question: 7. Sasha and Maxim (out of boredom) wrote non-zero digits in the cells of a $100 \times 100$ table. After this, Sasha said that among the 100 numbers formed by the digits in each row, all are divisible by 9. To this, Maxim replied that among the 100 numbers formed by the digits in each column, exactly one is not divisible by 9. Prove that one of them is wrong.
reference_solution: Solution: If we believe Sasha, then the sum of the digits in each row is divisible by 9, so the total sum of the digits in the table will also be divisible by 9. But if we believe Maksim, then the sum of the digits in all columns except one is divisible by 9, which means the sum of the digits in the table is not divisible by 9. Contradiction.

question: 3. Point $E$ is the midpoint of the base $A D$ of trapezoid $A B C D$. Segments $B D$ and $C E$ intersect at point $F$. It is known that $A F \perp B D$. Prove that $B C = F C$.
reference_solution: Solution. $F E$ is the median drawn to the hypotenuse of the right triangle $A F D$. Therefore, $F E=A D / 2=E D$ and $\angle E D F=\angle D F E$. But angles $E D F$ and $C B F$ are equal as alternate interior angles when the parallel lines $A D$ and $B C$ are cut by a transversal, and angles $D F E$ and $B F C$ are equal as vertical angles. Therefore, $\angle C B F=\angle B F C$, from which it follows that $B C=F C$.

question: 4. A square $20 \times 20$ is divided into unit squares. Some sides of the unit squares have been erased, with the erased segments having no common endpoints, and there are no erased segments on the top and right sides of the square. Prove that it is possible to travel from the bottom left corner of the square to the top right corner along the unerased segments.
reference_solution: Solution. From each cell corner, except the upper right corner of the $20 \times 20$ square, a move can be made either to the right or upwards - otherwise, two erased segments would have a common end. Therefore, starting from the lower left corner of the $20 \times 20$ square and making 40 such moves, we will end up at its upper right corner.

question: 5. Vasya calculated the sums of digits of 200 consecutive natural numbers and wrote these sums in a row in some order. Petya wrote the sums of digits of another 200 consecutive natural numbers under them (also in some order). Then Tanya multiplied each of Vasya's numbers by the number written under it and obtained 200 consecutive natural numbers as a result. Prove that someone made a mistake.
reference_solution: Solution. A number is divisible by 3 or 9 if and only if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3 or 9, respectively. Among 200 consecutive numbers, 66 or 67 are divisible by 3. Therefore, among the sums of their digits, the same is true. Let's say that among Vasya's numbers divisible by 3, exactly $k$ of Petya's numbers are also divisible by 3. Then the number of products divisible by 3 will be no less than $k + 2(66 - k) = 132 - k$. If Tanya obtained 200 consecutive natural numbers, the number $132 - k$ must be no more than 67, from which it follows that $k \geq 65$. But then among Tanya's numbers, there will be at least 65 that are divisible by 9, while the number of numbers divisible by 9 among two hundred consecutive natural numbers is no more than 23. Contradiction.

question: 1. Prove that for any natural number $n>1$ there exist such natural numbers $a, b, c, d$ that $a+b=c+d=ab-cd=4n$. (S. Berlov)
reference_solution: Solution. Let $a=2 n+x, b=2 n-x, c=2 n+y, d=2 n-y$. Then the equation can be rewritten as $y^{2}-x^{2}=4 n$. Now suppose that $y+x=2 n, y-x=2$. We get $x=n-1, y=n+1$, from which $a=3 n-1, b=n+1, c=3 n+1, d=n-1$.

question: 2. At a round table, 40 people are sitting. Could it happen that any two of them, between whom an even number of people sit, have a common acquaintance at the table, while any two, between whom an odd number of people sit, do not have a common acquaintance? (A. Shapovalov)
reference_solution: Answer. It cannot. First solution. Note that if there are $a$ people sitting between A and B, and $b$ people sitting between B and C, then there are $a+b+1$ or $|a-b|-1$ people sitting between A and C. Therefore, if the numbers $a$ and $b$ have the same parity, then there is an odd number of people sitting between A and C. Suppose there is a person B who has at least three acquaintances. Then among them, there will be such acquaintances A and C that the numbers $a$ and $b$ have the same parity, and they will have a common acquaintance B, although an odd number of people sit between them. If each person sitting has no more than two acquaintances, then for each person, there will be at most two people with whom they have common acquaintances, but according to the condition, there should be 20 such people. Second solution. Assume the opposite. Take any of the people sitting. An even number of people sit from him, 20 people. As shown in the first solution, these people sit from each other through an odd number of people, so they cannot have common acquaintances. Therefore, 20 different common acquaintances of the person we took with these people are required, that is, each of the people sitting has at least 20 acquaintances among them. But then, as is easily seen, any two of the people sitting have a common acquaintance - a contradiction.

question: 4. Inside a convex quadrilateral $A B C D$, in which $A B=C D$, a point $P$ is chosen such that the sum of the angles $P B A$ and $P C D$ is 180 degrees. Prove that $P B+P C<A D$. (S. Berlov)
reference_solution: Solution. Construct point $K$ on the extension of ray $PC$ beyond point $C$ such that $CK=BP$. Then triangles $ABP$ and $DCK$ will be equal by two sides and the included angle. Therefore, $DK=AP$ and $\angle BAP=\angle CDK$. Construct parallelogram $PKDL$. Since $\angle ABC + \angle BCD > 180^{\circ}$, then $\angle BAD + \angle ADC = \angle BAP + \angle PDC = \angle PDK = \angle DPL$. Therefore, ray $PL$ will go inside angle $APD$. But $AP=DK=LP$, so point $D$ will be on the same side of the perpendicular bisector of $AL$ as point $L$. Therefore, $AD > DL = PK = PC + PB$.

question: 5. In handball, 2 points are awarded for a win, 1 point for a draw, and 0 points for a loss. 14 handball teams conducted a tournament where each team played against each other once. It turned out that no two teams scored the same number of points. Could it have happened that each of the teams that took the top three places lost to each of the teams that took the last three places? (S. Berlov)
reference_solution: Answer: It could not. Solution: Let it could. We will show that the best of the last three teams scored no less than 9 points. Indeed, the last three teams in games among themselves played for 6 points, plus another 18 points taken from the top three. Therefore, together they scored no less than 24 points, and if each of them scored no more than 8 points, then all three scored exactly 8 points, which contradicts the problem's condition. By a similar consideration of the points lost by the top three teams, it is proven that the worst of the top three teams lost no less than 9 points, that is, scored no more than $26-9=17$ points. It turns out that each of the eight teams, ranking from 11th to 4th, scored no less than 10 and no more than 16 points. But in this range, there are only 7 whole numbers, and it follows that some two teams scored the same number of points. Contradiction.

question: 6. In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, where $AB=CD$, points $K$ and $M$ are chosen on sides $AB$ and $CD$ respectively. It turns out that $AM = KC$, $BM = KD$. Prove that the angle between lines $AB$ and $KM$ is equal to the angle between lines $KM$ and $CD$. (S. Berlov)
reference_solution:
First solution. Triangles $A B M$ and $C D K$ are equal by three sides, so their heights $K K_{1}$ and $M M_{1}$ are also equal. If they are equal to $K M$, then they coincide with $K M$, and the statement of the problem is obvious. If these heights are less than $K M$, then the right triangles $K K_{1} M$ and $M M_{1} K$ are equal by hypotenuse and leg; hence, their angles $K_{1} M K$ and $M_{1} K M$ are equal, which is what we needed to prove. The diagrams on the right show two possible cases of the relative positions of triangles $K K_{1} M$ and $M M_{1} K$.

Second solution. Lemma. By two sides $a$ and $b$ and the angle $\alpha$ opposite side $a$, no more than two different triangles can be constructed. If there exist two unequal triangles with such data, then the sum of their angles opposite the sides equal to $b$ is $180^{\circ}$. Proof. Take angle $X A Y$ equal to $\alpha$, and lay off segment $A C=b$ on side $A X$. The third vertices of the desired triangles lie at the intersection of ray $A Y$ and the circle of radius $a$ centered at $C$. There are no more than two such points. If there are exactly two - $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$ - then triangle $C B_{1} B_{2}$ is isosceles. Let $A B_{2} > A B_{1}$. Then $\angle C B_{1} A + \angle C B_{2} A = \angle C B_{1} A + \angle C B_{1} B_{2} = 180^{\circ}$. Solution of the problem. Triangles $A B M$ and $C D K$ are equal by three sides. Therefore, $\angle K A M = \angle B A M = \angle D C K = \angle M C K$. Thus, triangles $A K M$ and $C M K$ have a pair of equal sides $A M = C K$, a common side $K M$, and a pair of equal angles opposite the common side. If triangles $A K M$ and $C M K$ are equal, then $\angle A K M = \angle C M K$, and everything is proved. If they are not equal, then by the lemma $\angle A K M = 180^{\circ} - \angle C M K = \angle D M K$, and everything is proved.

question: 7. On a board, a sequence of n consecutive natural numbers in ascending order is written in a row. Under each of these numbers, a divisor is written, which is less than the number and greater than 1. It turns out that these divisors also form a sequence of consecutive natural numbers in ascending order. Prove that each of the original numbers is greater than $\frac{n^{k}}{p_{1} p_{2} \ldots p_{k}}$, where $p_{1}, p_{2}, \ldots, p_{k}$ are all prime numbers less than $n$. (S. Berlov)
reference_solution: Solution. Notice that all differences between the numbers and their divisors written below them are equal to the same number $c$. Let $p$ be a prime number less than $n$, and $p^{s}$ be the highest power of it not exceeding $n$. Then among the numbers in the second row, there will be one divisible by $p^{s}$. But then the number written above it in the first row is also divisible by $p^{s}$, and hence the number $c$ is also divisible by $p^{s}$. Thus, the number $c$ is divisible by the highest power of any prime number $p$ less than $n$ that does not exceed $n$, and therefore by the product of these powers for all such $p$. It remains to note that $p^{s}>n / p$ and any number in the original row is greater than $c$.

question: 3. On side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$, a point $D$ is marked. On side $AB$, a point $P$ is chosen. Segments $PC$ and $AD$ intersect at point $Q$. Point $R$ is the midpoint of segment $AP$. Prove that there exists a fixed point $X$ through which the line $RQ$ passes for any choice of point $P$. (A. Kuznetsov)
reference_solution:
Solution. Draw a line through point $C$ parallel to line $A B$, and let $E$ be the point of its intersection with line $A D$. The desired point $X$ is the midpoint of segment $C E$. Indeed, points $R, Q$, and $X$ lie on the same line for any choice of point $P$ as the midpoint of the sides and the point of intersection of the diagonals of trapezoid $APRE$.

question: 2. Points E and $\mathrm{F}$ are the midpoints of sides BC and CD, respectively, of rectangle $A B C D$. Prove that $A E<2 E F$.
reference_solution: First solution. $2 E F = B D = A C > A E$. The last inequality follows from the fact that angle $A E C$ is obtuse. Second solution. Let $B C = 2 x, C D = 2 y$. Then $A E^{2} = x^{2} + 4 y^{2} < 4 x^{2} + 4 y^{2} = (2 E F)^{2}$.

question: 3. Let $a, b, c$ be integers such that $(a+b+c)^{2}=-(ab+ac+bc)$ and the numbers $a+b, b+c, a+c$ are not equal to 0. Prove that the product of any two of the numbers $a+b, a+c, b+c$ is divisible by the third.
reference_solution: Solution. $(a+b)(a+c)=a^{2}+a b+a c+b c=a^{2}-(a+b+c)^{2}=-(b+c)(2 a+b+c)$. The other two cases are obtained by permuting the letters.

question: 4. A row of 101 cards is laid out. On each of the 50 cards lying in this row at even positions, a symbol > or < is drawn. Prove that, no matter how these symbols are drawn, the remaining cards can be filled with the numbers 1, 2, ... 51 (using each exactly once) so that all the resulting inequalities are true.
reference_solution: First solution. First, write a number above all the cards lying in odd positions. Above the first card, write the number 0. Then we will move to the right and each time after the sign “>” write a number that is 1 less than the previous one, and after the sign “b$ the inequality is true (since by construction $a$ is greater than all numbers to the right, in particular, greater than $b$ ).

question: 5. Alina outlined 22 different (but possibly overlapping) three-cell rectangles on a chessboard (8x8), and Polina - 22 non-overlapping two-cell rectangles (but possibly overlapping with Alina's rectangles). Prove that a cross made of 5 cells can be placed on the board, completely covering at least two of the outlined figures. (The cross can extend beyond the edges of the board.)
reference_solution: Solution. Note that a cross covers a 1x3 rectangle if their central cells coincide, and covers a 1x2 rectangle if the central cell of the cross lies within the rectangle. Mark the central cells of the long rectangles and all cells of the short ones; in total, 66 cells are marked, so some cell is marked twice. If we make this cell the central cell of the cross, it will cover two rectangles.

question: 1. Pete and Vasya ran the same distance. Vasya ran twice as fast as Pete, but started a minute later, and Pete finished first. Prove that Pete ran the distance in less than two minutes. (I. Rubanov)
reference_solution: Solution. Vasya runs twice as fast as Petya, and therefore covers as much distance in one minute as Petya does in two minutes. This means that if Petya does not finish the race within two minutes after the start, Vasya will catch up with him.

question: 3. Two numbers are such that their sum, the sum of their squares, and the sum of their cubes are all equal to the same number t. Prove that the sum of their fourth powers is also equal to t. (I. Rubanov)
reference_solution:
First solution. Let $a+b=a^{2}+b^{2}=a^{3}+b^{3}=m$. Then $m=a^{3}+b^{3}=(a+b)\left(a^{2}-a b+b^{2}\right)=m(m-a b)$, from which $m=0$ or $a b=m-1$. If $m=a^{2}+b^{2}=0$, then $a=b=0$ and $a^{4}+b^{4}=0=m$. If $a b=m-1$, then

$$
m^{2}=(a+b)\left(a^{3}+b^{3}\right)=a^{4}+b^{4}+a b\left(a^{2}+b^{2}\right)=a^{4}+b^{4}+(m-1) m, \text{ hence } a^{4}+b^{4}=m .
$$

Second solution. In the notation from the first solution, $(a+b)\left(a^{3}+b^{3}\right)=\left(a^{2}+b^{2}\right)^{2}=m^{2}$. Expanding the brackets and combining like terms, we get $a^{3} b+a b^{3}=2 a^{2} b^{2}$, from which $a b(a-b)^{2}=0$. From the last equality, it follows that either $a=0$, or $b=0$, or $a=b$. If $a=0$, then by the condition $b=b^{2}$, from which $b=0$ or $b=1$. Similarly, if $b=0$, then $a=0$ or $a=1$. Finally, if $a=b$, then by the condition $2 b=2 b^{2}$, from which $a=b=0$ or $a=b=1$. In all cases, each of the numbers $a$ and $b$ is 0 or 1, and therefore $a^{4}+b^{4}=a+b=m$.

question: 4. In triangle $A B C$, the bisector $B E$ and the perpendicular bisector $t$ of side $A B$ were drawn. It turned out that $B E=E C$, and line $t$ intersects side $B C$. Prove that angle $C$ is less than 36 degrees. (I. Rubanov)
reference_solution: Solution. Let $\angle A B C=2 \beta$, and the line $m$ intersects side $B C$ at point $D$. By the property of the perpendicular bisector, $D A=D B$, hence $\angle D A B=\angle A B D=2 \beta$. Therefore, by the exterior angle theorem of a triangle, $\angle A D C=\angle D A B+\angle A B D=4 \beta$. Moreover, since $B E=E C, \angle C=\angle D B E=\beta$. From triangle $A D C$, we have $180^{\circ}=\angle D A C+\angle A D C+\angle C=\angle D A C+4 \beta+\beta$, from which $\angle C=\beta=\left(180^{\circ}-\angle D A C\right) / 5<36^{\circ}$.

question: 2. (A. Shapovalov) For any natural number n greater than 2009, from the fractions $\frac{1}{n}, \frac{2}{n-1}, \frac{3}{n-2}, \ldots, \frac{n-1}{2}, \frac{n}{1}$, can two pairs of fractions with the same sums always be selected?
reference_solution: Answer: Yes. Solution. Each of the given fractions has the form $\frac{n+1-a}{a}=\frac{n+1}{a}-1$, where $1 \leq a \leq n$. Therefore, we need to find such distinct natural numbers $a, b$, $c$ and $d$, not greater than 2009, for which $\left(\frac{n+1}{a}-1\right)+\left(\frac{n+1}{b}-1\right)=\left(\frac{n+1}{c}-1\right)+\left(\frac{n+1}{d}-1\right)$. Removing the minus ones and then dividing by $n+1$, we obtain the equivalent equation $\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}=\frac{1}{c}+\frac{1}{d}$. It remains to find fractions that satisfy this equation. This can be done by taking any equality of two sums of distinct natural addends, the LCM of which is no more than 2009, and dividing it by this LCM. For example, the equality $1+4=2+3$, divided by 12, gives $\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{4}$.

question: 3. (S. Berlov) In triangle $ABC$, sides $AB$ and $BC$ are equal. Point $D$ inside the triangle is such that angle $ADC$ is twice the angle $ABC$. Prove that twice the distance from point $B$ to the line bisecting the angles adjacent to angle $ADC$ is equal to $AD + DC$.
reference_solution:
Solution. Let $l$ be the bisector of the angles adjacent to angle $A D C$, point $K$ be the projection of $B$ onto $l$, and points $B^{\prime}$ and $C^{\prime}$ be symmetric to points $A, B$, and $C$ respectively with respect to $l$. Then

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_fb2d18a585a6083255afg-2.jpg?height=451&width=440&top_left_y=177&top_left_x=1479)
$B B^{\prime}=2 B K$ - which is exactly twice the distance from $B$ to $l$. Moreover, point $D$ lies on the segment $A C$ (since lines $D A$ and $D C$ are symmetric with respect to $l$), and $A C^{2}=A D+D C^{\prime}=A D+D C$. From the same symmetry, we get $\angle A C^{\prime} B^{\prime}=\angle D C^{\prime} B^{\prime}=\angle D C B, \angle B B^{\prime} C^{\prime}=\angle B^{\prime} B C$. Let the segments $B B^{\prime}$ and $A C^{\prime}$ intersect at point $O$. From the right triangle $O K D$ we get

$$
\angle B O C=\angle K O D=90^{\circ}-\angle O D K=\left(180^{\circ}-\angle C D C^{\prime}\right) / 2=\angle A D C / 2=\angle A B C
$$

Thus,

$$
\angle A B B^{\prime}=\angle A B C-\angle B^{\prime} B C=\angle B O C^{\prime}-\angle O B^{\prime} C=\angle O C^{\prime} B^{\prime}
$$

Similarly,

$$
\angle B A O=\angle B O C^{\prime}-\angle A B O=\angle A B C-\angle A B O=\angle B^{\prime} B C=\angle B B^{\prime} C^{\prime}
$$

Therefore, triangles $A B O$ and $B^{\prime} C^{\prime} O$ are equal by side and two adjacent angles. Hence, $B B^{\prime}=B O+O B^{\prime}=C^{\prime} O+O A=A C^{\prime}=A D+D C$, which is what we needed to prove.

question: 4. (N. Gravin) In the country of Leonardia, all roads are one-way. Each road connects two cities and does not pass through other cities. The Department of Statistics calculated for each city the total number of residents in the cities from which roads lead to it, and the total number of residents in the cities to which roads lead from it. Prove that for at least one city, the first number is not less than the second.
reference_solution:
First solution. Construct a graph where the vertices correspond to the residents of the country, and two vertices are connected by a directed edge if and only if their cities are connected by a road (the direction of the edge will be the same as the direction of the road between the cities). For each vertex $v$ of this graph, denote by $f(v)$ the number of edges entering $v$ minus the number of edges leaving $v$. The sum of $f(v)$ over all vertices of the graph is 0, because each edge contributes one +1 and one -1 to it. Therefore, there exists a vertex $u$ such that $f(u) \geq 0$. It remains to note that $f(u)$ is exactly the difference between the first and second numbers for the city where $u$ lives.

Second solution. Let $n(A)$ be the number of residents in city $A$, and let $f(A)$ be the total population of the cities whose roads lead into $A$ minus the total population of the cities whose roads lead out of $A$. If the statement of the problem is false, then $f(A) < 0$ for every city $A$. Then the sum $S$ of the numbers $n(A) f(A)$ over all cities in the country is negative. On the other hand, consider any road from $A$ to $B$. This road "contributes" $+n(B) n(A)$ to the number $n(B) f(B)$, and $-n(A) n(B)$ to the number $n(A) f(A)$. Considering all roads, we get that $S=0$. Contradiction.

Remark. Note that in the second solution, we only used the fact that the "number of residents in a city" is positive. It does not need to be an integer.

question: 5. The integers $a, b$, and $c$ and the natural number $n$ are such that $a+b+c=1$ and $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}=2 n+1$. Prove that $a^{3}+b^{2}-a^{2}-b^{3}$ is divisible by $n$. (N. Agakhanov)
reference_solution: Solution. From the condition, it follows that $a^{2}+b^{2}+(1-a-b)^{2}=2 n+1$, from which $a^{2}+b^{2}+a b-(a+b)=n$. Therefore, $a^{3}+b^{2}-a^{2}-b^{3}=\left(a^{3}-b^{3}\right)+\left(b^{2}-a^{2}\right)=(a-b)\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+a b-(a+b)\right)=(a-b) \cdot n$, which is what we needed to prove.

question: 7. From a $70 \times 70$ checkerboard, 2018 cells were cut out. Prove that the board has split into no more than 2018 pieces. Two pieces that do not share any points other than the vertices of the cells are considered not connected to each other. (I. Rubanov)
reference_solution: Solution. It is not difficult to construct a cycle that passes through each cell of a $70 \times 70$ board exactly once, such that adjacent cells in the cycle share a common side: for example, one can walk the entire first vertical column from the bottom cell to the top, then move along the vertical columns in a "zigzag" pattern from the top horizontal row to the second from the bottom and back, and finally return to the first horizontal row via the last vertical column and walk along it to the starting cell. "Unstick" all the common sides of the cells on the board, except for the common sides between adjacent cells in our cycle. Even after this, 2018 removed cells will divide this cycle into no more than 2018 parts, and when the cycle is reassembled into the board, the number of parts will not increase.

question: 8. Vertex $F$ of parallelogram $A C E F$ lies on side $B C$ of parallelogram $A B C D$. It is known that $A C=A D$ and $A E=2 C D$. Prove that $\angle C D E=\angle B E F$. (A. Kuznetsov)
reference_solution:
First solution. Let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $CF$. Since quadrilateral $ACEF$ is a parallelogram, point $M$ is the midpoint of segment $AE$. Denote $\angle MAC = \angle MEF = \alpha$ and $\angle ABC = \angle ADC = \angle ACD = \beta$. Since $AM = AE / 2 = CD$, $AMCD$ is an isosceles trapezoid, from which we obtain that $\alpha = \angle MAC = \angle MDC$ and $MD = AC = AD$. Moreover, since $MA = CD = AB$ and $\angle ABM = \angle ADC = \beta$, the isosceles triangles $ABM$ and $ACD$ are similar, so $AB / BM = AC / CD$. Triangles $BME$ and $EMD$ are also similar, since

$$
\angle BME = 180^{\circ} - \beta = 180^{\circ} - \angle DMA = \angle EMD \text{ and } BM / ME = BM / MA = CD / AD = MA / MD = EM / MD.
$$

Thus, $\angle BEM = \angle EDM$, from which $\angle BEF = \angle BEM - \alpha = \angle EDM - \alpha = \angle CDE$, as required.

Second solution. As in the first solution, introduce point $M$ and show that $AMCD$ is an isosceles trapezoid. Lay off segment $CS = DC = ME$ on ray $DC$. Since $\angle SCB = \angle ABC = \beta = \angle EMC$, the perpendiculars dropped from points $E$ and $S$ to $BC$ are equal, from which $SE \parallel BC$. Therefore, quadrilaterals $MSEC$ and $ASED$ are also isosceles trapezoids; in particular, $ASED$ is inscribed in some circle $\omega$. On the other hand, since segments $AB$ and $CS$ are parallel and equal, $ACSB$ is a parallelogram, from which $BS = AC = AD$. Thus, $DABS$ is also an isosceles trapezoid. Since points $A, S$, and $D$ lie on $\omega$, point $B$ lies on the same circle. From the inscribed quadrilateral $BSED$, we now obtain $\angle SBE = \angle SDE = \angle CDE$. It remains to note that $BSEF$ is a parallelogram (since $BS$ is parallel and equal to $FE$), from which $\angle BEF = \angle SBE = \angle CDE$.

question: 5. Nезнayka wrote down 11 natural numbers in a circle. For each pair of adjacent numbers, he calculated their difference (subtracting the smaller from the larger). As a result, among the differences found, there were four ones, four twos, and three threes. Prove that Nезнayka made a mistake somewhere. (
reference_solution: Solution. Let's write each of our differences with a plus sign if in the corresponding pair of numbers the larger one stands before the smaller one clockwise, and with a minus sign otherwise. We have 11 differences between a number and the one following it clockwise; thus, the sum of all these numbers is zero, which is an even number. This is impossible, since among them there are exactly seven odd numbers - four numbers equal to 1 or -1, and three numbers equal to 3 or -3.

question: 6. In a company of six people, any five can sit at a round table such that every two neighbors are acquainted. Prove that the entire company can also be seated at a round table such that every two neighbors are acquainted. (S. Volchonkov)
reference_solution: Solution. Note that each person in the company has at least three acquaintances. Indeed, if someone $X$ were acquainted with fewer than three people, then by excluding one of his acquaintances from the company, we would end up with a group of five people in which $X$ has no more than one acquaintance, which means it would be impossible to seat them at a round table. Now, let's take any five people and seat them at a round table. The sixth person is acquainted with at least three of them; therefore, he is acquainted with some pair of adjacent people. If we seat the sixth person between them, we will obtain the required seating arrangement.

question: 8. The angle bisectors of angles $A$ and $C$ of trapezoid $A B C D$ intersect at point $P$, and the angle bisectors of angles $B$ and $D$ intersect at point $Q$, different from $P$. Prove that if segment $P Q$ is parallel to base $A D$, then the trapezoid is isosceles. (L. Emelyanov)
reference_solution:
Solution. Let $\rho(X, Y Z)$ denote the distance from point $X$ to line $Y Z$. Since point $P$ lies on the bisector of angle $C$, we have $\rho(P, B C)=\rho(P, C D)$. Similarly, $\rho(Q, A B)=\rho(Q, B C)$. But since $Q P \| B C$, we have $\rho(Q, B C)=\rho(P, B C)$, hence $\rho(Q, A B)=\rho(P, C D)$ (see figure). Similarly, $\rho(P, A B)=\rho(P, A D)=\rho(Q, A D)=\rho(Q, C D)$. Extend the lateral sides $A B$ and

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_46f4b6be2ad4bb1ee247g-1.jpg?height=175&width=302&top_left_y=2117&top_left_x=1551)
$C D$ until they intersect at point $S$. Let point $P^{\prime}$ be the reflection of $Q$ across the bisector $\ell$ of angle $A S D$. Then, by symmetry, $\rho\left(P^{\prime}, C D\right)=\rho(Q, A B)=\rho(P, C D)$ and $\rho\left(P^{\prime}, A B\right)=\rho(Q, C D)=$ $\rho(P, A B)$. Thus, points $P$ and $P^{\prime}$ lie inside angle $A S D$ on lines parallel to $A B$ and $C D$ and at distances $\rho(P, A B)$ and $\rho(P, C D)$ from them, respectively. Since these lines are not parallel, they have only one point of intersection; therefore, $P^{\prime}=P$, points $P$ and $Q$ are symmetric with respect to the bisector of angle $A S D$, and $\ell \perp P Q \| A D$. Thus, in triangle $S A D$, the bisector is an altitude, the angles at its base are equal, meaning trapezoid $A B C D$ is isosceles.

question: 1. On the board, three quadrilaterals are drawn. Petya said: "At least two trapezoids are drawn on the board." Vasya said: "At least two rectangles are drawn on the board." Kolya said: "At least two rhombuses are drawn on the board." It is known that one of the boys lied, while the other two told the truth. Prove that among the quadrilaterals drawn on the board, there is a square. (Recall that a trapezoid is a quadrilateral in which two sides are parallel, and the other two are not.) (I. Rubanov)
reference_solution:
Solution. A trapezoid cannot be a parallelogram. Therefore, if Petya is right, then there is no more than one parallelogram drawn on the board, and Vasya and Kolya are both wrong. But according to the condition, only one person lied. So, it must be Petya, and Vasya and Kolya told the truth. This means that at least one of the three quadrilaterals drawn on the board is both a rectangle and a rhombus, that is, a square.

Criteria. The statement equivalent to "consider the figures from the two true statements. Then one figure has both properties" is clearly formulated, with no further substantial progress - 1 point.

Only checked that in the case of "Petya lied" and "A square is both a rhombus and a rectangle at the same time," no contradictions arise - 2 points.

Proved only that Petya is lying - 4 points.

The phrase "at least two" is read as "exactly two," and a formally simpler problem is solved - do not reduce.

"If Petya is wrong, then one figure is both a rectangle and a rhombus" and similarly for others, without a more detailed explanation of why such a figure exists - do not reduce.

question: 2. It is known about three positive numbers that if you choose one of them and add to it the sum of the squares of the other two, you will get the same sum, regardless of which number you choose. Prove that at least two of the original numbers are the same. (L. Emelyanov)
reference_solution:
First solution. Let our numbers be $a, b, c$. Then $a+b^{2}+c^{2}=a^{2}+b+c^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}+c$. From the first two equalities, we have $a^{2}-a=b^{2}-b$, which is equivalent to $(a-b)(a+b-1)=0$. Therefore, $a=b$ or $b=1-a$. Similarly, $a=c$ or $c=1-a$. Consequently, if $a \neq b$ and $a \neq c$, then $b=1-a=c$, meaning that in any case, two numbers are equal.

Second solution. Let our numbers be $a, b, c$. Then $a+b^{2}+c^{2}=a^{2}+b+c^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}+c$. From this, we have $a^{2}-a=b^{2}-b=c^{2}-c=d$ (where $d$ is some number), i.e., the numbers $a, b$, and $c$ are solutions to the equation $x^{2}-x=d$. But a quadratic equation has no more than two solutions. This means that at least two of our numbers are equal.

Criteria. If the work claims that in any such example, all numbers are necessarily equal, the solution is not rated higher than 3 points.

If from equalities of the form $(a-b)(a+b)=a-b$, the equality $\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b}=1$ is obtained by "cancellation" without additional explanations (and everything else in the solution is correct; in particular, it does not claim without any qualifications that all numbers are necessarily equal) - 5 points.

If (essentially) a system of disjunctions of the form $\{a=b$ or $a+b=1\}$ is obtained, followed immediately by "thus, either all are equal, or two are equal ($a=b$), and the third is $=1-\mathrm{a}$" without any further explanation - 5 points.

If (essentially) a system of disjunctions of the form $\{a=b$ or $a+b=1\}$ is obtained, with no further substantial progress - 3 points.

If the equality $(a-b)(a+b)=a-b$ or $(a-b)(a+b-1)=0$ is obtained without further substantial progress - 1 point.

If the equality $a(1-a)=b(1-b) (=c(1-c))$ is obtained without further substantial progress - 0 points.

question:
3. Given a convex quadrilateral $A B C D$ such that $A D=A B+C D$. It turns out that the bisector of angle $A$ passes through the midpoint of side $B C$. Prove that the bisector of angle $D$ also passes through the midpoint of $B C$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_8aa2609a8219a75c6fb2g-1.jpg?height=254&width=477&top_left_y=2580&top_left_x=1463)
reference_solution:
Solution. Let $E$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Mark a point $F$ on side $AD$ such that $AB = AF$; then from the condition $FD = AD - AF = CD$. Triangles $AEB$ and $AEF$ are equal by two sides ($AB = AF$, $AE$ is common) and the angle between them. Therefore, $EF = BE = EC$. Now we get that triangles $DEF$ and $DEC$ are equal by three sides, hence $\angle EDF = \angle EDC$, and point $E$ lies on the bisector of angle $D$, which is what we needed to prove. Note. It is not difficult to show that $AB \parallel CD$. Indeed, $\angle ABE = \angle AFE = 180^{\circ} - \angle DFE = \angle DCE$, that is, the sum of the interior alternate angles is $180^{\circ}$.

question: 4. A closed broken line without self-intersections is drawn through the centers of some cells of an 8x8 chessboard. Each segment of the broken line connects the centers of adjacent cells, either horizontally, vertically, or diagonally. Prove that the total area of the black pieces within the region bounded by the broken line is equal to the total area of the white pieces. (D Kramtsov)
reference_solution:
First solution. Draw dashed vertical and horizontal lines through the centers of the cells of the board. On the resulting dashed grid, each segment of our broken line connects nodes that are adjacent vertically, horizontally, or diagonally. Therefore, the dashed lines divide the area bounded by the broken line into unit squares and half-squares, obtained by cutting them along the diagonal. It remains to note that in each such square and each such triangle, the areas of the black and white parts are equal. Indeed, each square contains two quarters of cells of both colors, and the triangle contains a quarter of a cell of one color and two triangles, each of which constitutes an eighth of a cell of the other color.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_8aa2609a8219a75c6fb2g-2.jpg?height=422&width=434&top_left_y=857&top_left_x=1462)

Second solution. Consider a new square grid formed by vertical and horizontal lines passing through the centers of the board's cells. Each square of this grid is divided by diagonals into four triangles. Obviously, each resulting triangle is half white and half black. On the other hand, the figure bounded by the broken line consists of such triangles, since by condition it does not intersect any of them.

Criteria. Considering some specific broken lines without describing the general idea of the solution - 0 points.

Only the idea that in the triangle and square mentioned in the solution, B=W - 1 point; additionally, it is claimed without justification that the figure can be divided into such triangles and squares - 3 points; substantial progress in justification adds 1 to 4 points to this three; reference to the square grid with nodes at the centers of the original squares is considered a complete justification.

question: 5. Businessman Boris Mikhailovich decided to have a race with tractor driver Vasya on the highway. Since his "Lexus" is ten times faster than Vasya's tractor, he gave Vasya a head start and set off an hour after Vasya. After Vasya's tractor had driven exactly half of the planned route, a spring fell off, so he covered the remaining part of the journey at half the speed of the first half. As a result, Boris Mikhailovich had to stop at a nearby service station for 4 hours after encountering Vasya's spring, and then continued his journey at half the speed he had before. Prove that as a result, he fell behind Vasya by at least an hour. (S. Berlov)
reference_solution:
First solution. Since Boris met with Vasya's spring, by the halfway point, he had not yet caught up with Vasya. Clearly, under normal conditions, he would have caught up with Vasya in $10 / 9$ hours; thus, Vasya took $10/9 - a$ hours to travel the first half of the distance for some $a \geq 0$, and then the entire journey took him $10/3 - 3a$ hours. Boris, on the other hand, took $1/9 - a/10$ hours to travel the first half of the distance, and the second half at half the speed, so he spent $4 + 1/3 - 3a/10 \geq 1 + (10/3 - 3a)$ hours on the entire journey, which is what was required. Second solution. According to the problem, one hour of a head start is enough for Vasya to prevent Boris from catching up on the first half of the journey. Therefore, on the second half of the journey (where all speeds are halved), Vasya needs only 2 hours of a head start. And he has at least a 4-hour head start (which Boris spent in the service station). Thus, Boris will complete the race no earlier than 2 hours after Vasya.

Criteria. In the provided solutions, it is shown that Boris spent at least one hour more on the entire journey than Vasya (i.e., considering the head start, he finished at least two hours after Vasya). This is the statement the author of the problem intended. However, the problem's formulation was ambiguous, and many participants proved that BM finished at least one hour after Vasya. Since the participants are not at fault, it has been decided to consider both possible interpretations as correct and evaluate the solutions based on which one the authors of the solutions intended.

Considering the "worst case," where the spring fell directly under the bumper of the "Lexus" without explaining why this case is indeed the "worst" (i.e., if the statement of the problem is true for it, then it is true for all other cases) - no more than 3 points.

Receiving only condition (3) from the following three conditions: (1) expression for Vasya's time; (2) expression for Boris's time; (3) condition on the spring (Boris will pass the halfway point later than Vasya). 1 point; receiving all three conditions with no further substantial progress - 2 points. Conditions (1) and (2) without condition (3) are not evaluated.

For considering strict inequalities instead of non-strict ones, the evaluation should not be reduced.

question: 8. In triangle $A B C$, points $M$ and $N$ are the midpoints of sides $A C$ and $A B$ respectively. On the median $B M$, a point $P$ is chosen, which does not lie on $C N$. It turns out that $P C=2 P N$. Prove that $A P=B C$. (C. Berlov)
reference_solution:
First solution. Mark a point $K$ such that $A K B P$ is a parallelogram. Then its diagonals are bisected by the point of intersection, that is, they intersect at point $N$ and $P K=2 P N=P C$. Let the lines $M B$ and $C K$ intersect at point $T$. Since $M T \| A K$ and $M$ is the midpoint of $A C$, then $M T$ is the midline of triangle $A K C$, hence $K T=T C$. Therefore, $P T$ is the median drawn to the base of the isosceles triangle $K P C$, from which $P T \perp C K$. Then $B T$ is the median and altitude of triangle $B K C$, hence $B C=B K$. Finally, $B K=A P$ since $A K B P$ is a parallelogram, from which $A P=B K=B C$.

Second solution. Let $G$ be the point of intersection of the medians of triangle $A B C$. Then $C G / G N=2=C P / P N$, so point $G$ divides side $NC$ of triangle $P N C$ in the ratio equal to the ratio of the adjacent sides. By the bisector criterion, we get $\angle C P G=\angle G P N$. Therefore, $\angle B P N=\angle B P C$. Let $X$ be the midpoint of $P C$. Then $P X=P N$, so $\triangle N P M=\triangle X P M$ by two sides and the included angle. Hence $N M=X M$. Finally, segments $X M$ and $N M$ are midlines in triangles $A P C$ and $A B C$, so $A P=2 X M=2 N M=B C$.

Third solution. Consider a point $Q$ such that $P$ is the midpoint of $A Q$. Then $B P \| Q C, B Q=2 N P=P C$, i.e., $B Q C P$ is an isosceles trapezoid ($B Q \| N P \Rightarrow$ not parallel to $P C$). Its diagonals $B C$ and $P Q$ are equal, and $P Q=A P$.

Criteria. Only additional construction: point $K$ such that $N$ is the midpoint of segment $P K$ (without explicit nonsense) -1 point.

Only the midpoint of $P C$ is constructed and it is understood that it is sufficient to prove $M N=M X$ (without explicit incorrect statements) -1 point.

The problem is reduced to proving that $B M$ is the bisector of angle $A P C$, without further substantial progress - 2 points.

Only proved that $B M$ is the bisector of angle $A P C-2$ points.

Only one specific position of point $P$ on $B M$ (before or after the intersection of medians) is used - the score is not reduced.

question: 2. In each of the 111 families, there are three people: a father, a mother, and a child. All 333 people lined up in a row. It turned out that the parents of each child are standing on different sides of the child (but not necessarily next to the child). Prove that among the central 111 people in this row, there is at least one child.
reference_solution:
Solution. Let's call a parent left (right) if their child stands to the left (right) of them in the row. Suppose all the central 111 people are parents. Then among them, either the left or the right parents will be more than 55, that is, at least 56. Suppose there are at least 56 left parents. Then all 56 of their children are among the first 111 people, and 56 of their second parents are also among those 111 people. Contradiction. The case of 56 right parents is handled similarly.

Grading Instructions. In a proof by contradiction, it is shown that among the left (right) 111 people, there are no fewer than 56 children, but there is no further substantial progress -1 point.

question: 3. Point $D$ lies on the hypotenuse $AB$ of a right triangle $ABC$, but does not coincide with its midpoint. Prove that among the segments $AD, BD$, and $CD$, there are no equal ones.
reference_solution:
Solution. $A D$ is not equal to $B D$ by the condition. Suppose $A D = C D$. Then the angles $D A C$ and $A C D$ are equal. Let each of them be $x$. But then each of the angles $D A B$ and $A B D$ is $90^{\circ} - x$, which implies $A D = B D = C D$ - a contradiction. Similarly, $C D$ cannot equal $B D$.

Grading Guidelines. If at least one of the inequalities is proven: $A D$ is not equal to $C D$ or $B D$ is not equal to $C D$ - the score should not be less than 6 points.

question: 4. A five-digit number x starts with 4 and ends with 7, and a five-digit number y starts with 9 and ends with 3. It is known that the numbers x and y have a common five-digit divisor. Prove that $2y - x$ is divisible by 11.
reference_solution:
Solution. Let $x=a z, y=b z$, where $z$ is a five-digit common divisor of the numbers $x$ and $y$. Obviously, $a$ and $b$ are odd, $b>a, a \leq 4$ and $b \leq 9$. From this it follows that $a$ is 1 or 3. If $a=1$, then $z=x, y=b x, b \geq 3$, but already $3 x>120000-$ a six-digit number. Therefore, $a=3$. The only digit whose product with 3 ends in 7 is 9. Therefore, $z$ ends in 9. The only single-digit $b$ for which the product $b z$ ends in 3 is 7.

Thus, $x=3 z, y=7 z$, from which $2 y-x=11 z$, which leads to the statement of the problem.

Grading guidelines. The equations $x=3 z, y=7 z$ are used without justification that other options are impossible - 1 point. Only proved that $x=3 z$ - 2 points. Proved that $x=3 z$ and $z$ ends in 9, with no further substantial progress - 3 points.

No justification that $y=7 z$ - no more than 3 points.

question: 1. Let's call good rectangles a square with side 2 and a rectangle with sides 1 and 11. Prove that any rectangle with integer sides, greater than 100, can be cut into good rectangles. (S. Volchendov)
reference_solution: Solution. A rectangle $2 n \times 2 m$ can be cut into squares $2 \times 2$. A rectangle $(2 n+1) \times 2 m$ can first be cut into rectangles $11 \times 2 m$ and $(2 n-10) \times 2 m$, then the first one can be cut into rectangles $1 \times 11$, and the second one - into squares $2 \times 2$. Finally, a rectangle $(2 n+1) \times (2 m+1)$ can first be cut into rectangles $11 \times (2 m+1), (2 n-10) \times 11$ and $(2 n-10) \times (2 m-10)$, then the first two rectangles can be cut into rectangles $1 \times 11$, and the last rectangle - into squares $2 \times 2$.

question: 2. In triangle $ABC$, side $AB$ is greater than side $BC$. On the extension of side $BC$ beyond point $C$, point $N$ is marked such that $2BN = AB + BC$. Let $BS$ be the bisector of triangle $ABC$, $M$ be the midpoint of side $AC$, and $L$ be a point on segment $BS$ such that $ML \parallel AB$. Prove that $2LN = AC$. (A. Antropov)
reference_solution:
Solution. Extend $BN$ beyond $N$ and $BL$ beyond $L$ to segments $NN' = BN$ and $LL' = BL$ respectively. Since $M$ is the midpoint of $AC$ and $ML \parallel AB$, the line $ML$ contains the midline $MK$ of triangle $ABC$. Since $L$ is the midpoint of $BL$, this line also contains the midline $LK$ of triangle $BCL$; hence,

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_2fbed22acb1306d1b27dg-1.jpg?height=428&width=485&top_left_y=700&top_left_x=1502)
$CL' \parallel LM \parallel AB$. Therefore, $\angle CL'B = \angle L'BA = \angle L'BC$, from which $CL' = CB$. Next, $CN' = BN' - BC = 2BN - BC = BA$ and $\angle N'CL' = \angle CBA$. Thus, triangles $N'CL'$ and $ABC$ are congruent, and therefore $AC = N'L' = 2LN$.

question: 3. Twenty fifteen positive numbers are written in a circle. The sum of any two adjacent numbers is greater than the sum of the reciprocals of the next two numbers in the clockwise direction. Prove that the product of all these numbers is greater than 1. (A. Gолованов, S. Berlov)
reference_solution: Solution. Let the numbers $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{2015}$ stand in a circle. Notice that $a+b>\frac{1}{c}+\frac{1}{d} \cdot(a+b) c d>c+d(*)$. Writing all 2015 inequalities given in the problem in the form (*), and multiplying them, we get the inequality $X \cdot\left(x_{1} x_{2} \ldots x_{2015}\right)^{2}>X$, where $X=\left(x_{1}+x_{2}\right)\left(x_{2}+x_{3}\right) \ldots\left(x_{2014}+x_{2015}\right)\left(x_{2015}+x_{1}\right)$. Dividing both sides of this inequality by $X$, we obtain the inequality $\left(x_{1} x_{2} \ldots x_{2015}\right)^{2}>1$, from which it follows that $x_{1} x_{2} \ldots x_{2015}>1$.

question: 1. Prove that the prime factorization of the product of ten consecutive three-digit numbers includes no more than 23 different prime numbers. (I. Rubanov)
reference_solution: Solution. Note that in the prime factorization of a three-digit number, there are no more than two factors greater than 10 - otherwise, the product would be greater than 1000. Moreover, among 10 consecutive natural numbers, there is a number divisible by 10, in the factorization of which there is at most one factor greater than 10. Thus, in the factorizations of ten consecutive three-digit numbers, there are no more than 19 prime factors greater than 10. Together with the factors 2, 3, 5, 7, this results in no more than 23 distinct prime factors, which is what we needed to prove.

question: 5. A certain natural number \( a \) was divided with a remainder by the numbers \( 1, 2, 3, \ldots, 1000 \). Could it happen that among the remainders, the numbers \( 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots, 99 \) each appear exactly 10 times? (S. Berlov)
reference_solution: Answer: It could not. Solution: From the condition, it follows that all remainders of the division of the number $a$ by numbers from 1 to 1000 are less than 100. Let the remainder of the division of the number $a$ by 100 be $r$. Then, when dividing $a$ by any number that is a multiple of 100, the remainder should be of the form $r+100k$, where $k$ is a non-negative integer. Since, by condition, the remainders of the division of $a$ by 200, 300, ..., 900, 1000 do not exceed 99, all of them are also equal to $r$. But then the same remainder will be obtained when dividing $a$ by any divisor of a thousand greater than 100, for example, by 250. Thus, the remainder $r$ must occur at least 11 times, which contradicts the condition of the problem.

question: 8. Given an odd natural number \( a \), greater than 100. On the board, all natural numbers of the form \( \frac{a-n^{2}}{4} \), where \( n \) is a natural number, were written. It turned out that for \( n \leq \sqrt{a / 5} \) all of them are prime. Prove that each of the other natural numbers written on the board is also prime or equal to one. (A. Khryabrov)
reference_solution:
Solution. If $a$ when divided by 4 gives 3, there are no integers on the board because squares when divided by 4 can only give remainders of 0 or 1. In this case, the statement of the problem is obviously true. From now on, we assume that $a$ gives a remainder of 1 when divided by 4. Then $a=4p+1$, where $p=\frac{a-1}{4}$ is prime. Note that the number $\frac{a-n^{2}}{4}$ is an integer if and only if $n$ is odd. Since for odd $n$ the difference $p-\frac{a-n^{2}}{4}=\frac{n^{2}-1}{4}$ is even, all integers of the form $\frac{a-n^{2}}{4}$ here are odd.

Suppose for some $a$ the condition of the problem is satisfied, but the conclusion is not. Consider the smallest such $n$ for which the number $b=\frac{a-n^{2}}{4}$ is composite. Let $u$ be its smallest prime divisor. Since $n>\sqrt{a / 5}$, the inequality $b=\frac{a-n^{2}}{4}<a / 5$ holds. Therefore, $u<\sqrt{\frac{a}{5}}<n$, from which $-n<n-2u<n$. Thus, $(n-2u)^{2}<n^{2}$, and $n-2u$ is not equal to 0, since $n$ is odd. It is easy to see that the number $\frac{a-(n-2u)^{2}}{4}$ is a natural number, divisible by $u$, and greater than $b$, that is, it is not prime and not one. Therefore, the number $|n-2u|$, which is less than $n$, also generates a composite natural number, which contradicts the minimality of $n$.

Remark. The condition of the problem is satisfied, for example, for $a=173$.

question: 3. In triangle $ABC$, angle $C$ is twice as large as angle $B$, and $CD$ is the angle bisector. From the midpoint $M$ of side $BC$, a perpendicular $MH$ is dropped to segment $CD$. On side $AB$, a point $K$ is found such that $KMN$ is an equilateral triangle. Prove that points $M$, $H$, and $A$ lie on the same line.
reference_solution:
First solution. Since $\angle D C B=\angle C / 2=\angle B, D M$ is the median, bisector, and altitude in the isosceles triangle $B D C$. Drop a perpendicular $M E$ from point $M$ to line $A B$. Then $M E=M H=M K$, from which it follows that $K=E$. Next, in the right triangles $C H M$ and $B K M$, the sum of the angles at vertex $M$ is $180^{\circ}-\angle H M K=120^{\circ}$, from which we find that each of the angles $\angle D C M$ and $\angle D B M$ is $30^{\circ}$. Therefore, in triangle $A B C$, $\angle C=30^{\circ}, \angle B=60^{\circ}, \angle A=90^{\circ}$. It remains to note that then triangle $A C M$ is equilateral, and hence $C H \perp A M$, from which the statement of the problem follows.

Second solution. Consider triangles $C H M$ and $K M B$. In them, two sides and one angle are equal (although the angle is not between the equal sides), and triangle $C H M$ is a right triangle. However, triangles with two equal sides and an equal pair of angles can only be unequal if one is obtuse and the other is acute. Therefore, triangles $C H M$ and $K M B$ are equal, from which it follows that $C H=B K$ and $\angle A K M=\angle C H M=90^{\circ}$. We then reason as in the first solution.

question: 4. Ten natural numbers were written on the board. If any three of the written numbers are marked, then the sum of all three will be divisible by two numbers from this triplet. Prove that among the written numbers there are equal ones.
reference_solution:
First solution. If $a \leq b \leq c \leq d \leq e$ are five of the given numbers, then among the sums $a+d+e, b+d+e, c+d+e$, two must be divisible by one of the numbers $d$ and $e$. But the difference between these two sums is equal to the difference between some two of the numbers $a, b, c$, and is therefore less than $d$. Hence, it is equal to 0, and thus, among the numbers $a, b, c$, there are two that are equal.

Second solution. Suppose all numbers in the set are distinct. Take the three smallest numbers: $a<b<c$. Consider any of the remaining numbers $x$ and the two triples $\{a, c, x\},\{b, c, x\}$. Both sums $a+c+x$ and $b+c+x$ cannot be divisible by $c$ simultaneously, since the difference between the second and the first sum is positive but less than $c$. Therefore, at least one of these sums is divisible by $x$. But $a+c<2 x$ and $b+c<2 x$, so one of the equalities $a+c=x$ or $b+c=x$ must hold. This means that any number not in the first triple is equal to the sum of two numbers from this triple. Hence, there are no more than six distinct numbers in the entire set.

Remark. Continuing the reasoning from the first solution, it is not difficult to show that among the given numbers, there are at least seven that are equal.

question: 1. Four numbers are written on the board, none of which are equal to 0. If each of them is multiplied by the sum of the other three, the results are four identical values. Prove that the squares of the numbers written on the board are equal. (I. Rubanov).
reference_solution: Solution. Let the numbers $a, b, c$ and $d$ be written. By the condition $a(b+c+d)=b(a+c+d)$, from which $(a-b)(c+d)=0$. Similarly, from the equality $c(a+b+d)=d(a+b+c)$ we get $(c-d)(a+b)=0$. Since either $c+d$ or $c-d$ is not equal to 0, then either $a=b$ or $a=-b$. In both cases, the squares of the numbers $a$ and $b$ are equal, from which, due to the arbitrariness of the choice of $a$ and $b$, the statement of the problem follows.

question: 3. A divisor of a natural number is called proper if it is less than the number but greater than 1. For a natural number \( n \), all proper divisors (there were at least three of them) were found and all possible pairwise sums of these divisors were recorded (repeated identical sums were not recorded). Prove that the resulting set could not be the set of all proper divisors of any natural number. (A. Khryabrov)
reference_solution: Solution. Suppose the obtained set of numbers turned out to be the set of all proper divisors of some number $m$. Since the number $n$ has at least three proper divisors, among them there will be two divisors of the same parity. Then their sum is even. The number $m$ is divisible by this sum, so it is also even. Therefore, the number 2, being a proper divisor of the number $m$, was also written down. But this is impossible, since the sum of any two proper divisors of the number $n$ is greater than 2.

question: 4. The perpendicular bisectors of sides $AB$ and $BC$ of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ intersect sides $CD$ and $DA$ at points $P$ and $Q$ respectively. It turns out that $\cdot A P B=\cdot B Q C$. Inside the quadrilateral, a point $X$ is chosen such that $Q X \| A B$ and $P X \| B C$. Prove that the line $B X$ bisects the diagonal $AC$. (S. Berlov)
reference_solution:
Solution. It is sufficient to prove that the distances from points $A$ and $C$ to the line $B X$ are equal. This is equivalent to $S_{A B X}=S_{B C X}$, since triangles $A B X$ and $B C X$ share the same base $B X$. Since $Q X \| A B$, we have $\quad S_{A B X}=S_{A B Q}$. Similarly, $\quad S_{C B X}=S_{C B P}$. Note that isosceles triangles $A B P$ and $C B Q$ are similar by two angles,

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_4f2190590c942c6c9afdg-1.jpg?height=448&width=439&top_left_y=2049&top_left_x=1548)
therefore $A B / B C=B P / B Q$, from which $A B \cdot B Q=C B \cdot B P$. Since $\cdot A B P=\cdot C B Q$, then $\cdot A B Q=\cdot C B P$. Consequently, the areas of triangles $A B Q$ and $C B P$ are proportional to the products of the sides enclosing equal angles, i.e., these areas are equal. Thus, $S_{A B X}=S_{A B Q}=S_{C B P}=S_{C B X}$, which is what we needed to prove.

question: 7. In trapezoid $A B C D$, where $A D \| B C$, angle $B$ is equal to the sum of angles $A$ and $D$. On the extension of segment $C D$ beyond vertex $D$, segment $D K=B C$ is laid out. Prove that $A K=B K$. (B. Obukhov)
reference_solution: Solution. On the ray $DA$, we mark off the segment $DE = BC$. Then the quadrilateral $DCBE$ is a parallelogram, so $\cdot CBE = \cdot CDE$. Using the given condition, we get $\cdot ABE = \cdot ABC - \cdot CBE = \cdot ABC - \cdot CDE = \cdot BAE$; hence, triangle $ABE$ is isosceles, $AE = BE$. Furthermore, since $ED = BC = KD$, we get $\cdot KED = \cdot EKD = \cdot CDE / 2$. Since $\cdot AEB = \cdot CDE$, the line $KE$ is the bisector of angle $AEB$ and, thus, the perpendicular bisector of the base $AB$ of the isosceles triangle $ABE$. Therefore, point $K$ is equidistant from the endpoints of segment $AB$, which is what we needed to prove.

question: 8. On a $20 \times 20$ chessboard, 220 knights are placed, each attacking all the free cells. Prove that it is possible to remove 20 knights such that the remaining knights still attack all the free cells. Recall that a knight attacks in an "L" shape (see figure). (S. Berlov)
reference_solution:
Solution. We will remove knights from the board one by one as follows. If at

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_4f2190590c942c6c9afdg-2.jpg?height=262&width=257&top_left_y=1728&top_left_x=1685)
any step, we can remove a knight such that the remaining knights still cover all free squares, we will do so. If after some step, 200 knights remain, we will have achieved the required result.

Suppose that at some point, it is impossible to remove any knight while maintaining the required condition. We will divide the cells of the board into pairs connected by a knight's move (this can be done, for example, as shown in the figure on the right). We will call a pair complete if it contains two knights, and empty if it contains no knights; let there be $f$ complete and $e$ empty pairs on the board. Consider any knight $\mathrm{R}$ standing in a complete pair. If it is removed,

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_4f2190590c942c6c9afdg-2.jpg?height=286&width=297&top_left_y=1353&top_left_x=1670)
its cell will be covered by its paired cell; therefore, some other cell $C$ will remain uncovered. Clearly, this cell is in an empty pair and is only covered by the knight $R$; we will associate cell $C$ with knight $R$. Clearly, different knights are associated with different cells; thus, the total number of associated cells (which is no more than $2e$) is $2f$, meaning $e \geq f$. But the total number of knights is $2f + (200 - e - f) = 200 + (f - e) \leq 200$. Therefore, at the moment when no knight can be removed, we have already achieved the required result.

question: 2. In Shvambania, some cities are connected by two-way non-stop flights. The flights are divided among three airlines, and if one airline serves a route between cities A and B, then planes of other airlines do not fly between these cities. It is known that from each city, flights of all three airlines depart. Prove that it is possible to fly out of some city and return to it, using flights of all three airlines along the way without visiting any of the intermediate cities more than once. (C. Berlov)
reference_solution: Solution. Fly out of any city A with the first company, arrive in city B, from there fly with the second company, then the third, and again the first, second, third, and so on. Consider the very first moment when we encounter a city C that we have already visited. Then the segment of our path from the first visit to city C to the second will be the one we are looking for. Indeed, if we flew from city C to city D for the first time, we could not have returned to C immediately from D. Therefore, between the two visits to city C, we made at least three flights and, thus, used flights of all three companies along the way.

question: 7. The angles of triangle $ABC$ satisfy the condition $2 \angle A + \angle B = \angle C$. Inside this triangle, on the bisector of angle $A$, a point $K$ is chosen such that $BK = BC$. Prove that $\angle KBC = 2 \angle KBA$. (S. Berlov)
reference_solution:
First solution. Since $\angle C > \angle A + \angle B$, then $\angle C > 90^{\circ}$. Choose a point $T$ on the ray $A C$ such that $B C = B T$. Note that $\angle A T B = \angle B C T = \angle A + \angle B$. Since $2 \angle A + \angle B = \angle C$, we have $3 \angle A + 2 \angle B = \angle A + \angle B + \angle C = 180^{\circ}$, from which $\angle C B T = \angle A \Rightarrow \angle A B T = \angle A + \angle B = \angle A T B$. Therefore, point $K$ lies on the axis of symmetry of the isosceles triangle $B A T$, from which $B K = K T$. Thus, $B T = B C = B K = K T$, meaning that triangle $B K T$ is equilateral, from which $\angle K B C = 60^{\circ} - \angle C B T = 60^{\circ} - \angle A$, and $\angle A B K = 30^{\circ}$, $\angle B A K = 30^{\circ} - \angle A / 2 = \angle K B C / 2$. 

Second solution. Choose a point $L$ on the angle bisector of $\angle A$ inside the triangle such that $\angle L B C = 2 \angle L B A$. To prove that points $L$ and $K$ coincide, it is sufficient to prove that $B L = B C$. Let the angle bisector of $\angle C B L$ intersect $A C$ at point $N$. Then $\angle B N C = \angle A + 2 \angle B / 3 = \angle A / 3 + \angle B / 3 + (\angle B / 3 + 2 \angle A / 3) = (\angle A + \angle B + \angle C) / 3 = 60^{\circ}$. Note that $L$ is the intersection point of the angle bisectors of triangle $A B N$. Therefore, $\angle L N B = 60^{\circ}$, and triangles $B C N$ and $B L N$ are equal by side $B N$ and the two angles adjacent to it, from which it follows that $B L = B C$.

question: 6. (S. Berlov) In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, the following relations are satisfied: $AB=BD; \angle ABD=\angle DBC$. On the diagonal $BD$, there is a point $K$ such that $BK=BC$. Prove that $\angle KAD=\angle KCD$.
reference_solution:
Solution. On side $A B$, we mark off a segment $B E = B C$. The isosceles triangles $E B K$ and $K B C$ are equal by two sides and the angle between them. Therefore, $E K = K C$, and

$$
\angle A E K = 180^{\circ} - \angle B E K = 180^{\circ} - \angle B K C = \angle C K D
$$

Moreover, $K D = B D - B K = B A - B E = E A$. Therefore, triangles $A E K$ and $D K C$ are equal. Furthermore, since both triangles $B E K$ and $B A D$ are isosceles, $\angle B E K = 90^{\circ} - \angle E B D / 2 = \angle B A D$. Therefore, $A D \| E K$, from which it follows that $\angle K A D = \angle E K A = \angle K C D$.

question: 3. Given a 1000-digit number with no zeros in its representation. Prove that from this number, several (possibly none) of the last digits can be erased so that the resulting number is not a natural power of a number less than 500. (S. Berlov)
reference_solution: Solution. We will erase at the end zero, one, two, three, ..., 499 digits. If all the time the results are powers of numbers less than 500, then the bases of some two of them must coincide. Let these be $a^{x}$ and $a^{y}(x<y)$. Multiply the number $a^{x}$ by a power of ten so that its notation has as many digits as the notation of $a^{y}$, and subtract the result from $a^{y}$. The difference will be a natural number, divisible by $a^{x}$. But it will have no more than 499 digits, while $a^{x}$ has no fewer than 501 digits. Contradiction.

question: 4. Given a convex quadrilateral $A B S C$. A point $P$ is chosen on the diagonal $B C$ such that $A P=C P>B$. Point $Q$ is symmetric to point $P$ with respect to the midpoint of diagonal $B C$, and point $R$ is symmetric to point $Q$ with respect to the line $A C$. It turns out that $\angle S A B=\angle Q A C$ and $\angle S B C=\angle B A C$. Prove that $S A=S R$. (S. Berlov)
reference_solution:
Solution. Mark a point $L$ on the segment $A C$ such that $Q L \| A P$. Then triangles $A P C$ and $L Q C$ are similar, and $L Q=Q C=B P$. Moreover, $B Q=P C=A P$ and $\angle A P B=\angle L Q B$, so triangles $A B P$ and $B L Q$ are equal by two sides and the angle between them. Therefore, $B A=B L$. Further,

$$
\angle A L R=\angle A L Q=180^{\circ}-\angle C L Q=180^{\circ}-\angle A C B=\angle C A B+\angle A B C=\angle A B C+\angle S B C=\angle A B S
$$

and $\angle B A S=\angle Q A C=\angle L A R$, so triangles $A B S$ and $A L R$ are similar by two angles, from which $A B / A L=A S / A R$. Thus, triangles $A B L$ and $A S R$ are similar by two proportional sides and the angle between them $(\angle S A R=\angle B A C$, since $\angle S A B=\angle Q A C=\angle R A L)$, but since $A B=B L$, then $A S=S R$.

Solution. We will prove a stronger statement b). Consider a $1 \times 10$ rectangle adjacent to the left side of the $2015 \times 2015$ square by its short side. If any of its cells falls into the cut-out $10 \times 10$ square, then the rightmost cell of this rectangle also falls into it. Therefore, if the rightmost cell of such a rectangle is not cut out, then none of its cells are cut out. It remains to note that the number 2015 gives a remainder of 5 when divided by 10, and therefore in the tenth column from the left of the $2015 \times 2015$ square, there will be at least five uncut cells.

question: 5. It is known that both the sum and the product of two natural numbers $a$ and $b$ are squares of natural numbers. Prove that the number $|16a - 9b|$ is not prime.
reference_solution:
Solution. If $16 a-9 b=0$, the statement of the problem is obvious. From now on, we assume that $16 a-9 b \neq 0$.

Let $d=\operatorname{GCD}(a, b)$, and let $a=d m, b=d n$. Then $a b=d^{2} m n=c^{2}$. Since the numbers $m$ and $n$ are coprime, in their factorization into prime factors, all prime numbers enter with even exponents. Therefore, $m$ and $n$ are squares of natural numbers: $m=u^{2}, n=v^{2}$.

Let $d>1$. Then $|16 a-9 b|=d\left|\left((4 u)^{2}-\left(3 v^{2}\right)\right)\right|=d(4 u+3 v)|(4 u-3 v)|$. This is a composite number, since $d>1$ and $4 u+3 v>1$.

Let $d=1$. Then $|16 a-9 b|=(4 u+3 v)|(4 u-3 v)|$. If $|4 u-3 v| \neq 1$, everything is proved. Otherwise $4 u-3 v= \pm 1$, that is, $4 u=3 v \pm 1$. By the condition $16(a+b)=16 f^{2}=16 u^{2}+16 v^{2}=(3 v \pm 1)^{2}+16 v^{2}=25 v^{2} \pm 6 v+1$. But the distance from the number $25 v^{2}=(5 v)^{2}$ to the nearest neighboring squares $(5 v \pm 1)^{2}$ is at least $(5 v)^{2}-(5 v-1)^{2}=10 v-1$, which is greater than $6 v+1$. Therefore, it turns out that the number $(4 f)^{2}=16 f^{2}$ is not a square of a natural number 一 a contradiction. Thus, the case $4 u-3 v= \pm 1$ is impossible, which completes the proof.

question: 4. On the side $B C$ of triangle $A B C$, a point $E$ is marked, and on the bisector $B D$ - a point $F$ in such a way that $E F \| A C$ and $A F=A D$. Prove that $A B=B E$.
reference_solution: Solution. From the condition of the problem, it follows that $\angle E F D=\angle A D F=\angle A F D$ (the first equality is true because $E F \| A C$, the second - since $A F=A D$). Therefore, the angles $A F B$ and $E F B$, adjacent to the angles $A F D$ and $E F D$, are also equal. In addition, by the condition $\angle A B F=\angle E B F$. Therefore, triangles $B F E$ and $B F A$ are equal by the common side $B F$ and two adjacent angles. Hence, their corresponding sides $B E$ and $A B$ are also equal.

question: 3. On the sides $A B$ and $A C$ of the isosceles triangle $A B C$, points $P$ and $Q$ are chosen respectively such that $P Q \| B C$. On the bisectors of triangles $A B C$ and $A P Q$, starting from vertices $B$ and $Q$, points $X$ and $Y$ are chosen respectively such that $X Y \| B C$. Prove that $P X = C Y$. (A. Kuznetsov, edited by S. Berlov and I. Bogdanov)
reference_solution:
Solution. Let $M$ and $N$ be the points of intersection of the line $X Y$ with the sides

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_c15415d85b2251483e80g-1.jpg?height=326&width=380&top_left_y=1496&top_left_x=1589)
$A B$ and $A C$ respectively. Note that $\cdot M X B=\cdot X B C=\cdot M B X=\cdot N Q Y=\cdot Y Q P=\cdot N Y Q$, so $M X=M B=N C$ and $N Y=N Q=M P$. Moreover, $\cdot C N Y=\cdot P M X$. Therefore, triangles $P M X$ and $Y N C$ are equal by two sides and the angle between them, from which $P X=Y C$. Remark. A similar solution can be obtained by denoting $T$ as the intersection of $B X$ and $P Q$ and proving that triangles $P T X$ and $C Q Y$ are equal.

question: 4. In a country, direct non-stop flights are organized between cities in such a way that from each city to any other city, one can travel (possibly with transfers). Moreover, for each city A, there exists a city B such that any other city is directly connected to A or B. Prove that from any city, one can reach any other city with no more than two transfers. (I. Bogdanov)
reference_solution: Solution. Let $X$ and $Y$ be any two cities, and $X, Z_{1}, \ldots, Z_{k}, Y$ be the route between them with the fewest number of transfers. Suppose $k \geq 3$. Then $Z_{2}$ is not connected by a flight to either $X$ or $Y$, otherwise our route could be shortened by using this flight. By the condition, there exists a city $B$ such that every city, different from $Z_{2}$ and $B$, is connected by a flight to at least one of them. Therefore, each of the cities $X$ and $Y$ is either connected to $B$ or is the city $B$ itself. However, if $X \neq B \neq Y$, then there is a route $X, B, Y$ with one transfer, otherwise there is even a direct flight between $X$ and $Y$. In any case, we have a contradiction with the choice of $k$. Therefore, the assumption is incorrect, and $k \leq 2$. Due to the arbitrariness of the choice of $X$ and $Y$, the required statement is proved.

question: 5. On a shelf, ten volumes of an encyclopedia, numbered from 1 to 10, are arranged in a random order. It is allowed to swap any two volumes if there are at least four other volumes between them. Is it always possible to arrange all the volumes in ascending order of their numbers? (D. Khramtsov)
reference_solution: Answer: Yes. Solution. Take any volume. It is removed by no less than 4 volumes, either from the one standing first or from the one standing last. Therefore, we can place it either in the first or in the last position, and then, if we want, move it from the last to the first or vice versa. Since the position where it should stand is removed by no less than 4 volumes, either from the first position or from the last, we will be able to place it in this position with the next move. By performing the described procedure with all volumes except volumes 1 and 10, we will place all of them in their places. Volumes 1 and 10 will end up at the edges, and we will get the arrangement of volumes in ascending order of numbers either immediately or by swapping the edge volumes.

question: 7. Prove that for arbitrary $a, b, c$ the equality $\frac{a(b-c)}{b+c}+\frac{b(c-a)}{c+a}+\frac{c(a-b)}{a+b}=0$ holds if and only if the equality $\frac{a^{2}(b-c)}{b+c}+\frac{b^{2}(c-a)}{c+a}+\frac{c^{2}(a-b)}{a+b}=0$ holds.
reference_solution:
Solution. By expanding the brackets on the left-hand side and combining like terms, it is easy to show that

$$
\left(\frac{a(b-c)}{b+c}+\frac{b(c-a)}{c+a}+\frac{c(a-b)}{a+b}\right)(a+b+c)=\frac{a^{2}(b-c)}{b+c}+\frac{b^{2}(c-a)}{c+a}+\frac{c^{2}(a-b)}{a+b}\left(^{*}\right)
$$

Therefore, if $\frac{a(b-c)}{b+c}+\frac{b(c-a)}{c+a}+\frac{c(a-b)}{a+b}=0$, then $\frac{a^{2}(b-c)}{b+c}+\frac{b^{2}(c-a)}{c+a}+\frac{c^{2}(a-b)}{a+b}=0$. Conversely, let $\frac{a^{2}(b-c)}{b+c}+\frac{b^{2}(c-a)}{c+a}+\frac{c^{2}(a-b)}{a+b}=0$. If $a+b+c \neq 0$, the equality $\frac{a(b-c)}{b+c}+\frac{b(c-a)}{c+a}+\frac{c(a-b)}{a+b}=0$ immediately follows from the equality $(*)$. If, however, $a+b+c=0$, then

$$
\frac{a(b-c)}{b+c}+\frac{b(c-a)}{c+a}+\frac{c(a-b)}{a+b}=\frac{a(b-c)}{-a}+\frac{b(c-a)}{-b}+\frac{c(a-b)}{-c}=(c-b)+(a-c)+(b-a)=0
$$

question: 5. Can a rectangle $1000 \times 2016$ be cut into rectangles $1 \times 2015$ and three-cell "corners" so that both types of figures are present? (E. Bakayev)
reference_solution:
Answer: No. Solution: Suppose it is possible. Clearly, each of the rectangles $1 \times 2015$ adjoins one of the short sides of the rectangle $1000 \times 2016$, and is one cell away from the other side. Let's call a rectangle $1 \times 2015$ black (respectively, white) if this cell is covered by a corner, the other two cells of which are located above (respectively, below) this rectangle.

The lowest of the rectangles $1 \times 2015$ must be black: otherwise, below it is a rectangle $2016 \times k$, the number of cells of which is divisible by 3 and which must be completely covered by three-cell corners and a "domino" of two cells, which is impossible. For the same reason, the highest of the rectangles $1 \times 2015$ must be white. But then among the rectangles $1 \times 2015$ there will be a black one and a white one lying above this black one, between which there are no other such rectangles. The rectangle $2016 \times$ lying between them must be completely covered by three-cell corners and two "dominoes" of two cells, which is impossible.

question: 6. In a school, there are 30 clubs, each attended by 40 children. For each $i=1,2, \ldots, 30$, let $n_{i}$ denote the number of children attending exactly $i$ clubs. Prove that in the same school, it is possible to organize 40 clubs with 30 children in each such that the numbers $n_{i}$ for these new clubs would be the same. (V. Dolnikov)
reference_solution: Solution. Let's write down the members of the first circle in a row, followed by those of the second, and so on. In this process, if a child is in both the $i$-th and the ( $i+1$ )-th circle, we record them in the same position in the list of the ( $i+1$ )-th circle as in the list of the $i$-th. By cutting the resulting long list into pieces of length 30, we will get 40 new circles, which obviously satisfy the conditions of the problem. In this way, no one will end up in the same circle twice, because the distance between two entries of the same child in the long list, by construction, is at least 40, and therefore at least 30.

question: 7. The sum of non-negative numbers $a, b, c$, and $d$ is 4. Prove that $(a b+c d)(a c+b d)(a d+b c) \leq 8$. (A. Khryabrov)
reference_solution: Solution. $\sqrt{(a b+c d)(a c+b d)} \leq \frac{a b+c d+a c+b d}{2}=\frac{(a+d)(b+c)}{2} \leq \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{a+b+c+d}{2}\right)^{2}=2$. Similarly, $\sqrt{(a b+c d)(a d+b c)} \leq 2$ and $\sqrt{(a c+b d)(a d+b c)} \leq 2$. Multiplying the three obtained inequalities, we get the desired result.

question: 8. Given a parallelogram $A B C D$. On sides $A B$ and $B C$ and the extension of side $C D$ beyond point $D$, points $K$, $L$, and $M$ are chosen respectively such that triangles $K L M$ and $B C A$ are equal (with this correspondence of vertices). Segment $K M$ intersects segment $A D$ at point $N$. Prove that $L N \| A B$. (B. Obukhov)
reference_solution:
First solution. Draw a line through $L$ parallel to $KM$; let it intersect lines $AB$ and $CD$ at points $P$ and $Q$ respectively. Note that the heights of triangles $BCA$ and $KLM$, dropped from the corresponding vertices $C$ and $L$, are equal; in turn, they are equal to the distances between the pairs of parallel lines $AB, CD$ and $KM, PQ$. Therefore, these lines form a rhombus $KPQM$, which means $PK = KM = AB$. From this, we have $BP = KP - KB = AB - KB = AK$. Additionally, from the parallelism, we get $\angle AKN = \angle BPL$ and $\angle NAK = \angle LBP$. Therefore, triangles $AKN$ and $BPL$ are congruent; in particular, $AN = BL$. Hence, quadrilateral $ANLB$ is a parallelogram, and $LN \parallel AB$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_50cb024ffeac238accdeg-1.jpg?height=420&width=289&top_left_y=1800&top_left_x=1683)

Second solution. Draw a line through point $L$ parallel to $AB$. Let it intersect line $KM$ at point $N'$. Then $\angle BKL = \angle KLN'$; moreover, by the condition $\angle KBL = \angle LKN'$. Therefore, triangles $BKL$ and $KLN'$ are similar by two angles, from which $K N' / BL = LN' / KL = LN' / BC$ (the last equality is true because $KL = BC$). On the other hand, in trapezoid $MKBC$, segment $N'L$ is parallel to the bases, so $K N' / BL = KM / BC = AB / BC$. Thus, $LN' / BC = K N' / BL = AB / BC$, that is, $LN' = AB$. Therefore, $ABLN'$ is a parallelogram, and hence point $N'$ lies on $AD$ and, consequently, coincides with $N$, from which $LN \parallel AB$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_50cb024ffeac238accdeg-1.jpg?height=380&width=325&top_left_y=2391&top_left_x=1662)

question: 3. Given an isosceles triangle \(ABC (AC = BC)\). Points \(A_1\), \(B_1\), and \(C_1\) are marked on the sides \(BC\), \(AC\), and \(AB\) respectively. It turns out that \(C_1 B_1\) is perpendicular to \(AC\), \(B_1 A_1\) is perpendicular to \(BC\), and \(B_1 A_1 = B_1 C_1\). Prove that \(A_1 C_1\) is perpendicular to \(AB\).
reference_solution: Solution. Let $\angle A=\angle B=\alpha$. Then $\angle C=\pi-2 \alpha$. Triangle $C A_{1} B_{1}$ is a right triangle, so $\angle C B_{1} A_{1}=\pi / 2-(\pi-2 \alpha)=2 \alpha-\pi$. Then $\angle A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}=\pi / 2-(2 \alpha-\pi / 2)=\pi-2 \alpha$. Since $B_{1} A_{1}=B_{1} C_{1}$, $\angle B_{1} C_{1} A_{1}=\angle B_{1} A_{1} C_{1}=\alpha$. Therefore, $\angle A C_{1} A_{1}=\angle A C_{1} B+\angle B C_{1} A_{1}=(\pi / 2-\alpha)+\alpha=\pi / 2$, which means $A_{1} C_{1}$ is perpendicular to $A B$.

question: 2. In triangle $ABC$, the bisector $BD$ is drawn, in triangle $BDC$ - the bisector $DE$, and in triangle $DEC$ - the bisector $EF$. It turned out that lines $BD$ and $EF$ are parallel. Prove that angle $ABC$ is twice the angle $BAC$.
reference_solution:
Solution. From the condition, it follows that $\angle A B D=\angle E B D=\angle C E F=\angle D E F=\angle B D E$. Thus, the alternate interior angles $A B D$ and $B D E$ formed by the intersection of line $B D$ with lines $A B$ and $D E$ are equal. Therefore, $A B \| D E$, from which $\angle B A C=\angle E D F=\angle E D B=\angle A B D=\angle A B C / 2$, as required to prove.
