question: 4. A company is called public if it has at least 15 shareholders. A shareholder of a company is called a minority shareholder if they own no more than $25 \%$ of the shares of that company. On the stock exchange where the shares are traded, one sixth of the companies are public. Prove that among all shareholders participating in the stock exchange, no less than $20 \%$ are minority shareholders. In the stock exchange, it is assumed that each shareholder owns shares of only one company.
reference_solution: Solution. Let the number of firms on the exchange be N. We will call a shareholder who owns more than $25 \%$ of a firm's shares a real shareholder. The number of real shareholders in one firm cannot exceed three. (If there are four, then one of them cannot own more than $25 \%$ of the shares). Therefore, the total number of real shareholders on the exchange cannot exceed $3 \mathrm{~N}$. Now consider a public company. Among its shareholders, there are no more than three real ones. This means that among the shareholders of a public company, there are at least 12 - minorities. The number of minorities on the exchange is no less than $12 \cdot \frac{1}{6} N$, i.e., no less than 2N. Thus, the number of minorities is no less than $2 \mathrm{~N}$, the number of real shareholders is no more than $3 \mathrm{~N}$, which means that minorities constitute no less than one fifth, i.e., no less than $20 \%$.

question: 8.4. Point $D$ lies on the hypotenuse $B C$ of a right triangle $A B C$, but does not coincide with its midpoint. Prove that among the segments $A D, B D$, and $C D$ there are no equal ones.
reference_solution:
First solution. We complete the right triangle $ABC$ to a rectangle $ABEC$. The point $O$ of intersection of the diagonals of this rectangle is the midpoint of the hypotenuse of the triangle. Since the diagonals of a rectangle are equal, it follows that $AO = BO = CO$. Considering now the isosceles triangles $AOB$ and $AOC$, we conclude that $\angle ABC = \angle BAO$ and $\angle ACB = \angle CAO$ (Fig. 1).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_01eaca71e034b8dd1883g-2.jpg?height=229&width=345&top_left_y=1322&top_left_x=547)

Fig. 1

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_01eaca71e034b8dd1883g-2.jpg?height=229&width=345&top_left_y=1322&top_left_x=1004)

Fig. 2

Now, take a point $D$ on the segment $OC$ that does not coincide with $O$ (Fig. 2). The segments $CD$ and $AD$ are sides of the triangle $CAD$, lying opposite the angles $CAD$ and $ACB$ respectively. Since the side opposite the larger angle in a triangle is longer, and $\angle ACB = \angle CAO > \angle CAD$, the segment $CD$ is shorter than the segment $AD$. Similarly, from triangle $BAD$, we obtain that the segment $BD$ is longer than the segment $AD$. Thus, $BD > AD > CD$, from which the statement of the problem follows. The case where point $D$ lies on the segment $OB$ is analyzed similarly.

Second solution. If any two of the segments $AD$, $BD$, and $CD$ were equal to each other, then point $D$ would lie on the perpendicular bisector of either $BC$, or $AC$, or $AB$, but all these perpendicular bisectors intersect the hypotenuse at its midpoint - point $O$, which is different from point $D$.

question:
9.8. In a state, there are $n$ cities, and an express train runs between each pair of them (in both directions). For any express train, the ticket prices for the "outbound" and "return" trips are the same, and for any two different express trains, these prices are different. Prove that a traveler can choose an initial city, leave it, and travel sequentially on $n-1$ express trains, paying less for each subsequent trip than for the previous one. (The traveler can visit the same city multiple times.) 

(I. Bogdanov)
reference_solution:
First solution. Remove all express trains, and then start launching them back one by one in ascending order of price (i.e., the first one launched is the cheapest, the second one is the cheapest of the remaining, and so on). At each moment, in each city, we will write the maximum number of express trains that can be sequentially taken, starting from this city, such that the prices of the rides monotonically decrease.

Initially, all numbers in the cities are zero. Suppose at some moment we introduce an express train connecting cities $A$ and $B$, in which the numbers $a$ and $b$ were written, respectively. After introducing the new express train, in $A$ there will be a number not less than $b+1$ (since now from $A$ one can take the new express train to $B$, and then follow a route of length $b$ starting from $B$). Similarly, in $B$ there will be a number not less than $a+1$. Therefore, the sum of the numbers in $A$ and $B$ will increase by at least 2, and the numbers in the other cities will not decrease. Thus, the sum of all numbers in the cities will increase by at least 2.

Therefore, when all $n(n-1) / 2$ express trains are introduced, the sum of the numbers in the cities will be at least $2 \cdot n(n-1) / 2 = n(n-1)$. This means that in at least one city, there will be a number not less than $n-1$. This indicates the existence of the required route from this city.

Remark. For any even $n$, one can construct an example showing that a monotonically decreasing route of $n$ express trains may not exist.

Second solution. Divide each express train running between $A$ and $B$ into two - one going from $A$ to $B$, and one going from $B$ to $A$. This results in $n(n-1)$ half-express trains. We will construct $n$ designated routes (one starting in each city) such that the price of the ride on each is monotonically decreasing, and each half-express train is included in at least one of the designated routes. Then, one of the designated routes will contain at least $n-1$ half-express trains, which is what we need.

A designated route starting in city $A$ looks like this. Let $A_{0} = A$. Consider all half-express trains $A_{0} X$ leaving from $A_{0}$, and choose the half-express train $A_{0} A_{1}$ with the maximum price $a_{1}$. Then consider all half-express trains $A_{1} Y$ leaving from $A_{1}$ with a price less than $a_{1}$; if such exist, choose the half-express train $A_{1} A_{2}$ with the maximum price $a_{2}$, and so on. The route ends with the half-express train $A_{k-1} A_{k}$ if no half-express trains with a price less than $a_{k}$ leave from $A_{k}$.

It remains to show that each half-express train $B C$ will be included in at least one of the designated routes. Let $B_{1} = B$, $B_{0} = C$, and let $b_{1}$ be the price of $B C$. Consider all half-express trains $X B_{1}$ leading to $B_{1}$ with a price greater than $b_{1}$. If such exist, choose the half-express train $B_{2} B_{1}$ with the minimum price $b_{2}$. Next, consider all half-express trains $Y B_{2}$ leading to $B_{2}$ with a price greater than $b_{2}$. Choose the half-express train $B_{3} B_{2}$ with the minimum price $b_{3}$, and so on. This selection process will end when, for some $k$, the half-express train $B_{k} B_{k-1}$ is the half-express train with the maximum price leaving from $B_{k}$. Then, according to our construction, the designated route starting from $B_{k}$ will sequentially pass through $B_{k-1}, \ldots, B_{1}, B_{0}$, i.e., it will include the express train $B C$, as required.

Remark. In fact, each half-express train will be included in exactly one of the designated routes.

question: 10.1. At each point $A$ in the plane, there stands a real number $f(A)$. It is known that if $M$ is the point of intersection of the medians of triangle $ABC$, then $f(M)=f(A)+f(B)+f(C)$. Prove that $f(A)=0$ for all points $A$.
reference_solution:
Solution. Let's take an arbitrary point $M$ on the plane and prove that $f(M)=0$. For this, consider an arbitrary triangle $ABC$ for which point $M$ is the centroid. Denote by $D$, $E$, and $F$ the centroids of triangles $BCM$, $CAM$, and $ABM$, respectively (see Fig. 2).

(A. S. Golvachev)

Note that point $M$ is also

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_0e15a0894cdaaa4705bag-1.jpg?height=466&width=436&top_left_y=405&top_left_x=856)

Fig. 2 the centroid of triangle $DEF$. Indeed, let $A'$, $B'$, and $C'$ be the midpoints of segments $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$, respectively. Then triangle $DEF$ is obtained from triangle $ABC$ by a homothety centered at $M$ with a coefficient of $-\frac{1}{3}$, since a homothety with a coefficient of $-\frac{1}{2}$ transforms triangle $ABC$ into $A'B'C'$, and a subsequent homothety with a coefficient of $\frac{2}{3}$ transforms it into triangle $DEF$.

Then the following chain of equalities holds:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(M)= & f(D)+f(E)+f(F)=(f(M)+f(B)+f(C))+ \\
& +(f(M)+f(C)+f(A))+(f(M)+f(A)+f(B))= \\
= & 2(f(A)+f(B)+f(C))+3 f(M)=5 f(M)
\end{aligned}
$$

from which it follows that $f(M)=0$, which is what we needed to prove.

question: 10.4. Given an acute-angled triangle $A B C$, where $A C < B C$. A circle passes through points $A$ and $B$ and intersects segments $C A$ and $C B$ again at points $A_{1}$ and $B_{1}$, respectively. The circumcircles of triangles $A B C$ and $A_{1} B_{1} C$ intersect again at point $P$. Segments $A B_{1}$ and $B A_{1}$ intersect at point $S$. Points $Q$ and $R$ are symmetric to $S$ with respect to lines $C A$ and $C B$. Prove that points $P, Q, R$ and $C$ lie on the same circle.
reference_solution:
Solution. Using circles $(P A B C)$ and $\left(P A_{1} B_{1} C\right)$, we get $\angle P A B=180^{\circ}-\angle P C B=\angle P A_{1} B_{1}$ and similarly $\angle P B A=\angle P B_{1} A_{1}$. Thus, $\triangle P A B \sim \triangle P A_{1} B_{1}$. From this similarity, it follows that $\angle A P A_{1}=\angle A P B \pm \angle B P A_{1}=\angle B P B_{1}$ and $P A / P A_{1}=P B / P B_{1}$. Therefore, $\triangle P A A_{1} \sim \triangle P B B_{1}$, and there exists a rotational homothety $h$ with center $P$, mapping $\overrightarrow{A A_{1}}$ to $\overrightarrow{B B_{1}}$. The rotation angle for $h$ is $\angle A P B=\angle A C B$ (see Fig. 3).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_0e15a0894cdaaa4705bag-4.jpg?height=681&width=620&top_left_y=790&top_left_x=445)

Triangle $A_{1} Q A$ is congruent to triangle $A_{1} S A$, which in turn is similar to triangle $B_{1} S B$ (since $A A_{1} B_{1} B$ is cyclic). Therefore, triangles $A_{1} Q A$ and $B_{1} S B$ are similar and have the same orientation, so $S=h(Q)$ and, hence, $\angle Q P S = \angle A C B$. Similarly, $\angle S P R = \angle A C B$. Then $\angle Q P R = 2 \angle A C B$.

But $\angle Q C R = \angle Q C A + \angle A B C + \angle B C R = \angle A C S + \angle A B C + \angle S C B = 2 \angle A B C$. Thus, we have proved the equality $\angle Q P R = \angle Q C R$, from which the statement of the problem follows.

Remark 1. In fact, the solution uses the well-known description of the Miquel point of the quadrilateral formed by the lines $A B, C A, B C$, and $A_{1} B_{1}$ as the center of the rotational homothety that maps $\overrightarrow{A A_{1}}$ to $\overrightarrow{B B_{1}}$.

Remark 2. The equalities of angles $\angle Q P S = \angle A C B = \angle S P R$ can be proved in different ways. Let's indicate another possible approach.

Let $Q_{1}$ and $R_{1}$ be the projections of $S$ onto $C A$ and $C B$ respectively. It can be shown that points $C, P, Q_{1}, R_{1}, S$ lie on the same circle $\Gamma$ with diameter $C S$. The lines $C P, A_{1} B_{1}$, and $A B$ are the radical axes of the three circles from the condition, and they intersect at a single point $S'$. From this, it is not difficult to understand that the quadruple of lines $C A, C P, C B, C S$ is harmonic. Projecting from $C$ onto $\Gamma$, we get that $S Q_{1} P R_{1}$ is harmonic. From this, $P R_{1} / R_{1} S = P Q_{1} / Q_{1} S = P Q_{1} / Q_{1} Q$, from which $\triangle P Q_{1} S \sim \triangle P R_{1} R$ (and also $\triangle P Q_{1} Q \sim \triangle P R_{1} S$), from which the required equalities of angles follow.

question: 10.6. In an acute-angled triangle $A B C$, the bisector $B L$ is drawn. Points $D$ and $E$ are the midpoints of the smaller arcs $A B$ and $B C$ of the circumcircle $\omega$ of triangle $A B C$. On the extension of segment $B D$ beyond point $D$, point $P$ is marked, and on the extension of segment $B E$ beyond point $E$, point $Q$ is marked such that $\angle A P B=\angle C Q B=90^{\circ}$. Prove that the midpoint of segment $B L$ lies on the line $P Q$. (A. Kuznetsov)
reference_solution:
Solution. Let $\angle B A C=2 \alpha, \angle A C B=2 \gamma$. Without loss of generality, assume that $\alpha \geqslant \gamma$. Since points $D$ and $E$ are the midpoints of arcs $A B$ and $A C$ of the circle $\omega$, we have $\angle A B D=\frac{\angle A C B}{2}=\gamma$ and $\angle C B E=\alpha$.

Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of sides $A B$ and $B C$ respectively (see Fig. 2). Then $M N$ is the midline of triangle $A B C$, it is parallel to side $A C$ and passes through the midpoint $K$ of segment $B L$. Also, $\angle A M K=180^{\circ}-\angle M A C=180^{\circ}-2 \alpha$ and $\angle B N K=\angle B C A=2 \gamma$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_0e15a0894cdaaa4705bag-7.jpg?height=515&width=698&top_left_y=142&top_left_x=400)

Fig. 2

Let $B M=M A=c, B N=N C=a$. Segment $M P$ is the median in the right triangle $A P B$, so $M P=c$ and $\angle M P B=\angle M B P=\gamma$; similarly, $N Q=a$ and $\angle N Q B=\alpha$. Therefore, $\angle Q N K=\angle B N K+\angle B N Q=2 \gamma+180^{\circ}-2 \alpha$ and $\angle P M K=\angle A M K+\angle P M A=180^{\circ}-2 \alpha+2 \gamma$. Since $\alpha \geqslant \gamma$, either points $P$ and $Q$ lie on the line $M N$, in which case the problem is already solved, or point $P$ lies in the same half-plane as point $A$ relative to the line $M N$, and point $Q$ lies in the other half-plane.

Note that $B K$ is the bisector of triangle $B M N$, so $\frac{M K}{K N}=\frac{c}{a}=\frac{M P}{Q N}$. Together with the equality $\angle P M K=\angle Q N K$, this means that triangles $P M K$ and $Q N K$ are similar. Therefore, $\angle M K P=\angle N K Q$. Since points $P$ and $Q$ also lie in different half-planes relative to the line $M N$, points $P, M$, and $K$ lie on the same line, as required.

question:
10.7. In a math club, 24 schoolchildren are participating. Each team of 6 schoolchildren is considered either played or not played by the leader. For a math battle tournament, the leader plans to divide the children into 4 teams of 6. Can it happen that in any division of the schoolchildren into 4 teams, either exactly three teams or exactly one team are played, and both scenarios are present?

(I. Bogdanov)
reference_solution:
Answer: Yes, it can.

Solution. Let's provide one of the possible examples. We will highlight three students. We will call teams played if they contain 1 or 3 highlighted students, and the rest - unplayed.

The highlighted students can either end up in three different teams, in which case we will get three played teams and one unplayed, or all in one team, and we will get one played and three unplayed teams, or two can be in one team and one in another, in which case we also get one played and three unplayed teams. Thus, all conditions are met.

Note. Also suitable are all examples where an odd number of students, greater than 1 and less than 23, are highlighted, and all teams in which there is an odd number of highlighted students are declared played, and all others unplayed.

question:
10.8. Given a non-constant polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients and a natural number $n$. Let $a_{0}=n, a_{k}=P\left(a_{k-1}\right)$ for all natural $k$. It turns out that for any natural number $b$, the sequence $a_{0}, a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ contains a number that is a $b$-th power of a natural number greater than 1. Prove that the polynomial $P(x)$ is linear.

(M. Antipov)
reference_solution:
Solution. Note immediately that for each natural number $b$, the sequence $a_{0}, a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ will contain infinitely many $b$-th powers of natural numbers greater than one. Indeed, if their number is finite, and the largest one is $N=x^{b}$, then the sequence will not contain any $N b$-th power, which is impossible.

Let $d_{k}=a_{k+1}-a_{k} ;$ then $a_{k+1} \equiv a_{k}\left(\bmod d_{k}\right)$. Since all coefficients of the polynomial are integers, from $a \equiv$ $\equiv a^{\prime}\left(\bmod d_{k}\right)$ it follows that $P(a) \equiv P\left(a^{\prime}\right) \quad\left(\bmod d_{k}\right)$. From this, by direct induction on $s$, we obtain that $a_{k+s+1} \equiv a_{k+s}$ $\left(\bmod d_{k}\right)$, that is, $a_{k+s} \equiv a_{k} \quad\left(\bmod d_{k}\right)$ for all $s \geqslant 0$.

Lemma. $a_{k}\left(a_{k}-1\right)$ is divisible by $d_{k}$.

Proof. Let $p^{\ell}$ be the maximum power of a prime number $p$ that divides $d_{k}$; it is sufficient to show that $a_{k}\left(a_{k}-1\right)$ is divisible by $p^{\ell}$. Let $b=p^{\ell-1}(p-1) \ell$; according to the above remark, there exists an index $s>k$ such that $a_{s}=m^{b}$ for some natural number $m$; in this case, $a_{s} \equiv a_{k}\left(\bmod p^{\ell}\right)$.

If $m$ is not divisible by $p$, then by Euler's theorem $a_{s}=$ $=\left(m^{p^{\ell-1}(p-1)}\right)^{\ell} \equiv 1^{\ell} \equiv 1 \quad\left(\bmod p^{\ell}\right)$, hence $a_{k} \equiv 1\left(\bmod p^{\ell}\right)$. If $m$ is divisible by $p$, then $a_{s}$ is divisible by $p^{\ell}$, and therefore so is $a_{k}$. In any case, $a_{k}\left(a_{k}-1\right)$ is divisible by $p^{\ell}$, which was to be shown.

According to the lemma, for any $k$ the number $a_{k}\left(a_{k}-1\right)$ is divisible by $d_{k}=P\left(a_{k}\right)-a_{k} ;$ and by the condition, among the integers $a_{k}$ there are infinitely many different ones. In particular, $|x(x-1)| \geqslant|Q(x)|$ for infinitely many integer values of $x$ (where $Q(x)=P(x)-x)$.

Now suppose that the degree of the polynomial $P(x)$ (and, consequently, of the polynomial $Q(x))$ is greater than 1. Then the above inequality can hold for infinitely many integers $x$ only if $Q(x)$ is a quadratic trinomial with the leading coefficient $\pm 1$, that is, $Q(x)= \pm x^{2}+u x+v$. In this last case, the values of the polynomial $Q(x) \mp x(x-1)=(u \pm 1) x+v$ are divisible by $Q(x)$ for infinitely many integers $x$; this can only be if $Q(x)= \pm x(x-1)$, that is, $P(x)=x^{2}$ or $P(x)=2 x-x^{2}=1-(x-1)^{2}$.

In the first case, $a_{k}=n^{2^{k}}$, so $a_{k}$ cannot be an odd power of a natural number unless $n$ is such a power. In the second case, $P(x) \leqslant 1$ for all $x$, so $P(x)$ cannot be a power of a natural number greater than 1. In both cases, the condition of the problem is not satisfied; hence, $P(x)$ is linear.

question: 11.5. Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial of degree $n \geqslant 2$ with non-negative coefficients, and let $a, b$, and $c$ be the lengths of the sides of some triangle. Prove that the numbers $\sqrt[n]{P(a)}, \sqrt[n]{P(b)}$, and $\sqrt[n]{P(c)}$ are also the lengths of the sides of some triangle. (N. Agakhanov)
reference_solution:
Solution. Let, without loss of generality, $a \geqslant b \geqslant c$; these three positive numbers are the lengths of the sides of a triangle if and only if $a < b + c$; this means we need to check that $\sqrt[n]{P(a)} < \sqrt[n]{P(b)} + \sqrt[n]{P(c)}$.

Let $P(x) = p_{n} x^{n} + p_{n-1} x^{n-1} + \ldots + p_{0}$. Denote $G(x) = P(x) / x^{n}$. Notice that

$$
G(a) = p_{n} + \frac{p_{n-1}}{a} + \ldots + \frac{p_{0}}{a^{n}} \leqslant p_{n} + \frac{p_{n-1}}{b} + \ldots + \frac{p_{0}}{b^{n}} = G(b)
$$

and, similarly, $G(a) \leqslant G(c)$. Therefore,

$$
\sqrt[n]{P(a)} = a \sqrt[n]{G(a)} < (b + c) \sqrt[n]{G(a)} \leqslant
$$

$$
\leqslant b \sqrt[n]{G(b)} + c \sqrt[n]{G(c)} = \sqrt[n]{P(b)} + \sqrt[n]{P(c)}
$$

which is what we needed to prove.

question:
9.1. Given quadratic trinomials $f_{1}(x)=x^{2}+2 a_{1} x+b_{1}, f_{2}(x)=$ $=x^{2}+2 a_{2} x+b_{2}, f_{3}(x)=x^{2}+2 a_{3} x+b_{3}$. It is known that $a_{1} a_{2} a_{3}=$ $=b_{1} b_{2} b_{3}>1$. Prove that at least one of these trinomials has two roots.

(N. Agakhanov)
reference_solution:
Solution. Suppose the opposite; then the discriminants of all trinomials are non-positive, that is, $a_{k}^{2} \leqslant b_{k}(k=1,2,3)$. The left (and therefore the right) parts of these inequalities are non-negative, so they can be multiplied, yielding $\left(a_{1} a_{2} a_{3}\right)^{2} \leqslant$ $\leqslant b_{1} b_{2} b_{3}$, that is, $N^{2} \leqslant N$, where $N=a_{1} a_{2} a_{3}$. But this contradicts the inequality $N>1$.

Comment. The proof by contradiction is started and the inequalities $a_{k}^{2} \leqslant b_{k}-1$ are obtained - 1 point. The legality of multiplying the inequalities is not justified - no more than 5 points.

question:
9.2. Seven skiers with numbers $1,2, \ldots, 7$ left the start one after another and completed the distance - each at their own constant speed. It turned out that each skier was involved in overtakes exactly twice. (In each overtake, exactly two skiers participate - the one who overtakes and the one who is overtaken.) At the end of the race, a protocol must be compiled, consisting of the numbers of the skiers in the order of their finishing. Prove that in a race with the described properties, no more than two different protocols can result.

(C. Volchonkov)
reference_solution:
Answer. Note that the parity of each skier's position changed with every overtake; therefore, their finishing position is of the same parity as their starting position.

Solution. Since the speeds are constant, any two skiers met no more than once. We will denote the skiers by their starting numbers.

The winner could not be overtaken by anyone, so he himself overtook two others. Therefore, he is 3, and he overtook skiers 1 and 2. Similarly, the one who finished last could not overtake anyone, so he was overtaken by two others, he is 5, and he was overtaken by 6 and 7. Next, skier 1 could not overtake anyone, so he finished third (and besides 3, he was overtaken by the skier who finished second), and skier 7 could not be overtaken by anyone, so he finished fifth (overtaking 5 and the skier who finished sixth).

Thus, it remains to determine how the skiers with even numbers finished. The second place could be taken by either 2 or 4. If 2 came in second, then he overtook 1, and no more overtakes occurred in the leading group $(1,2,3)$. Therefore, skier 4 could only be overtaken, he finished sixth, and skier 6 finished fourth.

If, however, 4 came in second, then 2 could only finish fourth (meaning 4 overtook 2 and 1), and 6 finished sixth (overtaking 5 and yielding to 7). In total, only two protocols are possible: $3,2,1,6,7,4,5$ and $3,4,1,2,7,6,5$

question:
9.3. Is it possible for some natural $k$ to divide all natural numbers from 1 to $k$ into two groups and write down the numbers in each group in a row in some order so that two identical numbers are obtained?

(N. Agakhanov)
reference_solution:
Answer: No

Solution. Assume the opposite. Clearly, $k \geqslant 10$, since the set of digits from 1 to 9 contains no repetitions. Consider the highest power of ten $10^{n}$ that does not exceed $k$. The sequence of digits of the number $10^{n}$ will entirely fit into one of the formed numbers. But then the same sequence of one and $n$ subsequent zeros must repeat in the second number. This sequence of digits could not have appeared from the union of two or more numbers (since natural numbers do not start with zeros), meaning it was contained in one number different from $10^{n}$. But the smallest number different from $10^{n}$ and containing such a set of digits is $10^{n+1}$. We have reached a contradiction with the fact that $10^{n}$ is the highest power of ten not exceeding $k$.

Comment. Only the correct answer (without proof) is provided - 0 points. The idea of considering the longest sequence of zeros is present - 4 points.

question:
9.4. In triangle $A B C$, angle $A$ is equal to $60^{\circ}$. Let $B B_{1}$ and $C C_{1}$ be the angle bisectors of this triangle. Prove that the point symmetric to vertex $A$ with respect to the line $B_{1} C_{1}$ lies on side $B C$.

(D. Prokopenko)
reference_solution:
Solution. Let $I$ be the point of intersection of the angle bisectors of triangle $ABC$. Then $\angle B_{1}IC_{1} = \angle BIC = 180^{\circ} - \angle IBC - \angle ICB = 180^{\circ} - (\angle ABC + \angle ACB) / 2 = 180^{\circ} - 60^{\circ} = 120^{\circ} = 180^{\circ} - \angle B_{1}AC_{1}$. Therefore, the quadrilateral $AB_{1}IC_{1}$ is cyclic. From this, $\angle AC_{1}B_{1} = \angle AIB_{1} = \angle ABI + \angle BAI = (\angle A + \angle B) / 2$ (since $\angle AIB_{1}$ is an exterior angle of $\triangle ABI$), and similarly, $\angle AB_{1}C_{1} = (\angle A + \angle C) / 2$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_e1ca9da53944ab5a6867g-3.jpg?height=429&width=537&top_left_y=1366&top_left_x=1939)

Let the circumcircle of triangle $BC_{1}I$ intersect the line $BC$ at point $K$ (it is easy to see that this point cannot lie on the extension of side $BC$). Then $\angle IKC = 180^{\circ} - \angle BKI = \angle BC_{1}I = 180^{\circ} - \angle AC_{1}I = \angle AB_{1}I = 180^{\circ} - \angle IB_{1}C$, so the quadrilateral $IB_{1}CK$ is also cyclic.

Finally, since the quadrilaterals $AB_{1}IC_{1}$, $BC_{1}IK$, and $CKIB_{1}$ are cyclic, we have $\angle KC_{1}B_{1} = \angle KC_{1}I + \angle IC_{1}B_{1} = \angle KBI + \angle IAB_{1} = (\angle B + \angle A) / 2 = \angle AC_{1}B_{1}$, and similarly, $\angle KB_{1}C_{1} = \angle KB_{1}I + \angle IB_{1}C_{1} = (\angle C + \angle A) / 2 = \angle AB_{1}C_{1}$. question:
9.1. Initially, there were 10 piles of candies on the table, containing $1, 2, \ldots, 10$ candies respectively. The Child decided to redistribute the candies. On each odd minute, he chooses one pile and divides it into two piles, each containing at least one candy. On each even minute, he chooses two piles and merges them into one (thus, his first action is to divide a pile into two). Can it happen at some point that all piles on the table contain the same number of candies?

(N. Agakhanov, jury)
reference_solution:
Answer: Yes.

Solution. We will provide an example of how Little One can achieve such a distribution. On the first minute, he divides the pile of 10 candies into two piles of 5 candies each. Then, on the 2nd, 4th, 6th, and 8th minutes, he combines the piles of 1+9, 2+8, 3+7, 4+6 respectively, and on the 3rd, 5th, 7th, and 9th minutes, he divides the pile of 10 candies he just received into two equal parts. By the 9th minute, he has 11 piles of 5 candies each.

Remark. There are other ways to get 11 piles of 5 candies. On the other hand, the number of piles on the table is always 10 or 11; from this, it is not hard to see that if the required result occurs, then there are exactly 11 piles of 5 candies each on the table.

Comment. Answer only - 0 points.

Any correct algorithm leading to the goal - 7 points.

question:
9.4. Let $p$ be a prime number greater than 3. Prove that there exists a natural number $y$, less than $p / 2$, such that the number $p y+1$ cannot be represented as the product of two integers, each greater than $y$.

(M. Antipov)
reference_solution:
Solution. Let $p=2k+1$. Assume the opposite: for each of the numbers $y=1,2, \ldots, k$ there exists a factorization $p y+1=a_{y} b_{y}$, where $a_{y}>y, b_{y}>y$. Note that each of the numbers $a_{y}$ and $b_{y}$ is strictly greater than 1, and that $a_{y} > p y + 1$. Therefore, each of the $p-1$ numbers in the set $a_{1}, b_{1}, a_{2}, b_{2}, \ldots a_{k}, b_{k}$ lies in the set of $p-2$ numbers
$\{2,3, \ldots, p-1\}$. Thus, there will be two equal numbers in this set. Let each of these two numbers be equal to $d$.

If these equal numbers have the same indices in the set, that is, $a_{y}=b_{y}=d$ for some $y$. Then $p y+1=d^{2}$, so the number $d^{2}-1=(d-1)(d+1)=p y$ is divisible by the prime $p$. Since $1 \leqslant d-1 < d+1 \leqslant p-1$, one of the numbers $d-1$ or $d+1$ is divisible by $p$. This is impossible because both $d-1$ and $d+1$ are greater than $k$. Contradiction (since $y \leqslant k$).

Otherwise, there exist indices $y_{1}<y_{2}$ such that $1 \leqslant y_{1}<y_{2}<d$, for which the numbers $p y_{1}+1$ and $p y_{2}+1$ are divisible by $d$. Then $p\left(y_{2}-y_{1}\right)=\left(p y_{2}+1\right)-\left(p y_{1}+1\right)$ is also divisible by $d$. From the coprimality of the numbers $d$ and $p$, we get that $y_{2}-y_{1}$ is divisible by $d$, which is impossible since $0<y_{2}-y_{1}<y_{2}<d$.

Thus, in each case, a contradiction is obtained, and therefore, the number $y$ specified in the problem statement always exists.

Comment. In the assumption of the opposite, it is only proven that there are two equal numbers in the set $a_{1}, b_{1}, a_{2}, b_{2}, \ldots a_{k}, b_{k}$ - 3 points.

In the assumption of the opposite, it is proven that there are two equal numbers in the set $a_{1}, b_{1}, a_{2}, b_{2}, \ldots a_{k}, b_{k}$, and the case $y_{1}<y_{2}$ (i.e., the case $y_{1}=y_{2}$ is missed or analyzed incorrectly) is reduced to a contradiction - 5 points.

In the assumption of the opposite, it is proven that there are two equal numbers in the set $a_{1}, b_{1}, a_{2}, b_{2}, \ldots a_{k}, b_{k}$, and the case $y_{1}=y_{2}$ (i.e., the case $y_{1}<y_{2}$ is missed or analyzed incorrectly) is reduced to a contradiction - 5 points.

question:
11.2 About numbers \(a\) and \(b\) it is known that the system of equations

\[
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
y=x^{2}+a x+b \\
x=y^{2}+a y+b
\end{array}\right.
\]

has a unique solution. Prove that \(a^{2}=2(a+2 b)-1\).
reference_solution:
Solution 1: Note that if $(x, y)$ is a solution to the system, then $(y, x)$ is also a solution. Since solutions with unequal $x$ and $y$ are paired, the system has a solution with $x=y$, and there is exactly one such solution. Then the quadratic equation $x=x^{2}+a x+b$ has one solution. Therefore, its discriminant $(a-1)^{2}-4 b$ is zero. This is equivalent to the statement of the problem.

Solution 2: The graphs of the equations $y=x^{2}+a x+b$ and $x=y^{2}+a y+b$ are symmetric with respect to the line $x=y$. If the parabola $y=x^{2}+a x+b$ does not intersect the axis of symmetry, then the two graphs lie on opposite sides of it and do not intersect. If there are two points of intersection with the axis, then each of these points is also passed through by the second parabola, so the system has at least two solutions. Therefore, the parabola touches the line, and the equation $x=x^{2}+a x+b$ has one solution.

## Criteria:

- Proved that there are no solutions when $x \neq y$ - 2 points.

question: 11.5 The tangents to the circumcircle of triangle $A B C$ at points $A$ and $C$ intersect at point $T$. The rays $A B$ and $T C$ intersect at point $S$. It is known that the areas of triangles $\triangle A C T, \triangle A B C$ and $\triangle B C S$ are equal. Prove that triangle $\triangle A B C$ is a right triangle.
reference_solution:
Solution: First, note that points $B$ and $T$ must lie on opposite sides of line $A C$, otherwise $S(\triangle A B C) < S(\triangle A C T)$. Triangles $\triangle A B C$ and $\triangle B C S$ have a common height, so the equality $S(\triangle A B C) = S(\triangle B C S)$ means that $A B = S B$ (1 point). Triangles $\triangle A B C$ and $\triangle A C T$ have a common base, so the equality of their areas means that points $B$ and $T$ are equidistant from line $A C$. Together with the fact that $A B = B S$, this means that point $S$ is twice as far from $A C$ as $T$ (1 point). This implies that $S C = 2 C T$ (1 point). Additionally, $C T = A T$ as segments of tangents from the same point. Since $S C$ is a tangent to the circumscribed circle, $S C^2 = S B \cdot S A$. Let $C T = 1$, then from the above relations we get $A T = 1, S T = S C + C T = 3, 4 = S C^2 = S B \cdot S A = \frac{S A}{2} \cdot S A$, from which $S A = 2 \sqrt{2}$ (1 point). Therefore, in $\triangle A B C$, $A T^2 + A S^2 = T S^2$, which means it is a right triangle by the converse of the Pythagorean theorem: $\angle S A T = 90^{\circ}$. It remains to note that $\angle S A T = \angle B A C + \angle A B C$, i.e., $\angle A C B = 90^{\circ}$.

## Criteria:

- If it is not stated that points $B$ and $T$ must lie on opposite sides of line $A C$ - 1 point is deducted;
- 1 point for proving each of the facts marked in the solution.

question: 9.1. In the country, some pairs of cities are connected by one-way direct flights (there is no more than one flight between any two cities). We say that city $A$ is accessible from city $B$ if it is possible to fly from $B$ to $A$, possibly with layovers. It is known that for any two cities $P$ and $Q$, there exists a city $R$ such that both $P$ and $Q$ are accessible from $R$. Prove that there exists a city from which all cities in the country are accessible. (It is assumed that it is possible to fly from a city to itself.) (V. Dolnikov)
reference_solution:
First solution. Let us renumber all cities in the country as $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}$. By the condition, there exists a city $B_{2}$, from which cities $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$ are accessible. Next, cities $A_{3}$ and $B_{2}$ are accessible from some city $B_{3}$. Since $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$ are accessible from $B_{2}$, they are also accessible from $B_{3}$. Continuing such reasoning, we will eventually get that there exists a city $B_{n}$, from which cities $A_{n}$ and $B_{n-1}$ are accessible. Then for $B_{n}$, cities $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n-1}$ will also be accessible, as they can be reached with a layover in $B_{n-1}$.

Second solution. Consider a city $A$, for which the maximum number of cities are accessible (if there are several such cities - any one of them). Suppose that some city $B$ is not accessible from $A$. Then by the condition, there exists a city $C$, from which both $A$ and $B$ are accessible. But then for $C$, $B$ is accessible, as well as all cities accessible from $A$. This contradicts the choice of $A$; hence, all cities are accessible from $A$.

question:
9.4. Does there exist an infinite increasing sequence $a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots$ of natural numbers such that the sum of any two 
distinct terms of the sequence is coprime with the sum of any three distinct terms of the sequence?

(S. Berlov)
reference_solution:
Answer. Yes, it exists.

Solution. We will construct an example of such a sequence. Let $a_{1}=1, a_{2}=7, a_{n+1}=\left(3 a_{n}\right)!+1$. To show that it meets the requirements, we need to strengthen these requirements somewhat. We will say that a pair (triple) of numbers is good if all its elements, different from one, are distinct (while one can appear in it several times). We will prove the following statement, from which it will follow that the constructed sequence is the required one.

Let $\left(a_{i}, a_{j}\right)$ and $\left(a_{p}, a_{q}, a_{r}\right)$ be a good pair and a good triple of elements of the sequence. Then

$$
\text { GCD }\left(a_{i}+a_{j}, a_{p}+a_{q}+a_{r}\right)=\text { GCD }\left(a_{i}+a_{j}, a_{p}+a_{q}-a_{r}\right)=1
$$

We will prove this by induction on the largest index $m$ among $i, j, p, q$ and $r$. If $m=1$, the statement is trivial. For the transition, assume that $m>1$. The number $a_{m}$ lies either only in the pair $\left(a_{i}, a_{j}\right)$, or only in the triple $\left(a_{p}, a_{q}, a_{r}\right)$, or in both.

Case 1. Suppose $a_{m}$ is only an element of the pair; say, $a_{m}=$ $=a_{j}$. Then, since $0<\left|a_{p}+a_{q} \pm a_{r}\right| \leqslant 3 a_{m-1}$, the number $a_{m}-1=$ $=\left(3 a_{m-1}\right)!$ divides $a_{p}+a_{q} \pm a_{r}$, so GCD $\left(a_{i}+a_{m}, a_{p}+\right.$ $\left.+a_{q} \pm a_{r}\right)=$ GCD $\left(\left(a_{i}+1\right)+\left(a_{m}-1\right), a_{p}+a_{q} \pm a_{r}\right)=$ GCD $\left(a_{i}+\right.$ $\left.+a_{1}, a_{p}+a_{q} \pm a_{r}\right)=1$ by the induction hypothesis.

Case 2. Suppose $a_{m}$ is only an element of the triple; say, $a_{m}=$ $=a_{q}$. Similarly, $a_{m}-1$ divides $a_{i}+a_{j}$, so GCD $\left(a_{i}+\right.$ $\left.+a_{j}, a_{p}+a_{m} \pm a_{r}\right)=$ GCD $\left(a_{i}+a_{j}, a_{p}+a_{1} \pm a_{r}\right)=1$ by the induction hypothesis.

Case 3. Suppose $a_{m}$ is an element of both the pair and the triple; say, $a_{m}=a_{j}=a_{q}$. Then $a_{m}-1$ divides $a_{p}-a_{i} \pm a_{r}$, so GCD $\left(a_{i}+a_{m}, a_{p}+a_{m} \pm a_{r}\right)=$ GCD $\left(a_{i}+a_{m},\left(a_{p}+a_{m} \pm a_{r}\right)-\left(a_{i}+\right.\right.$ $\left.\left.+a_{m}\right)\right)=$ GCD $\left(a_{i}+a_{m}, a_{p}-a_{i} \pm a_{r}\right)=$ GCD $\left(a_{i}+a_{1}, a_{p}-a_{i} \pm a_{r}\right)=1$ by the induction hypothesis. The transition of induction is proved.

question: 4. In an equilateral triangle $A B C$, points $N, T$, and $F$ are chosen on sides $A C, A B$, and $B C$ respectively, such that $A N=T B$ and $C F=F B$. Prove that the area of quadrilateral $T A N F$ is half the area of triangle $A B C$.
reference_solution:
The first solution. The area of triangle $ABC$ is equal to the sum of the areas of triangles $CNF$ and $FTB$ and quadrilateral $TANF$. We will prove that $S_{\triangle CNF} + S_{\triangle FTB} = \frac{1}{2} S_{\triangle ABC}$, from which it will immediately follow that the area of $TANF$ is the remaining half.

Let the side of triangle $ABC$ be $a$, and $NA$ be $b$. Then $CF = FB = \frac{1}{2} a$, and $CN = b - a$. Note immediately that $S_{\triangle ABC} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} a^2$.

$S_{\triangle CNF} + S_{\triangle FTB} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot CN \cdot CF \cdot \sin 60^\circ + \frac{1}{2} \cdot BT \cdot BF \cdot \sin 60^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{8} (a - b) a + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{8} b a = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{8} a^2$, which is half the area of triangle $ABC$.

The second solution. Triangles $CFA$ and $BFA$ are equal (for example, by two sides and the angle between them: $CF = FB$ by the condition, $AC = AB$, and $\angle ACF = \angle ABF = 60^\circ$, since triangle $ABC$ is equilateral). From this, it follows that the area of triangle $ABF$ is half the area of triangle $ABC$. Also, from the equality $\triangle CFA = \triangle BFA$, it follows that the heights of triangles $CFA$ and $BFA$ from point $F$ are equal. But these heights are also heights of triangles $NAF$ and $FTB$, and since $AN = TB$, the areas of triangles $NAF$ and $FTB$ are equal. It remains to note that $S_{\text{TANF}} = S_{\triangle NAF} + S_{\triangle ATF} = S_{\triangle FTB} + S_{\triangle ATF} = S_{\triangle ABF} = \frac{1}{2} S_{\triangle ABC}$.

Remark. Points are not deducted if the following facts are used without proof. The median $AF$ is the bisector and altitude in triangle $ABC$. $AF = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} AB$, $S_{\triangle ABF} = \frac{1}{2} S_{\triangle ABC}$, $\triangle CFA = \triangle BFA$.

Comment. If the proof uses the equality of the heights of triangles $NAF$ and $FTB$, but the proof of this fact is not provided (and the rest of the proof is correct) - 5 points.

question: 5. Non-zero real numbers $x, y, z$ and $t$ are such that $x+y+z+t=0$ and $\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}+$ $\frac{1}{z}+\frac{1}{t}=0$. Prove that among the numbers $x, y, z$ and $t$, two numbers can be chosen with a zero sum.
reference_solution:
Solution. Suppose that the sum of any two of the given numbers is not zero and arrive at a contradiction. From the first equality, it follows that $z+t=-(x+y)$. Since $\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{z}+\frac{1}{t}=0$, then $\frac{x+y}{x y}+\frac{t+z}{z t}=0$, which means $(x+y)\left(\frac{1}{x y}-\frac{1}{z t}\right)=0$. Given the assumption $x+y \neq 0$, it follows that $\frac{1}{x y}-\frac{1}{z t}=0, \frac{1}{x y}=\frac{1}{z t}, x y=z t$. Similarly, we obtain that $x z=y t$ and $x t=y z$.

If we add the equations $x y=z t$ and $x z=y t$, we get $x(y+z)=t(y+z)$. Given the assumption $y+z \neq 0$, it follows that $x=t$. By adding the equations $x y=z t$ and $x t=y z$ and conducting similar reasoning, we get that $x=z$. Finally, from the last possible variant, we get that $x=y$. Since $x+y+z+t=0$, then $4 x=0, x=0$, which contradicts the condition. Therefore, our initial assumption is false, meaning there will be two numbers with a zero sum.

$(x+y) f(x ; y ; s ; t)=0$ is obtained, but the subsequent solution is not correct: for example, only on the basis of this equality, it is concluded that $x+y=0-2$ points.

question:
10.1. On the coordinate plane, the graphs of two reduced quadratic trinomials and two non-parallel lines $\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}$ are drawn. It is known that the segments cut off by the graphs on $\ell_{1}$ are equal, and the segments cut off by the graphs on $\ell_{2}$ are also equal. Prove that the graphs of the trinomials coincide.

(A. S. Galkin)
reference_solution:
The first solution. Let $f_{1}(x)$ and $f_{2}(x)$ be the given reduced quadratic trinomials, and let $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$ be their graphs. Then there exists a unique vector $\vec{a}$ such that when the parabola $\Gamma_{1}$ is translated by this vector, it transforms into $\Gamma_{2}$ (the vector $\vec{a}$ connects the vertices of the parabolas).

Let the line $\ell_{1}$ intersect $\Gamma_{1}$ at points $A_{1}$ and $B_{1}$, and $\Gamma_{2}$ at points $A_{2}$ and $B_{2}$ such that $\overrightarrow{A_{1} B_{1}}=\overrightarrow{A_{2} B_{2}}$. When the parabola $\Gamma_{1}$ is translated by the vector $\overrightarrow{A_{1} A_{2}}$, the resulting parabola $\Gamma_{3}$ is the graph of the reduced trinomial $f_{3}(x)$, which intersects $\ell_{1}$ at the same points as $\Gamma_{2}$. Then the difference $f_{2}(x)-f_{3}(x)$ has at least two roots (the abscissas of points $A_{2}$ and $B_{2}$). However, since the degree of the polynomial $f_{2}(x)-f_{3}(x)$ is no higher than 1, we have $\underline{f_{2}(x)}-f_{3}(x) \equiv 0$, that is, $\Gamma_{3}=\Gamma_{2}$. Therefore, the translation vector $\vec{a}=\overrightarrow{A_{1} A_{2}}$ is parallel to the line $\ell_{1}$.

Similarly, $\vec{a} \| \ell_{2}$, thus $\vec{a}=\overrightarrow{0}$ and $\Gamma_{1}=\Gamma_{2}$.

The second solution. Let $f_{1}(x)=x^{2}+p_{1} x+q_{1}$ and $f_{2}(x)=x^{2}+p_{2} x+q_{2}$ be the given quadratic trinomials, $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$ be their graphs, and $y=k_{1} x+b_{1}$ and $y=k_{2} x+b_{2}$ be the equations of the lines $\ell_{1}$ and $\ell_{2}$ respectively.

Note that the length of the segment cut by the parabola $y=x^{2}+p x+q$ on the line $y=k x+b$ is the absolute value of the difference of the roots of the equation $x^{2}+p x+q=k x+b$, divided by the cosine of the angle of inclination of the line $y=k x+b$. The absolute value of the difference of the roots of a reduced quadratic trinomial is the square root of its discriminant. Therefore, the condition that $\Gamma_{1}$ and $\Gamma_{2}$ cut equal segments on $\ell_{1}$ is written as

$$
\left(p_{1}-k_{1}\right)^{2}-4\left(q_{1}-b_{1}\right)=\left(p_{2}-k_{1}\right)^{2}-4\left(q_{2}-b_{1}\right)
$$

Transforming this equality, we get $\left(p_{1}-p_{2}\right)\left(p_{1}+p_{2}-2 k_{1}\right)=4\left(q_{1}-q_{2}\right)$. If $p_{1}=p_{2}$, then $q_{1}=q_{2}$ and the problem is solved. Otherwise,

$$
k_{1}=\frac{p_{1}+p_{2}}{2}-\frac{2\left(q_{1}-q_{2}\right)}{p_{1}-p_{2}}
$$

The same reasoning can be applied to the line $\ell_{2}$. Therefore, if the parabolas do not coincide, then $k_{1}=k_{2}$, that is, $\ell_{1} \| \ell_{2}$, which is impossible by the condition.

question:
10.4. On a board, there are $n$ positive numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ written in a row. Vasya wants to write a number $b_{i} \geqslant a_{i}$ under each number $a_{i}$ such that for any two of the numbers $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$, the ratio of one to the other is an integer. Prove that Vasya can write the required numbers so that the inequality $b_{1} b_{2} \ldots b_{n} \leqslant 2^{(n-1) / 2} a_{1} a_{2} \ldots a_{n}$ holds.

(F. Petrov)
reference_solution:
Solution. We will prove that there exist even numbers $b_{1}, b_{2}$, $\ldots, b_{n}$, satisfying the following (stronger) conditions:

(1) $b_{i} \geqslant a_{i}$ for all $i \leqslant n$

(2) $b_{1} b_{2} \ldots b_{n} \leqslant 2^{(n-1) / 2} a_{1} a_{2} \ldots a_{n}$

(3) the ratio of any two of the numbers $b_{i}$ is a power of two (with an integer exponent).

Note that the statement to be proved will not change if some of the numbers $a_{k}$ (and the corresponding $b_{k}$) are multiplied by some power of two. Multiply each of the numbers $a_{k}$ by a power of two so that all the resulting numbers lie in the interval $[1,2)$.

Without loss of generality, we can assume that $1 \leqslant a_{1} \leqslant a_{2} \leqslant \leqslant \ldots \leqslant a_{n}a_{k}$, each of the sequences satisfies (1). Moreover, each of the sequences obviously satisfies (3). It remains to show that at least one of them satisfies (2).

For this, note that the product of all $n^{2}$ numbers in all

## $n$ sequences is

$$
2^{(n-1)+(n-2)+\ldots+0} \cdot a_{1}^{n} a_{2}^{n} \ldots a_{n}^{n}=\left(2^{(n-1) / 2} a_{1} a_{2} \ldots a_{n}\right)^{n}
$$

Therefore, the product of the numbers in at least one of the sequences does not exceed $2^{(n-1) / 2} a_{1} a_{2} \ldots a_{n}$, which is what we needed to prove.

question:
5. (7 points) Prove that the expression $5 x^{2}+5 y^{2}+5 z^{2}+6 x y-8 x z-8 y z$ is positive, provided that $x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}$ does not equal zero.

#
reference_solution:
# Solution.

Factor out the multiplier 5: $5\left(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}+\frac{6}{5} x y-\frac{8}{5} x z-\frac{8}{5} y z\right)$.

Estimate the sign of the expression in parentheses. For this, we complete the square for the variable $x$, and then for the variable $y$:

$x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}+\frac{6}{5} x y-\frac{8}{5} x z-\frac{8}{5} y z=x^{2}+2 x\left(\frac{3}{5} y-\frac{4}{5} z\right)+\left(z^{2}-\frac{8}{5} y z+y^{2}\right)=$

$$
\begin{gathered}
=\left(x^{2}+2 x\left(\frac{3}{5} y-\frac{4}{5} z\right)+\left(\frac{3}{5} y-\frac{4}{5} z\right)^{2}\right)+\left(z^{2}-\frac{8}{5} y z+y^{2}-\left(\frac{3}{5} y-\frac{4}{5} z\right)^{2}\right)= \\
=\left(x+\frac{3}{5} y-\frac{4}{5} z\right)^{2}+\frac{16}{25} y^{2}-\frac{16}{25} y z+\frac{9}{25} z^{2}= \\
=\left(x+\frac{3}{5} y-\frac{4}{5} z\right)^{2}+\frac{16}{25}\left(y-\frac{z}{2}\right)^{2}-\frac{4}{25} z^{2}+\frac{9}{25} z^{2}= \\
=\left(x+\frac{3}{5} y-\frac{4}{5} z\right)^{2}+\frac{16}{25}\left(y-\frac{z}{2}\right)^{2}+\frac{z^{2}}{5}
\end{gathered}
$$

This expression is a sum of squares. Therefore, it is non-negative. We need to exclude the possibility of this expression being zero. This is possible if each square is zero:

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{z^{2}}{5}=0, \text { that is } z=0 \\
\left(y-\frac{z}{2}\right)^{2}=0, \text { given } z=0, \text { we get } y=0 \\
\left(x+\frac{3}{5} y-\frac{4}{5} z\right)^{2}=0, \text { since } z=0, y=0, \text { we have } x=0
\end{gathered}
$$

But by the condition $x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}$ does not equal zero, so we exclude the possibility of the original expression being zero.

Thus, the expression $5 x^{2}+5 y^{2}+5 z^{2}+6 x y-8 x z-8 y z$ is positive.

Q.E.D.

question: 2. The sum of two integers is $S$. Masha multiplied the left number by an integer $a$, the right number by an integer $b$, added these products, and found that the resulting sum is divisible by $S$. Alyosha, on the contrary, multiplied the left number by $b$, and the right number by $a$. Prove that his analogous sum will also be divisible by $S$.
reference_solution:
Solution. Let $x$ be the left number and $y$ be the right number; according to the condition: $x+y=S$.. Then Masha got the number $a x+b y$, and Alyosha got the number $b x+a y$. The sum of these numbers is $a x+b y+b x+a y=(a+b)(x+y)=(a+b) S$, which means it is divisible by $S$. Since one of the two addends (Masha's number) is divisible by $S$, the other (Alyosha's number) is also divisible by $S$, as required.

question:
9.5. The numbers $b>0$ and $a$ are such that the quadratic trinomial $x^{2}+a x+b$ has two distinct roots, exactly one of which lies in the interval $[-1 ; 1]$. Prove that exactly one of these roots lies in the interval $(-b ; b)$.

(A. Khryabrov)
reference_solution:
First solution. Let $f(x)=x^{2}+a x+b$. If exactly one root lies on the interval $[-1,1]$, then the quadratic polynomial changes sign on this interval, that is,

$$
(1+a+b)(1-a+b)=f(1) f(-1) \leqslant 0
$$

Then

$0 \geqslant b^{2}(1+a+b)(1-a+b)=\left(b^{2}+a b+b\right)\left(b^{2}-a b+b\right)=f(b) f(-b)$. Therefore, there is a root on the interval $[-b, b]$, and if the inequality is strict, there is exactly one root (and it is not at the end of the interval). In the case of equality, one of the roots is $\pm b$, and the other is $\pm 1$, and $b>1$ (otherwise, there would be two roots on the interval $[-1,1]$). Then on the interval $(-b, b)$ there is exactly one root.

Second solution. Let $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ be the roots of the given quadratic polynomial, with $\left|x_{1}\right| \leqslant 1$ and $\left|x_{2}\right|>1$. By Vieta's theorem, we have $\left|x_{1}\right| \cdot\left|x_{2}\right|=b$. Then $\left|x_{2}\right|=b /\left|x_{1}\right| \geqslant b / 1=b$ and $\left|x_{1}\right|=b /\left|x_{2}\right|<b$. Thus, of the two roots, only $x_{1}$ lies in the interval $(-b ; b)$.

question:
9.7. Natural numbers $n>20$ and $k>1$ are such that $n$ is divisible by $k^{2}$. Prove that there exist natural numbers $a, b$, and $c$ such that $n=a b+b c+c a$.

(A. Khryabrov)
reference_solution:
Solution. Note that from the equality $n+a^{2}=(a+b)(a+c)$ follows the equality $n=a b+b c+c a$. Therefore, to solve the problem, it is sufficient to find a natural number $a$ such that the number $n+a^{2}$ can be factored into the product of two natural numbers $x$ and $y$, both greater than $a$ (then we can set $b=x-a$ and $c=y-a$). According to the condition, $n=\ell p^{2}$ for some prime $p$ and natural $\ell$.

If $\ell+1>p$, then due to the factorization $n+p^{2}=(\ell+1) \cdot p^{2}$, we can take $a=p$. Also, if the number $\ell+1$ is composite, then $\ell+1=s t$ for $s, t>1$; then again we can set $a=p$, since $n+p^{2}=(\ell+1) p^{2}=s p \cdot t p$.

In the remaining case, we have $n=(q-1) p^{2}$ for some prime $q \leqslant p$. If $p>q$, then $p=m q+r$ for some positive $r<q$; then $n+r^{2}=(q-1) p^{2}+r^{2}=(m q+r) r=(m r+1) \cdot q \cdot r$. Therefore, we can set $a=r$.

Finally, if $p=q$, then $n=p^{3}-p^{2}$, and $p \geqslant 5$ by the condition. Then $n+6^{2}=p^{3}-p^{2}+36=(p+3)\left(p^{2}-4 p+12\right)$, where both brackets are greater than 6; in this case, $a=6$ works.

Remark. It is not difficult to show that all natural numbers $n$ for which the number $n+1$ is composite can be represented in the form $a b+b c+c a$ - in particular, all odd numbers except 1. Using this observation and a calculator, it is not difficult to find the first 18 numbers that cannot be represented in the form $a b+b c+c a$ (all of them are less than five hundred). In the paper by Borwein and Choi, it is claimed that the number of numbers that cannot be represented in the form $a b+b c+c a$ is no more than 19, and the existence of the nineteenth such number would contradict the generalized Riemann hypothesis (which is currently neither proven nor disproven).

question: 9.8. A hundred sages were offered the following trial. They are brought into a hall one by one (in a predetermined order). In the hall, the warden offers the sage a choice of two different numbers from the set $1,2,3$. The sage chooses exactly one of them, reports the chosen number to the warden, and leaves the hall. Before making their choice, the sage has the right to ask the warden which number each of the two previous sages chose (the second sage has the right to know about the first). Any communication between the sages during the trial is prohibited. If at the end the sum of all 100 numbers chosen by the sages equals 200, the sages fail the trial; otherwise, they pass it. Prove that the sages can agree in advance on their actions so as to guarantee passing the trial. (S. Berlov)
reference_solution:
Solution. Let's present one of the possible agreements. Each sage will use one of two strategies: either choose the odd number (strategy H) from the two proposed numbers, or choose the larger of the two numbers (strategy B). They will choose them as follows:

(1) The first sage acts according to strategy B. The second sage acts according to strategy H if the first chose three, otherwise he uses strategy B.

(*) The $k$-th sage, for $3 \leqslant k \leqslant 99$, acts according to strategy H if the $(k-1)$-th sage chose three, and the $(k-2)$-th did not choose three; otherwise, he uses strategy B.

(100) The hundredth sage acts according to strategy B if the 99th chose three, and otherwise according to strategy H.

Let's analyze what will happen by the time the hundredth sage enters. We will write down the 99 numbers chosen by this moment in the order of their selection; let $S$ be their sum. If a one is written in the row, it was written according to strategy H, so immediately before it, a three was written, and immediately before this three, there cannot be another three. We will highlight these three and one in the written row. The highlighted pairs do not overlap, and the sum in each of them is 4. All other numbers in the row are either twos or threes.

Next, if there is a three among the unhighlighted numbers, consider the first such three. Either it stands at the end of the row (i.e., it was chosen by the 99th sage), or after it, there cannot be a one (otherwise it would be highlighted), nor a two (according to the algorithm (*)). Therefore, after our three, there can only be another three, and it is also not highlighted.

Thus, either all unhighlighted numbers are twos (and $S=198$), or there is exactly one three among them - the last one (and $S=199$), or there are at least two unhighlighted threes (and $S \geqslant 200$). In the latter case, the sages have already passed the test, because after the last sage's move, the sum will exceed 200.

Otherwise, we get that $S=198$ if the 99th sage did not name 3, and $S=199$ if he did. According to (100), in the first case, the sum of the 100 chosen numbers will be odd, and in the second case, it will be greater than 200. Therefore, in these cases, the test is also passed.

question:
9.6. Consider all 100-digit numbers divisible by 19. Prove that the number of such numbers that do not contain the digits 4, 5, and 6 is equal to the number of such numbers that do not contain the digits 1, 4, and 7.

(I. Efremov)
reference_solution:
Solution. To each remainder $a$ from division by 19, we associate a remainder $b(a)$ such that $b(a) \equiv 3a \pmod{19}$. Note that the remainders $0, 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 9$ are mapped to the remainders $0, 3, 6, 9, 2, 5, 8$ respectively. Moreover, from the remainder $b$, the remainder $a = a(b) \equiv -6b \pmod{19}$ can be restored such that $a(b(a)) \equiv -18a \equiv a \pmod{19}$ and $b(a(b)) = b$ (for similar reasons).

Now, let $\mathcal{A}$ be the set of numbers from the condition that do not contain the digits $4, 5, 6$, and let $\mathcal{B}$ be the set of such numbers that do not contain $1, 4, 7$. To each number $A = \overline{a_{99} a_{98} \ldots a_{0}} \in \mathcal{A}$, we associate the number $B = \overline{b(a_{99}) b(a_{98}) \ldots b(a_{0})}$. Note that $b(a_i)$ is a digit (and $b(a_{99}) \neq 0$), so we get a 100-digit number. Moreover,

\[
\begin{aligned}
& B = b_{0} + 10b_{1} + \ldots + 10^{99}b_{99} \equiv \\
& \equiv 3(a_{0} + 10a_{1} + \ldots + 10^{99}a_{99}) = 3A \quad \pmod{19}
\end{aligned}
\]

so $B$ is divisible by 19 and $B \in \mathcal{B}$. Since different numbers from $\mathcal{A}$ correspond to different numbers from $\mathcal{B}$, the number of numbers in $\mathcal{B}$ is not less than in $\mathcal{A}$.

Finally, to each number $B = \overline{b_{99} b_{98} \ldots b_{0}} \in \mathcal{B}$, there corresponds a number $A = \overline{a(b_{99}) a(b_{98}) \ldots a(b_{0})}$, which, for similar reasons, lies in $\mathcal{A}$. Therefore, the number of numbers in $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ are equal.

Comment. An incompletely described correspondence between numbers - 0 points.

An incomplete solution by induction - 0 points.

A correspondence between allowed (forbidden) digits using multiplication modulo $19$ - 1 point.

Using multiplication modulo 19 to construct a mapping from some set of 100-digit numbers, not covering all allowed numbers - 2 points.

Not verifying that the correspondence preserves divisibility by $19$ - 1 point is deducted.

question: 9.7. Given a trapezoid $A B C D$, where $A D \| B C$, and rays $A B$ and $D C$ intersect at point $G$. The common external tangents to the circumcircles of triangles $A B C$ and $A C D$ intersect at point $E$. The common external tangents to the circumcircles of triangles $A B D$ and $B C D$ intersect at point $F$. Prove that points $E, F$, and $G$ lie on the same line.
reference_solution:
Solution. Let the line $E C$ intersect the circle $(A B C)$ again at point $X$, and the line $E A$ intersect the circle $(A C D)$ again at point $Y$ (we will consider the arrangement of points as shown in Fig. 2; other cases are treated similarly).

Consider the homothety with center $E$ that maps $(A B C)$ to $(A C D)$. Under this homothety, point $X$ maps to $C$, and point $A$ maps to $Y$. Therefore, $A X \| Y C$ and $\angle A E C = \angle A Y C - \angle E C Y = \angle A Y C - \angle A X C$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_3533b1d4c3f264e872ebg-3.jpg?height=723&width=733&top_left_y=860&top_left_x=380)

Fig. 2

But $\angle A X C = 180^{\circ} - \angle A B C$ and $\angle A Y C = 180^{\circ} - \angle A D C$. Thus, $\angle A E C = \angle A B C - \angle A D C = \angle A B C - \angle B C G = \angle B G C$. From this equality, it follows that points $A, C, E, G$ lie on the same circle.

Since point $E$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $A C$ (i.e., on the axis of symmetry of the circles $(A B C)$ and $(A C D)$), it is the midpoint of the arc $A G C$ of the circle $(A C E G)$. Therefore, $E$ lies on the external bisector of angle $B G C$.

Similarly, it can be shown that $F$ also lies on the external bisector of angle $B G C$.

Remark. The problem has the following generalization. Let $A B C D$ be a quadrilateral, $G = A B \cap C D$, and $M$ be the second point of intersection of the circles $(A D G)$ and $(B C G)$ (i.e., the Miquel point of this quadrilateral). Let $E$ be the center of homothety with a positive coefficient that maps $(A B C)$ to $(A D C)$. Then points $A, C, M, E$ lie on the same circle, and $E$ is the midpoint of the arc $A C$ (i.e., $M E$ is the bisector of the angle between $A M$ and $C M$).

This can be proven similarly to the solution of the problem: we have (in directed angles) $\angle A E C = \angle A B C + \angle A D C = \angle G B C + \angle A M G = \angle G M C + \angle A M G = \angle A M C$.

Comment. Results about the configuration of the centers of circles and the positions of $E$ and $F$ relative to them (e.g., directions $O_{i} O_{j}$, similarity of the configuration of centers and $A B C D, A E = E C, E O_{1} / E O_{2} = r_{1} / r_{2}$, projections of $E O_{1}$ and $F O_{2}$ on $A D$ are equal, and equivalent advancements) do not add points.

Considering homotheties, compositions of homotheties, applications of the theorem about caps (without further advancement) do not add points.

It is shown that the ratios of the radii of the circles in pairs are equal (and equal to the ratio of the lateral sides) - 1 point.

Let $B A^{\prime} D^{\prime} C$ be the image of $A B C D$ under the homothety with center $G$. The problem is reduced to the fact that the centers of homothety of the pairs of circles $(A B C), (D^{\prime} B C)$ and $(D B C), (A^{\prime} B C)$ coincide - 1 point.

question:
# Task 8.4

Inside an acute angle, there is a convex quadrilateral $\mathrm{ABCD}$. It turns out that for each of the two lines containing the sides of the angle, the following condition is met: the sum of the distances from vertices A and C to this line is equal to the sum of the distances from vertices B and D to the same line. Prove that ABCD is a parallelogram.

## Number of points 7

#
reference_solution:
# Solution

Let the line $\mathrm{m}$ contain one of the sides of the given angle, and let $a$ and $c$ be the distances from vertices $A$ and $C$ to $\mathrm{m}$, and $P$ be the midpoint of segment $\mathrm{AC}$. Then the distance from $P$ to $\mathrm{m}$ is $(a + c) / 2$ (the midline of the trapezoid, see the figure).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_7041d088f4273961b51ag-2.jpg?height=240&width=388&top_left_y=2256&top_left_x=183)

Similarly, if $Q$ is the midpoint of segment $BD$, and $b$ and $d$ are the distances from vertices $B$ and $D$ to $\mathrm{m}$, then the distance from $Q$ to $\mathrm{m}$ is $(b + d) / 2$.

By the given condition, $a + c = b + d$, so points $P$ and $Q$ are equidistant from line $\mathrm{m}$. Conducting a similar reasoning for line $n$, which contains the other side of the given angle, we get that $P$ and $Q$ are equidistant from line $n$. The geometric locus of points that are at a given distance from a given line is a pair of lines parallel to the given line. According to the above proof, points $P$ and $Q$ belong to both geometric loci (for line $\mathrm{m}$ and for line $\mathrm{n}$), meaning they belong to their intersection. However, within the angle, only two lines intersect, one from each geometric locus, so points $P$ and $Q$ coincide. Thus, the diagonals $\mathrm{AC}$ and $\mathrm{BD}$ of the given quadrilateral intersect at their common midpoint, meaning that $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.

question: 7.2. Petya, Kolya, and Vasya were collecting mushrooms. Petya said that he found 7 fewer mushrooms than Kolya and Vasya combined, and Kolya said that he found 10 fewer mushrooms than Petya and Vasya combined. Prove that one of the boys was mistaken.
reference_solution:
First solution. Suppose that none of the boys made a mistake. Since Petya found 7 fewer mushrooms on an odd number than Kolya and Vasya found together, the number of mushrooms collected by Petya and the number of mushrooms collected by Kolya and Vasya together are of different parity. Therefore, the total number of collected mushrooms is odd. Similarly, we conclude that the number of mushrooms collected by Kolya and the number of mushrooms collected by Petya and Vasya together are of the same parity. Therefore, the total number of collected mushrooms is even. Contradiction.

Second solution. Let Petya find $p$ mushrooms, Vasya $-v$ mushrooms, and Kolya $-k$ mushrooms. Then the equations $p=k+v-7, k=p+v-10$ hold. Adding these equations, we get $2v=17$, which is impossible.

Comment. In the assumption of the contrary, it is only proven that the total number of mushrooms is even - 3 points.

In the assumption of the contrary, it is only proven that the total number of mushrooms is odd - 3 points.

question: 5. Four numbers are written on the board, none of which are equal to 0. If each of them is multiplied by the sum of the other three, the result is four identical values. Prove that the squares of the numbers written on the board are equal.
reference_solution: 5. Let the numbers $a, b, c$ and $d$ be given. By the condition $a(b+c+d)=b(a+c+d)$, we get $(a-b)(c+d)=0$. Similarly, from the equality $c(a+b+d)=d(a+b+c)$, we obtain $(c-d)(a+b)=0$. Since either $c+d$ or $c-d$ is not equal to 0, then either $a=b$ or $a=-b$. In both cases, the squares of the numbers $a$ and $b$ are equal, from which, due to the arbitrariness of the choice of $a$ and $b$, the statement of the problem follows.

question: 3. In a volleyball tournament, 6 teams participated. Prove that after one round of games (each team played with each other exactly once), there will be a team that won at least $3$ games (there are no draws in volleyball).
reference_solution: 3. Six teams played a total of $6 * 5 / 2 = 15$ games. The number of games matches the sum of the number of wins by each team. But if each team won fewer than three games, then the total number of games does not exceed $2 * 6 = 12$. Contradiction.

question: 11.3. On the sides $AB$, $BC$, and $CA$ of triangle $ABC$, points $M$, $N$, and $P$ were marked, respectively. It turned out that the areas of all four triangles $BMN$, $CNP$, $APM$, and $MNP$ are equal. Is it true that points $M$, $N$, and $P$ must be the midpoints of the corresponding sides of the triangle? Justify your answer.
reference_solution:
Solution: Let the sides of the triangle be denoted as $a = BC$, $b = AC$, and $c = AB$. Then, for some numbers $x, y, z$ from the interval $[0; 1]$, the following relationships hold: $BM = xc$, $MA = (1-x)c$, $AP = zb$, $PC = (1-z)b$, $CN = ya$, $NB = (1-y)a$ - see the figure.

Given that $S_{MBN} = \frac{1}{4} S_{ABC}$. Since $\frac{S_{MBN}}{S_{ABC}} = \frac{MB \cdot NB}{AB \cdot CB}$, it follows that $4x(1-y) = 1$. Similarly, we obtain the equations $4y(1-z) = 1$ and $4z(1-x) = 1$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_c5135f02f0293a986456g-6.jpg?height=368&width=914&top_left_y=130&top_left_x=571)

To the solution of problem 11.3

It remains to solve the system of the three obtained equations. This can be done in various ways, for example, as follows. Let's make the substitution $x = \sin^2 \alpha$, $y = \sin^2 \beta$, $z = \sin^2 \gamma$ for some numbers $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ from the interval $\left[0; \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$. (This is a valid substitution since $x, y, z \in [0; 1]$). Then the system will take the form

\[
\left\{
\begin{array}{l}
4 \sin^2 \alpha \cos^2 \beta = 1 \\
4 \sin^2 \beta \cos^2 \gamma = 1 \\
4 \sin^2 \gamma \cos^2 \alpha = 1
\end{array}
\right.
\]

Multiplying the left and right parts of all three equations and using the double-angle sine formula, we get the equality $\sin^2 2\alpha \cdot \sin^2 2\beta \cdot \sin^2 2\gamma = 1$. Since each of the factors does not exceed one, it follows that $\sin^2 2\alpha = \sin^2 2\beta = \sin^2 2\gamma = 1$. Considering that the numbers $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ lie in the interval $\left[0; \frac{\pi}{2}\right]$, we obtain the equality $\alpha = \beta = \gamma = \frac{\pi}{4}$. Therefore, $x = y = z = \frac{1}{2}$, which means that points $M, N, P$ are the midpoints of the sides of triangle $ABC$.

Answer: They must be.

question: 4. The bisector of angle $B A C$ of square $A B C D$ intersects side $B C$ at point $M$. Prove that $A C=A B+B M$.
reference_solution:
Solution. First method. Drop a perpendicular $M H$ from point $M$ to the diagonal $A C$ (see fig.). Then triangles $A B M$ and $A M H$ are equal (right triangles with a common hypotenuse and equal acute angles). We get $A H=A B=B C, M H=B M$. Triangle $H M C$ is isosceles (as a right triangle with an acute angle of $45^{\circ}$), hence $H C=H M=B M$. Then $A C=A H+H C=A B+B M$, which is what we need to prove.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_0643986526eb2c1054f2g-2.jpg?height=471&width=482&top_left_y=458&top_left_x=293)

Second method. On the extension of side $C D$ beyond point $D$, mark point $F$ such that $D F=B M$ (see fig.). Then triangles $A D F$ and $A B M$ are equal by two legs, so $\angle B A M=\angle D A F=22.5^{\circ}$, and $\angle A F D=90^{\circ}-\angle D A F=67.5^{\circ}$. Since $\angle C A F=\angle C A D+\angle D A F=45^{\circ}+22.5^{\circ}=67.5^{\circ}=\angle A F C$, triangle $A F C$ is isosceles and $A C=C F=C D+D F=A B+B M$, which is what we need to prove.

question: 3. (7 points) Prove that if the sides of a right triangle form an arithmetic progression, then its common difference is equal to the radius of the inscribed circle.
reference_solution:
Solution. Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be the sides of a right triangle, where $b=a+d, c=a+2d$.

Then on one hand, $c^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}=2a^{2}+2ad+d^{2}$.

On the other hand, $c^{2}=(a+2d)^{2}=a^{2}+4ad+4d^{2}$.

We obtain that $2a^{2}+2ad+d^{2}=a^{2}+4ad+4d^{2}, a^{2}-2ad-3d^{2}=0$.

Solving the quadratic equation for $a$, we get: $a=3d, b=4d, c=5d$. $r=\frac{S}{p}=\frac{S}{\frac{a+b+c}{2}}=\frac{ab}{a+b+c}=\frac{12d^{2}}{12d}=d$.

$$

S_{A M B}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot A B \cdot M H_{1}=\frac{1}{2} \cdot A B \cdot M C_{1} \cdot \cos \alpha
\end{gathered}
$$

We get that $\frac{S_{A B C}}{S_{A M B}}=\frac{C C_{1}}{M C_{1}}$.

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{C C_{1}}{M C_{1}}=\frac{S_{A B C}}{S_{A M B}}=\frac{S_{A M B}+S_{A C M}+S_{B C M}}{S_{A M B}}=1+\frac{S_{A C M}+S_{B C M}}{S_{A M B}} \\
\frac{S_{A C M}+S_{B C M}}{S_{A M B}}=\frac{C C_{1}}{M C_{1}}-1=\frac{C C_{1}-M C_{1}}{M C_{1}}=\frac{C M}{C_{1} M}

question:
9.5. Different real numbers $a$ and $b$ are such that the equation

$$
\left(x^{2}+20 a x+10 b\right)\left(x^{2}+20 b x+10 a\right)=0
$$

has no roots. Prove that the number $20(b-a)$ is not an integer.

(P. Kozlov)
reference_solution:
9.5. Suppose the opposite. Let, for definiteness, $b>a$; then $20(b-a) \geqslant 1$, that is, $b-a \geqslant \frac{1}{20}$.

The discriminant of the second quadratic polynomial in the original equation is negative, hence $100 b^{2}-10 a<0$. Therefore, $10 b^{2}<a \leqslant b-\frac{1}{20}$, which means $10 b^{2}-b+\frac{1}{20}<0$. But this is impossible, since the discriminant of the quadratic polynomial $f(b)=10 b^{2}-b+\frac{1}{20}$ is also negative, and the leading coefficient is positive.

question:
9.8. In an acute-angled triangle $A B C$, the median $A M$ is longer than the side $A B$. Prove that triangle $A B C$ can be cut into three parts from which a rhombus can be formed.

(S. Volchenkov)
reference_solution:
9.8. Let $N$ be the midpoint of side $AC$, and $K$ be a point on the line $MN$ such that $MK = MN$. Then triangles $MNC$ and $MKB$ are symmetric with respect to $M$ and therefore equal. We make a cut along the midline $MN$; by flipping triangle $MNC$ so that it coincides with $\triangle MKB$, we obtain parallelogram $ANKB$ (see Fig. 1). If $AN = AB$, then the rhombus is already obtained.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_1695894156295afed8e4g-1.jpg?height=440&width=402&top_left_y=1197&top_left_x=1693)

Fig. 1

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_1695894156295afed8e4g-1.jpg?height=291&width=444&top_left_y=1301&top_left_x=2082)

Fig. 2

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_1695894156295afed8e4g-1.jpg?height=399&width=284&top_left_y=1217&top_left_x=2520)

Fig. 3
Let $AN = AB$. Since triangle $ABC$ is acute-angled, the foot $H$ of the altitude $CH$ lies on the segment $AB$ (see Fig. 1). Further, the foot $T$ of the perpendicular dropped from $N$ to $AB$ is the midpoint of segment $AH$; hence, $BT > AT$, and then $BN > AN$. Therefore, the circle with center at point $B$ and radius $AN$ intersects side $AN$ at point $S$, because point $N$ lies outside and point $A$ lies inside this circle (see Fig. 3). By cutting off triangle $ABS$ from the parallelogram and sliding it until side $AB$ coincides with side $NK$, we obtain a rhombus.

Remark. It can be proven that any obtuse triangle can also be cut in the required manner. Indeed, if angle $B$ is obtuse and $AB \geqslant BC$, then the median $AM$ is definitely longer than side $AB$, and in this case $AN < AB$.

question:
# 6. CONDITION

Can 2005 non-zero vectors be drawn on a plane such that from any ten of them, three can be chosen with a zero sum?
reference_solution:
Solution. Suppose we managed to draw 2005 non-zero vectors on a plane such that from any 10 of them, we can choose 3 with a zero sum. Choose a line that is not perpendicular to any of the 2005 drawn vectors. Consider the projections of the drawn vectors onto the chosen line. None of these projections are zero vectors. At least 1003 projections are directed in the same direction. Choose 10 vectors whose projections are directed in the same direction. Then the projections of any three of them are directed in the same direction, and therefore their sum is not zero. (Since if the sum of vectors is zero, then the sum of the projections of these vectors onto the line is also zero).

Answer. It is impossible.

question: Problem 5. Do there exist 100 distinct natural numbers such that the product of any fifty-two of them is divisible by the product of the remaining forty-eight?
reference_solution:
Answer. They exist. The first solution. The numbers 100!, 100!/2, ..., 100!/100 will work. The product of any 52 of them is divisible by (100!)^51, and the product of any 48 of them is a divisor of (100!)^48, and thus of (100!)^51. The second solution. The numbers 2^n, 2^(n+1), ..., 2^(n+99), where n ≥ 575, will work. The product of any 52 of them is a power of two no less than 2^(n+(n+1)+...+(n+51)) = 2^(52n+51·52/2), and the product of any 48 of them is a power of two no greater than 2^((n+52)+...+(n+99)) = 2^(48n+151·48/2). Solving the inequality 52n + 51·52/2 > 48n + 151·48/2, we get n > 574.5, which leads to the statement made at the beginning of the solution, since any power of two divides any smaller power of two.

- See also Problem 5 for 6th grade.
- For the answer "they exist" without justification - 0 points. A correct example without justification of its correctness - 4 points. The idea to use powers of one number, not resulting in a correct example - no more than 2 points.

question:
11.2. Positive numbers $x, y$, and $z$ satisfy the condition $x y z \geqslant$ $\geqslant x y + y z + z x$. Prove the inequality

$$
\sqrt{x y z} \geqslant \sqrt{x} + \sqrt{y} + \sqrt{z}
$$

(A. Khryabrov)
reference_solution:
Solution. By the inequality of means, we have $x y+x z \geqslant 2 \sqrt{x y \cdot x z}, \quad x y+y z \geqslant 2 \sqrt{x y \cdot y z}, \quad x z+y z \geqslant 2 \sqrt{x z \cdot y z}$. Adding these three inequalities and dividing the result by 2, and considering the condition, we get

$$
x y z \geqslant x y+x z+y z \geqslant x \sqrt{y z}+y \sqrt{x z}+z \sqrt{x y}
$$

Dividing the obtained inequality by $\sqrt{x y z}$, we get the required result.

Remark. This solution is easier to come up with if we rewrite the given and required inequalities as $\frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{y}+\frac{1}{z} \leqslant 1$ and $\frac{1}{\sqrt{x y}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{x z}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{y z}} \leqslant 1$

question: 11.3. In triangle $A B C$, the bisector $B L$ is drawn. A point $M$ is chosen on the segment $C L$. The tangent at point $B$ to the circumcircle $\Omega$ of triangle $A B C$ intersects the ray $C A$ at point $P$. The tangents at points $B$ and $M$ to the circumcircle $\Gamma$ of triangle $B L M$ intersect at point $Q$. Prove that the lines $P Q$ and $B L$ are parallel.
reference_solution:
Solution. Since $BL$ is the bisector of $\angle ABC$, we have $\angle ABL = \angle LBC$. Since $PB$ is tangent to $\Omega$, we have $\angle PBA = \angle BCA$ (see Fig. 4). Additionally, $\angle PBL = \angle PBA + \angle ABL = \angle BCA + \angle LBC = \angle BLP$, so $\angle BPM = 180^\circ - (\angle PBL + \angle BLP) = 180^\circ - 2 \angle BLP$. This implies, in particular, that $\angle BLP$ is acute.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_cb4ef974dfe09c8ba0f5g-2.jpg?height=550&width=635&top_left_y=560&top_left_x=433)

Fig. 4

Since $\angle BLM = 180^\circ - \angle BLP$ is obtuse, the tangents to $\Gamma$ at points $B$ and $M$ intersect at a point $Q$ on the same side of $BM$ as point $L$ (and thus on the same side as point $P$). Further, we have $\angle QBM = \angle QMB = 180^\circ - \angle BLM = \angle BLP$. Therefore, $\angle BQM = 180^\circ - 2 \angle QBM = 180^\circ - 2 \angle BLP = \angle BPM$. Hence, points $B, M, P$, and $Q$ lie on the same circle. This implies that $\angle QPM = \angle QBM = \angle BLP$. This means that $PQ \parallel BL$.

Comment. It is proven that the quadrilateral $BPQM$ is cyclic - 3 points.

The problem is reduced to proving the cyclic nature of the quadrilateral $BPQM$ - 2 points.

It is proven that points $P$ and $Q$ lie on the same side of $BM$ - 0 points.

question:
10.7. Given a trapezoid $A B C D$, where $A D \| B C$, and rays $A B$ and $D C$ intersect at point $G$. The common external tangents to the circumcircles of triangles $A B C$ and $A C D$ intersect at point $E$. The common external tangents to the circumcircles of triangles $A B D$ and $B C D$ intersect at point $F$. Prove that points $E, F$, and $G$ lie on the same line.

(A. Kuznetsov)
reference_solution:
Solution. Let the line $EC$ intersect the circle $(ABC)$ again at point $X$, and the line $EA$ intersect the circle $(ACD)$ again at point $Y$ (we will consider the arrangement of points as shown in Fig. 5; other cases are treated similarly).

Consider the homothety with center $E$ that maps $(ABC)$ to $(ACD)$. Under this homothety, point $X$ maps to $C$, and point $A$ maps to $Y$. Therefore, $AX \parallel YC$ and $\angle AEC = \angle AYC - \angle ECY = \angle AYC - \angle AXC$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_306e95dfbf57b63cea3cg-5.jpg?height=721&width=733&top_left_y=487&top_left_x=380)

Fig. 5

But $\angle AXC = 180^\circ - \angle ABC$ and $\angle AYC = 180^\circ - \angle ADC$. Thus, $\angle AEC = \angle ABC - \angle ADC = \angle ABC - \angle BCG = \angle BGC$. From this equality, it follows that points $A, C, E, G$ lie on the same circle.

Since point $E$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AC$ (i.e., on the axis of symmetry of the circles $(ABC)$ and $(ACD)$), it is the midpoint of the arc $AGC$ of the circle $(ACEG)$. Therefore, $E$ lies on the external bisector of angle $BGC$.

Similarly, it can be shown that $F$ also lies on the external bisector of angle $BGC$.

Remark. The problem has the following generalization. Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral, $G = AB \cap CD$, and $M$ be the second point of intersection of the circles $(ADG)$ and $(BCG)$ (i.e., the Miquel point of this quadrilateral). Let $E$ be the center of homothety with a positive coefficient that maps $(ABC)$ to $(ADC)$. Then points $A, C, M, E$ lie on the same circle, and $E$ is the midpoint of the arc $AC$ (i.e., $ME$ is the bisector of the angle between $AM$ and $CM$).

This can be proven similarly to the solution of the problem: we have (in directed angles) $\angle AEC = \angle ABC + \angle ADC = \angle GBC + \angle AMG = \angle GMC + \angle AMG = \angle AMC$.

Comment. It is shown that the ratios of the radii of the circles in pairs are equal (and equal to the ratio of the lateral sides) - no additional points are awarded.

Results about the configuration of the centers of the circles and the positions of $E$ and $F$ relative to them (for example, the directions $O_iO_j$, the similarity of the construction of the centers and $ABCD$, $AE = EC$, $EO_1 / EO_2 = r_1 / r_2$, the projections of $EO_1$ and $FO_2$ on $AD$ are equal, and equivalent advancements) - no additional points are awarded.
