question: 8.1. If in the product of two natural numbers one factor is increased by 2, and the other is decreased by 2, the product of the numbers does not change. Prove that if 1 is added to this product, the result is a square of an integer.
reference_solution:
Solution. Let the natural numbers be denoted as $x$ and $y$. Then $x y = (x + 2)(y - 2)$. From this, we get $y = x + 2$. Therefore, $x y + 1 = x(x + 2) + 1 = (x + 1)^2$.

Comment. It has been proven that the difference between the natural numbers is 2 - 2 points.

question: 8.5. There are 90 cards - 10 with the digit 1, 10 with the digit $2, \ldots, 10$ with the digit 9. From all these cards, two numbers were formed, one of which is three times the other. Prove that one of these numbers can be factored into four not necessarily distinct natural factors, greater than one.
reference_solution:
Solution. Let these numbers be $A$ and $B=3A$. Then the sum of the digits of the number $B$ is divisible by 3. But the sum of the digits on all cards is divisible by 9 (and therefore by 3), so the sum of the digits of the number $A$ is divisible by 3. This means that the number $A$ is divisible by 3. But then the number $B=3A$ is divisible by 9 and the sum of its digits is divisible by 9. Since the sum of the digits on all cards is divisible by 9, then the sum of the digits of the number $A$ is also divisible by 9. This means that the number $A$ is divisible by 9. Therefore, the number
$B=3A$ is divisible by 27. Thus, the number $B$ is divisible by 27 and is greater than 27, so it can be factored into 4 multipliers $3,3,3$ and $\frac{B}{27}>1$.

Comment. It has been proven that the larger of the numbers is divisible by 9 - 3 points.

question: 10.5. The diagonals of trapezoid $ABCD$ intersect at point $O$. The circumcircles of triangles $AOB$ and $COD$ intersect at point $M$ on the base $AD$. Prove that triangle $BMC$ is isosceles.
reference_solution:
Solution

The first method. According to the theorem about angles inscribed in a circle, $\angle O B M=\angle O A M$ (see fig.). By the definition of a trapezoid, $\angle O A M=\angle O C B$. Thus, $\angle O B M=\angle O C B$. Similarly, it can be proven that $\angle O C M=\angle O B C$. Adding the obtained equalities, we find that $\angle M B C=\angle M C B$, which means $B M=C M$.

## The second method.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_93d92577b59f6996e8edg-3.jpg?height=348&width=571&top_left_y=180&top_left_x=822)

Consider the chain of equalities: $\angle C B M=\angle B M A=\angle B O A=\angle C O D=\angle C M D=\angle B C M$ (see fig.). The first and fifth equalities follow from the parallelism of the bases of the trapezoid, the second and fourth from the property of inscribed angles subtending the same arc, and the third from the equality of vertical angles. From the proven equalities, it follows that $\angle C B M=\angle B C M$, which means $B M=C M$.

question: 6. (7 points) For the tetrahedron $ABCD$, it is known that $AB \cdot CD = AC \cdot BD = AD \cdot BC$. Let $I_{A}, I_{B}, I_{C}, I_{D}$ be the centers of the inscribed circles of triangles $BCD, CDA, DAB$, and $ABC$ respectively. Prove that the segments $AI_{A}, BI_{B}, CI_{C}, DI_{D}$ intersect at one point.
reference_solution:
Solution. Let point $L$ be the foot of the bisector $AL$ of triangle $ABC$. By the property of the bisector, $BL / LC = BA / AC$. From the ratio of the lengths of the edges of the tetrahedron, it follows that $BA / AC = BD / DC$. By comparing these two equalities, we conclude that $BL / LC = BD / DC$. By the converse property of the bisector, segment $DL$ serves as the bisector in triangle $DBC$.

Consider triangle $ALD$. Points $I_D, I_A$ lie on its sides $AL$, $DL$ respectively, since the center of the inscribed circle of a triangle is the point of intersection of the bisectors. But then segments $DI_D$ and $AI_A$ intersect. Similarly, it can be proven that any two segments from the condition intersect. These four segments do not lie in the same plane (since their endpoints $A, B, C, D$ do not lie in the same plane) and intersect pairwise. This is only possible when they all have a common point.

Criteria. Any correct solution: 7 points.

Proven that the segments intersect pairwise, but not proven that all four have a common point: 4 points.

Proven that the bisectors of angles $BAC$ and $BDC$ intersect on edge $BC$, but no further progress: 2 points.

Incorrect or incomplete reasoning: 0 points.

question:
9.3. Given a parallelogram $A B C D$ with an obtuse angle $A$. Point $H$ is the foot of the perpendicular dropped from point $A$ to $B C$. The extension of the median of triangle $A B C$, drawn from vertex $C$, intersects the circumcircle of the triangle at point $K$. Prove that points $K, H, C$, and $D$ lie on the same circle.

(F. Ivlev)
reference_solution:
Solution. Let $E$ be the foot of the perpendicular dropped from point $B$ to $AD$. Then the quadrilateral $AHBE$ is a rectangle. Therefore, $\angle HED = \angle ABC = 180^\circ - \angle BCD$, which means that points $D, C, H, E$ lie on some circle $\omega$ (see Fig. 1).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_434c33a74f0761227f85g-2.jpg?height=367&width=470&top_left_y=1323&top_left_x=822)

Fig. 1

Let $M$ be the point of intersection of the diagonals of the rectangle $AHBE$, that is, $MA = MB = MH = ME$ (by the condition, point $M$ lies on $CK$). Since points $A, K, B, C$ lie on the same circle, we have $MK \cdot MC = MA \cdot MB = MH \cdot ME$. This equality means that points $C, K, H$, and $E$ lie on the same circle. This circle is the circumcircle of triangle $CHE$, which coincides with $\omega$; thus, all four points $K, H, C, D$ lie on $\omega$.

question:
9.4. Positive real numbers $a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n}$ and $k$ are such that $a_{1}+\ldots+a_{n}=3 k, a_{1}^{2}+\ldots+a_{n}^{2}=3 k^{2}$ and $a_{1}^{3}+\ldots+a_{n}^{3}>3 k^{3}+k$. Prove that some two of the numbers $a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n}$ differ by more than 1.

(N. Agakhanov)
reference_solution:
Solution. Multiplying the equality

$$
a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{n}=3 k
$$

and the inequality

$$
a_{1}^{3}+a_{2}^{3}+\ldots+a_{n}^{3}>3 k^{3}+k
$$

we obtain the inequality

$$
\begin{gathered}
a_{1}^{4}+a_{2}^{4}+\ldots+a_{n}^{4}+a_{1}^{3} a_{2}+a_{1} a_{2}^{3}+a_{1}^{3} a_{3}+a_{1} a_{3}^{3}+\ldots+a_{n-1}^{3} a_{n}+a_{n-1} a_{n}^{3}> \\
>9 k^{4}+3 k^{2}
\end{gathered}
$$

Now, let's square the equality

$$
a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}+\ldots+a_{n}^{2}=3 k^{2}
$$

We get

$$
a_{1}^{4}+a_{2}^{4}+\ldots+a_{n}^{4}+2 a_{1}^{2} a_{2}^{2}+2 a_{1}^{2} a_{3}^{2}+\ldots+2 a_{n-1}^{2} a_{n}^{2}=9 k^{4}
$$

Subtracting equality (4) from inequality (2), we get $\left(a_{1}^{3} a_{2}-2 a_{1}^{2} a_{2}^{2}+a_{1} a_{2}^{3}\right)+\ldots+\left(a_{n-1}^{3} a_{n}-2 a_{n-1}^{2} a_{n}^{2}+a_{n-1} a_{n}^{3}\right)>3 k^{2}$, or

$a_{1} a_{2}\left(a_{1}-a_{2}\right)^{2}+a_{1} a_{3}\left(a_{1}-a_{3}\right)^{2}+\ldots+a_{n-1} a_{n}\left(a_{n-1}-a_{n}\right)^{2}>3 k^{2}$.

Now, suppose that any two numbers differ by no more than 1. Then the square of their difference is no more than 1, and from (5) we get the inequality

$$
a_{1} a_{2}+a_{1} a_{3}+\ldots+a_{n-1} a_{n}>3 k^{2}
$$

But, if we subtract equality (3) from the square of equality (1), we get the equality

$$
2 a_{1} a_{2}+2 a_{1} a_{3}+\ldots+2 a_{n-1} a_{n}=6 k^{2}
$$

which contradicts (6). Therefore, there will be two numbers that differ by more than 1.

question: 3. Prove that there do not exist integers $x$ and $y$ such that the equation $(x+7)(x+6)=8y+3$ holds.
reference_solution: Solution. Let $x$ and $y$ be integers. Notice that $x+6$ and $x+7$ are consecutive integers, so one of them will be even, i.e., divisible by 2. Therefore, the product $(x+7)(x+6)$ will be divisible by 2. Next, we see that $8y$ is an even number for any integer value of $y$, and thus $8y+3$ is an odd number (as the sum of an even and an odd number). Therefore, for integer values of $x$ and $y$, the left side of the equation is an even number, while the right side is an odd number, so the equation has no solution in integers.

question: 4. In triangle $\mathrm{ABC}$, $\angle A=3 \angle C$. Point $D$ on side $B C$ has the property that $\angle D A C=2 \angle C$. Prove that $A B+A D=B C$.
reference_solution:
Solution. Let $\angle C=x$, then $\angle B A C=3 x$. Extend the segment $B A$ beyond point $A$ and mark a segment $A E=A D$ on it (see the figure). Clearly, $\angle E A C=180^{\circ}-\angle B A C=180^{\circ}-3 x$.

Notice that $\triangle E A C=\triangle A D C$ by the first criterion ( $A C$ is common, $A D=A E$ (by construction) and $\angle E A C=\angle A D C)$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_be4644d9f3fa48aba2e3g-2.jpg?height=417&width=437&top_left_y=203&top_left_x=887)

In $\triangle A E C$: $\angle A E C=2 x, \angle A C E=x$, i.e., $\angle B C E=2 x$, so $\triangle B E C$ is isosceles. Therefore, $A B+A D=A B+A E=B E=B C$.

question:
11.2. Set $A$ consists of $n$ distinct natural numbers, the sum of which is equal to $n^{2}$. Set $B$ also consists of $n$ distinct natural numbers, the sum of which is equal to $n^{2}$. Prove that there will be a number that belongs to both set $A$ and set $B$.

(D. Khramov)
reference_solution:
Solution. Suppose the opposite: sets $A$ and $B$ do not intersect. Then their union contains $2n$ distinct natural numbers. Consequently, the sum $S$ of all elements in the union of sets $A$ and $B$ will be no less than the sum $1+2+\ldots+2n=n(2n+1)$. On the other hand, by the condition $S=2n^2$, which is less than $n(2n+1)$. Contradiction.

Comment. In the assumption that sets $A$ and $B$ do not intersect, the estimate $S \geqslant 1+2+\ldots+2n-$ is worth no less than 5 points (in the case of an incorrect further calculation of the sum, 5 points are awarded).

question: 11.3. In a right triangle $ABC$ with hypotenuse $AC$, a height $BH$ is dropped. On side $BC$, point $D$ is marked, on segment $BH$ - point $E$, and on segment $CH$ - point $F$ such that $\angle BAD = \angle CAE$ and $\angle AFE = \angle CFD$. Prove that $\angle AEF = 90^{\circ}$.
reference_solution:
Solution. Construct point $E^{\prime}$, symmetric to point $E$ with respect to side $A C$ (see Fig. 3). Note that point $F$ lies on line $D E^{\prime}$, because $\angle D F C = \angle E F A = \angle E^{\prime} F A$ due to symmetry. From the right triangles $A B C$ and $B C H$, we get $\angle E^{\prime} B C = 90^{\circ} - \angle A C B = \angle B A C$.

Note that $\angle B A D = \angle C A E = \angle C A E^{\prime}$. Therefore, $\angle D A E^{\prime} = \angle C A E^{\prime} + \angle D A C = \angle B A D + \angle D A C = \angle B A C = \angle E^{\prime} B C$. This means that quadrilateral $A B D E^{\prime}$ is cyclic. Consequently, since $\angle A B D = 90^{\circ}$, then $\angle A E^{\prime} D = 90^{\circ}$. Then, by symmetry, $\angle A E F = 90^{\circ}$, which is what we needed to prove.

question: 11.4. Let $p$ be a prime number greater than 3. Prove that there exists a natural number $y$, less than $p / 2$, such that the number $p y+1$ cannot be represented as the product of two integers, each greater than $y$.
reference_solution:
Solution. Let $p=2k+1$. Assume the opposite: for each of the numbers $y=1,2, \ldots, k$ there exists a factorization $p y+1=a_{y} b_{y}$, where $a_{y}>y, b_{y}>y$. Note that each of the numbers $a_{y}$ and $b_{y}$ is strictly greater than 1, and that $a_{y} > p y + 1$. Therefore, each of the $p-1$ numbers in the set $a_{1}, b_{1}, a_{2}, b_{2}, \ldots a_{k}, b_{k}$ lies in the set of $p-2$ numbers $\{2,3, \ldots, p-1\}$. Thus, there will be two equal numbers in this set. Let each of these two numbers be equal to $d$.

If these equal numbers have the same indices in the set, that is, $a_{y}=b_{y}=d$ for some $y$. Then $p y+1=d^{2}$, so the number $d^{2}-1=(d-1)(d+1)=p y$ is divisible by the prime $p$. Since $1 \leqslant d-1 < d+1 \leqslant p-1$, one of the numbers $d-1$ or $d+1$ is divisible by $p$. This is impossible because both $d-1$ and $d+1$ are greater than $k$. Contradiction (since $y \leqslant k$).

Otherwise, there exist indices $y_{1}<y_{2}$ such that
$1 \leqslant y_{1}<y_{2}<d$, for which the numbers $p y_{1}+1$ and $p y_{2}+1$ are divisible by $d$. Then $p\left(y_{2}-y_{1}\right)=\left(p y_{2}+1\right)-\left(p y_{1}+1\right)$ is also divisible by $d$. From the coprimality of the numbers $d$ and $p$, we get that $y_{2}-y_{1}$ is divisible by $d$, which is impossible since $0<y_{2}-y_{1}<y_{2}<d$.

Thus, in each case, a contradiction is obtained, and therefore, the number $y$ specified in the problem statement always exists.

Comment. In the assumption of the opposite, it is only proven that there are two equal numbers in the set $a_{1}, b_{1}, a_{2}, b_{2}, \ldots a_{k}, b_{k}$ - 3 points.

In the assumption of the opposite, it is proven that there are two equal numbers in the set $a_{1}, b_{1}, a_{2}, b_{2}, \ldots a_{k}, b_{k}$, and the case $y_{1}<y_{2}$ (i.e., the case $y_{1}=y_{2}$ is omitted or resolved incorrectly) is reduced to a contradiction - 5 points.

In the assumption of the opposite, it is proven that there are two equal numbers in the set $a_{1}, b_{1}, a_{2}, b_{2}, \ldots a_{k}, b_{k}$, and the case $y_{1}=y_{2}$ (i.e., the case $y_{1}<y_{2}$ is omitted or resolved incorrectly) is reduced to a contradiction - 5 points.

question: 5. In each of the three schools in the microdistrict, 100 first-graders enrolled. On September 1, exactly 100 first-graders came to each school. However, some children got confused about which school they were supposed to go to, and exactly 40 children came to the wrong school. Prove that it is possible to choose two lost first-graders and swap their places so that as a result, each of them will be in their correct school.
reference_solution:
Solution. Let x students from other schools come to the first school (and, accordingly, x students from the first school went to the wrong place), y to the second school, and z to the third school, with $x \geq y \geq z$. Since 40 is not divisible by 3, then x > z and in the first school, there cannot be only "foreign" students from the third school.

If in the first school there are only "foreign" students from the second school, then $x = y$, because in the second school, there are at least x students missing, and thus there are at least x "foreign" students. And in this case, all students from the second school came specifically to the first. Then in the second school, there is at least one student from the first school, since $y = x > z$. And the students who came to the wrong place from the first and second schools can be swapped.

If, however, in the first school there are "foreign" students from both the second and the third schools, then a student from the first school who came to the wrong place can be swapped with the corresponding "foreign" student from the first school.

question: Problem 4. The difference of the roots of the quadratic equation with real coefficients $2018 x^{2} + a x + b = 0$ is an integer (while the roots themselves are not necessarily integers). Prove that the discriminant of this equation is divisible by $2018^{2}$.
reference_solution:
Solution. Let $D$ be the discriminant of this equation. Denote the roots of the equation by $x_{1}=\frac{-a+\sqrt{D}}{4036}$ and $x_{2}=\frac{-a-\sqrt{D}}{4036}$. Then $x_{1}-x_{2}=\frac{\sqrt{D}}{2018}=n-$ an integer. Thus, $\sqrt{D}=2018 \cdot n$ and $D=2018^{2} n^{2}$, which is divisible by $2018^{2}$.

question: Problem 6. In a country, there are 100 cities. Between any two cities, there is either no connection, or there is an air route, or there is a railway (both air routes and railways cannot exist simultaneously). It is known that if two cities are connected to a third city by railway, then there is an air route between them, and if two cities are connected to a third city by air routes, then there is a railway between them. Due to a natural disaster, all flights in the country have been canceled. The government has decided to place humanitarian aid centers in some cities, such that from each city, it is possible to reach such a center. Prove that at least 20 such centers need to be opened.
reference_solution:
Solution. Note that no city is connected by railway to more than two other cities. Indeed, suppose some three cities are connected by railway to one. Then all of them are connected to each other by air routes, which is impossible by the condition of the problem. Therefore, each city is connected by railway to no more than two others. Then the cities connected to each other by railway form a chain (possibly closed). We will prove that each such chain contains no more than 5 vertices. Let the cities $A, B, C, D$ and $E$ stand sequentially in the chain. Since $A$ and $C$ are connected to $B$ by railways, there is an air route between $A$ and $C$. Similarly, there is an air route between $C$ and $E$. Then there is a railway between $A$ and $E$, and thus the cities are connected in a circle and are not connected to any other city. Therefore, each chain contains no more than 5 cities. To be able to reach a humanitarian center from each city, it is necessary to open one in each such chain. This means that at least $100: 5=20$ centers need to be built, as required.

## Criteria

1 p. It is proven that each city is connected by railway to no more than two others, or an equivalent statement for air routes.

3 p. It is proven that each chain of railway connections contains no more than 5 cities, or an equivalent statement for air routes.

4 6. A correct proof is provided.

question: 10.1. Find all possible functions of the form $f(x)=k x-b$, where $k \neq 0$, such that $f(f(x))=2 f(x)-3 f(1-x)$, or prove that they do not exist. (7 points)
reference_solution:
# Solution:

1) $f(f(x))=f(k x-b)=k(k x-b)-b=k^{2} x-k b-b=k^{2} x+(-k b-b)$
2) $2 f(x)-3 f(1-x)=2(k x-b)-3(k(1-x)-b)=2 k x-2 b-3(k-k x-b)=2 k x-$ $2 b-3 k+3 k x+3 b=5 k x+(b-3 k)$
3) By equating the coefficients, we get: $\left\{\begin{array}{c}k^{2}=5 k \\ -k b-b=b-3 k\end{array}\right.$.
4) Using the fact that $k \neq 0$, we get: $\left\{\begin{array}{c}k=5 \\ -5 b-2 b=-15\end{array} \Rightarrow\left\{\begin{array}{c}k=5 \\ b=2 \frac{1}{7}\end{array}\right.\right.$.

Answer: $f(x)=5 x-2 \frac{1}{7}$.

question:
2. The magnitudes $\alpha$ and $\beta$ of acute angles satisfy the equation

$\sin ^{2} \alpha+\sin ^{2} \beta=\sin (\alpha+\beta)$. Prove that $\alpha+\beta=\frac{\pi}{2}$.
reference_solution:
Solution. From the condition, it follows that $\sin \alpha(\sin \alpha-\cos \beta)=\sin \beta(\cos \alpha-\sin \beta)$.

If $\sin \alpha>\cos \beta$ and $\cos \alpha>\sin \beta$, then $1=\sin ^{2} \alpha+\cos ^{2} \alpha>\sin ^{2} \beta+\cos ^{2} \beta=1-$ contradiction. Similarly, a contradiction arises if the signs in the two previous inequalities are reversed. Therefore, $\sin \alpha=\cos \beta$ and $\cos \alpha=\sin \beta$.

Thus, $\alpha+\beta=\frac{\pi}{2}$, which is what we needed to prove.

question: 11.4. Plane $\alpha$ intersects the edges $A B, B C, C D$ and $D A$ of the tetrahedron $A B C D$ at points $K, L, M$ and $N$ respectively. It turns out that the dihedral angles $\angle(K L A, K L M)$, $\angle(L M B, L M N)$, $\angle(M N C, M N K)$ and $\angle(N K D, N K L)$ are equal. (Here, $\angle(P Q R, P Q S)$ denotes the dihedral angle along the edge $P Q$ in the tetrahedron $P Q R S$.) Prove that the projections of the vertices $A, B, C$ and $D$ onto the plane $\alpha$ lie on a single circle.
reference_solution:
Solution. Let $A^{\prime}, B^{\prime}, C^{\prime}, D^{\prime}$ be the projections of vertices $A, B, C, D$ respectively onto the plane $\alpha$. Let $X$ be an arbitrary point on the extension of segment $K L$ beyond point $K$. Then we have $\angle(K X A, K X N)=\angle(K L A, K L M)$ and $\angle(K N A, K N X) = \angle(N K D, N K L)$. By the given condition, these angles are equal; hence, in the trihedral angle $K A N X$ (with vertex $K$), the dihedral angles at edges $K N$ and $K X$ are equal to each other. This means that the plane passing through the line $K A$ and perpendicular to the plane $\alpha$ is the plane of symmetry of the trihedral angle $K A N X$. Therefore, the point $A^{\prime}$ lies on the line containing the bisector of angle $X K N$, that is, on the external bisector of angle $N K L$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_19aef1b5960369e439f7g-16.jpg?height=540&width=926&top_left_y=464&top_left_x=287)

Fig. 3

Similarly, it can be shown that $A^{\prime}$ lies on the external bisector of angle $M N K$. Applying the same reasoning to points $B^{\prime}, C^{\prime}, D^{\prime}$, we find that points $A^{\prime}, B^{\prime}, C^{\prime}, D^{\prime}$ are the intersections of the external bisectors of adjacent angles of quadrilateral $K L M N$.

From triangle $A^{\prime} K N$, we find $\angle B^{\prime} A^{\prime} D^{\prime} = \angle K A^{\prime} N = 180^{\circ} - \angle A^{\prime} K N - \angle A^{\prime} N K = (90^{\circ} - \angle A^{\prime} K N) + (90^{\circ} - \angle A^{\prime} N K) = \frac{1}{2}(\angle N K L + \angle M N K)$. Similarly, we obtain $\angle B^{\prime} C^{\prime} D^{\prime} = \frac{1}{2}(\angle K L M + \angle L M N)$. Thus, $\angle B^{\prime} A^{\prime} D^{\prime} + \angle B^{\prime} C^{\prime} D^{\prime} = \frac{1}{2}(\angle N K L + \angle M N K + \angle K L M + \angle L M N) = 180^{\circ}$, from which it follows that quadrilateral $A^{\prime} B^{\prime} C^{\prime} D^{\prime}$ is cyclic.

Comment. If the location of the points is not justified in the solution - points are not deducted.

question:

Solution. The initial equality is equivalent to the following $(a+b)^{2}-c^{2}=2 c^{2}$, or $(a+b)^{2}=3 c^{2}$. If $c \neq 0$, we get $((a+b) / c)^{2}=3 .|(a+b) / c|={ }^{-}$. On the left, we have a rational number, since the sum, quotient, and absolute value of rational numbers are rational, while on the right, we have an irrational number, and the equality is impossible. question: 5. The bisectors $\mathrm{AD}$ and $\mathrm{BE}$ of triangle $\mathrm{ABC}$ intersect at point I. It turns out that $\mathrm{CA} \cdot \mathrm{CB}=\mathrm{AB} \cdot \mathrm{B}^{2}$. Prove that the area of triangle ABI is equal to the area of quadrilateral CDIE.
reference_solution:
Solution. Let $S(C D I E)=S_{1}, S(A B I)=S_{2}, S(B D I)=S_{3}, S(A I E)=S_{4}$ (see figure). Since the ratio of the areas of triangles with a common height is equal to the ratio of the bases, and the angle bisector divides the opposite side in the ratio of the adjacent sides, we have

$\left(S_{1}+S_{4}\right) /\left(S_{2}+S_{3}\right)=CD / BD=AC / AB$. Similarly, $\left(S_{2}+S_{4}\right) /\left(S_{1}+S_{3}\right)=AE / EC=AB / BC$. From the equality in the condition, it follows that

$AC / AB=AB / BC$. Therefore, $\left(S_{1}+S_{4}\right) /\left(S_{2}+S_{3}\right)=$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_60b8b9fe1297b29c11dag-2.jpg?height=504&width=473&top_left_y=367&top_left_x=927)

$\left(S_{2}+S_{4}\right) /\left(S_{1}+S_{3}\right)$. By the fundamental property of proportions,

$\left(S_{1}+S_{4}\right)\left(S_{1}+S_{3}\right)=\left(S_{2}+S_{4}\right)\left(S_{2}+S_{3}\right)$. Expanding the brackets, moving terms to one side, and factoring, we get

$\left(S_{1}-S_{2}\right)\left(S_{1}+S_{2}+S_{3}+S_{4}\right)=0$. The second factor is positive, so $S_{1}-S_{2}=0$ or $S_{1}=S_{2}$.

question: 6. In one company, among any 9 people, there are two people who know each other. Prove that in this company, there will be a group of eight people such that each of the others knows someone from this group.
reference_solution:
Solution. Consider the largest group $G$ of people who are pairwise unfamiliar with each other. In this group, there are no more than eight people, otherwise, there would be nine people among them, none of whom are familiar with each other, which contradicts the condition. Since this is the largest group, every other person is familiar with someone in this group. If necessary, we can add a few people to it to make it eight people, and we will get a group of eight people such that the rest are familiar with someone in this group.

Prove that Vasya can write a certain 30-digit natural number instead of the asterisk so that the resulting equation has an integer root. (A. Kuznetsov, A. Antropov)

question:
10.8. The bisector of angle $A$ of parallelogram $A B C D$ intersects side $B C$ at point $K$. A point $L$ is chosen on side $A B$ such that 
$A L=C K$. Segments $A K$ and $C L$ intersect at point $M$. On the extension of segment $A D$ beyond point $D$, point $N$ is marked. It is known that quadrilateral $A L M N$ is cyclic. Prove that $\angle C N L=90^{\circ}$.

First solution. Since $AM$ is the bisector of angle $LAN$, segments $LM$ and $MN$ are equal as chords subtending equal arcs (see Fig. 3). Now it is sufficient to prove that $CM = LM$ (then $CM = LM = MN$, so $CNL$ is a right triangle, and $NM$ is its median drawn from the right angle).

Since $\angle BKA = \angle NAK = \angle BAK$, triangle $ABK$ is isosceles (symmetric with respect to the perpendicular bisector of $AK$). Mark a point $X$ on side $BK$ such that $LX \parallel AK$. From the symmetry of triangle $ABK$, we have $KX = AL$. Then we have $KX = CK$ and $MK \parallel LX$, so $MK$ is the midline of triangle $CLX$, hence $CM = LM$, which completes the proof.

Second solution. Let $\angle BAD = 2\alpha$.

Notice that $DM$ is the bisector of angle $ADC$. Indeed, extend $AK$ to intersect $CD$ at point $Y$ (see Fig. 4). Then, using the similarity of triangles $AML \sim YMC$ and $AYD \sim KYC$, we have $AM / MY = AL / YC = CK / YC = AD / DY$. From the cyclic nature of $ALMN$, we have $\angle CMN = \angle LAD$, and from the parallelism $AB \parallel CD$, it follows that $\angle LAD = \angle CDN$. Therefore, $\angle CMN = \angle CDN$, so quadrilateral $CMDN$ is cyclic. Hence, $\angle MNC = \angle MDC = 90^\circ - \alpha$.

question: 8.4. Prove that there are infinitely many natural numbers $n$ for which the numbers $2 n-3$ and $3 n-2$ have a common divisor not equal to 1.
reference_solution: Solution. It is sufficient to note that for any positive integer $k$, when $n=5 k-1$, the numbers $2 n-3=10 k-5$ and $3 n-2=15 k-5$ are divisible by 5.

Solution. If among the 14 specified sets there is one consisting of a single element, then all the other sets include this element. There are a total of $2^{4}=16$ sets (including the empty set) without this element. By adding this element to them, we get 16 suitable sets. If among the 14 sets there are no single-element sets, then let's assume now that there is at least one set of two elements. If there is exactly one set of two elements, then excluding 5 single-element sets and 9 sets of two elements, as well as a set of three elements that does not intersect with the set of two elements included in the collection. There will be 15 suitable sets left (for example, 12, 123, 124, 125, 134, 135, 145, 234, 235, 245, 1234, 1235, 1245, 1345, 2345, 12345). If there are two sets of two elements (for example, 12 and 13), then 8 sets of three elements can be added (excluding sets 345 and 245), 5 sets of four elements, and one set of all five elements. In total, there are 16 sets. For three sets of two elements (for example, 12, 13, 23), 7 sets of three elements can be added, 5 sets of four elements, and one set of 5 elements. Again, there are 16 sets. For four sets of two elements (for example, 12, 13, 14, 15), 6 sets of three elements can be added, 5 sets of four elements, and one set of 5 elements. The last possible case: all sets contain more than two elements. Then they all will be suitable. And there are also 16 such sets. So, 16 sets can always be found.

Comments. The case where among the 14 specified sets there is one consisting of a single element is correctly considered $-\underline{\text { point. }}$

First, we zero out the corner cells with the number "3" along with their neighbors. Then we reduce the cells with the numbers 4, 11, and 5. Next, we reduce the cells with the numbers 6, 7, and 7. From the result, it is easy to obtain a table with zeros.

It remains to show the correct sequence of choosing such corners.

## Evaluation Criteria.

- If a chain of intermediate states of the table is indicated and it is clear how they are derived from each other, -7 points.

question: 11.2. In a row of 2009 weights, the weight of each weight is an integer number of grams and does not exceed 1 kg. The weights of any two adjacent weights differ by exactly 1 g, and the total weight of all the weights in grams is an even number. Prove that the weights can be divided into two piles such that the sums of the weights in each pile are equal. (D. Khramtsov)
reference_solution:
Solution. It is clear that the weights of all weights placed in odd positions have the same parity, while the weights of all other weights have a different parity. Since the total weight is even, the 1005 weights in odd positions have even weights.

Place the first weight on the left pan of the scales (let its weight be $2a \leqslant 1000$ g), and divide the remaining 2008 weights into 1004 pairs of adjacent weights (then the weights of the weights in any pair differ by 1 g). Now, in some $(502-a)$ pairs, place the lighter weights of each pair on the right pan of the scales, and the heavier ones on the left; in the remaining $(502+a)$ pairs, place the lighter weights on the left pan, and the heavier ones on the right. Then the difference between the total weights of the weights on the left and right pans will be $2a + (502 - a) - (502 + a) = 0$, as required.

Comment. The idea of dividing all weights, except one, into pairs of adjacent weights and distributing the weights from one pair onto different pans - 2 points.

question:
11.3. Quadrilateral $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle with diameter $AC$. Points $K$ and $M$ are the projections of vertices $A$ and $C$ respectively onto the line $BD$. A line through point $K$ parallel to $BC$ intersects $AC$ at point $P$. Prove that angle $KPM$ is a right angle.

(T. Emelyanova)
reference_solution:
Solution. First solution. Let $E$ be the point of intersection of the diagonals $A C$ and $B D$. Suppose, for definiteness, that point $K$ lies on the segment $B E$. Let the line passing through $K$ parallel to $P M$ intersect $A C$ at point $N$ (see Fig. 6). Then $\triangle N K E \sim \triangle P M E$ (since their sides are parallel), from which $\frac{P E}{E M}=\frac{N E}{E K} \cdot$ On the other hand, the right triangles $A K E$ and $C M E$ are also similar (by the acute angle at vertex $E$), so $\frac{E M}{E C}=\frac{E K}{E A}$. Multiplying the obtained equalities, we get $\frac{P E}{E C}=\frac{N E}{E A}$. But by Thales' theorem, $\frac{P E}{E C}=\frac{K E}{E B}$. Thus, we have $\frac{N E}{E A}=\frac{P E}{E C}=\frac{K E}{E B}$, from which $K N \| A B$. Therefore, $P M\|A B \perp B C\| K P$, as required.

The case when point $K$ lies on the segment $D E$ is considered similarly.

Second solution. Again, let $E$ be the point of intersection of the diagonals $A C$ and $B D$ and consider the case when point $K$ lies on the segment $B E$. Notice that $\angle P A D=\angle C A D=\angle C B D=\angle P K D$, so the quadrilateral $A K P D$ is cyclic (see Fig. 7). Thus, $\angle A K D=\angle A P D=90^{\circ}$. Then, from the equality $\angle C P D=\angle C M D=90^{\circ}$, it follows that the quadrilateral $C P M D$ is cyclic, from which $\angle E P M=180^{\circ}-\angle C P M=\angle E D C=\angle B A C=\angle B A E$. Therefore, $P M\|A B \perp B C\| K P$, as required.

The case when $K$ lies on the segment $D E$ is again considered similarly.

question:
11.4. We will call a triple of natural numbers $(a, b, c)$ square if they form an arithmetic progression (in that order), the number $b$ is coprime with each of the numbers $a$ and $c$, and the number $a b c$ is a perfect square. Prove that for any square triple, there exists another square triple that shares at least one common number with it.

(V. Senderov)
reference_solution:
Solution. If $b=1$, then $a=c=1$, and another triplet can be chosen as $(1,25,49)$. If $b \neq 1$, then from the mutual simplicity of the difference of the progression $d$ cannot be zero. Then, without loss of generality, $d=b-a=c-b>0$.

Since $b$ is coprime with both $a$ and $c$, it is coprime with $ac$. Furthermore, the product of coprime numbers $ac$ and $b$ is a square, so each of them is also a square, that is, $b=f^{2}, ac=m^{2}=(b-d)(b+d)=b^{2}-d^{2}$ for some natural numbers $f$ and $m$. Here, $m \neq d$, because otherwise $b^{2}=m^{2}+d^{2}=2m^{2}$, which is impossible.

Now consider the triplet $(b-m, b, b+m)$. Its members form an arithmetic progression, are natural numbers (since $b^{2}-m^{2}=d^{2}>0$), and their product
$(b-m)b(b+m)=f^{2}(b^{2}-m^{2})=(df)^{2}$ is a square. Moreover, $\gcd(b, m^2) = \gcd(b, ac) = 1$, hence $1 = \gcd(b, m) = \gcd(b, b-m) = \gcd(b, b+m)$. Therefore, this triplet is square, it has a common element $b$ with the original one, and is different from it (since $b-m \neq b-d$), which is what was required.

Comment. The solution is generally correct, but the case of the triplet $(1,1,1)$ is missed - deduct 1 point. For each triplet, another one is presented that has exactly one common number with it, but it is not verified that these triplets are different - award 4 points.

question: 2. In a right triangle $\mathrm{ABC}$, from the right angle $\mathrm{B}$, the altitude $\mathrm{BH}$, the angle bisector $\mathrm{BL}$, and the median $\mathrm{BM}$ are drawn. Prove that $\angle \mathrm{LBM} = \angle \mathrm{HBL}$.
reference_solution:
Solution. Let $\angle \mathrm{CAB} \leq 45^{\circ}$. Denote $\angle \mathrm{CAB}=\alpha$. Then $\angle \mathrm{ACB}=90^{\circ}-\alpha$.

1) In the right triangle $\triangle \mathrm{BHC}$, $\angle \mathrm{CBH}=90^{\circ}-\angle \mathrm{HCB}=90^{\circ}-(90^{\circ}-\alpha)=\alpha$. $\angle \mathrm{CBL}=45^{\circ}$ (BL is the bisector of the right angle). Since $\angle \mathrm{CBH}=\alpha \leq 45^{\circ}=\angle \mathrm{CBL}$, point $\mathrm{H}$ is located on segment CL (as shown in the diagram) and $\angle \mathrm{HBL}=\angle \mathrm{CBL}-\angle \mathrm{CBH}=45^{\circ}-\alpha$.
2) $\mathrm{AM}=\mathrm{CM}=\mathrm{BM}$ (by the property of the median in a right triangle) $\Rightarrow \triangle \mathrm{AMB}$ and $\triangle \mathrm{BMC}$ are isosceles $\Rightarrow \angle \mathrm{MBA}=\angle \mathrm{MAB}=\alpha$. $\angle \mathrm{LBA}=45^{\circ}$ (BL is the bisector of the right angle). Since $\angle \mathrm{ABM}=\alpha \leq 45^{\circ}=\angle \mathrm{ABL}$, point $\mathrm{M}$ is located on segment AL (as shown in the diagram) and $\angle \mathrm{LBM}=\angle \mathrm{LBA}-\angle \mathrm{MBA}=45^{\circ}-\alpha$.

Thus, $\angle \mathrm{HBL}=\angle \mathrm{LBM}=45^{\circ}-\alpha$, which is what we needed to prove.

The case $\angle \mathrm{CAB}>45^{\circ}$ is considered similarly, with the points A and C being relabeled.

Criteria. Only one configuration of points M, L, H is considered, without mentioning that the points can be in a different order - 6 points.

question: 5. There are candies in five bags. In different bags, there are different numbers of candies, and in total, there are 21 candies. It is known that candies from any two bags can be distributed into the three remaining bags so that the number of candies in these three bags becomes equal. Prove that there is a bag with exactly 7 candies.
reference_solution:
Solution. Suppose there is a bag A, which contains 8 or more candies. Then, according to the condition, candies from other bags D, E can be distributed into bags A, B, C so that the number of candies in them becomes equal. Since the number of candies in A has not decreased, there are at least 8 candies in each bag, meaning there are at least 24 candies in total. But there are only 21. Contradiction, so in all bags, there are no more than 7 candies.

Suppose there is no bag with 7 candies. Then there are no more than 6 candies in each. But then in 5 bags, there are a maximum of \(6+5+4+3+2=20\) candies. Again, a contradiction, so there must be a bag with 7 candies.

Criteria. Proof that there cannot be a bag with 8 or more candies - 4 points (if it talks about exactly 8 candies - 3 points). Proof that there cannot be 6 or fewer candies in all bags - 3 points.

question: 11.3. Given 11 different natural numbers, not greater than 20. Prove that among their pairwise differences, there will be four that are the same in absolute value.
reference_solution: 11.3. The number of pairwise differences is $11 \cdot 10 / 2=55$ (each of the 11 numbers forms a difference with ten others, and each difference is counted twice). The maximum absolute value of the difference is 19, the minimum is -1, and there are 19 different values. However, the difference of 19 can be obtained in only one way: $19=20-1$, the difference of 18 can be obtained in two ways: $18=20-2=19-1$. Therefore, at least 52 differences are left for the remaining 17 values, and one of them will occur at least 4 times.

question: 11.4. On the graph of the function $y=\frac{1}{x}$, two points $A$ and $B$ with positive abscissas are selected. Points $H_{A}$ and $H_{B}$ are the bases of the perpendiculars dropped from these points to the x-axis, and $O$ is the origin. Prove that the area of the figure bounded by the lines $O A, O B$ and the arc $A B$ is equal to the area of the figure bounded by the lines $A H_{A}, B H_{B}$, the x-axis, and the arc $A B$.
reference_solution: 11.4. We can assume that the abscissa of point $A$ is less than the abscissa of point $B$. Let $K$ be the intersection point of segments $A H_{A}$ and $O B$. Since $O H_{A} \cdot A H_{A} = O H_{B} \cdot B H_{B} = 1$, the areas of triangles $O A H_{A}$ and $O B H_{B}$ are equal, and thus the areas of triangle $O A K$ and trapezoid $H_{A} K B H_{B}$ are equal, which implies the equality of the specified figures.

question:
11.6. Quadrilateral $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle $\Gamma$ with center at point $O$. Its diagonals $AC$ and $BD$ are perpendicular and intersect at point $P$, and point $O$ lies inside triangle $BPC$. A point $H$ is chosen on segment $BO$ such that $\angle BHP=90^{\circ}$. The circle $\omega$, circumscribed around triangle $PHD$, intersects segment $PC$ again at point $Q$. Prove that $AP = CQ$.

(A. Kuznetsov)
reference_solution:
Solution. Draw the diameter $B T$ in the circle $\Gamma$ (see Fig. 4). Note that $\angle P D T = \angle B D T = 90^{\circ}$. Therefore, $\angle P H T + \angle P D T = 180^{\circ}$, which means that point $T$ lies on the circle $\omega$. Hence, $\angle P Q T = \angle P H T = 90^{\circ}$, and quadrilateral $P Q T D$ is a rectangle.

Consider the common perpendicular bisector $\ell$ of segments $D T$ and $P Q$. It passes through $O$, and thus is also the perpendicular bisector of $A C$. Therefore, segments $A P$ and $C Q$ are symmetric with respect to $\ell$ and are therefore equal.

question: 11.7. On a plane, several lines are drawn, no two of which are parallel and no three pass through the same point. Prove that the numbers can be placed in the regions into which the lines divide the plane, such that the sums of the numbers on either side of any of the drawn lines are equal.
reference_solution:
Solution. Let us denote the drawn lines as $\ell_{1}, \ell_{2}, \ldots, \ell_{n}$, ordering their directions clockwise (see Fig. 5). Formally, this means the following. Consider an arbitrary point $O$ on the plane. Draw lines through it parallel to ours, number them clockwise, and then assign the same numbers to our lines as the new lines received.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_4a7c63dffbb4bfda6df0g-2.jpg?height=440&width=488&top_left_y=1010&top_left_x=2284)

Fig. 5 Among the regions into which our lines cut the plane, there are $2 n$ infinite pieces; denote them clockwise as $S_{1}, S_{2}, \ldots, S_{2 n}$ such that the line $\ell_{i}$ separates the pieces $S_{i}$ and $S_{i+1}$, as well as the pieces $S_{i+n}$ and $S_{i+n+1}$. (Here and below, we assume that $S_{2 n+1}=S_{1}$.)

First, place 1 in each region (finite and infinite). For each line $\ell_{i}$, let $\Sigma_{i}$ be the difference between the sums of the numbers to the right and to the left of $\ell_{i}$ (we consider that the pieces $S_{i}$ and $S_{i+n+1}$ lie to the left of $\ell_{i}$). If $\Sigma_{i}>0$, then add $\frac{1}{2} \Sigma_{i}$ to the numbers in $S_{i}$ and $S_{i+1+n}$. In this case, all numbers $\Sigma_{j}$ for $j \neq i$ remain unchanged, since the regions $S_{i}$ and $S_{i+1+n}$ lie on different sides of any line except $\ell_{i}$. The number $\Sigma_{i}$ becomes zero. Similarly, if $\Sigma_{i}<0$, then add $\frac{1}{2}|\Sigma_{i}|$ to the numbers in $S_{i+1}$ and $S_{i+n}$; again, $\Sigma_{i}$ becomes zero, and the other $\Sigma_{j}$ remain unchanged.

By such operations, we sequentially make each $\Sigma_{i}$ equal to zero without changing the others.

Remark. In some works, there may be an attempt to correct some initial arrangement by adding negative numbers to the numbers in the regions. In such a solution, one must be very careful to ensure that the final numbers in the regions remain positive; usually, achieving this is quite difficult.

Comment. If the work presents an algorithm that, by the end of its operation, may result in non-positive numbers in the regions - no more than 2 points for the problem.

question:
11.8. Initially, 100 cards are placed on the table, each with a natural number written on it; among them, exactly 28 cards have odd numbers. Then, every minute, the following procedure is carried out. For every 12 cards lying on the table, the product of the numbers written on them is calculated, all these products are summed, and the resulting number is written on a new card, which is added to those on the table. Can the initial 100 numbers be chosen such that for any natural number $d$, a card with a number divisible by $2^{d}$ will eventually appear on the table?

(I. Bogdanov)
reference_solution:
Answer. No, it cannot.

Solution. If at some moment there are exactly $k$ odd numbers among the numbers on the cards, then among the products of 12 numbers, there are exactly $C_{k}^{12}$ odd products; therefore, the number on the next added card will be odd if and only if $C_{k}^{12}$ is odd (and in that case, $k$ will increase by 1).

It is not hard to notice that the number $C_{28}^{12}$ is odd (this follows from the fact that the powers of two entering $28 \cdot 27 \cdot \ldots \cdot 17$ and $12 \cdot 11 \cdot \ldots \cdot 1$ are equal). Further, since $C_{28+t}^{12}=\frac{(28+1)(28+2) \ldots(28+t)}{(16+1)(16+2) \ldots(16+t)} \cdot C_{28}^{12}$, we get that the smallest $t$ for which $C_{28+t}^{12}$ is even is 4. Thus, the number of odd numbers on the cards will increase until it reaches 32 (on the 4th minute), and after that, there will always be exactly 32 odd numbers on the cards.

Consider the numbers on the cards after $n \geqslant 4$ minutes. Let $T_{n}$ be the sum of all products of 12 of these numbers, and $D_{n}$ be the sum of all products of 11 of these numbers. The number $T_{n+1}$ differs from $T_{n}$ by the addition of all products of 12 numbers, among which is the one just added, i.e., by the addition of $T_{n} E_{n}$; thus, $T_{n+1}=T_{n}+E_{n} T_{n}=T_{n}\left(1+E_{n}\right)$. Note that $E_{n} \equiv C_{32}^{11}(\bmod 2)$ for $n \geqslant 4$, and the number $C_{32}^{11}=\frac{12}{21} \cdot C_{32}^{12}$ is even. Therefore, for $n \geqslant 4$, the number $1+E_{n}$ is odd, and the power of two by which $T_{n+1}$ is divisible is equal to the power of two by which $T_{n}$ is divisible.

Now choose $d$ such that after the fifth minute, no number on the cards is divisible by $2^{d}$; in particular, the number just added, $T_{4}$, will also not be divisible by $2^{d}$. This means that none of the numbers $T_{5}, T_{6}, \ldots$ will be divisible by $2^{d}$, and these are precisely the numbers written on the cards added after the fifth minute. Thus, a number divisible by $2^{d}$ will never appear on the cards.

Comment. Only the correct answer - 0 points.

Described in which cases the number on the added card is odd (for example, as in the first paragraph of the solution) - 1 point.

Proved that, starting from the fifth minute, only even numbers are added - another 1 point is added.

question: 11.3. The midpoint of the edge $S A$ of the triangular pyramid $S A B C$ is equidistant from all vertices of the pyramid. Let $SH$ be the height of the pyramid. Prove that the point $H$ does not lie inside the triangle $A B C$.
reference_solution:
Solution. See fig.

question: 10.2. Given a convex quadrilateral with a perimeter of $10^{100}$, where the lengths of all sides are natural numbers, and the sum of the lengths of any three sides is divisible by the length of the remaining fourth side. Prove that this quadrilateral is a rhombus. (P. Kozhevnikov)

Solution. Let $a, b, c$ and $d$ be the lengths of the sides, and let $N=10^{100}$.

First solution. Suppose $d$ is the largest side. According to the condition, $a+b+c$ is divisible by $d$, that is, $a+b+c=k d$ for some natural number $k$. Moreover, since $a \leqslant d, b \leqslant d$ and $c \leqslant d$, we have $a+b+c \leqslant 3 d$, that is, $k \leqslant 3$.

The case $k=3$ is possible only if $a=b=c=d$. In this case, our quadrilateral is a rhombus.

question:
10.4. An infinite sequence of non-zero numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots$ is such that for all natural $n \geqslant 2018$ the number $a_{n+1}$ is the smallest root of the polynomial

$$
P_{n}(x)=x^{2 n}+a_{1} x^{2 n-2}+a_{2} x^{2 n-4}+\ldots+a_{n} .
$$

Prove that there exists an $N$ such that in the infinite sequence $a_{N}, a_{N+1}, a_{N+2}, \ldots$ each term is less than the previous one.
reference_solution:
Solution. Let $n \geqslant 2018$. Notice that $P_{n}(a)=P_{n}(-a)$ for all $a$. Therefore, since $P_{n}(x)$ has a non-zero root, it also has a negative root, from which it follows that $a_{n+1}<0$.

Furthermore, since $P_{n+1}(x)=x^{2} P_{n}(x)+a_{n+1}$, we have

$$
P_{n+1}\left(a_{n+1}\right)=a_{n+1}^{2} P_{n}\left(a_{n+1}\right)+a_{n+1}=0+a_{n+1}<0
$$

Since the degree of the polynomial $P_{n+1}(x)$ is even and the leading coefficient is positive, for sufficiently large negative $x$, it takes positive values. Now it follows from $(*)$ that this polynomial has a root in the interval $\left(-\infty, a_{n+1}\right)$. Therefore, $a_{n+2}<a_{n+1}$.

Thus, we have obtained that $a_{n+2}<a_{n+1}$ for all $n \geqslant 2018$. This means that the sequence $\left(a_{2019}, a_{2020}, a_{2021}, \ldots\right)$ is decreasing.

Comment. It is noted that $a_{n}<0$ if $n$ is sufficiently large - 1 point.

It is noted that the relation $P_{n+1}(x)=x^{2} P_{n}(x)+a_{n+1}$ holds - 1 point (can be combined with the previous point).

In an otherwise correct solution, it is claimed that the sequence is necessarily decreasing starting from the 2018th (rather than the 2019th) term - 1 point is deducted.

question:
10.5. In an isosceles triangle \(ABC\), the bisector \(BL\) is drawn. The extension of the median drawn from vertex \(B\) intersects the circumcircle \(\omega\) of triangle \(ABC\) at point \(D\). Through the center of the circumcircle of triangle \(BDL\), a line \(\ell\) is drawn parallel to the line \(AC\). Prove that the circumcircle \(\omega\) is tangent to the line \(\ell\).

(A. Kuznetsov)
reference_solution:
Solution. Let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $AC$, $S$ be the second intersection point of line $BL$ with circle $\omega$, and $N$ be the midpoint of arc $ABC$ (see Fig. 4). Then $S$ is the midpoint of the smaller arc $AC$ of circle $\omega$, and points $M, S, N$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of segment $AC$. Line $BN$ is the external bisector of angle $ABC$, so $BN \perp BL$. Then $\angle LBN + \angle LMN = 90^\circ + 90^\circ = 180^\circ$, from which we conclude that quadrilateral $BLMN$ is cyclic. Let $\angle MBL = \alpha$. Then $\angle MNL = \alpha$. Also, since

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_b90afe8f09b154de199fg-09.jpg?height=832&width=511&top_left_y=775&top_left_x=786)
$BND S$ is cyclic, $\angle SND = \angle SBD = \alpha$.

On the extension of segment $DN$ beyond point $N$, mark point $T$ such that $LN = NT$. Then $\angle LNT = 180^\circ - \angle LNM - \angle SND = 180^\circ - 2\alpha$, from which it follows that $\angle LTN = \angle TLN = \alpha$. Therefore, $\angle LTD = \alpha = \angle LBD$, so point $T$ lies on the circle $\Gamma$ circumscribed around triangle $BDL$. Let $\ell'$ be the tangent at point $N$ to circle $\omega$. Since $SN$ is the diameter of $\omega$, $\ell' \perp SN$ and $\ell' \parallel AC$. As we know, $SN$ is the external bisector of angle $LNT$, so $\ell'$ is the bisector of angle $LNT$. Since $TL = TN$, $\ell'$ is the perpendicular bisector of segment $TL$, and thus passes through the center of circle $\Gamma$. Therefore, lines $\ell$ and $\ell'$ coincide, and line $\ell$ is tangent to $\omega$.

question:
11.5. Do there exist 2013 different natural numbers such that the sum of any 2012 of them is not less than the square of the remaining one?

(O. Podlipsky)
reference_solution:
Answer. They do not exist.

Solution. Suppose such numbers were found. Since they are distinct and there are 2013 of them, the largest one is at least 2013; let's denote it by $a$. Then the sum of all the others does not exceed $2012a$, while its square is $a^{2} \geqslant 2013a$, meaning it is greater than this sum. Contradiction.

Comment. The maximum of the numbers was considered and it was noted that it is not less than 2013 - 2 points.

question:
1. The sum of the factorials of the first $k$ natural numbers is equal to the square of the sum of the first $n$ natural numbers.

a) Find all such pairs $(k, n)$ (3 points);

b) prove that there are no other pairs besides those found in part a) (4 points).

(For reference: The factorial of a natural number $m$ is the product of all numbers in sequence from 1 to $m$. It is denoted by $m!$. For example, $4!=4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1=24$. By definition, $1!=1$)
reference_solution: Solution. Obviously, the pairs $(1,1)$ and $(3,2)$ work: $1!=1^{2}=1$ and $1!+2!+3!=$ $(1+2)^{2}=9$. We will prove that there are no other suitable pairs. For $k=2$, we have $1!+2!=3$ - this is not a square of an integer. For $k=4$, we have $1!+2!+3!+4!=1+2+6+$ $24=33$ - also not a square. For $k \geqslant 5$, the subsequent terms in the sum of factorials all end in 0. Therefore, the sum of the factorials of the first $k$ natural numbers ends in the digit 3 for $k \geqslant 4$. But a perfect square cannot end in 3. Therefore, there are no solutions for $k \geqslant 4$.

question: 4. On the sides $AB, BC, CD$ and $DA$ of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, points $P, Q, R$ and $S$ are taken such that $BP: AB = CR: CD = 1: 3$ and $AS: AD = BQ: BC = 1: 4$. Prove that the segments $PR$ and $QS$ are divided by their point of intersection in the ratios $1: 3$ and $1: 2$.
reference_solution: Solution. Consider the auxiliary parallelogram $A B C D_{1}$. We can assume that points $D$ and $D_{1}$ do not coincide (otherwise, the statement of the problem is obvious). Take points $S_{1}$ and $R_{1}$ on sides $A D_{1}$ and $C D_{1}$ such that $S S_{1} \| D D_{1}$ and $R R_{1} \| D D_{1}$. Let $N$ be the intersection point of segments $P R_{1}$ and $Q S_{1}$; $N_{1}$ and $N_{2}$ be the intersection points of the line passing through $N$ parallel to $D D_{1}$ with segments $P R$ and $Q S$ respectively. Then $N_{1} N=\frac{1}{4} R R_{1}=\frac{1}{4} \cdot \frac{1}{3} D D_{1}$ and $N_{2} N=\frac{1}{3} S S_{1}=\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{4} D D_{1}$. Therefore, $N_{1}=N_{2}$ is the intersection point of segments $P R$ and $Q S$. It is clear that $P N_{1}: P R=P N: P R_{1}=1: 4$ and $Q N_{2}: Q S=1: 3$.

question: 8.2 In a triangle, one side is three times smaller than the sum of the other two. Prove that the angle opposite to it is the smallest angle in the triangle.
reference_solution:
8.2 In a triangle, one side is three times smaller than the sum of the other two. Prove that the angle opposite to it is the smallest angle in the triangle.

Solution: It is sufficient to prove that the given side is the smallest side of the triangle (the smaller side has the smaller angle opposite to it). Let $a$ be its length, $b$ and $c$ be the lengths of the other sides. According to the condition, $3a = b + c$. Therefore, $3a < b + a + b$, from which it follows that $a < b$. Similarly, $a < c$.

question: 8.3 On a grid board of $10 \times 20$, several cells are painted red. Kostya cut the board into rectangles along the grid lines such that each rectangle contained 5 red cells. Vlad cut the same board into rectangles such that each contained 7 red cells. Prove that Dima will not be able to cut the same board into rectangles such that each contains 6 red cells.
reference_solution:
8.3 On a grid board $10 \times 20$, several cells are painted red. Kostya cut the board into rectangles along the grid lines such that each rectangle contained 5 red cells. Vlad cut the same board into rectangles such that each contained 7 red cells. Prove that Dima cannot cut the same board into rectangles such that each contains 6 red cells.

Solution: Let $n$ be the total number of red cells. If $k$ is the number of Kostya's rectangles, then $n=5k$. Therefore, $n$ is divisible by 5. Similarly, $n$ is divisible by 7. If Kostya could cut the board into rectangles with 6 red cells, then $n$ would also be divisible by 6. Since the numbers 5, 6, and 7 are pairwise coprime, $n$ would be divisible by their product $5 \cdot 6 \cdot 7 = 210$. Therefore, $n \geq 210$. However, the board has only 200 cells.

question: 8.4 An infinite sequence of positive numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots$ is formed according to the rule: $a_{1}=1, a_{n+1}^{2}=a_{n}^{2}+\frac{1}{a_{n}}$ for $n=1,2,3, \ldots$ Prove that the sequence $b_{1}, b_{2}, b_{3}, \ldots$, where $b_{n}=a_{n+1}-a_{n}$, is decreasing, i.e., $b_{1}>b_{2}>b_{3}>\ldots$
reference_solution:
8.4 An infinite sequence of positive numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots$ is formed according to the rule: $a_{1}=1, a_{n+1}^{2}=a_{n}^{2}+\frac{1}{a_{n}}$ for $n=1,2,3, \ldots$. Prove that the sequence $b_{1}, b_{2}, b_{3}, \ldots$, where $b_{n}=a_{n+1}-a_{n}$, is decreasing, i.e., $\mathrm{b}_{1}>\mathrm{b}_{2}>\mathrm{b}_{3}>\ldots$

Solution: It is clear that $a_{n+1}>a_{n}$. We have $a_{n+1}^{2}-a_{n}^{2}=\frac{1}{a_{n}}$, $\left(a_{n+1}-a_{n}\right)\left(a_{n+1}+a_{n}\right)=\frac{1}{a_{n}}$,

$b_{n}=a_{n+1}-a_{n}=\frac{1}{a_{n}\left(a_{n+1}+a_{n}\right)}>\frac{1}{a_{n+1}\left(a_{n+2}+a_{n+1}\right)}=b_{n+1}$, since the denominator of the second fraction is greater than the denominator of the first fraction. Q.E.D.

question: 8.5 Around a circle, 10 iron weights are placed. Between each pair of adjacent weights, there is a bronze ball. The mass of each ball is equal to the difference in mass between its adjacent weights. Prove that the balls can be divided into two groups such that the scales will balance.
reference_solution:
8.5 Around a circle, 10 iron weights are placed. Between each pair of adjacent weights, there is a bronze ball. The mass of each ball is equal to the difference in mass between the adjacent weights. Prove that the balls can be divided into two groups such that the scales will balance.

Solution: Let \(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{10}\) be the masses of the weights in order as we move around the circle (say, clockwise). Then the masses of the balls between them are \(m_{1} = |a_{2} - a_{1}|, \quad m_{2} = |a_{3} - a_{2}|, \ldots, \quad m_{9} = |a_{10} - a_{9}|, \quad m_{10} = |a_{1} - a_{10}|.\) Therefore, \(a_{2} - a_{1} = \pm m_{1}\) with some sign + or, \(- a_{3} - a_{2} = \pm m_{2}\) with some sign + or, \(- a_{1} - a_{10} = \pm m_{10}\) with some sign + or - . The sum of the numbers \((a_{2} - a_{1}), (a_{3} - a_{2}), \ldots, (a_{10} - a_{9}), (a_{1} - a_{10})\) is equal to \(0\). Therefore, the sum \(\pm m_{1} \pm m_{2} \pm \ldots \pm m_{10}\), where the sign before each term is chosen as indicated above, is equal to 0. Consequently, the sum of those terms with a + sign is equal to the sum of those terms with a - sign. This gives the required division of the balls into two groups on the scales.

Petya ran down a moving escalator and counted 30 steps. Then he ran up the same escalator with the same speed relative to the escalator and counted 70 steps. How many steps would he have counted if he had gone down a stationary escalator?

Answer: 42.

Solution: Let $S$ be the length of the escalator in steps, $x$ be the speed of the escalator, and $V$ be Petya's own speed.

Petya's movement relative to the ground:

|  | $V$ | $t$ | $S$ |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Movement down | $V+x$ | $t_{1}$ | $(V+x) t_{1}=S$ |
| Movement up | $V-x$ | $t_{2}$ | $(V-x) t_{2}=S$ |

Petya's movement relative to the escalator:

|  | $V$ | $t$ | $S$ |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Movement down | $V$ | $t_{1}$ | 30 |
| Movement up | $V$ | $t_{2}$ | 70 |

We set up the system:

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
(V+x) t_{1}=S \\
(V-x) t_{2}=S \\
V \cdot t_{1}=30 \\
V \cdot t_{2}=70
\end{array}\right.
$$

Express

from

the last

equalities

$t_{1}, t_{2}$ and substitute into the first two equations respectively:

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
(V+x) \cdot \frac{30}{V}=S \\
(V-x) \cdot \frac{70}{V}=S
\end{array}\right.
$$

Solving this system for $S$, we get: $S=42$.

question:
# 10.3. (7 points)

Prove that for any non-zero numbers $a, b$ and at least one of the quadratic equations $a x^{2}+2 b x+c=0, b x^{2}+2 c x+a=0$ and $c x^{2}+2 a x+b=0$ has a root.
reference_solution:
Solution: We will prove by contradiction. Suppose the equations do not have real roots. Then $4 b^{2}-4 a c<0, 4 c^{2}-4 a b<0, 4 a^{2}-4 b c<0$.

Therefore, $b^{2}<a c, c^{2}<a b, a^{2}<b c$.

Since the right-hand sides are positive, the left-hand sides will also be positive, and we have the right to multiply the inequalities term by term. We get that $a^{2} b^{2} c^{2}<a^{2} b^{2} c^{2}$. We have reached a contradiction. Therefore, at least one equation has a root.

question:
# 10.4. (7 points)

Prove that if in an arbitrary quadrilateral $A B C D$ internal angle bisectors are drawn, then the four points of intersection of the bisectors of angles $A$ and $C$ with the bisectors of angles $B$ and $D$ lie on a single circle.

#
reference_solution:
# Solution:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_29cbc05fa9d64c546048g-2.jpg?height=571&width=948&top_left_y=1351&top_left_x=700)

Let $A P, B Q, C R, D S$ be the angle bisectors of the internal angles of quadrilateral $A B C D$, and let $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \varphi$ be the measures of these angles. Then,

$$
\angle A S D=180^{\circ}-\frac{\alpha}{2}-\frac{\varphi}{2}, \quad \angle B Q C=180^{\circ}-\frac{\beta}{2}-\frac{\gamma}{2} .
$$

Adding these equations:

$$
\angle A S D+\angle B Q C=360^{\circ}-\frac{1}{2}(\alpha+\beta+\varphi+\gamma)=360^{\circ}-\frac{1}{2} \cdot 360^{\circ}=180^{\circ}
$$

Or

$$
\angle P S R+\angle P Q R=180^{\circ} .
$$

Therefore, points $P, S, R, Q$ lie on the same circle.

question:
11.5. Given a natural number $n>1$. Prove that there exist such $n$ consecutive natural numbers that their product is divisible by all prime numbers not exceeding $2 n+1$, and is not divisible by any other prime number.

(I. Bogdanov)
reference_solution:
11.5. Suppose that the number $n+1$ is composite; we will show that then the numbers $n+2, \ldots, 2 n+1$ work. Clearly, their product is divisible by all prime numbers in the interval $[n+2,2 n+1]$, but is not divisible by prime numbers greater than $2 n+1$ (since all factors do not exceed $2 n+1$). For any prime $p \leqslant n$, one of $p$ consecutive numbers is divisible by $p$; hence, one of our $n$ numbers is also divisible by $p$.

Now suppose the number $n+1>2$ is prime; then it is odd, and the number $n+2>2$ is even and therefore composite. In this case, the numbers $n+3, \ldots, 2 n+2$ work. Indeed, for similar reasons, their product $P$ is divisible by all prime numbers in the intervals $[1, n]$ and $[n+3,2 n+2]$, but is not divisible by prime numbers greater than $2 n+1$ (since the number $2 n+2$ is composite). Moreover, $P$ is divisible by $n+1=\frac{2 n+2}{2}$

question: 11.6. Can the 4 centers of the circles inscribed in the faces of a tetrahedron lie in the same plane? (I. Bogdanov, O. Podlipsky)
reference_solution:
11.6. Answer. They cannot.

Let $I_{A}, I_{B}, I_{C}, I_{D}$ be the centers of the inscribed circles of triangles $B C D, A C D, A B D, A B C$ respectively. Suppose they lie in the same plane. Then either they form a convex quadrilateral, or one of these points lies inside the triangle formed by the other three.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_cd2a505f44b1268d3f6cg-1.jpg?height=362&width=518&top_left_y=475&top_left_x=1695)

Fig. 5

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_cd2a505f44b1268d3f6cg-1.jpg?height=299&width=432&top_left_y=503&top_left_x=2282)

Fig. 6
Case 1. Suppose without loss of generality that $I_{A} I_{B} I_{C} I_{D}$ is a convex quadrilateral: then the segments $I_{A} I_{C}$ and $I_{B} I_{D}$ intersect. Let $M, N, K, L$ be the midpoints of the edges $A B$, $A D, C D, B C$ respectively (see Fig. 5). Consider triangle $A B C$. Draw a line $\ell$ through point $B$ parallel to $A C$; then the inscribed circle of this triangle lies between the lines $\ell$ and $A C$, touching $A C$ but not touching $\ell$. This means that points $I_{D}$ and $B$ lie on opposite sides of the midline $M L$ (see Fig. 6). Similarly, we obtain that points $I_{B}$ and $I_{D}$ will be on one side of the plane $M N K L$, and points $I_{A}$ and $I_{C}$ on the other. But then the segments $I_{B} I_{D}$ and $I_{A} I_{C}$ cannot intersect - a contradiction.

Case 2. It remains to show that point $I_{A}$ cannot lie inside triangle $I_{B} I_{C} I_{D}$. This follows from the fact that points $I_{B}, I_{C}, I_{D}$ lie strictly on one side of the plane $B C D$, while point $I_{A}$ lies in this plane.

question:
11.8. In a boarding school, 9 subjects are taught and 512 children are enrolled, accommodated in 256 double rooms (children living in the same room are called neighbors). It is known that any two children have different sets of subjects they are interested in (in particular, exactly one child is not interested in anything). Prove that all the children can be arranged in a circle so that any two neighbors stand next to each other, and for any two non-neighbors standing next to each other, one of them is interested in all the subjects the other is interested in, plus exactly one additional subject.

(D. Fon-Der-Flaass)
reference_solution:
11.8. We will prove the statement of the problem in a more general form, for $n \geqslant 2$ items and $2^{n}$ children, arbitrarily divided into $2^{n-1}$ pairs of neighbors. Note that there are exactly $2^{n}$ sets of $n$ items; hence, each set of items is interesting to exactly one student.

Induction on $n$. For $n=2$, the statement can be easily verified directly. Let $n>2$; consider any two neighbors, choose some item that they have different interests in (say, physics), and divide all the children into two groups of $2^{n-1}$ children: group $A$ will include those who are interested in physics, and group $B$ will include all the others.

Isolate group $A$ in another boarding school, with $2^{n-2}$ rooms. In this case, we will keep the pairs that were neighbors before as neighbors. The others (according to the choice of the item, they exist; and their number is obviously even) will be divided into pairs of neighbors arbitrarily. We will call such pairs "new."

By the induction hypothesis, now group $A$ can be arranged in a circle $K$ satisfying the conditions. Let $\left(x_{1}, x_{2}\right), \ldots$, $\left(x_{2 k-1}, x_{2 k}\right)$ be all the new pairs in the order of traversal of this circle clockwise ( $x_{2 i-1}$ is in front of $x_{2 i}$; we will assume that $x_{2 k+1}=x_{1}$ ). Denote by $x_{i}^{\prime}$ the original neighbor of person $x_{i}$ (by construction, $x_{i}^{\prime}$ is in group $B$), and declare pairs $\left(x_{2}^{\prime}, x_{3}^{\prime}\right), \ldots,\left(x_{2 k-2}^{\prime}, x_{2 k-1}^{\prime}\right),\left(x_{2 k}^{\prime}, x_{1}^{\prime}\right)$ as "new" pairs in group $B$. Clearly, the new pairs, together with the old ones, give us a partition of group $B$ into pairs of neighbors.

Now, applying the induction hypothesis to group $B$ with this partition, arrange it in a circle satisfying the conditions. Insert now between any children of the new pair $\left(x_{2 i}^{\prime}, x_{2 i+1}^{\prime}\right)$ the segment of circle $K$ from $x_{2 i}$ to $x_{2 i+1}$. It is not difficult to see that now all the children are standing in a circle, and the arrangement satisfies all the conditions.
