$$

From triangle $L B N$ we see that the right side of this equality is $N L$, and the left side, by the sine theorem for triangle $B C K$, is equal to twice the radius of the circle, which

question: 58. On the base $AD$ of trapezoid $ABCD$, a point $E$ is marked. It is known that $\angle CAD = \angle ADC = \angle ABE = \angle DBE$. Prove that triangle $BCE$ is isosceles.
reference_solution: 58. Let $\alpha$ denote the angle $C A D$ and the angles equal to it. Let $C^{\prime}$ be the point symmetric to point $C$ with respect to the line $A D$. Then $A C D C^{\prime}$ is a rhombus. In triangle $A D C^{\prime}: 180^{\circ}=\angle A C^{\prime} D+2 \alpha=\angle A C^{\prime} D+\angle A B D$, so the quadrilateral $A B D C^{\prime}$ is cyclic. Then $\angle A D C^{\prime}=\angle A B C^{\{\prime}}=\alpha=\angle A B E$. Therefore, the line $B C^{\prime}$ passes through point $E$, and then $E$ is the midpoint of segment $B C^{\prime}$. Consequently, $E C=E C^{\prime}=B E$.

question: 60. From point $O$, rays $\ell, \ell_{1}, \ell_{2}$ emanate, the angle between $\ell$ and $\ell_{2}$ is acute, and ray $\ell_{1}$ lies inside this angle. On ray $\ell$ lies a fixed point $F$ and an arbitrary point $L$. Through points $F$ and $L$ pass a circle tangent to ray $\ell_{1}$ at point $L_{1}$, and a circle tangent to ray $\ell_{2}$ at point $L_{2}$. Prove that the circle $F L_{1} L_{2}$ passes through some point, different from point $F$ and independent of the choice of point $L$.
reference_solution: 60. Note that $O F \cdot O L=O L_{1}^{2}=O L_{2}^{2}$. Therefore, the perpendicular bisector of the segment $L_{1} L_{2}$ coincides with the bisector of the angle $L_{1} O L_{2}$. Hence, any circle passing through the points $L_{1}$ and $L_{2}$ is symmetric with respect to this bisector. This means that the circle passing through the points $F, L_{1}$, and $L_{2}$ also passes through the point $F^{\prime}$, which is symmetric to the point $F$ with respect to the bisector of the angle $L_{1} O L_{2}$.

61. A social network can be represented as a graph where people are vertices and the "friendship" relationship is the edges. It is sufficient to consider the case where this graph is a tree. According to the conditions of the problem, a group with 1 to 100 members will be called small, and a group with 100 to 900 members will be called large. We will prove the statement of the problem by induction on the number of users in the network. Base of induction: \( n \leqslant \) 900. If there are no more than 100 users in the network, we will declare them all a small group. If there are from 101 to 900 users in the network, we will designate a small group as any user corresponding to a pendant vertex, and all the others will be recorded in the large group.

Inductive step. It is sufficient to check that if the number of users is greater than 900, then it is possible to select a large group, the removal of which will leave the graph connected. Let's suspend our tree and consider the vertex \( A \) (one of the vertices) farthest from the root, which has more than 900 descendants. Each of the children of vertex \( A \) has no more than 900 descendants, and the number of children is no more than 9. If each of the children of \( A \) has no more than 99 descendants, then in total \( A \) has no more than \( 9 \cdot 99 < 900 \) descendants, which contradicts the choice of vertex \( A \). Therefore, one of the children of \( A \) has from 100 to 900 descendants, and we will designate him and his descendants as a large group.

question: 68. Let's consider the mathematicians' acquaintance graph. By condition, this graph is chordal, i.e., any cycle of 4 or more vertices contains a chord (a pair of adjacent vertices not adjacent in the cycle). We will prove that for a chordal graph $G$, the expression $f(G):=c_{1}-c_{2}+c_{3}-\ldots$, where $c_{i}$ is the number of cliques in $G$ with $i$ vertices, equals the number $k(G)$ of connected components of the graph $G$.
reference_solution:
Solution 1. Assume the contrary and consider $G$ as the smallest counterexample in terms of the number of vertices. It is clear that the graph $G$ contains more than one vertex and is connected (otherwise, one of the connected components would be a smaller counterexample). Remove an arbitrary vertex $v$ from the graph $G$, and let the new graph $G \backslash v$ split into components $G_{1}, \ldots, G_{k}$. Let $H_{1}$, $H_{2}, \ldots, H_{k}$ be the subgraphs in $G_{1}, \ldots, G_{k}$, respectively, on the neighbors of vertex $v$. It is not hard to see that

$$
f(G)=1+\sum_{i=1}^{k} f\left(G_{i}\right)-\sum_{i=1}^{k} f\left(H_{i}\right)
$$

where the term 1 corresponds to the clique $\{v\}$, the terms $f\left(G_{i}\right)$ correspond to cliques not containing $v$, and the terms $-f\left(H_{i}\right)$ correspond to cliques containing $v$ (upon removing vertex $v$ from them, the parity changes, and thus the sign in the expression for $f$ changes). Due to the minimality of the counterexample, $f\left(G_{i}\right)=1, f\left(H_{i}\right)=k\left(H_{i}\right)$. We will check that $k\left(H_{i}\right)=1$ for all $i$. Suppose the contrary, then the vertices of one of the graphs $H_{i}$ can be partitioned into two non-empty subsets $V^{-}, V^{+}$ such that no edge connects $V^{-}$ to $V^{+}$. Consider the shortest path $x \ldots y$ from $V^{-}$ to $V^{+}$ in the graph $G_{i}$. Then the cycle $v x \ldots y v$ has no chord in the graph $G$.

We have verified that $f\left(H_{i}\right)=f\left(G_{i}\right)$ for all $i$. Then, by formula (*), $f(G)=1=k(G)$, i.e., the graph $G$ turned out to be a non-counterexample.

Solution 2. We call a vertex admissible if all its neighbors are pairwise adjacent to each other.

Lemma. In a chordal graph with at least two vertices, there are at least two admissible vertices.

Proof. Assuming the contrary, consider the smallest counterexample by the number of vertices - the graph $G$. Note that $G$ has no vertex $v$ adjacent to all others (otherwise, $G \backslash v$ would be a smaller counterexample). Let $v$ be an inadmissible vertex in $G$, $N$ be the set of neighbors of vertex $v$, and $H=G \backslash(N \cup v)$ be the graph on the remaining vertices. Note that if $u_{1}, u_{2}$ are non-adjacent neighbors of $v$, then there is no path from $u_{1}$ to $u_{2}$ with all intermediate vertices in $H$ - otherwise, the smallest path by the number of edges, supplemented by the path $u_{2} v u_{1}$, would be a cycle without a chord. Let $H_{1}$ be one of the connected components of the graph $H$, and $N_{1}$ be the set of vertices in $N$ that have a neighbor in $H_{1}$. By the proven fact, $N_{1}$ is a clique, so $N_{1} \neq N$. Consider the (chordal, of course) graph on the vertices $v, N_{1}, H_{1}$. In it, due to the minimality of the counterexample, there is an admissible vertex $w$ different from $v$. It cannot belong to $N_{1}$ because each vertex in $N_{1}$ has neighbors $v$ and some vertex in $H_{1}$. Therefore, it belongs to $H_{1}$ and is admissible in $G$. To find an admissible vertex different from $w$, repeat the reasoning, taking as the initial vertex $v$ a neighbor of vertex $w$.

Returning to the solution of the problem, we will reason by induction on the number of vertices. For an admissible vertex $v$, the inductive step from the graph $G \backslash v$ to the graph $G$ is very simple: if it is isolated, the sum of interest increases by 1; otherwise, neither the sum nor the number of connected components changes.

question:
57. Let's color the vertices of a 2018-gon in two colors such that any two adjacent vertices are of different colors. If the sum of the angles at the vertices of one color is equal to the sum of the angles at the vertices of the other color, we will call such a 2018-gon interesting. In a convex 2019-gon, one vertex is marked. It turns out that removing any unmarked vertex leaves an interesting 2018-gon. Prove that removing the marked vertex also leaves an interesting 2018-gon.

(A. Kuznetsov)
reference_solution:
57. Let's denote the adjacent vertices of the 2019-gon by the letters $A, B, C$ and $D$ (clockwise). Suppose vertices $B$ and $C$ are not marked. Consider the angles of the 2019-gon, taken every other one counterclockwise, starting from $A$ and ending at $D$. Denote their sum by $u$. Consider the remaining angles, and denote their sum by $v$. Since removing vertex $B$ results in an interesting 2018-gon, we have the equality of the sums of the angles

\[
u - \angle CAB = v - \angle ACB - \angle ABC
\]

(The angle $\angle B$ does not belong to this polygon, and the angles $\angle A$ and $\angle C$ must be reduced by $\angle CAB$ and $\angle ACB$ respectively). Similarly, since removing vertex $C$ results in an interesting 2018-gon, we have the equality of the sums of the angles

\[
u - \angle CDB = v - \angle CBD - \angle BCD
\]

Subtracting equality $(**)$ from equality $(*)$, we get

\[
\angle CAB - \angle CDB = \angle ACB + \angle ABC - \angle CBD - \angle BCD = \angle ABD - \angle ACD
\]

Adding to this the valid equality $\angle CAB + \angle ABD = \angle CDB + \angle ACD$, we obtain that $\angle CAB = \angle CDB$. Therefore, the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is cyclic. Note also that the converse is true. Specifically, if equality $(*)$ holds (i.e., the 2018-gon without vertex $B$ is interesting) and the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is cyclic, then equality $(**)$ also holds, meaning that the 2018-gon without vertex $C$ is interesting.

By acting in this manner sequentially, we will prove that the original 2019-gon is cyclic. Consequently, if we consider a marked vertex $P$ and its adjacent vertex $Q$, then from the interestingness of the 2018-gon without vertex $Q$ and the cyclic nature of the 2019-gon, we will obtain that the 2018-gon without vertex $P$ is interesting.

question:
59. The coefficients of the polynomial $f(x)$ are integers, in absolute value not exceeding 5000000. Moreover, each of the equations

$$
f(x)=x, \quad f(x)=2 x, \quad \ldots, \quad f(x)=20 x
$$

has an integer root. Prove that $f(0)=0$.

(M. Antipov)
reference_solution:
59. We will prove that $f(0)$ is divisible by all prime numbers less than 20, from which it will follow that $f(0)=0$, since this product is too large.

Indeed, suppose $f(0)$ is not divisible by some $p$. Then $x \equiv 0(\bmod p)$ cannot be a solution to any of the equations in the condition (the left side is not divisible by $p$, while the right side is).

But it is obvious that the solutions to the equations $f(x)=x, f(x)=2 x, \ldots f(x)=p x$ must give pairwise distinct remainders when divided by $p$, provided that these remainders are non-zero. However, we have $p$ equations, and there are $p-1$ possible remainders - a contradiction.

question: 60. Given a cyclic quadrilateral $A B C D$. A line perpendicular to $B D$ intersects segments $A B$, $B C$ and rays $D A$, $D C$ at points $P, Q, R, S$ respectively. It is known that $P R=Q S$. Prove that the midpoint of segment $P Q$ is equidistant from points $A$ and $C$.
reference_solution:
60. Let $T$ be the midpoint of segment $P Q$. Suppose point $A^{\prime}$ is symmetric to point $A$ with respect to point $T$. Triangles $S A^{\prime} Q$ and $R A P$ are symmetric and, therefore, equal. Then

$$
\angle S A^{\prime} Q=\angle R A P=180^{\circ}-\angle B A D=\angle Q C D
$$

Thus, point $A^{\prime}$ lies on the circle $C Q S$. Let's check that angle $\angle A^{\prime} C A$ is a right angle. Indeed, note that $\angle A^{\prime} C Q=\angle A^{\prime} S Q=\angle P R A, \angle B C A=\angle B D A$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_d6d52d604bd4c064fabfg-3.jpg?height=352&width=434&top_left_y=41&top_left_x=1553)

Adding these equalities, we get that

$$
\angle A^{\prime} C A=\angle A^{\prime} C Q+\angle B C A=\angle P R A+\angle B D A=90^{\circ}
$$

Now the statement of the problem follows from the fact that in the right triangle $A A^{\prime} C$, the median is equal to half the hypotenuse.

question:
61. Let \(a, b, c, d > 0\). Prove the inequality

\[
a^{4} + b^{4} + c^{4} + d^{4} - 4abcd \geq 4(a - b)^{2} \sqrt{abcd}
\]

(S. Gorsky, F. Petrov)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_9edb286abaeee11d94cfg-1.jpg?height=294&width=334&top_left_y=1321&top_left_x=1638)

26. In the tetrahedron $A B C D$, the median $A E$ of face $A B C$ is perpendicular to edge $B D$, and the median $A F$ of face $A B D$ is perpendicular to edge $B C$. Prove that edge $A B$ is perpendicular to edge $C D$.

(A. Golev)
reference_solution:
26. Let $\vec{b}=\overrightarrow{A B}, \vec{c}=\overrightarrow{A C}, \vec{d}=\overrightarrow{A D}$. Then $\overrightarrow{B D}=\vec{d}-\vec{b}, \overrightarrow{B C}=\vec{c}-\vec{b}, \overrightarrow{C D}=\vec{d}-\vec{c}$. The vectors along the medians are $\overrightarrow{A E}=\frac{1}{2}(\vec{b}+\vec{c})$ and $\overrightarrow{A F}=\frac{1}{2}(\vec{b}+\vec{d})$. The conditions $A E \perp B D$ and $A F \perp B C$ can be rewritten in terms of the dot product:

$$
(\vec{b}+\vec{c})(\vec{d}-\vec{b})=0 \quad \text { and } \quad(\vec{b}+\vec{d})(\vec{c}-\vec{b})=0
$$

Expanding the brackets and subtracting the second equation from the first, we get: $2(\vec{b} \cdot \vec{d}-\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c})=0$, i.e., $\vec{b} \cdot (\vec{d}-\vec{c})=0$. This means that the vectors $\overrightarrow{A B}$ and $\overrightarrow{C D}$ are perpendicular.

question: 5. The altitudes $A A_{1}, B B_{1}, C C_{1}$ of an acute triangle $A B C$ intersect at point $H$. A perpendicular $H Q$ is dropped from point $H$ to the tangent line drawn from point $C$ to the circumcircle of triangle $A B_{1} C_{1}$ (point $Q$ lies inside triangle $A B C$). Prove that the circle passing through point $B_{1}$ and tangent to line $A B$ at point $A$ is also tangent to line $A_{1} Q$.
reference_solution:
Solution. Let the circle $(A B_{1} C_{1})$ be denoted by $s_{1}$, and the circle passing through point $B_{1}$ and tangent to the line $A B$ at point $A$ - by $s_{2}$. The chords $B_{1} C_{1}$ and $B_{1} A$ of these circles cut off arcs of the same angular magnitude. Indeed, the halves of these arcs in both cases are equal to $\angle B_{1} A C_{1}$: for the circle $s_{1}$, this is an inscribed angle, and for $s_{2}$, it is the angle between the tangent and the chord.

Consider a rotational homothety with center at point $B_{1}$, mapping $C_{1}$ to $A$ and $C$ to $A_{1}$: triangles $B_{1} C_{1} A$ and $B_{1} C A_{1}$ are similar (and similar to triangle $B A C$). The circle $s_{1}$ will transform into $s_{2}$, since the chords $B_{1} C_{1}$ and $B_{1} A$, which cut off equal arcs, transform into each other. Since point $C$ maps to $A_{1}$, the secant $C C_{1}$ of the circle $s_{1}$ transforms into the secant $A_{1} A$ of the circle $s_{2}$, and the tangent $C Q$ to the circle $s_{1}$ - into the tangent from point $A_{1}$ to $s_{2}$. Thus, the angles between the secant and the tangent in both cases are equal. It remains to note that the angle between $C C_{1}$ and $C Q$ is equal to the angle between $A_{1} A$ and $A_{1} Q$: these inscribed angles subtend the same arc $H Q$ in the circle with diameter $C H$.

question: 29. On September 1st, children brought roses and carnations to school. 101 boys and 3 girls stood in a circle, each holding all their flowers. It turned out that each boy had exactly 50 flowers. At the principal's signal, each child passed all their carnations to the child on their left. After this, it turned out that each boy had exactly 49 flowers. Prove that no two girls stood next to each other.
reference_solution: 29. If a boy received $k$ nails from the neighbor on the right, then he himself passed $k+1$ nails to the neighbor on the left. Since each boy has no more than 50 nails, no more than 50 boys can stand in a row. Therefore, there are at least three groups of boys standing in a row. Since there are only 3 girls in total, this is possible only when there are exactly three groups of boys, and exactly one girl stands between adjacent groups. In particular, the girls do not stand next to each other.

question: 32. A ten-digit number is written on the board. You can take any digit of this number that is less than 8, add 1 or 2 to it, and write the resulting new number on the board instead of the old one. This operation was performed 55 times. Prove that at least one of the 56 numbers written on the board in this experiment was composite.
reference_solution: 32. To ensure the number never divides by 3 at any point, one must alternately add ones and twos, i.e., either $82=1+2+\cdots+1$, or $83=2+1+\cdots+2$. But the last digit could increase by no more than 2 (from 1 to 3, or from 7 to 9), the first digit by no more than 8, and the rest by no more than 9. Thus, no more than 82 was added, i.e., exactly 82, and the first was a one. But then the original number must have been 1000000001 or 1000000007, and after the first move, it would be divisible by 3.

question: 34. In the gym, 200 schoolchildren gathered. Every pair of acquaintances shook hands. It turned out that any two strangers made at least 200 handshakes in total. Prove that there were at least 10000 handshakes in total.
reference_solution:
34. Let's write the solution in the language of graphs. If the degree of a vertex is not less than 100, we call it rich; if it is less than 100, we call it poor. From the condition, it follows that all poor vertices are pairwise adjacent to each other.

We will prove that each poor vertex can be paired with a non-adjacent rich vertex such that different poor vertices correspond to different rich vertices. Suppose we have constructed pairs for $k$ poor vertices. If there are still poor vertices left, then $k < 100$. Take the next poor vertex; it is non-adjacent to at least 100 (rich) vertices. Out of these, no more than $k$ have already been paired with some poor vertex, so there will be at least one that has not yet been included in any pair.

As a result, we have several non-adjacent pairs of vertices, and in each such pair, the sum of the degrees is at least 200, and there are still several rich vertices with a degree of at least 100. In total, the sum of all degrees is at least $200 \cdot 100$, and the number of edges is at least 10000.

12. Solution 1. Mark a point \( E' \) on the segment \( AD \) such that \( DE' = DE \). Notice that then triangles \( BDE' \) and \( CDE \) are equal by two sides and the angle, which means \( BE' = CE \). We need to check that the perimeter of triangle \( ADC \) is greater than the perimeter of quadrilateral \( ABDE \), i.e., that

\[
A E' + E' D + D C + A E + E C > B D + A B + A E + E D
\]

Remove the common segment \( A E \) from both sides, the equal segments \( D C = B D \), \( E' D = E D \), and replace \( E C \) with \( E' B \) in the left part, we get the inequality

\[
A E' + E' B > A B
\]

This is the triangle inequality for triangle \( A E' B \).
reference_solution:
Solution 2. Construct triangle $D A^{\prime} C$ symmetric to triangle $D A B$ with respect to the perpendicular bisector of segment $B C$. Then $A D=A^{\prime} D=A^{\prime} E+E D$, $A B=A^{\prime} C$. Remove the equal segments $B D=D C$ from the perimeters of triangle $A D C$ and quadrilateral $A B D E$. Then we need to prove the inequality

$$

question: 26. In a kindergarten group, there are 26 children. When the children went out for a walk, each had two mittens of the same color, and the mittens of different children were of different colors. During the walk, the children formed pairs three times (not necessarily in the same way). During the first formation, the children in each pair exchanged left mittens, and during the second formation, they exchanged right mittens. When they formed pairs for the third time, it turned out that each pair of children had two mittens of one color and two of another. Prove that at this moment, there is a child with matching mittens.
reference_solution:
26. If child A is wearing mittens of colors x and y (x on the left hand, y on the right), we will denote this fact by the notation $\mathrm{A}(\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y})$.

If any child exchanges mittens twice with the same child, they will end up with two identical mittens. Therefore, we will assume that this did not happen. Let's take an arbitrary child $\mathrm{A}(1,1)$ just before the first exchange. Suppose he exchanges for the first time with $\mathrm{B}(2,2)$, and for the second time with child $\mathrm{C}$, while child $\mathrm{C}(3,3)$ exchanges for the first time with $\mathrm{D}(4,4)$. After the first exchanges, we get: $\mathrm{A}(2,1), \mathrm{B}(1,2), \mathrm{C}(4,3), \mathrm{D}(3,4)$. After the second exchange between A and C, we get: $\mathrm{A}(2,3), \mathrm{C}(4,1)$. For the third pairing, child A needs another child with mittens of colors 2 and 3. But such a child can only appear after the second exchange if $\mathrm{B}(1,2)$ exchanges with $\mathrm{D}(3,4)$. In this case, during the third pairing, $\mathrm{A}(2,3)$ will be paired with $\mathrm{D}(3,2)$, and child $\mathrm{B}(1,4)$ will be paired with $\mathrm{C}(4,1)$.

Thus, all children must be divided into groups of four (each group of four can be split into three pairs in three different ways). But the number of children is not divisible by 4, so such a division is impossible!

question:
28. Given natural numbers $m$ and $n (m < n)$ and a large chocolate bar, the sides of which are divisible by $n^5$. (All chocolate bars in this problem are grid rectangles, with the side of each cell equal to 1.) Lesha ate several cells five times such that each time a smaller chocolate bar was left, the area of which was $\frac{m}{n}$ of the area of the previous chocolate bar. Prove that he can eat several more cells so that a very small chocolate bar is left, the area of which is $\left(\frac{m}{n}\right)^{10}$ of the area of the original large chocolate bar.

(O. Ivanova)
reference_solution: 28. Let the original chocolate bar have dimensions $a n^{5} \times b n^{5}$. Then its area was $a b n^{10}$. Suppose after five bites, the resulting chocolate bar is $x \times y$ with an area of $x y = a b m^{5} n^{5}$. Since $x \leqslant a n^{5}, y \leqslant b n^{5}$, then $x \geqslant b m^{5}, y \geqslant a m^{5}$. This means that the chocolate bar $x \times y$ can be reduced to dimensions $b m^{5} \times a m^{5}$, and this chocolate bar differs in area from the chocolate bar $x \times y$ by a factor of $(m / n)^{5}$.

question:
42. Hooligan Vasya is dissatisfied with his average math grade, which has dropped below 3. As a measure to sharply improve his grade, he managed to get to the school journal and changed all his twos to threes. Prove that after this, his average grade will still not exceed 4.

(K. Tyschuk $)$
reference_solution: 42. Let Vasya receive $a$ units, $b$ twos, $c$ threes, $d$ fours, and $e$ fives. Then, by the condition, $a+2b+3c+4d+5e+2e$, from which $a+b>e$. It is required to prove that $2b+3(a+c)+4d+5e \leqslant 4(a+b+c+d+e)$, which is equivalent to the inequality $a+2b+c \geqslant e$. This easily follows from the derived inequality $a+b>e$.

question: 43. Triangles $A B C$ and $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ are such that $\angle A=\angle A_{1}$ and $\angle B+\angle B_{1}=180^{\circ}$. Prove that if $A_{1} B_{1}=$ $A C+B C$, then $A B=A_{1} C_{1}-B_{1} C_{1}$.
reference_solution: 43. Let's mark a point \( B' \) on the ray \( AC \) (beyond point \( C \)) such that \( CB' = CB \). Then, by the condition, \( AB' = A_1B_1 \). Let's mark a point \( C' \) on the ray \( AB \) such that \( \triangle AB'C' = \triangle A_1B_1C_1 \). The point \( C' \) will fall on the extension of side \( AB \) beyond point \( B \), since otherwise \( \angle ABC + \angle C'B'A \leq \angle ABB' + \angle BB'A < 180^\circ \), which contradicts the condition \( \angle B + \angle B_1 = 180^\circ \). Since \( CB' = CB \) and \( \angle CB'C' = 180^\circ - \angle ABC = \angle CBC' \), the quadrilateral \( CBC'B' \) is symmetric with respect to the diagonal \( CC' \). Therefore, triangles \( BCC' \) and \( B'CC' \) are equal. From this, we obtain the required: \( AB = AC' - BC' = AC' - B'C' = A_1C_1 - B_1C_1 \).

question:
45. A natural number $n$ has exactly 1000 natural divisors (including 1 and $n$ itself). These 1000 divisors are listed in ascending order. It turns out that any two consecutive divisors have different parity. Prove that the number $n$ has more than 150 digits.

( $\Phi$. Petrov $)$

36. In a convex quadrilateral $A B C D$, the angles at vertices $A, B$ and $C$ are equal. A point $E$ is marked on side $A B$. It is known that $A D=C D=B E$. Prove that $C E$ is the bisector of angle $B C D . \quad(A$. Kuznetsov)
reference_solution:
36. Since $A D=C D$, then $\angle D A C=\angle D C A$, this together with $\angle A=\angle C$ means that $\angle B A C=\angle B C A$, so $A B=B C$. Then triangles $B D A$ and $B D C$ are equal by three sides. From this it follows that $B D$ is the bisector of angle $A B C$, and moreover, triangles $B C D$ and $C B E$ are equal by the first criterion, from which

$$
\angle B C E=\angle C B D=\frac{\angle A B C}{2}=\frac{\angle B C D}{2}
$$

so $C E$ is the bisector of angle $B C D$.

question: 37. Several people are standing in a row, some of them are knights who always tell the truth, while the others are liars who always lie. Each of them said one of two phrases: There are more knights to the right of me than to the left or There are more knights to the left of me than to the right, and the number of people who said each phrase was equal. Then each of them said one of two phrases: There are more liars to the right of me than to the left or There are more liars to the left of me than to the right. Prove that again both phrases were said an equal number of times.
reference_solution:
37. We will call the phrase "To my right, there are more knights than to my left" the first phrase, and the phrase "To my left, there are more knights than to my right" the second phrase. The number of knights cannot be odd, because in that case, the central knight (who has an equal number of knights on both sides) could not say either the first or the second phrase. Therefore, the number of knights is even, and there exists a pair of "central" knights A and B (A stands to the left of B, with no other knights between them, and there are as many knights to the left of A as there are to the right of B). Then A and all the knights to the left of him say the first phrase, while B and all the knights to the right of him say the second phrase. Therefore, the knights say the first and second phrases an equal number of times, and thus the liars also say these phrases an equal number of times. This means the number of liars is even.

Let V and \(\Gamma\) be a pair of central liars (V stands to the left of \(\Gamma\), with no other liars between them, and there are as many liars to the left of V as there are to the right of \(\Gamma\)). If V stood to the right of B, then to the left of V, \(\Gamma\), and the liars standing to the right of \(\Gamma\), there would be more knights than to the right, so all the mentioned liars (more than half of the liars) would have said the first phrase, which is impossible. Therefore, V stands to the left of B. If \(\Gamma\) stands to the right of B, then there would be an equal number of liars on both sides of B, and he would have nothing to say the second time, so \(\Gamma\) must also be to the left of B. Similarly, V and \(\Gamma\) are positioned to the right of A. In particular, V and \(\Gamma\) stand between A and B. It remains to note that then V, together with the liars to the left of him, and B, together with the knights to the right of him, will say the phrase "To my left, there are more liars than to my right," while \(\Gamma\), all the liars to the right of \(\Gamma\), A, and all the knights to the left of A will say the phrase "To my right, there are more liars than to my left." But we have already understood that there are an equal number of each.

question:
39. In front of Andrey, there are 2019 plates, on which there are a total of 2019 pastries. Andrey can perform two operations.

I. If there are an equal number of pastries on any two plates, he can eat all the pastries on one of these plates.

II. He can transfer one pastry from each non-empty plate to an empty plate.

Prove that Andrey can perform several operations so that he can eat at least 3 pastries.

(A. Solynin)
reference_solution:
39. Let it be that sad moment when Andryusha can no longer eat another pastry. Having nothing else to do, let Andryusha arrange the non-empty plates in ascending order of the number of pastries. Since there are no plates with the same number of pastries, the last non-empty plate (let it have the number $k$ and be called the plate with the blue rim) has at least $k$ pastries.

If the plate with the blue rim has exactly $k$ pastries, then on the first plate there is one pastry, on the second $-2, \ldots$, on the $k$-th - exactly $k$ pastries. In total, they give the triangular number $\frac{k(k+1)}{2}$ pastries, and the largest triangular number not exceeding 2019 is 2016. It turns out that in this case, three pastries have already been eaten.

Now consider the case when the plate with the blue rim has at least $k+1$ pastries. Now Andryusha will perform the second operation. A new plate will form (possibly, some old ones will disappear) with exactly $k$ pastries, and on the plate with the blue rim, there will be at least $k$ pastries. If Andryusha still cannot eat any pastries, then the plate with the blue rim remains the plate with the maximum number of pastries.

We continue to perform the second operation. Either at some point it will be possible to eat one plate of pastries, or after each operation, the plate with the blue rim will still have more pastries than any other. But this is impossible because with each operation, the number of pastries on it decreases, and sooner or later they will disappear from this plate altogether.

40. Note that if Sasha chose two identical numbers (for example, $x$ and $y$), then he wrote two fractions equal to 1 (in our example, $x / y$ and $y / x$), and the statement of the problem is obvious. Therefore, we can assume that all of Sasha's numbers are distinct.

Let's list Sasha's fractions in ascending order: $q_{1}, q_{2}, q_{3}, \ldots, q_{12}$. Then the fractions $q_{1}, q_{2}, \ldots, q_{6}$ are less than 1, and $q_{7}$ is the smallest of the fractions greater than 1. It is not hard to guess that $q_{7}=\frac{1}{q_{6}}, q_{8}=\frac{1}{q_{5}}$, and so on.

Suppose that any two fractions differ by at least $d=\frac{11}{6}$. Then $q_{1}>0, q_{2}>q_{1}+d>d$, $q_{3}>q_{2}+d>2 d, \ldots, q_{7}>q_{6}+d>6 d$. Consequently, $1=q_{6} q_{7}>5 d \cdot 6 d=5 \cdot \frac{11}{60} \cdot 6 \cdot \frac{11}{60}=\frac{121}{120}$. Contradiction.

question: 41. On the side $AC$ of triangle $ABC$, a point $K$ is marked. It turns out that $\angle ABK=7^{\circ}$ and $\angle ABC=77^{\circ}$. Prove that $2AK + AC > BC$.
reference_solution: 41. Let point $K^{\prime}$ be symmetric to $K$ with respect to line $A B$, and point $A^{\prime}$ be symmetric to $A$ with respect to $B K^{\prime}$. Then $A K=A K^{\prime}=A^{\prime} K^{\prime}$ and $\angle A^{\prime} B C=7^{\circ}+7^{\circ}+77^{\circ}=91^{\circ}>90^{\circ}$. Therefore, $B C<A^{\prime} C \leqslant A^{\prime} K^{\prime}+A K^{\prime}+A C=$ $2 A K+A C$.

2. In childhood, Kostya was taught to add natural numbers incorrectly: he believes that after the usual addition, the digits of the sum should be rearranged in descending order. Let's denote Kostya's addition by the symbol $\oplus$ (for example, $99 \oplus 2=110$.) Do there exist such natural numbers $a$ and $b$ for which $a \oplus b=a?$

(K. Kokhas)
reference_solution: 2. Answer: No. With regular addition, the number will increase, and with the rearrangement of digits, it will increase even more (or at least not decrease). Therefore, $a \oplus b$ is always strictly greater than $a$.

question: 4. The teacher considers some students in class $6^{a}$ to be excellent students, while the rest are poor students. During the quarter, there were 6 math tests in the class (grades from 2 to 5 were given). All students were present at each test, and they sat in pairs at desks (possibly different pairs for different tests). A poor student miraculously received a three if they sat with an excellent student, and a two if they sat with another poor student. In total, the number of fives received during these tests was three times the number of fours, and the number of threes was ten less than the number of twos. Prove that there will be an excellent student who received at least one grade not higher than a three.
reference_solution:
4. In fact, there is even an excellent student who received a two.

Suppose that such an excellent student does not exist. Then all the twos were received by poor students. The total number of twos for all six tests is even, because they were received by poor students sitting at the same desk. Let the number of twos be $2k$. Then the total number of threes is $2k-10$.

Further, if the total number of fours is $\ell$, then the number of fives received is $3\ell$. The total number of all grades for the quarter is $2k+(2k-10)+\ell+3\ell=4k+4\ell-10$ and, thus, does not divide by 4. But this is impossible, since on each of the six tests, the same even number of grades was given!

52. Solution 1 (complete residue system). Let $p-$ be the smallest of the prime numbers. Then $p<q<2 p$. Consider the integers from $-\frac{p-1}{2}$ to $\frac{p-1}{2}$. These are $p$ consecutive numbers, so they all give different remainders when divided by $p$. Now multiply these $p$ numbers by $q$. We will show that the numbers in the new set will also give different remainders when divided by $p$. If $q a$ and $q b$ (for $a<b$) give the same remainder when divided by $p$, then the natural number $q b - q a = q(b-a)$ is divisible by $p$, and thus $b-a$ is divisible by $p$, which is impossible, since $b-a$ is positive and less than $p$. Therefore, the numbers in the new set give different remainders when divided by $p$. Since there are $p$ of them, there will be a number that gives a remainder of $p-1$. Thus, we have shown that there exists a number $k$ such that $q k + 1$ is divisible by $p$ and $|k| \leqslant \frac{p-1}{2}$. Then

$$
|q k + 1| \leqslant q|k| + 1 \leqslant 2 p \cdot \frac{p-1}{2} + 1 = p(p-1) + 1 < p^2
$$

Therefore, the number $q k + 1$ cannot have prime divisors greater than $p$, because the product of such a divisor with $p$ is already greater than $p^2$ and even more so greater than $q k + 1$.

If $k \geqslant 0$, then the numbers $q k$ and $q k + 1$ will work. Otherwise, the numbers $-q k$ and $-q k - 1$ will work.
reference_solution: Solution 2 (Chinese Remainder Theorem). Let $p-$ be the smallest of the prime numbers. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, there exists a number $a$ that is divisible by $q$ and gives a remainder of 1 when divided by $p$. Note that any number of the form $a-k p q$ for integer $k$ also satisfies this condition. Choose $k$ such that $0 < a - k p q < p^2$. Then consider the natural number $c = p q - b$. It is divisible by $q$ and the result of the division is less than $p$, so the greatest prime divisor of $c$ is $q$. Moreover, $c + 1 = p q - (b - 1) > 2 p > q$. Contradiction.
