Problem 3. On the table lie 6 apples (not necessarily of the same weight). Tanya divided them into 3 on each of the two pans of the scales, and the scales remained in balance. And Sasha divided the same apples differently: 2 apples on one pan and 4 on the other, and the scales were again in balance. Prove that it is possible to place one apple on one pan and two on the other so that the scales remain in balance. [6 points]

(A. V. Shipovalov)
reference_solution:
Solution. Let's look at the three apples that Tanya put on one of the pans. Let's call them green.

Could all of them have ended up on one pan with Sasha as well? No, because their weight is already half of the total weight of the apples. This means that two green apples will end up on one of the pans, and the third on the other. Could only these two green apples remain on one pan? No, because their weight is less than half of the total weight. Therefore, Sasha added two apples from the other pan (let's call them red).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_4fbead29144343cd679ag-2.jpg?height=200&width=686&top_left_y=538&top_left_x=384)

So, Tanya had three green apples on one pan, while Sasha has two green apples and two red apples on one of the pans. By replacing one of the green apples with two red ones, the total weight of the apples on the pan did not change (it is equal to half of the total weight of the apples). This means we have found an apple that weighs as much as two others.

Provide an example and prove that it is impossible to shade fewer triangles.

question: Problem 4. Anya wanted to write one digit in each cell of a $5 \times 8$ table in such a way that each digit appears exactly in four rows. (We consider both columns and rows as rows of the table.) Prove that she cannot achieve this. [6 points] (E.V. Bakayev)
reference_solution:
Solution. Let's assume that the table has 5 rows and 8 columns, and suppose that Anya managed to arrange the digits. Note that each digit in the table can appear no more than 4 times. Indeed, if among the four rows where it appears, there are two vertical rows and two horizontal rows, then there are exactly four cells at their intersections for our digit (it can be written in two, three, or all four cells), and if there are three rows in one direction and one in the other, then only three cells.

However, there are 10 digits in total, and 40 cells, so each digit appears exactly 4 times, and they are located precisely at the intersections of two horizontal and two vertical rows. This, in particular, means that in each column, the same digits appear in pairs, which is impossible, since there is an odd number of digits in the column (five).

question: Problem 5. One angle of a triangle is $60^{\circ}$, and the side opposite this angle is equal to one third of the perimeter of the triangle. Prove that the given triangle is equilateral. $[10$ points] (M.A. Volchkevich)
reference_solution:
Solution. Suppose the opposite. Let in triangle $ABC$ angle $A$ be $60^{\circ}$, $BC=a$, $AB=a-x$, then $AC=$ $=p-AB-BC=3a-a-(a-x)=a+x$. Choose point $B'$ on ray $AB$ and point $C'$ on ray $AC$ such that $AB'=AC'=a$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_79cfe44052259f2639fcg-10.jpg?height=404&width=442&top_left_y=1084&top_left_x=502)

Triangle $AB'C'$ is isosceles with an angle of $60^{\circ}$. Therefore, it is also equilateral, i.e., $B'C'=a$.

It remains to note that triangles $BC'B'$ and $BC'C$ are equal by three sides. Therefore, $\angle BCC'=\angle BB'C'=60^{\circ}$. That is, in triangle $ABC$, not only angle $A$, but also angle $C$ is $60^{\circ}$, i.e., it is equilateral.

question: Problem 5. Six mathematicians went fishing. Together they caught 100 fish, and each caught a different number of fish. After fishing, they noticed that any one of them could distribute all their fish to the other five fishermen so that each of the remaining five would have an equal number of fish. Prove that one fisherman can go home with his catch and still, each of the remaining can distribute all their fish to the others so that they all end up with an equal number of fish. $\quad[7$ points] (A.V. Shapovalov)
reference_solution: Solution. After one fisherman distributes his fish, the others should each have $100: 5=20$ fish. This means that each caught no more than 20 fish. Suppose Fisherman Ivan has exactly 20 fish. When another mathematician distributes his fish, Ivan does not receive anything, but everyone ends up with the same amount. Therefore, if Ivan leaves, the others can continue distributing as before, and everyone will again have 20 fish. It remains to show that there is indeed a fisherman who caught exactly 20 fish. Indeed, if there is no such fisherman, then the fishermen together have no more than $19+18+17+16+15+14=99<100$ fish - a contradiction.

Task 5. A curious tourist wants to stroll through the streets of the Old Town from the station (point $A$ on the map) to their hotel (point $B$). The tourist wants their route to be as long as possible, but it is not interesting for them to visit the same intersection twice, and they do not do so. Draw the longest possible route on the map and prove that there is no longer one.

$[7$ points] (I. V. Yashchenko)
reference_solution:
Solution. One of the possible routes of the tourist is shown in the figure. By following this path, the tourist will walk 34 streets (a street is defined as a segment between two adjacent intersections). We-
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_37ba496d27b0f6814cf4g-04.jpg?height=568&width=276&top_left_y=1150&top_left_x=1097)
claim that a longer route is impossible.

There are a total of 36 intersections in the Old Town. Every time the tourist walks another street, he arrives at a new intersection. Therefore, the tourist cannot walk more than 35 streets (the initial intersection $A$ is not counted). We will show that the curious tourist cannot visit 35 intersections (and, consequently, walk 35 streets). To do this, we will color the intersections in black and white in a checkerboard pattern (see the figure). Every time the tourist walks a street, he arrives at an intersection of the opposite color. Both the hotel and the station are located on white intersections. Therefore, any route contains an even number of streets, and the number 35 is odd.

Problem 4. Two squares are arranged as shown in the figure, the marked segments are equal. Prove that triangle $B D G$ is isosceles.

$[6$ points]

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_6c835588f80e91073398g-3.jpg?height=343&width=438&top_left_y=1193&top_left_x=839)
reference_solution:
Solution 1. Consider triangles $D E G$ and $D E B$. They share the side $D E$, and the sides $E G$ and $E B$ are equal (as two sides of the square). It remains to prove that the angles $D E G$ and $D E B$ are equal, - then the specified triangles will be equal (by two sides and the angle between them), and therefore, the corresponding sides $D G$ and $D B$ will also be equal.

The equality of these angles can be proven as follows. Mark $H$ - the midpoint of the segment $E B$. Note that $H B = E C$ as halves of the side of the right square, and also $B C = D C$, $\angle H B C = 90^{\circ} - \angle E C B = \angle E C D$. Therefore, triangles $H B C$ and $E C D$ are equal by two sides and the angle between them. Since triangle $E H C$ is an isosceles right triangle, $\angle E H C = 45^{\circ}$, and $\angle D E G = \angle C H B = 180^{\circ} - \angle E H C = 135^{\circ}$. But then $\angle D E B = 360^{\circ} - \angle D E G - \angle G E B = 360^{\circ} - 135^{\circ} - 90^{\circ} = 135^{\circ}$.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_6c835588f80e91073398g-4.jpg?height=340&width=940&top_left_y=544&top_left_x=255)

Solution 2. Note that $B D = A C$ as the diagonals of the square. If we prove that triangles $C E A$ and $G C D$ (marked in gray on the right) are equal, then from the equality of the corresponding sides $A C$ and $D G$ it will follow that $D G = A C = B D$. How to prove the equality of these triangles?

Consider triangles $A B E$ and $C B F$. Each of them has two sides equal to the sides of the original squares. The angles between these sides are also equal: each of them complements the angle $E B C$ to the right angle of the square. Therefore, these triangles are equal.

But triangle $B C F$ is isosceles (since it is "symmetrically located in the square"; more formally: $C B$ and $C F$ are the hypotenuses of right triangles $C B E$ and $C F G$, equal by two legs). Therefore, $C F = C B = A B = A E$.

Now we know that in the gray triangles, the sides $A E$ and $D C$ are equal, and the sides $C E$ and $C G$ are equal by condition. It remains to prove that the angles between the sides are equal.

If the angle at the base of the isosceles triangles $A B E$ and $C B F$ is $\alpha$, then $\angle A E C = 90^{\circ} + \alpha$. But $\angle D C G = 360^{\circ} - \angle B C D - \angle B C G = 360^{\circ} - 90^{\circ} - (180^{\circ} - \alpha) = 90^{\circ} + \alpha$.

($\angle C B F = \alpha$ and $\angle B C G$ sum to $180^{\circ}$ as consecutive interior angles when the sides of the square are parallel and $B C$ is the transversal).

The equality of the gray triangles (and thus the statement of the problem) is proven.

Solution 3. Transfer the drawing to graph paper. Start with the square $B E G F$: let it be a $2 \times 2$ grid square. Construct the square $A B C D$ along the segment $B C$. Now it is clear that the segments $D G$ and $D B$ are equal as the hypotenuses of right triangles with legs of length 1 cell and 3 cells.

Comment. There are many additional constructions that also allow solving the problem. Here are some of them:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_6c835588f80e91073398g-5.jpg?height=694&width=1010&top_left_y=852&top_left_x=218)

Problem 2. Two identical rectangular triangles made of paper were placed one on top of the other as shown in the figure (with the vertex of the right angle of one landing on the side of the other). Prove that the shaded triangle

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_03d5e2dee9da9ea28fdcg-08.jpg?height=251&width=261&top_left_y=363&top_left_x=1012)
is equilateral. [4 points] (E.V. Bakayev)
reference_solution:
Solution. In triangle $A B C$, angles $A$ and $C$ are equal (as corresponding angles of equal paper triangles); therefore, its sides $A B$ and $B C$ are equal. But its sides $A B$ and $A C$ are also equal (as corresponding sides of equal paper triangles); therefore, triangle $A B C$ is equilateral.

Comments. 1. The solution does not use the fact that the paper triangles have a right angle; it is only important that they are equal.

Problem 6. On the board, two numbers are written: 2014 and 2015. Petya and Vasya take turns, with Petya starting. In one move, they can

- either decrease one of the numbers by its non-zero digit or by a non-zero digit of the other number;
- or divide one of the numbers by two if it is even.

The player who first writes a single-digit number wins. Who among them can win, regardless of how the opponent plays? Describe their strategy and prove that it is a winning strategy.

[8 points] (A. V. Shapovalov)
reference_solution:
Answer: Petya can win.

Solution. Let Petya first replace 2015 with 2014, and with each subsequent move, he will equalize the numbers (he can always do this by repeating Vasya's move with the number Vasya did not change):

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_03d5e2dee9da9ea28fdcg-11.jpg?height=178&width=783&top_left_y=323&top_left_x=335)

If Petya acts this way throughout the game, of course, at some point Vasya will make one of the two identical numbers a single-digit number and win.

But let's look at this moment more closely. If Vasya wins by replacing one of the two numbers $X$ with a single-digit number, then before that, on Petya's turn, one of the two numbers $X$ on the board was already there. At this moment, Petya can replace $X$ with a single-digit number and win:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_03d5e2dee9da9ea28fdcg-11.jpg?height=297&width=686&top_left_y=897&top_left_x=384)

(Petya can do this because he has all the options that Vasya had on his last, winning move: to divide the number $X$ in half if it is even, and to subtract its own digit from it.)

So, let's formulate Petya's strategy completely: "if one of the numbers can be replaced with a single-digit number - do it; otherwise, equalize the two numbers."

Problem 4. The Smeshariki live on the shores of a pond in the shape of an equilateral triangle with a side length of 600 meters. Krosh and Barash live on one shore, 300 meters apart from each other. In the summer, it is 900 meters for Losharik to walk to Krosh, and 900 meters for Barash to walk to Nyusha. Prove that in the winter, when the pond freezes and it is possible to walk directly across the ice, the distance for Losharik to walk to Krosh will again be the same as the distance for Barash to walk to Nyusha.

[6 points] (E.V. Bakayev, A.V. Khachatryan)
reference_solution:
Solution. Let Krosh live at a distance $x$ from the nearest corner of the pond, $A K=x$. Then the distance from Barash to his corner of the pond is $B B=600-300-x=300-x$. Now, by the condition, $B J=900-B K=300+x$ (note that since 900 is exactly half the perimeter of the pond, it doesn't matter which of the two paths Losyash takes to reach Krosh), $A H=$ $=900-A B=600-x$. It remains to note that triangles АНБ and ВКЛ are equal by angle ( $\angle A=60^{\circ}=\angle B$ ) and two sides adjacent to it ( $A B=300+x=B Л, A H=B K=$ $=600-x)$. Therefore, their corresponding sides ЛК and $Б Н$ are also equal.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_569060baad9798200f98g-08.jpg?height=462&width=491&top_left_y=617&top_left_x=477)

Comment. The fact that Yusha indeed lives on side $A C$ (and not on side $B C$) is evident from the fact that $600-x<600$ (after Barash has walked $300+x$ to vertex $A$, he still has $600-x<A C$ left to Yusha). Similarly, Losyash lives precisely on side $B C$.

Problem 6. Five friends approached a river and found a boat on the shore that could accommodate all five of them. They decided to go for a ride in the boat. Each time, a group of one or several people would cross from one bank to the other. The friends want to organize the ride so that each possible group crosses exactly once. Will they be able to do this?

[9 points] (A. V. Grigalko)
reference_solution:
Answer: It won't work.

Solution: Suppose the friends manage to achieve their goal. Let's calculate how many different groups can be formed from five people (and, accordingly, how many times the boat will cross from one bank to the other). Each person can either be in the group or not, so there are two options for each, meaning there are $2^{5}=32$ options in total. This includes the option where no one is in the group. However, an empty boat does not float, so there are $32-1=31$ groups in total. Since this number is odd, the friends must cross the river an odd number of times, which means the boat will end up on the opposite bank. Therefore, at least one of the friends will finish the ride on the other bank, let's say it's Vasya.

Let's see how many times he could have crossed. Each of his friends can either go with him or not, so Vasya is part of $2^{4}=16$ different groups (including the option where he goes alone). But this number is even, so after the ride, Vasya should return to the original bank. The contradiction obtained proves that it is impossible to have the ride as required.

question: Problem 5. Around a circular lake, 2019 trees grow at equal intervals: 1009 pines and 1010 spruces. Prove that there must be a tree next to which a pine grows and on the other side, one tree away, another pine also grows. $[8$ points] ( (E. V. Bakayev)
reference_solution: Solution. Let's walk around the lake in a circle and write the letters: A, B, C, then again A, B, C, and so on. There will be $2019: 3=673$ trees with each letter. If there were no more than 336 pines with each letter, then there would be no more than $336 \cdot 3=1008$ pines in total. Since there are 1009 pines, there will be at least 337 pines with some letter (say, A). (This kind of reasoning is often found in mathematical problem solutions and is called the Pigeonhole Principle.) Now let's consider only the trees with the letter A. If any two pines stand next to each other, the problem is solved—the tree with the letter C between them meets the conditions. If, however, there is at least one fir between every pair of adjacent pines with the letter A, then there would be no fewer than $337 \cdot 2=674$ trees with the letter A, which is not the case.

Task 2. On two cards, four different digits are written - one on each side of the card. Can it be that every two-digit number that can be formed from these cards is prime? (You cannot flip the digits upside down, i.e., turn a 6 into a 9 and vice versa.)

$[4$ points] (A.V. Shapovalov)
reference_solution:
Answer: No, it cannot.

Solution: All two-digit numbers ending in 0, $2, 4, 6$ or 8 are even, and those ending in 5 are multiples of five. Therefore, such numbers cannot be prime, and it makes no sense to write these digits on cards. The remaining digits are 1, 3, 7, and 9. If the digits 3 and 9 are written on different cards, then they can form the composite number 39. If they are written on the same card, then 1 and 7 are on the second card, and then the composite number $91=7 \cdot 13$ can be formed.

question:
Problem 3. Among all the faces of eight identical cubes, one third are blue, and the rest are red. These cubes are used to form a larger cube. Now, among the visible faces of the smaller cubes, exactly one third are red. Prove that it is possible to form a cube that is completely red on the outside from these smaller cubes.

[2 points] (A.V. Shapovalov)
reference_solution:
Solution. Eight cubes have $8 \cdot 6=48$ faces. Of these, $48: 3=16$ are blue. On the faces of the large cube $2 \times 2 \times 2$, we see $6 \cdot 4=24$ faces of the small cubes, of which $24: 3=8$ are red, and the remaining $24-8=16$ are blue. Thus, all 16 blue faces of the small cubes are on the surface of the large cube, i.e., all the invisible faces are red. Now we can rotate each cube so that its three hidden red faces are on the outside.

We can do without counting the number of faces. According to the condition, blue faces make up $1 / 3$ of their total number. On the surface of the large cube, we see exactly half of the faces of each cube (three out of six), i.e., we see half of all the faces. Two-thirds of these are blue, i.e., $2 / 3 \cdot 1 / 2=1 / 3$ of their total number. Therefore, all blue faces are on the outside, and we can rotate each cube, hiding these faces inside.

Problem 6. Among 49 schoolchildren, each is acquainted with at least 25 others. Prove that they can be divided into groups of 2 or 3 people such that everyone in a group is acquainted with everyone else in their group.

$[8$ points $]$

(A. V. Shapovalov)
reference_solution:
Solution. Let's assume that initially all 49 students are standing in the corridor, and we will gradually let them into the classroom.

We will do this in such a way that at any moment in time, the children in the classroom are divided into the required groups.

Let's say that a student named Fyodor is standing in the corridor. If he is acquainted with any other student standing in the corridor, we will simply let them both into the classroom.

Otherwise, all of Fyodor's acquaintances are already in the classroom. Since there are fewer than 50 students in the classroom, they are divided into fewer than 25 groups. Therefore, among Fyodor's acquaintances, there are at least two who are in the same group. If this is a group of 2 students, we will let Fyodor into the classroom and add him to this group. If it is a group of 3 students, we will ask one of Fyodor's acquaintances to form a group with him, and leave the remaining students in a pair.

By gradually letting students into the classroom, we will achieve the goal of dividing all students into the required groups.

Problem 3. An equilateral triangle with a side length of 8 was divided into smaller equilateral triangles with a side length of 1 (see figure). What is the minimum number of small triangles that need to be shaded so that all intersection points of the lines (including those on the edges) are vertices of at least one shaded triangle? Provide an example and prove that it is impossible to shade fewer triangles.

[6 points] (

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_451a0d7107599630d1d3g-04.jpg?height=364&width=420&top_left_y=1455&top_left_x=517)
reference_solution:
Answer: 15 small triangles. See the example in the figure.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_451a0d7107599630d1d3g-05.jpg?height=361&width=420&top_left_y=201&top_left_x=517)

Solution: The total number of intersection points of the lines is $1+2+3+\ldots+9=45$. Since a triangle has three vertices, at least $45: 3=15$ triangles will need to be shaded.

Comment: It can be shown that there is only one (up to axial symmetry) way to shade 15 triangles.

In the coloring we found, no vertex is shaded twice. The side length of 8 of the large triangle is the minimum for which such an "economical" coloring is possible. It is definitely impossible if the side length is a multiple of three. A more complex version of this problem (for a triangle with side length 2015) was published in the "Problems" section of the journal "Mathematics in School" (Issue 1, 2016).

question:
Problem 6. A row of 100 coins lies on a table, some showing heads and the rest showing tails. In one operation, it is allowed to select seven coins lying at equal intervals (i.e., seven consecutive coins, or seven coins lying every other coin, etc.), and flip all seven coins. Prove that using such operations, it is possible to have all the coins show heads.

$[9$ points] (S.I. Tokarev, A.V. Shapovalov)
reference_solution:
Solution. It is clear that it is enough to learn how to flip each of the coins (while keeping the position of the others).

First, let's show how to flip a pair of coins, with exactly 6 coins lying between them. If we mentally combine this pair with the coins between them, we get a group of 8 coins in a row. We will flip 7 of the leftmost coins, then 7 of the rightmost. Then the outermost coins will flip once, while the intermediate ones will flip twice (i.e., return to their original position).

Now suppose we want to flip a single coin. We will assume that it lies in the left half (for the right half, the reasoning is analogous). Let's look at a group of 7 coins, the first of which is the one we have chosen, the next one lies 6 coins away, the next one another 6 coins away, and so on.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_b15c0281e21ba8d77df7g-5.jpg?height=78&width=1054&top_left_y=726&top_left_x=204)

This group of 7 consists of the chosen coin and three pairs, in which the coins lie 6 apart. Therefore, we can flip each of these pairs (as described above), and then the entire group of 7. In the end, only the chosen coin will change its position.

question:
Problem 6. On the sides \(AB\) and \(BC\) of square \(ABCD\) with side length 10, points \(K\) and \(L\) are marked such that \(AK = CL = 3\). On segment \(KL\), a point \(P\) is chosen, and on the extension of segment \(AB\) beyond point \(B\), a point \(Q\) is chosen such that \(AP = PQ = QL\) (see figure).

a) Prove that \(\angle PAB = \angle BLQ\).

b) Find the length of segment \(BQ\).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_966677e2574743a5a289g-3.jpg?height=337&width=378&top_left_y=304&top_left_x=897)

[4 points]

[4 points] * In solving part b), you can use the statement from part a).

(F. A. Ivlev, A. A. Mardanov)

a) Solution. Note that \(KB = AB - AK = 10 - 3 = BC - CL = BL\). Therefore, triangle \(KBL\) is isosceles and right-angled, so \(\angle KLB = 45^\circ\).

Let \(\angle BLQ = \alpha\). Since triangle \(PQL\) is isosceles, we have \(\angle LPQ = \angle PLQ = 45^\circ + \alpha\). From the sum of the angles in triangle \(PQL\), we find \(\angle PQL = 180^\circ - 2 \cdot (45^\circ + \alpha) = 90^\circ - 2\alpha\).

From the sum of the angles in triangle \(BLQ\), we find that \(\angle LQB = 90^\circ - \alpha\). Now we find \(\angle PQA = \angle LQA - \angle LQP = 90^\circ - \alpha - (90^\circ - 2\alpha) = \alpha\). Finally, since triangle \(APQ\) is isosceles, \(\angle PQA = \angle PAQ = \alpha = \angle BLQ\), which is what we needed to prove.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_966677e2574743a5a289g-3.jpg?height=432&width=517&top_left_y=1383&top_left_x=468)
b) Answer. \(BQ = 4\).
reference_solution:
Solution. Drop a perpendicular $PH$ from point $P$ to side $AB$. Since triangle $KBL$ is isosceles and right-angled, $\angle PKH = 45^\circ$. Therefore, triangle $KPH$ is also isosceles and $KH = HP$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_966677e2574743a5a289g-4.jpg?height=432&width=507&top_left_y=369&top_left_x=477)

Notice that right triangles $APH$ and $LQB$ are equal by hypotenuse ($AP = LQ$) and acute angle ($\angle PAH = \angle BLQ$). Therefore, $KH = PH = BQ$.

Since $PH$ is the height in the isosceles triangle $APQ$ drawn to its base, it is also the median. Then $AH = HQ$ and we can write the following relationship:

\[
\begin{gathered}
AB + BQ = AQ = 2AH = 2(AK + KH) = 2(AK + BQ) \\
10 + BQ = 2(3 + BQ) = 6 + 2BQ
\end{gathered}
\]

from which $BQ = 4$.

question:
Problem 4. Two squares and an isosceles triangle are arranged as shown in the figure (vertex $K$ of the larger square lies on the side of the triangle). Prove that points $A, B$, and $C$ lie on the same line.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_3fb59c7075fbe0bc8ea2g-3.jpg?height=379&width=363&top_left_y=325&top_left_x=545)

$[8$ points] (M.A. Evdokimov)
reference_solution:
First solution. An isosceles triangle has an axis of symmetry. When reflecting over this axis, $K$ maps to $C$, and $D$ maps to $A$ (see the left figure). Therefore, $AC$ forms the same angle with the base as the diagonal of the square $KD$, which is $45^{\circ}$. But $AB$ also forms an angle of $45^{\circ}$ with the base, as the diagonal of the smaller square. Therefore, points $A, B$, and $C$ indeed lie on the same straight line.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_3fb59c7075fbe0bc8ea2g-3.jpg?height=432&width=862&top_left_y=1096&top_left_x=298)

Second solution (without using symmetry). Let's introduce the notation as shown in the right figure and draw segments $AB$ and $BC$. Since $\angle ABH=45^{\circ}$, it is sufficient to prove that $\angle KBC=\angle BCK=45^{\circ}$ (then $\angle ABH + \angle HBK + \angle KBC = 45^{\circ} + 90^{\circ} + 45^{\circ} = 180^{\circ}$, which is equivalent to the statement of the problem).

Using the equality of corresponding angles when parallel lines are cut by a transversal and the isosceles property of triangle $AGD$, we get: $\angle GKC = \angle GAD = \angle GDA = \angle GCK$. Therefore, $GK = GC$, so $AK = CD$. This means that the right triangles $AKF$ and $CDE$ are equal (by hypotenuse and leg). Consequently, $CE = AF = BF$, then $BK = CK$, from which $\angle KBC = \angle BCK = 45^{\circ}$, as required.

question:
Problem 4. Two squares are arranged as shown in the figure, the marked segments are equal. Prove that triangle $B D G$ is isosceles.

$[6$ points]

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_8a4168ef17f569e28eb1g-3.jpg?height=343&width=438&top_left_y=1193&top_left_x=839)
reference_solution:
Solution 1. Consider triangles $D E G$ and $D E B$. They share a common side $D E$, and have equal sides $E G$ and $E B$ (as two sides of the square). It remains to prove that angles $D E G$ and $D E B$ are equal, - then the specified triangles will be equal (by two sides and the angle between them), and therefore, the corresponding sides $D G$ and $D B$ will also be equal.

The equality of these angles can be proven as follows. Mark $H$ - the midpoint of segment $E B$. Note that $H B=E C$ as halves of the side of the right square, and also $B C=D C$, $\angle H B C=90^{\circ}-\angle E C B=\angle E C D$. Therefore, triangles $H B C$ and $E C D$ are equal by two sides and the angle between them. Since triangle $E H C$ is an isosceles right triangle, $\angle E H C=45^{\circ}$, and $\angle D E G=\angle C H B=180^{\circ}-\angle E H C=135^{\circ}$. But then $\angle D E B=360^{\circ}-\angle D E G-\angle G E B=360^{\circ}-135^{\circ}-90^{\circ}=$ $=135^{\circ}$.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_8a4168ef17f569e28eb1g-4.jpg?height=340&width=940&top_left_y=544&top_left_x=255)

Solution 2. Note that $B D=A C$ as diagonals of the square. If we prove that triangles $C E A$ and $G C D$ (marked gray on the right) are equal, then from the equality of corresponding sides $A C$ and $D G$ it will follow that $D G=$ $=A C=B D$. How to prove the equality of these triangles?

Consider triangles $A B E$ and $C B F$. Each of them has two sides equal to the sides of the original squares. The angles between these sides are also equal: each of them complements angle $E B C$ to the right angle of the square. Therefore, these triangles are equal.

But triangle $B C F$ is isosceles (since it is "symmetrically located in the square"; more formally: $C B$ and $C F$ are the hypotenuses of right triangles $C B E$ and $C F G$, equal by two legs). Therefore, $C F=C B=A B=A E$.

Now we know that in the gray triangles, sides $A E$ and $D C$ are equal, and sides $C E$ and $C G$ are equal by condition. It remains to prove that the angles between the sides are equal.

If the angle at the base of the isosceles triangles $A B E$ and $C B F$ is $\alpha$, then $\angle A E C=90^{\circ}+\alpha$. But $\angle D C G=$ $=360^{\circ}-\angle B C D-\angle B C G=360^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-\left(180^{\circ}-\alpha\right)=90^{\circ}+\alpha$

( $\angle C B F=\alpha$ and $\angle B C G$ sum to $180^{\circ}$ as consecutive interior angles when the sides of the square are parallel and $B C$ is the transversal ).

The equality of the gray triangles (and thus the statement of the problem) is proven.

Solution 3. Transfer the drawing to graph paper. Start with the square $B E G F$: let it be a $2 \times 2$ grid square. Construct the square $A B C D$ along segment $B C$. Now it is clear that segments $D G$ and $D B$ are equal as the hypotenuses of right triangles with legs of length 1 cell and 3 cells.

Comment. There are many additional constructions that also allow solving the problem. Here are some of them:
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_8a4168ef17f569e28eb1g-5.jpg?height=694&width=1010&top_left_y=852&top_left_x=218)

question:
3. In triangle $ABC$, the altitudes $BE$ and $CF$ intersect at point $H$, point $M$ is the midpoint of side $BC$, and $X$ is the intersection point of the internal tangents to the incircles of triangles $BMF$ and $CME$. Prove that points $X$, $M$, and $H$ lie on the same line.

(I. N. Mikhailov)
reference_solution:
Solution.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_3347677eef7d1364dccag-2.jpg?height=807&width=1214&top_left_y=407&top_left_x=217)

Method 1. Let $S, T$ be the midpoints of the altitudes $B E$ and $C F$, and $L, N$ be the midpoints of the segments $B F$ and $C E$. Denote the incircles of triangles $B M F$ and $C M E$ by $\omega_{1}, \omega_{2}$, and their centers by $I_{b}$ and $I_{c}$, respectively. Triangles $B M F$ and $C M E$ are isosceles, so points $I_{b}$ and $I_{c}$ lie on the corresponding altitudes $M L$ and $M N$ of these triangles. Segments $B I_{b}$ and $C I_{c}$ are the angle bisectors of triangles $M L B$ and $M N C$, so by the Angle Bisector Theorem, we have the ratios: $\frac{M I_{c}}{N I_{c}}=\frac{M C}{N C}, \frac{M I_{b}}{L I_{b}}=\frac{M B}{L B}$. Dividing the first by the second and considering that $M B = M C$, we get $\frac{M I_{c}}{M I_{b}} \cdot \frac{L I_{b}}{N I_{c}}=\frac{L B}{N C}$. Since $X$ is the center of homothety mapping $\omega_{1}$ to $\omega_{2}$, $X$ lies on the line of centers $I_{b} I_{c}$ and the equality $\frac{L I_{b}}{N I_{c}}=\frac{X I_{b}}{X I_{c}}$ holds. Therefore, $\frac{M I_{c}}{M I_{b}} \cdot \frac{L I_{b}}{N I_{c}}=\frac{M I_{c}}{M I_{b}} \cdot \frac{X I_{b}}{X I_{c}}=\frac{M I_{c}}{M I_{b}} \cdot \frac{S_{M X I_{b}}}{S_{M X I_{c}}}=\frac{\rho\left(X, M I_{b}\right)}{\rho\left(X, M I_{c}\right)}$, where $\rho(X, A B)$ denotes the distance from point $X$ to line $A B$. On the other hand, by the property of the midline, $M S \| A C$ and $M T \| A B$, so $M S \perp B E$ and $M T \perp C F$. Thus, $M L F T$ and $M N E S$ are rectangles, so $M T = L F$ and $M S = N E$. Then the equalities $\frac{L B}{N C}=\frac{L F}{N E}=\frac{M T}{M S}=\frac{\rho(H, M L)}{\rho(H, M N)}$ hold, where the last equality holds because $M S$ and $M T$ are the common perpendiculars to the pairs of parallel lines $B E \| M N$ and $C F \| M L$. Combining all the proven equalities, we get $\frac{\rho(H, M L)}{\rho(H, M N)}=\frac{L B}{N C}=\frac{M I_{c}}{M I_{b}} \cdot \frac{L I_{b}}{N I_{c}}=\frac{\rho\left(X, M I_{b}\right)}{\rho\left(X, M I_{c}\right)}$, from which it immediately follows that points $M, X$, and $H$ lie on the same line.

Method 2. As in the first solution, denote the incircles of triangles $B M F$ and $C M E$ by $\omega_{1}, \omega_{2}$, their centers by $I_{b}$ and $I_{c}$, respectively, and the midpoints of segments $B F$ and $C E$ by $L$ and $N$. Let $Y$ be the point of intersection of the external tangents to $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$. Note that the quadruple of points $(I_{b}, I_{c}, X, Y)$ is harmonic, meaning the cross-ratio $(I_{b}, I_{c}; X, Y)$ equals -1. Project this quadruple of points onto the line $B E$ with the center at point $M$. Point $Y$ lies on the line $A C$ because this line is one of the external tangents to $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$, so $Y$ maps to $B$. Point $I_{b}$ maps to point $R$, the intersection of lines $M L$ and $B H$, which is the midpoint of $B H$ because in triangle $B F C$, segment $M L$ is the midline. Point $I_{c}$ maps to the point at infinity on line $B H$ because $M I_{c} \| B H$. Since the cross-ratio of a quadruple of points is preserved under central projection, and the quadruple $(R, \infty; H, B)$ is harmonic, the image of point $X$ under this projection is point $H$, which is what we needed to prove.

question:
4. We have perfectly accurate two-pan scales and a set of 50 weights, the weights of which are equal to $\operatorname{arctg} 1$, $\operatorname{arctg} \frac{1}{2}$, $\operatorname{arctg} \frac{1}{3}$, ..., $\operatorname{arctg} \frac{1}{50}$. Prove that it is possible to choose 10 of them and distribute 5 weights on each pan of the scales so that equilibrium is established.

(M.A. Evdokimov)
reference_solution:
Solution. First, we will show that in this set, there are triples of weights, one of which balances the other two. All weights do not exceed $\pi / 4$, so the equality $\operatorname{tg}\left(\operatorname{arctg} \frac{1}{n}+\operatorname{arctg} \frac{1}{m}\right)=\operatorname{tg}\left(\operatorname{arctg} \frac{1}{k}\right)$ is equivalent to the equality $\operatorname{arctg} \frac{1}{n}+\operatorname{arctg} \frac{1}{m}=\operatorname{arctg} \frac{1}{k}$.

Using the formula $\operatorname{tg}(x+y)=\frac{\operatorname{tg} x+\operatorname{tg} y}{1-\operatorname{tg} x \cdot \operatorname{tg} y}$, we get

$$
\frac{n+m}{n m-1}=\frac{1}{k}
$$

i.e., $n m-k(n+m)=1$. Adding $k^{2}$ to both sides of this equation and factoring, we obtain $(n-k)(m-k)=k^{2}+1$. Now, choosing different natural $k$ and factoring $k^{2}+1$, we find suitable triples in which each number does not exceed 50. The result for $k \leqslant 5$ and $n$ $(5,8)$ | $(5,21)$ | $(6,31)$ |
|  |  |  |  | $(7,18)$ |  |

Now we will show how to distribute the weights on the pans:

| 1st pan |  | 2nd pan |
| :---: | :--- | :---: |
| 1 | $=$ | 2,3 |
| 5,21 | $=$ | 4 |
| 6,31 | $=$ | 7,18 |

(in the table, the value of $n$ is indicated for the weight $\operatorname{arctg} \frac{1}{n}$).

Thus, we managed to select 10 weights and distribute 5 weights on each of the different pans of the scales so that equilibrium is established.

question:
5. In a convex polyhedron, let B, P, and T denote the number of vertices, edges, and the maximum number of triangular faces that share a common vertex, respectively. Prove that $B \sqrt{P+T} \geqslant 2P$.

For example, for a tetrahedron ( $B=4, P=6, T=3$ ), the equality holds, while for a triangular prism ( $B=6, P=9, T=1$ ) or a cube ( $B=8, P=12, T=0$ ), the inequality is strict.

(O.N. Kosukhin)
reference_solution:
Solution. The degree of a vertex of a polyhedron is the number of edges emanating from it. Vertices are called adjacent if they are connected by an edge.

Let $A$ be an arbitrary vertex of the polyhedron, $k$ its degree, and $m_{j}$ the degrees of all vertices adjacent to it $(j=1,2, \ldots, k)$, numbered in any order. Then $m_{1}+m_{2}+\ldots+m_{k}$ is the number of all edges emanating from the vertices adjacent to $A$, counted once or twice, where the edges that lie opposite vertex $A$ in some triangular face of the polyhedron are counted twice. Therefore, $m_{1}+m_{2}+\ldots+m_{k} \leqslant \mathrm{P}+\mathrm{T}$. From this, using the known inequality between the arithmetic mean and the quadratic mean, we get

$$
\frac{\sqrt{m_{1}}+\sqrt{m_{2}}+\ldots+\sqrt{m_{k}}}{k} \leqslant \sqrt{\frac{m_{1}+m_{2}+\ldots+m_{k}}{k}} \leqslant \frac{\sqrt{\mathrm{P}+\mathrm{T}}}{\sqrt{k}}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\sqrt{\frac{m_{1}}{k}}+\sqrt{\frac{m_{2}}{k}}+\ldots+\sqrt{\frac{m_{k}}{k}} \leqslant \sqrt{\mathrm{P}+\mathrm{T}}
$$

Let us denote the sum on the left side of the last inequality by $S(A)$.

Let $A_{i}(i=1,2, \ldots, \mathrm{B})$ be all the vertices of the polyhedron, numbered in any order, and $n_{i}(i=1,2, \ldots, \mathrm{B})$ their respective degrees. For any pair of adjacent vertices $A_{i}$ and $A_{j}$, by the inequality between the arithmetic mean and the geometric mean, the following inequality holds:

$$
\sqrt{\frac{n_{j}}{n_{i}}}+\sqrt{\frac{n_{i}}{n_{j}}} \geqslant 2
$$

Summing these inequalities over all unordered pairs $\left\{A_{i}, A_{j}\right\}$ of adjacent vertices of the polyhedron, we get

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{\mathrm{B}} S\left(A_{i}\right) \geqslant 2 \mathrm{P}
$$

From the proven inequality $S(A) \leqslant \sqrt{\mathrm{P}+\mathrm{T}}$, it follows the required estimate.

question:
1. For four integers $a, b, c, d$ it is known that

$$
a+b+c+d=ab+bc+cd+da+1
$$

Prove that the absolute values of some two of these numbers differ by one.

$$
\text { (2023-64, A. Dolodenok) }
$$
reference_solution:
Solution. Transform the equation to the form

$$
a+b+c+d=(a+c)(b+d)+1
$$

After substituting $x=a+c$ and $y=b+d$, we get

$$
x+y=x y+1
$$

Move all terms to one side and factorize

$$
(x-1)(y-1)=0
$$

Thus, $a+c=1$ or $b+d=1$. Suppose $a+c=1$. The sum of two positive integers is no less than two, so $a \leqslant 0$ or $c \leqslant 0$. Without loss of generality, let $a \leqslant 0$. Then $c>0$. Therefore, $|c|-|a|=c+a=1$. This completes the proof.

5. First solution. We will prove that this is true for the partition of any rectangular parallelepiped. For brevity, we will call the encompassing parallelepiped a box, its three non-parallel faces - the left, the bottom, and the front, the parallelepipeds of the partition - bricks, and the partitions that satisfy the condition of the problem - correct.

Lella. If a box and bricks are cut by a plane parallel to a face, then we get two smaller correctly partitioned boxes.

Proof. If the projections of two bricks overlapped on a face parallel to the cut, then the projections of their pieces that ended up in one smaller box do not change and therefore overlap. Otherwise, the intersection of the projections is either (a) cut by the cut, or (b) empty. In case (a), the projections of the pieces of the bricks overlap along the corresponding part of the intersection of the projections. In case (b), one of the bricks is entirely in one smaller box, and the overlap of its projection with the projection of the corresponding piece of the other brick does not change.

Let's return to the problem. Suppose the statement is false. Then there is a counterexample, and in it, there are three bricks $X, Y$, and $Z$ such that the projections of $X$ and $Y$ overlap on the bottom, the projections of $X$ and $Z$ - on the left face, and the projections of $Y$ and $Z$ - on the front. Choose a counterexample with the smallest number of bricks. Suppose $X$ and $Y$ do not touch. We can assume that $Y$ is higher than $X$. Consider the part of the box in the form of a parallelepiped between the bottom face of $Y$ and the top face of $X$, the projection of which on the bottom coincides with the intersection of the projections of $X$ and $Y$. This part does not belong to $X$, $Y$, or $Z$. It belongs to one or several bricks; let $K$ be one of them. Let's see on which face the projections of $K$ and $Z$ overlap: on the left or on the front (the bottom is obviously not suitable). If on the left, then $K, Y$, and $Z$ also serve as a counterexample. Cut the box with a plane passing through the top face of $X$. In the upper of the resulting boxes lie $K, Y$, and a part of $Z$, forming a counterexample. But since this box contains no part of $X$, there are fewer bricks in the upper box, which contradicts the minimality of the counterexample. Similarly, if the projections of $K$ and $Z$ overlapped on the front, a smaller counterexample could be obtained by cutting off the upper part with $Y$.

Thus, $X$ and $Y$ touch, and for similar reasons, $X$ touches $Z$ and $Y$ touches $Z$. Let $M$ be the common point of $X, Y$, and $Z$. Two oppositely directed octants with vertex $M$ are not covered by them, and bricks from these octants cannot have overlapping projections - a contradiction.
reference_solution:
The second solution (proposed by Alexander Skutin, an Olympiad participant). Let's introduce a coordinate system with the origin at the vertex of the cube and axes parallel to its edges. Instead of projections onto the faces, we will consider projections onto the coordinate planes (let's call them the bottom, front, and left planes).

Notice that the faces of all parallelepipeds must be parallel to the coordinate planes. Also, note that two parallelepipeds can overlap in projections on no more than one plane: if they overlap on at least two planes, then the projections on all three axes overlap, and thus the parallelepipeds themselves overlap.

Suppose there are three parallelepipeds \(A, B\), and \(C\) that violate the problem's requirement. Then for each of the three pairs, there is a plane on which their projections overlap. Let \(a\) be the distance between parallelepipeds \(B\) and \(C\) along the axis perpendicular to the corresponding plane, similarly \(b\) - the distance between \(A\) and \(C\), and \(c\) - the distance between \(A\) and \(B\). Among all triples that violate the problem's requirement, let's take one where \(a + b + c\) is minimal.

Case 1: \(a + b + c = 0\) (Fig. 28). Then \(a = b = c = 0\) and all three pairs of parallelepipeds have a common point. From this point, two opposite octants not covered by parallelepipeds \(A, B\), and \(C\) extend. Therefore, they are covered by some other parallelepipeds \(D\) and \(E\). But these parallelepipeds must lie entirely within their octants, and the projections of the octants do not overlap on any plane. Therefore, the same is true for \(D\) and \(E\), which contradicts the condition.

Case 2: \(a + b + c > 0\) (Fig. 29). Suppose for definiteness that \(a > 0\), \(B\) is to the left of \(C\), \(C\) is below \(A\), and \(A\) is further from \(B\). Consider all parallelepipeds lying between \(B\) and \(C\) and overlapping with them in the projection on the left plane. Among them, there must be a parallelepiped \(F\) whose top face is not lower than the top face of \(C\), and whose far face is not closer than the far face of \(B\). If \(F\) overlaps with \(A\) in the projection on the bottom plane, then consider the triple \((A, B, F)\), if on the front plane - the triple \((A, F, C)\). In any case, we get a triple that violates the problem's condition with a smaller sum \(a + b + c\): in one dimension, the distance has not changed, in another it has not increased, and in the third it has decreased, which contradicts the initial choice of the triple.

In both cases, we arrive at a contradiction, therefore, the sought-after triple of parallelepipeds does not exist.

6. Answer: a) yes; b) no.

a) First solution. Divide the chests into three pairs. The total number of coins in each pair of chests is even, so the number of coins in all six chests is even as well. Now divide the chests into two triplets. The number of coins in each triplet is divisible by three, so the total number of coins in all the chests is also divisible by three. Thus, this total number of coins is divisible by 2 and 3, and therefore by 6 (since 2 and 3 are coprime). Therefore, all the coins can be evenly distributed into 6 chests.
reference_solution:
Second solution. First, note that the number of coins in all chests has the same parity. After all, it is impossible to evenly divide the contents of two chests with different parities of coins.

Then, pay attention to the fact that the total number of coins in the first three chests is divisible by three. If we replace chest No. 3 with chest No. 4, the divisibility by 3 will not be violated. This means that the number of coins in the fourth chest gives the same remainder when divided by 3 as the third chest. In the same way, for any two chests, it can be proven that the number of coins in one gives the same remainder when divided by 3 as the other. Therefore, the remainders of these numbers when divided by 3 are the same.

If numbers give the same remainders when divided by both 2 and 3, then their difference is divisible by both 2 and 3, which means it is also divisible by 6. This means that the remainders of any two (and therefore all six) numbers when divided by 6 are equal to each other. The sum of six such numbers will be divisible by 6. Therefore, all the coins can be evenly distributed among all the chests.

b) Reasoning in the same way as in part a), we can prove that all eight numbers corresponding to the quantities of coins in the chests give the same remainders when divided by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7. This means that these numbers give the same remainders when divided by 420 (420 is the least common multiple of the numbers 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7). However, since 420 is not divisible by 8, these numbers can have different remainders when divided by 8, which will prevent the coins from being evenly distributed among eight chests.

For example, there could have been 421 coins in the first chest, and one coin in each of the other seven. Then in two chests, the total is either 2 or 422 coins, both of which are even. In three chests, the total is either 3 or 423 coins, each of which is divisible by 3, and so on. In seven chests, the total is 7 or 427 coins. Both numbers are divisible by 7. However, the total number of coins, 428, is not divisible by 8. That is, in this case, it is impossible to distribute the coins evenly among eight chests.

On the other hand, there could have been an equal number of coins in all chests from the beginning. Therefore, it is impossible to answer the question without knowing what is in the chests.

3. A n s w e r: $p+1$.

If $\left(p^{2}\right)!$ is divisible by $(p!)^{n}, n \in \mathbb{N}$, then $n \leqslant p+1$, because $p$ enters the factorization of the number $p!$ into prime factors with an exponent of 1 (and thus in the factorization of the number $(p!)^{n}$ - with an exponent of $n$), while in the factorization of the number $\left(p^{2}\right)!$ - with an exponent of $p+1$. We will prove that $\left(p^{2}\right)!$ is divisible by $(p!)^{p+1}$.
reference_solution:
First solution. Write down $p^{2}$ different elements in the form of a $p \times p$ table. Two such tables are called equivalent if one can be obtained from the other by some permutations of elements within rows, as well as some permutation of the rows themselves (a total of $p+1$ permutations of $p$ objects). Since $m$ objects can be permuted in $m!$ ways, there are a total of $(p^{2})!$ tables, and they are divided into classes of equivalent tables, with $(p!)^{p+1}$ tables in each class, so $(p^{2})!$ is divisible by $(p!)^{p+1}$.

Second solution. For all natural numbers $k \leqslant n$, the number

$$
C_{n}^{k}=\frac{n(n-1) \ldots(n-k+1)}{k!}
$$

is an integer because it equals the number of $k$-element subsets of an $n$-element set. Indeed, any $k$-element subset can be ordered in $k!$ ways, and the number of ordered sequences of length $k$ from $n$ elements is $n(n-1) \ldots(n-k+1)$.

Therefore, $\frac{(p^{2})!}{(p!)^{p}}=\prod_{i=1}^{p} C_{p i}^{p}$ is divisible by $p!$, since

$$
C_{p i}^{p}=\frac{p i(p i-1) \ldots(p i-p+1)}{p \cdot(p-1)!}=i C_{p i-1}^{p-1}
$$

is divisible by $i$ for all $i=1, \ldots, p$.

Third solution. Take an arbitrary prime number $q \leqslant p$ and prove that in the factorization of the number $(p!)^{p+1}$ into prime factors, it enters in a power no greater than in the factorization of the number $(p^{2})!$.

Since among the numbers $1, \ldots, p$ there are exactly $\left[\frac{p}{q^{i}}\right]$ numbers divisible by $q^{i}$ (where $[x]$ denotes the integer part of $x$, i.e., the greatest integer not exceeding $x$), the number $q$ enters in the factorization of the number $(p!)^{p+1}$ into prime factors in the power $(p+1) \sum_{i=1}^{\left[\log _{q} p\right]}\left[\frac{p}{q^{i}}\right]$ (the upper index of summation is the greatest integer $k$ such that $q^{k} \leqslant p$), and in the factorization of the number $(p^{2})!$, for similar reasons, in the power $\sum_{i=1}^{\left[\log _{q} p^{2}\right]}\left[\frac{p^{2}}{q^{i}}\right]$.

Using the estimate $n[x] \leqslant[n x], n \in \mathbb{N}$ (following from the inequality $n[x] \leqslant n x$ taking into account that $n[x] \in \mathbb{Z}$), we obtain the inequalities

$$
p\left[\frac{p}{q^{i}}\right] \leqslant\left[\frac{p^{2}}{q^{i}}\right], \quad i=1, \ldots,\left[\log _{q} p\right]
$$

And estimating $\left[\log _{q} p\right] \leqslant \log _{q} p$, we obtain the inequalities

$$
\left[\frac{p}{q^{i}}\right] \leqslant\left[\frac{p^{2}}{q^{\left[\log _{q} p\right]+i}}\right], \quad i=1, \ldots,\left[\log _{q} p\right]
$$

Summing the inequalities (1) and (2) over all specified $i$, we get

$$
(p+1) \sum_{i=1}^{\left[\log _{q} p\right]}\left[\frac{p}{q^{i}}\right] \leqslant \sum_{i=1}^{2\left[\log _{q} p\right]}\left[\frac{p^{2}}{q^{i}}\right] \leqslant \sum_{i=1}^{\left[\log _{q} p^{2}\right]}\left[\frac{p^{2}}{q^{i}}\right]
$$

5. First solution. We will prove by induction on $k$ a more general fact: if in the conditions of the problem for each $p$ the polynomial $Q_{p}(x)$ has a degree not greater than $k$, then $f(x)$ at integer points coincides with some polynomial, the degree of which is also not greater than $k$.

Base: $k=0$. In this case, we know that for each prime $p$ there is a constant $Q_{p}$ such that $f(x)-Q_{p}$ is divisible by $p$ for any integer $x$. But then

$$
\left(f(x)-Q_{p}\right)-\left(f(y)-Q_{p}\right)=f(x)-f(y)
$$

is divisible by $p$ for any integers $x$ and $y$ and any prime $p$. But this can only be if $f(x)=f(y)$, that is, $f(x)$ is constant at integers. The base is proved.

Transition from $k$ to $k+1$. For a function $h(x)$, denote by $\Delta h(x)$ the function equal to $h(x+1)-h(x)$. We will need two lemmas.

Lemma 1. If $h(x)$ is a polynomial of degree not more than $m$, then $\Delta h(x)$ is a polynomial of degree not more than $m-1$.

Proof. The degrees of the polynomials $h(x+1)$ and $h(x)$ are equal, as are their leading coefficients. Therefore, the degree of the polynomial $h(x+1)-h(x)$ is less than the degree of the polynomial $h(x)$.

Lemma 2. If $\Delta h(x)$ coincides with a polynomial of degree not more than $m-1$ at integer points, then $h(x)$ coincides with a polynomial of degree not more than $m$ at integer points.

Proof. We will prove this by induction on $m$. Base: $m=1$. If $\Delta h(x)$ is equal to a constant $c$ at integer points, then $h(x)=h(0)+c x$ for all integers $x$. Transition from $m$ to $m+1$. Suppose $\Delta h(x)$ coincides with a polynomial of degree not more than $m$ and the coefficient at $x^{m}$ is $a$ (possibly zero). Then denote by $h_{0}(x)$ the function

$$
h(x)-\frac{a}{m+1} x(x-1)(x-2) \ldots(x-m+1)(x-m)
$$

Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta h_{0}(x)=h_{0}(x+1)- & h_{0}(x)= \\
& =\Delta h(x)-a x(x-1)(x-2) \ldots(x-m+1)
\end{aligned}
$$

and is equal to a polynomial of degree not more than $m-1$ at integer points. Therefore, by the induction hypothesis, $h_{0}(x)$ coincides with a polynomial of degree not more than $m$ at integer points.[^3]

Since $h(x)-h_{0}(x)$ is a polynomial of degree not more than $m+1$, then $h(x)$ coincides with a polynomial of degree not more than $m+1$ at integer points. The transition is proved.

So, let's return to the proof of the transition in the main problem. It is easy to see that the function $\Delta f(x)$ satisfies the induction hypothesis, since $\Delta f(x)-\Delta Q_{p}(x)$ is divisible by $p$ for any integer $x$, and $\Delta Q_{p}(x)$ is a polynomial of degree not higher than $k-1$ by Lemma 1. Therefore, $\Delta f(x)$ coincides with a polynomial of degree not higher than $k-1$ at integer points. Hence, by Lemma 2, we conclude that $f(x)$ coincides with a polynomial of degree not higher than $k$ at integer points. The transition is proved.
reference_solution:
The second solution. Let's try to approach the solution of the problem: we will find a polynomial $f_{0}(x)$ of degree not higher than 2013, which coincides with $f(x)$ at the points $1,2, \ldots, 2014$. Such a polynomial is known and is called the Lagrange interpolation polynomial. In our case, it is given by the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}
& f_{0}(x)=f(1) \cdot \frac{(x-2)(x-3) \ldots(x-2014)}{(1-2)(1-3) \ldots(1-2014)}+ \\
&+ f(2) \cdot \frac{(x-1)(x-3)(x-4) \ldots(x-2014)}{(2-1)(2-3)(2-4) \ldots(2-2014)}+\ldots \\
& \ldots+f(i) \cdot \frac{(x-1) \ldots(x-(i-1))(x-(i+1)) \ldots(x-2014)}{(i-1) \ldots(i-(i-1))(i-(i+1) \ldots(i-2014)}+\ldots \\
& \ldots+f(2014) \cdot \frac{(x-1)(x-2) \ldots(x-2013)}{(2014-1)(2014-2) \ldots(2014-2013)}
\end{aligned}
$$

It is clear that in the expression for $f_{0}(i)$, all terms of the sum are zero except the $i$-th term, which, in turn, equals $f(i)$. Therefore, the polynomial $f_{0}(x)$ satisfies the desired conditions. (For the Lagrange polynomial, see, for example, [1].)

For brevity, let $c=(2013!)^{2}$. Then the coefficients of the polynomial $c f_{0}(x)$ are integers. Let $p$ be a prime number greater than $c$. Then the polynomial $c Q_{p}(x)-c f_{0}(x)$ has a degree not higher than 2013 and has 2014 distinct roots modulo $p$ - these are the numbers $1,2, \ldots, 2014$ (since

$$
c Q_{p}(i)-c f_{0}(i)=c\left(Q_{p}(i)-f(i)\right)
$$

for $1 \leqslant i \leqslant 2014$). Therefore, this polynomial is identically zero modulo $p$. Hence, the number

$$
c\left(f(x)-Q_{p}(x)\right)+\left(c Q_{p}(x)-c f_{0}(x)\right)=c f(x)-c f_{0}(x)
$$

is divisible by any sufficiently large prime $p$ for any integer $x$. Consequently, $f(x)=f_{0}(x)$ for all integers $x$.

Literature. [1] N. B. Alfutova, A. V. Ustinov. Algebra and Number Theory. A Collection of Problems for Mathematical Schools. - M.: MCCME, 2009.

Second solution. Let $x^{2}+p_{1} x+q_{1}, x^{2}+p_{2} x+q_{2}$ be the quadratic trinomials given in the problem, $D_{1}=p_{1}^{2}-4 q_{1}$ and $D_{2}=p_{2}^{2}-4 q_{2}$ be their discriminants. Then the discriminant of their sum

$$
2 x^{2}+\left(p_{1}+p_{2}\right) x+\left(q_{1}+q_{2}\right)
$$

is

$$
D=\left(p_{1}+p_{2}\right)^{2}-8\left(q_{1}+q_{2}\right)
$$

By the problem's condition, $D_{1}+D_{2}=D$, therefore,

$$
p_{1}^{2}+p_{2}^{2}-4 q_{1}-4 q_{2}=p_{1}^{2}+2 p_{1} p_{2}+p_{2}^{2}-8 q_{1}-8 q_{2}
$$

from which $p_{1} p_{2}=2\left(q_{1}+q_{2}\right)$.

Now let $x_{0}, x_{1}$ be the roots of the first trinomial, and $x_{0}, x_{2}$ be the roots of the second. By Vieta's theorem,

$p_{1}=-\left(x_{0}+x_{1}\right), \quad p_{2}=-\left(x_{0}+x_{2}\right), \quad q_{1}=x_{0} x_{1}, \quad q_{2}=x_{0} x_{2}$.

Therefore,

$$
\begin{gathered}
\left(x_{0}+x_{1}\right)\left(x_{0}+x_{2}\right)=2\left(x_{0} x_{1}+x_{0} x_{2}\right) \\
x_{0}^{2}+x_{0} x_{1}+x_{0} x_{2}+x_{1} x_{2}=2 x_{0} x_{1}+2 x_{0} x_{2} \\
x_{0}^{2}-x_{0} x_{1}-x_{0} x_{2}+x_{1} x_{2}=0 \\
\left(x_{0}-x_{1}\right)\left(x_{0}-x_{2}\right)=0
\end{gathered}
$$

Thus, $x_{0}=x_{1}$ or $x_{0}=x_{2}$, i.e., $D_{1}=0$ or $D_{2}=0$ respectively.

Third solution. Let again $x^{2}+p_{1} x+q_{1}, x^{2}+p_{2} x+q_{2}$ be the given quadratic trinomials, $D_{1}$ and $D_{2}$ be their discriminants, and $D$ be the discriminant of their sum. As in the previous solution, from the condition $D_{1}+D_{2}=D$ we obtain the equality $p_{1} p_{2}=2\left(q_{1}+q_{2}\right)$. Then

$$
D=\left(p_{1}+p_{2}\right)^{2}-8\left(q_{1}+q_{2}\right)=\left(p_{1}+p_{2}\right)^{2}-4 p_{1} p_{2}=\left(p_{1}-p_{2}\right)^{2}
$$

Now use the condition that the trinomials have a common root. This means that for some arrangement of the signs + and - instead of the signs $\pm$ the equality holds

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{-p_{1} \pm \sqrt{D_{1}}}{2}=\frac{-p_{2} \pm \sqrt{D_{2}}}{2} \\
& p_{1}-p_{2}= \pm \sqrt{D_{1}} \pm \sqrt{D_{2}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Square the last equality:

$$
D=\left(p_{1}-p_{2}\right)^{2}=\left( \pm \sqrt{D_{1}} \pm \sqrt{D_{2}}\right)^{2}=D_{1}+D_{2} \pm 2 \sqrt{D_{1} D_{2}}
$$

Again, taking into account the condition $D_{1}+D_{2}=D$, we get $\sqrt{D_{1} D_{2}}=0$, from which $D_{1}=0$ or $D_{2}=0$.

Fourth solution. Note that the discriminant of a quadratic trinomial $f(x)=x^{2}+p x+q$ does not change under a shift of the variable, i.e., under the replacement of $x$ with $x+h$. Indeed, the discriminant of the trinomial $f(x+h)=(x+h)^{2}+p(x+h)+q=x^{2}+(2 h+p) x+\left(h^{2}+p h+q\right)$
is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& (2 h+p)^{2}-4\left(h^{2}+p h+q\right)= \\
& \quad=4 h^{2}+4 p h+p^{2}-4 h^{2}-4 p h-4 q=p^{2}-4 q
\end{aligned}
$$

i.e., the discriminant of the trinomial $f(x)$. Therefore, we can assume that the common root of the quadratic trinomials given in the problem is $x_{0}=0$. Then the trinomials have the form $x^{2}+p_{1} x$, $x^{2}+p_{2} x$, and their sum is $2 x^{2}+\left(p_{1}+p_{2}\right) x$. By the problem's condition, their discriminants are related by the equality $\left(p_{1}+p_{2}\right)^{2}=p_{1}^{2}+p_{2}^{2}$, from which $2 p_{1} p_{2}=0$, which means that $p_{1}$ or $p_{2}$ is zero, and thus the discriminant of one of the trinomials is zero.

$$
2 a+\frac{1}{x-b}=2 c+\frac{1}{x-d}=a+c
$$

when $x=\frac{b+d}{2}$. This condition is equivalent to the equality $(a-c) \times (b-d)=2$. Similarly, it can be proved that this equality is also equivalent to the condition that the graphs of the functions $y=2 b+\frac{1}{x-a}$ and $y=2 d+\frac{1}{x-c}$, which are centrally symmetric with respect to the point with coordinates $(\frac{a+c}{2}, b+d)$, have exactly one common point.
reference_solution:
The second solution. Let's rephrase the problem statement as follows: the equation $2 a+\frac{1}{x-b}=2 c+\frac{1}{x-d}$ has exactly one solution. It is not hard to see that if $a=c$ or $b=d$, this equation cannot have exactly one solution. When $a \neq c$ and $b \neq d$, this equation is equivalent to the quadratic equation

$$
2(a-c) x^{2}-2(a-c)(b+d) x+2(a-c) b d+(b-d)=0
$$

(neither $b$ nor $d$ can be its roots under these conditions). It has a unique root if and only if its discriminant is zero, that is, when

$$
4(a-c)^{2}(b+d)^{2}-8(a-c)(2(a-c) b d+(b-d))=0 .
$$

Transforming the last equality and considering that $a-c \neq \mathbf{0}$, we get $(a-c)(b-d)=2$. Similarly, it can be shown that the equality $(a-c)(b-d)=2$ is equivalent to the statement that the graph of the function $y=2 b+\frac{1}{x-a}$ intersects the graph of the function $y=2 d+\frac{1}{x-c}$ at exactly one point.

The third solution. It is not hard to see that a point with coordinates $(x, y)$ is a common point of the graphs $y=2 b+\frac{1}{x-a}$ and $y=2 d+\frac{1}{x-c}$ if and only if the pair of numbers $(x, y)$ is a solution to the system

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
(y-2 b)(x-a)=1 \\
(y-2 d)(x-c)=1 .
\end{array}\right.
$$

Note that the pair of numbers ( $x_{0}, y_{0}$ ) is a solution to this system if and only if the pair of numbers ( $y_{0} / 2,2 x_{0}$ ) is a solution to the system

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
(y-2 a)(x-b)=1, \\
(y-2 c)(x-d)=1 .
\end{array}\right.
$$

The last system, as follows from the problem statement, has a unique solution. Therefore, the graphs of the functions $y=$ $=2 b+\frac{1}{x-a}$ and $y=2 d+\frac{1}{x-c}$ will have a unique common point.

5. First solution. Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots$ be a non-increasing sequence of natural numbers. For $k \geqslant 2$, denote by $S_{k}=a_{1}+\ldots+a_{k-1}$ the sum of the first $k-1$ terms of this sequence, and set $S_{1}=0$.

We will prove that any natural number can be represented as the sum of distinct terms of the sequence $\left\{a_{k}\right\}$ if and only if for any $k$ the inequality

$$
a_{k} \leqslant S_{k}+1
$$

holds.

Indeed, if for some $k$ we have $a_{k}>$ $>S_{k}+1$, then the natural number $S_{k}+1$ cannot be represented in the required form.

To verify the sufficiency, we will prove by induction that any natural number from 1 to $S_{k}$ inclusive can be represented in the required form using only the terms that are included in $S_{k}$, that is, $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{k-1}$.

Base case. From $a_{1} \leqslant S_{1}+1=1$ we have $a_{1}=1, S_{2}=$ $=a_{1}=1$, and for $k=2$ the statement is true.

Inductive step. Without using $a_{k}$, by the inductive hypothesis, we can obtain all numbers from 1 to $S_{k}$. By adding $a_{k}$ to these numbers, we can obtain all natural numbers from $a_{k}+1$ to $a_{k}+S_{k}=S_{k+1}$, and $a_{k}$ itself is also representable in the required form. The intervals $\left[1, S_{k}\right]$ and $\left[a_{k}, S_{k+1}\right]$ cover all natural numbers from 1 to $S_{k+1}$ due to $a_{k} \leqslant S_{k}+1$. The statement is proved.
reference_solution:
The solution to the original problem applies the proven statement to the sequence $\left\{a_{k}\right\}$, which consists of the terms of the geometric progressions $1,3,3^{2}, 3^{3}, \ldots, 1,4,4^{2}$, $4^{3}, \ldots$ and $1,5,5^{2}, 5^{3}, \ldots$, arranged in non-decreasing order: $1,1,1,3,4,5,9,16,25,27,64,81,125,243,256$, $625,729,1024,2187,3125,4096, \ldots$

Let's check inequality (1). For $k=1,2,3$, it is satisfied because $a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=1$. Suppose for $k>3$ the sum $S_{k}$ consists of exactly $n$ terms of the first geometric progression (from $3^{0}$ to $3^{n-1}$), $m$ terms of the second (from $4^{0}$ to $4^{m-1}$), and $l=k-1-n-m$ terms of the third (from $5^{0}$ to $5^{l-1}$). Then the next number in the sequence $a_{k}$ is the minimum of the numbers $3^{n}, 4^{m}, 5^{l}$. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{k}= & \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} 3^{j}+\sum_{j=0}^{m-1} 4^{j}+\sum_{j=0}^{l-1} 5^{j}=\frac{3^{n}-1}{2}+\frac{4^{m}-1}{3}+\frac{5^{l}-1}{4} \geqslant \\
& \geqslant\left(\min \left(3^{n}, 4^{m}, 5^{l}\right)-1\right) \cdot\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{4}\right)= \\
& =\frac{13}{12}\left(\min \left(3^{n}, 4^{m}, 5^{l}\right)-1\right)>\min \left(3^{n}, 4^{m}, 5^{l}\right)-1=a_{k}-1
\end{aligned}
$$

Second solution. By direct verification, we can confirm that the statement to be proven is true for the numbers $1,2, \ldots, 9$. Indeed, $1=0+0+1,2=0+1+1$, $3=3+0+0,4=0+4+0,5=0+0+5,6=1+4+1,7=3+4+$ $+0,8=3+4+1,9=0+4+5$.

We will prove by mathematical induction that the statement of the problem is true for all $N>9$. Assume that for all natural numbers less than $N$, this statement has already been proven. We will deduce from this that this statement is also true for $N$. The main idea of the further solution is that the required representation of the number $N$ as a sum of a number of the first type, a number of the second type, and a number of the third type can be obtained by using such a representation for some smaller natural number $N$.

Let $3^{k}, 4^{l}$, and $5^{m}$ be the largest terms of the three progressions specified in the problem that do not exceed $N$ (where $k, l, m$ are natural numbers, $k \geqslant 2$). If $N > 3^{k} + 4^{l} + 5^{m}$, then $N - 3^{k} - 4^{l} - 5^{m} > 0$. If $N - 3^{k} - 4^{l} - 5^{m} > 0$, then either $N - 3^{k} - 4^{l} - 5^{m} > 0$ or $N - 3^{k} - 4^{l} - 5^{m} < 0$. In the last case, either $N - 3^{k} - 4^{l} - 5^{m} > 0$ or $N - 3^{k} - 4^{l} - 5^{m} < 0$. Since $3^{k+1} > N$, $4^{l+1} > N$, and $5^{m+1} > N$, we have $c > N / 5$,

$$
N - 3^{k} - 4^{l} - c \geqslant c > \frac{N}{5} > 3^{k-1}
$$

and

$$
N - 3^{k} - 4^{l} - c < N - \frac{N}{3} - \frac{N}{4} - \frac{N}{5} < \frac{2 N}{9} < 2 \cdot 3^{k-1}
$$

From this, we get

$$
0 < N - 3^{k} - 4^{l} - c - 3^{k-1} < 3^{k-1}
$$

and, representing the number $N - 3^{k} - 4^{l} - c - 3^{k-1}$ as a sum of a number of the first type, a number of the second type, and a number of the third type, and then adding $3^{k-1} + 3^{k}$ to the first number, $4^{l}$ to the second number, and $-5^{m}$ to the third number, we obtain the required representation as a sum for the number $N$. All cases have been considered.

Problem 2. The cells of a paper square $8 \times 8$ are painted in two colors. Prove that Arseny can cut out from it two $2 \times 2$ squares along the grid lines, which do not share any cells, and whose colorings are identical. (Colorings that differ by a rotation are considered different.)

(L. Popov, A. Gushev)
reference_solution:
Solution 1. Suppose that Arseny will not be able to cut out two such squares. This means that any two squares that match in coloring intersect in at least one cell.

Let's divide our square into 16 squares $2 \times 2$, as shown in Fig. 1a; all of them must be colored differently. Since there are exactly 16 different ways to color a $2 \times 2$ square in two colors, all colorings are present exactly once.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_59e7fc10fe4b38ee956dg-2.jpg?height=307&width=308&top_left_y=93&top_left_x=274)

(a)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_59e7fc10fe4b38ee956dg-2.jpg?height=305&width=299&top_left_y=94&top_left_x=870)

(b)

Fig. 1: to the solution of problem 2

Now let's highlight 12 "descendant" squares $2 \times 2$, marked in Fig. 1b, each of which intersects with two "parent" squares from the first division, joined horizontally. Note that each "descendant" matches the coloring of one of the "parents" (since it must match one of the squares from the first division, and it cannot match those with which it does not intersect).

But if two squares, shifted relative to each other by one cell horizontally, match in coloring, then their top cells must be the same color, and their bottom cells must also be the same color. This gives only four possible colorings for such "descendant" squares. But there are 12 of them, so some two of them will match in coloring; while they all do not intersect pairwise. Contradiction.

Solution 2. As in the previous solution, suppose that Arseny was not able to cut out such two squares.

Consider all 49 squares $2 \times 2$. Since there are 16 possible colorings for such squares, by the pigeonhole principle, some quadruples of squares match in coloring.

First, note that more than 4 squares cannot match in coloring. Indeed, in this case, either their vertical coordinates or horizontal coordinates take at least three different values, meaning that the coordinates of two squares differ by at least 2 (for definiteness, we can consider the coordinates of the centers of the squares). Such squares cannot intersect.

Similar considerations allow us to note that three or four squares with the same coloring must necessarily have a common cell.

Consider some triplet of squares with the same coloring. Without loss of generality, let's assume they are arranged as shown in Fig. 2. Then from the matching colorings it follows that cells $1, 2, 4$ have the same color; similarly for the triplets of cells $\{2, 3, 5\}, \{4, 5, 7\}, \{5, 6, 8\}$. It turns out that all these cells have the same color.

It is clear that for four squares with the same coloring, the conclusion will be similar. This means that in a triplet or quadruplet of squares with matching coloring, they are all either

| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 4 | 5 | 6 |
| 7 | 8 | 6 |

entirely of the first color, or entirely of the second. This means that the remaining 14 ways to color a $2 \times 2$ square can be represented by no more than 2 instances.

Then the total number of $2 \times 2$ squares is no more than $2 \cdot 4 + 14 \cdot 2 = 36$. But there are 49. Contradiction.

Problem 4. Point $M$ is the midpoint of side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$. Circle $\omega$ passes through point $A$, is tangent to line $BC$ at point $M$, and intersects side $AB$ at point $D$ and side $AC$ at point $E$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the midpoints of segments $BE$ and $CD$ respectively. Prove that the circle circumscribed around triangle $MXY$ is tangent to $\omega$.

(A. Doledenok)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_59e7fc10fe4b38ee956dg-4.jpg?height=395&width=495&top_left_y=931&top_left_x=479)

Fig. 3: for the solution of problem 4
reference_solution:
Solution. Note that $M X$ and $M Y$ are the midlines of triangles $B C E$ and $B C D$ (Fig. 3), so $\angle X M B = \angle C$ and $\angle C M Y = \angle B$. Then

$$
\angle Y M X = 180^{\circ} - \angle X M B - \angle C M Y = \angle A
$$

By the property of a tangent and a secant to a circle, we have $B M^{2} = B D \cdot B A$, from which

$$
M Y = \frac{B D}{2} = \frac{B M^{2}}{2 A B}
$$

Similarly, we get $M X = \frac{C M^{2}}{2 A C}$. Dividing one by the other and using $B M = C M$, we find

$$
\frac{M Y}{M X} = \frac{B M^{2}}{C M^{2}} \cdot \frac{2 A C}{2 A B} = \frac{A C}{A B}
$$

Thus, triangles $B A C$ and $X M Y$ are similar by an angle and the ratio of the adjacent sides.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_59e7fc10fe4b38ee956dg-5.jpg?height=287&width=305&top_left_y=212&top_left_x=574)

Fig. 4: to the solution of problem 4

Lemma (converse of the angle between a tangent and a chord theorem). Let in triangle $P Q R$ the angle $Q$ be equal to the angle between the segment $P R$ and the line $\ell$ passing through $R$, as in Fig. 4. Then the line $\ell$ is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $P Q R$.

Proof of the lemma. Draw the line $\ell^{\prime}$ tangent to the circle at point $R$. Then, by the theorem of the angle between a chord and a tangent, the angle between the line and the segment $P R$ is also equal to the angle $Q$ of the triangle. Hence, $\ell$ and $\ell^{\prime}$ coincide. The lemma is proved.

Then $\angle X Y M = \angle A C B = \angle X M B$. It follows that in the circumcircle of triangle $X M Y$, the angle subtended by the chord $X M$ is equal to the angle between the chord $X M$ and the line $B C$. Using the lemma, we conclude that the line $B C$ is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $X M Y$. This means that the considered circles are tangent.

question:
Problem 5. In a row, there are $100 N$ sandwiches, each with sausage and cheese. Uncle Fyodor and the cat Matroskin are playing a game. Uncle Fyodor, in one move, eats one sandwich from one of the ends. Matroskin, in one move, can remove the sausage from one sandwich (or do nothing). Uncle Fyodor makes 100 moves in a row, while Matroskin makes only 1 move; Uncle Fyodor goes first, Matroskin second, and the moves alternate until Uncle Fyodor eats all the sandwiches. Uncle Fyodor wins if the last sandwich he eats has sausage. Is it true that for every natural number $N$, he can win regardless of Matroskin's moves?

(I. Mitrofanov)
reference_solution:
Answer: No.

Solution. We will prove that with $N=3^{100}$, the cat Matroskin will win. For this to happen, all 100 remaining sandwiches must be without sausage by the last move of Uncle Fyodor (otherwise, he can choose a sequence of actions to end on a sandwich with sausage).

Let's number the sandwiches in order. We will divide the cat Matroskin's strategy into several stages. First, we will show that he can act in such a way that by the time one-third of the initial number of sandwiches remains, all sandwiches whose number gives a remainder of 1 when divided by 100 will be without sausage.

In each hundred sandwiches, mark the sandwich whose number gives a remainder of 1 when divided by 100. Let the cat Matroskin, in the first $3^{99}$ moves, take the sausage from each marked sandwich among the central third of the sandwiches. Since Uncle Fyodor eats $3^{99} \cdot 100$ sandwiches during this time, no sandwiches among the central third will be eaten. In the next $3^{99}$ moves, the cat Matroskin will take the sausage from any marked sandwich, and if there are no marked sandwiches with sausage left, he will do nothing. Since Uncle Fyodor eats no more than one marked sandwich per move (see Remark 1), after another $3^{99}$ moves, all remaining marked sandwiches will be without sausage.

In the next stage of his strategy, the cat Matroskin will similarly ensure that all sandwiches whose number gives a remainder of 2 when divided by 100 are without sausage; at this point, the number of sandwiches will again decrease by a factor of 3. On each subsequent stage, he will free from sausage the next remainder when divided by 100; after a hundred stages, when exactly 100 sandwiches remain, they will all be without sausage.

Remark 1. Each move, Uncle Fyodor will eat sandwiches with numbers giving different remainders when divided by 100, even if he eats them from both sides. This can be understood by noting that before his move, the number of sandwiches for each remainder is the same, as the total number is a multiple of 100; and after his move, the situation is the same.

Remark 2. The cat Matroskin's strategy can be refined to show that he also wins with $N=2^{100}$; on each stage, the number of sandwiches will decrease by a factor of 2. For this, he needs to take the sausage only from those sandwiches (with numbers giving the given remainder when divided by 100) that Uncle Fyodor is guaranteed not to reach on the current stage. It is not difficult to understand that such a sandwich will always be found.

However, with $N=2^{100}-1$, Uncle Fyodor wins. Indeed, in the first $2^{99}-1$ moves, he can eat any $2^{99}-1$ hundreds of sandwiches; during this time, the opponent's efforts will result in no more than $2^{99}-1$ sandwiches without sausage. Next, if Uncle Fyodor has $2^{k}$ hundreds of sandwiches in front of him, of which no more than $(100-k) \cdot 2^{k}-1$ are without sausage, then for $k>0$ he can eat the half of the row (right or left) where there are more sandwiches without sausage. Then, in the row, there will be no more than $(100-k) \cdot 2^{k-1}-1$ plus, thanks to the cat Matroskin, no more than $2^{k-1}$ new ones - a total of no more than $(100-k+1) \cdot 2^{k-1}-1$. Continuing this way, when $k=0$, Uncle Fyodor will have a hundred sandwiches, of which no more than 99 will be without sausage.
