Problem 6. Let $p$ and $q$ be coprime natural numbers. A frog jumps along the number line, starting at point 0, each time either $p$ to the right or $q$ to the left. One day, the frog returned to 0. Prove that for any natural number $d < p+q$, there are two numbers visited by the frog that differ by $d$.

(
reference_solution:
Solution 1. Suppose, for some $d1$.

Let the frog return to 0, having made $n$ steps to the right and $m$ steps to the left. Then $n p = m q$, which means $\frac{n}{m} = \frac{q}{p}$. We will assume that the frog repeats this sequence of $m+n$ steps infinitely many times in a cycle; it is clear that the points it visits will be the same.

Take $k > \frac{a+b}{m+n}$. Arrange letters in a circle describing $(m+n) k$ consecutive steps of the frog. We will write them clockwise, one letter per step; if it is a step to the right, we will write the letter "R", and if it is a step to the left - "L". In total, we have arranged $n k$ letters "R" and $m k$ letters "L" in a circle.

Suppose we find a segment of $a+b$ consecutive letters, among which "R" appears exactly $a$ times (and "L" exactly $b$ times). Then these letters correspond to $a+b$ consecutive steps, during which the frog moves exactly $a p - b q = d$. Contradiction. Therefore, on no such segment can the letter "R" appear $a$ times.

Consider some segment of $a+b$ consecutive letters. Suppose the letter "R" appears no more than $a-1$ times. Look at the segment of $a+b$ letters, differing from the previous one by a shift of 1 clockwise, i.e., obtained by removing one letter and adding another. Note that on the new segment, the letter "R" appears no more than $a-1+1=a$ times, and since exactly $a$ is impossible, it also appears no more than $a-1$ times. Repeating these arguments, we get that on any segment of this length, the letter "R" appears no more than $a-1$ times. We can consider the average number of letters "R" in all sets of $a+b$ consecutive letters and conclude that the proportion of letters "R" in the entire circle is no more than $\frac{a-1}{a+b}$. Therefore, the ratio of the number of letters "R" to the number of letters "L" in the entire circle does not exceed $\frac{a-1}{b+1}$.

Similarly, if on some segment of $a+b$ consecutive letters the letter "R" appears no less than $a+1$ times, then the ratio of the number of letters "R" to the number of letters "L" in the entire circle is no less than $\frac{a+1}{b-1}$. Therefore,

$$
\text { either } \quad \frac{n k}{m k} \leqslant \frac{a-1}{b+1}, \quad \text { or } \quad \frac{n k}{m k} \geqslant \frac{a+1}{b-1} \text {. }
$$

Since $\frac{n k}{m k} = \frac{n}{m} = \frac{q}{p}$. To arrive at a contradiction, it is enough to show that

$$
\frac{a-1}{b+1}(b-1) q$, which follows from $a p - b q = d > -p - q$.

We have arrived at a contradiction, so points at a distance $d$ will be found.

Solution 3. As in the previous solution, we will assume that the frog jumps in an infinite cycle. We will also use the representation $d = a p - b q$ for positive $a$ and $b$, with the sum $a+b$ denoted by $r$.

Let $\delta_{i}$ denote the difference between the positions of the frog at moment $i+r$ (i.e., after $i+r$ steps from the start) and at moment $i$. Since they are separated by $r$ steps, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\delta_{i} & = x p - (r - x) q = a p + (x - a) p - b q - (r - x - b) q = \\
& = d + (x - a) p + (x - (r - b)) q = d + (x - a)(p + q)
\end{aligned}
$$

If $\delta_{i}$ equals $d$, then we have found the desired positions. Suppose the opposite, that $\delta_{i} \neq d$ for all $i$. Then all numbers $\delta_{i}$ have the form $d + (p + q) k$ for integers $k \neq 0$.

Note that the difference between $\delta_{i}$ and $\delta_{i+1}$ is determined by the $(i+1)$-th and $(i+r+1)$-th steps; by considering the cases, it is not difficult to convince oneself that it is equal to $-(p+q), 0$, or $p+q$. This means that the numbers $\delta_{i}$ are either all less than 0 (have the form $d - (p+q) k$ for natural $k$), or all greater than 0 (have the form $d + (p+q) k$ for natural $k$).

Then consider the position of the frog after $r T$ steps, where $T$ is the number of steps in its cycle. On the one hand, it is equal to the sum $\delta_{0} + \delta_{r} + \delta_{2r} + \ldots + \delta_{r(T-1)}$, which, by the above, must be either negative or positive. On the other hand, after $r T$ steps, the frog returns to position 0. Contradiction.

question: 3. (E. Bakayev) Prove that in a right-angled triangle with a 30-degree angle, one bisector is twice as short as the other.
reference_solution:
Solution 1: Let there be a right-angled triangle $ABC$, $\angle A=30^{\circ}$, $\angle C=90^{\circ}$. We will prove that the bisector $AK$ is twice as long as the bisector $CL$ of the given triangle. Extend $ABC$ to an equilateral triangle $ABB'$. In this case, $AK$ forms an angle of $15^{\circ}$ with the side of the equilateral triangle.

Let the line passing through $B'$ parallel to $CL$ intersect $AB$ at point $N$. Then $CL$ is the midline in triangle $B'NB$, hence $BN = 2CL$. At the same time, the segment $BN$, like $AK$, forms an angle of $60^{\circ}-45^{\circ}=15^{\circ}$ with the side of the equilateral triangle, thus $AK = BN = 2CL$.

Solution 2: Let there be a right-angled triangle $ABC$, $\angle A=30^{\circ}$, $\angle C=90^{\circ}$. We will prove that the bisector $AK$ is twice as long as the bisector $CL$ of the given triangle. Draw the midline $DF$ in triangle $ABC$ parallel to $BC$. Let it intersect the bisector $AK$ at point $G$. Then $FG$ is the midline of triangle $ACK$ (since $FG \parallel CK$ and $F$ is the midpoint of $AC$), hence $G$ is the midpoint of $AK$. Since $CG$ is the median of the right-angled triangle $ACK$, $\angle CAG = \angle ACG = 15^{\circ}$. Since $CD$ is the median of the right-angled triangle $ABC$, $\angle DAC = \angle DCA = 30^{\circ}$, hence $\angle GCD = \angle ACD - \angle ACG = 15^{\circ}$, $\angle DCL = \angle ACL - \angle ACD = 15^{\circ}$, $\angle ADF = \angle ABC = 60^{\circ}$ (corresponding angles when $DF$ and $BC$ are cut by $AB$), $\angle FDC = \angle FDA = 60^{\circ}$ ($DF$ is the median and thus the bisector in the isosceles triangle $ACD$), $\angle CDL = \angle DAC + \angle DCA = 60^{\circ}$. Triangles $CGD$ and $CLD$ are congruent by side $CD$ and pairs of angles $\angle GCD, \angle LCD$ and $\angle CDG, \angle CDL$. Therefore, $CL = CG = AG = AK / 2$, as required.

Solution 3: Let there be a triangle $ABC$, where $\angle A=30^{\circ}$, $\angle C=90^{\circ}$, $AK$ and $CL$ are bisectors, and $CD$ is the median. Then, by the property of a right-angled triangle, $CD = AD = BD$, and in triangle $\triangle BCD$ there are two equal sides and an angle of $60^{\circ}$, so it is equilateral. Then $\angle ABK = \angle CDL = 60^{\circ}$. At the same time, $\angle KAB = \frac{1}{2} \angle BAC = 15^{\circ}$ and $\angle LCD = \angle ACL - \angle ACD = \frac{1}{2} \angle ACB - \angle BAC = 15^{\circ}$. Then triangles $ABK$ and $CDL$ are similar by two angles. Therefore, $AK / CL = AB / CD = AB / BC = 2$, as required.

Solution 4: Let there be a triangle $ABC$, where $\angle A=30^{\circ}$, $\angle C=90^{\circ}$, $AK$ and $CL$ are bisectors. Construct point $M$ such that $CLAM$ is a parallelogram. Then $\angle BCM = 90^{\circ} + \angle ACM = 90^{\circ} + \angle CAB = 120^{\circ}$, and $\angle KAM = 15^{\circ} + \angle CAM = 15^{\circ} + \angle ACL = 60^{\circ}$. This means that points $A$, $K$, $C$, and $M$ lie on the same circle. Consider triangle $AKM$. In it, $\angle KAM = 60^{\circ}$, and $\angle AMK = \angle ACK = 90^{\circ}$ due to the inscribed quadrilateral $AKCM$. Therefore, its hypotenuse $AK$ is twice the length of the leg $AM$ by the property of a right-angled triangle with an angle of $60^{\circ}$. Then $AK = 2AM = 2CL$ due to the property of the parallelogram.

question: 4. (V. Kleptsyn, K. Knop) We will call a natural number good if its decimal representation contains only zeros and ones. Suppose the product of two good numbers is also a good number. Is it true that then the sum of the digits of the product equals the product of the sums of the digits of the factors?
reference_solution:
Answer: Not necessarily.

Solution: Consider the product of two good numbers

$$
\left(10^{2}+10^{4}+10^{8}+\cdots+10^{1024}\right)\left(10^{N-2}+10^{N-4}+10^{N-8}+\cdots+10^{N-1024}\right)
$$

where $N$ is a large even number (for example, a million). When we expand all the brackets, we get many terms, each of which is a power of 10. If all the terms were different, we would get a good number with the sum of its digits equal to the product of the sums of the digits of the original numbers. Let's see if any of the terms are the same. If $10^{a} \cdot 10^{N-b}=10^{x} \cdot 10^{N-y}$, where $x \neq y$, then $a+N-b=x+N-y$, from which $a+y=b+x$. Since $a, b, x, y$ are powers of two, equality is possible only in the case $a=b, x=y$. Therefore, we will have 10 matching terms, equal to $10^{N}$, which in total will give $10^{N+1}$.

Notice that no other terms are equal to $10^{N+1}$, since the exponent of all terms is even.

Therefore, the sum of the terms will be a good number, but the sum of its digits will be 9 less than the product of the sums of the digits of the original numbers.

1. Tangents were drawn to the graphs of the functions $y=\cos x$ and $y=a \operatorname{tg} x$ at some point of their intersection. Prove that these tangents are perpendicular to each other for any $a \neq 0$.

(V.A. Klypin, G.A. Merzon)
reference_solution: Solution. The abscissa $x_{0}$ of any intersection point of the given functions' graphs satisfies the equation $\cos x_{0}=a \operatorname{tg} x_{0}$. At this point, the tangent to the graph of the function $y=\cos x$ has a slope $k_{1}=-\sin x_{0}$, and the tangent to the graph of the function $y=a \operatorname{tg} x$ has a slope $k_{2}=\frac{a}{\cos ^{2} x_{0}}$. Since $k_{1} k_{2}=-\frac{a \operatorname{tg} x_{0}}{\cos x_{0}}=-1$, these tangents are perpendicular to each other.

question:
2. Let $A B C D$ be a parallelogram different from a rectangle, and let point $P$ be chosen inside it such that the circumcircles of triangles $P A B$ and $P C D$ have a common chord perpendicular to $A D$. Prove that the radii of these circles are equal.

(A. A. Zaslavsky)
reference_solution:
Solution.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_4f99c5bf3497360ef676g-1.jpg?height=540&width=943&top_left_y=901&top_left_x=190)

Method 1. Notice that the line of centers $O_{1} O_{2}$ is perpendicular to the common chord of the given circles, and therefore parallel to the lines $A D$ and $B C$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of segment $A B$, and $N$ be the midpoint of segment $C D$. Then $O_{1} M \perp A B$, $O_{2} N \perp C D$, and since $A B \| C D$, the lines $O_{1} M$ and $O_{2} N$ are parallel. Furthermore, $O_{1} O_{2} \| A D$ and since $A D \| M N$, it follows that $O_{1} O_{2} \| M N$. Therefore, the quadrilateral $O_{1} M N O_{2}$ is a parallelogram by definition, hence $O_{1} M = O_{2} N$. Additionally, since segments $M B$ and $N C$ are equal, the right triangles $O_{1} M B$ and $O_{2} N C$ are equal by the two legs, and therefore their hypotenuses $O_{1} B$ and $O_{2} C$, which are also the radii of our circles, are equal, as required.

Method 2. Assume the contrary, that the radii of the circles $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$, circumscribed around triangles $P A B$ and $P C D$ respectively, are different.

When the segment $C D$ is translated by $\overrightarrow{C B}$, it will become the segment $A B$, the circle $\omega_{2}$ will become the circle $\omega_{3}$, and the line $O_{1} O_{2}$ will remain unchanged. Moreover, $\omega_{3}$ cannot coincide with $\omega_{1}$ because their radii are different. Therefore, the line of centers $O_{3} O_{1}$, which coincides with the line $O_{1} O_{2}$, is perpendicular to the common chord $A B$. Thus, the line $A B$ is parallel to the common chord of the circles $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$ and, consequently, perpendicular to the line $A D$. But then the parallelogram $A B C D$ is a rectangle, which contradicts the problem's condition. Therefore, the radii of the circles $\omega_{1}$ and $\omega_{2}$ are equal.

question: 4. In a tennis tournament (where there are no draws), more than 4 athletes participated. Each game day, each tennis player participated in exactly one game. By the end of the tournament, everyone played against each other exactly once. We will call a player persistent if they won at least one match and never lost after their first win. All other players will be called non-persistent. Is it true that the number of game days when a match between non-persistent players took place is more than half?
reference_solution:
(B.R. Frenkin) Solution. On the last day, all the persistent players won. Therefore, there are no more than half of them. If there are fewer than half, then every day there was a meeting between non-persistent players. It remains to consider the case where the number of persistent players $k$ is half of the total number of players $2k$.

Such a tournament lasted $2k-1$ days, and it needs to be proven that there were at least $k$ days when there was a meeting between non-persistent players. This is equivalent to saying that there were at least $k$ days when there was a meeting between persistent players, since there are exactly half of each (if all persistent players play with non-persistent players, then all non-persistent players participate in these meetings, and vice versa).

Assume the opposite: let the meetings between non-persistent players take place in fewer than half of all tournament days. Then, due to the above observation, the same can be said about meetings between persistent players. Since there are $k$ persistent players, each persistent player played with other persistent players for $k-1$ days. Therefore, the only possible scenario in which meetings between persistent players took place in fewer than half of the tournament days is when all persistent players play among themselves on the same days. In other words, persistent players hold a mini-tournament on these $k-1$ days, which is only possible if the number of persistent players is even.

Now recall that $2k > 4$, so $k > 2$, and since $k$ is even, $k \geq 4$. Then, on the first day of the mini-tournament, at least two pairs of persistent players played, which means that at least two persistent players won on that day. In the future, they must play against each other, but then one of them will lose after winning. Contradiction. Therefore, our assumption is incorrect, and the number of game days when there was a meeting between non-persistent players is not less than half.

question:
5. The midpoints of all altitudes of a certain tetrahedron lie on its inscribed sphere. Is it true that the tetrahedron is regular?

(M.A. Evdokimov)

#
reference_solution:
# Solution.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_4f99c5bf3497360ef676g-3.jpg?height=704&width=1350&top_left_y=346&top_left_x=190)

Consider the tetrahedron \(ABCD\) satisfying the condition of the problem. Note that by the condition, for any height \(h_i\) of the given tetrahedron, the inequality \(\frac{h_i}{2} \leqslant 2r\) holds, where \(r\) is the radius of the inscribed sphere, i.e., \(h_i \leqslant 4r, i=1,2,3,4\).

Let \(S_i\) be the area of the face to which the height \(h_i\) is dropped. We will prove that \(S_1 = S_2 = S_3 = S_4\).

Assume the opposite. Choose the face with the smallest area (if there are several such faces, take any one of them). Without loss of generality, we can assume that its area is \(S_1\) (otherwise, we can introduce new notations). Since not all \(S_i\) are equal and \(S_1\) is the smallest of them, we have

\[
\frac{S_1 + S_2 + S_3 + S_4}{4} > S_1
\]

Express the volume of the tetrahedron in two ways:

\[
V = \frac{1}{3} h_1 S_1 = \frac{1}{3} r (S_1 + S_2 + S_3 + S_4) > \frac{1}{3} r \cdot 4 S_1
\]

From this, \(h_1 > 4r\), which contradicts the inequality \(h_1 \leqslant 4r\).

Thus, all \(S_i\) are equal, so all \(h_i\) are also equal, since \(h_i = \frac{3V}{S_i}\). Let \(h\) be the length of these equal heights. From the above volume relation, we get \(h = 4r\), i.e., the inequality \(h \leqslant 4r\) becomes an equality. This is possible only if the height contains the center of the sphere and the point of tangency with the face (and so for each height).

Let \(H\) be the foot of the height of the tetrahedron dropped from point \(A\). Then \(H\) coincides with the point of tangency of the sphere and the face \(BCD\). Let \(BH = a\), then by the theorem of the tangent and the secant \(a^2 = \frac{h}{2} \cdot h\). By the Pythagorean theorem in the right triangle \(ABH\), we get

\[
AB^2 = AH^2 + BH^2 = h^2 + a^2 = h^2 + \frac{h^2}{2} = \frac{3h^2}{2}
\]

Similarly, we obtain the same expression for the other edges of the tetrahedron, so they are equal to each other, i.e., the tetrahedron is regular.

question:
5. Two triangles intersect along a hexagon, which cuts off 6 small triangles from them. The radii of the inscribed circles of these six triangles are equal. Prove that the radii of the inscribed circles of the two original triangles are also equal.

(A. Kushnir)
reference_solution:
Solution. Let the radii of the six equal circles be denoted by $r$, and their centers by $A, B, C, D, E, F$ in counterclockwise order. Consider the triangle $A C E$. Note that if we consider the circle inscribed in the original triangle containing triangle $A C E$, and then reduce its radius by $r$ while keeping the center the same, we obtain the circle inscribed in triangle $A C E$ (see Figure 1). Similarly, the radius of the circle inscribed in triangle $B D F$ is $r$ less than the radius of the circle inscribed in the original triangle containing $B D F$. Thus, the statement of the problem is equivalent to the equality of the radii of the circles inscribed in triangles $A C E$ and $B D F$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_dcfac8f96fa27961912cg-3.jpg?height=811&width=811&top_left_y=329&top_left_x=321)

Fig. 1: to the solution of problem 5

Drop perpendiculars from $A$ to $B F$, from $B$ to $A C$, and so on. Denote their feet by $A_{1}, B_{1}, \ldots$, and the intersection point of segments $A B_{1}$ and $A_{1} B$ by $X$. It is easy to see that the lengths of segments $A A_{1}, B B_{1}, \ldots$ are $2 r$. Consider the quadrilateral $A A_{1} B_{1} B$. It is cyclic because $\angle A A_{1} B = \angle A B_{1} B$, and since $A A_{1} = B B_{1}$, it is an isosceles trapezoid with bases $A B$ and $A_{1} B_{1}$. Therefore, $\triangle A X A_{1} = \triangle B X B_{1}$ and $A B_{1} = A_{1} B$. Considering trapezoids $B B_{1} C_{1} C, C C_{1} D_{1} D, \ldots$, we obtain similar equalities of triangles and segments (see Figure 2; on it, three pairs of equal triangles out of six are shaded).

It is easy to see that the perimeters of triangles $A C E$ and $B D F$ are equal:

$$
\begin{array}{rl}
P_{A C E} = A B_{1} + B_{1} C + C & C D_{1} + D_{1} E + E F_{1} + F_{1} A = \\
& = A_{1} B + B C_{1} + C_{1} D + D E_{1} + E_{1} F + F A_{1} = P_{B D F}
\end{array}
$$

The areas of triangles $A C E$ and $B D F$ are also equal, since when cutting out the common hexagon from them, six right triangles remain, which can be divided into pairs of equal triangles.

Since the area of a triangle is the product of the radius of the circle inscribed in the triangle and the semiperimeter, it follows from the equality of the areas and the equality of the perimeters of the two triangles that the radii of the circles inscribed in them are equal.

Comment. There are quite asymmetrical examples of the construction described in the problem, such as the one depicted in Fig. 3. In particular, it cannot be claimed that the original triangles are equal to each other, nor that the circles inscribed in them coincide (i.e., that the hexagon of intersection is circumscribed).

question:
6. Andrei Mikhailovich wrote on the board all possible sequences of length 2022, consisting of 1011 zeros and 1011 ones. Let's call two sequences compatible if they coincide in exactly 4 positions. Prove that Andrei Mikhailovich can divide all the sequences into 20 groups so that no two compatible sequences end up in the same group.

(A. Raigorodsky)
reference_solution: Solution. It is clear that compatible sequences coincide in two positions by ones, and in two - by zeros. Consider the first five positions. There are $C_{5}^{3}=10$ ways to place three ones in these five positions. For each of these ten ways, Andrey Mikhailovich groups the sequences written on the board, the first three ones of which are in the corresponding three positions. Thus, Andrey Mikhailovich divides all the sequences written on the board, which have at least three ones in the first five positions, into ten groups. Moreover, any two sequences from one group coincide by ones in at least three positions, hence they are not compatible. Similarly, Andrey Mikhailovich divides all the sequences written on the board, which have at least three zeros in the first five positions, into ten groups. Since each sequence has either three zeros or three ones in the first five positions, Andrey Mikhailovich has divided all the sequences into 20 groups.

question:
# 2. A. Blinkov

Given an isosceles trapezoid, the sum of the lateral sides of which is equal to the larger base. Prove that the acute angle between the diagonals is no more than 60 degrees.
reference_solution:
Solution 1.

Consider trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $BC$ and $AD$, where $AD = AB + CD = 2AB$. In triangle $ABD$, the angle $\sin \angle ADB = \frac{AH}{AD} \leqslant \frac{AB}{AD} = \frac{1}{2}$, where $AD$ is the height from point $A$. Therefore, $\angle ADB \leqslant 30^{\circ}$, similarly $\angle CAD \leqslant 30^{\circ}$. In triangle $AOD$, where point $O$ is the intersection of the diagonals, $\angle AOB \geqslant 120^{\circ}$, which means the smaller angle is no more than $60^{\circ}$ degrees as the adjacent angle.

## Solution 2.

Trapezoid $ABCD$ is inscribed in a circle. Its lateral side is half the length of the base and, therefore, no longer than the radius of the circle. Thus, the lateral sides subtend arcs no greater than 60 degrees. The angle between the diagonals is equal to half the sum of these arcs.

The first solution.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_df35a4934f33dda81cacg-3.jpg?height=555&width=393&top_left_y=476&top_left_x=693)

$$

$$
1=\frac{B X}{X C} \cdot \frac{C R}{R A} \cdot \frac{A Y}{Y B}=\frac{P B}{P C} \cdot \frac{C R}{R A} \cdot \frac{P A}{P B}=\frac{P D}{P C} \cdot \frac{C R}{R A} \cdot \frac{P A}{P D}=\frac{D Z}{Z C} \cdot \frac{C R}{R A} \cdot \frac{A X}{X D}
$$

Applying Menelaus' theorem for triangle $A C D$, we get that points $Z, R, X$ lie on the same line. It remains to recall that point $Y$ also lies on this line.

The second solution.

$$
\begin{gathered}
{[X D, X T, X Z, X C]=[D, T, Z, C]=[P D, P T, P Z, P C]=[P A, P S, P Y, P B]=} \\
=[A, S, Y, B]=[X A, X S, X Y, X B]=[X D, X T, X Y, X C]

Let $p$ and $q$ be coprime natural numbers. A frog jumps along the number line, starting at point 0. Each time, it jumps either $p$ to the right or $q$ to the left. One day, the frog returned to 0. Indeed, the numbers $0, p, 2 p, \ldots,(A-1) p$ give different remainders when divided by $A$ (otherwise for some $0 \leqslant i0$. If $a_{k}$ is the rightmost point, then $r_{k}0$. Then $r_{i+1}<A$, because

$$
r_{i+1}-r_{i}=\left(a_{i+s+1}-a_{i+s}\right)-\left(a_{i+1}-a_{i}\right) \leqslant p-(-q)=A
$$

question:
6. D. Krekov

Prove that there exists a real number $A$, such that the distance from the upper integer part of $A^{n}$ to the nearest square is two for any $n$.
reference_solution:
Solution.

Let $t$ be the larger root of the polynomial $x^{2}-10 x+1$, then $t+\frac{1}{t}=10$. We will prove by induction that the number $t^{n}+\frac{1}{t^{n}}$ is an integer for any non-negative integer $n$. Indeed, this is true for $n=0,1$. Moreover,

$$
t^{n+1}+\frac{1}{t^{n+1}}=\left(t^{n}+\frac{1}{t^{n}}\right)\left(t+\frac{1}{t}\right)-\left(t^{n-1}+\frac{1}{t^{n-1}}\right)
$$

which allows us to perform the induction step.

Let $A=t^{2}$, then $A^{n}+\frac{1}{A^{n}}=\left(t^{n}+\frac{1}{t^{n}}\right)^{2}-2$ and $\frac{1}{A^{n}}<1$, so $A^{n}+\frac{1}{A^{n}}$ is the upper integer part of $A^{n}$, and the nearest square of an integer to it is $\left(t^{n}+\frac{1}{t^{n}}\right)^{2}$.

Note. Of course, $t$ can be any number that is the larger root of a polynomial of the form $x^{2}-n x+1=0$, where $n$ is a natural number not less than 3. It is easy to see that the distance from the $n$-th power of such a number to the nearest integer tends to 0 (this follows from the fact that $t^{n}+\frac{1}{t^{n}}$ is an integer). More generally, if $P(x)$ is a monic polynomial with integer coefficients, all of whose roots, except one, have a modulus less than 1, then this root is real and has the property that the distance from its $n$-th power to the nearest integer tends to 0 (this follows from the fact that the sum of the $n$-th powers of the roots with integer coefficients is expressed as an integer through the elementary symmetric functions of these roots, which are integers).

Numbers with this property, which are roots of polynomials with rational coefficients, are called Pisot numbers. They are of interest in connection with Diophantine approximation problems and have been studied in the works of Thue, Hardy, and Pisot. They were named after Charles Pisot, who discovered many remarkable properties of these numbers in his dissertation, see [3].

## References

[1] Zaslavsky A. A., Geometric Transformations., Moscow: MCCME, 2004.

[2] Elements of Mathematics in Problems. Through Olympiads and Circles to a Profession., Moscow: MCCME, 2018.

[3] Pisot Charles, La répartition modulo un et les nombres algébriques, Thèses de l'entre-deux-guerres, no. 203 (1938).

Problem 4. Given a natural number $n>1$. We will call a positive common fraction (not necessarily irreducible) good if the sum of its numerator and denominator equals $n$. Prove that any positive common fraction, the denominator of which is less than $n$, can be expressed through good fractions (not necessarily distinct) using addition and subtraction if and only if $n$ is a prime number.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_1b4f6750e3c0642144d1g-6.jpg?height=656&width=618&top_left_y=92&top_left_x=418)

Fig. 3: to the solution of problem 3

Let's recall that a common fraction is the ratio of an integer to a natural number.

(T. Kazitsyna)
reference_solution:
Solution. First, we prove that if $n$ is composite, then not every fraction with a denominator less than $n$ can be expressed. If among the good fractions there are reducible ones, then reduce them. Let the least common multiple (LCM) of the denominators of all the fractions obtained after reduction be denoted by $N$. Note that the denominators of all irreducible fractions that can be expressed will be divisors of $N$. Indeed, this statement is true for all good fractions, and the denominators of the sum or difference of fractions, whose denominators divide $N$, will also divide $N$.

Let $n$ be divisible by a prime number $p$, and let the natural number $\alpha$ be such that $p^{\alpha}<n \leqslant p^{\alpha+1}$. Consider any good fraction $\frac{n-a}{a}$, where the denominator $a$ is divisible by $p$. Since $a<n \leqslant p^{\alpha+1}$, $a$ does not divide $p^{\alpha+1}$. Note that $n-a$ is divisible by $p$, so the fraction $\frac{n-a}{a}$ can be reduced by $p$. After reduction, the denominator will not be divisible by $p^{\alpha}$. Thus, $N$ will not be divisible by $p^{\alpha}$, and therefore the fraction $\frac{1}{p^{\alpha}}$ cannot be expressed.

We prove that if $n$ is equal to a prime number $p$, then any fraction with a denominator less than $n$ can be expressed. Consider the fraction $\frac{a}{b}$, where $b<p$. Since $p$ is prime, the numbers $p-a$ and $a$ are coprime. As is known, there exists a natural number $k$ such that $(p-a) k \equiv 1(\bmod a)$. Let $(p-a) k=a l+1$ for some integer non-negative $l$. Then

$$
\frac{1}{a}=\frac{(p-a) k-a l}{a}=k \cdot \frac{p-a}{a}-l=k \cdot \frac{p-a}{a}-(n-1) l \cdot \frac{1}{n-1}
$$

Thus, by adding $k$ good fractions $\frac{p-a}{a}$ and $(n-1) l$ good fractions $\frac{1}{n-1}$, we obtain the fraction $\frac{1}{a}$. The fraction $\frac{b}{a}$ can be represented as the sum of $b$ fractions $\frac{1}{a}$, so it can also be expressed.

question:
Problem 5. A regular 100-gon was cut into several parallelograms and two triangles. Prove that these triangles are equal.

(A. Yuran)
reference_solution:
Solution. For each figure - the parallelogram and the triangle - consider all the vertices of the figures on the boundary. For each figure, draw vectors between adjacent points on the boundary so that their direction corresponds to the traversal of the boundary of the figure counterclockwise.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_1b4f6750e3c0642144d1g-7.jpg?height=260&width=460&top_left_y=544&top_left_x=497)

Fig. 4: to the solution of problem 5

Consider an arbitrary line $\ell$ and all vectors parallel to it. The sum of these vectors is zero. Indeed, to each cut line parallel to $\ell$, there are sets of opposite vectors. If $\ell$ is parallel to the sides of the 100-gon, then the sum of the vectors corresponding to opposite sides of the 100-gon is also zero, as they will be directed in opposite directions and equal in length.

On the other hand, in each parallelogram, the sum of the vectors corresponding to opposite sides is zero. Therefore, in the two triangles, the sum of all vectors parallel to $\ell$ will also be zero.

Choose $\ell$ as a line parallel to one of the sides of the first triangle. We get that the set of vectors of the second triangle parallel to $\ell$ are vectors opposite to the vectors of the first triangle. Similarly for the other two sides. Therefore, for each side of the first triangle, there is a parallel and equal in length side of the second triangle. Consequently, the triangles are equal.

Remark. The dissections from the condition exist, and they can be arranged in a sufficiently asymmetric manner (for example, not all sides of the triangles need to be parallel to the sides of the 100-gon, the triangles do not necessarily form a parallelogram, do not necessarily adjoin the sides of the 100-gon, and are not necessarily symmetric relative to the center of the 100-gon). Figure 5 provides an example of a dissection of a 10-gon.

question: 3. In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$, the bisector $AL$ is drawn. On the extension of the segment $LA$ beyond point $A$, a point $K$ is chosen such that $AK = AL$. The circumcircles of triangles $BLK$ and $CLK$ intersect segments $AC$ and $AB$ at points $P$ and $Q$ respectively. Prove that the lines $PQ$ and $BC$ are parallel.
reference_solution:
Solution.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_c9eb608fba8b4c875be2g-3.jpg?height=593&width=807&top_left_y=403&top_left_x=735)

First method. Consider the segment $K L$, which is the common chord of the circumcircles of triangles $B L K$ and $C L K$. Point $A$ is the midpoint of $K L$, so it lies on the line of centers $O O_{1}$ of these circles. Extend $B A$ and $C A$ to intersect the circles at points $C_{1}$ and $B_{1}$, respectively. Due to the symmetry of the resulting construction with respect to the line $O O_{1}$, segments $A B$ and $A C$ are equal to segments $A B_{1}$ and $A C_{1}$, respectively. Introduce the following notations: $B L=m, C L=n, B A=A B_{1}=c, C A=A C_{1}=b, A Q=x, A P=y$. By the property of the secant, $m(m+n)=B L \cdot B C=B Q \cdot B C_{1}=(B A-Q A) \cdot B C_{1}=(c-x)(b+c)$. Similarly, for the secants $C B$ and $C A_{1}$, we get $n(m+n)=(b-y)(b+c)$. Dividing one equation by the other, we obtain $\frac{m}{n}=\frac{c-x}{b-y}$. By the property of the angle bisector $A L$ of triangle $A B C$, we get $\frac{m}{n}=\frac{B L}{L C}=\frac{A B}{A C}=\frac{c}{b}$. Therefore, $\frac{c}{b}=\frac{c-x}{b-y}$, or $c(b-y)=b(c-x)$. Expanding the brackets and combining like terms, we get $c y=b x$, or $\frac{y}{b}=\frac{x}{c}$, from which, by the converse of the theorem on proportional segments, it follows that $Q P \| B C$.

Second method. Mark points $B_{1}$ and $C_{1}$, which are symmetric to points $B$ and $C$ with respect to the external angle bisector $\ell$ of angle $B A C$. Since the line $\ell \perp K L$, it is the perpendicular bisector of segment $K L$. Since $K L$ is the common chord of the circumcircles $(B L K)$ and $(C L K)$, under symmetry with respect to $\ell$ they map to themselves, so points $B_{1}$ and $C_{1}$ lie on $(B L K)$ and $(C L K)$, respectively. Note that $A B_{1} \cdot A P=K A \cdot A L=A C_{1} \cdot A Q$, so quadrilateral $B_{1} Q P C_{1}$ is cyclic, therefore $\angle A Q P=\angle C_{1} B_{1} A=\angle A B C$, which proves the required.

4. First solution. Mark the pears with the smallest and the largest weights (we will call them pears $X$ and $Y$ respectively). Obviously, if the pears placed between them are sorted by weight (separately in a clockwise direction from $X$ to $Y$ and separately in a counterclockwise direction from $X$ to $Y$, thus dividing our pears into two parts), the weights of any two adjacent pears will still differ by no more than 1 g. Indeed, if between two pears, the weights of which differ by no more than 1 g, we place a pear that is lighter than one of them and heavier than the other, the difference in weight between adjacent pears will not exceed 1 g. We will reduce the problem to a more convenient situation where pears $X$ and $Y$ are diametrically opposite.

For this, we will arrange the pears in a row in ascending order of weight, with pear $X$ in the first place and pear $Y$ in the last. We will prove that for any pear in this row, the two subsequent, heavier pears (if they exist) also differ from it by no more than 1 g. Indeed, consider an arbitrary pear $Z$ in the row. There are at least two pears that are heavier than $Z$ by no more than 1 g. One of them is the one that was adjacent to it in the circle after sorting, and the second will be found because if we moved $Z$ to another part after sorting in the circle (it will find a place because it is not lighter than $X$ and not heavier than $Y$), the main property will not be violated - the weights of any two adjacent pears will still differ by no more than 1 g, and the adjacent pear, heavier than $Z$, will fit. From this, the required follows obviously.

Now we will again arrange the pears in a circle so that $X$ and $Y$ are opposite each other. Clockwise from $X$ to $Y$, we will place the pears from the odd positions in the row in ascending order of weight, and counterclockwise from $X$ we will similarly place the pears from the even positions in the row. Note that the condition about the weights of any two adjacent pears is preserved, which follows from the proven statement. After that, we will start, for example, with pear $X$ and move counterclockwise, taking a pear, placing it in a bag together with the opposite one, and laying them out sequentially in a circle. It is not difficult to check that the weights of two adjacent bags will differ by no more than 1 g.
reference_solution:
Second solution. We will prove the following statement by mathematical induction.
$A_{n}:$ if the number of pears laid out is $2 n+2$, then they can be paired as required by the condition.

B a s e. The number of pears is 4. We combine the lightest and heaviest pears into one pair, and the remaining two into another. It is obvious that the masses of the pairs differ by less than 1 g.

S t e p. Suppose the statement is proven for $2 n$ pears, $n \geqslant 2$. Consider $2 n+2$ pears and remove the lightest and heaviest pears ($A$ and $B$ respectively). The remaining set still satisfies the condition, so by the induction hypothesis, these $2 n$ pears can be arranged in pairs in a circle in the correct manner. There are three possible cases:

1) the pair $(A, B)$ is not the lightest or heaviest among the pairs formed from $2 n$ pears;
2) the pair $(A, B)$ is the lightest;

3) the pair $(A, B)$ is the heaviest.

We will show how to arrange all $2 n+2$ pears in pairs in a circle in each of the three cases.

Case 1: there will be such pairs $\left(C_{1}, C_{2}\right)$ and ( $D_{1}, D_{2}$ ), that

$$
m\left(C_{1}\right)+m\left(C_{2}\right)<m(A)+m(B)<m\left(D_{1}\right)+m\left(D_{2}\right)
$$

Then on either of the two arcs connecting the pairs of pears $\left(C_{1}, C_{2}\right)$ and ( $D_{1}, D_{2}$ ), there will be a place for the new pair $(A, B)$.

Cases 2 and 3 are analogous to each other; for definiteness, let's consider case 2. Let $A^{\prime}$ and $A^{\prime \prime}$ be the two lightest pears among the remaining $2 n$. It is clear that $A^{\prime}$ and $A^{\prime \prime}$ differ from $A$ by no more than 1 g, since this was true for the two neighbors of the pear $A$. There are two possible scenarios.

1) $A^{\prime}$ and $A^{\prime \prime}$ ended up in different pairs $\left(A^{\prime}, B^{\prime}\right)$ and ( $\left.A^{\prime \prime}, B^{\prime \prime}\right)$. Then the two lightest pairs of pears ( $\left.X_{1}, Y_{1}\right),\left(X_{2}, Y_{2}\right)$ (for definiteness, assume that $m\left(X_{1}\right)+m\left(Y_{1}\right) \geqslant m\left(X_{2}\right)+$ $\left.+m\left(Y_{2}\right)\right)$ differ from the pair $(A, B)$ by no more than one gram, since already

$$
0 \leqslant\left(m\left(A^{\prime}\right)+m\left(B^{\prime}\right)\right)-(m(A)+m(B)) \leqslant 1
$$

and

$$
0 \leqslant\left(m\left(A^{\prime \prime}\right)+m\left(B^{\prime \prime}\right)\right)-(m(A)+m(B)) \leqslant 1
$$

If the pairs ( $X_{1}, Y_{1}$ ) and ( $X_{2}, Y_{2}$ ) are not adjacent, then we remove the pair ( $X_{1}, Y_{1}$ ) and place it next to ( $X_{2}, Y_{2}$ ). This will not violate the conditions for the pairs of pears. After that, we place the pair of pears $(A, B)$ between the pairs ( $X_{1}, Y_{1}$ ) and ( $X_{2}, Y_{2}$ ).
2) $A^{\prime}$ and $A^{\prime \prime}$ ended up in the same pair. Then consider the heaviest pair of pears ( $X_{1}, X_{2}$ ). Remove the pairs ( $A^{\prime}, A^{\prime \prime}$ ) and ( $X_{1}, X_{2}$ ) from the circle (this will not violate the condition). Form the pairs ( $A^{\prime}, X_{1}$ ) and ( $A^{\prime \prime}, X_{2}$ ). For these pairs, on each of the two arcs connecting the former positions of ( $A^{\prime}, A^{\prime \prime}$ ) and ( $X_{1}, X_{2}$ ), there will be a place (analogous to case 1). The reasoning from point 1 can now be applied to the resulting arrangement of pears.

question:
Problem 2. Rectangles $A B C D$ and $D E F G$ are positioned such that point $D$ lies on segment $B F$, and points $B, C, E, F$ lie on the same circle (see figure). Prove that $\angle A C E = \angle C E G$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_3fff55d9eed9f4edd9eag-01.jpg?height=350&width=807&top_left_y=1028&top_left_x=323)

$(2022-1$ / Bakayev E.)
reference_solution:
Solution. Since points $B, C, E, F$ lie on the same circle, then

$$
\angle A C E=\angle B C E-\angle A C B=\left(180^{\circ}-\angle B F E\right)-\angle A C B=180^{\circ}-\angle D F E-\angle A C B
$$

Similarly,

$$
\angle C E G=\angle C E F-\angle F E G=\left(180^{\circ}-\angle C B F\right)-\angle F E G=180^{\circ}-\angle C B D-\angle F E G
$$

Since $A B C D$ and $D E F G$ are rectangles, then $\angle A C B=\angle C B D$ and $\angle D F E=\angle F E G$. Therefore, the expressions on the left sides of equations (1) and (2) are equal, so $\angle A C E=\angle C E G$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_3fff55d9eed9f4edd9eag-02.jpg?height=424&width=811&top_left_y=91&top_left_x=321)

question:
Problem 4. Some cells of a $100 \times 100$ board are painted black. In all rows and columns where there are black cells, their number is odd. In each row where there are black cells, we place a red chip in the middle black cell. In each column where there are black cells, we place a blue chip in the middle black cell. It turns out that all red chips are in different columns, and all blue chips are in different rows. Prove that there will be a cell where both a blue and a red chip are placed.

$(2022-65$ / Frengkin B.)
reference_solution:
Solution. Remove all rows and columns from the board that do not contain black cells. Note that after this, the condition of the problem will still be satisfied. Now all black cells lie within some rectangle $n \times m$, in each row and each column of which there is at least one black cell.

By the condition, there is exactly one red chip in each of the $n$ rows. Then there are a total of $n$ red chips. But these $n$ red chips must be in different columns, so $m \geqslant n$. Similarly, considering the blue chips, we conclude that $n \geqslant m$. Thus, $n=m$. Since there are as many red chips as there are columns and the red chips are in different columns, there is exactly one red chip in each column. Similarly, there is exactly one blue chip in each row.

Consider the top row, which contains a blue chip. Consider the column with this blue chip. In this column, the blue chip is in the topmost cell. It follows that the topmost cell of this column is the middle black cell in this column. This is only possible if there is only one black cell in the column.

It has been proven that there is exactly one red chip in any column. Considering the column with the single black cell, we conclude that the red chip must be in this cell. But there is already a blue chip in this cell. Thus, the required cell is found.

Comment. The constructions described in the problem exist, and it is not necessary that there is exactly one black cell in each row and each column. Possible examples are shown in Figure 2.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_3fff55d9eed9f4edd9eag-04.jpg?height=292&width=620&top_left_y=530&top_left_x=416)

Fig. 2: to problem 3

question:
Problem 5. Two triangles intersect along a hexagon, which cuts off 6 small triangles from them. The radii of the inscribed circles of these six triangles are equal. Prove that the radii of the inscribed circles of the two original triangles are also equal.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_3fff55d9eed9f4edd9eag-04.jpg?height=660&width=656&top_left_y=1172&top_left_x=397)

(2022-62 / Kushnir A.)
reference_solution:
Solution. Let the radii of the six equal circles be denoted by $r$, and their centers by $A, B, C, D, E, F$ in counterclockwise order. Consider the triangle $A C E$. Note that if we consider the circle inscribed in the original triangle containing triangle $A C E$, and then reduce its radius by $r$ while keeping the center the same, we obtain the circle inscribed in triangle $A C E$ (see Figure 3). Similarly, the radius of the circle inscribed in triangle $B D F$ is $r$ less than the radius of the circle inscribed in the original triangle containing $B D F$. Thus, the statement of the problem is equivalent to the equality of the radii of the circles inscribed in triangles $A C E$ and $B D F$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_3fff55d9eed9f4edd9eag-05.jpg?height=808&width=797&top_left_y=488&top_left_x=332)

Fig. 3: to the solution of problem 5

Drop perpendiculars from $A$ to $B F$, from $B$ to $A C$, and so on. Denote their feet by $A_{1}, B_{1}, \ldots$, and the intersection point of segments $A B_{1}$ and $A_{1} B$ by $X$. It is easy to see that the lengths of segments $A A_{1}, B B_{1}, \ldots$ are $2 r$. Consider the quadrilateral $A A_{1} B_{1} B$. It is cyclic because $\angle A A_{1} B = \angle A B_{1} B$, and since $A A_{1} = B B_{1}$, it is an isosceles trapezoid with bases $A B$ and $A_{1} B_{1}$. Therefore, $\triangle A X A_{1} = \triangle B X B_{1}$ and $A B_{1} = A_{1} B$. Considering trapezoids $B B_{1} C_{1} C, C C_{1} D_{1} D, \ldots$, we obtain similar equalities of triangles and segments (see Figure 4; on it, three pairs of equal triangles out of six are shaded).

It is easy to see that the perimeters of triangles $A C E$ and $B D F$ are equal:

$P_{A C E} = A B_{1} + B_{1} C + C D_{1} + D_{1} E + E F_{1} + F_{1} A = A_{1} B + B C_{1} + C_{1} D + D E_{1} + E_{1} F + F A_{1} = P_{B D F}$. Also, the areas of triangles $A C E$ and $B D F$ are equal, since when cutting out the common hexagon from them, there remain six right triangles, which can be divided into pairs of equal triangles.

Since the area of a triangle is the product of the radius of the circle inscribed in the triangle and the semiperimeter, it follows from the equality of the areas and the equality of the perimeters of the two triangles that the radii of the circles inscribed in them are equal.

Comment. There are quite asymmetrical examples of the construction described in the problem, such as the one depicted in Figure 5. In particular, one cannot assert that the original triangles are equal to each other, nor that the circles inscribed in them coincide (i.e., that the hexagon of intersection is circumscribed).

4. First solution. If one of these numbers (for example, $n$) equals 1, then the inequality takes the form $|m-1|>\frac{1}{m}$ and is satisfied for any $m \geqslant 2$. Further, without loss of generality, we will assume that $m>n \geqslant 2$. Then $m \geqslant n+1$, so

$$
\sqrt[n]{m}-\sqrt[m]{n}>\sqrt[n]{n+1}-\sqrt[n]{n} \quad \text { and } \quad \frac{1}{n(n+1)} \geqslant \frac{1}{m n}
$$

Therefore, it is sufficient to prove the inequality $\sqrt[n]{n+1}$ $-\sqrt[n]{n}>\frac{1}{n(n+1)}$ for all $n \geqslant 2$. Using the identity

$$
a^{n}-b^{n}=(a-b)\left(a^{n-1}+a^{n-2} b+\ldots+a b^{n-1}+b^{n-1}\right)
$$

in which we set $a=\sqrt[n]{n+1}$ and $b=\sqrt[n]{n}$, and also considering the inequality $a>b$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sqrt[n]{n+1}-\sqrt[n]{n}=\frac{1}{a^{n-1}+a^{n-2} b+\ldots+a b^{n-2}+b^{n-1}}> \\
& >\frac{1}{n a^{n-1}}=\frac{1}{n(n+1)^{\frac{n-1}{n}}}>\frac{1}{n(n+1)}
\end{aligned}
$$
reference_solution:
The second solution. First, let's prove an auxiliary statement: if the derivative \( f'(x) \) of the function \( f(x) \) is positive and increasing on the interval \([a; b]\), then \( f(b) - f(a) > f'(a)(b - a) \). Indeed, in this case, the tangent at the point \( a \) to the graph of the function \( y = f(x) \) lies below this graph, and therefore intersects the segment between the points \((b, f(a))\) and \((b, f(b))\) at some point \(\left(b, y_0\right)\), where \( f(a) < y_0 < f(b) \) and \( y_0 - f(a) = f'(a)(b - a) \).

Let, for definiteness, \( m > n \), then \( \sqrt[n]{m} > \sqrt[m]{n} \). Apply the proven statement to the function \( f(x) = e^x \) (its derivative is \( f'(x) = e^x \)) on the interval \(\left[\frac{\ln n}{m}; \frac{\ln m}{n}\right]\):

\[
m^{\frac{1}{n}} - n^{\frac{1}{m}} = e^{\frac{\ln m}{n}} - e^{\frac{\ln n}{m}} > e^{\frac{\ln n}{m}} \left( \frac{\ln m}{n} - \frac{\ln n}{m} \right) \geq \frac{m \ln m - n \ln n}{mn}
\]

Applying the same statement again to the function \( g(x) = x \ln x \) (then \( g'(x) = \ln x + 1 \)) on the interval \([n; m]\), we get

\[
m \ln m - n \ln n > (\ln n + 1)(m - n) \geq m - n \geq 1
\]

From this, the required inequality follows.

question: Problem 4. Each point on the plane is painted in one of three colors. Is it necessarily true that there exists a triangle of area 1, all vertices of which have the same color?
reference_solution:
4. Answer. Yes.

First solution. Suppose that such a triangle does not exist, and we will prove that there exists a line, all points of which have the same color.

Let there be two points $A, B$ of the same color (denote this color 1) on some line $l$, with the distance between them being $d$. Let $l_{1}, l_{2}$ be two lines parallel to $l$ and at a distance of $2 / d$ from it. If there is a point of color 1 on any of these lines, then it forms a triangle of area 1 with points $A, B$, all vertices of which have the same color. If each of the lines $l_{1}, l_{2}$ contains two colors and there are two points of the same color at a distance of $d / 2$ on one of them, then these points together with a point of the same color on the other line form a triangle of area 1, all vertices of which have the same color. If, however, each of the lines $l_{1}, l_{2}$ contains two colors and any two points at a distance of $d / 2$ are of different colors, then any two points at a distance of $d$ will be of the same color, which means that all points on the line $A B$ are of color 1.

Now suppose all points of some line $a$ are painted in color 1. Then the remaining points of the plane are painted in the two remaining colors. Take a line not parallel to $a$ and two points $C, D$ on it of the same color (denote this color 2). If there is a point of color 2 on any of the two lines parallel to $C D$ and at a distance of $2 / C D$ from it, then $C, D$ and this point form a triangle of area 1, all vertices of which have the same color. If such points do not exist, then there will be a triangle of area 1 with vertices of color 3.

Second solution. ${ }^{1}$ Suppose not all points of the plane are painted in one color. Then on some line there are points of different colors: points $A$ and $B$ of color 1 and point $X$ of color 2. Let $A_{1} B_{1} B_{2} A_{2}$ be a rectangle where $A, B$ are the midpoints of sides $A_{1} A_{2}, B_{1} B_{2}$ respectively, the lengths of these sides are $4 / A B$, $C_{1}, C_{2}$ are the midpoints of $A_{1} B_{1}$ and $A_{2} B_{2}$ respectively, and $D$ is the point symmetric to $C_{1}$ with respect to $B_{1}$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_3ef5a8ceb2d598e1bed2g-2.jpg?height=242&width=573&top_left_y=967&top_left_x=448)

If among the points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}, A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ there is a point of color 1, it forms the desired triangle with points $A, B$.

If among the points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}, A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ there are no points of color 1, the following cases are possible.

1) Points $A_{1}$ and $B_{1}$ (the reasoning for points $A_{2}$ and $B_{2}$ is analogous) are of different colors. Then the color of $C_{1}$ matches the color of one of them, for example, $A_{1}$. If any of the points $A_{2}$, $C_{2}$ are of the same color, these three points form the desired triangle. Otherwise, the desired triangle is $A_{2} C_{2} B_{1}$.
2) If one of the pairs $A_{1}, B_{1}$ or $A_{2}, B_{2}$ is of color 2, it forms the desired triangle with point $X$.
3) If all points $A_{1}, B_{1}, A_{2}, B_{2}$ are of color 3 and one of the points $C_{1}, D$ is also of color 3, then the triangle $B_{1} C_{1} B_{2}$ or $B_{1} D B_{2}$ is the desired one. Otherwise, the triangle $C_{1} D X$ is the desired one.

question:
5. First solution. First, we will show that the distance to the nearest integer from a number of the form $c - m q$ (where $m \in \mathbb{N}$, $q$ is irrational, and $c$ is any fixed number) can be made arbitrarily small by choosing $m$. Consider $n+1$ numbers $q, 2q, 3q, \ldots, (n+1)q$. Their fractional parts fall into one of $n$ intervals

$$
\left(0 ; \frac{1}{n}\right),\left(\frac{1}{n} ; \frac{2}{n}\right), \ldots,\left(\frac{n-1}{n} ; 1\right)
$$

By the pigeonhole principle, there will be two numbers $m_{1} q$ and $m_{2} q$ ($m_{2} > m_{1}$), whose fractional parts fall into the same interval. Their difference $\left(m_{2} q - m_{1} q\right) = \left(m_{2} - m_{1}\right) q$ is also a number of the form $m q$, and since the difference of their fractional parts in absolute value is less than $1 / n$, for some integer $N$ the inequality

$$
N - \frac{1}{n} < m q < N + \frac{1}{n}
$$

holds. This means that the distance from $m q$ to the nearest integer is less than $1 / n$.

Now, let's consider the problem of the grasshopper. Suppose the grasshopper is initially at point $-a$ and can jump to the right by 1 and to the left by $b$ (where $b > a > 0$). We will transform the problem by scaling the line with a coefficient of $1 / a$. The point $-a$ will then map to the point -1, and the point $b$ will map to the point $b / a > 1$. The grasshopper will now jump to the right by 1 and to the left by $q = b / a$. At some point, the grasshopper will cross the midpoint of the segment $[-1 ; q]$ with a jump to the right by 1 and land at some point $c$. After this, the grasshopper will never make jumps of length $q$ more than once in a row. When jumping to the right by 1, the fractional parts of the points where the grasshopper was before and after the jump are the same.

Suppose the grasshopper is at point $c$. Choose a natural number $m$ such that the distance from $c - m q$ to the nearest integer is less than $10^{-6} / a$. If the grasshopper makes $m$ jumps to the left, it will be within a distance of less than $10^{-6} / a$ from some integer, regardless of how many jumps to the right by 1 it has made. Since the point 0 is to the left of the midpoint of our segment, by jumping to the right by 1, the grasshopper will definitely be within a distance of less than $10^{-6} / a$ from the point 0, and on the original line, it will be within a distance of less than $10^{-6}$ from the point 0.
reference_solution:
The second solution. Regardless of its initial position $x_{0}$, the grasshopper will eventually end up in the interval $\Delta=\left[-\frac{a+b}{2} ; \frac{a+b}{2}\right)$. Indeed, if $x_{0}<\frac{b-a}{2}$, it will jump to the right by $a$ until it jumps past the point $\frac{b-a}{2}$ and ends up in the interval $\Delta_{r}=\left[\frac{b-a}{2} ; \frac{a+b}{2}\right) \subset \Delta$, and if $x_{0} \geqslant \frac{b-a}{2}$, it will jump to the left by $b$ until it jumps past the point $\frac{b-a}{2}$ and ends up in the interval $\Delta_{l}=\left[-\frac{a+b}{2} ; \frac{b-a}{2}\right) \subset \Delta$.

With further jumps, the grasshopper will no longer leave the interval $\Delta$: if it lands on $\Delta_{r}$, it will jump to the left by $b$ and land on $\Delta_{l}$, and if it lands on $\Delta_{l}$, it will jump to the right by $a$ and land on $\Delta_{r}$.

If we glue the interval $\Delta$ into a circle of the same length $a+b$, the grasshopper's jumps on this circle will already be jumps in one direction by $a$ (or in the other direction by $b$, which is the same on this circle).

Since the ratio of the jump $a$ to the length $a+b$ of the circle is irrational, the grasshopper's traces will be dense everywhere on the circle, meaning that sooner or later the grasshopper will land on any arc of the circle. Consequently, the grasshopper's traces are also dense everywhere on the original interval $\Delta$, so sooner or later it will land in any predetermined neighborhood of zero.

5. First solution. Let's divide all guests into ordered triples; we will put a hat with the letter A on the first person in the triple, a hat with the letter B on the second, and a hat with the letter C on the third. To do this, we will line up the guests (which can be done in $(3n)!$ ways), combine the first three into one triple, the next three into another, and so on. Since the triples can be rearranged within the line and still result in the same partition into triples, each partition has been counted $n!$ times. Therefore, the number of ways to divide the guests into ordered triples is $(3n)! / n!$.

Now, to divide the guests into circles, it is sufficient to divide the first $n$ people from their triples into circles (these circles can consist of one person), and then place the rest of the triple after each person, which can be done in a unique way. We will prove by induction on $n$ that the number of ways to do this is $n!$, which will complete the solution.

The base case for $n=1$ is obvious. Suppose the statement is true for $n$, let's prove it for $n+1$. Arrange $n$ people into circles, which can be done in $n!$ ways. In each partition of $n$ people into circles, there are exactly $n+1$ places where the remaining person can be placed: in each existing circle of $k$ people, there are exactly $k$ such places, and we can also isolate this person into a new circle.

Remark. The last argument can be simplified if we notice that each partition into circles corresponds to a permutation of a set of $n$ elements represented in cycle form, and the number of permutations, as is known, is $n!$.
reference_solution:
The second solution. Number the people from 1 to $3 n$. There are exactly (3n)! ways to arrange these people in a row, so it is sufficient to establish a one-to-one correspondence between such arrangements and partitions into circles.

Take any arrangement, put top hats on everyone in the order ABABAB...ABAB from left to right. Mentally divide the people in a row into $n$ triples. In the first circle, take all the people in a row from the beginning to and including the triple where the person with number 1 stands (and close into a circle); in the second circle, take the next triples in a row to and including the triple where the person with the smallest of the remaining numbers stands (and close into a circle), and so on.

Conversely, from a set of circles, it is easy to restore the arrangement: take the circle where the person 1 stands, find the triple ABAB where he is, "cut" the circle immediately after this triple, stretch it into a line and place it at the beginning of the arrangement. Then take the person with the smallest number of the remaining, find "his" circle, cut it in the same way and attach it to the arrangement, and so on.

question:
1. Some non-negative numbers $a, b, c$ satisfy the equation $a+b+c=2 \sqrt{abc}$. Prove that $bc \geqslant b+c$.

(D. V. Goryashin)
reference_solution:
Solution. Method 1. Move all terms to the left side of the equation and complete the square:

$$
a-2 \sqrt{a} \sqrt{b c}+b+c=(\sqrt{a}-\sqrt{b c})^{2}+b+c-b c
$$

Therefore, $b c=b+c+(\sqrt{a}-\sqrt{b c})^{2} \geqslant b+c$.

Method 2. The numbers $a, b$, and $c$ are non-negative, so the original equation can be considered as a quadratic equation in $\sqrt{a}:(\sqrt{a})^{2}-2 \sqrt{b c} \sqrt{a}+b+c=0$. By the condition, this equation has at least one solution, which means $D / 4=b c-b-c \geqslant 0$.

Method 3. If $a=0$, then $b=c=0$, and the inequality is satisfied. Let $a>0$. By the inequality of means, we have $a+b+c \geqslant 2 \sqrt{a(b+c)}$. Then, by the condition, $2 \sqrt{a b c} \geqslant 2 \sqrt{a(b+c)}$, from which, dividing by $2 \sqrt{a}$ and squaring, we obtain the required inequality.

Method 4. By the inequality of means, we have $a+b c \geqslant 2 \sqrt{a b c}=a+b+c$, from which $b c \geqslant b+c$.

question: 4. In an isosceles trapezoid, a diagonal is drawn. A beetle crawls along the perimeter of each of the two resulting triangles. The speeds of the beetles are constant and equal. The beetles do not change the direction of their traversal of their respective perimeters, and they crawl along the diagonal of the trapezoid in opposite directions. Prove that regardless of their initial positions, the beetles will eventually meet. (P. A. Borodin)
reference_solution:
Solution. Let in an isosceles trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $AB > CD$, a diagonal $AC$ is drawn, so that the first beetle crawls along the cycle $A \rightarrow C \rightarrow D \rightarrow A$, and the second one - along the cycle $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C \rightarrow A$. Consider the moments when the first beetle is at point $A$. During the time it takes for the first beetle to complete a full cycle from $A$ back to $A$, the second beetle shifts along its cycle by $AB - CD$ in the same direction. Since

$$
AB - CD < BC + AC - CD = AD + AC - CD < AC + CD + AC - CD = 2AC
$$

with such shifts, at one of the considered moments, the second beetle will be less than $2AC$ away from point $A$ in the direction of its movement, and thus will meet the first beetle on the diagonal $AC$.

question:
Problem 3. (M. Diden) In a room, several children stand by a pile of 2021 candies. Each of them, in turn, approaches the pile, divides the number of candies in it by the number of children in the room (including themselves), rounds the result, takes the obtained number of candies, and leaves the room. Boys round up, while girls round down. Prove that the total number of candies the boys will have after this procedure does not depend on the order of the children in the queue.

In the solutions to this problem, we will assume variables to be integers.
reference_solution:
The first solution. We will prove that if any two children are swapped, the number of candies taken by boys and girls will not change. Since such permutations can achieve any order of children in the queue, this will mean that the total number of candies taken by boys does not depend on this order.

Indeed, it is clear that if two girls or two boys are swapped, nothing will change for the children before or after this pair, and the total number of candies taken by boys will not change.

Now, let there be only $k$ children left, and in front of a pile of $n$ candies stands a pair of a boy and a girl. If $n$ is divisible by $k$, it is easy to see that they will both take $\frac{n}{k}$ candies regardless of the order. Further, we will assume that $n$ is divisible by $k$ with a remainder $r>0$. Then $n=k q+r$, the boy will take $q+1$ candies and leave $(k-1) q+r-1$ candies, the girl will take $q$ candies after him. If the girl had approached first, she would have taken $q$ candies and left $(k-1) q+r$, and the boy would have taken $q+1$ candies after her. Thus, this pair takes the same number of candies regardless of the order, which means nothing changes for them or for the children behind them, as required.

The second solution. Suppose there are $n$ children in the room, and $2021=a n+r$, $0 \leq r<n$. The first child approaches the pile and divides it into piles of size $a$ and piles of size $a+1$ (the total number of piles is $n$, and the number of piles of size $a+1$ is exactly $r$), with all the larger piles lying to the right of the smaller ones.

If the first child is a boy, he takes the rightmost pile and leaves. If it turns out to be a girl, she takes the leftmost pile and also leaves. Then the next child approaches the candies; in front of him lie $n-1$ piles of $a$ or $a+1$ candies.

If piles of both types remain, this means that the quotient of the number of candies divided by the number of children is $a$ and the process continues similarly: boys, rounding up, take piles from the right, girls, rounding down, take piles from the left.

If only piles of one type remain, then the number of candies is divisible by the number of children, and any child can take any pile, which means that in this case, boys can take piles from the right, and girls from the left.

Then, in the end, boys will take all the right piles (as many as there were boys), regardless of the order in which the children approached the candies.

question: Problem 4. (A.Blinkov) In a regular pentagon $A B C D E$, point $F$ is the midpoint of $C D$. The perpendicular bisector of $A F$ intersects $C E$ at point $H$. Prove that line $A H$ is perpendicular to line $C E$.
reference_solution:
First solution. The angle of a pentagon is $108^{\circ}$, then $\angle E C D=\angle C E D=$ $\frac{180^{\circ}-108^{\circ}}{2}=36^{\circ}$, and $\angle A C D=108^{\circ}-36^{\circ}=72^{\circ}$. Thus, $C E$ contains the bisector of triangle $A C F$ and consequently, intersects the perpendicular bisector of side $A F$ at a point on the circumcircle of this triangle. But $\angle F$ is a right angle, so $\angle A H C$ is also a right angle, as it subtends the same arc.

Second solution. Similarly to the first solution, $\angle A C E=\angle E C D=36^{\circ}$. Since $H P \| C D$, by Thales' theorem, $A P=P C$, where $P$ is the intersection point of the perpendicular bisector of $A F$ with diagonal $A C$, and also as alternate interior angles, $\angle P H C=\angle E C D=36^{\circ}$. Therefore, triangle $P H C$ is isosceles and $P H=P C$. Finally, we get that $H P=$ $P A=P C$ and triangle $A H C$ is a right triangle, as its median equals half the side to which it is drawn.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_89d73d034ee0bef24fcbg-3.jpg?height=591&width=671&top_left_y=2029&top_left_x=698)

Third solution. Let's rephrase the problem slightly: let $H$ be the foot of the perpendicular dropped from point $A$ to line $C E$. Then it is sufficient to prove that the point $H$ obtained in this way is equidistant from $A$ and $F$. Let the diagonals $A D$ and $C E$ intersect at point $I$. Mark another point $G$ - the midpoint of segment $D I$. Note that triangle $A E I$ is isosceles $\left(\angle A E I=\angle A I E=72^{\circ}\right)$. Then $H$ is the midpoint of $E I$. Quadrilateral $H G F C$ is an isosceles trapezoid, since $G F \| I C$ (as the midline of triangle $I D C$), and $H G=1 / 2 D E=1 / 2 D C=F C$. $A H G C$ is also an isosceles trapezoid because $H G\|D E\| A C$ and $A G=C H$. Finally, we get that $A H=C G=H F$. Which is what we needed to prove.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_06_89d73d034ee0bef24fcbg-4.jpg?height=611&width=654&top_left_y=831&top_left_x=701)

question: Problem 6. (A. Zaslavsky) In a certain state, there are 32 cities, each of which is connected by a road with one-way traffic. The Minister of Communications, a secret villain, decided to organize traffic in such a way that after leaving any city, it would be impossible to return to it. To achieve this, he can change the direction of traffic on one of the roads every day, starting from June 1, 2021. Prove that he can achieve his goal by 2022 (that is, he has 214 days).
reference_solution:
Solution. We will prove the general formula. Let there be $2^{n}$ cities in the state. Then the prime minister can achieve the desired result in no more than $2^{n-2}\left(2^{n}-n-1\right)$ days.

Lemma. Suppose there are $2k$ cities in the state, each two of which are connected by a one-way road. Choose half of them with the largest number of outgoing roads. Then the total number of roads outgoing from the selected cities is not less than $k^{2}$.

Proof. Suppose from $k$ selected cities, the total number of outgoing roads is less than $k^{2}$. Then, by the pigeonhole principle, there is a city from which no more than $k-1$ roads go out. Since the cities with the largest number of outgoing roads are chosen, from each of the remaining $k$ cities, no more than $k-1$ roads also go out. In total, there are fewer than $k^{2}+k(k-1)=2k^{2}-k$ outgoing roads, while the total number of roads is exactly $\frac{2k(2k-1)}{2}=2k^{2}-k$. Contradiction, the lemma is proved.

Now let's proceed to the proof of the main formula. We will prove it by induction. Base case $n=1$: between two cities, there is only one road, and it is already in one direction. No changes are needed.

Step. Suppose the statement is true for $2^{n}$ cities. We will prove it for $2^{n+1}$. Divide the cities into two groups of $2^{n}$ cities each. In the first group, place the cities with the largest number of outgoing roads. According to the lemma, from all cities in this group, the total number of outgoing roads is not less than $2^{2n}$.

Of these roads, $\frac{2^{n}(2^{n}-1)}{2}$ are roads within the group, so from the first group to the second, there are not fewer than $2^{n-1}(2^{n}+1)$ roads. Then, out of $2^{2n}$ roads between the first and second groups, no more than $2^{n-1}(2^{n}-1)$ are directed into the first group. The prime minister can redirect all these roads to the second group in no more than $2^{n-1}(2^{n}-1)$ days. And in no more than $2 \cdot 2^{n-2}(2^{n}-n-1)$ days, he will ensure that in each group, it is impossible to leave a city and return to it. Therefore, in total, it will take no more than $2^{n-1}(2^{n+1}-n-2)$ days.

Since $32=2^{5}$, the minister will need no more than $2^{3}(2^{5}-5-1)=208$ days, which is less than the 214 days remaining until 2022.

Comment. If there are $n$ cities in the country, then an estimate for the number of $f(n)$ changes can be obtained from the relations $f(2n) \leq \frac{n(n-1)}{2} + 2f(n)$ (essentially proven in the problem) and $f(2n+1) \leq n + f(2n)$ (obvious). The jury does not know whether this estimate is exact.

question:
(!) 1. The midline of a quadrilateral is a segment connecting the midpoints of two opposite sides.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_27f86caa754616304e40g-015.jpg?height=291&width=481&top_left_y=417&top_left_x=197)

Fig. 4. For example, in Fig. 4, these are the segments $K M$ and $L N$. Two geometers, the Englishman Simson and the Frenchman Gergonne, noted such an interesting theorem: The midlines of any quadrilateral and the segment connecting the midpoints of its diagonals pass through a common point and are bisected by it. Prove this theorem. (U. 119, P. 128.)
reference_solution: 1. Place a mass of one unit at each vertex of the quadrilateral \(ABCD\) (Fig. 4). Let \(O\) be the center of gravity of the resulting system of four material points. The masses from \(A\) and \(B\) can be transferred to their center of gravity \(K\), and the masses from \(C\) and \(D\) to their center of gravity \(M\)-this does not change the position of the center of gravity of the entire system. Since the masses at points \(K\) and \(M\) are equal, the center of gravity \(O\) of the material points \((K, 2)\) and \((M, 2)\) (which is also the center of gravity of the entire system) is the midpoint of segment \(KM\). Thus, point \(O\) lies on the midline \(KM\) and divides it in half. Similarly, we can show that \(O\) lies on segments \(LN\) and \(PQ\) (and divides each of them in half). Therefore, segments \(KM\), \(LN\), and \(PQ\) pass through the common point \(O\) and are bisected by it. The theorem is proved.

question:
2. Let masses be placed at the vertices of a triangle. Prove that the line connecting a vertex of the triangle with the center of gravity of the resulting system of material points intersects the opposite side at the center of gravity of the two material points placed at the ends of this side.

The following problem is given as preparatory for problems 4, 5, and 6.
reference_solution:
2. Let masses $m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{s}$ be placed at vertices $A, B$ and $C$ respectively. Denote by $O$ the center of gravity of the three resulting material points. Let $C_{1} \equiv Z\left[\left(A, m_{1}\right),\left(B, m_{2}\right)\right]$.

We need to show that the line $C O$ intersects the segment $A B$ at point $C_{1}$.

Replace the two material points ( $A, m_{1}$ ) and ( $B, m_{2}$ ) with their combination ( $C_{1}, m_{1}+m_{2}$ ) - the position of the center of gravity of the system will not change. But now the system consists of only two material points: ( $C_{1}, m_{1}+m_{2}$ ) and ( $C, m_{s}$ ).

Therefore, the points $O, C$ and $C_{1}$ lie on the same straight line, i.e., $C_{1}$ lies on the line $C O$. Since $C_{1}$ also lies on the segment $A B$, $C_{1}$ is indeed the point where the line $C O$ meets the side $A B$, which is what we needed to prove.

question:
(!) 3. Of course, you know the theorem that in any triangle, the three medians intersect at one point, and each median is divided by this point in the ratio $2: 1$, counting from the vertex. Prove this theorem based on mechanical considerations. (U. 119, P. 128.)

Note that this theorem was known even to Archimedes, who arrived at it based on mechanical considerations. Without using the concept of the center of gravity, it was proved much later, about 14 centuries after Archimedes, by the Italian mathematician Leonardo Fibonacci.
reference_solution: 3. Place a mass of one unit at each vertex of the triangle $ABC$. Let $O$ (Fig. 118) be the center of gravity of the entire system, and let $CC_{1}$ be one of the three medians. The masses of the material points $(A, 1)$ and $(B, 1)$ can be concentrated at their center of gravity $C_{1}$ - the midpoint of the segment $AB$. Now the entire system consists of two material points: $(C, 1)$ and $(C_{1}, 2)$. The center of gravity of the entire system $O$ lies on the segment $CC_{1}$. Similarly, we can show that $O$ lies on the medians $AA_{1}$ and $BB_{1}$. Therefore, all three medians pass through one point (through $O$). By the lever rule, $1 \cdot OC = 2 \cdot OC_{1}$, i.e., $OC : OC_{1} = 2 : 1$.

question:
4. We have just once again recalled that a line passing through the vertex of the base and the midpoint of the lateral side of a triangle cuts off one third of the median of the base. This statement remains valid if the expressions "median of the base" and "lateral side" are swapped, that is:

A line passing through the vertex of the base and the midpoint of the median of the base cuts off one third of the lateral side (of the triangle).

Prove this theorem. (U. 119, P. 129.)
reference_solution:

question: 9. Prove the "trapezoid lemma": the point of intersection of the diagonals of a trapezoid, the point of intersection of the extensions of the non-parallel sides, and the midpoints of the bases of the trapezoid lie on the same line. (
reference_solution: 9. Let $ABCD$ be a trapezoid (see Fig. 113), $AB > CD$, $AM = MB$, $DN = NC$, $AC \times BD \equiv F$, $AD \times BC \equiv E$. We will limit ourselves to proving that points $M, F$, and $E$ lie on the same line. Place masses at points $A, B, E$ such that $F$ becomes the center of gravity of the resulting three material points. Place an arbitrary mass, for example, 1 unit, at $E$. Choose masses $p$ (at $A$) and $q$ (at $B$) such that point $D$ (respectively $C$) becomes the center of gravity of the material points $(A, p)$ and $(E, 1)$ (respectively $(B, q)$ and $(E, 1)$). Then $p \cdot AD = 1 \cdot DE$, i.e., $p = DE : AD$. Similarly, $q = CE : BC$. But $DE : AD = CE : BC$ (since parallel lines cut off proportional segments on the sides of an angle), so $p = q$. Replace the material points $(A, p)$ and $(E, 1)$ with their combination $(D, p+1)$. Then it is clear that the center of gravity of the entire system lies on $BD$. Similarly, we show that it lies on $AC$, i.e., it coincides with point $F$. Moreover, the center of gravity of the material points $(A, p)$ and $(B, q)$ is the midpoint $M$ of segment $AB$. The center of gravity of the entire system must lie on $ME$, i.e., $F$ lies on $ME$, which is what we needed to prove.

question: 10. Prove: in any triangle, the segment of the angle bisector at the vertex, enclosed between the base and the point of intersection of the bisectors, is as many times smaller than the entire bisector as the base is smaller than the perimeter of the triangle. Let in $\triangle A B C$ (see Fig. 6) $A A_{1}, B B_{1}, C C_{1}$ be the bisectors, $O$ - the point of their intersection; $a, b, c$ - the sides. We need to prove that $\frac{A_{1} O}{A_{1} A}=\frac{a}{a+b+c} \cdot(У .119$, p. 131.)
reference_solution:
10. Place an arbitrary mass $p_{3}$ at point $C$ and choose the mass $p_{1}$ at point $A$ such that point $B_{1}$ is the center of gravity of the material points $\left(A, p_{1}\right)$ and $\left(C, p_{3}\right)$. Then $\frac{p_{1}}{p_{3}}=\frac{C B_{1}}{A B_{1}}$. But $\frac{C B_{1}}{A B_{1}}=\frac{a}{c}$ (due to the known property of the angle bisector). Thus,

$$
p_{1}=p_{3} \frac{a}{c}
$$

Similarly, choose the mass $p_{2}$ at point $B$ such that point $A_{1}$ is the center of gravity of the material points $\left(B, p_{2}\right)$ and $\left(C, p_{3}\right)$. We get $p_{2}=p_{3} \frac{b}{c}$.

Let $M$ be the center of gravity of the entire system. The masses $p_{2}$ and $p_{3}$ could be concentrated at point $A_{1}$. Then the entire system would consist of two material points, and the center of gravity $M$ must lie on the line $A A_{1}$. Similarly, it can be shown that $M$ lies on the line $B B_{1}$. Therefore, $M$ coincides with $O$, i.e., $O$ is the center of gravity of the entire system.

By the lever rule, $\frac{A_{1} O}{A O}=\frac{p_{1}}{p_{2}+p_{3}}=\frac{\frac{a}{c} p_{3}}{\frac{b}{c} p_{3}+p_{3}}=\frac{a}{b+c}$.

Forming the derived proportion, we get: $\frac{A_{1} O}{A_{1} O+A O}=$ $=\frac{a}{a+b+c}$, i.e., $\frac{A_{1} O}{A_{1} A}=\frac{a}{a+b+c}$, which is what we needed to prove.

then their areas are proportional to their bases. Therefore, $\frac{S_{\triangle B R A}}{S_{\triangle B B 1 A}}=\frac{B R}{B B_{1}}$.

Let's place masses at the vertices of $\triangle A B C$ such that point $R$ becomes the center of gravity of the resulting three material points. For this purpose, it is sufficient to place masses of 1, 2, and 4 units at $B, C, A$ respectively. question:
16. Let $A B C A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ be an arbitrary truncated triangular pyramid. Then the point of intersection of the planes of triangles $A B C_{1}, B C A_{1}$ and $C A B_{1}$ and the point of intersection of the extended lateral edges $A A_{1}, B B_{1}$ and $C C_{1}$ lie on the same line with the points of intersection of the medians of the bases. (U. 120, P. 134.)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_27f86caa754616304e40g-018.jpg?height=489&width=443&top_left_y=433&top_left_x=661)

Fig. 8.
reference_solution:
16. Place in $S$ ( $S$-the intersection point of lines $A A_{1}$, $B B_{1}$, and $C C_{1}$ ) a mass of one unit, and in $A, B, C$ choose masses $m_{1}, m_{2}$, and $m_{3}$ such that

$$
\begin{gathered}
Z\left[\left(A, m_{1}\right),(S, 1)\right] \equiv A_{1}, \quad Z\left[\left(B, m_{2}\right),(S, 1)\right] \equiv B_{1}, \\
Z\left[\left(C, m_{3}\right),(S, 1)\right] \equiv C_{1} .
\end{gathered}
$$

By the lever rule

$$
\frac{S A_{1}}{A A_{1}}=\frac{m_{1}}{1}, \quad \frac{S B_{1}}{B B_{1}}=\frac{m_{2}}{1}, \quad \frac{S C_{1}}{C C_{1}}=\frac{m_{3}}{1}
$$

Since the planes of triangles $A B C$ and $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ are parallel, then

$$
\frac{S A_{1}}{A A_{1}}=\frac{S B_{1}}{B B_{1}}=\frac{S C_{1}}{C C_{1}}
$$

Therefore, $m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{3}$. Let $O$ be the center of gravity of the system of four material points $\left(A, m_{1}\right),\left(B, m_{2}\right),\left(C, m_{3}\right)$, $(S, 1)$. Two pairs of material points $\left(A, m_{1}\right),\left(B, m_{2}\right)$ and ( $\left.C, m_{3}\right)$, $(S, 1)$ can be replaced by their combinations ( $C_{2}, m_{1}+m_{2}$ ) and ( $C_{1}, m_{3}+1$ ). Therefore, $O$ lies on the segment $C_{1} C_{2}$.

Similarly, we can show that $O$ lies on $A_{1} A_{2}$ and $B_{1} B_{2}$.

From this, it is clear that $O$ is the common point of the three triangles $A B C_{1}, B C A_{1}$, and $C A B_{1}$. But the same four material points can be grouped differently.

Replace the three material points $\left(A, m_{1}\right),\left(B, m_{2}\right)$, and ( $\left.C, m_{3}\right)$ with their combination ( $M, m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}$ ). $M$ is the intersection point of the medians of triangle $A B C$ (since $m_{1}=m_{2}=m_{3}$). The point $O$ lies on the segment $M S$. It is then easy to show that the intersection point of the medians of triangle $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ also lies on $M S$.
