6. Let $0<b_{1}<b_{2}<\ldots<b_{n}$. Then for any $k$, less than $n$,

$$
\frac{b_{1}+b_{2}+\ldots+b_{k}}{k}<\frac{b_{1}+b_{2}+\ldots+b_{n}}{n}
$$

(У. 121, P. 139.)
reference_solution:
6. Choose on some ray $S T$ (Fig. $126, a$) $n$ points $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{n}$ such that $S B_{1}=b_{1}, S B_{2}=b_{2}, \ldots, S B_{n}=b_{n}$. Distribute a mass of 1 equally among $k$ points $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{k}$ (Fig. $126, b$). Let $Z$ be the center of gravity of the resulting system of $k$ material points $\left(B_{1}, \frac{1}{k}\right), \ldots, \left(B_{k}, \frac{1}{k}\right)$. Then

$$
S Z=\frac{b_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots+b_{k}}{k}
$$

Now redistribute the entire mass of this system (equal to 1), specifically, move part of the mass to the right so that each of the points $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{k}, B_{k+1}, \ldots, B_{n}$ (Fig. $126, c$) has a mass of $\frac{1}{n}\left(\frac{1}{n}k\right)$. As a result, the center of gravity of the system will move to the right: if $Z^{\prime}$ is the center of gravity of the new system of material points $\left(B_{1}, \frac{1}{n}\right), \ldots, \left(B_{k}, \frac{1}{n}\right)$, then

$$
S Z^{\prime}>S Z
$$

and

$$
S Z^{\prime}=\frac{b_{1}+b_{2}+\cdots+b_{k}+\cdots+b_{n}}{n}
$$

From (1) - (3) follows the desired inequality.

Another solution. Choose on some ray $S T$ (see Fig. $126, c$) $n$ points $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{n}$ such that $S B_{1}=b_{1}$, $S B_{2}=b_{2}, \ldots, S B_{n}=b_{n}$. Place a mass of 1 unit in each of the points $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{k}, B_{k+1}, \ldots, B_{n}$. Then the center of gravity of the system of $k$ material points $\boldsymbol{B}_{1}, \ldots, \boldsymbol{B}_{k}$ is at a distance from $S$ of

$$
S Z=\frac{b_{1}+\ldots+b_{k}}{k}
$$

The center of gravity $Z^{\prime \prime}$ of the system of material points $\boldsymbol{B}_{k+1}, \ldots, \boldsymbol{B}_{n}$ is at a distance from $S$ of

$$
S Z^{\prime \prime}=\frac{b_{k+1}+\ldots+b_{n}}{n-k}
$$

Since $S B_{1}<S B_{2}<\ldots<S B_{k}<S B_{k+1}<\ldots<S B_{n}$, then $S Z<S Z^{\prime \prime}$.

The overall center of gravity $Z^{\prime \prime}$ of the entire system is located between them, i.e., $S Z<S Z^{\prime}<S Z^{\prime \prime}$, and

$$
S Z^{\prime}=\frac{b_{1}+\ldots+b_{n}}{n}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{b_{1}+\ldots+b_{k}}{k}<\frac{b_{1}+\ldots+b_{n}}{n}<\frac{b_{k+1}+\ldots+b_{n}}{n-k} .
$$

Remark. As can be seen from these arguments, the requirement for the positivity of the numbers $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ could have been omitted.

question:
7. Prove: if

$$
0 < a_i, b_i \quad (i = 1, 2, \ldots, n)
$$

then

$$
\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{n}\right)\left(b_{1}+b_{2}+\ldots+b_{n}\right) \geq n^2 \sqrt[n]{a_1 a_2 \ldots a_n} \sqrt[n]{b_1 b_2 \ldots b_n}
$$

(y. 121, P. 141.)

$$
\text { * }
$$
reference_solution:
7. Let

$$
b_{1}+b_{2}+\ldots+b_{n}=M
$$

On an arbitrary ray OT (Fig. $127, a$), choose $n$ points $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}$ such that $O A_{1}=a_{1}, O A_{2}=a_{2}, \ldots O A_{n}=a_{n}$.

Place a mass of $\frac{M}{n}$ at each of these points (Fig. $127, \sigma$). Let $Z$ be the center of mass of the resulting system of $n$ material points $\left(A_{1}, \frac{M}{n}\right),\left(A_{2}, \frac{M}{n}\right), \ldots,\left(A_{n}, \frac{M}{n}\right)$. Then

$$
O Z=\frac{a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+z_{n}}{n}
$$

Now we will move some masses of this system of material points to the right.

1st step. Clearly, $\frac{M}{n}>b_{1}$. Leave a mass of $b_{1}$ at $A_{1}$, and move the remainder $\left(\frac{M}{n}-b_{1}\right)$ to $A_{2}$ (Fig. 127,8). As a result, the center of mass of the system will move to the right.

2nd step. As a result of the first step, the total mass of the first two material points has not changed (it remains equal to $\left.\frac{2 M}{n}\right)$. Leave a mass of $b_{1}$ at $A_{1}$; at $A_{2}$ leave a mass of $b_{2}$ (Fig. 127,2), and move the remaining mass $\left(\frac{2 M}{n}-\left(b_{1}+b_{2}\right)\right)$ to $A_{3}$. This is possible because, by the previous problem (for $k=2$),

$$
\frac{2 M}{n}-\left(b_{1}+b_{2}\right)>0
$$

By problem 5, the center of mass of the system has moved to the right.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_27f86caa754616304e40g-143.jpg?height=736&width=980&top_left_y=546&top_left_x=132)

Fig. 127.

3rd step. The total mass of the first three material points has not changed (it remains equal to $\frac{3 M}{n}$). Leave the masses $b_{1}$ and $b_{2}$ at $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$, respectively; at $A_{3}$ leave a mass of $b_{3}$ (Fig. $127, \grave{o}$), and move the remainder $\frac{3 M}{n}-\left(b_{1}+b_{2}+b_{3}\right)$ (which is positive by problem 6) to $A_{4}$. As a result, the center of mass of the system will move to the right.

We will perform similar mass transfer operations a total of $n-1$ times; each time the center of mass of the system will move to the right. After $n-1$ steps, we will obtain a system of $n$ material points $\left(A_{1}, b_{1}\right),\left(A_{2}, b_{2}\right), \ldots,\left(A_{n}, b_{n}\right)$ (Fig. 127, e), and its center of mass $Z^{\prime}$ will be located to the right of point $Z$:

$$
O Z^{\prime}>O Z
$$

But by problem 2,

$$
O Z^{\prime}=\frac{a_{1} b_{1}+a_{2} b_{2}+\ldots+a_{n} b_{n}}{M} .
$$

From (1) - (4), the desired inequality follows.

Remark. The proven inequality can be refined as follows: If

$$
\begin{gathered}
a_{1} \leqslant a_{2} \leqslant a_{3} \leqslant \ldots \leqslant a_{n} \\
b_{1} \leqslant b_{2} \leqslant b_{3} \leqslant \ldots \leqslant b_{n} \\
a_{1}>0, b_{1}>0
\end{gathered}
$$

then

$$
\begin{aligned}
& n\left(a_{1} b_{1}+a_{2} b_{2}+\ldots+a_{n} b_{n}\right) \geqslant \\
& \quad \geqslant\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{n}\right)\left(b_{1}+b_{2}+\ldots+b_{n}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

with strict equality holding if and only if the equalities in (5) and (6) are strict. Another solution. Let $b_{1}+b_{2}+\ldots+b_{n}=M$. On an arbitrary ray $O T$, as in the first solution, choose $n$ points $\Lambda_{1}, \ldots, A_{n}\left(O A_{1}=a_{1}, O A_{2}=a_{2}, \ldots, O A_{n}=a_{n}\right)$. Then for the center of mass of $n$ material points $\left(A_{1}, \frac{M}{n}\right), \ldots$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \ldots,\left(A_{n}, \frac{M}{n}\right) \text { we have } \\
& \qquad O Z=\frac{a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{n}}{n}
\end{aligned}
$$

Then place masses $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ at these same points $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}$. In this case, for the center of mass $Z^{\prime}$ of the system of material points $\left(A_{1}, b_{1}\right), \ldots,\left(A_{n}, b_{n}\right)$, we have

$$
O Z^{\prime}=\frac{a_{1} b_{1}+\alpha_{2} b_{2}+\ldots+a_{n} b_{n}}{M}
$$

Since $b_{1}O Z$, the desired inequality follows.

15. Consider the line

$$
y=\sin x \quad\left(0 \leqslant x \leqslant \frac{\pi}{2}\right)

with points

$$

such that (Fig. 132)

$$

$$

Place a mass of one unit at each of these points. Let the point $Z$ with coordinates $(x_{0}, y_{0})$ be the center of gravity of the resulting $n$ material points. Then (see formulas (8)-(9) § 2)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& x_{0}=O X=\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}+\ldots+x_{n}}{n} \\
& y_{0}=X Z=\frac{\sin x_{1}+\sin x_{2}+\ldots+\sin x_{n}}{n}
\end{aligned}
$$

If the line $X Z$ intersects the arc $O S$ of the sine curve at point $P$, and the chord $O S$ at point $Q$, then (see formula (10) § 2)

$$
X Q<y_{0}<X P .
$$

Let's find the equation of the line $O S$. Since it passes through the origin, the equation is of the form: $y=k x$. Since it passes through the point $S$ with coordinates $\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, 1\right)$, then $y=1$ when

$$

where \( x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n} \) are different positive numbers (some of which may be less than 1). First consider the case where each of these numbers is greater than 1.

From this, derive the Cauchy inequality

$$

$$
\left(x_{1}^{m m_{1}} x_{2}^{m m_{2}} \ldots x_{n}^{m}\right)^{\frac{1}{M}} < \frac{m_{1} x_{1} + m_{2} x_{2} + \ldots + m_{n} x_{n}}{M}
$$

where \( m_{1}, m_{2}, \ldots, m_{n} \) are arbitrary positive numbers and \( M = m_{1} + m_{2} + \ldots + m_{n} \). (Ref. 122, p. 150.)

(*) The reader, after considering the problems in § 1, probably has the following doubt: "Yes, the solutions to these problems were simple, but were they mathematically rigorous?" Let's try to clarify this. We used such concepts: mass, material point, center of gravity. In our reasoning, they appeared as purely mathematical concepts. Mass always appeared as some positive number. Every time we had to use this concept, we used it only as some positive number. When we considered a material point, we always, in fact, considered two purely mathematical objects: some geometric point and some positive number. Material points were needed for us only for one purpose - to find centers of gravity. But the center of gravity of two material points always appeared as some mathematical object, as a geometric point, defined in a known way depending on two (geometric) points and two positive numbers. Specifically, the center of gravity appeared as the point dividing the distance between two given points in a ratio equal to the ratio of two given positive numbers. And dividing a segment in a given ratio is already a problem of elementary geometry.

To emphasize the purely geometric nature of the concept of the center of gravity (in the form in which we used this concept here), some geometers refuse to use this term altogether.

They replace the term "center of gravity of two material points $(A, a)$ and $(B, b)$" with the purely geometric term "center of proportional distances of points $A$ and $B$ with corresponding coefficients $a$ and $b$".

The concept of "center of gravity of several material points" is defined through the concept of "center of gravity of two material points" and, consequently, can also be considered a purely geometric concept.

Thus, the introduction of the concept of the center of gravity, even from the point of view of elementary geometry, does not contain anything that could be called "mathematically non-rigorous". However, in solving problems, we used without proof two properties of the center of gravity (see p. 13): the "theorem of the uniqueness of the center of gravity" and the "theorem of the possibility of grouping material points". To make our reasoning truly rigorous, it is necessary to prove these theorems. Let's start with the theorem of the uniqueness of the center of gravity. Let's limit ourselves to the case of three material points, which we will denote as follows: $\left(A_{1}, m_{1}\right),\left(A_{2}, m_{2}\right),\left(A_{3}, m_{3}\right)$ (Fig. 32). To find their center of gravity, we proceeded as follows: we found the center of gravity $B$ of the first two material points $\left(A_{1}, m_{1}\right)$ and $\left(A_{2}, m_{2}\right)$, and then we found the point $S$ - the center of gravity of two other material points: $\left(B, m_{1}+m_{2}\right)$ and $\left(A_{3}, m_{3}\right)$.

This point, by definition, is called the center of gravity of three material points $\left(A_{1}, m_{1}\right),\left(A_{2}, m_{2}\right),\left(A_{3}, m_{3}\right)$.

But we could have proceeded differently: first, find the center of gravity, say, of points $\left(A_{2}, m_{2}\right)$ and ( $A_{3}, m_{3}$ ) (denote it as $C$), and then find the center of gravity $T$ of material points ( $C, m_{2}+m_{3}$ ) and ( $A_{1}, m_{1}$ ). Could it turn out that point $T$ is different from point $S$? Why should they coincide? But they do indeed coincide; this is the essence of the theorem of the uniqueness of the center of gravity (applied to three material points). So, prove such a theorem.

(*) 21. The center of gravity of three material points does not depend on the order in which these points are combined.

Let $\left(A_{1}, m_{1}\right),\left(A_{2}, m_{2}\right)$ and $\left(A_{3}, m_{3}\right)$ be three material points: $B$ - the center of gravity of points $\left(A_{1}, m_{1}\right)$ and $\left(A_{2}, m_{2}\right), C$ the center of gravity of points $\left(A_{2}, m_{2}\right)$ and ( $A_{3}, m_{3}$ ), $D$ - the center of gravity of points $\left(A_{s}, m_{s}\right)$ and $\left(A_{1}, m_{1}\right)$. (U. 122, P. 155.)

(*) 22. Prove the theorem of the uniqueness of the center of gravity of $n$ material points: the position of the center of gravity of $n$ material points does not depend on the order in which these points are sequentially combined. (U. 122, P. 156.)

Now let's move on to the "theorem of the possibility of grouping material points". Consider a special case first.

The property observed by Van Aubel could be formulated as follows:

If three segments connecting the vertices of a triangle to points on the opposite sides have a common point $O$, then the ratio in which $O$ divides each of these segments (measured from the vertex) is equal to the sum of the ratios in which the other two segments divide the sides of the triangle (measured from the same vertex).

reference_solution:
7. As we saw in the proof of Ceva's theorem (necessity), masses \( m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3} \) can be placed at vertices \( A, B, C \) such that conditions (13) - (15) are satisfied.

Fig. 140. In this case, \( O \) becomes the center of gravity of the material points \( \left(A, m_{1}\right), \left(B, m_{2}\right), \left(C, m_{3}\right) \). Replacing the points \( \left(A, m_{1}\right) \) and \( \left(B, m_{2}\right) \) with their combination \( \left(C_{1}, m_{1}+m_{2}\right) \), we get by the "lever rule"

\[
\frac{C O}{O C_{1}} = \frac{m_{1} + m_{2}}{m_{3}} = \frac{m_{1}}{m_{3}} + \frac{m_{2}}{m_{3}}
\]

Applying the "lever rule" to the points \( \left(A, m_{1}\right) \) and \( \left(C, m_{3}\right) \), \( \left(B, m_{2}\right) \) and \( \left(C, m_{3}\right) \), we find

\[
\frac{m_{1}}{m_{3}} = \frac{C B_{1}}{B_{1} A}, \quad \frac{m_{2}}{m_{3}} = \frac{C A_{1}}{A_{1} B}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\frac{C O}{O C_{1}} = \frac{C B_{1}}{B_{1} A} + \frac{C A_{1}}{A_{1} B}
\]

question:
8. Let $A A_{1}, B B_{1}, C C_{1}$ be the medians of triangle $A B C$, and $O$ be the point of their intersection. Then

$$
\frac{A_{1} O}{A_{1} A}=\frac{1}{3}, \quad \frac{B_{1} O}{B_{1} B}=\frac{1}{3}, \quad \frac{C_{1} O}{C_{1} C}=\frac{1}{3}
$$

so that $\frac{A_{1} O}{A_{1} A}+\frac{B_{1} O}{B_{1} B}+\frac{C_{1} O}{C_{1} C}=1$. The French geometer Gergonne, whom we have already mentioned, claimed that this equality is preserved if $A A_{1}, B B_{1}, C C_{1}$ are any three segments having a common point $O$ and connecting the vertices of the triangle with points on the opposite sides. Prove this statement by Gergonne. (U. 122, P. 159.)

8. We load the vertices in the same way as in the solution of the previous problem. Then

$$
\frac{C_{1} O}{O C}=\frac{m_{3}}{m_{1}+m_{2}}
$$

From this,

$$
\frac{C_{1} O}{C_{1} C}=\frac{m_{3}}{m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}}
$$

Similarly, we find:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{A_{1} O}{A_{1} A}=\frac{m_{1}}{m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}} \\
& \frac{B_{1} O}{B_{1} B}=\frac{m_{2}}{m_{1}+m_{2}+m_{3}}

Adding the last three equalities term by term, we get:

$$
\frac{A_{1} O}{A_{1} A}+\frac{B_{1} O}{B_{1} B}+\frac{C_{1} O}{C_{1} C}=1
$$

Thus, Gergonne's statement is proved.

$$
\text { 9. } \begin{aligned}

11. Let condition (18) § 3 be satisfied. Then, by the solution of the previous problem, we can choose four masses $m_{1}, m_{2}, m_{3}, m_{4}$ such that conditions (1) - (4) of this solution are met.

Let $O$ be the center of gravity of the four material points $\left(A_{1}, m_{1}\right),\left(A_{2}, m_{2}\right),\left(A_{3}, m_{3}\right),\left(A_{4}, m_{4}\right)$. We can replace the two material points ( $A_{1}, m_{1}$ ) and ( $A_{2}, m_{2}$ ) with their combination $\left(A_{12}, m_{1}+m_{2}\right)$, and the other two material points $\left(A_{3}, m_{3}\right)$ and $\left(A_{4}, m_{4}\right)$ with their combination ( $A_{34}, m_{3}+m_{4}$ ).

From this, it is clear that $O$ lies on the segment $A_{12} A_{34}$. Similarly, we can show that $O$ lies on $A_{23} A_{41}$. Therefore, $A_{12} A_{34}$ and $A_{23} A_{41}$ intersect (at point $O$ ).

Conversely, let the segments $A_{12} A_{34}$ and $A_{23} A_{41}$ have a common point $O$. We will show that it is then possible to choose four masses such that conditions (1) - (4) of the solution to the previous problem are satisfied.

Place any mass $m_{1}$ at $A_{1}$. Then choose masses $m_{2}, m_{3}$, and $m_{4}$ such that conditions (1) - (3) of the previous problem are satisfied. These conditions uniquely determine the masses $m_{2}, m_{3}, m_{4}$. We will show that $Z\left[\left(A_{4}, m_{4}\right),\left(A_{1}, m_{1}\right)\right] \equiv A_{41}$. Let $F$ (see Fig. 37) be the center of gravity of the system of four material points $\left(A_{1}, m_{1}\right), \ldots,\left(A_{4}, m_{4}\right)$, and let $D$ be the center of gravity of the material points $\left(A_{4}, m_{4}\right)$ and $\left(A_{1}, m_{1}\right)$. Then $F$ lies on $A_{12} A_{34}$ and on $D A_{23}$. Suppose $D$ is different from $A_{41}$. Then $F$ is also different from $O$. Therefore, the lines $A_{1} A_{4}$ and $A_{12} A_{34}$ lie in the same plane - the plane of the triangle $A_{41} A_{23} D$. Then the lines $A_{1} A_{2}$ and $A_{1} A_{3}$ also lie in the same (that) plane, so the quadrilateral $A_{1} A_{2} A_{3} A_{4}$ is planar, contrary to the condition of the theorem. Therefore, $A_{41} \equiv D$, i.e., $A_{41} \equiv Z\left[\left(A_{4}, m_{4}\right), \quad\left(A_{1}, m_{1}\right)\right] ;$ conditions (1)-(4) are satisfied, and consequently, condition (18) § 3 of Ceva's theorem is also satisfied.

question:
1. Prove Menelaus' theorem under the assumption that of the three points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$, two lie on two sides of triangle $A B C$, and the third lies on the extension of the third side. (U. 123, P. 167.)

Menelaus' theorem is often advantageous to apply when it is required to prove that some three points lie on one straight line. As an example, prove, using Menelaus' theorem, the following interesting theorem of Simson ${ }^{1}$ ).
reference_solution:
1. Sufficiency. Let the condition of Menelaus be satisfied. It is required to prove that the points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ lie on one straight line.

Without loss of generality, we can assume that $B_{1}$ and $C_{1}$ lie on the segments $A C$ and $A B$, respectively, and the point $A_{1}$ lies on the ray $C B$ outside the segment $C B$ (see Fig. 41).

We will choose masses in such a way: place an arbitrary mass $a$ at point $A$, a mass $c$ at point $C$ such that
$Z[(A, a),(C, c)] \equiv B_{1} ; \quad$ place a mass $a_{1}$ at $A_{1}$ such that $Z\left[(C, c),\left(A_{1}, a_{1}\right)\right] \equiv B$. Then

$$
\frac{A B_{1}}{B_{1} C}=\frac{c}{a}, \quad \frac{C B}{B A_{1}}=\frac{a_{1}}{c}, \quad \frac{C A_{1}}{A_{1} B}=\frac{a_{1}+c}{c}
$$

But then, by the condition of Menelaus,

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{c}{a} \cdot \frac{a_{1}+c}{c} \cdot \frac{B C_{1}}{C_{1} A}=1 \\
\left(a_{1}+c\right) B C_{1}=a \cdot A C_{1}
\end{gathered}
$$

From this, by the "lever rule," it follows that $C_{1}$ is the center of mass of the material points $(A, a)$ and ( $B, c+a_{1}$ ). But then $C_{1}$ is the center of mass of the system of three material points: $(A, a),(C, c)$ and $\left(A_{1}, a_{1}\right)$. Replacing the points $(A, a)$ and $(C, c)$ with their union ( $B_{1}, a+c$ ), the entire system reduces to two material points ( $B_{1}, a+c$ ) and ( $A_{1}, a_{1}$ ). Therefore, the center of mass of the entire system, i.e., the point $C_{1}$, lies on the line $A_{1} B_{1}$, which is what we needed to prove.

Necessity. Let $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ lie on one straight line. We need to prove that the condition of Menelaus is satisfied. Choosing the loads in the same way as in the proof of sufficiency, we see, as before, that

$$
\frac{A B_{1}}{B_{1} C}=\frac{c}{a}, \quad \frac{C A_{1}}{A_{1} B}=\frac{a_{1}+c}{c}
$$

Moreover, the center of mass of the system of three material points $(A, a),(C, c),\left(A_{1}, a_{1}\right)$ must lie on the lines $B_{1} A_{1}$ and $B A$, so it is the point $C_{1}$. Since $C_{1}$ is the center of mass of the material points ( $A, a$ ) and ( $B, c+a_{1}$ ), then

$$
\frac{B C_{1}}{C_{1} A}=\frac{a}{c+a_{1}}
$$

Multiplying the obtained three equalities term by term, we get the condition of Menelaus.

By slightly modifying the reasoning, we could also prove Menelaus' theorem in the case when all three points lie on the extensions of the sides of the triangle. We omit this, as we will give another proof of this theorem below, covering both cases.

question: 7. On the extensions of sides $A B, B C$, and $C A$ of triangle $A B C$ (fig. 61), points $C_{1}, A_{1}, B_{1}$ are chosen respectively such that $\overline{A C}_{1}=2 \overline{A B}, \overrightarrow{B A_{1}}=2 \overline{B C}, \overline{C B_{1}}=2 \overline{C A}$. Prove that the points of intersection of the medians of triangles $A B C$ and $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ coincide.
reference_solution:
7. Let's take triangle $ABC$ as the base. We will find the barycentric coordinates of points $A_1, B_1, C_1$. We will assign masses $a$ and $b$ to points $A$ and $B$ such that point $C$ is the center of gravity of the material points $(A, a)$ and $(B, b)$. Then $\frac{b}{a} = \frac{\overline{AC_1}}{\overline{C_1B}} = -2$. From this, it is clear that we can take $b = 2$, $a = -1$. Thus,

$$
(A, -1) + (B, 2) = (C_1, 1)
$$

Point $C_1$ is "expressed" through material points with carriers at the vertices of triangle $ABC$. Similarly, we find that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& (B, -1) + (C, 2) = (A_1, 1) \\
& (C, -1) + (A, 2) = (B_1, 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

The center of gravity of the three material points $(A_1, 1)$, $(B_1, 1)$, and $(C_1, 1)$ is the point of intersection of the medians of triangle $A_1B_1C_1$. We will denote this point by $O_1$. Therefore,

$$
(A_1, 1) + (B_1, 1) + (C_1, 1) = (O_1, 3)
$$

From equalities (1) - (4), we find

$$
\begin{aligned}
(O_1, 3) = [(A, -1) + (A, 2)] + [(B, -1) + (B, 2)] + \\
& + [(C, -1) + (C, 2)]
\end{aligned}
$$

That is,

$$
(O_1, 3) = (A, 1) + (B, 1) + (C, 1)
$$

This means that $O_1$ is also the center of gravity of triangle $ABC$.

question:
11. You probably found the proof of Gauss's theorem given on pp. $51-52$ somewhat artificial. A more natural proof can be obtained using the method of barycentric coordinates. Conduct this proof. (P. 174.)

We limited ourselves to considering the method of barycentric coordinates on the plane. But the same idea can be applied in space. Then instead of the coordinate triangle of Möbius, a coordinate tetrahedron of Möbius appears; each point $P$ is characterized not by a triplet, but by a quartet of numbers - the four masses that must be placed at the vertices of the tetrahedron so that the center of gravity of the resulting four material points is the point $P$.

We do not dwell on a more detailed consideration of the method of barycentric coordinates. In questions of elementary (Euclidean) geometry, this method does not provide anything new compared to the methods of vector algebra - a discipline that is now part of the university mathematics curriculum. Moreover, it is possible to indicate a fairly simple recipe for translating any proof found using the method of barycentric coordinates into a "vector" proof.

Historically, the method of barycentric coordinates arose before the vector method and served as one of the foundations in the creation of vector calculus.

It should be noted that in one branch of geometry - so-called "projective geometry" - the method of barycentric coordinates is still very valuable and allows solving problems to which the vector method is not applicable.
reference_solution:
11. Let's keep the notation used in § 5 and Fig. 46. Let $(p, q, b)$ be the barycentric coordinates of point $D$. Then

$$
(D, p+q+b)=(P, p)+(Q, q)+(B, b)
$$

Dividing all masses by $p+q+b$, we get the valid equality

$$
\begin{aligned}
(D, 1)=\left(P, \frac{p}{p+q+b}\right)+\left(Q, \frac{q}{p+q+b}\right) & + \\
+ & +\left(B, \frac{b}{p+q+b}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

It is clear that

$$
A \equiv Z[(P, p),(B, b)], \quad C \equiv Z[(Q, q),(B, b)]
$$

Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}
& (A, p+b)=(P, p)+(B, b) \\
& (C, q+b)=(Q, q)+(B, b)
\end{aligned}
$$

From this

$$
\begin{aligned}
& (A, 1)=\left(P, \frac{p}{p+b}\right)+\left(B, \frac{b}{p+b}\right) \\
& (C, 1)=\left(Q, \frac{q}{q+b}\right)+\left(B, \frac{b}{q+b}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $M$ is the midpoint of segment $A C$, then

$$
\begin{array}{r}
(M, 2)=(A, 1)+(C, 1)=\left(P, \frac{p}{p+b}\right)+\left(Q, \frac{q}{q+b}\right)+ \\
+\left(B, \frac{b}{p+b}+\frac{b}{q+b}\right) .
\end{array}
$$

Since $N$ is the midpoint of segment $D B$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
& (N, 2)=(D, 1)+(B, 1)=\left(P, \frac{p}{p+q+\dot{b}}\right)+\left(Q, \frac{q}{p+q+b}\right)+ \\
& +\left(B, \frac{b}{p+q+b}+1\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $R$ is the midpoint of segment $P Q$, so

$$
(R, 2)=(P, 1)+(Q, 1)
$$

We need to prove that $M$ lies on the line $N R$. For this, it is sufficient to show that it is possible to choose a number $x$ such that the center of gravity of the material points $(N, 2)$ and $x(R, 2)$ is the point $M$. In other words, that the equality

$$
(N, 2)+x(R, 2)=(M, 2(1+x))
$$

holds. By (7)-(9), this is equivalent to the following equality:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(P, \frac{p}{p+q+b}+x\right)+\left(Q, \frac{q}{p+q+b}+x\right)+ \\
& +\left(B, \frac{b}{p+q+b}+1\right)=\left(P, \frac{p(I+x)}{b+p}\right)+ \\
& +\left(Q, \frac{q(1+x)}{q+b}\right)+\left(B,\left(\frac{b}{p+b}+\frac{b}{q+b}\right)(1+x)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's choose $x$ such that the material points with carrier $B$, written in the left and right parts of the last equality, are equal to each other:

$$
\frac{b}{p+q+b}+1=\left(\frac{b}{p+b}+\frac{b}{q+b}\right)(1+x)
$$

From this, $1+x=\frac{(p+b)(q+b)}{b(p+q+b)}$, or

$$
x=\frac{p q}{b(p+q+b)}
$$

But with such $x$, the left part of equality (11) is equal to

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(P, \frac{p}{p+q+b}+\frac{p q}{b(p+q+b)}\right)+ \\
& \quad+\left(Q, \frac{q}{p+q+b}+\frac{p q}{b(p+q+b)}\right)+\left(B, \frac{p+q+2 b}{p+q+b}\right)= \\
& =\left(P, \frac{p(q+b)}{b(p+q+b)}\right)+\left(Q, \frac{q(p+b)}{b(p+q+b)}\right)+\left(B, \frac{p+q+2 b}{p+q+b}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

and the right part of equality (11) is equal to

$$
\begin{array}{r}
\left(P, \frac{p}{p+b} \cdot \frac{(p+b)(q+b)}{b(p+q+b)}\right)+\left(Q, \frac{q}{q+b} \frac{(p+b)(q+b)}{b(p+q+b)}\right)+ \\
+\left(B,\left(\frac{b}{p+b}+\frac{b}{q+b}\right) \frac{(p+b)(q+b)}{b(p+q+b)}\right)=\left(P, \frac{p(q+b)}{b(p+q+b)}\right)+ \\
+\left(Q, \frac{q(p+b)}{b(p+q+b)}\right)+\left(B, \frac{p+q+2 b}{p+q+b}\right)
\end{array}
$$

Thus, if $x$ is determined by formula (13), then in (11), and therefore in (10), the left part is equal to the right. Consequently, point $M$ lies on the line $N R$ (since $M$ is the center of gravity of two material points: $(N, 2)$ and $(R, 2 x)$).

Note also that by the lever rule

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\overline{N M}}{\overline{M R}}=\frac{2 x}{2}=\frac{p q}{b(p+q+b)} & =\frac{\frac{p}{b} \cdot \frac{q}{b}}{\frac{p}{b}+\frac{q}{b}+1}= \\
& =\frac{\frac{B A}{A P} \cdot \frac{B C}{C Q}}{\frac{B A}{A P}+\frac{B C}{C Q}+1}
\end{aligned}
$$

question:
5. The following theorem is true: The sum of the squares of the distances from the vertices of a regular $n$-gon to any point taken on the circle circumscribed around it is a constant value, independent of the position of the point on the circle (it is equal to $2 n R^{2}$, where $R$ is the radius of the circle).

Prove this theorem for $n=6$. (U. 123, P. 178.)
reference_solution:
5. Let $A_{1} A_{2} \ldots A_{8}$ be a regular hexagon, $O$ the center of the circumscribed circle, and $R$ its radius.

Place a mass of 1 unit at each vertex of the hexagon. Then (retaining the notation of problem 4) we will have $J_{P}=J_{0}+6 \cdot P O^{2}$, i.e.

$$
P A_{1}^{2}+\ldots+P A_{6}^{2}=A_{1} O^{2}+\ldots+A_{6} O^{2}+6 P O^{2}=12 R^{2}
$$

for any position of point $P$ on the circle.

Prove that the sum $PA^2 + PB^2 + PC^2 + PD^2$ does not depend on the choice of point $P$ on the sphere. (P. 178.)

question: 7. A circle is inscribed in a regular $n$-gon. Then the sum of the squares of the distances from any point on the circle to the vertices of the $n$-gon is a constant value, independent of the position of this point on the circle. Prove this theorem for $n=3$. (P. 178.)

7. Let $ABC$ be a given triangle, $O$ the center of the inscribed circle, $r$ its radius, $R$ the radius of the circumscribed circle, and $P$ an arbitrary point on the inscribed circle. We will assign equal masses (1 unit each) to the vertices of the triangle.

$$
J_{P}=J_{O}+3 P O^{2}
$$

i.e.

$$
\begin{array}{r}
P A^{2}+P B^{2}+P C^{2}=O A^{2}+O B^{2}+O C^{2}+3 P O^{2}= \\
=3\left(R^{2}+r^{2}\right)

question: (!) 12. In triangle $A B C$, the bisector $C C_{1}$ of angle $C$ is drawn (Fig. 67). Prove: $C C_{1}^{2}=C A \cdot C B-C_{1} A \cdot C_{1} B$. (U. 123, P. 180.)
reference_solution:
12. Let's introduce the notations: $A C=b$, $B C=a, A C_{1}=b_{1}, B C_{1}=a_{1}$ (Fig. 144). We will choose such masses at points $A$ and $B$ that point $C_{1}$ becomes the center of gravity of the resulting material points. For example, we can place a mass of $a_{1}$ units at $A$ and a mass of $b_{1}$ units at $B$. Then $a_{1} A C_{1}=b_{1} B C_{1}$, so $C_{1}$ is indeed the center of gravity of the system of two material points $\left(A, a_{1}\right)$ and ( $B, b_{1}$ ). According to Lagrange's theorem

$$
\left(a_{1}+b_{1}\right) C C_{1}^{2}=J_{C}-J_{C_{1}}=\left(a_{1} \cdot b^{2}+b_{1} \cdot a^{2}\right)-\left(a_{1} b_{1}^{2}+b_{1} a_{1}^{2}\right) .
$$

Since $C C_{1}$ is the bisector of angle $C$, then

$$
\frac{a_{1}}{a}=\frac{b_{1}}{b}=\frac{a_{1}+b_{1}}{a+b}=\frac{c}{a+b}
$$

from which

$$
a_{1}=\frac{a c}{a+b}, \quad b_{1}=\frac{b c}{a+b}
$$

Moreover, $a_{1}+b_{1}=c$. Therefore,

$$
c \cdot C C_{1}^{2}=\frac{b^{2} a c}{a+b}+\frac{a^{2} b c}{a+b}-a_{1} b_{1}\left(a_{1}+b_{1}\right)
$$

or

$$
c \cdot C C_{1}^{2}=\frac{a b c}{a+b}(a+b)-a_{1} b_{1} c
$$

thus,

$$
C C_{1}^{2}=a b-a_{1} b_{1}
$$

which is what we needed to prove.

question:
(!) 14. The English geometer $M$. Stewart (1717-1785) obtained an interesting theorem:

If $C_{1}$ is any point on the side $A B$ of triangle $A B C$, then

$$
C A^{2} \cdot C_{1} B + C B^{2} \cdot C_{1} A - C C_{1}^{2} \cdot A B = C_{1} A \cdot C_{1} B \cdot A B
$$

Prove Stewart's theorem. (U. 123, P. 181.)
reference_solution:
14. Let's introduce the notations: $C A=b, \quad C B=a, C_{1} A=b_{1}$, $C_{1} B=a_{1}, C C_{1}=d$. We will choose the loads at $A$ and $B$ such that point $C_{1}$ is their center of mass. For this, it is sufficient to place a mass of $a_{1}$ units at $A$ and a mass of $b_{1}$ units at $B$. Applying the theorem of Lagrange to the system of two points $\left(A, a_{1}\right)$ and $\left(B, b_{1}\right)$, we get

$$
J_{C}=J_{C_{1}}+\left(a_{1}+b_{1}\right) \cdot C C_{1}^{2}
$$

or

$$
a_{1} b^{2}+b_{1} a^{2}=a_{1} b_{1}^{2}+b_{1} a_{1}^{2}+\left(a_{1}+b_{1}\right) d^{2}
$$

Considering that $a_{1}+b_{1}=c$, we get:

$$
a^{2} b_{1}+h^{2} a_{1}-d^{2} c=a_{1} b_{1} c
$$

which is what we needed to prove.

question: 15. A quadrilateral with perpendicular diagonals is inscribed in a circle (see Fig. 8). Prove that the sum of the squares of two opposite sides is equal to the square of the diameter of the circumscribed circle. (U. 123, P. 181.)

(!) 16. It is known that the sum of the squares of the sides of a parallelogram is equal to the sum of the squares of its diagonals. What is the relationship between the sum of the squares of the sides and the sum of the squares of the diagonals in other quadrilaterals, for example, in a trapezoid? The answer to this question was given by Leonhard Euler in a work published in the "Commentaries of the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences." Euler established the following theorem:

The sum of the squares of the sides of any quadrilateral (planar or spatial) is greater than the sum of the squares of its diagonals by four times the square of the segment connecting the midpoints of its diagonals.

Thus, if \(A_{1} A_{2} A_{3} A_{4}\) is any quadrilateral (Fig. 68), and \(P\) and \(Q\) are the midpoints of its diagonals \(A_{1} A_{3}\) and \(A_{2} A_{4}\), then \(A_{1} A_{2}^{2} + A_{2} A_{3}^{2} + A_{3} A_{4}^{2} + A_{4} A_{1}^{2} = A_{1} A_{3}^{2} + A_{2} A_{4}^{2} + 4 P Q^{2}\). Prove this theorem. (U. 123, P. 182.)

The geometric locus of points \(M\) for which \(A M^{2} - B M^{2} = c^{2}\) is the line \(M_{0} N\), perpendicular to \(A B\). Indeed, if \(M\) lies on \(M_{0} N_{0}\), then \(A M^{2} - B M^{2} = (A M_{0}^{2} + M_{0} M^{2}) - (B M_{0}^{2} + M_{0} M^{2}) = A M_{0}^{2} - B M_{0}^{2} = c^{2}\). (The converse can also be proven by contradiction: if \(A M^{2} - B M^{2} = c^{2}\), then \(M\) is located on the line \(M_{0} N\).
reference_solution:
16. Place equal masses (1 unit each) at the vertices of a quadrilateral. It is clear that the center of gravity $O$ of the entire system is the midpoint of the segment $P Q$ (see § 1, problem 1). According to Lagrange's theorem,

$$
J_{A_{1}}=J_{0}+4 \cdot O A_{1}^{2}
$$

or

$$
A_{1} A_{2}^{2}+A_{1} A_{3}^{2}+A_{1} A_{4}^{2}=O A_{1}^{2}+O A_{2}^{2}+O A_{3}^{2}+O A_{4}^{2}+4 O A_{1}^{2} .
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& A_{2} A_{1}^{2}+A_{2} A_{3}^{2}+A_{2} A_{4}^{2}=O A_{1}^{2}+O A_{2}^{2}+O A_{3}^{2}+O A_{4}^{2}+4 O A_{2}^{2} \\
& A_{3} A_{1}^{2}+A_{3} A_{2}^{2}+A_{3} A_{3}^{2}=O A_{1}^{2}+O A_{2}^{2}+O A_{3}^{2}+O A_{4}^{2}+4 O A_{3}^{2} \\
& A_{4} A_{1}^{2}+A_{4} A_{2}^{2}+A_{4} A_{3}^{2}=O A_{1}^{2}+O A_{2}^{2}+O A_{3}^{2}+O A_{4}^{2}+4 O A_{4}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations term by term, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 2\left(A_{1} A_{2}^{2}+A_{2} A_{3}^{2}+A_{3} A_{4}^{2}+A_{4} A_{1}^{2}\right)+2 A_{1} A_{3}^{2}+2 A_{2} A_{4}^{2}= \\
&=8\left(O A_{1}^{2}+O A_{2}^{2}+O A_{8}^{2}+O A_{4}^{2}\right) .
\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Lagrange's theorem to the system of points $\left(A_{1}, 1\right)$ and $\left(A_{8}, 1\right)$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
O A_{1}^{2}+O A_{3}^{2}=P A_{1}^{2}+P A_{3}^{2}+2 O P^{2} & =\left(\frac{1}{2} A_{1} A_{s}\right)^{2}+ \\
& +\left(\frac{1}{2} A_{1} A_{s}\right)^{2}+2\left(\frac{1}{2} P Q\right)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

That is,

$$
O A_{1}^{2}+O A_{3}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left(A_{1} A_{3}^{2}+P Q^{2}\right)
$$

Similarly, considering the system of two points $\left(A_{2}, 1\right)$ and $\left(A_{4}, 1\right)$, we get

$$
O A_{2}^{2}+O A_{4}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left(A_{2} A_{4}^{2}+P Q^{2}\right)
$$

From the obtained equalities, it follows that:

$$
\begin{gathered}
A_{1} A_{2}^{2}+A_{2} A_{3}^{2}+A_{3} A_{4}^{2}+A_{4} A_{1}^{2}+A_{1} A_{3}^{2}+A_{2} A_{1}^{2}= \\
=2 A_{1} A_{3}^{2}+2 A_{2} A_{4}^{2}+4 P Q^{2}
\end{gathered}
$$

from which

$$
A_{1} A_{2}^{2}+A_{2} A_{3}^{2}+A_{3} A_{4}^{2}+A_{4} A_{1}^{2}=A_{1} A_{3}^{2}+A_{2} A_{4}^{2}+4 P Q^{2}
$$

which is what we needed to prove.

question:
19. Prove: if $R$ is the radius of the circumcircle of a triangle, $p$ is the radius of some excircle, and $d$ is the distance between the centers of these circles, then $d^{2}=R^{2}+2 R$. (U. 124, P. 185.)

The following problem was considered by the famous German mathematician G. W. Leibniz.
reference_solution:
19. Let (Fig. 148) $S$ be the center of the circumscribed circle, and $O$ be the center of the excircle tangent to side $c$ and the extensions of sides $a$ and $b$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_27f86caa754616304e40g-186.jpg?height=638&width=671&top_left_y=869&top_left_x=270)

Fig. 148.

The reasoning conducted in solving the previous problem (up to formula (5) inclusive) remains valid if we replace $c$ with $-c$, $z$ with $-z$, $r$ with $\rho$, and $A$ with $180^{\circ}-A$.

However, for the excircle, $2 x + 2 y - 2 z = -(a + b - c)$. Therefore,

$$
J_{O} = -2 R_{\mathrm{p}}(a + b - c)
$$

Substituting the expressions for $J_{S}$ and $J_{O}$ into (1), we get

$$
(a + b - c) R^{2} = -2 R p (a + b - c) + (a + b - c) d^{2}
$$

and, consequently, $d^{2} = R^{2} + 2 R p$.

question:
21. Prove that the arithmetic mean of several positive numbers \(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}\) does not exceed their quadratic mean

$$
\frac{a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{n}}{n} \leqslant \sqrt{\frac{a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}+\ldots+a_{n}^{2}}{n}}
$$

Equality holds if and only if:

$$
a_{1}=a_{2}=\ldots=a_{n}
$$

(
reference_solution:
21. Let points $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}$ be chosen as suggested in the "instructions". Place a mass of 1 unit in each of them. Then

$$
M=n, \quad J_{S}=a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}+\ldots+a_{n}^{2}
$$

By problem 2 of § 2

$$
S Z=\frac{a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{n}}{n}
$$

Therefore (see inequality (51))

$$
n\left(\frac{a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{n}}{n}\right)^{2} \leqslant a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}+\ldots+a_{n}^{2}

hence,

question:
22. Prove the inequality:

$$
\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{n}\right)\left(\frac{1}{a_{1}}+\frac{1}{a_{2}}+\ldots+\frac{1}{a_{n}}\right) \geqslant n^{2}
$$

$\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}\right.$ - positive numbers). (U. 124, P. 187.)
reference_solution:
22. For the choice of the system of material points mentioned in the instruction,

\[
\begin{gathered}
M=\frac{1}{a_{1}}+\frac{1}{a_{2}}+\ldots+\frac{1}{a_{n}} \\
J_{S}=\frac{1}{a_{1}} a_{1}^{2}+\frac{1}{a_{1}} \cdot a_{2}^{2}+\ldots+\frac{1}{a_{n}} \cdot a_{n}^{2}=a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{n} \\
S Z=\frac{\frac{1}{a_{1}} a_{1}+\frac{1}{a_{2}} \cdot a_{2}+\cdots+\frac{1}{a_{n}} \cdot a_{n}}{M}=\frac{n}{M}
\end{gathered}
\]

Therefore,

\[

question:
5. If the size of a polygonal plate is increased by several ($k$) times (without changing its shape), then the distances from the center of gravity of the plate to the sides of the polygon will also increase by the same ($k$) times. Accepting this property without proof, derive from this that the center of gravity of a triangular plate is the point of intersection of its medians.

In the following, by the center of gravity of a given polygon, we mean the center of gravity of a homogeneous plate having the shape of such a polygon. By the center of gravity of the vertices of an $n$-gon, we mean the center of gravity of $n$ material points that are formed if equal masses are placed at all vertices of the $n$-gon.
reference_solution:
5. Let $z$ be the distance from the center of gravity $Z$ (Fig. 155) of triangle $ABC$ to one of its sides (let this be $AB$), and $h$ be the height dropped to $AB$. By connecting the midpoints of the sides of the triangle, we divide it into four equal triangles. Let the centers of gravity of these triangles be denoted by $T_{1}, T_{2}, T_{3}, T_{4}$, and their distances from the line $AB$ by $y_{1}, y_{2}, y_{3}, y_{4}$. Each of the resulting four triangles is similar to triangle $ABC$ and has sides that are half the length of the corresponding sides of triangle $ABC$. Therefore, the distances from the points $T_{1}, T_{2}, T_{3}, T_{4}$ to the largest sides of the corresponding triangles are $\frac{z}{2}$ (by the condition of the problem).

If the area of the large triangle is $S$, then the area of each of the small triangles is $\frac{S}{4}$. We will consider the entire mass of each triangle to be concentrated at its center of gravity. Then $Z$ is the center of gravity of four material points

\[
\begin{aligned}
& \left(T_{1}, \frac{S}{4}\right),\left(T_{2}, \frac{S}{4}\right),\left(T_{3}, \frac{S}{4}\right),\left(T_{4}, \frac{S}{4}\right): \\
& z=\frac{\frac{S}{4} y_{1}+\frac{S}{4} y_{2}+\frac{S}{4} y_{3}+\frac{S}{4} y_{4}}{S}=\frac{y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{8}+y_{4}}{4}.
\end{aligned}
\]

However,

\[
y_{1}=y_{2}=\frac{z}{2}, \quad y_{3}=\frac{h}{2}-\frac{2}{2}, y_{4}=\frac{h}{2}+\frac{z}{2}
\]

Therefore,

\[
z=\frac{\frac{z}{2}+\frac{z}{2}+\left(\frac{h}{2}-\frac{z}{2}\right)+\left(\frac{h}{2}+\frac{z}{2}\right)}{4}
\]

From this,

\[
3 z=h, \quad z=\frac{h}{3}
\]

Thus, the center of gravity $Z$ of the triangular plate $ABC$ is at a distance $\frac{h}{3}$ from the side $AB$. Similarly, it can be shown that the distance from point $Z$ to each of the other two sides is also equal to one third of the height dropped to that side. The only point with this property is the point of intersection of the medians of triangle $ABC$. Therefore, $Z$ (the center of gravity of the triangular plate) is the point of intersection of its medians, which is what we needed to prove.

question: (!) 10. Prove that the center of gravity of any trapezoid lies on the segment $M N$, connecting the midpoints of the bases. (
reference_solution:
10. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of the bases of trapezoid $ABCD$ (Fig. 161), and $T$ be the point of intersection of its diagonals. $T$ lies on $MN$ (see problem 9 § 1). Let $EF$ be the midline of the trapezoid and $R \equiv EF \times MN$. Then it is clear that $ER = RF$, so $TR$ is the median in $\triangle ETF$.

Let $K, L, P, Q$ be the centroids of triangles $ATD, BTC, ATB, CTD$, and $S_{1}, S_{2}, S_{3}, S_{4}$ be their areas.

The centroid of the trapezoid coincides with the centroid of four material points: $\left(K, S_{1}\right), \left(L, S_{2}\right), \left(P, S_{3}\right), \left(Q, S_{4}\right)$. We will show that the centroid of the material points $\left(K, S_{1}\right)$ and $\left(L, S_{2}\right)$ is located on the line $MN$. We have

$$
\begin{gathered}
S_{\triangle ATD} = S_{\triangle ADB} - S_{\triangle ATB} \\
S_{\triangle BTC} = S_{\triangle BAC} - S_{\triangle ATB}
\end{gathered}
$$

But $S_{\triangle ADB} = S_{\triangle BAC}$, because $\triangle ADB$ and $\triangle BAC$ have equal bases and equal heights. Therefore, $S_{\triangle ATD} = S_{\triangle BTC}$, $S_{1} = S_{2}$, so the masses of $\triangle ATD$ and $\triangle BTC$ are equal; therefore, the centroid of the two material points $\left(K, S_{1}\right)$ and $\left(L, S_{2}\right)$ is the midpoint $H$ of segment $KL$. It is clear that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{TK}{TE} = \frac{2}{3} \\
& \frac{TL}{TF} = \frac{2}{3}
\end{aligned}
$$

so

$$
\frac{TK}{TE} = \frac{TL}{TF}
$$

and therefore $KL \parallel EF$. Consequently, the median $TR$, and thus the line $MN$ of triangle $ETF$, passes through the midpoint of segment $KL$, i.e., through point $H$. Therefore, the centroid of the trapezoid coincides with the centroid of three material points: $\left(H, S_{1} + S_{2}\right), \left(P, S_{3}\right), \left(Q, S_{4}\right)$. All these points lie on the line $MN$, so the centroid of the trapezoid also lies on $MN$, which was to be proved.

Another proof (intuitive but not rigorous). One can imagine the trapezoid as consisting of a very large number of very thin homogeneous wires, all parallel to the bases of the trapezoid. The centroid of each wire, i.e., its midpoint, lies on the segment $MN$. Therefore, the centroid of the entire trapezoid cannot lie outside the segment $MN$.

Similarly, from $\triangle K R E \sim \triangle A B E$, we get

From (1) and (2), it follows that

question: (!) 10. Prove the second theorem of Guldin for the case when the plate is composed of a certain number of rectangles, each of which has two sides parallel to the axis of rotation. ( ( 208 .)
reference_solution:
10. Let $S_{1}$, $S_{2}, \ldots, S_{n}$ denote the $n$ rectangles that make up the plate, as well as their areas; let $y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n}$ denote the distances from the centers of gravity of these rectangles to the axis of rotation.

It is clear that the volume $V$ of the body obtained by rotating the entire plate is equal to the sum of the volumes of the bodies obtained by rotating each individual rectangle. Therefore,

\[
\begin{aligned}
& V=2 \pi \cdot y_{1} \cdot S_{1}+2 \pi \cdot y_{2} \cdot S_{2}+\ldots+2 \pi \cdot y_{n} S_{n}= \\
& \quad=2 \pi \frac{y_{1} S_{1}+y_{2} S_{2}+\ldots+y_{n} S_{n}}{S} S \left(\text{ here } S=S_{1}+S_{2}+\ldots+S_{n}\right)
\end{aligned}
\]

But we have already seen (p. 86) that the quantity $\frac{y_{1} S_{1}+y_{2} S_{2}+\ldots+y_{n} S_{n}}{S}$ is precisely the distance $z$ from the center of gravity of the plate to the axis of rotation. Therefore,

\[
V=2 \pi \cdot z \cdot S
\]

which is what we needed to prove.

question: 7. Generalize the theorem from problem 1 to the case of $n$ mixtures $(n>2)$. (O. 117, У. 126, P. 218.)
reference_solution:
7. Let the theorem (see "answers") be true for $n=p$. This means: when mixing mixtures

$$
\left(K_{1}, m_{1}\right),\left(K_{2}, m_{2}\right), \ldots,\left(K_{p}, m_{p}\right)
$$

the resulting mixture is ( $C, m_{1}+m_{2}+\ldots+m_{p}$ ), determined by the condition: $\left(C, m_{1}+\ldots+m_{p}\right)=\left(K_{1}, m_{1}\right)+\left(K_{2}, m_{2}\right)+\ldots+\left(K_{p}, m_{p}\right)$.

We will prove that the theorem is also true for $n=p+1$. Indeed, the mixture resulting from mixing $p+1$ mixtures

$$
\left(K_{1}, m_{1}\right), \ldots,\left(K_{p}, m_{p}\right),\left(K_{p+1}, m_{p+1}\right)
$$

obviously coincides with the mixture that results from mixing two mixtures:

$$
\left(C, m_{1}+\ldots+m_{p}\right) \text { and }\left(K_{p+1}, m_{p+1}\right)
$$

But by problem 1, this mixture is characterized by a material point determined by the condition:

$$
(K, m)=\left(C, m_{1}+\ldots+m_{p}\right)+\left(K_{p+1}, m_{p+1}\right)
$$

If we also take into account the equality (1) written above, we get:

$$
(K, m)=\left(K_{1}, m_{1}\right)+\ldots+\left(K_{p}, m_{p}\right)+\left(K_{p+1}, m_{p+1}\right) .
$$

Thus, the theorem is true for $n=p+1$ if it is true for $n=p$. Moreover, it is true for $n=1$. Therefore, it is true for any natural $n$.

question:
17. If two three-component mixtures are characterized by material points ( $K_{1}, m_{1}$ ) and ( $K_{2}, m_{2}$ ) (Fig. I11), then their mixing results in a mixture characterized by

A material point ( $K, m$ ), which is the combination of the two material points ( $K_{1}, m_{1}$ ) and ( $K_{2}, m_{2}$ ).

Prove this statement. (P. 220.)
reference_solution:
17. Let the concentrations of components $A, B, C$ in the first mixture be $a_{1}, b_{1}, c_{1}$, and in the second mixture $a_{2}, b_{2}, c_{2}$. Then the first mixture contains $m_{1} \cdot a_{1}$ units of component $A$, $m_{1} b_{1}$ units of component $B$, and $m_{1} c_{1}$ units of component $C$; the second mixture contains $m_{2} a_{2}$ units of component $A$, $m_{2} b_{2}$ units of component $B$, and $m_{2} c_{2}$ units of component $C$. Therefore, in the combined mixtures, components $A, B, C$ will be present in quantities $m_{1} a_{1}+m_{2} a_{2}$, $m_{1} b_{1}+m_{2} b_{2}$, $m_{1} c_{1}+m_{2} c_{2}$. Thus, in the new mixture with mass $m\left(m=m_{1}+m_{2}\right)$, the concentrations of components $A, B, C$ are respectively

$$
\frac{m_{1} a_{1}+m_{2} a_{2}}{m}, \quad \frac{m_{1} b_{1}+m_{2} b_{2}}{m}, \quad \frac{m_{1} c_{1}+m_{2} c_{2}}{m}
$$

Therefore, if the material point

$$
K \equiv(K, m)
$$

corresponds to the new mixture, then the point $K$ is the center of gravity of three material points

$$
\left(A, \frac{m_{1} a_{1}+m_{2} a_{2}}{m}\right), \quad\left(B, \frac{m_{1} b_{1}+m_{2} b_{2}}{m}\right), \quad\left(C, \frac{m_{1} c_{1}+m_{2} c_{2}}{m}\right)
$$

and thus, of such material points:

$$
\left(A, m_{1} a_{1}+m_{2} a_{2}\right), \quad\left(B, m_{1} b_{1}+m_{2} b_{2}\right), \quad\left(C, m_{1} c_{1}+m_{2} c_{2}\right)
$$

Thus,

$K=\left(A, m_{1} a_{1}+m_{2} a_{2}\right)+\left(B, m_{1} b_{1}+m_{2} b_{2}\right)+\left(C, m_{1} c_{1}+m_{2} c_{2}\right)$.

On the other hand, the combination of two material points $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ can be transformed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& K_{1}+K_{2}=\left[\left(A, m_{1} a_{1}\right)+\left(B, m_{1} b_{1}\right)+\left(C, m_{1} c_{1}\right)\right]+ \\
& \quad+\left[\left(A, m_{2} a_{2}\right)+\left(B, m_{2} b_{2}\right)+\left(C, m_{2} c_{2}\right)\right]= \\
& =\left(A, m_{1} a_{1}+m_{2} a_{2}\right)+\left(B, m_{1} b_{1}+m_{2} b_{2}\right)+\left(C, m_{1} c_{1}+m_{2} c_{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
K=K_{1}+K_{2}
$$

which was to be proved.

question: 12. Let a line intersect one circle at points $A$ and $B$, and another circle at points $C$ and $D$. Prove that the points of intersection of the tangents to the first circle drawn at points $A$ and $B$ with the tangents drawn to the second circle at points $C$ and $D$ (considering the points where the tangents to different circles intersect) lie on one circle, the center of which lies on the line passing through the centers of the given circles.
reference_solution: 12. Let (Fig. 15) $K$ and $L$ be the points of intersection of the tangent to the second circle passing through $D$ with the tangents to the first circle passing through $B$ and $A$, and let $M$ and $N$ be the other two points. It is easy to see that $\angle D K B = \angle C M A$ (each of these angles is equal to half the difference of the angles corresponding to the arcs $A B$ and $C D$). Therefore (in our figure) $\angle L M N + \angle L K N = 180^{\circ}$. Hence, the quadrilateral $K L M N$ is cyclic. Further, we have: $\frac{|D K|}{|K B|} = \frac{\sin \angle D B K}{\sin \angle B D K} = \frac{\sin \frac{1}{2} \cup A B}{\sin \frac{1}{2} \cup D C}$. Similarly, the ratios of the lengths of the tangents drawn through points $L, M$, and $N$ are found. All these ratios are equal to each other; therefore, the center of the circle circumscribed around $K L M N$ lies on the line passing through the centers of the given circles (see problem II.6).

question: 14. Given a triangle $ABC$. Consider all possible pairs of points $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ such that $\left|A M_{1}\right|:\left|B M_{1}\right|:\left|C M_{1}\right|=$ $=\left|A M_{2}\right|:\left|B M_{2}\right|:\left|C M_{2}\right|$. Prove that all lines $M_{1} M_{2}$ pass through a fixed point on the plane.
reference_solution: 14. Let $\left|A M_{1}\right|:\left|B M_{1}\right|:\left|C M_{1}\right|=p: q: r$. Then the set of points $M$ such that $\left(r^{2}-q^{2}\right)|A M|^{2}+\left(p^{2}-r^{2}\right)|B M|^{2}+\left(q^{2}-p^{2}\right)|C M|^{2}=0$, is a straight line passing through $M_{1}, M_{2}$ and the center of the circumcircle of $\triangle A B C$ (see problem II.7).

question: 15. The distances from point $M$ to the vertices $A, B$, and $C$ of the triangle are 1, 2, and 3, respectively, and from point $M_{1}$ they are $3, \sqrt{15}, 5$, respectively. Prove that the line $M M_{1}$ passes through the center of the circle circumscribed around triangle $A B C$.
reference_solution: 15. Points $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ belong to the set of points $M$ for which $5|M A|^{2}-8|M B|^{2}+3|M C|^{2}=0$. This set is a straight line, and obviously, the center of the circumscribed circle satisfies the condition defining this set (see problem II.7).

question: 17. Given an equilateral triangle $A B C$ and an arbitrary point $D$; $A_{1}, B_{1}$, and $C_{1}$ are the centers of the circles inscribed in triangles $B C D, C A D$, and $A B D$. Prove that the perpendiculars dropped from vertices $A, B$, and $C$ to $B_{1} C_{1}, C_{1} A_{1}$, and $A_{1} B_{1}$ respectively, intersect at one point.
reference_solution: 17. Let $|A D|=x,|B D|=y,|C D|=z,|A B|=a$. Denote by $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ the points of tangency of the incircles of triangles $B C D$, $C A D$, $A B D$ with sides $B C, C A, A B$. The perpendiculars drawn through points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ to sides $B C, C A$, and $A B$ coincide with the perpendiculars erected to the same sides at points $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$. But $\left|B A_{2}\right|=\frac{a+y-z}{2},\left|A_{2} C\right|=\frac{a+z-y}{2} ;$ similarly, $\left|A C_{2}\right|,\left|C_{2} B\right|,\left|A B_{2}\right|,\left|B_{2} C\right|$ can be found. Now it is easy to verify the condition of problem II. 3.

question: 18. Given three pairwise intersecting circles. Prove that the three common chords of these circles pass through one point.
reference_solution: 18. Apply the condition of problem II.3, taking points $A, B$ and $C$ as the centers of the circles, and points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ as one of the intersection points of the circles ( $A_{1}$ - one of the intersection points of the circles with centers $B$ and $C$ and so on.)

question: 19. On the lines $A B$ and $A C$, points $M$ and $N$ are taken respectively. Prove that the common chord of the two circles with diameters $C M$ and $B N$ passes through the orthocenter of triangle $A B C$.
reference_solution: 19. Let's take the third circle with diameter $B C$. The common chords of the 1st and 3rd, as well as the 2nd and 3rd circles, are the altitudes of the triangle dropped from vertices $B$ and $C$. Therefore (see problem II.18), the common chord of these circles also passes through the orthocenter of triangle $A B C$.

question: 22. Given numbers $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ and $k$. Let $x, y, z$ be the distances from a point $M$ inside a triangle to its sides. Prove that the geometric locus of points $M$ such that $\alpha x + \beta y + \gamma z = k$ is either empty, a segment, or coincides with the set of all points of the triangle.
reference_solution: 22. Show that if $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ are two distinct points belonging to our set, then any point $M$ on the line segment $M_{1} M_{2}$ inside the triangle also belongs to this set. For this, denoting by $x_{1}, y_{1}, z_{1}$ the distances from $M_{1}$ to the sides of the triangle, and by $x_{2}, y_{2}, z_{2}$ the distances from $M_{2}$, we can express the distances $x, y, z$ from $M$ to the sides in terms of these quantities and the distances between $M_{1}, M_{2}, M$. For example, if $\left|M_{1} M\right|=k\left|M_{1} M_{2}\right|$ and the directions of $M_{1} M$ and $M_{1} M_{2}$ coincide, then $x=(1-k) x_{1}+k x_{2}, y=(1-k) y_{1}+k y_{2}, z=(1-k) z_{1}+k z_{2}$. From this it follows that if the equality holds for three points inside the triangle that do not lie on the same line, then it will hold for all points of the triangle. Remark. The statement of the problem remains true for any convex polygon. Moreover, all points of the plane can be considered, but in this case the distances to the line from points located on opposite sides of it should be taken with opposite signs.

question: 24. Let $A_{1}, B_{1}$ and $C_{1}$ be the midpoints of the sides $B C, C A$ and $A B$ of triangle $A B C$. On the perpendiculars dropped from some point $M$ to the sides $B C, C A$ and $A B$, points $A_{2}, B_{2}$ and $C_{2}$ are taken. Prove that the perpendiculars dropped from $A_{1}$, $B_{1}$ and $C_{1}$ to the lines $B_{2} C_{2}, C_{2} A_{2}$ and $A_{2} B_{2}$, respectively, intersect at one point.
reference_solution: 24. Since the perpendiculars dropped from $A_{2}, B_{2}$ and $C_{2}$ to $B_{1} C_{1}, C_{1} A_{1}$ and $A_{1} B_{1}$, respectively, intersect at one point, then (problem II.4) and the perpendiculars dropped from $A_{1}, B_{1}$ and $C_{1}$ to $B_{2} C_{2}, C_{2} A_{2}$ and $A_{2} B_{2}$, respectively, also intersect at one point.

question: 25. Given a line $l$ and three lines $l_{1}, l_{2}$ and $l_{3}$, perpendicular to $l$. Let $A, B$ and $C$ be three fixed points on line $l$; $A_{1}$ be an arbitrary point on $l_{1}$, $B_{1}$ be on $l_{2}$, and $C_{1}$ be on $l_{3}$. Prove that if for some position of points $A_{1}, B_{1}$ and $C_{1}$ the perpendiculars dropped from $A, B$ and $C$ to the lines $B_{1} C_{1}, C_{1} A_{1}$ and $A_{1} B_{1}$ respectively, intersect at one point, then these perpendiculars will always intersect at one point.
reference_solution: 25. Let $a_{1}$ and $a_{2}$ be the distances from $A$ to the lines $l_{2}$ and $l_{3}$ respectively, $b_{1}$ and $b_{2}$ be the distances from $B$ to the lines $l_{3}$ and $l_{1}$ respectively, $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$ be the distances from $C$ to the lines $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ respectively, $x$, $y, z$ be the distances from $A_{1}, B_{1}$ and $C_{1}$ respectively to $l$. For the perpendiculars dropped from $A, B$ and $C$ to $B_{1} C_{1}, C_{1} A_{1}$ and $A_{1} B_{1}$ respectively to intersect at one point, it is necessary and sufficient that the equality (problem II.3) $\left|A B_{1}\right|^{2}-\left|B_{1} C\right|^{2}+\left|C A_{1}\right|^{2}-$ $-\left|A_{1} B\right|^{2}+\left|B C_{1}\right|^{2}-\left|C_{1} A\right|^{2}=0$, or $\left(a_{1}^{2}+y^{2}\right)-\left(c_{2}^{2}+y^{2}\right)+\left(c_{1}^{2}+x^{2}\right)-$ $-\left(b_{2}^{2}+x^{2}\right)+\left(b_{1}^{2}+z^{2}\right)-\left(a_{2}^{2}+z^{2}\right)=0$, which leads to the condition $a_{1}^{2}-a_{2}^{2}+$ $+b_{1}^{2}-b_{2}^{2}+c_{1}^{2}-c_{2}^{2}=0$, independent of $x, y, z$.

question:
26. $A A_{1}, B B_{1}, C C_{1}$ - altitudes of triangle $A B C, A_{2}, B_{2}$ and $C_{2}$ - projections of $A, B$ and $C$ respectively onto $B_{1} C_{1}, C_{1} A_{1}$ and $A_{1} B_{1}$. Prove that the perpendiculars dropped from $A_{2}, B_{2}$ and $C_{2}$ respectively to $B C, C A$ and $A B$ intersect at one point.

## § 2. Theorems of Ceva and Menelaus. Affine Problems
reference_solution: 26. It is sufficient for us to check the condition (problem II.3) $\left|A B_{2}\right|^{2}-\left|B_{2} C\right|^{2}+\left|C A_{2}\right|^{2}-\left|A_{2} B\right|^{2}+\left|B C_{2}\right|^{2}-\left|C_{2} A\right|^{2}=0$. Note that triangles $B B_{2} C_{1}$ and $A A_{2} C_{1}$ are similar, hence, $\left|A C_{1}\right| \cdot\left|C_{1} B_{2}\right|=$ $=\left|B C_{1}\right| \cdot\left|C_{1} A_{2}\right|$, moreover, $\angle A C_{1} B_{2}=\angle B C_{1} A_{2}$, therefore, $\left|A B_{2}\right|^{2}-\left|B A_{2}\right|^{2}=\left(\left|A C_{1}\right|^{2}-\left|C_{1} B\right|^{2}\right)+\left(\left|C_{1} B_{2}\right|^{2}-\left|C_{1} A_{2}\right|^{2}\right)$. Writing the corresponding equalities for $\left|C A_{2}\right|^{2}-\left|A C_{2}\right|^{2}$ and $\left|B C_{2}\right|^{2}-\left|C B_{2}\right|^{2}$ and adding them, we get that the differences in the first parentheses will sum to zero (applying the condition of problem II.3 to triangles $A B C$ and $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$; we get zero, since the altitudes intersect at one point). It is not difficult to prove that $A A_{2}, B B_{2}$ and $C C_{2}$ pass through the center of the circumcircle around $A B C$, i.e., the sum of the differences in the second parentheses is also zero.

question: 30. Given a quadrilateral $A B C D ; O$ - the intersection point of diagonals $A C$ and $B D, M$ - a point on $A C$ such that $|A M|=$ $=|O C|, N$ - a point on $B D$ such that $|B N|=|O D|, K$ and $L-$ midpoints of $A C$ and $B D$. Prove that the lines $M L, N K$, and the line connecting the points of intersection of the medians of triangles $A B C$ and $A C D$, intersect at one point.
reference_solution:
30. The statement of the problem follows from the following two facts.
1) If points $K$, $L$, $M$, and $N$ are taken on the sides of quadrilateral $ABCD$ such that the sides $AB$, $BC$, $CD$, and $DA$ are divided by these points in the same ratio $\left(\frac{|BK|}{|KA|}=\frac{|CM|}{|MD|}=\frac{|BL|}{|LC|}=\frac{|AN|}{|ND|}\right)$, then the segments $KM$ and $LN$ are also divided by their point of intersection $P$ in the same ratio.

Indeed, from the fact that lines $KL$ and $NM$ are parallel to diagonal $AC$, it follows: $\frac{|KP|}{|PM|}=\frac{|KL|}{|NM|}=\frac{|KL|}{|AC|} \cdot \frac{|AC|}{|NM|}=\frac{|BK|}{|BA|} \cdot \frac{|AD|}{|ND|}=$ $=\frac{|BK|}{|BA|} \cdot \frac{|BA|}{|KA|}=\frac{|BK|}{|KA|}$.

2) If points $K_1$ and $K$, $M_1$ and $M$ are taken on the sides $AB$ and $CD$ of the quadrilateral such that $\frac{|K_1K|}{|AB|}=\frac{|M_1M|}{|CD|}=\frac{1}{m}, |AK_1|=|KB|, |DM_1|=$ $=|CM|$, then the area of quadrilateral $K_1KMM_1$ is $\frac{1}{m}$ of the area of quadrilateral $ABCD$. Indeed, $S_{BKC}=$ $=\frac{|BK|}{|BA|} S_{ABC}, \quad S_{AM_1D}=\frac{|M_1D|}{|CD|} S_{ACD}=\frac{|BK|}{|BA|} S_{ACD} . \quad$ Therefore, $S_{AKCM_1}=\left(1-\frac{|BK|}{|BA|}\right) S_{ABCD}=\frac{|AK|}{|BA|} S_{ABCD} . \quad$ Similarly, $\quad S_{K_1KMM_1}=$ $=\frac{|K_1K|}{|AK|} S_{AKCM_1}$. Thus, $S_{K_1KMM_1}=\frac{|K_1K|}{|AB|} S_{ABCD}=\frac{1}{m} S$.

question: 37. A line passing through the midpoints of the diagonals $A C$ and $B C$ of quadrilateral $A B C D$ intersects sides $A B$ and $D C$ at points $M$ and $N$ respectively. Prove that $S_{D C M}=S_{A B N}$.
reference_solution: 37. Let $K$ be the midpoint of $DB$, $L$ be the midpoint of $AC$, $S_{ANM}=S_{CNM}$ (since $|AL|=|LC|$), similarly $S_{BNM}=S_{DMN}$; from which the statement of the problem follows.

question: 38. In parallelogram $A B C D$, vertices $A, B, C$, and $D$ are connected to the midpoints of sides $C D, A D, A B$, and $B C$ respectively. Prove that the area of the quadrilateral formed by these lines is $1 / 5$ of the area of the parallelogram.
reference_solution: 38. If $M$ is the midpoint of $DC$, $N$ is the midpoint of $BC$, and $K$ and $L$ are the points of intersection of $DN$ with $AM$ and $AB$ respectively, then $\frac{|KM|}{|AK|} = \frac{|DM|}{|AL|} = \frac{1}{4}$, i.e., $|AK| = \frac{4}{5}|AM|$; therefore, $S_{ADK} = \frac{4}{5} S_{ADM} = \frac{4}{5} \cdot \frac{1}{4} S = \frac{1}{5} S$ (where $S$ is the area of the parallelogram). Thus, the area of the desired figure will be $S - 4 S_{ADK} = \frac{1}{5} S$.

question: 39. Prove that the area of the octagon formed by the lines connecting the vertices of a parallelogram to the midpoints of the opposite sides is $1 / 6$ of the area of the parallelogram.
reference_solution:
39. Let $Q$ be the midpoint of $A D$, $N$ be the midpoint of $B C$, $M$ be the midpoint of $D C$, and $K, P, R$ be the points of intersection of $D N$ and $A M$, $Q C$ and $D N$, $Q C$ and $A M$. Then $|D K|=\frac{2}{5}|D N|$, $|D P|=|P N|$, $|Q P|=|P C|$, $|Q R|=\frac{1}{3}|Q C|$, $\frac{S_{R P Q}}{S_{Q P D}}=$ $=\frac{|R P|}{|Q P|} \cdot \frac{|K P|}{|D P|}=\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{5}=\frac{1}{15}$, $S_{R P K}=\frac{1}{15} \cdot \frac{S}{8}=\frac{S}{120}$.

Therefore, from the quadrilateral considered in the previous problem, four triangles of area $\frac{S}{120}$ are cut off; thus, the area of the desired octagon will be $\frac{S}{5}-\frac{4 S}{120}=\frac{S}{6}$.

question: 40. On the sides $AC$ and $BC$ of triangle $ABC$, two parallelograms $ACDE$ and $BCFG$ are constructed outwardly. The extensions of $DE$ and $FD$ intersect at point $H$. On side $AB$, a parallelogram $ABML$ is constructed, with sides $AL$ and $BM$ equal and parallel to $HC$. Prove that the parallelogram $ABML$ is equal in area to the sum of the parallelograms constructed on $AC$ and $BC$.
reference_solution: 40. Let the line $H C$ intersect $A B$ and $L M$ at points $T$ and $N$, respectively, the line $A L$ intersect $E D$ at point $K$, and the line $B M$ intersect $P G$ at point $P$. We have: $S_{A C D E}=S_{A C H K}=S_{A T N L}, S_{B C F G}=S_{B C H P}=$ $=S_{B M N T};$ thus, $S_{A C D E}+S_{B C F G}=S_{A B M L}$.

question: 41. Through the ends of the smaller base of the trapezoid, two parallel lines are drawn intersecting the larger base. The diagonals of the trapezoid and these lines divide the trapezoid into seven triangles and one pentagon. Prove that the sum of the areas of the three triangles adjacent to the lateral sides and the smaller base of the trapezoid is equal to the area of the pentagon.
reference_solution: 41. Let $Q$ denote the area of the pentagon, $s_{1}, s_{2}$, and $s_{3}$ the areas of the triangles adjacent to one lateral side, the smaller base, and the other lateral side; $x$ the area of the triangle enclosed between the triangles of areas $s_{1}$ and $s_{2}$, $y$ the area of the triangle enclosed between the triangles of areas $s_{2}$ and $s_{3}$. Then $s_{1}+x+s_{2}=s_{2}+y+s_{3}=\frac{1}{2}\left(x+y+s_{2}+Q\right)$. Therefore, $s_{1}+x+s_{2}+s_{2}+y+s_{3}=x+y+s_{2}+Q \Rightarrow s_{1}+s_{2}+s_{3}=Q$.

question:
42. Let $A B C D$ be a parallelogram, point $E$ lies on line $A B$, and point $F$ lies on line $A D$ ($B$ is on segment $A E$, $D$ is on segment $A F$), $K$ is the intersection point of lines $E D$ and $F B$. Prove that quadrilaterals $A B K D$ and $C E K F$ have equal areas.
