reference_solution: 42. If $S$ is the area of the parallelogram, then $S_{A B K}+S_{K C D}=\frac{1}{2} S$, on the other hand, $S_{D B C}=S_{E K C}+S_{K C D}=\frac{1}{2} S$, hence, $S_{A B K}=S_{E K C}$; similarly, $S_{A K D}=S_{K C P}$; adding the last two equalities, we get: $S_{A B K D}=S_{C E K F}$.

question:
43. Consider an arbitrary triangle $ABC$. Let $A_{1}$, $B_{1}$, $C_{1}$ be three points on the lines $BC$, $CA$, $AB$ respectively.

We introduce the following notations:

$$
\begin{gathered}
R=\frac{\left|A C_{1}\right|}{\left|C C_{1} B\right|} \cdot \frac{\left|B A_{1}\right|}{\left|A_{1} C\right|} \cdot \frac{\left|C B_{1}\right|}{\left|B_{1} A\right|} \\
R^{*}=\frac{\sin \angle A C C_{1}}{\sin \angle C_{1} C B} \cdot \frac{\sin \angle B A A_{1}}{\sin \angle A_{1} A C} \cdot \frac{\sin \angle C B B_{1}}{\sin \angle B_{1} B A} \cdot
\end{gathered}
$$

Prove that $R=R^{*}$.
reference_solution: 43. Given: $\frac{\left|A C_{1}\right|}{\left|C_{1} B\right|}=\frac{S_{A C C_{1}}}{S_{C C_{1} B}}=\frac{\frac{1}{2}|A C| \cdot\left|C C_{1}\right| \sin \angle A C C_{1}}{\frac{1}{2}\left|C C_{1}\right| \cdot|C B| \sin \angle O_{1} C B}=$ $=\frac{|A C|}{|B C|} \cdot \frac{\sin \angle A C C_{1}}{\sin \angle C_{1} C B}$. By obtaining similar equalities for the ratios $\frac{\left|B A_{1}\right|}{\left|A_{1} C\right|}$ and $\frac{\left|C B_{1}\right|}{\left|B_{1} A\right|}$ and multiplying them, we get the required statement.

question: 44. Ceva's Theorem. For the lines $A A_{1}, B B_{1}$, $C C_{1}$ to intersect at one point (or all three to be parallel), it is necessary and sufficient that $R=1$ (see problem II.43) and that an odd number (i.e., one or all three) of the points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ lie on the sides of the triangle $A B C$, and not on the extensions of the sides.
reference_solution: 44. Let's show that if the lines $A A_{1}, B B_{1}$, and $C C_{1}$ intersect at one point (denote it by $M$), then $R^{*}=1$ (and therefore, $R=1$; see problem II.43). By the Law of Sines for $\triangle A M C$, we have: $\frac{\sin \angle A C C_{1}}{\sin \angle A_{1} A C} = \frac{|A M|}{|M C|}$. Writing similar equalities for triangles $A M B$ and $B M C$ and multiplying them, we obtain the required statement. Conversely, if $R=1$ and all points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ lie on the sides of the triangle (or only one of them), then, drawing the lines $A A_{1}$ and $B B_{1}$, denote their intersection point by $M_{1}$; let the line $C M_{1}$ intersect $A B$ at point $C_{2}$. Considering the conditions of the problem and the necessity of the condition $R=1$ that has been proven, we will have that $\frac{|A C_{1}|}{|C_{1} B|} = \frac{|A C_{2}|}{|C_{2} B|}$, and points $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ lie simultaneously either on the segment $A B$ or outside it. Therefore, $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ coincide.

question:
45. Theorem of Menelaus. For points $A_{1}, B_{1}$, $C_{1}$ to lie on the same line, it is necessary and sufficient that $R=1$ (see problem II.43) and that an even number (i.e., zero or two) of the points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ lie on the sides of triangle $A B C$, and not on their extensions.

Note. Instead of the ratio $\frac{\left|A C_{1}\right|}{\left|C_{1} B\right|}$ and others, we can consider the ratio of directed segments, which we will denote as $\frac{A C_{1}}{C_{1} B}$ and define as follows: $\left|\frac{A C_{1}}{C_{1} B}\right|=\frac{\left|A C_{1}\right|}{\left|C_{1} B\right|}$, $\frac{A C_{1}}{C_{1} B}$ is positive when the vectors $\overrightarrow{A C_{1}}$ and $\overrightarrow{C_{1} B}$ are directed the same way, and negative if they are directed oppositely. $\left(\frac{A C_{1}}{C_{1} B}\right.$ makes sense only for points located on the same line.) It is easy to see that the ratio $\frac{A C_{1}}{C_{1} B}$ is positive if point $C_{1}$ lies on the segment $A B$, and negative if $C_{1}$ is outside $A B$. Accordingly, instead of $R$, we will consider the product of ratios of directed segments, which we will denote as $\tilde{R}$. We will now introduce directed angles. By $\Varangle A C C_{1}$ and others, we will mean the angle through which $C A$ must be rotated around $C$ counterclockwise until the ray $C A$ coincides with the ray $C C_{1}$. Now, instead of $R^{*}$, we will consider $\tilde{R}^{*}$ - the corresponding product of ratios of sines of directed angles.

Problems II. 43, II. 44, and II. 45 should now be reformulated. 43*. Prove that $\tilde{R}=\tilde{R}^{*}$.
reference_solution: 45. Let $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ lie on the same line. Draw a line through $C$ parallel to $A B$, and denote by $M$ the point of its intersection with the line $A_{1} B_{1}$. From the similarity of the corresponding triangles, we get: $\frac{\left|B A_{1}\right|}{\left|A_{1} C\right|}=\frac{\left|B C_{1}\right|}{|C M|}, \frac{\left|C B_{1}\right|}{\left|B_{1} A\right|}=\frac{|C M|}{\left|A C_{1}\right|}$. By substituting the corresponding ratios in the expression $R$ (see problem II. 43), we obtain that $R=1$. The converse statement is proved similarly to how it was done in problem II. 44 (draw the line $B_{1} A_{1}$, denote by $C_{2}$ the point of its intersection with $A B$, and so on).

question: 46. Prove that if three lines passing through the vertices of a triangle intersect at one point, then the lines symmetric to them with respect to the corresponding angle bisectors of the triangle also intersect at one point or are parallel.
reference_solution: 46. Check that if for the given lines $R^{*}=1$, then it will also be the same for the symmetric ones. At the same time, if a line passing through, for example, vertex $A$ intersects side $B C$, then the line symmetric to it with respect to the angle bisector will also intersect side $B C$ (see problems II. 43, II. 44).

question: 47. Let $O$ be an arbitrary point in the plane, $M$ and $N$ be the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from point $O$ to the bisectors of the internal and external angles at $A$ of triangle $ABC$; $P$ and $Q$ are similarly defined for angle $B$; $R$ and $T$ are defined for angle $C$. Prove that the lines $MN$, $PQ$, and $RT$ intersect at one point or are parallel.
reference_solution: 47. If $A_{0}, B_{0}, C_{0}$ are the midpoints of the segments $A O, B O, C O$ respectively, then the constructed lines turn out to be symmetric to the lines $A_{0} O, B_{0} O, C_{0} O$ with respect to the angle bisectors of triangle $A_{0} B_{0} C_{0}$ (see problem II. 46).

question: 48. Let $O$ be the center of the circle inscribed in triangle $ABC$, and let $A_{0}, B_{0}, C_{0}$ be the points of tangency of this circle with the sides $BC, CA, AB$ respectively. On the rays $OA_{0}, OB_{0}, OC_{0}$, points $L, M, K$ are taken, respectively, at equal distances from $O$. a) Prove that the lines $AL, BM$, and $CK$ intersect at one point. b) Let $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ be the projections of $A, B, C$ onto an arbitrary line $l$ passing through $O$. Prove that the lines $A_{1}L, B_{1}M$, and $C_{1}K$ intersect at one point (Harano).

49. For the diagonals $A D, B E$ and $C F$ of a hexagon $A B C D E F$ inscribed in a circle to intersect at one point, it is necessary and sufficient that the equality $|A B| \cdot|C D| \cdot|E F|=|B C| \cdot|D E| \cdot|F A|$ holds.
reference_solution: 49. Consider the triangle $A C E$, through the vertices of which the lines $A D, C F$ and $E B$ are drawn. The sines of the angles formed by these lines with the sides of the triangle $A C E$ are proportional to the chords on which they stand; therefore, the condition $R=1$ (see problem II. 44) is equivalent to the condition given in the problem.

question: 51. A circle intersects side $A B$ of triangle $A B C$ at points $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$, side $C A$ - at points $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$, and side $B C$ - at points $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$. Prove that if the lines $A A_{1}, B B_{1}$ and $C C_{1}$ intersect at one point, then the lines $A A_{2}, B B_{2}$ and $C C_{2}$ also intersect at one point.
reference_solution: 51. By the property of secants drawn from an external point to a circle, or by the property of segments of chords of a circle passing through one point, we have: $\left|B C_{1}\right| \cdot\left|B C_{2}\right|=\left|B A_{1}\right| \cdot\left|B A_{2}\right|,\left|C B_{1}\right| \cdot\left|C B_{2}\right|=$ $=\left|C A_{1}\right| \cdot\left|C A_{2}\right|,\left|A B_{1}\right| \cdot\left|A B_{2}\right|=\left|A C_{1}\right| \cdot\left|A C_{2}\right|$. It is now easy to verify that if the statement of Ceva's theorem (the equality $R=1$) holds for the points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$, then it also holds for the points $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$. From the statement of the problem, it follows that either all three points $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ lie on the corresponding sides of the triangle, or only one of them (see problem II. 44).

question: 52. On the sides $AB, BC$, and $CA$ of triangle $ABC$, points $C_{1}, A_{1}$, and $B_{1}$ are taken. Let $C_{2}$ be the point of intersection of the lines $AB$ and $A_{1} B_{1}$, $A_{2}$ be the point of intersection of the lines $BC$ and $B_{1} C_{1}$, and $B_{2}$ be the point of intersection of the lines $AC$ and $A_{1} C_{1}$. Prove that if the lines $A A_{1}, B B_{1}$, and $C C_{1}$ intersect at one point, then the points $A_{2}, B_{2}$, and $C_{2}$ lie on one line.
reference_solution: 52. Writing the equality $R=1$ (according to Ceva's and Menelaus' theorems - see problems II.44 and II.45) for the points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1} ; A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{2} ; A_{1}, B_{2}, C_{1}$; $A_{2}, B_{1}, C_{1}$, we obtain that the equality $R=1$ also holds for the points $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$. Now it remains to prove that either all three points $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ lie on the extensions of the sides of the triangle (which will be the case if the points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ lie on the sides of the triangle), or only one is on the extension (if one of the points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ lies on the sides of the triangle), and then use Menelaus' theorem (see problem II.45).

question: 53. A line intersects sides $A B, B C$ and the extension of side $A C$ of triangle $A B C$ at points $D, E$ and $F$ respectively. Prove that the midpoints of segments $D C, A E$ and $B F$ lie on one line (Gauss line).
reference_solution: 53. Use Menelaus' theorem (see problem II. 45). As the vertices of the given triangle, take the midpoints of the sides of triangle $A B C$, on the sides and extensions of which the considered points lie.

question: 54. Given a triangle $A B C$. Let's define a point $A_{1}$ on the side $B C$ as follows: $A_{1}$ is the midpoint of the side $K L$ of a regular pentagon $M K L N P$, where vertices $K$ and $L$ lie on $B C$, and vertices $M$ and $N$ lie on $A B$ and $A C$, respectively. Similarly, points $C_{1}$ and $B_{1}$ are defined on the sides $A B$ and $A C$. Prove that the lines $A A_{1}, B B_{1}$ and $C C_{1}$ intersect at one point.
reference_solution: 54. If $a$ is the length of the side of pentagon $M K L N P, b$ is the length of the side of the pentagon with one side on $A B, c$ is the length of the side of the pentagon, one of whose sides is on $A C$, then $\frac{\left|B A_{1}\right|}{\left|C_{1} B\right|}=\frac{a}{b}$, $\frac{\left|A C_{1}\right|}{\left|B_{1} A\right|}=\frac{b}{c}, \frac{\left|C B_{1}\right|}{\left|A_{1} C\right|}=\frac{c}{a}$. Multiplying these equalities, we find that $R=1$, and we will use Ceva's theorem (problem II. 44).

question: 55. Given three pairwise non-intersecting circles. Let $A_{1}, A_{2}, A_{3}$ be the three points of intersection of the common internal tangents to any two of them, and $B_{1}, B_{2}$, $B_{3}$ be the corresponding points of intersection of the external tangents. Prove that these points lie on four lines, three on each ( $A_{1}, A_{2}, B_{3} ; A_{1}, B_{2}, A_{3} ; B_{1}, A_{2}, A_{3} ; B_{1}$, $\left.B_{2}, B_{3}\right)$).
reference_solution: 55. Check that points $A_{1}, A_{2}, A_{3}$ and $B_{1}, B_{2}, B_{3}$ lie on the sides of triangle $O_{1} O_{2} O_{3}$ (where $O_{1}, O_{2}, O_{3}$ are the centers of the circles) or on the extensions of these sides, and the ratio of the distances from each of these points to the corresponding vertices of triangle $O_{1} O_{2} O_{3}$ is equal to the ratio of the radii of the corresponding circles. Then, one can use Menelaus' theorem (see problem II. 45) for each of these sets of three points.

question: 57. Given a triangle $A B C$, $M$ is an arbitrary point on the plane. The bisectors of two angles formed by the lines $A M$ and $B M$ intersect the line $A B$ at points $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ ( $C_{1}$ is on the segment $A B$ ), similarly, points $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$, $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$ are determined on $B C$ and $C A$. Prove that $A_{1}, A_{2}, B_{1}, B_{2}, C_{1}, C_{2}$ are located three on four lines.
reference_solution: 57. Let us use the equality $\frac{\sin \angle B_{1} A A_{2}}{\sin \angle A_{2} A C_{1}}=\frac{\left|A C_{1}\right|}{\left|A B_{1}\right|} \cdot \frac{\left|B_{1} A_{2}\right|}{\left|A_{2} C_{1}\right|}$. By obtaining similar equalities for other angles and multiplying them, we get our statement based on the results of problems II. 43 and II. 44.

question: 61. Given a triangle $A B C$. On the sides $B C, C A$ and $A B$, points $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}, B_{1}$ and $B_{2}, C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ are taken such that $A A_{1}$, $B B_{1}$ and $C C_{1}$ intersect at one point and $A A_{2}, B B_{2}$ and $C C_{2}$ also intersect at one point. Prove that: a) the points of intersection of the lines $A_{1} B_{1}$ and $A B, B_{1} C_{1}$ and $B C, C_{1} A_{1}$ and $C A$ lie on one line $l_{1}$. Similarly, the points $A_{2}, B_{2}$ and $C_{2}$ define a line $l_{2}$; b) the point $A$, the point of intersection of the lines $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$, and the point of intersection of the lines $B_{1} C_{1}$ and $B_{2} C_{2}$ lie on one line; c) the points of intersection of the lines $B C$ and $B_{2} C_{1}, C A$ and $C_{2} A_{2}, A B$ and $A_{1} B_{1}$ lie on one line.
reference_solution:
61. Let $S$ be the point of intersection of the lines $A_{1} M, B_{1} L$, and $C_{1} K$. Applying Menelaus' theorem (problem II. $45^{*}$, note) to triangles $S M K, S K L$, and $S L M$, we get $\frac{K L_{1}}{L_{1} M} \cdot \frac{M A_{1}}{A_{1} S} \cdot \frac{S C_{1}}{C_{1} K}=-1, \frac{L M_{1}}{M_{1} K} \times$ $\times \frac{K C_{1}}{C_{1} S} \cdot \frac{S B_{1}}{B_{1} L}=-1, \frac{M K_{1}}{K_{1} L} \cdot \frac{L B_{1}}{B_{1} S} \cdot \frac{S A_{1}}{A_{1} M}=-1$. Multiplying these equalities, we obtain:

$$
\frac{K L_{1}}{L_{1} M} \cdot \frac{L M_{1}}{M_{1} K} \cdot \frac{M K_{1}}{K_{1} L}=-1
$$

Equality (1) is a necessary and sufficient condition for the lines $A_{1} M, B_{1} L$, and $C_{1} K$ to intersect at one point. The necessity has already been proven. The sufficiency is proven by contradiction. (Let $S^{\prime}$ be the point of intersection of $A_{1} M$ and $B_{1} L$, draw $S^{\prime} C_{1}$, and denote by $K^{\prime}$ its point of intersection with the given line, and prove that $K$ and $K^{\prime}$ coincide.) Since equality (1) remains unchanged when $K, L, M$ are replaced by $K_{1}, L_{1}, M_{1}$ and vice versa, the statement of the problem is proven.

question: 63. Given a triangle $A B C$ and a point $D$. Points $E, F$ and $G$ are located on the lines $A D, B D$ and $C D$, respectively. $K$ is the intersection point of $A F$ and $B E$, $L$ is the intersection point of $B G$ and $C F$, and $M$ is the intersection point of $C E$ and $A G$. The points $P, Q$ and $R$ are the intersections of $D K$ and $A B$, $D L$ and $B C$, $D M$ and $A C$, respectively. Prove that the six lines $A L, E Q, B M, F R, C K$ and $G P$ intersect at one point.
reference_solution: 63. Applying Ceva's theorem (problem II. 44*, note) to triangles $A B D, \quad B D C \quad$ and $C D A$, we get: $\frac{A P}{P B} \cdot \frac{B F}{F D} \cdot \frac{D E}{E A}=1$, $\frac{B Q}{Q C} \cdot \frac{C G}{G D} \cdot \frac{D F}{F B}=1, \frac{C R}{R A} \cdot \frac{A E}{E D} \cdot \frac{D G}{G C}=1$. Multiplying these equalities, we obtain: $\frac{A P}{P B} \cdot \frac{B Q}{Q C} \cdot \frac{C R}{R A}=1$, i.e., the lines $A Q, B R$ and $C P$ intersect at one point. Let's denote it by $N$. Let $T$ be the point of intersection of $P G$ and $D N$. By Menelaus' theorem (problem II. $45^{*}$, note), we have $\frac{D T}{T N} \cdot \frac{N P}{P C} \cdot \frac{C G}{G D}=-1$, from which $\frac{D T}{T N}=-\frac{P C}{N P} \frac{G D}{C G}=-\frac{C P}{P N} \cdot \frac{G D}{C G}$. If $\frac{A E}{E D}=\alpha, \quad \frac{B F}{F D}=\beta, \quad \frac{C G}{G D}=\gamma, \quad$ then $\quad \frac{A P}{P B}=\frac{\alpha}{\beta}, \quad \frac{C R}{R A}=\frac{\gamma}{\alpha}, \quad \frac{C N}{N P}=$ $=-\frac{B A}{P B} \cdot \frac{R C}{A R}=\frac{\alpha+\beta}{\beta} \cdot \frac{\gamma}{\alpha}, \frac{C P}{P N}=-\left(1+\frac{C N}{N P}\right)=-\frac{\alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha}{\alpha \beta}$. Thus, $\frac{D T}{T N}=\frac{\alpha \beta+\beta \gamma+\gamma \alpha}{\alpha \beta \gamma}$. The segment $D N$ will be divided in the same ratio by other lines.

question: 64. Points $A$ and $A_{1}$, $B$ and $B_{1}$, $C$ and $C_{1}$ are symmetric with respect to the line $l$, and $N$ is an arbitrary point on $l$. Prove that the lines $A N, B N, C N$ intersect the lines $B_{1} C_{1}$, $C_{1} A_{1}$, $A_{1} B_{1}$ respectively at three points lying on one straight line.
reference_solution:
64. Let us first consider the limiting case when point $N$ is at "infinity"; then the lines $A N, B N$ and $C N$ are parallel to line $l$. Let the distances from points $A, B$ and $C$ to line $l$ be $a, b$ and $c$ (for convenience, assume that $A, B$ and $C$ are on the same side of $l$). The lines parallel to $l$ and passing through $A, B$ and $C$ intersect the lines $B_{1} C_{1}$, $C_{1} A_{1}$ and $A_{1} B_{1}$ at points $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$, respectively. It is easy to see that $\frac{\left|A_{1} C_{2}\right|}{\left|C_{2} B_{1}\right|}=\frac{a+c}{c+b}, \frac{\left|B_{1} A_{2}\right|}{\left|A_{2} C_{1}\right|}=\frac{b+a}{a+c}, \frac{\left|C_{1} B_{2}\right|}{\left|B_{2} A_{1}\right|}=\frac{c+b}{b+a}$. Multiplying these equalities, we get that the statement of Menelaus' theorem for problem II. 45 holds (it is also necessary to check that an odd number of points from $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ lie on the extensions of the sides of triangle $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$). Therefore, points $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ lie on the same line.

The general case can be reduced to the one considered if, for example, we project the given arrangement of triangles from some point in space onto another plane. In this way, we can ensure that the symmetry of the triangles is not violated, and point $N$ will move to infinity. We can also avoid spatial considerations. Introduce a coordinate system, choosing the line $l$ as the $x$-axis and taking the origin at point $N$. Perform the transformation $x^{\prime}=1 / x$, $y^{\prime}=y / x$. In this transformation, points on the $x$-axis ($y=0$) will move to the line $y^{\prime}=0$; points symmetric with respect to the $x$-axis will move to points symmetric with respect to the line $y^{\prime}=0$; lines will move to lines; lines passing through the origin will move to lines parallel to the line $y^{\prime}=0$ (this transformation is essentially the projection mentioned above). After such a transformation, we obtain the arrangement already considered.

question:
65. Let $A_{1}, A_{3}, A_{5}$ be three points on one line, and $A_{2}, A_{4}, A_{6}$ be on another. Prove that the three points where the lines $A_{1} A_{2}$ and $A_{4} A_{5}, A_{2} A_{3}$ and $A_{5} A_{6}, A_{3} A_{4}$ and $A_{6} A_{1}$ intersect pairwise lie on one line (Pappus).

## § 3. Geometric Loci
reference_solution:
65. We will consider that these lines are parallel. This can be achieved through appropriate design or coordinate transformation (see the solution to problem II. 64). Apply Menelaus' theorem (problem II. 45) to triangle \(A_{1} A_{6} M\) (Fig. 16, \(N^{\prime} K^{\prime}\) is parallel to the given lines):

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_35c23d544adcc44dca41g-125.jpg?height=362&width=673&top_left_y=385&top_left_x=291)

Fig. 16

We will have: \(\frac{\left|A_{1} L\right|}{\left|L A_{6}\right|} \cdot \frac{\left|A_{6} K\right|}{|K M|} \cdot \frac{|M N|}{\left|N A_{1}\right|} = \frac{\left|A_{1} A_{3}\right|}{\left|A_{4} A_{6}\right|} \cdot \frac{\left|A_{6} A_{2}\right|}{\left|K^{\prime} M\right|} \cdot \frac{\left|M N^{\prime}\right|}{\left|A_{5} A_{1}\right|} = \frac{\left|A_{1} A_{3}\right|}{\left|K^{\prime} M\right|} \cdot \frac{\left|M N^{\prime}\right|}{\left|A_{4} A_{6}\right|} \cdot \frac{\left|A_{6} A_{2}\right|}{\left|A_{5} A_{1}\right|} = \frac{\left|A_{1} A_{2}\right|}{\left|A_{2} M\right|} \times \frac{\left|M A_{5}\right|}{\left|A_{5} A_{6}\right|} \cdot \frac{\left|A_{6} A_{2}\right|}{\left|A_{5} A_{1}\right|} = \frac{\left|A_{1} M\right|}{\left|A_{2} M\right|} \cdot \frac{\left|M A_{5}\right|}{\left|A_{5} M\right|} \cdot \frac{\left|A_{2} M\right|}{\left|M A_{1}\right|} = 1\). Thus, the points \(L, N\), and \(K\) lie on the same line. According to the note to problems II. 44 and II. 45, instead of \(\frac{\left|A_{1} L\right|}{\left|L A_{6}\right|}\) and others, we could consider the ratios \(\frac{A_{1} L}{L A_{6}}\) and others. In this case, the product of the corresponding ratios would be equal to \((-1)\).

question: 95. Given a segment $A B$. Take an arbitrary point $M$ on $A B$ and consider two squares $A M C D$ and $M B E F$, located on the same side of $A B$. Describe circles around these squares and denote by $N$ their point of intersection, different from $M$. Prove that: a) $A F$ and $B C$ intersect at $N$; b) $M N$ passes through a fixed point on the plane. Find the geometric locus of the midpoints of the segments connecting the centers of the squares.
reference_solution:
95. a) Since $\angle F N B=90^{\circ}, \angle C N M=135^{\circ}, \angle F N M=45^{\circ}$ (assuming $|A M|>|M B|$), then $\angle F N C=90^{\circ}$ and $C, N$ and $B$ are collinear, etc.

b) Consider the isosceles right triangle $A B K$ with hypotenuse $A B$ ( $K$ is on the opposite side of $A B$ from the squares). The quadrilateral $A N B K$ is cyclic, therefore, $\angle A N K=\angle A B K=45^{\circ}$, i.e., $N K$ passes through $M$.

The desired geometric locus of points is the midline of triangle $A L B$, where $L$ is the point symmetric to point $K$ with respect to $A B$.

question: 99. The sides of the given triangle are the diagonals of three parallelograms. The sides of these parallelograms are parallel to two lines $-l$ and $p$. Prove that the three diagonals of these parallelograms, different from the sides of the triangle, intersect at one point $M$. Find the geometric locus of points $M$ if $l$ and $p$ are two arbitrary perpendicular lines.
reference_solution:
99. The union of three constructed parallelograms represents a parallelogram circumscribed around a given triangle, divided into four smaller ones. It is not difficult to express the ratios in which each of the considered diagonals is divided by another diagonal in terms of the segments of the sides of the larger parallelogram.

If the parallelograms are rectangles, then by parallelly translating two of the three considered diagonals, we form a triangle equal to the given one; and this means that the angles between them are either equal to the corresponding angles of the triangle or supplement them to $180^{\circ}$. The sought geometric locus of points is a circle passing through the midpoints of the sides of the given triangle.

question: 115. The circle inscribed in triangle $ABC$ touches sides $AB$ and $AC$ at points $C_{1}$ and $B_{1}$, and the circle that touches side $BC$ and the extensions of $AB$ and $AC$ touches the lines $AB$ and $AC$ at points $C_{2}$ and $B_{2}$. Let $D$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Line $AD$ intersects lines $B_{1} C_{1}$ and $B_{2} C_{2}$ at points $E$ and $F$. Prove that $BECF$ is a parallelogram.
reference_solution: 115. Draw a line through $D$ perpendicular to the bisector of angle $A$, and denote the points of its intersection with $A B$ and $A C$ as $K$ and $M$, and prove that $|A K|=|A M|=\frac{b+c}{2}$. Since $\left|A C_{1}\right|=\left|A B_{1}\right|=p-a$, $\left|A C_{2}\right|=\left|B C_{2}\right|=p$ ( $p$ - the semiperimeter of $\triangle A B C, a, b, c$ - its sides), the points $K$ and $M$ will be the midpoints of segments $C_{1} C_{2}$ and $B_{1} B_{2}$.

question: 116. In triangle $ABC$, the bisector of the internal angle $AD$ is drawn. Construct the tangent $l$ to the circumscribed circle at point $A$. Prove that the line drawn through $D$ parallel to $l$ is tangent to the inscribed circle of triangle $ABC$.
reference_solution: 116. Prove that $l$ forms the same angles with $A D$ as the line $B C$, which is tangent to our circle. It follows from this that the other tangent to the circle passing through $D$ will be parallel to $l$.

question: 117. In triangle $ABC$, a line is drawn intersecting sides $AC$ and $BC$ at points $M$ and $N$ such that $|MN| = |AM| + |BN|$. Prove that all such lines are tangent to the same circle.
reference_solution: 117. Let's construct a circle that is tangent to the lines $M N, A C$ and $B C$ in such a way that the points of tangency $P$ and $Q$ with the lines $A C$ and $B C$ are outside the segments $C M$ and $C N$ (this will be the excircle of triangle $M C N$). If $R$ is the point of tangency with $M N$, then $|M P|=|M R|,|N Q|=|N R|$, hence $|M N|=|M P|+|N Q|$; but by the condition $|M N|=|M A|+|N B|$. Therefore, one of the points $P$ or $Q$ lies inside the corresponding side, and the other lies on its extension. In this case, $|C P|=|C Q|=\frac{1}{2}(|C P|+|C Q|)=$ $=\frac{1}{2}(|A C|+|C B|)$, i.e., the constructed circle is constant for all lines.

question: 118. Prove that the points symmetric to the center of the circle circumscribed around a triangle with respect to the midpoints of its medians lie on the heights of the triangle.
reference_solution: 118. If $O$ is the center of the circle circumscribed around $\triangle A B C, D$ is the midpoint of $C B, H$ is the point of intersection of the altitudes, $L$ is the midpoint of $A H$, then $|A L|=|O D|$ and, since $A L \| O D$, $O L$ bisects $A D$, i.e., $L$ is symmetric to $O$ with respect to the midpoint of $A D$.

question: 119. Prove that if the height of a triangle is $\sqrt{2}$ times the radius of the circumscribed circle, then the line connecting the bases of the perpendiculars dropped from the base of this height to the sides containing it passes through the center of the circumscribed circle.
reference_solution:
119. Let $B D$ be the height of the triangle, and $|B D|=R \sqrt{2}$, where $R$ is the radius of the circumscribed circle. $K$ and $M$ are the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from $D$ to $A B$ and $B C$, and $O$ is the center of the circumscribed circle. If angle $C$ is acute, then $\angle K B O=90^{\circ}-\angle C$. Since quadrilateral $B M$ $\angle M K B=180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}-\left(90^{\circ}-\angle C\right)=\angle C$; therefore, $B O \perp K M$. But $S_{B K M}=\frac{1}{2}|B D|^{2} \sin A \sin B \sin C=R^{2} \sin A \sin B \sin C=\frac{1}{2} S_{A B C}$. (We used the formula $S=2 R^{2} \sin A \sin B \sin C$.) On the other hand, if $h_{1}$ is the height of $\triangle B K M$ drawn from vertex $B$, then $\frac{1}{2} S=$ $=\frac{1}{4}|A C| \cdot|B D|=S_{B K M}=\frac{1}{2}|K M| h_{1}=\frac{1}{2}|B D| h_{1} \sin B, \quad$ hence, $\quad h_{1}=$
$=\frac{|A C|}{2 \sin B}=R$; considering that $B O \perp K M$, we get that point $O$ lies on $K M$.

question: 120. Let $A B C$ be a right triangle ( $\angle C=90^{\circ}$ ), $C D$ be the altitude, $K$ be a point on the plane such that $|A K|=|A C|$. Prove that the diameter of the circumcircle of triangle $A B K$, passing through vertex $A$, is perpendicular to the line $D K$.
reference_solution: 120. Note that $\triangle A D K$ is similar to $\triangle A B K$, since $|A K|^{2}=$ $=|A C|^{2}=|A D| \cdot|A B|$. If $O$ is the center of the circumcircle of $\triangle A B K$, then $\angle O A D+\angle A D K=90^{\circ}-\angle A K B+\angle A D K=90^{\circ}$ (it was assumed that $\angle A K B$ is acute; if $\angle A K B$ is obtuse, the reasoning is analogous).

question: 122. Two circles pass through the vertex of an angle and a point lying on the bisector. Prove that the segments of the sides of the angle, enclosed between the circles, are equal.
reference_solution: 122. If $O$ is the vertex of the angle, $A$ is a point on the bisector, $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$ are the points of intersection with the sides of the angle of one circle, $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ ( $B_{1}$ and $C_{1}$ are on the same side) are the points of intersection of another circle, then $\triangle A B_{1} C_{1}=\triangle A B_{2} C_{2}$.

question: 130. Given a right triangle $A B C$; angle $C$ is right, $O$ is the center of the inscribed circle, $M$ is the point of tangency of the inscribed circle with the hypotenuse, the circle with center at $M$, passing through $O$, intersects the angle bisectors of angles $A$ and $B$ at points $K$ and $L$, different from $O$. Prove that $K$ and $L$ are the centers of the circles inscribed in triangles $A C D$ and $B C D$, where $C D$ is the altitude of triangle $A B C$.
reference_solution:
130. If $K N$ is the perpendicular from $K$ to $A B, \angle C A B=\alpha$, then

\[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{|K N|}{|O M|}=\frac{|A K|}{|A O|}=\frac{|A O|-|K O|}{|A O|}=\frac{|A O|-2|O M| \sin \frac{\alpha}{2}}{|A O|}= \\
& =\frac{|A O|-2|A O| \sin ^{2} \frac{\alpha}{2}}{|A O|}=\cos \alpha=\frac{|C D|}{|C B|}. \text{ Since } \triangle A C B \text{ and } \triangle A C D
\end{aligned}
\]

are similar, it follows from the above that $K N$ is equal to the radius of the circle inscribed in $\triangle A C D$, and since $K$ lies on the bisector of angle $A$, $K$ is the center of the circle inscribed in $\triangle A C D$. Similarly for $L$.

question: 131. Prove that in triangle $ABC$, the bisector of angle $A$, the midline parallel to $AC$, and the line connecting the points of tangency of the inscribed circle with sides $CB$ and $CA$, intersect at one point.
reference_solution: 131. Let $C_{1}$ and $A_{1}$ be the midpoints of $A B$ and $B C$, $B^{\prime}$ and $A^{\prime}$ - the points of tangency of the inscribed circle with $A C$ and $B C$. Suppose, for definiteness, that $c \geqslant b$ (where $c$ and $b$ are the sides of $\triangle A B C$), then the angle bisector of $\angle A$ intersects the extension of $C_{1} A_{1}$ at a point $K$ such that $\left|A_{1} K\right|=\frac{c-b}{2}$, and the line $B^{\prime} A^{\prime}$ should also pass through the same point $K$, since triangles $K A_{1} A^{\prime}$ and $A^{\prime} B^{\prime} C$ are isosceles, $\left|A^{\prime} C\right|=\left|B^{\prime} C\right|,\left|A_{1} K\right|=\left|A_{1} A^{\prime}\right|, \angle A^{\prime} A_{1} K=$ $=\angle A^{\prime} C B^{\prime}$.

question: 132. Prove that three lines, passing respectively through the bases of two altitudes of a triangle, the ends of two of its angle bisectors, and through two points of tangency of the inscribed circle with its sides (all points are located on two sides of the triangle), intersect at one point.
reference_solution:
132. Consider an angle with vertex $A$. On one side of the angle, three points $-B_{1}, B_{2}, B_{3}$ are taken, and on the other side, $C_{1}, C_{2}, C_{3}$. From Menelaus' theorem (Problem II. 45, note), it follows that for the lines $B_{1} C_{1}, B_{2} C_{2}, B_{3} C_{3}$ to intersect at one point, it is necessary and sufficient that the equality

$$
\frac{A B_{2}}{B_{2} B_{1}} \cdot \frac{C_{1} C_{2}}{C_{2} A}=\frac{A B_{3}}{B_{3} B_{1}} \cdot \frac{C_{1} C_{3}}{C_{3} A}
$$

(holding the ratios in the sense indicated in the note) is satisfied. Indeed, if equality (1) is satisfied, then from Menelaus' theorem it will follow that the lines $B_{2} C_{2}$ and $B_{3} C_{3}$ intersect the side $B_{1} C_{1}$ of the triangle $A B_{1} C_{1}$ at one point.

question: 133. On the sides $B C, C A$ and $A B$ of triangle $A B C$, points $A_{1}, B_{1}$ and $C_{1}$ are taken such that the lines $A A_{1}, B B_{1}$ and $C C_{1}$ intersect at one point. Prove that if $A A_{1}$ is the bisector of angle $B_{1} A_{1} C_{1}$, then $A A_{1}$ is the altitude of triangle $A B C$.
reference_solution: 133. Draw a line through $A$ parallel to $B C$, and denote by $K$ and $L$ the points of its intersection with $A_{1} C_{1}$ and $A_{1} B_{1}$, respectively. We have: $\frac{|K A|}{\left|B A_{1}\right|}=\frac{\left|A C_{1}\right|}{\left|C_{1} B\right|}, \frac{\left|C B_{1}\right|}{\left|B_{1} A\right|}=\frac{\left|A_{1} C\right|}{|A L|}$. By Ceva's theorem (problem II.44) $\frac{\left|A C_{1}\right|}{\left|C_{1} B\right|} \cdot \frac{\left|B A_{1}\right|}{\left|A_{1} C\right|} \cdot \frac{\left|C B_{1}\right|}{\left|B_{1} A\right|}=1$, hence, $|K A|=|A L|$. If $A A_{1}$ is the bisector of angle $K A_{1} L$, then, since $|K A|=|A L|, A A_{1}$ is perpendicular to $K L$, i.e., $A A_{1}$ is the altitude of $\triangle A B C$.

question: 134. On the sides $B C, C A$ and $A B$ of triangle $A B C$, points $A_{1}, B_{1}$ and $C_{1}$ are taken respectively such that $\angle A A_{1} C = \angle B B_{1} A = \angle C C_{1} B$ (angles are measured in the same direction). Prove that the center of the circle circumscribed around the triangle bounded by the lines $A A_{1}, B B_{1}$ and $C C_{1}$ coincides with the orthocenter of triangle $A B C$.
reference_solution: 134. Let $K$ be the point of intersection of $A A_{1}$ and $B B_{1}$, and $H$ be the point of intersection of the altitudes of triangle $A B C$. Points $A, K, H$, and $B$ lie on the same circle (angles $A K B$ and $A H B$ are either equal or their sum is $180^{\circ}$, depending on whether points $K$ and $H$ are on the same side or opposite sides of line $A B$). The radius of this circle is equal to $R$, the radius of the circumcircle of $\triangle A B C$. If $\varphi$ is the angle between $A A_{1}$ and $A H$, then $|K H|=2 R \sin \varphi$.

question: 135. The vertices of triangle $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ are located on the lines $B C, C A$ and $A B\left(A_{1}\right.$ - on $B C, B_{1}$ - on $C A, C_{1}$ - on $\left.A B\right)$. Prove that if triangles $A B C$ and $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ are similar (corresponding vertices are $A$ and $A_{1}, B$ and $B_{1}, C$ and $C_{1}$ ), then the point of intersection of the altitudes of triangle $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ is the center of the circumcircle of triangle $A B C$. Is the converse statement true?
reference_solution: 135. Let $H$ be the orthocenter of triangle $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$. Points $A_{1}, H, B_{1}$, and $C$ lie on the same circle, and points $B_{1}, H, C_{1}$, and $A$ also lie on the same circle, with the radii of these circles being equal. Angles $H B_{1} C$ and $H B_{1} A$ are either equal or supplementary to $180^{\circ}$. Therefore, $|H A|=|H C|$. The converse statement is false. For each point $A_{1}$ on line $BC$, there generally exist two triangles $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ and $A_{1} B_{1}^{\prime} C_{1}^{\prime} \left(B_{1}\right.$ and $B_{1}^{\prime}$ on $AC$, $C_{1}$ and $C_{1}^{\prime}$ on $\left.AB\right)$, the orthocenters of which coincide with the circumcenter of $\triangle ABC$, with one of them being similar to $\triangle ABC$ and the other not. For example, if $\triangle ABC$ is an equilateral triangle and $A_{1}$ is the midpoint of $BC$, then $B_{1}$ and $C_{1}$ can be the midpoints of $AC$ and $AB$, and $B_{1}^{\prime}$ and $C_{1}^{\prime}$ can be points on the extensions of $AC$ and $AB$ beyond $C$ and $B$, with $\left|C B_{1}^{\prime}\right|=|CB|,\left|B C_{1}^{\prime}\right|=|BC|$. The converse statement would be true if we required that points $A_{1}, B_{1}$, and $C_{1}$ be located on the sides of $\triangle ABC$ and not on their extensions.

question: 136. On each side of a triangle, two points are taken such that all six segments connecting each point with the opposite vertex are equal to each other. Prove that the midpoints of these six segments lie on the same circle.
reference_solution: 136. We will prove that the center of the desired circle coincides with the orthocenter (the point of intersection of the altitudes). Let $B D$ be the altitude, $H$ be the point of intersection of the altitudes, and $K$ and $L$ be the midpoints of the constructed segments originating from vertex $B, |B K|=|B L|=l, M$ be the midpoint of $B D$. Then $|K H|^{2}=|L H|^{2}=|M H|^{2}+|K M|^{2}=l^{2}-|B M|^{2}+|M H|^{2}=l^{2}-\frac{|B D|^{2}}{4}+$ $+\left(|B H|-\frac{|B D|}{2}\right)^{2}=l^{2}+|B H|^{2}-|B H| \cdot|B D|=l^{2}-|B H| \cdot|H D| . \quad$ It remains to prove that the products of the segments of the altitudes, into which each is divided by their point of intersection, are equal. Draw the altitude $A E$. Due to the similarity of $\triangle B H E$ and $\triangle A H D$ we have: $|B H| \cdot|H D|=|A H| \cdot|H E|$, which is what we needed to prove.

question: 137. In triangle $ABC$, on the rays $AB$ and $CB$, segments $|AM|=|CN|=p$ are laid out, where $p$ is the semiperimeter of the triangle (with $B$ lying between $A$ and $M$, and between $C$ and $N$). Let $K$ be the point on the circumcircle of $ABC$ that is diametrically opposite to $B$. Prove that the perpendicular dropped from $K$ to $MN$ passes through the incenter of the inscribed circle.
reference_solution:
137. Let (Fig. 28): \( |BC| = a, |CA| = b, |AB| = c \). Draw lines through the center of the inscribed circle parallel to \( AB \) and \( BC \), intersecting \( AK \) and \( KC \) at points \( P \) and \( Q \); in triangle \( OPQ \) we have: \( \angle POQ = \angle ABC, \quad |OQ| = p - c, \quad |OP| = p - a \), where \( p \) is the semiperimeter of \( \triangle ABC \). By the given condition, \( \angle NBM = \angle ABC \), \( |NB| = p - a, \quad |MB| = p - c \). Therefore, \( \triangle POQ = \triangle NBM \). If on line \( OP \) we take \( M_1 \) such that \( |OM_1| = |OQ| \), and on \( OQ \) - point \( N_1 \) such that \( |ON_1| = |OP| \), then \( \triangle ON_1M_1 = \triangle NBM \) and the corresponding sides \( BM \) and \( OM_1 \), \( BN \) and \( ON_1 \) will be parallel respectively. Thus, \( N_1M_1 \parallel NM \). We will prove that \( OK \perp N_1M_1 \), since in quadrilateral \( OPKQ \) two opposite angles are right, it is inscribed, therefore, \( \angle OKP = \angle OQP \). Further, \( \angle KOP + \angle OM_1N_1 = \angle KOP + \angle OQP = \angle KOP + \angle OKP = 90^\circ \), which means,

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_35c23d544adcc44dca41g-140.jpg?height=503&width=369&top_left_y=1057&top_left_x=749)

Fig. 28 that \( OK \perp M_1N_1 \).

question: 138. From a certain point on the circumcircle of an equilateral triangle $ABC$, lines parallel to $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ are drawn, intersecting $CA$, $AB$, and $BC$ at points $M$, $N$, and $Q$ respectively. Prove that $M$, $N$, and $Q$ lie on the same line.
reference_solution: 138. Let $P$ lie on the arc $A C$ for definiteness. Points $A, M$, $P, N$ lie on the same circle, so $\angle N M P=\angle N A P$. Similarly, $P, M, Q, C$ lie on the same circle, $\angle P M Q=180^{\circ}-\angle P C Q=$ $=180^{\circ}-\angle P A N=180^{\circ}-\angle P M N$.

question: 139. Prove that three lines, symmetric to an arbitrary line passing through the orthocenter of a triangle with respect to the sides of the triangle, intersect at one point.
reference_solution:
139. Let $A B C$ be the given triangle (Fig. 29), and $H$ be the point of intersection of its altitudes. Note that the points symmetric to $H$ with respect to its sides lie on the circumcircle of triangle $A B C$ (see problem II.107). If $H_{1}$ is the point symmetric to $H$ with respect to

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_35c23d544adcc44dca41g-141.jpg?height=310&width=325&top_left_y=275&top_left_x=459)

Fig. 29

side $B C$, then the line $l_{1}$, symmetric to $l$ with respect to the same side, passes through $H_{1}$. When $l$ is rotated around $H$ by an angle $\varphi$, the line $l_{1}$ rotates around $H_{1}$ by the same angle $\varphi$ in the opposite direction. Therefore, if $P$ is the second intersection point of the line $l_{1}$ with the circumcircle, then the radius $O P$ (where $O$ is the center of the circumcircle) rotates around $O$ by an angle $2 \varphi$ in the corresponding direction. The same reasoning applies to the other two lines symmetric to $l$. However, if $l$ coincides with one of the altitudes of the triangle, the statement of the problem is obvious (the point $P$ will coincide with the corresponding vertex of the triangle). Therefore, this statement is always true.

question:
140. Theorem of Leibniz. Let $M$ be an arbitrary point on the plane, and $G$ be the centroid of triangle $A B C$. Then the following equality holds:
$3|M G|^{2}=|M A|^{2}+|M B|^{2}+|M C|^{2}-$ $-\frac{1}{3}\left(|A B|^{2}+|B C|^{2}+|C A|^{2}\right)$.
reference_solution:
140. Let points $A, B, C$ and $M$ in the Cartesian coordinate system have coordinates respectively $\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right),\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right),\left(x_{3}, y_{3}\right),(x, y)$,

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_35c23d544adcc44dca41g-141.jpg?height=379&width=384&top_left_y=1100&top_left_x=133)

Fig. 30 coordinates of point $G-\left(\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}}{3}\right.$, $\left.\frac{y_{1}+y_{2}+y_{3}}{3}\right)$. Then the validity of the statement to be proved follows from the identity $3\left(x-\frac{x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}}{3}\right)^{2}=$ $=\left(x-x_{1}\right)^{2}+\left(x-x_{2}\right)^{2}+\left(x-x_{3}\right)^{2}-$ $-\frac{1}{3}\left(\left(x_{1}-x_{2}\right)^{2}+\left(x_{2}-x_{3}\right)^{2}+\left(x_{3}-x_{1}\right)^{2}\right)$ and a similar relation for the ordinates.

question: 141. Let $A B C$ be an equilateral triangle with side $a$, and $M$ be some point on the plane at a distance $d$ from the center of the triangle $A B C$. Prove that the area of the triangle with sides equal to the segments $M A, M B$, and $M C$ is given by the formula $S=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{12}\left|a^{2}-3 d^{2}\right|$.
reference_solution: 141. Consider the case when point $M$ (Fig. 30) lies inside triangle $ABC$. Rotate triangle $ABM$ around $A$ by an angle of $60^{\circ}$ so that $B$ moves to $C$. We obtain triangle $AM_1C$, which is equal to $\triangle ABM$, and $\triangle AMM_1$ is equilateral. Therefore, the sides of $\triangle CMM_1$ are equal to the segments $MA$, $MB$, and $MC$. Similarly, we obtain points $M_2$ and $M_3$. The area of the hexagon $AM_1CM_3BM_2$ is twice the area of $\triangle ABC$, i.e., it is equal to $a^2 \sqrt{3} / 2$. On the other hand, the area of this hexagon is composed of three equilateral triangles: $AMM_1$, $CMM_3$, $BMM_2$, and three triangles equal to the desired one. Therefore, $3S + \left(|MA|^2 + |MB|^2 + |MC|^2\right) \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} = a^2 \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. Using the result of problem II. 140, we get: $3S + \left(3d^2 + a^2\right) \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} = a^2 \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}$, from which $S = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{12} \left(a^2 - 3d^2\right)$. Similarly, other cases of the position of point $M$ are considered.

question: 143. Given a triangle $A B C$. On the rays $A B$ and $C B$, segments $A K$ and $C M$ are laid off, equal to $A C$. Prove that the radius of the circumcircle of triangle $B K M$ is equal to the distance between the centers of the inscribed and circumscribed circles of triangle $A B C$, and that the line $K M$ is perpendicular to the line connecting the centers of the inscribed and circumscribed circles.
reference_solution:
143. Let (Fig. $31, a$) $O$ be the center of the circumscribed circle, and $I$ be the center of the inscribed circle. Drop perpendiculars from $O$ and $I$ to $AB$ and $BC$; $ON, OP$,

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_35c23d544adcc44dca41g-142.jpg?height=357&width=340&top_left_y=625&top_left_x=226)

$a$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_35c23d544adcc44dca41g-142.jpg?height=394&width=419&top_left_y=610&top_left_x=605)

$\delta$

Fig. 31

$IL, IQ$. If $a, b, c$ are the lengths of the sides $BC, CA$, and $AB$, and $p$ is the semiperimeter of $\triangle ABC$, then $|BK|=|c-b|$, $|BM|=|a-b|$, $|BN|=c/2$, $|BP|=a/2$, $|BL|=|BQ|=p-b$, $|NL|=\frac{1}{2}|a-b|$, $|PQ|=\frac{1}{2}|c-b|$ (see problem I.18). Therefore, if we draw lines through $O$ parallel to the sides $AB$ and $BC$ until they intersect the perpendiculars dropped from $I$, we obtain $\triangle ORS$, similar to $\triangle BKM$, with a similarity coefficient of $1/2$. But the circle constructed on $OI$ as its diameter is the circumcircle of $\triangle ORS$. Therefore, the radius of the circumcircle of $\triangle BKM$ is $OI$. For the proof of the second part of the problem, note that if we lay off the segment $OR_1$ equal to $OR$ on the line $OS$, and the segment $OS_1$ equal to $OS$ on the line $OR$, then the line $S_1R_1$ will be parallel to $KM$ (Fig. 31, b); but $\angle OR_1S_1 + \angle IOR_1 = \angle ORS + \angle IOS = 90^\circ$, i.e., $S_1R_1 \perp OI$.

question: 145. Prove that if the lengths of the sides of a triangle form an arithmetic progression, then: a) the radius of the inscribed circle is equal to $1 / 3$ of the height dropped to the middle side; b) the line connecting the centroid of the triangle with the center of the inscribed circle is parallel to the middle side; c) the bisector of the internal angle opposite the middle side is perpendicular to the line connecting the centers of the inscribed and circumscribed circles; d) for all points on this bisector, the sum of the distances to the sides of the triangle is constant; e) the center of the inscribed circle, the midpoints of the largest and smallest sides, and the vertex of the angle they form lie on the same circle.
reference_solution:
145. Let the sides of the triangle be $a, b$, and $c$, with $b = (a + c) / 2$.
a) From the equality $p r = \frac{1}{2} b h_{b}$ (where $p$ is the semiperimeter, $r$ is the radius of the inscribed circle, and $h_{b}$ is the height dropped to side $b$), we get: $\frac{1}{2}(a + b + c) = \frac{1}{2} b h_{b}$; but $a + c = 2b$, so $h_{b} = 3r$.

b) This statement follows from the fact that $r = \frac{1}{3} h_{b}$, and the point of intersection of the medians divides each median in the ratio $2:1$.

c) Extend the bisector $BD$ to intersect the circumscribed circle at point $M$. If we prove that $O$ - the center of the inscribed circle - bisects $BM$, then our statement will also be proven. (Draw the diameter $BN$, then the line connecting the centers of the inscribed and circumscribed circles will be parallel to $NM$, and $\angle BMN = 90^{\circ}$.) But $\triangle COM$ is isosceles, since $\angle COM = \angle OCM = \frac{1}{2}(\angle C + \angle B)$. Therefore, $|CM| = |OM|$. From the condition $b = (a + c) / 2$ and the property of the bisector, we get that $|CD| = a / 2$. Let $K$ be the midpoint of $CB$; $\triangle CKO = \triangle CDO (|CK| = |CD|, \angle KCO = \angle OCD)$; hence, $\angle BKO = \angle CDM$, and $\angle DCM = \angle OBC = \angle B / 2, |CD| = |BK|$, i.e., $\triangle BKO = \triangle CDM, |CM| = |BO|$, so $|BO| = |OM|$, which is what we needed to prove.

d) Take any point on the bisector. Let the distances to sides $BC$ and $BA$ be $x$, and to side $AC - y$. We have: $\frac{1}{2}(ax + cx + by) = S_{\triangle} \Rightarrow b(2x + y) = 2S_{\Delta} \Rightarrow 2x + y = h_{b}$.

e) If $L$ is the midpoint of $BA$, then the quadrilateral we need is homothetic to the quadrilateral $BCMA$ with a coefficient of $1 / 2$ (see part c)).

question:
146. Let $K$ be the midpoint of side $BC$ of triangle $ABC$, and $M$ be the foot of the altitude dropped to $BC$. The incircle of triangle $ABC$ touches side $BC$ at point $D$; the excircle opposite to $A$, which touches the extensions of $AB$ and $AC$ and side $BC$, touches $BC$ at point $E$. The common tangent to these circles, different from the sides of the triangle, intersects the circle passing through $K$ and $M$ at points $F$ and $G$. Prove that points $D, E, F$, and $G$ lie on the same circle.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_35c23d544adcc44dca41g-055.jpg?height=86&width=144&top_left_y=244&top_left_x=544)
reference_solution: 146. Let $N$ be the point of intersection of the common tangent with $B C$. It is sufficient to check that $|F N| \cdot|N G|=|K N| \cdot|N M|=|D N| \cdot|N E|$. All segments are easily calculated, since $|B D|=|C E|=p-b$, $|D E|=|b-c|, \frac{|D N|}{|N E|}=\frac{r}{r_{a}}=\frac{p-a}{p}\left(r_{a}-\right.$ radius of the circle touching side $B C$ and the extensions of sides $A B$ and $A C$ ), and so on.

question: 147. Prove that the centroid of a triangle, the orthocenter, and the circumcenter lie on the same line (Euler's line).
reference_solution: 147. Draw lines through the vertices of triangle $A B C$ parallel to the opposite sides. They form $\triangle A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$, similar to $\triangle A B C$; it is obtained from $\triangle A B C$ by a homothety with the center at the common centroid of $\triangle A B C$ and $\triangle A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$, and the coefficient is -2. The orthocenter of $\triangle A B C$ is the circumcenter of the circumcircle of $\triangle A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$. Therefore, the points $O$ (circumcenter), $G$ (centroid), and $H$ (orthocenter of $\triangle A B C$) lie on the same line, and $|O G|=\frac{1}{2}|G H|$, with $\boldsymbol{G}$ on the segment $O H$.

question: 149. Let $K$ be the point symmetric to the center of the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ with respect to the side $BC$. Prove that the Euler line of triangle $ABC$ bisects the segment $AK$.
reference_solution: 149. Show that the required property is possessed by a point $P$ on the Euler line for which $|P O|=|O H|$ (where $O$ is the circumcenter and $H$ is the orthocenter); in this case, for each triangle, the distance from the centroid to the opposite vertex of the original triangle is $\frac{4}{3} R$, where $R$ is the radius of the circumcircle of $\triangle A B C$, and the line passing through the centroid of this triangle and the opposite vertex of the original triangle passes through $O$.

question: 150. Prove that on the Euler line of triangle $ABC$ there exists a point $P$ such that the distances from the centroids of triangles $ABP$, $BCP$, $CAP$ to the vertices $C$, $A$, and $B$ respectively are equal to each other.
reference_solution: 150. Let $C_{1}$ be the center of the circumcircle of $\triangle A P B$, and $C_{2}$ be the point symmetric to $C_{1}$ with respect to $A B$. Similarly, for triangles $B P C$ and $C P A$, define points $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}, B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$. Since triangles $A C_{1} B, A C_{2} B, B A_{1} C, B A_{2} C, C B_{1} A, C B_{2} A$ are isosceles with angles at the vertices of $120^{\circ}$, triangles $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ and $A_{2} B_{2} C_{2}$ are equilateral (see problem II.296). By calculating the angles of the quadrilaterals with vertices $P, A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$, it can be proven that these points ($P, A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$) lie on the same circle. Furthermore, if $H$ is the orthocenter of triangle $A P B$, then since $|P H|=\left|C_{1} C_{2}\right|$ and, therefore, $\mathrm{PHC}_{2} \mathrm{C}_{1}$ is a parallelogram, the line $C_{1} H$ (the Euler line of triangle $A P B$) passes through the midpoint of $P C_{2}$. Since $P C_{2}$ is a chord of the circle with center $C_{1}$, $C_{1} H$ is perpendicular to $P C_{2}$. Thus, the three Euler lines coincide with the perpendicular bisectors of the segments $P C_{2}, P B_{2}$, and $P A_{2}$. Since points $P, A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ lie on the same circle, these lines intersect at its center, which is the center of the equilateral triangle $A_{2} B_{2} C_{2}$. From the result of problem II.296, it follows that these three Euler lines intersect at the centroid of triangle $A B C$.

question: 155. Let $M$ be a point on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. A line passing through $M$ and perpendicular to $BC$ intersects the circle again at point $N$. Prove that the Simson line corresponding to point $M$ is parallel to the line $AN$.
reference_solution: 155. The distance between the projections of $M$ on $A C$ and $B C$ is $|C M| \sin C$. If $K$ and $L$ are the projections of $M$ on $A B$ and $B C$, then the projection of $A B$ on the line $K L$ (which is the Simson line) is $|A B||\cos \angle B K L|=$ $=|A B||\cos \angle \dot{B} M L|=|A B| \sin \angle C B M=|C M| \sin C$.

question: 157. Let $A A_{1}, B B_{1}, C C_{1}$ be the altitudes of triangle $A B C$. The lines $A A_{1}, B B_{1}, C C_{1}$ intersect the circumcircle of triangle $A B C$ again at points $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$, respectively. The Simson lines corresponding to points $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ form triangle $A_{3} B_{3} C_{3}$ (where $A_{3}$ is the intersection of the Simson lines corresponding to points $B_{2}$ and $C_{2}$, and so on). Prove that the centroids of triangles $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ and $A_{3} B_{3} C_{3}$ coincide, and that the lines $A_{2} A_{3}, B_{2} B_{3}$, and $C_{2} C_{3}$ intersect at a single point.
reference_solution: 157. Prove that the Simson line corresponding to $A_{1}$ is perpendicular to $B_{1} C_{1}$ (the same applies to other points). Further, it can be proven that the Simson line corresponding to point $A_{1}$ passes through the midpoint of $A_{1} H$, where $H$ is the orthocenter of triangle $A B C$ (see also the solution to problem II.166). Consequently, the Simson lines are the altitudes of the triangle whose vertices are the midpoints of the segments $A_{1} H, B_{1} H, C_{1} H$. Note. It can be proven that for arbitrary points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$, the Simson lines of these points with respect to triangle $A B C$ form a triangle similar to triangle $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$, and the center of the circumcircle of this triangle coincides with the midpoint of the segment connecting the orthocenters of triangles $A B C$ and $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$.

question: 163. The height dropped from vertex $A$ of triangle $ABC$ intersects the circumscribed circle at point $A_{1}$. Prove that the distance from the center of the nine-point circle to side $BC$ is equal to $\frac{1}{4}\left|A A_{1}\right|$.
reference_solution: 163. Let $M_{0}$ be the midpoint of $H P$, $A_{0}$ be the midpoint of $H A$, and $A_{0}, A_{1}$, and $M_{0}$ lie on the nine-point circle. Therefore, $M$ also lies on this circle, since from the problem statement it follows that $\left|M_{0} H\right| \cdot|H M|=\left|A_{0} H\right| \cdot\left|H A_{1}\right|$ and $H$ is simultaneously either inside or outside each of the segments $M_{0} M$ and $A_{0} A_{1}$.

question: 164. In triangle $A B C$, $A A_{1}$ is the altitude, $H$ is the orthocenter. Let $P$ be an arbitrary point on the circumcircle of triangle $A B C$, and $M$ be a point on the line $H P$ such that $|H P| \cdot|H M|=\left|H A_{1}\right| \cdot|H A|(H$ is on the segment $M P$ if triangle $A B C$ is acute and outside it if it is obtuse). Prove that $M$ lies on the nine-point circle of triangle $A B C$.
reference_solution:
164. We will prove that $M$ and $N$ are on the corresponding midlines of triangle $ABC$. If $P$ is the midpoint of $AB$, then $\angle MPA = 2 \angle ABM = \angle ABC = \angle APL$. Let, for definiteness, $ABC$ be an acute triangle, $\angle C \geqslant \angle A$, then $\angle MNK = 180^{\circ} - \angle KNB = \angle KCB = \angle MLK$ (we used the fact that points $K, N, B$ and $C$ lie on the same circle, as well as the fact that $ML$ is parallel to $BC$). Therefore, $M, L, N$ and $K$ lie on the same circle. Further, $\angle LMK = \angle PMB + \angle NMK = \frac{1}{2} \angle B + \angle BMK = \frac{1}{2} \angle B + \angle A$. If $O$ is the center of the circle circumscribed around $\triangle LMK$, then

$\angle LOK = 2 \angle LMK = \angle B + 2 \angle A = 180^{\circ} - \angle C + \angle A = 180^{\circ} -$

$- \angle LPK \left(\angle LPK = \angle APK - \angle APL = 180^{\circ} - 2 \angle A - \angle B = \angle C - \angle A\right)$,

i.e., $O$ lies on the circle passing through $L, P$ and $K$, and this is the nine-point circle.

question: 166. Let $H$ be the orthocenter of a triangle, and $F$ be an arbitrary point on the circumcircle. Prove that the Simson line corresponding to point $F$ passes through one of the points of intersection of the line $F H$ with the nine-point circle (see problems II. 153, II. 159).
reference_solution:
166. Since the midpoint of $F H$ lies on the nine-point circle (see problem II.160), it is sufficient to show that the Simson line corresponding to point $F$ also bisects $F H$. Let $K$ be the projection of $F$ onto some side of the triangle, $D$ the foot of the altitude drawn to the same side, $H_{1}$ the intersection of this altitude with the circumcircle, $\left|H_{1} D\right|=|H D|$ (see problem II.107, solution), $L$ the intersection of the Simson line with the same altitude, and finally, $M$ a point on the line $H H_{1}$ such that $F M \| K D$; then $\triangle F M H_{1}=\triangle K D L$ ( $|F M|=|K D|$ ), both are right triangles and $\angle D L K=\angle M H_{1} F$, since the altitude of the triangle is the Simson line corresponding to the vertex from which it is drawn, and we can use the statement of problem II.154. It is also not difficult to show that the directions of $\overrightarrow{H_{1} M}$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_35c23d544adcc44dca41g-147.jpg?height=384&width=462&top_left_y=535&top_left_x=121)

Fig. 32 and $\overrightarrow{D L}$ coincide, i.e., $F K H L-$ is a parallelogram, from which our statement follows.

question: 167. Let $l$ be an arbitrary line passing through the center of the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$, and let $A_1$, $B_1$, and $C_1$ be the projections of $A$, $B$, and $C$ onto $l$. Draw a line through $A_1$ perpendicular to $BC$, a line through $B_1$ perpendicular to $AC$, and a line through $C_1$ perpendicular to $AB$. Prove that these three lines intersect at a single point located on the nine-point circle of triangle $ABC$.
reference_solution: 167. In Fig. $32 O$ is the center of the circumscribed circle, $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ are the midpoints of the sides, $L$ and $K$ are the projections of $A$ and $B$ onto $l$, $M$ is the intersection point of the lines passing through $L$ and $K$ perpendicular to $BC$ and $CA$. The triangle $ABC$, for definiteness, is an acute-angled triangle. First, we will prove that $C_{1}$ is the center of the circle circumscribed around $\triangle KLM$. Points $A_{1}, O, K, C_{1}, B$ lie on the same circle. Therefore, $\angle C_{1} K L=\angle O A_{1} C_{1}=90^{\circ}-\angle C$, similarly $\angle C_{1} L K=90^{\circ}-$ - $\angle C$. Thus, $\left|K C_{1}\right|=\left|C_{1} L\right|, \angle L C_{1} K=2 \angle C$, and since $\angle K M L=$ $=\angle C$, our statement is proved. Further, $K M$ is perpendicular to $A_{1} C_{1}$, $\left|K C_{1}\right|=\left|C_{1} M\right|$, hence $\angle C_{1} M A_{1}=\angle C_{1} K A_{1}=180^{\circ}-\angle B$, that is, $M$ lies on the circle circumscribed around $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$.

question: 168. Given a triangle $A B C ; A A_{1}, B B_{1}$ and $C C_{1}$ are its altitudes. Prove that the Euler lines of triangles $A B_{1} C_{1}, A_{1} B C_{1}$, $A_{1} B_{1} C$ intersect at a point $P$ on the nine-point circle, such that one of the segments $P A, P B, P C$ is equal to the sum of the other two segments (Victor Tebo).
reference_solution:
168. Let $H$ be the orthocenter of triangle $ABC$, and let $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ be the midpoints of segments $AH, BH, CH$. Note that triangles $AB_{1}C_{1}, A_{1}BC_{1}, A_{1}B_{1}C$ are similar to each other (corresponding vertices are denoted by the same letters), and $A_{2}, B_{2}$, and $C_{2}$ are the centers of the circumcircles of these triangles. First, let's prove the following statement: three lines passing through points $A_{2}, B_{2}$, and $C_{2}$ and equally positioned relative to triangles $AB_{1}C_{1}, A_{1}BC_{1}, A_{1}B_{1}C$ intersect at one point on the nine-point circle. Note that lines $A_{2}B_{1}, B_{2}B$, and $C_{2}B_{1}$ are equally positioned relative to triangles $AB_{1}C_{1}, A_{1}BC_{1}$, and $A_{1}B_{1}C$ and intersect at point $B_{1}$, which lies on the nine-point circle. Since points $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ lie on the nine-point circle, it is obvious that three lines obtained from lines $A_{2}B_{1}, B_{2}B$, and $C_{2}B_{1}$ by rotating them by the same angle around points $A_{2}, B_{2}$, and $C_{2}$ respectively, will also intersect at one point located on the nine-point circle. Let $P$ be the intersection point of the Euler lines of triangles $AB_{1}C_{1}, A_{1}BC_{1}, A_{1}B_{1}C$. Denote: $\angle PA_{2}A=\varphi$. For convenience, we will assume that triangle $ABC$ is acute-angled, and point $P$ lies on the arc $B_{1}A_{2}$ of the nine-point circle (Fig. 33). Then $\angle PA_{2}A_{1}=180^{\circ}-\varphi, \quad \angle PA_{2}B_{1}=180^{\circ}-\varphi-\angle B_{1}A_{2}A_{1}=180^{\circ}-\varphi-\angle B_{1}C_{1}A_{1}=2\angle C-\varphi, \quad \angle PA_{2}C_{1}=180^{\circ}-\varphi+180^{\circ}-2\angle B=360^{\circ}-\varphi-2\angle B$. Since the chords $PA_{1}, PB_{1}$, and $PC_{1}$ are proportional to the sines of the angles subtended by them, it remains to prove that one of the three quantities $\sin \varphi, \sin (2C-\varphi), -\sin (2B+\varphi)$ (in our case, the first one) is equal to the sum of the other two, i.e., $\sin \varphi = \sin (2C-\varphi) - \sin (2B+\varphi)$. But in triangle $AA_{2}H_{1}: |AA_{2}|=R$, $|AH_{1}|=2R \cos A$ (where $R$ is the circumradius, and $R \cos A$ is the distance from the center of the circumcircle $A_{2}$ to $B_{1}C_{1}$), $\angle H_{1}AA_{2}=\angle A + 2\angle B - 180^{\circ}$. By the Law of Sines for $\triangle AA_{2}H_{1}: \frac{2 \cos A}{\sin \varphi} = \frac{1}{\sin (2B+A+\varphi)} \Rightarrow -\sin (2B+2A+\varphi) - \sin (2B+\varphi) = \sin \varphi \Rightarrow \sin (2C-\varphi) - \sin (2B+\varphi) = \sin \varphi$, which is what we needed to prove. Thus, the statement is proved for the case of an acute-angled triangle. The case of an obtuse-angled $\triangle ABC$ is considered in the same way.

question: 169. Prove that three circles, each passing through a vertex of a triangle, the foot of the altitude dropped from this vertex, and tangent to the radius of the circumcircle of the triangle drawn to this vertex, intersect at two points located on the Euler line of the given triangle.
reference_solution: 169. Let $A B C$ be a given triangle, and $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ the midpoints of the corresponding sides. Prove that the circle passing through vertex $A$ and satisfying the condition of the problem passes through the points of intersection of the internal and external bisectors of angle $A$ with the midline $B_{1} C_{1}$. Therefore, for all points $M$ on this circle, the equality $\left|B_{1} M\right|:\left|C_{1} M\right|=\left|B_{1} A\right|:\left|C_{1} A\right|=b: a$ holds (see problem II.9). Thus, if $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ are the points of intersection of two such circles, then $\left|A_{1} M_{1}\right|:\left|B_{1} M_{1}\right|:\left|C_{1} M_{1}\right|=a: b: c$ (the same for point $M_{2}$), so $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ will belong to the third circle. Moreover, $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ belong to a line for all points $M$ on which the equality $\left(c^{2}-b^{2}\right)\left|A_{1} M\right|^{2}+\left(a^{2}-c^{2}\right)\left|B_{1} M\right|^{2}+$ $+\left(b^{2}-a^{2}\right)\left|C_{1} M\right|^{2}=0$ holds (see problem II.14 and its solution). This line passes through the center of the circumcircle of $\triangle A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ and through the point of intersection of its medians (verify this by expressing the lengths of the medians in terms of the sides), i.e., it coincides with the Euler line of $\triangle A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$, and thus of $\triangle A B C$.

question: 170. Consider three circles, each passing through one vertex of a triangle and the bases of the two angle bisectors - internal and external, emanating from this vertex (these circles are known as Apollonian circles). Prove that: a) these three circles intersect at two points ($M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$); b) the line $M_{1} M_{2}$ passes through the center of the circle circumscribed around the given triangle; c) the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from points $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ to the sides of the triangle serve as the vertices of two equilateral triangles.
reference_solution:
170. a) Similarly to how it was done in the previous problem, it can be proven that these three circles intersect at two points $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$, and that $\left|A M_{1}\right|:\left|B M_{1}\right|:\left|C M_{1}\right|=b c: a c: a b$ (also for $\left.M_{2}\right)$.

b) Follows from a) and problem II.14.

c) Prove that if $M$ is inside $\triangle A B C$, then $\angle A M_{1} C=60^{\circ}+\angle B$, $\angle B M_{1} A=60^{\circ}+\angle C, \angle C M_{1} B=60^{\circ}+\angle B$ (Bretschneider's theorem - problem II.236 can be used for this).

question: 171. A line symmetric to the median of a triangle with respect to the bisector of the same angle is called a symmedian. Let the symmedian from vertex $B$ of triangle $A B C$ intersect $A C$ at point $K$. Prove that $|A K|:|K C| = |A B|^{2}:|B C|^{2}$.
reference_solution: 171. Let's take point $A_{1}$ on $BC$ and point $C_{1}$ on $BA$ such that $\left|B A_{1}\right| = |B A|$, $\left|B C_{1}\right| = |B C|$ (triangle $\triangle A_{1} B C_{1}$ is symmetric to $\triangle A B C$ with respect to the bisector of angle $B$). Clearly, $B K$ bisects $A_{1} C_{1}$. We construct two parallelograms $B A_{1} M C_{1}$ and $B C N D$ (corresponding sides of the parallelograms are parallel, points $B, K, M$ and $N$ lie on the same line); $|C N| = \left|A A_{1}\right| \frac{|B C|}{\left|B A_{1}\right|} = \frac{|B C|^{2}}{|B A|}$, therefore, $\frac{|A K|}{|K C|} = \frac{|A B|}{|C N|} = \frac{|A B|^{2}}{|B C|^{2}}$.

question: 172. Let $D$ be an arbitrary point on side $BC$, and let $E$ and $F$ be points on $AC$ and $AB$ such that $DE$ is parallel to $AB$, and $DF$ is parallel to $AC$. The circle passing through $D$, $E$, and $F$ intersects $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ again at points $D_{1}$, $E_{1}$, and $F_{1}$, respectively. Let $M$ and $N$ be the points of intersection of $DE$ and $F_{1}D_{1}$, and $DF$ and $D_{1}E_{1}$. Prove that $M$ and $N$ lie on the symmedian from vertex $A$. Furthermore, if $D$ coincides with the foot of the symmedian, then the circle passing through $D$, $E$, and $F$ is tangent to side $BC$. (This circle is called the Tucker circle.)
reference_solution:
172. We have (Fig. 34) $\angle F E_{1} A = \angle E D F = \angle A$; therefore, $|A F| = |E_{1} F|, \quad \angle F E_{1} N = \angle F D B = \angle C, \quad \angle E_{1} F N = \angle A. \quad$ Consequently, $\triangle E_{1} F N$ is similar to $\triangle A B C, \frac{|A F|}{|F N|} = \frac{|E_{1} F|}{|F N|} = \frac{|A C|}{|A B|}, \quad \angle A F N = 180^{\circ} - \angle A$. Now we can show that $A N$ is the symmedian. For this, we consider the parallelogram $A C A_{1} B ; A A_{1}$ bisects $B C, \triangle A C A_{1}$ is similar to $\triangle A F N$, hence $\angle N A F = \angle A_{1} A C$.
