reference_solution: 290. Using the formulas of problems II.193, II.194, II.289 (see the solution of the last problem), we find $\frac{\left|F_{b} F_{c}\right|}{\left|B_{1} C_{1}\right|}=\frac{(a+b)(b+c)(c+a) R^{3}}{a b c \cdot\left|O I_{a}\right| \cdot\left|O I_{b}\right| \cdot\left|O I_{c}\right|}$. The ratios of the other corresponding sides of triangles $F_{a} F_{b} F_{c}$ and $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ will be the same. Similarly, the similarity of other pairs of triangles is proved. For the quantities $\left|A_{1} B_{2}\right|$ and others, formulas analogous to the formula of problem II.194 should be obtained.

question: 291. On the sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ of triangle $ABC$, squares $BCDE$, $ACFG$, and $BAHK$ are constructed outwardly. Let $FCDQ$ and $EBKP$ be parallelograms. Prove that triangle $APQ$ is an isosceles right triangle.
reference_solution:
291. Prove that $\triangle A B P = \triangle A C Q$. For this, it is sufficient to prove that $\triangle K B P = \triangle A B C$ and $\triangle F C Q = \triangle A B C$ (by two sides and the angle between them): $\angle Q A P = \angle C A B + \angle C A Q + \angle B A P = \angle C A B + \angle C A Q + \angle C Q A = \angle C A B + 180^{\circ} - \angle Q C A = \angle C A B + 90^{\circ} - \angle Q C F = 90^{\circ}$
(it was assumed that $\angle C A B \leqslant 90^{\circ}$; the reasoning in the case $\angle C A B > 90^{\circ}$ is analogous).

question: 292. Let $A B C D$ be a rectangle, $E$ a point on $B C$, $F$ on $D C$, $E_{1}$ the midpoint of $A E$, and $F_{1}$ the midpoint of $A F$. Prove that if $\triangle A E F$ is equilateral, then the triangles $D E_{1} C$ and $B F_{1} C$ are also equilateral.
reference_solution: 292. Since $\angle F E_{1} E=\angle F C E=90^{\circ}$, the quadrilateral $F E_{1} E C$ is cyclic, $\angle F C E_{1}=\angle F E E_{1}=60^{\circ}$. Similarly, the quadrilateral $F E_{1} A D$ is cyclic and $\angle E_{1} D F=\angle E_{1} A F=60^{\circ}$, i.e., $\triangle D E_{1} C$ is equilateral. In the same way, it can be proved that $\triangle B F_{1} C$ is also equilateral.

question: 293. On the legs $AC$ and $BC$ of a right triangle, squares $ACKL$ and $BCMN$ are constructed outward. Prove that the quadrilateral bounded by the legs and the lines $LB$ and $NA$ is equal in area to the triangle formed by the lines $LB$, $NA$, and the hypotenuse $AB$.
reference_solution: 293. Let $P, Q$, and $R$ be the points of intersection of $L B$ and $A C$, $A N$ and $B C$, $L B$ and $A N$, respectively. Let $|B C|=a,|A C|=b$. It is sufficient to show that $S_{A C Q}=S_{A P B}$ (both these areas differ from the considered ones by the addition of the area of $\triangle A P R$). From the similarity of the corresponding triangles, we get $|C Q|=|P C|=\frac{a b}{a+b}$. Therefore, $S_{A C Q}=$ $=\frac{1}{2}|A C||C Q|=\frac{a b^{2}}{2(a+b)}, \quad S_{A P B}=S_{A C B}-S_{P C B}=\frac{1}{2} a b-\frac{a^{2} b}{2(a+b)}=$ $=\frac{a b^{2}}{2(a+b)}$.

question: 295. Prove that if the centers of squares constructed on the sides of a given triangle outwardly serve as the vertices of a triangle, the area of which is twice the area of the given one, then the centers of the squares constructed on the sides of the triangle inwardly lie on one straight line.
reference_solution:
295. Let: $\angle A_{1} B C=\alpha, \angle A_{1} C B=\beta$; then $A A_{1}$ divides $B C$ in the ratio equal to

$$
\frac{S_{A B A_{1}}}{S_{A C A_{1}}}=\frac{\frac{1}{2}|A B| \cdot\left|B A_{1}\right| \sin (\angle B+\alpha)}{\frac{1}{2}|A C| \cdot\left|C A_{1}\right| \sin (\angle C+\beta)}=
$$

$=\frac{c}{b} \frac{\sin \beta}{\sin \alpha} \frac{\sin (\angle B+\alpha)}{\sin (\angle C+\beta)}$. Performing the same calculations for the other sides of triangle $A B C$, use Ceva's theorem (problem II.44).

question: 297. Let $A B C$ be an isosceles triangle $(|A B| = |B C|)$; $B D$ is its height. A circle of radius $B D$ rolls along the line $A C$. Prove that while the vertex $B$ is inside the circle, the arc of the circle located inside the triangle has a constant length.
reference_solution:
297. Let $K L$ be an arc of a circle located inside triangle $A B C$. Extending sides $A B$ and $B C$ beyond point $B$, we obtain arc

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_35c23d544adcc44dca41g-183.jpg?height=421&width=463&top_left_y=1320&top_left_x=134)

Fig. 54 $M N$, which is symmetric to arc $K L$ with respect to the diameter parallel to $A C$. Since $\angle B$ is measured by an arc equal to $\frac{1}{2}(\cup K L + \cup M N) = \cup K L$, the arc $K L$ has a constant length and corresponds to a central angle equal to angle $B$.

question: 298. Two points move along two intersecting straight lines with equal speeds. Prove that there exists a fixed point in the plane that is equidistant from them at all times.
reference_solution: 298. Let $O$ (Fig. 54) - the point of intersection of the lines, $A$ and $A_{1}$ - two positions of a point on one line, $B$ and $B_{1}$ - positions of another point at the same moments in time. Construct perpendiculars to $A B$ and $A_{1} B_{1}$ at their midpoints and denote their point of intersection by $M$; $\triangle A A_{1} M = \triangle B B_{1} M$ by three sides - one is obtained from the other by a rotation through the angle $A O B$ with center $M$. During this rotation, any position of a point on $A O$ comes to the corresponding position of a point on $O B$, so $M$ has the required property.

question: 299. Two cyclists are riding along two intersecting circles. Each is riding along their own circle at a constant speed. Starting simultaneously from one point where the circles intersect and completing one revolution, the cyclists meet again at this point. Prove that there exists a fixed point such that the distances from this point to the cyclists are always equal if they are riding: a) in the same direction (clockwise); b) in opposite directions.
reference_solution:
299. a) Let $A$ and $B$ be the points of intersection of the circles, $A$ be the point from which the cyclists started, and $M$ and $N$ be the positions of the cyclists at some moment in time. If $M$ and $N$ are on the same side of $AB$, then $\angle ABM = \angle ABN$. If they are on opposite sides, then $\angle ABM + \angle ABN = 180^\circ$, i.e., points $B$, $M$, and $N$ lie on the same straight line. If $L$ and $K$ are the points on the circles diametrically opposite to $B$ (with $L$ and $K$ fixed), then since $\angle LNM = \angle NMK = 90^\circ$, the midpoint of $LK$—point $P$—will be equidistant from $N$ and $M$. One can verify that $P$ is symmetric to point $B$ with respect to the midpoint of the segment connecting the centers of the circles (Fig. 55, a).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_35c23d544adcc44dca41g-184.jpg?height=304&width=415&top_left_y=640&top_left_x=183)

a

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_35c23d544adcc44dca41g-184.jpg?height=307&width=415&top_left_y=671&top_left_x=653)

$\delta$

Fig. 55

b) Let $O_1$ and $O_2$ be the centers of the circles. Take a point $A_1$ such that $O_1 A O_2 A_1$ is a parallelogram. It is easy to see that $\triangle M O_1 A_1 = \triangle N O_2 A_1$, since $|MO_1| = |O_1 A| = |O_2 A_1|$, $|O_1 A_1| = |O_2 A| = |NO_2|$, and $\angle MO_1 A_1 = \varphi + \angle AO_1 A_1 = \varphi + \angle AO_2 A_1 = \angle NO_2 A_1$, where $\varphi$ is the angle corresponding to the arcs traveled by the cyclists (Fig. 55, b). Thus, the desired points are symmetric to the points of intersection of the circles with respect to the midpoint of the segment $O_1 O_2$. Note. In part a), the same approach could have been used as in part b). Specifically, by taking point $P$ such that $\triangle O_1 P O_2 = \triangle O_1 A O_2$ (with $A$ and $P$ on the same side of $O_1 O_2$ and not coinciding), the equality of the corresponding triangles can be easily proven.

question: 300. Prove that: a) a rotation around point $O$ by an angle $\alpha$ is equivalent to the sequential application of two axial symmetries, the axes of which pass through point $O$, and the angle between the axes is $\alpha / 2$; a parallel translation is equivalent to two axial symmetries with parallel axes; b) two consecutive rotations around point $O_{1}$ by an angle $\alpha$ and around point $O_{2}$ by an angle $\beta$ ( $0 \leqslant \alpha<2 \pi, 0 \leqslant \beta<2 \pi$, the rotations are made in the same direction) are equivalent to a single rotation by an angle $\alpha+\beta$ around some point $O$, if $\alpha+\beta \neq 2 \pi$. Find the angles of triangle $O_{1} O_{2} O$.
reference_solution: 300. b) Use the result from part a). Replace the rotation around $O_{1}$ with two axial symmetries, taking the line $O_{1} O_{2}$ as the axis of the second symmetry, and the rotation around point $O_{2}$ with two symmetries, taking the line $O_{1} O_{2}$ as the axis of the first symmetry. Remark. If $\alpha+\beta=2 \pi$, then the sequential application of these rotations, as is easy to verify, is equivalent to a parallel translation. Answer: if $\alpha+\beta=2 \pi$, then the angles are $\pi-\frac{\alpha}{2}, \pi-\frac{\beta}{2}, \frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}$.

question: 301. Given an arbitrary triangle $A B C$. On its sides as bases, three isosceles triangles $A K B, B L C, C M A$ are constructed with angles at the vertices $K, L$, and $M$ equal to $\alpha, \beta$, and $\gamma$, respectively, where $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 2 \pi$. Moreover, all three triangles are either outside triangle $A B C$ or inside it. Prove that the angles of triangle $K L M$ are $\alpha / 2, \beta / 2, \gamma / 2$.
reference_solution:
301. Let us perform three consecutive rotations in the same direction around points $K, L$ and $M$ (or around $K_{1}, L_{1}$ and $M_{1}$) by angles $\alpha, \beta$ and $\gamma$. Since $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=2 \pi$, the resulting transformation is a parallel translation (see problem II.300). But since one of the vertices of the original triangle remains fixed, all points of the plane must remain fixed.

Thus, the center of the third rotation (point $M$) must coincide with the center of the rotation obtained by the consecutive application of the first two: around points $K$ and $L$. Now we can use the result of problem II. 300.

question: 302. Let $A B C D E F$ be an inscribed hexagon, in which $|A B|=|C D|=|E F|=R$, where $R$ is the radius of the circle, and $O$ is its center. Prove that the points of pairwise intersections of the circumcircles of triangles ВОС, DOE, FOA, distinct from $O$, are the vertices of an equilateral triangle with side $R$.
reference_solution: 302. Let's denote: $\angle B O C=2 \alpha, \angle D O E=2 \beta, \angle F O A=2 \gamma$. Let $K$, $M$, and $L$ be the points of intersection of the circumcircles of triangles $B O C$ and $A O F$, $B O C$ and $D O E$, $A O F$ and $D O E$. Point $K$ is inside triangle $A O B$, and $\angle B K O=180^{\circ}-\angle B C O=90^{\circ}+\alpha$, $\angle A K O=90^{\circ}+\gamma$, and since $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=90^{\circ}, \angle A K B=90^{\circ}+\beta$. Similarly, $L$ is inside triangle $F O E$ and $\angle O L F=90^{\circ}+\gamma, \angle O L E=90^{\circ}+\beta, \angle F L E=90^{\circ}+\alpha$. Therefore, $|O L|=|A K|, \angle K O L=2 \gamma+\angle K O A+\angle L O F=2 \gamma+\angle K O A+\angle K A O=90^{\circ}+\gamma=\angle A K O$; thus, triangles $K O L$ and $A K O$ are congruent, i.e., $|K L|=|A O|=R$. Similarly, it can be proven that the other two sides of triangle $K L M$ are also equal to $R$.

question: 303. On the sides of a convex quadrilateral, rhombi are constructed outwardly, with each having an acute angle of $\alpha$. Moreover, the angles of two rhombi adjacent to one vertex of the quadrilateral are equal. Prove that the segments connecting the centers of opposite rhombi are equal, and the acute angle between these segments is $\alpha$.
reference_solution: 303. Notations: $A B C D$ - the given quadrilateral, $O_{1}, O_{2}, O_{3}$, $O_{4}$ - the centers of rhombuses constructed respectively on $A B, B C, C D, D A$; $K$ and $L$ - midpoints of sides $A B$ and $B C, M$ - midpoint of diagonal $A C$. Triangles $O_{1} K M$ and $O_{2} L M$ are equal $\left(\left|O_{1} K\right|=\frac{1}{2}|A B|=|L M|,|K M|=\right.$ $\left.=\frac{1}{2}|B C|=\left|O_{2} L\right|, \angle O_{1} K M=\angle O_{2} L M\right)$. In this case, if $\angle A B C+\alpha\pi$, then these triangles are outside triangle $O_{1} M O_{2}$ (angles of rhombuses with vertex $B$ are equal to $\alpha$). Thus, $\left|O_{1} M\right|=\left|O_{2} M\right|, \angle O_{1} M O_{2}=\pi-\alpha$. Similarly, $\left|O_{3} M\right|=\left|O_{4} M\right|$, $\angle O_{3} M O_{4}=\pi-\alpha$. Therefore, triangles $O_{1} M O_{3}$ and $O_{2} M O_{4}$ are equal, and one is obtained from the other by a rotation around $M$ by an angle $\pi-\alpha$. This leads to the statement of the problem.

question: 304. Given an arbitrary triangle. On its sides, equilateral triangles are constructed outward, the centers of which serve as the vertices of triangle $\Delta$. The centers of the equilateral triangles constructed on the sides of the original triangle inward serve as the vertices of another triangle $\delta$. Prove that: a) triangles $\Delta$ and $\delta$ are equilateral; b) the centers of triangles $\Delta$ and $\delta$ coincide with the centroid of the original; c) the difference in the areas of triangles $\Delta$ and $\delta$ is equal to the area of the original.
reference_solution:
304. Let $ABC$ be a given triangle, $A_1B_1C_1$ be triangle $\Delta$, and $A_2B_2C_2$ be triangle $\delta$ (where $A_1$ and $A_2$ are the centers of triangles constructed on $BC$), and the sides of triangle $ABC$ are, as usual, $a, b, c$.

a) The fact that triangles $A_1B_1C_1$ and $A_2B_2C_2$ are equilateral follows, for example, from the result of problem II. 301.

b) Let's prove a more general statement. If on the sides of $\triangle ABC$ similar triangles $A_1BC, B_1CA, C_1AB$ are constructed outward (or inward) such that $\angle A_1BC = \angle B_1CA = \angle C_1AB$ and $\angle A_1CB = \angle B_1AC = \angle C_1BA$, then the points of intersection of the medians of triangles $ABC$ and $A_1B_1C_1$ coincide. Note first that if $M$ is the point of intersection of the medians of $\triangle ABC$, then $\overrightarrow{MA} + \overrightarrow{MB} + \overrightarrow{MC} = 0$, and conversely, if this equality holds, then $M$ is the point of intersection of the medians of $\triangle ABC$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_35c23d544adcc44dca41g-185.jpg?height=48&width=979&top_left_y=1736&top_left_x=136)
$+\left(\overrightarrow{MB} + \overrightarrow{BA_1}\right) + \left(\overrightarrow{MC} + \overrightarrow{CB_1}\right) = 0$. But $\overrightarrow{MA} + \overrightarrow{MB} + \overrightarrow{MC} = 0$. Moreover, $\overrightarrow{AC_1} + \overrightarrow{BA_1} + \overrightarrow{CB_1} = 0$, since each of the vectors $\overrightarrow{AC_1}, \overrightarrow{BA_1}, \overrightarrow{CB_1}$ is obtained from $\overrightarrow{AB}, \overrightarrow{BC}, \overrightarrow{CA}$ by a rotation by the same angle ($\angle A_1BC$) and multiplication by the same number.

c) Consider a more general case. On the sides of $\triangle ABC$ outside and inside it, isosceles triangles $A_1BC, B_1CA, C_1BA$ and $A_1'BC, B_1'CA, C_1'BA$ are constructed with the ratio of the height dropped to the base to the length of the base equal to $k$. Let $O$ be the center of the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$, $a, b, c$ be its sides, and $A_0, B_0, C_0$ be the midpoints of $BC, CA, AB$, respectively. For definiteness, assume that $\triangle ABC$ is an acute triangle. Then $S_{A_1OC_1} = \frac{1}{2} |A_1O| \cdot |C_1O| \sin B = \frac{1}{2} (|OA_0| + ka)(|OC_0| + kc) \sin B = \frac{1}{2} |OA_0| \cdot |OC_0| \sin B + \frac{1}{2} k^2 ac \sin B + \frac{k}{2} (a|OC_0| + c|OA_0|) \sin B = k^2 S_{ABC} + S_{A_0OC_0} + \frac{k}{4} b^2$. By obtaining similar relations for triangles $A_1OB_1$ and $B_1OC_1$ and summing them, we find: $S_{A_1B_1C_1} = (3k^2 + \frac{1}{4}) S_{ABC} + \frac{k}{4} (a^2 + b^2 + c^2)$ (this equality remains valid if $\triangle ABC$ is obtuse). For $\triangle A_1'B_1'C_1'$, we will have: $S_{A_1'B_1'C_1'} = \left| \frac{k}{4} (a^2 + b^2 + c^2) - (3k^2 + \frac{1}{4}) S_{ABC} \right|$. Therefore, if $\frac{k}{4} (a^2 + b^2 + c^2) - (3k^2 + \frac{1}{4}) S_{ABC} \geq 0$, then $S_{A_1B_1C_1} - S_{A_1'B_1'C_1'} = (6k^2 + \frac{1}{2}) S_{ABC}$, and if $\frac{k}{4} (a^2 + b^2 + c^2) - (3k^2 + \frac{1}{4}) S_{ABC} < 0$, then $S_{A_1B_1C_1} - S_{A_1'B_1'C_1'} = \frac{k}{2} (a^2 + b^2 + c^2)$. It can be proven that always $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 \geq 4\sqrt{3} S_{ABC}$ (in problem II. 362, a stronger inequality is proven), which means that for $k = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}$, the difference in the areas of triangles $A_1B_1C_1$ and $A_1'B_1'C_1'$ is $S_{ABC}^2$.

question:
306. Given a triangle $A B C$. On the line passing through vertex $A$ and perpendicular to side $B C$, two points $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$ are taken such that $\left|A A_{1}\right|=\left|A A_{2}\right|=|B C|$ ($A_{1}$ is closer to the line $B C$ than $A_{2}$). Similarly, on the line perpendicular to $A C$ and passing through $B$, points $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$ are taken such that $\left|B B_{1}\right|=\left|B B_{2}\right|=$ $=|A C|$. Prove that the segments $A_{1} B_{2}$ and $A_{2} B_{1}$ are equal and mutually perpendicular.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_35c23d544adcc44dca41g-076.jpg?height=81&width=126&top_left_y=520&top_left_x=551)
reference_solution: 306. We will prove that triangles $C B_{1} A_{2}$ and $C A_{1} B_{2}$ are obtained from each other by a rotation about point $C$ by an angle of $90^{\circ}$. Indeed, $\triangle C A A_{1}=\triangle C B B_{1}\left(\left|B B_{1}\right|=|A C|,|B C|=\left|A A_{1}\right|, \angle C B B_{1}=\angle C A A_{1}\right)$, and since $A A_{1} \perp B C$ and $B B_{1} \perp A C$, then $B_{1} C \perp A_{1} C$. Similarly, $A_{2} C$ and $B_{2} C$ are equal and perpendicular.

question: 307. Prove that a circumscribed polygon, all sides of which are equal, is regular if the number of sides is odd.
reference_solution: 307. Prove that the tangents to the circle, drawn from the vertices between which one vertex of the polygon is located, are equal. It follows from this that for a polygon with an odd number of sides, the points of tangency are the midpoints of the sides.

question: 309. Prove that the sum of the distances from an arbitrary point inside a convex polygon to its sides is constant if: a) all sides of the polygon are equal; b) all angles of the polygon are equal.
reference_solution:
309. a) If the side of a polygon is $a$, $S$ is its area, and $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ are the distances from some point inside it to the sides, then the statement of the problem follows from the equality $S=\left(a x_{1}+a x_{2}+\ldots+\right.$ $\left.+a x_{n}\right) / 2$.
b) Consider a regular polygon containing the given one inside it, whose sides are parallel to the sides of the given one. The sum of the distances from any point inside the given polygon to the sides of the regular one is constant (point a) and differs from the sum of the distances to the sides of the given one by a constant value.

question: 310. A semicircle is divided into $2 n+1$ equal arcs by points $A_{0}, A_{1}, \ldots, A_{2 n+1}$ ( $A_{0}$ and $A_{2 n+1}$ are the endpoints of the semicircle), $O$ is the center of the semicircle. Prove that the lines $A_{1} A_{2 n}$, $A_{2} A_{2 n-1}, \ldots, A_{n} A_{n+1}$ form segments with the lines $O A_{n}$ and $O A_{n+1}$, the sum of the lengths of which is equal to the radius of the circle.
reference_solution: 310. Let $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{n+1}$ be the points symmetric to $A_{1}$, $A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n+1}$ with respect to the diameter $A_{0} A_{2 n+1}, C_{k}$ and $C_{k}^{\prime}$ - the points of intersection of the line $A_{k} A_{2 n+1-k}$ with $O A_{n}$ and $O A_{n+1}$. Let $D_{k-1}$ and $D_{k}$ be the points of intersection of the lines $A_{k} B_{k-1}$ and $A_{k} B_{k+1}$ with the diameter. It is clear that these same points are the points of intersection of the diameter with the lines $B_{k} A_{k-1}$ and $B_{k} A_{k+1}$. It is clear that $\triangle D_{k-1} A_{k} D_{k}=\triangle C_{k} O C_{k}^{\prime}$. Thus, the sum of the segments $C_{k} C_{k}^{\prime}$ is equal to the sum of the segments $D_{k-1} D_{k}(k=1, \ldots, n), D_{0}=A_{0}$, $D_{n}=O$, i.e., it is equal to the radius.

question: 311. Prove that if perpendiculars are dropped from an arbitrary point on a circle to the sides of an inscribed $2 n$-gon, then the products of the lengths of these perpendiculars taken alternately will be equal.
reference_solution:
311. Let $A$ (Fig. 56) be a given point, $A_{k}$ be some vertex of a $2n$-gon, $B_{k-1}$ and $B_{k}$ be the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from $A$ to the sides containing $A_{k}$, $\alpha_{k}$ and $\beta_{k}$ be the angles formed by the line $A A_{k}$ with these sides $\left(\beta_{k}=\right.$ $\left.=\angle A A_{k} B_{k-1}, \quad \alpha_{k}=\angle A A_{k} B_{k}\right)$. Since a circle can be circumscribed around the quadrilateral $A B_{k-1} A_{k} B_{k}$, then $\angle A B_{k-1} B_{k}=\alpha_{k}, \angle A B_{k} B_{k-1}=$ $=\beta_{k}$ (or these angles are supplementary to $180^{\circ}$); thus, by the Law of Sines $\frac{\left|A B_{k-1}\right|}{\left|A B_{k}\right|}=\frac{\sin \beta_{k}}{\sin \alpha_{k}}, \frac{\left|A B_{k-1}\right|\left|A B_{k+1}\right|}{\left|A B_{k}\right|^{2}}=\frac{\sin \beta_{k} \sin \alpha_{k+1}}{\sin \alpha_{k} \sin \beta_{k+1}}$. Multiplying these equalities for $k=2,4, \ldots, 2 n$, and replacing the index $2 n+1$ with 1, we obtain the desired result.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_35c23d544adcc44dca41g-188.jpg?height=350&width=384&top_left_y=403&top_left_x=732)

Fig. 56

question: 312. Let $A_{1} A_{2} \ldots A_{n}$ be an inscribed polygon; the center of the circle is inside the polygon. A system of circles touches the given one from the inside at points $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}$, and one of the intersection points of two adjacent circles lies on the corresponding side of the polygon. Prove that if $n$ is odd, then all the circles have equal radii. The length of the outer boundary of the union of the inscribed circles is equal to the length of the given circle.
reference_solution: 312. Prove that if $O_{k}$ and $O_{k+1}$ are the centers of circles touching a given circle at points $A_{k}$ and $A_{k+1}, B$ is their intersection point lying on the chord $A_{k} A_{k+1}; r_{k}, r_{k+1}$ are their radii, then $r_{k}+r_{k+1}=r$, $\angle A_{k} O_{k} B=\angle A_{k+1} O_{k+1} B=\angle A_{k} O A_{k+1}$ ( $r$ is the radius of the given circle, $O$ is its center). From this, it follows that the radii are equal every other one, which for $n$ odd will result in all of them being $r / 2$. In addition, $\cup A_{k} B + \cup B A_{k+1} = \cup A_{k} A_{k+1}$ (the smaller arcs of the corresponding circles are taken).

question:
313. Consider a circle in which a regular $(2 n+1)$-gon $A_{1} A_{2} \ldots A_{2 n+1}$ is inscribed. Let $A$ be an arbitrary point on the arc $A_{1} A_{2 n+1}$.
a) Prove that the sum of the distances from $A$ to the vertices with even indices is equal to the sum of the distances from $A$ to the vertices with odd indices.

b) Construct equal circles that are tangent to the given circle at points $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{2 n+1}$. Prove that the sum of the tangents drawn from $A$ to the circles tangent to the given circle at the vertices with even indices is equal to the sum of the tangents drawn to the circles tangent to the given circle at the vertices with odd indices.
reference_solution:
313. a) Let $A$ be an arbitrary point on the circle ( $A$ is on the arc $A_{1} A_{2 n+1}$ ). Denote the side of the polygon by $a$, and the length of the diagonal connecting vertices through one, by $b$. By Ptolemy's theorem (problem II.237) for the quadrilateral $A A_{k} A_{k+1} A_{k+2}$ we have: $\left|A A_{k}\right| a + \left|A A_{k+2}\right| a = \left|A A_{k+1}\right| b (k=1,2, \ldots, 2 n-1)$. Similar relations can be written for the quadrilaterals $A_{2 n} A_{2 n+1} A A_{1}$ and $A_{2 n+1} A A_{1} A_{2}:$

$$
\begin{gathered}
\left|A A_{1}\right| a + \left|A A_{2 n+1}\right| b = \left|A A_{2 n}\right| a \\
\left|A A_{2 n+1}\right| a + \left|A A_{1}\right| b = \left|A A_{2}\right| a
\end{gathered}
$$

By adding all these equations, leaving the vertices with even numbers on the right and the odd ones on the left, we obtain the required statement.
b) Our statement follows from part a) and the result of problem I. 206. (A similar formula can be obtained in the case of internal tangency.)

question:
314. a) Two tangents are drawn to a given circle. Let $A$ and $B$ be the points of tangency, and $C$ be the point of intersection of the tangents. Draw an arbitrary line $l$ tangent to the given circle, not passing through $A$ and $B$. Let $u$ and $v$ be the distances from $A$ and $B$ to $l$, and $w$ be the distance from $C$ to $l$. Find $uv / w^2$ if $\angle ACB = \alpha$.

b) A polygon is circumscribed around a circle. Let $l$ be an arbitrary line tangent to the circle and not coinciding with any side of the polygon. Prove that the ratio of the product of the distances from the vertices of the polygon to $l$ to the product of the distances from the points of tangency of the sides of the polygon with the circle to $l$ does not depend on the position of the line $l$.

c) Let $A_1 A_2 \ldots A_{2n}$ be a $2n$-sided polygon circumscribed around a circle, and $l$ be an arbitrary tangent to the circle. Prove that the product of the distances from the vertices with odd indices to $l$ and the product of the distances from the vertices with even indices to $l$ are in a constant ratio, independent of $l$ (assuming that $l$ does not contain any vertices of the polygon).
reference_solution:
314. a) Let $l$ intersect $A C$ and $B C$ at points $K$ and $N$ respectively and touch the circle at point $M$ (Fig. 57). Denote:

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_35c23d544adcc44dca41g-189.jpg?height=300&width=434&top_left_y=305&top_left_x=131)

Fig. 57 $|A C|=|B C|=a,|A K|=|K M|=x$, $|B N|=|N M|=y$. Clearly, $\frac{w^{2}}{u v}=$ $=\frac{(a-x)(a-y)}{x y}$, but by the cosine theorem for $\triangle C K N$ the equality $(x+y)^{2}=(a-x)^{2}+(a-y)^{2}-$ $-2(a-x)(a-y) \cos \alpha \Rightarrow \sin ^{2} \frac{\alpha}{2}=$

$$
=\frac{x y}{(a-x)(a-y)}
$$

Thus, $\frac{u v}{w^{2}}=\sin ^{2} \frac{\alpha}{2}$. (Similarly, other cases of the position of the line $l$ are considered.)

b) Use the result from part a). Multiplying the corresponding equalities for all angles of the $n$-gon, we obtain the square of the desired ratio, and the ratio itself will be equal to $1 /\left(\sin \frac{\alpha_{1}}{2} \sin \frac{\alpha_{2}}{2} \ldots \sin \frac{\alpha_{n}}{2}\right)$, where $\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \ldots, \alpha_{n}$ are the angles of the polygon.

c) Use the result from part a). If we denote the points of tangency of the sides $A_{1} A_{2}, A_{2} A_{3}, \ldots, A_{2 n-1} A_{2 n}, A_{2 n} A_{1}$ with the circle as $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{2 n-1}, B_{2 n}$, and the distances from $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{2 n}$ to $l$ as $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{2 n-1}, x_{2 n}$, and the distances from $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{2 n}$ to $l$ as $y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{2 n}$, then we get:

$$
\frac{x_{1}^{2}}{y_{2 n} y_{1}}=\frac{1}{\sin ^{2} \frac{\alpha_{1}}{2}}, \frac{x_{2}^{2}}{y_{1} y_{2}}=\frac{1}{\sin ^{2} \frac{\alpha_{2}}{2}}, \ldots, \frac{x_{2 n}^{2}}{y_{2 n-1} y_{2 n}}=\frac{1}{\sin ^{2} \frac{\alpha_{2 n}}{2}}
$$

where $\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \ldots, \alpha_{2 n}$ are the angles of the polygon. Multiplying the equalities containing $x_{1}, x_{3}, \ldots, x_{2 n-1}$, and dividing by the product of the remaining equalities, we get:

$$
\left(\frac{x_{1} x_{3} \ldots x_{2 n-1}}{x_{2} x_{4} \ldots x_{2 n}}\right)^{2}=\left(\frac{\sin \frac{\alpha_{2}}{2} \sin \frac{\alpha_{4}}{2} \ldots \sin \frac{\alpha_{2 n}}{2}}{\sin \frac{\alpha_{1}}{2} \sin \frac{\alpha_{3}}{2} \ldots \sin \frac{\alpha_{2 n-1}}{2}}\right)^{2}
$$

question: 315. In a cyclic polygon, non-intersecting diagonals are drawn, dividing it into triangles. Prove that the sum of the radii of the circles inscribed in these triangles does not depend on how the diagonals are drawn.
reference_solution:
315. The statement of the problem can be proved by induction. The base case, $n=4$, is considered in problem II.235.

However, another approach can be suggested, based on the following equality. Let in triangle $ABC$ angle $A$ be the largest, $r$ and $R$ be the radii of the inscribed and circumscribed circles, respectively, and $d_{a}$, $d_{b}$, $d_{c}$ be the distances from the center of the circumscribed circle to the corresponding sides of the triangle. Then

$$
r+R=d_{a}+d_{b}+d_{c}
$$

for an acute triangle and

$$
r+R=-d_{a}+d_{b}+d_{c}
$$

for an obtuse triangle (for a right triangle, $d_{a}=0$ and either of the above relations holds).

Proof. Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle, $A_{0}, B_{0}, C_{0}$ be the midpoints of sides $BC, CA, AB$, respectively, and $O$ be the center of the circumscribed circle. By Ptolemy's theorem (problem II.237) for quadrilateral $AB_{0}OC_{0}$, we have: $\frac{b}{2} d_{c}+\frac{c}{2} d_{b}=\frac{a}{2} R$. Writing two more such relations for quadrilaterals $BC_{0}OA_{0}$ and $CB_{0}OA_{0}$ and adding them, we get:

$$
\left(\frac{a}{2}+\frac{b}{2}\right) d_{c}+\left(\frac{a}{2}+\frac{c}{2}\right) d_{b}+\left(\frac{b}{2}+\frac{c}{2}\right) d_{a}=\frac{1}{2}(a+b+c) R=p R
$$

from which $p\left(d_{a}+d_{b}+d_{c}\right)-\frac{1}{2}\left(c d_{c}+b d_{b}+a d_{a}\right)=p R$. Since $\frac{1}{2}\left(c d_{c}+b d_{b}+a d_{a}\right)=S=p r$, after canceling by $p$, we obtain equality (1). The case $\angle A>90^{\circ}$ is considered similarly.

From relations (1), (2), the statement of the problem follows. For this, write the corresponding equalities for all triangles of the partition. Note that each diagonal is a side for two triangles. Therefore, in the relations corresponding to these triangles, the distance to the chosen diagonal will enter with opposite signs. Thus, if we add all these equalities, we get, under the condition that the center of the circle is inside the polygon $\sum r+R=d_{1}+d_{2}+\ldots+d_{n}$, where $d_{1}, d_{2}, \ldots, d_{n}$ are the distances from the center of the circle to the sides of the polygon. If the center of the circle is outside the polygon, then the distance to the largest side must be taken with a negative sign.

question:
316. Let $A_{1} A_{2} \ldots A_{n}$ be a polygon with perimeter $2 p$, circumscribed around a circle of radius $r$, and let $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{n}$ be the points of tangency of the sides $A_{1} A_{2}, A_{2} A_{3}, \ldots, A_{n} A_{1}$ with the circle. Let $M$ be a point at a distance $d$ from the center of the circle. Prove that

$$
\begin{array}{r}
\left|M B_{1}\right|^{2} \cdot\left|A_{1} A_{2}\right|+\left|M B_{2}\right|^{2} \cdot\left|A_{2} A_{3}\right|+\ldots+\left|M B_{n}\right|^{2} \cdot\left|A_{n} A_{1}\right|= \\
\\
=2 p\left(r^{2}+d^{2}\right) .
\end{array}
$$
reference_solution:
316. Let's consider, for definiteness, the case when point $M$ is inside the polygon. Denote by $u$ and $v$ the distances from $M$ to $A_{1} A_{2}$ and $A_{1} A_{n}$, respectively, and by $x$ and $y$ the projections of $A_{1} M$ onto $A_{1} A_{2}$ and $A_{1} A_{n}$ (the values of $x$ and $y$ should be considered positive if these projections lie on the rays $A_{1} A_{2}$ and $A_{1} A_{n}$, and negative otherwise), $\left|A_{1} B_{1}\right|=\left|A_{1} B_{n}\right|=a$, $\angle A_{2} A_{1} A_{n}=\alpha$. We can express $u$ and $v$ in terms of $x$ and $y$: $u=\frac{y}{\sin \alpha}-x \frac{\cos \alpha}{\sin \alpha}$, $v=\frac{x}{\sin \alpha}-y \frac{\cos \alpha}{\sin \alpha} ; \quad$ from this $\quad u+v=(x+y) \frac{1-\cos \alpha}{\sin \alpha}=(x+y) \operatorname{tg} \frac{\alpha}{2}=$ $=(x+y) \frac{r}{a}$. Now we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(\left|M B_{1}\right|^{2}+\left|M B_{n}\right|^{2}\right) a=\left((x-a)^{2}+u^{2}+(y-a)^{2}+v^{2}\right) a= \\
& =\left((x-a)^{2}+(u-r)^{2}+(y-a)^{2}+(v-r)^{2}+2 r(u+v)-2 r^{2}\right) a= \\
& \quad=2 d^{2} a+2 r a(u+v)-2 r^{2} a=2 d^{2} a+2 r^{2}(x+y)-2 r^{2} a
\end{aligned}
$$

By writing similar equalities for each vertex and summing them, we obtain the statement of the problem.

question:
317. Let $A B C D$ be a cyclic quadrilateral, and $M$ be an arbitrary point on the circle. Prove that the projections of point $M$ onto the Simson lines (see problem II.153) corresponding to point $M$ relative to triangles $A B C, B C D, C D A$, and $D A B$, lie on one line (the Simson line of the quadrilateral).

Further, by induction, we define the Simson line of an $(n+1)$-gon through the Simson line of an $n$-gon. Specifically, for any inscribed $(n+1)$-gon and a point $M$ on the circle, the projections of this point onto all possible Simson lines of this point relative to all possible $n$-gons formed by $n$ vertices of this $(n+1)$-gon lie on one line - the Simson line of the $(n+1)$-gon.
reference_solution:
317. Consider three triangles - $A B C, A C D$ and $A D B$, having a common vertex $A$. Let $B_{1}, C_{1}$ and $D_{1}$ be the projections of $M$ onto $A B, A C$ and $A D$, respectively. The lines $B_{1} C_{1}, C_{1} D_{1}$ and $D_{1} B_{1}$ are the Simson lines of point $M$ with respect to triangles $A B C, A C D$ and $A D B$. However, points $A, M, B_{1}, C_{1}, D_{1}$ lie on the same circle (with $A M$ as its diameter). Therefore, the projections of point $M$ onto $B_{1} C_{1}, C_{1} D_{1}$ and $D_{1} B_{1}$ lie on the same line - the Simson line of point $M$ with respect to triangle $B_{1} C_{1} D_{1}$. By then considering the projections of the point onto the Simson lines corresponding to the three triangles with a common vertex $B$, we find that these three projections also lie on the same line, which means - all four projections lie on the same line.

The same process is used for the inductive step from $n$ to $n+1$.

question: 318. Inside the circle $\alpha$ there is a circle $\beta$. On the circle $\alpha$ there are two sequences of points: $A_{1}, A_{2}$, $A_{3} \ldots$ and $B_{1}, B_{2}, B_{3} \ldots$, following in the same direction, such that the lines $A_{1} A_{2}, A_{2} A_{3}, A_{3} A_{4} \ldots$ and $B_{1} B_{2}, B_{2} B_{3}, B_{3} B_{4} \ldots$ are tangent to the circle $\beta$. Prove that the lines $A_{1} B_{1}, A_{2} B_{2}$, $A_{3} B_{3} \ldots$ are tangent to one circle, the center of which lies on the line passing through the centers of the circles $\alpha$ and $\beta$.
reference_solution:
318. Let, for definiteness, $B_{1}$ be on the arc $A_{1} A_{2}$, bounding a segment that does not contain the circle $\beta$. Denote by $C_{1}, C_{2}, \ldots$ the points of tangency of $A_{1} A_{2}, A_{2} A_{3}, \ldots$ with the circle $\beta$, and by $D_{1}, D_{2}, \ldots$ the points of tangency of $B_{1} B_{2}, B_{2} B_{3}, \ldots$ with the same circle (Fig. 58). $K, L$ and $P$ are the points of intersection of $D_{1} C_{1}$ and $A_{1} B_{1}$, $D_{1} C_{1}$ and $A_{2} B_{2}$, $A_{1} B_{1}$ and $A_{2} B_{2}$, respectively.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_35c23d544adcc44dca41g-191.jpg?height=790&width=844&top_left_y=799&top_left_x=196)

Fig. 58

In triangles $A_{1} K C_{1}$ and $D_{1} L B_{2}$, we have: $\angle K C_{1} A_{1} = \angle L D_{1} B_{2}$, $\angle C_{1} A_{1} K = \angle D_{1} B_{2} L$; hence, $\angle C_{1} K A_{1} = \angle D_{1} L B_{2}$, i.e., $\triangle K P L$ is isosceles, $|K P| = |P L|$.

Consider the circle $\gamma$ that is tangent to $K P$ and $P L$ at points $K$ and $L$, respectively. The center of this circle lies on the line passing through the centers of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ (see problem II.12).

Let the line $D_{2} C_{2}$ intersect $A_{2} B_{2}$ and $A_{3} B_{3}$ at points $L^{\prime}$ and $M$, respectively. As in the previous case, we will prove that there exists a circle $\gamma^{\prime}$ with its center on the line passing through the centers of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ and tangent to $A_{2} B_{2}$ and $A_{3} B_{3}$ at points $L^{\prime}$ and $M$, respectively. We will prove that $\gamma$ and $\gamma^{\prime}$ coincide. For this, it is sufficient to prove that $L$ and $L^{\prime}$ coincide. We have: $\frac{|A_{2} L|}{|L B_{2}|} = \frac{S_{A_{2} C_{1} D_{1}}}{S_{B_{2} C_{1} D_{1}}} = \frac{\frac{1}{2}|D_{1} C_{1}| \cdot |A_{2} C_{1}| \sin \angle A_{2} C_{1} D_{1}}{\frac{1}{2}|D_{1} C_{1}| \cdot |B_{2} D_{1}| \sin \angle B_{2} D_{1} C_{1}} = \frac{|A_{2} C_{1}|}{|B_{2} D_{1}|}$. Similarly, $\frac{|A_{2} L^{\prime}|}{|L^{\prime} B_{2}|} = \frac{|A_{2} C_{2}|}{|B_{2} D_{2}|} = \frac{|A_{2} C_{1}|}{|B_{2} D_{1}|}$, i.e., $L$ and $L^{\prime}$ coincide. Note. From the reasoning, it follows that in the considered case, the points of tangency of $\gamma$ with the lines $A_{1} B_{1}, A_{2} B_{2}, \ldots$ lie within the segments $A_{1} B_{1}, A_{2} B_{2}, \ldots$.

question: 319. Using the result of the previous problem, prove the following statement (Poncelet's theorem). If there exists one $n$-gon inscribed in some circle $\alpha$ and circumscribed about another circle $\beta$, then there exist infinitely many $n$-gons inscribed in circle $\alpha$ and circumscribed about circle $\beta$, and one of the vertices of such an $n$-gon can be taken as any point on circle $\alpha$.
reference_solution: 319. In the notation of the previous problem, the statement reduces to the following: if $A_{n+1}$ coincides with $A_{1}$, then $B_{n+1}$ also coincides with $B_{1}$. Suppose this is not the case. Then $A_{1} B_{1}$ and $A_{1} B_{n+1}$ are tangent to the circle $\gamma$, $A_{1} A_{2}$ intersects $\gamma$, and $B_{1}$ and $B_{n+1}$ lie on the arc $A_{1} A_{2}$ corresponding to the segment not containing $\beta$. The points of tangency of $A_{1} B_{1}$ and $A_{1} B_{n+1}$ with $\gamma$ lie within the segments $A_{1} B_{1}$ and $A_{1} B_{n+1}$. This means that two tangents are drawn from $A_{1}$ to $\gamma$, and the points of tangency with $\gamma$ are on the same side of the secant $A_{1} A_{2}$. This is impossible.

question:
320. On the sides of an equilateral triangle $P Q R$, isosceles triangles $P X Q, Q Y R$, and $R Z P$ are constructed outward with respect to triangle $P Q R$, such that $\angle P X Q=\frac{1}{3}(\pi+2 \angle A), \angle Q Y R=\frac{1}{3}(\pi+2 \angle B)$, and $\angle R Z P=\frac{1}{3}(\pi+2 \angle C)$, where $A, B, C$ are the angles of some triangle $A B C$. Let $A_{0}$ be the intersection point of the lines $Z P$ and $Y Q$, $B_{0}$ be the intersection point of the lines $X Q$ and $Z R$, and $C_{0}$ be the intersection point of the lines $Y R$ and $X P$. Prove that the angles of triangle $A_{0} B_{0} C_{0}$ are equal to the corresponding angles of triangle $A B C$.

Using the obtained result, prove the following Morley's theorem: if the angles of any triangle are each divided into three equal parts (the resulting lines are called trisectors), then the three points of intersection of pairs of trisectors adjacent to the corresponding sides of the triangle are the vertices of an equilateral triangle.
reference_solution: 320. Consider $\triangle B_{0} X C_{0}$. The line $X R$ is the bisector of angle $C_{0} X B_{0}$. It is easy to verify that $\angle C_{0} R B_{0}=\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \angle C_{0} X B_{0}$. From this, it follows that $C_{0} R$ and $B_{0} R$ are the bisectors of angles $X C_{0} B_{0}$ and $X B_{0} C_{0}$ (see problem I.46). Similarly, in triangles $C_{0} Y A_{0}$ and $A_{0} Z B_{0}$, points $P$ and $Q$ are the points of intersection of the bisectors. Therefore, considering that $\angle P A_{0} Q=\angle A / 3, \angle Q B_{0} R=\angle B / 3, \angle R C_{0} P=\angle C / 3$, we obtain the statement from which Morley's theorem follows.

question: 322. At the beginning of the 19th century, the Italian geometer Malfatti posed the following problem: to cut three circles from a given triangle so that the sum of their areas is the largest. In later research, the Malfatti circles came to be understood as three circles that are pairwise tangent to each other, each of which also touches two sides of the given triangle. Prove that for an equilateral triangle, the Malfatti circles do not provide a solution to the original problem. (It was only in the mid-20th century that it was established that the Malfatti circles do not provide a solution to the original problem for any triangle.)
reference_solution: 322. For an equilateral triangle with side 1, the radius of each of the Malfatti circles is $\frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{4}$. The sum of the areas of the corresponding circles is $\frac{3 \pi(2-\sqrt{3})}{8}$. The sum of the areas of three circles, one of which is inscribed in this triangle, and the other two each touch the triangle and two of its sides, is $\frac{11 \pi}{108}>\frac{3 \pi(2-\sqrt{3})}{8}$.

question: 323. Prove that $p \geqslant \frac{3}{2} \sqrt{6 R r}$, where $p$ is the semiperimeter, and $r$ and $R$ are the radii of the inscribed and circumscribed circles of the triangle.
reference_solution: 323. Use the equality $R r=\frac{a b c}{4 p}$ and the inequality $2 p=$ $=a+b+c \geqslant 3 \sqrt[3]{a b c}$ (the theorem of means).

question: 324. Prove that the perimeter of the triangle, the vertices of which are the bases of the altitudes of a given acute-angled triangle, does not exceed half the perimeter of the given triangle.
reference_solution: 324. If $p_{1}$ is the semiperimeter of the triangle with vertices at the bases of the altitudes of a given triangle, and $p, S, r$, and $R$ are the semiperimeter, area, inradius, and circumradius of the given triangle, respectively, then $S = p r$ and, moreover, $S = p_{1} R$ (the latter follows from the fact that the radius of the circumcircle, drawn to a vertex of the triangle, is perpendicular to the segment connecting the bases of the altitudes dropped from the sides emanating from that vertex). Therefore, $p_{1} = p \frac{r}{R} \leqslant \frac{1}{2} p$.

question: 326. Let $A B C D$ be a convex quadrilateral. Prove that at least one of the four angles $B A C, D B C, A C D, B D A$ does not exceed $\pi / 4$.
reference_solution:
326. Let $O$ be the point of intersection of the diagonals of quadrilateral $ABCD$. Suppose all angles specified in the condition are greater than $\pi / 4$. Then on segments $OB$ and $OC$, we can take points $B_{1}$ and $C_{1}$ respectively, such that $\angle B_{1} A O=\angle O B_{1} C_{1}=\pi / 4$. Let $\angle B O A=\alpha>\pi / 4$. We have:

\[
\begin{aligned}
& |O C|>\left|O C_{1}\right|= \\
& =\frac{\left|O B_{1}\right|}{\sqrt{2} \sin \left(\alpha-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}=\frac{|O A|}{2 \sin \left(\alpha-\frac{\pi}{4}\right) \sin \left(\alpha+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}=-\frac{|O A|}{\cos 2 \alpha} \geqslant|O A|
\end{aligned}
\]

Similarly, we will prove the inequality $|O A|>|O C|$. Contradiction.

question: 327. Prove that the median to the largest side of a triangle forms angles with the sides enclosing it, each of which is not less than half the smallest angle of the triangle.
reference_solution: 327. Let in $\triangle A B C$ the sides are related by $c \leqslant b \leqslant a$. Take a point $M$ on $C B$ such that $\angle C A M=\frac{1}{2} \angle C$. We need to prove that $|C M| \leqslant \frac{a}{2}$. By the Law of Sines for $\triangle C A M$ we have: $|C M|=$ $=\frac{b \sin \frac{C}{2}}{\sin \frac{3 C}{2}}=\frac{b}{2 \cos C+1}=\frac{a b^{2}}{a^{2}+a b+b^{2}-c^{2}} \leqslant \frac{a}{2}$.

question: 328. Prove that if in triangle $ABC$ angle $B$ is obtuse and $|AB|=|AC| / 2$, then $\angle C>\angle A / 2$.
reference_solution: 328. Let $D$ be the midpoint of $A C$. Construct a perpendicular to $A C$ at $D$ and denote by $M$ the point of intersection of this perpendicular with $B C$; $\triangle A M C$ is isosceles, so $\angle M A C = \angle B C A$. By the problem's condition, $\triangle A B D$ is also isosceles, $\angle A B D = \angle B D A$, $\angle A B M > 90^{\circ}$ (by the problem's condition), $\angle A D M = 90^{\circ}$; hence, $\angle M B D > \angle M D B$ and $|M D| > |B M|$. Therefore, $\angle M A D > \angle M A B$ (if we reflect $B$ symmetrically with respect to the line $A M$, we get a point $B_{1}$ inside the angle $M A D$, since $M D \perp A D$ and $|M D| > |M B| = |M B_{1}|$; thus, $\angle C > \angle A - \angle C$, $\angle C > \frac{1}{2} \angle A$.

question: 329. Prove that the circumcircle of a triangle cannot pass through the center of an excircle.
reference_solution: 329. If a circle touches the extensions of sides $A B$ and $A C$ of triangle $A B C$ and its center is $O$, it is easy to find that $\angle B O C=90^{\circ}-$ $-\frac{1}{2} \angle A$. Therefore, $\angle B O C+\angle A=90^{\circ}+\frac{1}{2} \angle A \neq 180^{\circ}$.

question: 331. Prove that if the medians drawn from vertices $B$ and $C$ of triangle $ABC$ are perpendicular, then $\operatorname{ctg} B + \operatorname{ctg} C \geqslant \geqslant 2 / 3$.
reference_solution: 331. If $A D$ is the altitude, $A N$ is the median, and $M$ is the point of intersection of the medians, then $\operatorname{ctg} B+\operatorname{ctg} C=\frac{|D B|}{|A D|}+\frac{|C D|}{|A D|}=\frac{|C B|}{|A D|} \geqslant \frac{|C B|}{|A N|}=\frac{|C B|}{3|M N|}=\frac{2}{3}$.

question: 333. From an external point $A$ to a circle, two tangents $A B$ and $A C$ are drawn, and the midpoints of these tangents, $D$ and $E$, are connected by a line $D E$. Prove that this line does not intersect the circle.
reference_solution: 333. If $|O A|=a, R$ is the radius of the circle, and $K$ is the intersection point of $O A$ and $D E$, it is easy to find that $|O K|=a-\frac{a^{2}-R^{2}}{2 a}=\frac{a^{2}+R^{2}}{2 a}>R$.

question: 335. In triangle $A B C$, the angles are related by $3 \angle A-\angle C<\pi$. Angle $B$ is divided into four equal parts by lines intersecting side $A C$. Prove that the third segment, counting from vertex $A$, into which side $A C$ is divided, is less than $|A C| / 4$.
reference_solution:
335. Let $K, L$ and $M$ be the points of intersection of the drawn lines with $AC$. Denote: $|AC|=b$, $|BC|=a$, $|AB|=c$, $|BL|=$ $=l$. By the angle bisector theorem for the internal angle,

we find: $|LC|=\frac{ab}{a+c}$; applying this theorem again for $\triangle BCL$, we find: $|LM|=\frac{ba}{a+c} \cdot \frac{l}{l+a}=\frac{ba}{a+c}\left(1-\frac{a}{a+l}\right) ; \quad$ but $\quad \angle BLA=$ $=\frac{1}{2} \angle B + \angle C = \frac{\pi - \angle A + \angle C}{2} > \angle A$ (since $\angle C > 3 \angle A - \pi$). Therefore, $c > l$ and $|LM| < \frac{ba}{a+c}\left(1-\frac{a}{a+c}\right) = b \frac{ac}{(a+c)^2} \leqslant \frac{b}{4}$.

question: 336. Let $a, b, c, d$ be the consecutive sides of a quadrilateral. Prove that if $S$ is its area, then $S \leqslant(a c + b d) / 2$, and equality holds only for a cyclic quadrilateral with perpendicular diagonals.
reference_solution: 336. Let $A B C D$ be the given quadrilateral. Consider the quadrilateral $A B_{1} C D$, where $B_{1}$ is symmetric to $B$ with respect to the perpendicular bisector of the diagonal $A C$. Obviously, the areas of $A B C D$ and $A B_{1} C D$ are equal, and the sides of $A B_{1} C D$ in order are $b, a, c, d$. The inequality $S \leqslant 1 / 2(a c+b d)$ for the quadrilateral $A B_{1} C D$ is obvious. Equality holds if $\angle D A B_{1}=\angle B_{1} C D=90^{\circ}$, i.e., the quadrilateral $A B_{1} C D$ is cyclic, with two opposite angles of $90^{\circ}$; hence, the quadrilateral $A B C D$ is also cyclic (in the same circle) and its diagonals are perpendicular.

question: 337. Prove that if the lengths of the bisectors of a triangle are less than 1, then its area is less than $\sqrt{3} / 3$.
reference_solution:
337. Let's consider two cases.
1) The given triangle $(A B C)$ is acute-angled. Let $\angle B$ be the largest: $60^{\circ} \leqslant \angle B<90^{\circ}$. Since the angle bisectors of angles $A$ and $C$ are less than 1, the heights of these angles $h_{A}$ and $h_{C}$ are also less than 1. We have $S_{A B C}=$ $=\frac{h_{A} h_{C}}{2 \sin B}<\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$.
2) If one of the angles of the triangle, for example $B$, is not acute, then the sides enclosing it are less than the corresponding bisectors, i.e., less than 1, and the area does not exceed $1 / 2$.

question: 338. Prove that a triangle will be acute, right, or obtuse depending on whether the expression $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}-8 R^{2}$ is positive, zero, or negative ( $a, b, c$ - sides of the triangle, $R$ - radius of the circumscribed circle).
reference_solution: 338. Let $c$ be the largest side, opposite vertex $\cdot C$. If $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}-8 R^{2}>0$, then $a^{2}+b^{2}>8 R^{2}-c^{2} \geqslant c^{2}$ (since $c \leqslant 2 R$), i.e., the triangle is acute-angled. Conversely, let the triangle be acute-angled; then $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}=2 m_{c}^{2}+\frac{3}{2} c^{2}$ ($m_{c}$ is the median to side $c$); therefore, the smaller the median, the smaller $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}$, but the median is maximal when $C$ is the midpoint of the arc, and decreases as $C$ moves along the arc; when the triangle becomes right-angled, $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}-8 R^{2}$ will be equal to 0.

question: 339. Prove that a triangle will be acute, right, or obtuse depending on whether its semiperimeter is respectively greater than, equal to, or less than the sum of the diameter of the circumscribed circle and the radius of the inscribed circle.
reference_solution:
339. By substituting $R$ and $r$ using the formulas $R=\frac{a b c}{4 S}, r=\frac{S}{p}$, use Heron's formula for $S$ and the equality

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 4 S^{2}\left(p-\frac{a b c}{2 S}-\frac{S}{p}\right)\left(p+\frac{a b c}{2 S}+\frac{S}{p}\right)= \\
& \quad=\frac{1}{8}\left(a^{2}+b^{2}-c^{2}\right)\left(a^{2}-b^{2}+c^{2}\right)\left(-a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

question: 340. Prove that if the lengths of the sides of a triangle are related by the inequality $a^{2}+b^{2}>5 c^{2}$, then $c-$ is the smallest side.
reference_solution: 340. Suppose the opposite, for example, that $c \geqslant a$; then $2 c \geqslant c+a >$ $>b$; squaring the inequalities and adding them, we get: $5 c^{2}>a^{2}+$ $+b^{2}$ - a contradiction.

question: 341. In triangle $ABC$, angle $B$ is the middle in size: $\angle A < \angle B < \angle C, I$ is the center of the inscribed circle, $O$ is the center of the circumscribed circle, $H$ is the intersection point of the altitudes. Prove that $I$ lies inside triangle $BOH$.
reference_solution: 341. The bisector of angle $B$ is the bisector of $\angle O B H$, and the bisector of angle $A$ is the bisector of $\angle O A H$. Further, $\angle B A H=90^{\circ}-\angle B|B H|$. If $K$ and $M-$ are the points of intersection of the bisectors of angles $A$ and $B$ with $O H$, then $\frac{|H K|}{|K O|}=$ $=\frac{|A H|}{|A O|}=\frac{|A H|}{R}>\frac{|B H|}{R}=\frac{|B H|}{|O B|}=\frac{|H M|}{|M O|}$. Therefore, $|H K|>$ $>|H M|$ and the point of intersection of the bisectors of angles $A$ and $B$ lies inside $\triangle B O H$.

question: 343. In triangle $ABC$, point $M$ lies on side $BC$. Prove that $(|AM|-|AC|)|BC| \leqslant(|AB|-|AC|)|MC|$.
reference_solution:
343. Draw a line through $M$ parallel to $AC$ until it intersects $AB$ at point $K$. It is easy to find: $|AK| = |CM| \cdot \frac{|AB|}{|CB|}, |MK| = |MB| \cdot \frac{|AC|}{|CB|}$. Since $|AM| \leqslant |AK| + |KM|$, by substituting $|AK|$ and $|KM|$, we get:

$|AM| \leqslant \frac{|CM| \cdot |AB|}{|BC|} + \frac{|MB| \cdot |AC|}{|CB|} \Rightarrow$

$\Rightarrow (|AM| - |AC|)|BC| \leqslant (|AB| - |AC|)|MC|$,

which is what was required.

and required.
344 The minimum is equal to $\frac{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}{3}$ and is achieved if $M$ is the centroid of $\triangle ABC$. (This can be proven, for example, using the method of coordinates or by using Leibniz's theorem - see problem II.140.)

question: 349. Given an angle with vertex $A$ and two points $M$ and $N$ inside it. A line through $M$ intersects the sides of the angle at points $B$ and $C$. Prove that for the area of quadrilateral $A B N C$ to be the smallest, it is necessary and sufficient that the line $B C$ intersects $A N$ at a point $P$ such that $|B P|=|M C|$. Provide a method for constructing this line.
reference_solution: 349. Let the line $BC$ satisfy the condition of the problem: $|BP| = |MC|$ (the order of the points is $B, P, M, C$). We will prove that the area of the quadrilateral $ABNC$ is the smallest. Draw another line intersecting the sides of the angle at points $B_1$ and $C_1$. Suppose point $B$ lies between points $A$ and $B_1$, then point $C_1$ lies between points $A$ and $C$. We need to prove that $S_{BB_1N} > S_{CC_1N}$. This inequality is equivalent to the inequality $S_{BB_1P} > S_{CC_1P}$, since $\frac{S_{BB_1P}}{S_{BB_1N}} = \frac{S_{CC_1P}}{S_{CC_1N}} = \frac{|AP|}{|AN|}$. Add $S_{BPC_1}$ to both sides of the last inequality. On the left, we get $S_{BB_1P} + S_{BPC_1} = S_{BB_1PC_1} = S_{C_1CB_1}$ (follows from the equality $|BP| = |MC|$), and on the right, $S_{CC_1P} + S_{BPC_1} = S_{C_1CB}$. But, obviously, $S_{C_1CB_1} > S_{C_1CB}$. The case when point $B_1$ lies between points $A$ and $B$ is considered similarly. Construction. It is sufficient to draw any line intersecting the sides of the given angle and the lines $AN$ and $AM$ at points $B_0, P_0, M_0$, and $C_0$ such that $|B_0P_0| = |M_0C_0|$, and then draw a line through $M$ parallel to $B_0C_0$. Consider the parallelogram $AB_0DC_0$; denote by $K$ and $L$ the points of intersection of the lines $AP_0$ and $AM_0$ with $B_0D$ and $C_0D$, respectively. From the equality $|B_0P_0| = |M_0C_0|$, it follows that $S_{AB_0K} = S_{AC_0L}$. The problem reduces to constructing two equal-area triangles $AB_0K$ and $AC_0L$, all angles of which are known. Take $B_0$ arbitrarily, construct $\triangle AB_0K$. Take a point $E$ on $AB_0$ such that $\angle B_0KE = \angle ALC_0$. Construct the segment $AC_0$ equal to $\sqrt{|B_0E||B_0A|}$. The line $B_0C_0$ is the desired one. Remark. Consider the following problem. Through a point $M$ inside a given angle, draw a line intersecting the sides of the angle at points $B$ and $C$ such that the segment $BC$ is the shortest. From the considered problem, it follows that the segment $BC$ will be the shortest in the case when $|BP| = |MC|$, where $P$ is the projection of the vertex of the given angle onto $BC$. (Even more follows, namely: if the segment $BC$ has the specified property, then for any other line passing through $M$ and intersecting the sides of the angle at points $B_1$ and $C_1$, the projection of the segment $B_1C_1$ onto the segment $BC$ will be greater than $|BC|$.) Constructing such a segment, however, is not always possible with a compass and straightedge.

question: 353. Let $A B C D$ be a cyclic quadrilateral. The diagonal $A C$ is equal to $a$ and forms angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$ respectively with the sides $A B$ and $A D$. Prove that the area of the quadrilateral is between $\frac{a^{2} \sin (\alpha+\beta) \sin \beta}{2 \sin \alpha}$ and $\frac{a^{2} \sin (\alpha+\beta) \sin \alpha}{2 \sin \beta}$.
reference_solution: 353. Let $\sin \alpha \geqslant \sin \beta$ for definiteness; take a point $K$ on the extension of $A B$ such that $\angle B K C=\beta$; since $\angle C B K=\angle A D C$ (because quadrilateral $A B C D$ is cyclic), $\triangle K B C$ is similar to $\triangle A C D$. But $|B C| \geqslant|C D|$, therefore, $S_{B C K} \geqslant S_{A D C}$ and $S_{A K C} \geqslant S_{A B C D}$. But $S_{A K C}=\frac{a^{2} \sin (\alpha+\beta) \sin \alpha}{2 \sin \beta}$, hence, $S_{A B C D} \leqslant \frac{a^{2} \sin (\alpha+\beta) \sin \alpha}{2 \sin \beta}$. Similarly, it can be shown that $S_{A B C D} \geqslant \frac{a^{2} \sin (\alpha+\beta) \sin \beta}{2 \sin \alpha}$.

question: 354. Given an angle $\alpha$ with vertex at point $O$ and a point $A$ inside it. Consider all possible quadrilaterals OMAN, where vertices $M$ and $N$ are located on the sides of the angle and such that $\angle M A N=\beta(\alpha+\beta>\pi)$. Prove that if among these quadrilaterals there is a convex quadrilateral such that $|M A|=|A N|$, then this quadrilateral has the smallest area among all the considered quadrilaterals.
reference_solution: 354. Consider another position of points $M_{1}$ and $N_{1}\left(\angle M_{1} A N_{1}=\beta\right)$ and show, given the condition $\alpha+\beta>180^{\circ}$, that the "added" triangle has a greater area than the triangle whose area is reduced (analogous to the solution of problem II.350).

question: 360. In triangle $ABC$, points $M$ and $N$ are taken on sides $AC$ and $BC$, and point $L$ is taken on segment $MN$. Let the areas of triangles $ABC$, $AML$, and $BNL$ be $S$, $P$, and $Q$ respectively. Prove that $\sqrt[3]{S} \geqslant \sqrt[3]{P} + \sqrt[3]{Q}$.
reference_solution: 360. Let the ratios $\frac{|A M|}{|M C|}, \frac{|C N|}{|N B|}$ and $\frac{|M L|}{|L M|}$ be denoted by $\alpha, \beta$ and $\gamma$. Then (see the solution of problem I.221) $P=Q \alpha \beta \gamma, S=Q(\alpha+1)(\beta+1)(\gamma+1)$. Next, we will use the inequality $(\alpha+1)(\beta+1)(\gamma+1) \geqslant(\sqrt[3]{\alpha \beta \gamma}+1)^{3}$.

question: 361. Let $a, b, c, S$ be the sides and area of a certain triangle, and $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ be the angles of another triangle. Prove that $a^{2} \operatorname{ctg} \alpha+b^{2} \operatorname{ctg} \beta+c^{2} \operatorname{ctg} \gamma \geqslant 4 S$, with equality holding only when both triangles are similar.
reference_solution: 361. Let $\operatorname{ctg} \alpha=x, \operatorname{ctg} \beta=y$, then $\operatorname{ctg} \gamma=\frac{-x y+1}{x+y}=\frac{x^{2}+1}{x+y}-x$, $a^{2} \operatorname{ctg} \alpha+b^{2} \operatorname{ctg} \beta+c^{2} \operatorname{ctg} \gamma=\left(a^{2}-b^{2}-c^{2}\right) x+b^{2}(x+y)+c^{2} \frac{x^{2}+1}{x+y}$. The minimum value of the expression $b^{2}(x+y)+c^{2} \frac{x^{2}+1}{x+y}$ for a fixed $x$ and $x+y>0$ is achieved when $b^{2}(x+y)=c^{2} \frac{x^{2}+1}{x+y} \Rightarrow \frac{x+y}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}=\frac{c}{b}$. Thus, $\frac{c}{b}=\frac{x+y}{\sqrt{x^{2}+1}}=$ $=\frac{\sin \gamma}{\sin \beta}$. Therefore, the minimum value of the given expression is achieved for such $\alpha, \beta$ and $\gamma$, the sines of which are proportional to the sides $a, b$ and $c$, i.e., when the considered triangles are similar. In this case, the equality (which is easy to verify) holds.

question: 362. Prove the inequality $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2} \geqslant 4 S \sqrt{3}+(a-b)^{2}+$ $+(b-c)^{2}+(c-a)^{2}$, where $a, b, c, S-$ are respectively the sides and area of a triangle (Finsler, Hadwiger).
reference_solution: 362. Let's denote: $p-a=x, p-b=y, p-c=z$ ( $p-$ is the semiperimeter). Leaving $4 S \sqrt{3}$ on the right side of the inequality, after transforming the left side (for example, $a^{2}-(b-c)^{2}=4(p-b)(p-c)=4 y z$) and substituting $S$ using Heron's formula, we get the inequality $x y+y z+z x \geqslant \geqslant \sqrt{3(x+y+z) x y z}$. Dividing both sides of the inequality by $\sqrt{x y z}$ and making the substitution $u=\sqrt{(x y) / z}, v=\sqrt{(y z) / x}, w=\sqrt{(z x) / y}(x=u w, y=v u, z=w v)$, we obtain the inequality $u+v+w \geqslant \sqrt{3(u v+v w+w u)}$, which, after squaring, reduces to the well-known inequality $u^{2}+v^{2}+w^{2} \geqslant \geqslant u v+v w+w u$.

question: 364. Let $M$ be an arbitrary point inside triangle $ABC$. The line $AM$ intersects the circumcircle of $ABC$ at point $A_1$. Prove that $\frac{|BM| \cdot |CM|}{|A_1 M|} \geqslant 2r$, where $r$ is the radius of the inscribed circle, and equality is achieved when $M$ coincides with the center of the inscribed circle.
reference_solution: 364. Describe a circle around triangle $A M C$. All triangles $A_{1} M C$, obtained by moving $M$ along the arc $A C$, are similar to each other, so the ratio $\frac{|C M|}{\left|A_{1} M\right|}$ will be the same for them. Therefore, if $M$ is the point of minimum of the expression $f(M)=$ $=\frac{|B M| \cdot|C M|}{\left|A_{1} M\right|}$, then $B M$ should pass through the center of the circle circumscribed around triangle $A M C$, otherwise, one can decrease $|B M|$, keeping the ratio $\frac{|C M|}{\left|A_{1} M\right|}$ constant. Let $B_{1}$ and $C_{1}$ be the points of intersection of the lines $B M$ and $C M$ with the circle circumscribed around triangle $A B C$, then $\frac{|B M| \cdot|C M|}{\left|A_{1} M\right|}=\frac{|C M| \cdot|A M|}{\left|B_{1} M\right|}=$ $=\frac{|A M| \cdot|B M|}{\left|C_{1} M\right|}$. Therefore, the lines $A M$ and $C M$ should also pass through the centers of the circles circumscribed around triangles $B M C$ and $A M B$ respectively. Thus, the point $M$ is the incenter (see problem II.125). Moreover, in this case, $A_{1}$ is the center of the circle circumscribed around triangle $C M B$, $\sin \angle M B C=\frac{r}{|M B|}, \frac{|C M|}{\sin \angle M B C}=2\left|A_{1} M\right|$; hence, $\frac{|B M| \cdot|C M|}{\left|A_{1} M\right|}=2 r$. Let's return to the question of the function $f(M)$ achieving its minimum value. A known theorem in analysis states that a function continuous on a closed set attains its maximum and minimum values. This theorem is also true for a function of two variables defined on a polygon. However, this theorem is not directly applicable to this problem - the function $f(M)$ is not defined at the vertices of triangle $A B C$. If, however, we cut off the corners of the triangle, we get a hexagon on which $f(M)$ is already a continuous function and, therefore, will have a minimum value. It can be proven that near the boundary of the triangle $f(M)>2 r$. Therefore, if the cut-off corners are sufficiently small, the minimum value of $f(M)$ on the hexagons, and hence on the triangle, is achieved when $M$ is the incenter, and this minimum value is $2 r$. On the other hand, the maximum value of $f(M)$ is not attained, although it is bounded. Prove that $f(M)<l$, where $l$ is the length of the longest side of triangle $A B C$, for all points of the triangle, excluding the vertices, and $f(M)$ can take values arbitrarily close to $l$.

question: 365. Let $M$ be an arbitrary point inside triangle $ABC$. Prove that $|AM| \sin \angle BMC + |BM| \sin \angle AMC + |CM| \sin \angle AMB \leqslant p$ (where $p$ is the semiperimeter of triangle $ABC$) and equality is achieved when $M$ coincides with the incenter of the inscribed circle.
reference_solution:
365. Let's take points \(C_1\) and \(B_1\) on rays \(MB\) and \(MC\) respectively, such that \(|MC_1| = |MC|\) and \(|MB_1| = |MB|\) (\(\triangle MC_1B_1\) is symmetric to \(\triangle MBC\) with respect to the bisector of angle \(BMC\)), \(C_2\) and \(B_2\) are the projections of \(C_1\) and \(B_1\) onto the line \(AM\). We have: 
\[ |BM| \sin \angle AMC + |CM| \sin \angle AMB = |B_1M| \sin \angle AMC + |C_1M| \sin \angle AMB = |B_1B_2| + |C_1C_2| \geq |B_1C_1| = a. \]
By writing two more such inequalities and adding them, we can prove the statement of the problem. It is easy to verify that if \(M\) coincides with the center of the inscribed circle, then the inequality becomes an equality.

question:
366. Let $h_{1}, h_{2}, h_{3}$ be the altitudes of triangle $ABC$, and $u, v, w$ be the distances from a point $M$ inside triangle $ABC$ to the corresponding sides. Prove the inequalities:

a) $\frac{h_{1}}{u}+\frac{h_{2}}{v}+\frac{h_{3}}{w} \geqslant 9$;

b) $h_{1} h_{2} h_{3} \geqslant 27 u v w$

c) $\left(h_{1}-u\right)\left(h_{2}-v\right)\left(h_{3}-w\right) \geqslant 8 u v w$.
reference_solution: 366. a) Let's first solve the following problem. Let $M$ be a point on side $AB$ of triangle $ABC$, the distances from $M$ to sides $BC$ and $AC$ are $u$ and $v$ respectively, and $h_{1}$ and $h_{2}$ are the altitudes dropped to $BC$ and $AC$ respectively. Prove that the expression $\frac{h_{1}}{u}+\frac{h_{2}}{v}$ reaches its minimum value when $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$. Let $|BC|=a$, $|AC|=b$, and $S$ be the area of $\triangle ABC$. We have: $a u + b v = 2 S$, $v = \frac{2 S - a u}{b}$. Substituting $v$ into the expression $\frac{h_{1}}{u} + \frac{h_{2}}{v} = t$, we get: $a t u^2 - 2 S t u + 2 h_{1} S = 0$. The discriminant of this equation is non-negative, $S^2 (t^2 - 4 t) \geqslant 0$, from which $t \geqslant 4$. The minimum value $t = 4$ is achieved when $u = S / a = h_{1} / 2$, $v = h_{2} / 2$. From this problem, it follows that the minimum value of the left side of the inequality in part a) is achieved when $M$ is the intersection of the medians. Similarly, the inequalities in parts b) and c) can be proven. In part b), we need to determine for which point $M$ on side $AB$ the product $uv$ reaches its maximum value. In part c), we first divide both sides of the inequality by $uvw$ and solve the problem of minimizing the function $\left(h_{1} / u - 1\right)\left(h_{2} / v - 1\right)$ for the point $M$ on $AB$.

question: 367. Let $h$ be the length of the greatest altitude of an acute-angled triangle, $R$ and $r$ be the radii of the circumcircle and the incircle, respectively. Prove that $R + r \leqslant h$ (Erdős).
reference_solution: 367. Let for an acute-angled triangle $A B C$ the inequality $|A C| \leqslant|A B| \leqslant|B C|$ holds; $B D$ is the altitude, $O$ is the circumcenter, $I$ is the incenter of $\triangle A B C, E$ is the projection of $I$ onto $B D$. Since $|E D|=r$, it is necessary to prove that $|B E| \geqslant R=|B O|$. But $B I$ is the bisector of angle $E B O$ ( $B I$ is the bisector of angle $A B C$ and $\angle A B D=$ $=\angle O B C$ ), $\angle B E I=90^{\circ}, \angle B O I \geqslant 90^{\circ}$ (the latter follows from the fact that the projection of $C I$ onto $B C$ does not exceed $|B C| / 2$ ). Therefore, $|B E| \geqslant|B O|$ (reflect $B O$ symmetrically with respect to $B I$ ).

question: 368. Prove that the radius of the circle circumscribed around the triangle formed by the medians of an acute-angled triangle is greater than $5 / 6$ of the radius of the circle circumscribed around the original triangle.
reference_solution:
368. Since the area of a triangle formed by the medians of another triangle is $3 / 4$ of the area of the original triangle, and for any triangle $a b c=4 R S$, it is necessary to prove that for an acute-angled triangle, the inequality

$$
m_{a} m_{b} m_{c}>\frac{5}{8} a b c
$$

holds. For convenience of calculations, let one of the sides be $2 d$, and the median to this side be $m$. Since the triangle is acute-angled, $m>d$. Let $t$ be the cosine of the acute angle formed by this median with the side $2 d, 0 \leqslant t t^{2} d^{2} m^{2}\left(64 m^{2}-100 d^{2}\right)$. The left side of the inequality can be reduced to $\left(m^{2}-4 d m+5 d^{2}\right)\left(m^{2}+4 d m+\right.$ $\left.+5 d^{2}\right)\left(m^{2}-d^{2}\right)$. For $m>d$, this expression is positive. Moreover, if $m=d$ (the triangle is right-angled), the left side of the inequality is not less than the right side (equality when $t=0$). Further, if $d\frac{5}{4} d$. In this case, the right side of the inequality is less than the value obtained when $t=d / m$. But when $t=d / m$, the original triangle is right-angled, and for right-angled triangles, the validity of the non-strict inequality has already been proven. (It is sufficient to repeat the same reasoning for another side of the triangle.) Thus, it is proven that for any non-obtuse triangles except isosceles right-angled ones, inequality (1) holds; for isosceles right-angled triangles, equality holds.

question: 369. Prove that the sum of the squares of the distances from an arbitrary point in the plane to the sides of a triangle takes its minimum value for a point inside the triangle for which the distances to the corresponding sides are proportional to these sides. Also prove that this point is the intersection of the symmedians (see problem II.171) of the given triangle (the Lemoine point).
reference_solution: 369. Let $M$ lie inside $ABC$ at distances $x, y$, and $z$ from the sides $BC, CA$, and $AB$, respectively. The problem is to find the minimum of $x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}$ under the condition $ax + by + cz = 2S_{ABC}$. It is clear that this minimum is achieved at the same values of $x, y, z$ as the minimum of $x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}-2\lambda(ax + by + cz) = (x-\lambda a)^{2} + (y-\lambda b)^{2} + (z-\lambda c)^{2} - \lambda^{2}(a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2})$, where $\lambda$ is an arbitrary fixed number (under the same condition $ax + by + cz = 2S_{ABC}$). Taking $\lambda = \frac{2S_{ABC}}{a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2}}$ (where $\lambda$ is found from the equations $x = \lambda a, y = \lambda b, z = \lambda c, ax + by + cz = 2S_{ABC}$), we see that the minimum of the last expression will be achieved at $x = \lambda a, y = \lambda b, z = \lambda c$. Now, let the point $M$ be at distances $\lambda a, \lambda b$, and $\lambda c$ from $BC, CA$, and $AB$, respectively, and let the point $M_{1}$ be symmetric to $M$ with respect to the bisector of angle $A$. Since $S_{AM_{1}C} = S_{AM_{1}B}$, $M_{1}$ lies on the median of angle $A$, which means that $M$ lies on the symmedian of this angle (see problem II.171).

question: 370. Given a triangle, all angles of which are less than $120^{\circ}$. Prove that the sum of the distances from an arbitrary point to the vertices of this triangle takes the minimum value for a point inside it from which each side of the triangle is seen at an angle of $120^{\circ}$.
reference_solution: 370. Let $M$ be a point inside triangle $ABC$, all angles of which are less than $120^{\circ}$. Rotate $\triangle AMC$ around point $A$ by an angle of $60^{\circ}$ outward relative to $\triangle ABC$. In this case, point $C$ will move to point $C_{1}$, and point $M$ will move to point $M_{1}$. The sum $|AM| + |BM| + |CM|$ is equal to the broken line $BMM_{1}C$. This broken line will be the smallest when points $M$ and $M_{1}$ lie on segment $BC_{1}$. This leads to the statement of the problem.

question: 371. Prove that among all triangles inscribed in a given acute triangle, the one with the smallest perimeter has its vertices at the feet of the altitudes of the given triangle.
reference_solution: 371. Let $ABC$ be a given acute-angled triangle, $A_1$ a point on side $BC$, $B_1$ on $CA$, $C_1$ on $AB$, $A_2$ and $A_3$ the points symmetric to $A_1$ with respect to sides $AB$ and $AC$ (respectively). The broken line $A_2 C_1 B_1 A_3$ equals the perimeter of triangle $A_1 B_1 C_1$; therefore, this perimeter, for a fixed point $A_1$, will be the smallest when points $C_1$ and $B_1$ lie on the segment $A_2 A_3$, and will be equal to $|A_2 A_3|$. But $\triangle A A_2 A_3$ is isosceles, $\angle A_2 A A_3 = 2 \angle B A C, |A_2 A| = |A_3 A| = |A A_1|$. Thus, $|A_2 A_3|$ will be the smallest if $A A_1$ is the altitude of $\triangle B A C$. Similarly, $B B_1$ and $C C_1$ must also be altitudes.

question: 373. For an arbitrary triangle, prove the inequality (using standard notation) $\frac{b c \cos A}{b+c}+a<p<\frac{b c+a^{2}}{a}$.
reference_solution:
373. Let's prove the right part of the inequality. Let for definiteness $b \geqslant c$.
1) If $a \leqslant b$, then $2 p=a+b+c=(b-a)+c+2 a<2 c+2 a \leqslant 2 \frac{b}{a} c+$ $+2 a=2 \frac{b c+a^{2}}{a}$.
2) If $a \geqslant b \geqslant c$, then $a<2 b$ and $2 p=a+b+c=(b+c-a)+2 a \leqslant c+$ $+2 a<\frac{2 b c}{a}+2 a=2 \frac{b c+a^{2}}{a}$.

The left part of the inequality follows from the right part and the identity $(b+c)(p-a)-b c \cos A=a\left(\frac{b c+a^{2}}{a}-p\right)$.

question: 374. Let $K$ be the point of intersection of the diagonals of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$, $L$ a point on side $AD$, $N$ on side $BC$, and $M$ on diagonal $AC$, such that $KL$ and $MN$ are parallel to $AB$, and $LM$ is parallel to $DC$. Prove that $KLMN$ is a parallelogram and its area is less than $8/27$ of the area of quadrilateral $ABCD$ (X a t tori).

377. On the sides $B C, C A$ and $A B$ of triangle $A B C$, points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ are taken respectively. Prove that the area of triangle $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ is not less than the area of at least one of the three triangles: $A B_{1} C_{1}, A_{1} B C_{1}, A_{1} B_{1} C$.
reference_solution: 377. Let: $\frac{\left|A C_{1}\right|}{|A B|}=x, \frac{\left|B A_{1}\right|}{|B C|}=y, \frac{\left|C B_{1}\right|}{|C A|}=z$. We will assume that $x \leqslant 1 / 2$. If we assume that the areas of triangles $A B_{1} C_{1}$, $B C_{1} A_{1}$, and $C A_{1} B_{1}$ are greater than the area of triangle $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$, then $z \leqslant 1 / 2$ (otherwise $S_{A C_{1} B_{1}} \leqslant S_{A_{1} C_{1} B_{1}}$) and $y \leqslant 1 / 2$. The areas of all considered triangles can be easily expressed through $S_{A B C}$ and $x, y, z$, for example: $S_{A B_{1} C_{1}}=$ $=x(1-z) S_{A B C}$. The inequality $S_{A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}}<S_{A B_{1} C_{1}}$ can be transformed into $1-$ $-x(1-z)-y(1-x)-z(1-y)<x(1-z)$. Adding three such inequalities, we get: $3-4 x(1-z)-4 y(1-x)-4 z(1-y)<0$. Since the last inequality is linear with respect to $x, y, z$, if it were satisfied for some $x, y, z$ between 0 and $1 / 2$, then it should also be satisfied for some set of extreme values of the variables, i.e., when each variable is equal to 0 or $1 / 2$. However, it can be verified that this is not the case. The obtained contradiction proves our statement.

question: 378. Let $O, I, H$ be the centers of the circumcircle, incircle, and the intersection point of the altitudes of a certain triangle, respectively. Prove that $|O H| \geqslant|I H| \sqrt{2}$.
reference_solution:
378. Let $Q$ be the midpoint of $O H$, and $Q$ is the center of the nine-point circle (see problem II.160). We have: $|O H|^{2}+4|Q I|^{2}=2|O I|^{2}+2|H I|^{2}$. Since $|Q I|=R / 2-r$ (based on Feuerbach's theorem, problem II.287), $|O I|^{2}=R^{2}-2 R r$ (Euler's formula, problem II.193), taking into account that $R \geqslant 2 r$, we get:

$$
|O H|^{2}=2|I H|^{2}+R^{2}-4 r^{2} \geqslant 2|I H|^{2}
$$

question:
379. Let $M$ be an arbitrary point inside triangle $ABC$; $x, y$, and $z$ be the distances from $M$ to $A, B$, and $C$ respectively; $u, v$, and $w$ be the distances from $M$ to the sides $BC, CA$, and $AB$ respectively; $a, b, c$ be the corresponding sides of triangle $ABC$; $S$ be its area; $R$ and $r$ be the radii of the circumcircle and incircle. Prove the inequalities:

a) $a x + b y + c z \geqslant 4 S$

b) $x + y + z \geqslant 2(u + v + w) \quad (\text{Erdös-Mordell inequality})$

c) $x u + y v + z w \geqslant 2(u v + v w + w u)$

d) $2\left(\frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{z}\right) \leqslant \frac{1}{u} + \frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{w}$

e) $x y z \geqslant \frac{R}{2 r}(u + v)(v + w)(w + u)$

f) $x y z \geqslant \frac{4 R}{r} u v w$

g) $x y + y z + z x \geqslant \frac{2 R}{r}(u v + v w + w u)$.
reference_solution:
379. An elegant idea for proving inequalities of this type was proposed by Kazarinoff (Michigan Mathematical Journal, 1957, No. 2, pp. $97-98$). The essence of it is as follows. Take points $B_{1}$ and $C_{1}$ on rays $A B$ and $A C$ respectively. It is obvious that the sum of the areas of the parallelograms constructed on $A B_{1}$ and $A M$ and on $A C_{1}$ and $A M$ is equal to the area of the parallelogram, one side of which is $B_{1} C_{1}$, and the other is parallel to $A M$ and equal to $|A M|$ (see also problem II.40). Therefore,

$$
\left|A C_{1}\right| v+\left|A B_{1}\right| w \leqslant\left|B_{1} C_{1}\right| x
$$

a) Take points $B_{1}$ and $C_{1}$ coinciding with points $B$ and $C$; then inequality (1) will give the inequality $b v+c w \leqslant a x$. Adding three such inequalities, we get the required one.

b) If $\left|A B_{1}\right|=|A C|,\left|A C_{1}\right|=|A B|$, then inequality (1) will give the inequality $c v+b w \leqslant a x$, or $x \geqslant \frac{c}{a} v+\frac{b}{a} w$. Adding three such inequalities, we get:

$$
x+y+z \geqslant\left(\frac{b}{c}+\frac{c}{b}\right) u+\left(\frac{c}{a}+\frac{a}{c}\right) v+\left(\frac{b}{a}+\frac{a}{b}\right) w \geqslant 2(u+v+w)
$$

c) In part a), the inequality $a x \geqslant b v+c w$ was proved, from which $x u \geqslant \frac{b}{a} u v+\frac{c}{a} w u$. Similarly, $y v \geqslant \frac{a}{b} u v+\frac{c}{b} w v, z w \geqslant \frac{a}{c} u w+\frac{b}{c} v w$. Adding these three inequalities, we get $x u+y v+z w \geqslant\left(\frac{a}{b}+\frac{b}{a}\right) u v+$

$$
+\left(\frac{b}{c}+\frac{c}{b}\right) v w+\left(\frac{a}{c}+\frac{c}{a}\right) w u \geqslant 2(u v+v w+w u)
$$

d) Let $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ be the projections of point $M$ on the sides $B C, C A, A B$ of triangle $A B C$. Take points $A^{\prime}, A_{1}^{\prime}, B^{\prime}, B_{1}^{\prime}, C^{\prime}, C_{1}^{\prime}$ on rays $M A$, $M A_{1}, M B, M B_{1}, M C, M C_{1}$ respectively, such that $|M A|\left|M A^{\prime}\right|=\left|M A_{1}\right| \cdot\left|M A_{1}^{\prime}\right|=|M B|\left|M B^{\prime}\right|=\left|M B_{1}\right|\left|M B_{1}^{\prime}\right|=$
$\left.=|M C| \cdot\left|M C^{\prime}\right|=\left|M C_{1}\right| \cdot\left|M C_{1}^{\prime}\right|=d^{2 *}\right)$. It can be proved that points $A^{\prime}$, $B^{\prime}, C^{\prime}$ lie on lines $B_{1}^{\prime} C_{1}^{\prime}, C_{1}^{\prime} A_{1}^{\prime}, A_{1}^{\prime} B_{1}^{\prime}$ respectively, and $M A^{\prime}$, $M B^{\prime}, M C^{\prime}$ are perpendicular to these lines. Thus, in $\triangle A_{1}^{\prime} B_{1}^{\prime} C_{1}^{\prime}$, the distances from $M$ to the vertices are $\frac{d^{2}}{u}, \frac{d^{2}}{v}, \frac{d^{2}}{w}$, and to the opposite sides $-\frac{d^{2}}{x}, \frac{d^{2}}{y}, \frac{d^{2}}{z}$. Applying the inequality from part b), we get the required inequality.

e) Take in inequality (1) $b_{1}=c_{1}=l$; then $a_{1}=2 l \sin \frac{A}{2}$. We will have $x \geqslant \frac{1}{2 \sin \frac{A}{2}}(u+v)$. Obtaining similar inequalities for $y$ and $x$ and multiplying them, we get:

$x y z \geqslant \frac{1}{8 \sin \frac{A}{2} \sin \frac{B}{2} \sin \frac{C}{2}}(u+v)(v+w)(w+u)=\frac{R}{2 r}(u+v)(v+w)(w+u)$ (the equality $\sin \frac{A}{2} \cdot \sin \frac{B}{2} \cdot \sin \frac{C}{2}=\frac{r}{4 R}$ was proved in the solution of problem I.240).

f) From the inequality of the previous part, it follows: $x y z \geqslant$ $\geqslant \frac{R}{2 r} 2 \sqrt{u v} \cdot 2 \sqrt{v w} \cdot 2 \sqrt{w u}=\frac{4 R}{r} u v w$.

g) Dividing the inequalities of parts d) and f) by each other, we get the required inequality.

Remark. In the inequality of part a), equality is achieved for any acute-angled triangle when $M$ coincides with the intersection point of the heights of the triangle. In parts b), c), d), and g), equality is achieved for an equilateral triangle when $M$ is the center of this triangle. In parts d) and f), equality is achieved in any triangle when $M$ is the center of the inscribed circle.

reference_solution:
4. Let angle $A$ of quadrilateral $A B C D$ be acute, and the other three angles be obtuse. We construct a circle with segment $A C$ as its diameter (Fig. 33). Since $\angle B$ and $\angle D$ are obtuse, points $B$ and $D$ will be inside this circle, from which it follows that the distance $B D$ between them will be less than the diameter of the circle-segment $A C$.
