question: 7. Inside triangle $A B C$, a point $O$ is chosen; on the rays $O A, O B$, and $O C$, vectors of length 1 are laid out. Prove that the length of the sum of these vectors is less than 1.
reference_solution:
7. Since rays $A O$ and $B O$ intersect sides $B C$ and $A C$ of triangle $A B C$, ray $O C=O C_{0}$ lies inside angle $A^{\prime} O B^{\prime}$, which is the vertical angle of $A O B$ (Fig. 37). We construct two rhombi $O A_{0} D_{0} B_{0}$ and $O A^{\prime} D B^{\prime}$, symmetric with respect to point $O$, with side length 1. It is obvious that

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \overline{O A}_{0}+\overline{O B}_{0}+\overline{O C}_{0}=-\overline{O A^{\prime}}-\overline{O B^{\prime}}+\overline{O C}_{0}=-\overline{O D}+\overline{O C}_{0}= \\
&=\overline{D O}+\overline{O C}_{0}=\overline{D C}_{0}
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we only need to prove that the length of segment $D C_{0}$ is less than 1. However, point $C_{0}$ lies on the arc $A^{\prime} m B^{\prime}$ of circle $s$ with center $O$ and radius 1, which is intercepted by angle $A^{\prime} O B^{\prime}$, while the arc $A^{\prime} M B^{\prime}$ of circle $S$ with center $D$ and radius 1, intercepted by the same angle, encompasses arc $A^{\prime} m B^{\prime}$: this follows from the fact that if $A^{\prime} t$ and $A^{\prime} T$ are tangents to arcs $A^{\prime} m B^{\prime}$ and $A^{\prime} M B^{\prime}$ at point $A^{\prime}$, then $\angle O A^{\prime} t=90^{\circ}$ and $\angle O A^{\prime} T=\angle O A^{\prime} D+\angle D A^{\prime} T=\angle O A^{\prime} D+90^{\circ}>90^{\circ}$ (see

Fig. 37). Therefore, point $C_{0}$ lies inside the circle $K$ bounded by circle $S$, and thus,

$$
D C_{0}<1
$$

which is what we needed to prove.

question:
22. a) Inside a square $A B C D$ with side length 1, there is a convex polygon $M$ with an area greater than $1 / 2$. Prove that there exists a line $l$, parallel to the side $A B$ of the square, that intersects the polygon $M$ along a segment of length greater than $1 / 2$.

b)* Inside a square $A B C D$ with side length 1, there is a non-self-intersecting broken line $L$ with a length greater than 10.00. Prove that there exists a line $l$, parallel to one of the sides of the square, that intersects the broken line $L$ in more than 350 points:
reference_solution:
22. a) Draw lines through all vertices of the polygon $M$ parallel to the side $AB$. Then the polygon will be divided into a series of triangles and trapezoids (Fig. 67). The area of each of these triangles and trapezoids is equal to the length of the midline multiplied by the height. If all midlines were no more than $1/2$, then the area of each triangle or trapezoid would be no more than half the height, and consequently, the area of the entire polygon $M$ would be no more than half the sum of all heights of the considered triangles and trapezoids, i.e., no more than $1/2$ (since the sum of all heights is no more than $AD=1$), which contradicts the condition.

Thus, the midline of some triangle or trapezoid must be greater than $1/2$.

The line on which this midline lies will be the desired one.

Note. From the proof, it is clear that if the polygon $M$ is not assumed to be convex, then there exists a line $l \| AB$,

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_15011fcc7946713185f0g-098.jpg?height=575&width=574&top_left_y=872&top_left_x=105)

Fig. 68. intersecting the polygon along segments whose total length is $>1/2$.

b) Let $O$ be the center of the square $ABCD$ (Fig. 68). Consider separately all segments of the broken line that have directions of rays located inside the angle $AOB$, and all segments of the broken line that have directions of rays located inside the angle $BOC$ (segments of the broken line that have the direction $OB$ are included in both of these sets of segments). At least one of the two considered sets of segments will have a total length of no less than 500; let it be, for definiteness, the set of segments that have directions of rays located inside the angle $AOB$.

Project all segments of this set onto the side $BC$ of the square. Since each of the segments of the considered set forms an acute angle with the side $BC$ that is no greater than $45^\circ$, the projection of each segment is no less than the length of the segment multiplied by $\cos 45^\circ = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{2}$. Therefore, the sum of the lengths of all projections of the segments onto the side $BC$ is no shorter than $500 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{2} \approx 353.5$. Since the length of the side $BC$ is 1, there must be segments on this side onto which projections of more than 353 different segments of the broken line fall.

Let $P$ be a point on the side $BC$ of the square that belongs to the projections of 354 (or more) different segments of the broken line. In this case, the line $PQ \| AB$ intersects the original broken line in no fewer than 354 points, i.e., definitely more than 350 points. This completes the proof.

question: 23. Inside a square with side 1, a broken line is drawn such that each straight line parallel to the side of the square intersects it in no more than one point. Prove that the length of the broken line is less than 2, and for each number $l<2$ there exists a broken line of length $l$ that satisfies the required condition.
reference_solution: 23. Let the directions of the sides of the square coincide with the horizontal and vertical directions; denote the consecutive segments of the broken line by $l_{1}, l_{2}, \ldots, l_{n}$, and their projections on the horizontal and vertical sides of the square by $l_{1}^{\prime}$, $l_{2}^{\prime}, \ldots, l_{n}^{\prime}$ and $l_{1}^{\prime \prime}, l_{2}^{\prime \prime}, \ldots, l_{n}^{\prime \prime}$, respectively. It is clear that no two of the segments $l_{1}^{\prime}, l_{2}^{\prime}, \ldots, l_{n}^{\prime}$ overlap: indeed, if the segments $l_{i}^{\prime}$ and $_{i}^{\prime} l_{i}^{\prime}$ (where $1 \leqslant i0$, we obtain all values of the length $l$ of the broken line $A_{0} C B$ in the interval $\sqrt{2} \leqslant l<2$. For any value $l<\sqrt{2}$, we can take the segment $A_{0} D$ as the desired broken line, where $D$ is a point on the diagonal $A_{0} B_{0}$, at a distance $l$ from $A_{0}$.

question:
27. All sides of a convex polygon $m$ with perimeter $p=12$ and area $s$ are moved outward by a distance of 1; the perimeter of the larger polygon $M$ formed by the moved lines (Fig. 5) is denoted by $P$, and its area by $S$. Prove that

a) $P-p>6$

b) $S-s>15$

c) * if the polygon $m$ is a quadrilateral, then $P-p \geqslant 8$ and $S-s \geqslant 16$;

d) * if all angles of the polygon $m$ are obtuse, then $P-p<8$ and $S-s<16$.

30. On a plane, there are 25 points; it is known that from any three points, two can be chosen such that the distance between them is less than 1. Prove that among these points, there are 13 that can be covered by a circle of radius 1.
reference_solution:
30. Let $A$ be one of the given points (it does not matter which one!). If all points are at a distance $<1$ from $A$, then all of them can be covered by a circle of radius 1 (with center $A$); therefore, assume that there is a point $B$ among our points such that $A B \geqslant 1$. For each third point $M$ in our system of points, by the condition of the problem, either $A M<1$ or $B M<1$; therefore, all the remaining 23 points can be divided into two classes: points $C$ such that $A C<1$, and points $D$ such that $A D \geqslant 1$, but $B D<1$. If we have 12 (or more) points $C$, then a circle of radius 1 with center $A$ covers 13 (or more) points; if the number of points $C$ is less than 12, then we have

12 (or more) points $D$-and a circle with center $B$ and radius 1 covers 13 (or more) points.

question: 31*. On a plane, there are 100 points. Prove that they can be covered by one or several non-overlapping circles, the sum of whose diameters is less than 100, and such that the distance between any two points in different circles exceeds 1.
reference_solution:
31. Consider 100 circles of radius $1 / 2$ with centers at the given points; thus, we cover all points with 100 circles (some of which may intersect or touch each other!), the sum of whose diameters is 100. If any two $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ of these circles intersect or touch, we replace them with a larger circle $K$, whose diameter is the segment of the line of centers of $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ contained within them, and whose center $O$ coincides with the midpoint of this segment (Fig. $83, a$, b). Since this
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_15011fcc7946713185f0g-115.jpg?height=440&width=872&top_left_y=464&top_left_x=222)

Fig. 83.

larger circle fully covers the two original circles, the new system of circles still covers all the points; the number of circles has decreased by one; the sum of the diameters of the circles has not increased (since the diameter of the newly constructed circle is no greater than the sum of the diameters of the two original circles; see Fig. 83, $a$, b, where the two circles being replaced by one larger one are not equal to each other). If in the new system of circles there are still intersecting or touching circles, we again replace two such circles with one larger one, and so on. Ultimately, we will arrive at a system of non-intersecting (and non-touching) circles (possibly just one circle) that cover all our points, and the sum of the diameters of these circles does not exceed the sum of the diameters of the original circles, i.e., $\leqslant 100$.

Next, note that the smallest distance between points of two (non-intersecting) circles $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ with radii $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ (which is called the distance between the circles $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$) is equal to the length of the segment $N_{1} N_{2}$ of the line of centers $O_{1} O_{2}$ contained between the circles (this follows from the fact that if $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ are arbitrary points of circles with radii $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$, then

$$
O_{1} O_{2} \leqslant O_{1} M_{1} + M_{1} M_{2} + M_{2} O_{2}
$$

and, therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& M_{1} M_{2} \geqslant O_{1} O_{2} - O_{1} M_{1} - O_{2} M_{2} \geqslant O_{1} O_{2} - r_{1} - r_{2} = \\
&= O_{1} O_{2} - O_{1} N_{1} - O_{2} N_{2} = N_{1} N_{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

(Fig. 84, a); the smallest distance from a point $Q$ of circle $K$ to the boundary $S$ of circle $K$ with center $O$ and radius $r$ (which is called the distance from point $Q$ to the circumference $S$) is the smaller of the segments $Q B_{1}$ and $Q B_{2}$ of the diameter $B_{1} B_{2}$ of circle $S$ passing through $Q$ (since if $A$ is an arbitrary point on the circumference $S$ and $Q B_{1} \leqslant Q B_{2}$, then $O A \leqslant O Q + Q A$, and therefore, $Q A \geqslant O A - Q O = O B_{1} - Q O = O B_{1}$; see Fig. $\left.84, b\right)$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_15011fcc7946713185f0g-116.jpg?height=287&width=470&top_left_y=333&top_left_x=196)
a)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_15011fcc7946713185f0g-116.jpg?height=336&width=344&top_left_y=331&top_left_x=688)

Fig. 84.

Furthermore, in the original system of 100 circles, each point was at a distance of $1 / 2$ from the circumference of the circle containing it (it was the center of a circle of radius $1 / 2$); when replacing two circles $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ with one larger circle $K$, the smallest distance from each of the given points $Q$ to the circumference of the circle covering it does not decrease (since if $Q B_{1}$ is the smallest distance from point $Q$ to the circumference of circle $K$, $Q b_{1}$ is the smallest distance from point $Q$ to the circumference of the circle $K_{1}$ covering it, and $B$ is the point of intersection of segment $O B_{1}$ with the circumference of circle $K_{1}$, then, obviously, $Q B_{1} \geqslant Q B \geqslant Q b_{1}$; see, for example, Fig. $83, a$). Thus, in the obtained system of circles covering our points, each point is at a distance of at least $1 / 2$ from the circumference of the circle covering it.

If the obtained system of circles consists of a single circle, we only need to slightly (by a value less than 1) reduce its diameter if this diameter turned out to be

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_15011fcc7946713185f0g-116.jpg?height=359&width=503&top_left_y=1032&top_left_x=601)

Fig. 85. equal to 100. If the number of circles is more than one and the distance between any two circles is $>1$, then we again need only slightly reduce (by less than $1 / 2$) the radius of any one circle if the sum of the diameters of the circles turned out to be exactly 100. Finally, if the smallest distance between any two circles in the system (denoted by $\alpha$) $\leqslant 1$, then we reduce all circles by replacing a circle of radius $R$ with a concentric circle of radius $R - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{\alpha}{3}$ (since the distance between any two circles in the system was previously $\geqslant \alpha$; see Fig. 85).

question:
33. On a round table with a radius of 25, there are $n$ coins with a radius of 1. Prove that if $n>625$, the coins probably overlap, and if $n<144$, another coin can be placed on the table without overlapping with the previously placed ones.

The estimates given in problem 33 (in the general case of a table with radius $R$; on which coins with a radius of 1 are placed) have the following form: if the number $n$ of coins is greater than $R^{2}$, the coins probably overlap, and if $n<0.25(R-1)^{2}$, another coin can be placed on the table without overlapping with the previously placed ones. These estimates are relatively easy to obtain; however, they are quite rough. More subtle reasoning allows proving that for a large radius $R$ of the table, the number of non-overlapping coins cannot significantly exceed $0.9 \cdot R^{2}$, and the number of coins placed in such a way that no more coins can be placed on the table without overlapping with the previously placed ones cannot be significantly less than $0.3 \cdot R^{2}$ (see Chapter II of L. Fejes Tóth's book [21]).
reference_solution:
33. It is clear that if \( n > 625 \), then the total area of all the coins is greater than

\[
625 \cdot \left(\pi \cdot 1^{2}\right) = \pi \cdot 625 = \pi \cdot 25^{2},
\]

i.e., greater than the area of the table with a radius of 25; therefore, the coins cannot be placed on the table without overlapping. On the other hand, if \( n < 144 \), then the total area of the concentric circles with the coins, each with a radius of 2, is less than

\[
144 \cdot \left(\pi \cdot 2^{2}\right) = \pi \cdot 576 = \pi \cdot 24^{2}
\]

i.e., these circles cannot fully cover the part \( Q \) of the table obtained by cutting off a narrow "rim" of width 1 (Fig. 86). But if \( A \) is a point in the region \( Q \) not covered by any circle of radius 2, then this point is at a distance \(\geqslant 2\) from the centers of all the coins and at a distance \(\leqslant 1\) from the edge of the table; therefore, a coin with center \( A \) will fit entirely on the table and will not touch any of the previously placed \( n \) coins.

question: 34. An irrigated field has the shape of a square with a side of 12; from a source $J$ located within the field, a system of straight ditches has been laid out such that the distance from any point in the field to the nearest ditch does not exceed 1. Prove that the total length of the ditches is greater than 70 (we neglect the width of the ditches).
reference_solution:
34. The network of irrigation ditches represents a "branched" broken line (Fig. 87) passing through the field; in this case, the considered broken line is "connected," i.e., consists of one piece, since all ditches are connected to the source J. Let us single out from the system of ditches some "main ditch," i.e., a "simple" (unbranched) broken line $A B$. If the network of ditches has another end $C$ different from $A$ and $B$, consider the "additional ditch" going from $C$, i.e., a simple broken line $C C^{\prime}$, which at some point $C^{\prime}$ (possibly coinciding with the source $J$) flows into the main ditch $A B$; further, if the broken line has another end $D$ different from $A, B$, and $C$, then consider the "additional ditch" $D D^{\prime}$ leading from $D$, which at some point $D^{\prime}$ flows into the system of ditches $A B$ and $C C^{\prime}$, and so on.

Now let us consider what the "irrigated area" represents, i.e., the set of points located no more than 1 unit away from the nearest ditch. For a straight ditch $A B$ of length $l$, the irrigated area is a rectangular strip $A_{1} B_{1} B_{2} A_{2}$ of length $l$ and width 2, supplemented by two semicircles of radius 1 (Fig. 88); the area of the corresponding figure is $2 l + \pi$. If two straight ditches $A M$ and $M B$ meet at point $M$, forming a broken line $A M B$ (Fig. 89, a, b), then the rectangles $A_{1} M_{1} M_{2} A_{2}$ and $M_{1}^{\prime} B_{1} B_{2} M_{2}^{\prime}$ corresponding to segments $A M$ and $M B$ are supplemented by a circular sector $M_{2} M M_{2}^{\prime}$ of radius 1, with a central angle of $180^{\circ} - \angle A M B$; however, the centrally symmetric sector $M_{1} M M_{1}^{\prime}$ relative to point $M$ (and not only it!) is covered twice, so the area irrigated by the "broken ditch" $A M B$ does not exceed $2 A M + 2 M B + \pi = 2 l + \pi$, where $l$ is the length of the broken line $A M B$. Similarly, it is shown that for a "broken ditch" $A M N \ldots R B$ with any number of "internal vertices" $M, N, \ldots, R$, the irrigated area (Fig. 90) does not exceed $2 l + \pi$, where $l$ is the length of the broken line $A M N \ldots R B$.

Now consider a straight ditch $C C^{\prime}$ of length $m$; "flowing into" the ditch $A B$ at point $C^{\prime}$ (Fig. 91, a). The addition of the ditch $C C^{\prime}$ to the ditch $A B$ increases the area irrigated by the ditch $A B$ by (overlapping with the area irrigated by the ditch $A B!$) the rectangle $C_{1} C_{1}^{\prime} C_{2}^{\prime} C_{2}$ and the semicircle $C_{1} C_{2}$ of radius 1 centered at $C$. However, the shaded semicircle $C_{1}^{\prime} C_{2}^{\prime}$ centered at $C^{\prime}$ (and not only it!) is covered twice, so the addition of the ditch $C C^{\prime}$ of length $m$ to the ditch $A B$ increases the irrigated area by no more than $2 m$. This conclusion remains valid even if the straight ditches $A B$ and $C C^{\prime}$ are replaced by broken ditches $A M N \ldots R B$ and $C S T \ldots U C^{\prime}$, the total length of the latter being $m$ (Fig. 91, b).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_15011fcc7946713185f0g-119.jpg?height=365&width=365&top_left_y=540&top_left_x=177)
a)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_15011fcc7946713185f0g-119.jpg?height=467&width=590&top_left_y=477&top_left_x=558)

Fig. 91.

From the above, it follows that if the total length of the ditches is $L$, then the irrigated area does not exceed $2 L + \pi$. In particular, if the total length of the ditches does not exceed 70, then the irrigated area does not exceed

$$
2 \cdot 70 + \pi < 140 + 3.15 < 144 = 12^{2}
$$

from which it follows that it cannot coincide with the entire field.

question: 50. Let $h_{a}=m_{b}$, where $h_{a}=A P$ is the largest altitude of an acute-angled triangle $A B C$, and $m_{b}=B E$ is the median drawn from vertex $B$. Prove that $\angle B \leqslant 60^{\circ}$,
reference_solution:

Since $E Q=\frac{1}{2} A P=\frac{1}{2} h_{a}$ and $B E=m_{b}=h_{a}$, then $\angle E B C=30^{\circ}$. On the other hand, $E Q_{1}=\frac{1}{2} C R=\frac{1}{2} h_{c} \leqslant \frac{1}{2} h_{a}$ (since the height $h_{a}$ is the largest), and

51. If $A K=\beta_{a}$ is the angle bisector of triangle $A B C$ (Fig. 130), then obviously,

$$
S_{\triangle B A K}+S_{\triangle C A K}=S_{\triangle A B C},
$$

or

$$
\frac{1}{2} c \beta_{a} \sin \frac{A}{2}+\frac{1}{2} b \beta_{a} \sin \frac{A}{2}=\frac{1}{2} b c \sin A
$$

Therefore,

$$
\beta_{a}=\frac{b c \sin A}{(b+c) \sin \frac{A}{2}}=\frac{2 b c \sin \frac{A}{2} \cos \frac{A}{2}}{(b+c) \sin \frac{A}{2}}=\frac{2 b c \cos \frac{A}{2}}{b+c}
$$

Thus,

$$
\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{a}=\frac{b+c}{b c}=\frac{2 \cos \frac{A}{2}}{\beta_{a}}
$$

Next, we use the fact that, according to the result of problem 48, $h_{a} \leqslant \beta_{a} \leqslant m_{a}$, i.e., $\frac{1}{h_{a}} \geqslant \frac{1}{\beta_{a}} \geqslant \frac{1}{m_{a}}$; therefore,

a) if $\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}=\frac{1}{h_{a}}$, then

$$
\frac{2 \cos \frac{A}{2}}{\beta_{a}} \geqslant \frac{1}{\beta_{a}}
$$

i.e.,

$$
\cos \frac{A}{2} \geqslant \frac{1}{2}
$$

and consequently, $\frac{A}{2} \leqslant 60^{\circ}, \angle A \leqslant 120^{\circ}$;

b) if $\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}=\frac{1}{\beta_{a}}$, then

$$
\frac{2 \cos \frac{A}{2}}{\beta_{a}}=\frac{1}{\beta_{a}}
$$

i.e.,

$$
\cos \frac{A}{2}=\frac{1}{2}
$$

and consequently, $\frac{A}{2}=60^{\circ}, \angle A=120^{\circ}$;

c) if $\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}=\frac{1}{m_{a}}$, then

$$
\frac{2 \cos \frac{A}{2}}{\beta_{a}} \leqslant \frac{1}{\beta_{a}}, \text { i.e., } \cos \frac{A}{2} \leqslant \frac{1}{2}
$$

and consequently, $\frac{A}{2} \geqslant 60^{\circ}, \angle A \geqslant 120^{\circ}$.

question: 62. Triangle $A B C$ is divided into two triangles $A B D$ and $C B D$ by the straight line $B D$. Prove that the sum of the radii $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ of the circles inscribed in triangles $A B D$ and $C B D$ is greater than the radius $r$ of the circle inscribed in triangle $A B C$.
reference_solution:
62. Let $O, P, Q$ be the centers of the circles inscribed in triangles $ABC, ABD$, and $BCD$; $O', P', Q'$ be the points of tangency of these circles with the line $AC$ (Fig. 145). Draw the line $PK \parallel AC$ ($K$ is a point on the segment $OO'$); we need to prove that $PP' + QQ' > OO'$, or that $QQ' > OK$.

Let's compare the right triangles $POK$ and $DQQ'$ with legs $OK$ and $QQ'$ and hypotenuses $PO$ and $DQ$. Note that probably

$$
PO^2 + QO^2 < 90^\circ;
$$

therefore, triangle $OPQ$ is obtuse, and thus,

$$
PO^2 + QO^2 < QD^2.
$$

Since $QD > QO$, we have the right to assume that

$$
QD > PO,
$$

otherwise, we would replace triangle $POK$ with triangle $Q0L$, where $QL \parallel AC$ and $L$ is a point on the segment $00'$, and use the inequality $PD > QO$.

Furthermore, $\angle KPO = \angle CAO = \frac{1}{2} \angle A$ and $\angle Q'DQ = \frac{1}{2} \angle CDB$; therefore,

$$
\angle KPO < \angle Q'DQ
$$

since $\angle CDB$ is an exterior angle for triangle $DAB$ and is thus greater than $\angle A$. If the hypotenuse of triangle $KPO$ is less than the hypotenuse of triangle $Q'DQ$ and the angle opposite the leg $OK$ in triangle $KPO$ is less than the angle opposite the leg $QQ'$ in triangle $Q'DQ$, then

$$
OK < QQ',
$$

which proves the statement of the problem.

question:
63. Let $M$ be an arbitrary point inside triangle $ABC$; the points of intersection of $AM$, $BM$, and $CM$ with the opposite sides $BC$, $AC$, and $AB$ of the triangle are denoted by $A_{1}$, $B_{1}$, and $C_{1}$ (Fig. 15). Prove that the sum

$$
M A_{1} + M B_{1} + M C_{1}
$$

does not exceed the length of the largest side of triangle $ABC$.
reference_solution:
63. First Solution. Let

$$
a=BC \geqslant b=AC \geqslant c=AB \text{; }
$$

then $BC=a$ is the greatest distance between any two points of triangle $ABC$: if $M$ and $N$ are two points of triangle $ABC$ and $M_{1}, N_{1}$ are the points of intersection of segment $MN$ with the boundary of the triangle, then

$$
MN \leqslant M_{1}N_{1} \leqslant BC
$$

since we can increase segment $M_{1}N_{1}$ by moving one, and then the other of its endpoints to coincide with the vertices of the triangle (Fig. 146; we assume that $\angle M_{1}N_{1}A$ is not acute, so $M_{1}A > M_{1}N_{1}$,

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_15011fcc7946713185f0g-177.jpg?height=307&width=483&top_left_y=434&top_left_x=165)

Fig. 146.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_15011fcc7946713185f0g-177.jpg?height=312&width=534&top_left_y=437&top_left_x=653)

Fig. 147.

and $\angle AM_{1}C$ is not acute, so $AC > AM_{1}$; note that $BC$ is the largest side, and thus, $BC \geqslant AC$). Further, if $AP$ and $MP_{1}$ are the altitudes of triangles $ABC$ and $MBC$ (Fig. 147), then

$$
\frac{MA_{1}}{AA_{1}}=\frac{MP_{1}}{AP}=\frac{S_{\triangle MBC}}{S_{\triangle ABC}}
$$

and therefore,

$$
MA_{1}=\frac{S_{\triangle MBC}}{S_{\triangle ABC}} AA_{1} < \frac{S_{\triangle MBC}}{S_{\triangle ABC}} a
$$

Similarly, it can be shown that

$$
MB_{1} < \frac{S_{\triangle MAC}}{S_{\triangle BAC}} a \text{ and } MC_{1} < \frac{S_{\triangle MAB}}{S_{\triangle CAB}} a
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& MA_{1} + MB_{1} + MC_{1} < \frac{S_{\triangle MAC}}{S_{\triangle ABC}} a + \frac{S_{\triangle MAC}}{S_{\triangle ABC}} a + \frac{S_{\triangle MAB}}{S_{\triangle ABC}} a = \\
& = \frac{S_{\triangle MBC} + S_{\triangle MAC} + S_{\triangle MAB}}{S_{\triangle ABC}} a = a
\end{aligned}
$$

which is what we needed to prove.

Second Solution. Here is another solution to the problem, the connection of which with the first solution is left to the reader. Draw through point $M$ segments $A^{\prime}B^{\prime \prime}, A^{\prime \prime}C^{\prime}$, and $B^{\prime}C^{\prime \prime}$ parallel to the sides of the triangle, as shown in Fig. 148. Then triangles $MA^{\prime \prime}B^{\prime}, MB^{\prime \prime}C^{\prime}$, and $MC^{\prime \prime}A^{\prime}$ will be similar to $ABC$; their greatest sides will be segments $B^{\prime}M = BB^{\prime \prime}, B^{\prime \prime}C^{\prime}$, and $MC^{\prime \prime} = C^{\prime}C$. But the sum

$$
B^{\prime}M + B^{\prime \prime}C^{\prime} + MC^{\prime \prime} = BB^{\prime \prime} + B^{\prime \prime}C^{\prime} + C^{\prime}C = BC = a
$$

On the other hand, since the greatest distance between any two points of the triangle is its greatest side (see the first solution of the problem), then

$$
MA_{1} \leqslant B^{\prime \prime}C^{\prime}, MB_{1} \leqslant MC^{\prime \prime} \text{ and } MC_{1} \leqslant B^{\prime}M
$$

Therefore,

$$
MA_{1} + MB_{1} + MC_{1} \leqslant B^{\prime \prime}C^{\prime} + MC^{\prime \prime} + B^{\prime}M = a
$$

where equality cannot hold if point $M$ lies inside the triangle $ABC$.

## 3. PROBLEMS ON FINDING MAXIMUM AND MINIMUM VALUES OF GEOMETRICAL QUANTITIES

The central problems in this series are probably the classical problems 70 b) and 75, which have been the subject of considerable literature (see, for example, 4, 5, and Chapter VII of the book by R. Courant and H. Robbins [2], §8 of the book by H. S. M. Coxeter [12], and §2 of the article by V. G. Boltyansky and I. M. Yaglom [1]), or even all the problems $69-80$ related to this circle of problems. Further development of some of the themes initiated by the problems collected here can be found in the following series of problems.
reference_solution:
64. It is obvious that segment $E C$ intersects either $B D$ or $A D$; let it, for example, intersect $A D$ at some point $F$ (Fig. 149; point $F$ may coincide with $D$). By a known property of triangles,

$$
E F+D F \geqslant E D, \quad A F+C F \geqslant A C
$$

Adding these two inequalities, we get

$$
E F+D F+A F+C F=E C+A D \geqslant E D+A C
$$

Subtracting the sum $E D+A D$ from both sides of the last inequality, we obtain

$$
E C-E D \geqslant A C-A D \geqslant 1
$$

which is what we needed to prove.

question:
89. Prove that the sum of the medians of an arbitrary triangle $ABC$ is always less than the perimeter of the triangle and greater than $3/4$ of its perimeter:

$$
2 p > m_{a} + m_{b} + m_{c} > \frac{3}{2} p, \text{ or } 2 > \frac{m_{a} + m_{b} + m_{c}}{p} > 1^{1/2}
$$

Can the (double) inequality

$$
2 > \frac{m_{a} + m_{b} + m_{c}}{p} > 11 / 2
$$

be improved (i.e., is there a number $M < 2$ such that for all triangles $\frac{m_{a} + m_{b} + m_{c}}{p} \leqslant M$)?
reference_solution:
89. Let $M$ be the point of intersection of the medians $A D=m_{a}, B E=m_{b}$, and $C F=m_{c}$ of triangle $A B C$ (Fig. 230); then $A M=\frac{2}{3} m_{a}, B M=\frac{2}{3} m_{b}$, $C M=\frac{2}{3} m_{c} ; \quad M D=\frac{1}{3} m_{a}, \quad M E=\frac{1}{3} m_{b}, \quad M F=\frac{1}{3} m_{c}$. From the consideration of triangles $B M C, C M A$, and $A M B$, it follows that

$$
\frac{2}{3} m_{b}+\frac{2}{3} m_{c}>a, \frac{2}{3} m_{c}+\frac{2}{3} m_{a}>b, \frac{2}{3} m_{a}+\frac{2}{3} m_{b}>c
$$

Adding these three inequalities, we get

$$
\frac{4}{3}\left(m_{a}+m_{b}+m_{c}\right)>a+b+c=2 p, \text { i.e., } m_{a}+m_{b}+m_{c}>\frac{3}{2} p
$$

On the other hand, by extending $A D$ beyond point $D$ and marking a segment $D A_{1}=A D$, and noting that $B A_{1}=A C=b$ (since quadrilateral $A B A_{1} C$ is a parallelogram), we find from triangle $A B A_{1}$ that

$$
b+c>2 m_{a}
$$

Similarly, it can be shown that

$$
a+c>2 m_{b} \quad \text { and } \quad a+b>2 m_{c} .
$$

Adding these last three inequalities, we have

$$
2(a+b+c)>2\left(m_{a}+m_{b}+m_{c}\right)
$$

i.e., $2 p=a+b+c>m_{a}+m_{b}+m_{c}$.

The obtained inequalities cannot be improved, as the sum $m_{a}+m_{b}+m_{c}$ of the medians of a triangle can be arbitrarily close to either the value $\frac{3}{2} p$ or the value $2 p$. Indeed, if vertex $A$ of the triangle is very close to side $B C$ (Fig. 231, a), then

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_15011fcc7946713185f0g-237.jpg?height=533&width=367&top_left_y=205&top_left_x=205)

Fig. 230.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& B C=a \approx b+c, m_{a} \approx 0, m_{b} \approx c+\frac{b}{2} \text { and } m_{c} \approx b+\frac{c}{2}, \text { so that } \\
& m_{a}+m_{b}+m_{c} \approx 0+\left(c+\frac{b}{2}\right)+\left(b+\frac{c}{2}\right)=\frac{3}{2}(b+c)= \\
& \quad=\frac{3}{2} \frac{b+c+b+c}{2} \approx \frac{3}{2} \frac{a+b+c}{2}=\frac{3}{2} p
\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\frac{m_{a}+m_{b}+m_{c}}{p} \approx \frac{3}{2}
$$

On the other hand, if vertices $B$ and $C$ of the triangle are very close to each other (Fig. 231, b), then $a \approx 0, b \approx c, m_{a} \approx b(\approx c)$. $m_{b} \approx \frac{b}{2}, \quad m_{c} \approx \frac{c}{2}$, so

$$
m_{a}+m_{b}+m_{c} \approx b+\frac{b}{2}+\frac{c}{2}=\frac{3}{2} b+\frac{1}{2} c \approx 2 \frac{b+c+0}{2} \approx 2 p
$$

i.e., $\frac{m_{a}+m_{b}+m_{c}}{p} \approx 2$.

question:
90. Prove that for any triangle

$$
A a+B b+C c \geqslant \frac{1}{2}(A b+B a+A c+C a+B c+C b)
$$

In which case does this inequality become an equality?
reference_solution:
90. Let $a \geqslant b \geqslant c$; then, since in a triangle the larger side is opposite the larger angle, $A \geqslant B \geqslant C$. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
(a-b)(A-B)+(b-c) & (B-C)+ \\
& +(c-a)(C-A) \geqslant 0
\end{aligned}
$$

since each term on the left side is non-negative.

Expanding the brackets and moving the negative terms to the right, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
2 A a+2 B b+2 C c & \\
& \geqslant A b+B a+B c+C b+A c+C a
\end{aligned}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_15011fcc7946713185f0g-238.jpg?height=271&width=320&top_left_y=495&top_left_x=766)

Fig. 232.

Dividing both sides by 2, we obtain the required inequality.

It is easy to see that equality holds if and only if $a=b=c$, i.e., if the triangle is equilateral and $A=B=C$ (Fig. 232).

question:
92. a) Prove that if the bases $BC$ and $B_{1}C_{1}$, as well as the angles $A$ and $A_{1}$, of two triangles $ABC$ and $A_{1}B_{1}C_{1}$ are equal, then the one with the smaller (in absolute value) difference of the angles at the base has the larger perimeter.

b) What perimeter can triangle $ABC$ with a known side $BC=a$ and angle $\angle A=\alpha$ have?
reference_solution:
92. a) Let's align the bases $BC$ and $B_1C_1$ of triangles $ABC$ and $A_1B_1C_1$; then extend their sides $BA$ and $BA_1$ to segments $AD = AC$ and $A_1D_1 = A_1C$ (here we assume that $AB \leq AC$ and $A_1B \leq A_1C$; see Fig. 234). From the isosceles triangles $ACD$ and $A_1CD_1$, we have: $\angle ADC = \frac{\angle A}{2}$ and $\angle A_1D_1C = \frac{\angle A}{2}$; therefore, while points $A$ and $A_1$ (which we assume are located on the same side of the line $BC$) belong to the arc of the segment constructed on the segment $BC$ that contains the angle $A$, points $D$ and $D_1$ belong to the arc of the segment constructed on the same segment $BC$ that contains the angle $A/2$. Since $AB$ and $A_1B$ are the smaller of the lateral sides of triangles $ABC$ and $A_1BC$, points $A$ and $A_1$ belong to the same half $BM$ of the arc of the segment that contains the angle $A$, and thus $\angle ACB \angle A_1BT$, where $BT$ is the tangent to the considered arc at point $B$, i.e., $\cup BD > \cup BD_1$, then

$$
BA + AC = BD > BD_1 = BA_1 + A_1C
$$

(Note that, since $\angle BCD = \angle BCA + \frac{\alpha}{2} \geq 90^\circ$, $\cup BD$ is less than a semicircle). This is where the statement of the problem follows from.

b) From the result of part a), it follows that the perimeter $2p$ of triangle $ABC$ is bounded between $2a$ (the case when $\beta = 0$; see Fig. 235)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_15011fcc7946713185f0g-240.jpg?height=58&width=363&top_left_y=426&top_left_x=721)

Fig. 235. and $a + 2 \cdot \frac{\alpha}{2} \operatorname{cosec} \frac{\alpha}{2} = a\left(1 + \operatorname{cosec} \frac{\alpha}{2}\right)$ (the case when $\beta = \frac{180^\circ - \alpha}{2}$, and triangle $ABC$ is isosceles) and can, obviously, take any value in the interval $2a < 2p \leq a\left(1 + \operatorname{cosec} \frac{\alpha}{2}\right)$.

question:
95. Prove that for any triangle $ABC$

a) $9 r \leqslant h_{a}+h_{b}+h_{c} \leqslant \beta_{a}+\beta_{b}+\beta_{c} \leqslant m_{a}+m_{b}+m_{c} \leqslant \frac{9}{2} R$;

b) $\beta_{a}+\beta_{b}+\beta_{c} \leqslant \sqrt{r_{a} r_{b}}+\sqrt{r_{b} r_{c}}+\sqrt{r_{c} r_{a}} \leqslant p \sqrt{3} \leqslant$

$$
\leqslant r_{a}+r_{b}+r_{c}=r+4 R
$$

c) $27 r^{2} \leqslant h_{a}^{2}+h_{b}^{2}+h_{c}^{2} \leqslant \beta_{a}^{2}+\beta_{b}^{2}+\beta_{c}^{2} \leqslant p^{2} \leqslant m_{a}^{2}+m_{b}^{2}+m_{c}^{2}=$

$$
=\frac{3}{4}\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}\right) \leqslant \frac{27}{4} R^{2}
$$

d) $\frac{1}{r}=\frac{1}{r_{a}}+\frac{1}{r_{b}}+\frac{1}{r_{c}}=\frac{1}{h_{a}}+\frac{1}{h_{b}}+\frac{1}{h_{c}} \geqslant \frac{1}{\beta_{a}}+\frac{1}{\beta_{b}}+\frac{1}{\beta_{c}} \geqslant$ $\geqslant \frac{1}{m_{a}}+\frac{1}{m_{b}}+\frac{1}{m_{c}} \geqslant \frac{2}{R}$.

In what case does each of these inequalities turn into an equality?

It is clear that the "complex" inequalities of problems 95 a), c) and d) contain, in particular, the result of problem 94 a): if $9 r \leqslant \frac{9}{2} R$, or $27 r^{2} \leqslant \frac{27}{4} R^{2}$, or $\frac{1}{r} \geqslant \frac{2}{R}$, then, of course, $r \leqslant \frac{1}{2} R$. The inequalities of problems 95 a) and b) can also be written in the form of the following "chain" of inequalities:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 9 r \leqslant h_{a}+h_{b}+h_{c} \leqslant \beta_{a}+\beta_{b}+\beta_{c} \leqslant \sqrt{r_{a} r_{b}}+\sqrt{r_{b} r_{c}}+\sqrt{r_{c} r_{a}} \leqslant p \sqrt{3} \leqslant \\
& \leqslant r_{a}+r_{b}+r_{c}=r+4 R,
\end{aligned}
$$

${ }^{1}$ ) The symbol $\min (x, y)$ denotes the smaller of the numbers $x$ and $y$ (and the number equal to both if $x=y$ ).
including the same relationship between $r$ and $R$; if $9 r \leqslant r+4 R$, then, of course, $r \leqslant \frac{R}{2} \cdot\left[\right.$ On the contrary, taking into account the inequality $r \leqslant \frac{R}{2}$, the last chain of inequalities can also be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 9 r \leqslant h_{a}+h_{b}+h_{c} \leqslant \beta_{a}+\beta_{b}+\beta_{c} \leqslant \sqrt{r_{a} r_{b}}+\sqrt{r_{b} r_{c}}+\sqrt{r_{a} r_{c}} \leqslant \\
&\left.\leqslant p \sqrt{3} \leqslant r_{a}+r_{b}+r_{c}=r+4 R \leqslant \frac{9}{2} R .\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

96*. Prove that for any triangle $ABC$

a) $r_{a}^{2}+r_{b}^{2}+r_{c}^{2} \geqslant 27 r^{2}$

b) $4 R < r_{a}+r_{b}+r_{c} \leqslant 4 \frac{1}{2} R$

Can these inequalities be improved?

Problem 96 b) indicates the range within which the sum $r_{a}+r_{b}+r_{c}$ of the radii of the excircles of a triangle can vary if the radius of its circumcircle is known. More profound are the inequalities

$$
\frac{r_{a}+r_{b}+r_{c}}{3} \leq \frac{3}{2} R \leqslant \sqrt{\frac{r_{a}^{2}+r_{b}^{2}+r_{c}^{2}}{3}}
$$

which follow from the result of problem 96 b) and from the inequality

$$
r_{a}^{2}+r_{b}^{2}+r_{c}^{2} \geqslant \frac{27}{4} R^{2}
$$

(where equality holds only for an equilateral triangle), the proof of which, however, is quite difficult (see G. Hajós [47]): it shows that the quantity $\frac{3}{2} R$ is bounded between the arithmetic mean and the quadratic mean (between the power means of order 1 and 2) of the radii of the excircles of the triangle (see below, pp. $52-53$).
reference_solution:
96. a) Above (p. 250) we have already seen that

$$
r_{a} r_{b} + r_{b} r_{c} + r_{a} r_{c} = p^{2}
$$

Therefore, using inequality (B) (p. 250) and the inequality derived from the results of problem 95 a), b):

$$
9 r \leqslant p \sqrt{3}, \text{ or } p^{2} \geqslant 27 r^{2}
$$

(see also problem 97 below), we obtain

$$
r_{a}^{2} + r_{b}^{2} + r_{c}^{2} \geqslant r_{a} r_{b} + r_{a} r_{c} + r_{b} r_{c} = p^{2} \geqslant 27 r^{2}
$$

where equality can only hold in the case of an equilateral triangle.

b) From the fact that \( r_{a} + r_{b} + r_{c} = 4 R + r \) (problem 95 b)) and \( R \geqslant 2 r \) (problem 94 a)), it directly follows that

$$
r_{a} + r_{b} + r_{c} \leqslant 4 R + \frac{1}{2} R = \frac{9}{2} R
$$

where equality holds when \( R = 2 r \), i.e., for an equilateral triangle. On the other hand, it is obvious that

$$
4 R < 4 R + r = r_{a} + r_{b} + r_{c}
$$

and the ratio \(\frac{r_{a} + r_{b} + r_{c}}{R}\) will be closer to 4 the smaller the ratio \( \frac{r}{R} \).

It is clear that the inequalities in parts a) and b) cannot be improved.

question:
97. Prove that for any triangle $ABC$

$$
r \leqslant \frac{\sqrt{\sqrt{3} S}}{3} \leqslant \frac{\sqrt{3}}{9} p \leqslant \frac{1}{2} R
$$

In what case do the inequalities in this problem become equalities?

The results of problem 97 deserve a more detailed discussion. By discarding the intermediate terms of the inequality (*), we obtain the dependence

$$
r \leqslant \frac{1}{2} R, \quad \text { or } \quad R \geqslant 2 r
$$

between the radii of the circumscribed and inscribed circles of the triangle, which was already mentioned above (see problem 94 a)). Conversely, the "intermediate" inequality of problem 97

$$
\frac{\sqrt{\sqrt{3} S}}{3} \leq \frac{\sqrt{3}}{9} p, \quad \text { or } \quad S \leqslant \frac{\sqrt{3}}{36}(2 p)^{2}
$$

is nothing but the famous "isoperimetric inequality" for a triangle, which answers the question of what the maximum area a figure (in our case, a triangle) with a given perimeter can have («what is the maximum area that can be enclosed by a triangular fence if the building material allows for a fence of length $2 p$?») or, conversely, what the minimum perimeter a figure (triangle) with a given area can have (see the book by D. A. Kryzhansky [28] dedicated to this problem). From inequality (II), it follows that the area of a triangle with a unit perimeter cannot be greater than $\sqrt{3} / 36$ $\left(\approx 0.048\right)$; if $2 p=1$, then inequality (II) gives $\left.S \leq \frac{\sqrt{3}}{36}\right)$, and the perimeter of a triangle with a unit area cannot be less than $2 \sqrt[4]{27}(\approx 4.56)$; if $S=1$, then inequality (II) gives $2 p \geqslant 2 \sqrt[4]{27})$. Finally, the inequalities

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\sqrt{\sqrt{3} S}}{3} \leqslant \frac{1}{2} R, \text { or } \quad S \leqslant \frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{4} R^{2} \\
& \frac{\sqrt{\sqrt{3} S}}{3} \geqslant r, \text { or } S \geqslant 3 \sqrt{3} r^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\sqrt{3}}{9} p \leqslant \frac{1}{2} R, \text { or } \quad 2 p \leqslant 3 \sqrt{3} R ; \quad \frac{\sqrt{3}}{9} p \geqslant r, \text { or } 2 p \geqslant 6 \sqrt{3} r,
$$

establish dependencies between the area and perimeter of the triangle, on the one hand, and the radii of its circumscribed and inscribed circles, on the other. From these, it follows that if triangle $ABC$ is inscribed in a circle of radius 1, then

$$
S \leqslant \frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{4}(\approx 1.30) \quad \text { and } \quad 2 p \leqslant 3 \sqrt{3}(\approx 5.20)
$$

and if it is circumscribed around a circle of radius 1, then

$$
S \geqslant 3 \sqrt{3}(\approx 5.20) \quad \text { and } \quad 2 p \geqslant 6 \sqrt{3}(\approx 10.39)
$$

All these results can be extended to arbitrary (convex!) polygons (see sections 3 and 4 of chapter I of the book by L. Fejes Tóth [21] or sections 2.6 and 2.7 of the article by V. G. Boltyansky and I. M. Yaglom [29]). Regarding the extension of inequality (I) to the case of an arbitrary convex $n$-gon, we have already discussed it above; further, it can be established that the radius $R$ of the circumscribed circle, the radius $r$ of the inscribed circle, the perimeter $2 p$, and the area $S$ of any convex $n$-gon are related by the inequalities

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{1}{2} n R^{2} \sin \frac{360^{\circ}}{n} \geqslant S \geqslant n r^{2} \tan \frac{180^{\circ}}{n} \\
2 n R \sin \frac{180^{\circ}}{n} \geqslant 2 p \geqslant 2 n r \tan \frac{180^{\circ}}{n}
\end{gathered}
$$

and, finally,

$$
(2 p)^{2} \geqslant 4 n \tan \frac{180^{\circ}}{n} \cdot S, \quad \text { or } \quad S \leq \frac{1}{4 n} \cot \frac{180^{\circ}}{n}(2 p)^{2}
$$

the "isoperimetric inequality" for an $n$-gon!). [Equalities in (I'), (II'), (III'), and (IV') are achieved for a regular $n$-gon.]
reference_solution:
97. In problem 95 b), it was already shown that

$$
27 r^{2} \leqslant p^{2} \leqslant \frac{27}{4} R^{2}
$$

from which

$$
r \leqslant \frac{\sqrt{3} p}{9} \leqslant \frac{1}{2} R
$$

and equality holds only for an equilateral triangle. Thus, we need to prove that

$$
r \leqslant \frac{\sqrt{\sqrt{3}} S}{3} \leq \frac{\sqrt{3}}{9} p
$$

But this clearly follows from the inequality

$$
r \leqslant \frac{\sqrt{3} p}{9}
$$

and from the fact that $p r = S$; multiplying both sides of the inequality (*) first by $r$, and then by $p$, we get $r^{2} \leqslant \frac{\sqrt{3} p r}{9} = \frac{\sqrt{3} S}{9}$, i.e., $r \leqslant \frac{\sqrt{\sqrt{3} S}}{3}$ and $S = p r \leqslant \frac{\sqrt{3} p^{2}}{9}$, i.e., $\frac{\sqrt{3} S}{9} \leqslant \frac{3 p^{2}}{81}$, or $\frac{\sqrt{\sqrt{3}} S}{3} \leqslant \frac{\sqrt{3} p}{9}$, where equality is achieved when $r = \frac{1}{2} R$, i.e., when the triangle $ABC$ is equilateral.

question:
98. Prove that for any tetrahedron

$$
V \leqslant \frac{8 \sqrt{3}}{27} \mathrm{P}^{3}
$$

In what case does the equality $V=\frac{8 \sqrt{3}}{27} \mathrm{P}^{3}$ hold?

99 * %. Prove that for any tetrahedron

a) $\Delta \geqslant 6 \sqrt[3]{\sqrt{3} V^{2}}$

b) $\Pi \geqslant 3 \sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt[3]{3 V}$

In what case do the inequalities a) and b) become equalities?

Problems 98 and 99 (as well as problem 94 v); see also problems 101 a) and 106) illustrate the nature of the dependencies between the main characteristics $V, \Delta, \Pi, \mathbf{P}$ of a tetrahedron $A B C D$; from them it follows that for each tetrahedron inscribed in a sphere of radius 1,

$$
V \leqslant \frac{8 \sqrt{3}}{27}
$$

and for each tetrahedron of unit volume

$$
\Delta \geqslant 6 \sqrt[6]{3} \quad \text { and } \quad \Pi \geqslant 3 \sqrt[6]{72}
$$

(for a tetrahedron of unit surface area $V \leqslant \frac{\sqrt[4]{12}}{36}$ ). The complete set of dependencies between the listed characteristics of a tetrahedron is given by

$$
\rho \leqslant \frac{\sqrt[3]{9 \sqrt{3} V}}{6} \leqslant \frac{\sqrt{2 \sqrt{3} \Delta}}{12} \leqslant \frac{\sqrt{6}}{36} \Pi \leqslant \frac{1}{3} \mathrm{P}
$$

here all inequalities are strict if the tetrahedron $A B C D$ is irregular; for a regular tetrahedron, all of them become equalities, since, as it is easy to calculate, if the edge of a regular tetrahedron is $a$, then

$$
V=\frac{a^{3} \sqrt{2}}{12}, \quad \Delta=a^{2} \sqrt{3}, \quad \Pi=3 a, \quad \mathrm{P}=\frac{a \sqrt{\overline{6}}}{4} \text { and } \rho=\frac{a \sqrt{6}}{12}
$$

The most important of these inequalities is the inequality of problem 99 a), which can be called the "isoperimetric inequality for a tetrahedron" (cf. the "isoperimetric inequality for a triangle" mentioned on p. 45). All inequalities (**) can be established by indirect reasoning; however, a direct proof of some of them is quite tedious (cf. the remarks on pp. 7-9 of the book's preface). It should also be noted that while the inequalities (*) (p. 44), relating the characteristics $S, p, R$ and $r$ of a triangle, are fairly easily extended to an arbitrary (convex) polygon, the question of generalizing the inequalities (**) (extending them to an arbitrary convex polyhedron) is much more complex (see chapter $V$ of book [21]).

The proof of other dependencies of the same nature is the subject of problem 103.
reference_solution:
98. First solution. Let the tetrahedron \(ABCD\) be inscribed in a sphere \(\Sigma\) of radius \(P\). If the base \(BCD\) of this tetrahedron lies in a fixed plane \(\pi\), which is at a distance \(d\) from the center \(O\) of the sphere \(\Sigma\), then the volume \(V\) of the tetrahedron does not exceed \(\frac{1}{3} S(P + d)\), where \(S\) is the area of the triangle \(BCD\), since the height \(AP\) of the tetrahedron cannot exceed the distance \(A_0Q = P + d\) from the farthest point \(A_0\) of the sphere \(\Sigma\) to the plane \(\pi\) (Fig. 246). On the other hand, the radius \(QB = r\) of the circumcircle \(s\) of the triangle \(ABC\) - the section of the sphere \(\Sigma\) by the plane \(\pi\) - is obviously equal to

\[ r = \sqrt{OB^2 - OQ^2} = \sqrt{P^2 - d^2} \]

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_15011fcc7946713185f0g-256.jpg?height=521&width=557&top_left_y=478&top_left_x=513)

Fig. 246.

Therefore, the area \(S\) of the triangle \(BCD\) satisfies the inequality

\[ S \leq \frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{4} r^2 = \frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{4} (P^2 - d^2) \]

(see problem 97).

Thus, we have

\[ V \leq \frac{1}{3} S(P + d) \leq \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} (P^2 - d^2)(P + d) \]

and it remains to determine for which \(d\) (satisfying the inequality \(0 \leq d \leq P\)) the product

\((P^2 - d^2)(P + d) = (P - d)(P + d)(P + d) = \frac{1}{2} (2P - 2d)(P + d)(P + d)\) takes the maximum possible value.

But by the inequality (A), p. 246

\[ (2P - 2d)(P + d)(P + d) \leq \left[ \frac{(2P - 2d) + (P + d) + (P + d)}{3} \right]^3 = \left( \frac{4}{3} P \right)^3 = \frac{64}{27} P^3 \]

where equality holds if and only if

\[ 2P - 2d = P + d, \quad \text{i.e.,} \quad d = \frac{P}{3} \]

Hence, we have

\[ V \leq \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} (P^2 - d^2)(P + d) = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{8} [(2P - 2d)(P + d)^2] \leq \frac{\sqrt{3}}{8} \cdot \frac{64}{27} P^3 = \frac{8 \sqrt{3}}{27} P^3 \]

which is what we needed to prove.

Equality \(V = \frac{8 \sqrt{3}}{27} P^3\) holds if the triangle \(BCD\) is equilateral and the vertex \(A\) of the tetrahedron \(ABCD\) projects onto the plane \(\pi\) of the face \(BCD\) at the center \(Q\) of the circumcircle \(s\) of \(BCD\) (i.e., if the triangular pyramid \(ABCD\) is regular) and if, in addition, the distance \(d\) from the center \(O\) of the circumscribed sphere of \(ABCD\) to the plane \(\pi\) is \(\frac{1}{3}\) of the radius \(P\) of the circumscribed sphere. In this case, the square of the radius \(r\) of the circle \(s\) is

\[ r^2 = P^2 - d^2 = P^2 - \left( \frac{P}{3} \right)^2 = \frac{8}{9} P^2 \]

and the lateral edges \(AB, AC, AD\) of the tetrahedron (triangular pyramid) \(ABCD\) are equal to

\[ AB = \sqrt{AQ^2 + QB^2} = \sqrt{\left( \frac{4}{3} P \right)^2 + \frac{8}{9} P^2} = \sqrt{\frac{16}{9} P^2 + \frac{8}{9} P^2} = \frac{2 \sqrt{6}}{3} P \]

i.e., equal to the side \(BC\) (or \(CD\), or \(DB\)) of the equilateral triangle inscribed in the circle \(s\) of radius \(r = \frac{2 \sqrt{2}}{3} P\) (this side is equal to \(r \sqrt{3} = \frac{2 \sqrt{6}}{3} P\)), i.e., if the tetrahedron \(ABCD\) is regular.

Second solution. The result of this problem can also be easily obtained from the inequalities of problems 106a) and 94b). Indeed, by dividing the tetrahedron \(ABCD\) into four smaller tetrahedra \(BCD, ACD, ABD, ABC\) with a common height \(\rho\) (where \(O\) is the center of the inscribed sphere of the tetrahedron), we easily obtain that

\[ V = \frac{1}{3} \Delta \cdot \rho \]

Therefore, from the inequality \(P \geq \frac{\sqrt{2 \sqrt{3} \Delta}}{4}\), or \(\Delta \leq \frac{8 \sqrt{3}}{3} P^2\), of problem 106a) and the inequality \(\rho \leq \frac{1}{3} P\) of problem 94b), it follows that

\[ V = \frac{1}{3} \rho \cdot \Delta \leq \frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{3} P \cdot \frac{8 \sqrt{3}}{3} P^2 = \frac{8 \sqrt{3}}{27} P^3 \]

where equality holds if and only if \(\Delta = \frac{8 \sqrt{3}}{3} P^2\) and \(\rho = \frac{1}{3} P\), i.e., if the tetrahedron \(ABCD\) is regular.

question:
100. a) Prove that for any triangle $ABC$

$$
a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2} \geqslant 4 \sqrt{3} S
$$

where equality holds only for an equilateral triangle $ABC$.

b)* Prove that, moreover,

$$
a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}-(a-b)^{2}-(b-c)^{2}-(c-a)^{2} \geqslant 4 \sqrt{3} S
$$

where equality also holds only when $a=b=c$.

101*. a) Prove that for each tetrahedron \(ABCD\)

\[
\Pi^{2} \geqslant 3 \sqrt{3} \Delta
\]

where equality holds only if the tetrahedron \(ABCD\) is regular.

b) Prove that, moreover,

\[
\begin{aligned}
& \Pi^{2} \geqslant 3 \sqrt{3} \Delta + 1 / 2\left[\left(a + a_{1} - b - b_{1}\right)^{2} + \left(a + a_{1} - c - c_{1}\right)^{2} + \right. \\
& \left.\quad + \left(b + b_{1} - c - c_{1}\right)^{2}\right] + 3 / 4\left[\left(a - a_{1}\right)^{2} + \left(b - b_{1}\right)^{2} + \left(c - c_{1}\right)^{2}\right]
\end{aligned}
\]

where, of course, equality also holds only if \(a = b = c = a_{1} = b_{1} = c_{1}\).
reference_solution:
101. Since the inequality of problem a) obviously follows from the stronger inequality of problem b), we will limit ourselves to proving the latter. We apply the inequality of problem 100 b) to each face of the tetrahedron $A B C D$ (Fig. 252):

$$
a_{1}^{2}+b_{1}^{2}+a_{1}^{2}-\left(a_{1}-b_{1}\right)^{2}-\left(b_{1}-c_{1}\right)^{2}-\left(c_{1}-a_{1}\right)^{2} \geqq 4 \sqrt{3} S_{\triangle A B C}
$$

$\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{n}!}$

$$
2 a_{1} b_{1}+2 b_{1} c_{1}+2 c_{1} a_{1}-a_{1}^{2}-b_{1}^{2}-c_{1}^{2} \geqslant 4 \sqrt{3} S_{\triangle A B C}
$$

Adding these four inequalities, we get

$$
\Sigma^{\prime}(2 a b)-2 \Sigma a^{2} \geqslant 4 \sqrt{3} \Delta
$$

where $\Sigma a^{2}$ denotes the sum of the squares of the six edges of the tetrahedron $A B C D$, and $\Sigma^{\prime}(2 a b)$ denotes the sum of twelve doubled products of edges, excluding the products of $a_{1}, b b_{1}$ and $c c_{1}$ of the tetrahedron.

Now consider the expression

$$

107. Prove that for any triangle $ABC$ and any point $M$ inside it

a) $\min \left(h_{a}, h_{b}, h_{c}\right) \leqslant d_{a}+d_{b}+d_{c} \leqslant \max \left(h_{a}, h_{b}, h_{c}\right)$, where $\min \left(h_{a}, h_{b}, h_{c}\right)$ denotes the smallest and $\max \left(h_{a}, h_{b}, h_{c}\right)$ the largest of the heights of the triangle;

b) $d_{a} d_{b} d_{c} \leqslant \frac{8 S^{3}}{27 a b c}$.

In what cases do the inequalities in parts a) and b) become equalities?

Since for an equilateral triangle, obviously, $\min \left(h_{a}, h_{b}, h_{c}\right)=\max \left(h_{a}, h_{b}, h_{c}\right)(=h)$, it follows from the result of problem 107 a) that for an equilateral triangle the sum $d_{a}+d_{b}+d_{c}=h=$ const, i.e., this sum is completely independent of the choice of point $M$ inside the triangle.
reference_solution:
107. From the consideration of triangles $MBC$, $M$ and $C$, and $MAB$ (see Fig. 26 on p. 48), we easily obtain

$$
S_{\triangle ABC}=\frac{1}{2} a d_{a}+\frac{1}{2} b d_{b}+\frac{1}{2} c d_{c}, \text{ i.e., } a d_{a}+b d_{b}+c d_{c}=2 S \text{. }
$$

## From this, it follows:

a) If $a \geqslant b \geqslant c$, then

$$
2 S=a d_{a}+b d_{b}+c d_{c} \leqslant a d_{a}+a d_{b}+a d_{c}=a\left(d_{a}+d_{b}+d_{c}\right)
$$

and

$$
2 S=a d_{a}+b d_{b}+c d_{c} \cong c d_{a}+c d_{b}+c d_{c}=c\left(d_{a}+d_{b}+d_{c}\right)
$$

Thus,

$\min \left(h_{a}, h_{b}, h_{c}\right)=h_{a}=\frac{2 S}{a} \leqslant d_{a}+d_{b}+d_{c} \leqslant \frac{2 S}{c}=h_{c}=\max \left(h_{a}, h_{b}, h_{c}\right)$.

Equality $d_{a}+d_{b}+d_{c}=h_{a}=111$ in $\left(h_{a}, h_{b}, h_{c}\right)$ when $a>b \geqslant c$ holds only in the case where in the equality $a d_{a}+b d_{b}+c d_{c}=2 S$ the terms with coefficients different from $a$ are absent, i.e., when $d_{b}=d_{c}=0$, and point $M$ coincides with vertex $A$ of the triangle; when $a=b>c$, equality holds when $d_{c}=0$, and point $M$ lies on side $AB$; when $a=b=c$, i.e., when triangle $ABC$ is equilateral, it holds for any point $M$ (inside $ABC$). Similarly, equality $d_{a}+d_{b}+d_{c} \cdot=$ $=\max \left(h_{a}+h_{b}+h_{c}\right)$ when $a \geqslant b>c$ holds only when point $M$ coincides with vertex $C$ of the triangle; when $a>b=c$, it holds when point $M$ lies on side $BC$; when $a=b=c$, i.e., if triangle $ABC$ is equilateral, it holds for any point $M$ inside $ABC$.

b) From the equality

$$
a d_{a}+b d_{b}+c d_{c}=2 S
$$

by inequality (A) (p. 246), we obtain

$$
\left(a d_{a}\right)\left(b d_{b}\right)\left(c d_{c}\right) \leq\left(\frac{a d_{a}+b d_{b}+c d_{c}}{3}\right)^{3}=\left(\frac{2 S}{3}\right)^{3}
$$

Thus,

$$
d_{a} d_{b} d_{c} \leqslant \frac{8 S^{3}}{27 a b c}
$$

Equality is achieved only when

a d_{a}=b d_{b}=c d_{c}, \text{ i.e., } d_{a}: d_{b}: d_{c}=\frac{1}{a}: \frac{1}{b}: \frac{1}{c}
$$

In which case $d_{a}^{2}+d_{b}^{2}+d_{c}^{2}=12 \frac{r^{4}}{R^{2}}$?

If point $M$ coincides with the center of the inscribed circle of the triangle, then the sum $d_{a}^{2}+d_{b}^{2}+d_{c}^{2}$ becomes equal to $3 r^{2}$, and the result of problem 109 turns into the result of problem 94 a):

$$
3 r^{2} \geqslant 12 \frac{r^{4}}{R^{2}}, \text { or } R^{2} \geqslant 4 r^{2}, \quad \text { i.e. } R \geqslant 2 r
$$

Let us now move on to inequalities involving the quantities $R_{a}$, $R_{b}, R_{c}$ and $d_{a}, d_{b}, d_{c}$. We will start with the following simple problem.

109. $$

Equality $d_{a}^{2}+d_{b}^{2}+d_{c}^{2}=12 \frac{r^{4}}{R^{2}}$ is achieved only in the case when $S=3 \sqrt{3} r^{2}$ and $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}=9 R^{2}$, i.e., when the triangle $ABC$ is equilateral, and $d_{a}: d_{b}: d_{c}=a: b: c=1: 1: 1$, i.e., if the point $M$ coincides with the center of the inscribed circle of the triangle $ABC$ (the center of the triangle $ABC$).

(from which, in particular, it follows that

$$

this result is obtained if we assume that the point $M$ coincides with the center of the inscribed circle of the triangle $ABC$) can be considered as a strengthening of the inequality

110. Since, obviously (compare with the beginning of the solution to problem 107),

$$

$$

then

Adding the last three equations, we get

h_{l}-d_{b} \leqslant R_{b}, \quad h_{c}-d_{c} \leqslant R_{c}

From here, the required inequality follows:

Equality is achieved when \( h_{a}-\lambda_{\alpha}=A K=A M=R_{\alpha} \), i.e., when \( A M \perp B C \) and similarly \( B M \perp A C, C M \perp A B \), i.e., when point \( M \) coincides with the orthocenter (the point of intersection of the altitudes) of the triangle. question:
112*. a) Prove that for any triangle $ABC$ and for any point $M$ inside it,

$$
R_{a} R_{b} R_{c} \geqslant 8 d_{a}^{\prime} d_{b}^{\prime} d_{c}^{\prime}
$$

In what case does this inequality become an equality?

b) Prove that for any triangle $ABC$ and for any point $M$ inside it,

$$
R_{a}+R_{b}+R_{c}>d_{a}^{\prime}+d_{b}^{\prime}+d_{c}^{\prime}
$$

Can this inequality be improved (i.e., does there exist a number $\lambda>1$ such that

$$
R_{a}+R_{b}+R_{c}>\lambda\left(d_{a}^{\prime}+d_{b}^{\prime}+d_{c}^{\prime}\right)
$$

for all triangles $ABC$ and any point $M$ inside $ABC$)?

It is clear that the inequality of problem 112 a) is a strengthening of the inequality of problem 111 a). [See also L. Carlitz [57], where many diverse inequalities involving the quantities $R_{a}, R_{b}$, $R_{c}$ and $\left.d_{a}^{\prime}, d_{b}^{\prime}, d_{c}^{\prime}.\right]$
reference_solution:
112. a) Let

$$
d_{a}^{\prime}=M A_{1}, d_{b}^{\prime}=M B_{1}, \quad d_{c}^{\prime}=M C_{1}
$$

where $A_{1}, B_{1}$, and $C_{1}$ are the points of intersection of the lines $A M, B M$, and $C M$ with the opposite sides of the triangle (see Fig. 26 on p. 48 or Fig. 260 on p. 284). It is clear that the altitudes $A P$ and $M U$ of triangles $A B C$ and $M B C$ are related as the segments $A A_{1}$ and $M A_{1}$, therefore

$$
\frac{d_{a}^{\prime}}{d_{a}^{\prime}+R_{a}}=\frac{M A_{1}}{A A_{1}}=\frac{S_{\triangle M B C}}{S_{\triangle A B C}}
$$

analogously

$$
\frac{d_{b}^{\prime}}{d_{b}^{\prime}+R_{b}}=\frac{S_{\triangle M A C}}{S_{\triangle A B C}} \quad \text { and } \frac{d_{c}^{\prime}}{d_{c}^{\prime}+R_{c}}=\frac{S_{\triangle M A B}}{S_{\triangle A B C}}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{d_{a}^{\prime}}{d_{a}^{\prime}+R_{a}}+\frac{d_{b}^{\prime}}{d_{b}^{\prime}+R_{b}}+\frac{d_{c}^{\prime}}{d_{c}^{\prime}+R_{c}}=\frac{S_{\triangle M B C}+S_{\triangle M A C}+S_{\triangle M A B}}{S_{\triangle A B C}}=1
$$

i.e.,

$$
\frac{1}{1+R_{a} / d_{a}^{\prime}}+\frac{1}{1+R_{b} / d_{b}^{\prime}}+\frac{1}{1+R_{c} / d_{c}^{\prime}}=1,
$$

or

$$
\frac{1}{1+x_{a}}+\frac{1}{1+x_{b}}+\frac{1}{1+x_{c}}=1
$$

where for brevity we denote $\frac{R_{a}}{d_{a}^{\prime}}=x_{a}, \frac{R_{b}}{d_{b}^{\prime}}=x_{b}$, and $\frac{R_{c}}{d_{c}^{\prime}}=x_{c}$,

Bringing all the fractions in the equality (*) to a common denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\left(1+x_{b}\right)\left(1+x_{c}\right)+\left(1+x_{a}\right)\left(1+x_{c}\right)+\left(1+x_{a}\right)\left(1+x_{b}\right)= \\
&=\left(1+x_{a}\right)\left(1+x_{b}\right)\left(1+x_{c}\right) .
\end{aligned}
$$

Expanding the brackets and moving all terms of the equality to one side, we will have

$$
2+\left(x_{a}+x_{b}+x_{c}\right)-x_{a} x_{b} x_{c}=0
$$

Further, from the inequality (A) (p. 246)

$$
x_{a}+x_{b}+x_{c} \geqslant 3 \sqrt[3]{x_{a} x_{b} x_{c}}
$$

it follows that

$$
2+3 \sqrt[3]{x_{a} x_{b} x_{c}}-x_{a} x_{b} x_{c} \leqslant 0
$$

or

$$
2+3 Z-Z^{3} \leqslant 0
$$

where $Z=\sqrt[3]{x_{a} x_{b} x_{c}}$.

Factoring the left side of the last inequality, we get

$$
\begin{gathered}
(2-Z)(1+Z)^{2} \leqslant 0 \\
2-Z \leqslant 0
\end{gathered}
$$

i.e.,

$$
Z=\sqrt[3]{x_{a} x_{b} x_{c}}=\sqrt[3]{\frac{R_{a}}{d_{a}^{\prime}} \frac{R_{b} R_{c}}{d_{b}^{\prime}} \frac{d_{c}^{\prime}}{2}} \geqslant 2, \quad \text { or } \quad \frac{R_{a} R_{b} R_{c}}{d_{a}^{\prime} d_{b}^{\prime} d_{c}^{\prime}} \geqslant 8
$$

in other words, that

$$
R_{a} R_{b} R_{c} \geqslant 8 d_{a}^{\prime} d_{b}^{\prime} c_{c}^{\prime}
$$

It is clear that the equality $R_{a} R_{b} R_{c}=8 d_{a}^{\prime} d_{b}^{\prime} d_{c}^{\prime}$ holds only in the case when

$$
\frac{R_{a}}{d_{a}^{\prime}}=\frac{R_{b}}{d_{b}^{\prime}}=\frac{R_{c}}{d_{c}^{\prime}} \quad(=2)
$$

in other words, in the case when the point $M$ coincides with the centroid (the point of intersection of the medians) of the triangle $A B C$.

b) Let the sides of the triangle $A B C$ be denoted by $a, b, c$, as usual; then, obviously (see, for example, Fig. 26 on p. 48),

$$
R_{a}+R_{b}>c, \quad R_{b}+R_{c}>a, \quad R_{c}+R_{a}>b
$$

and therefore

$$
R_{a}+R_{b}+R_{c}>\frac{a+b+c}{2}=p
$$

On the other hand (see problem 63),

$$
d_{a}^{\prime}+d_{b}^{\prime}+d_{c}^{\prime}\frac{p}{c}>1
$$

since $a+b>c$, and thus $2 p=a+b+c>2 c$.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_15011fcc7946713185f0g-295.jpg?height=484&width=896&top_left_y=754&top_left_x=242)

Fig. 266.

The inequality of the problem cannot be improved, and if $A B C$ is an isosceles triangle with a very large angle at the vertex $C$ and the point $M$ is very close to the midpoint of the side $A B$ (Fig. $266, a$ ), then

$$
R_{a} \approx \frac{c}{2}, \quad R_{b} \approx \frac{c}{2}, \quad R_{c} \approx 0 ; \quad d_{a}^{\prime} \approx \frac{c}{2}, \quad d_{b}^{\prime} \approx \frac{c}{2}, \quad d_{c}^{\prime} \approx 0
$$

!

$$
R_{a}+R_{b}+R_{c} \approx d_{a}^{\prime}+d_{b}^{\prime}+d_{c}^{\prime}
$$

where the ratio $\frac{R_{a}+R_{b}+R_{c}}{d_{a}^{\prime}+d_{b}^{\prime}+d_{c}^{\prime}}$ can be made arbitrarily close to 1. [Similarly, if $A B C$ is an isosceles triangle with a very small angle at the vertex $A$ and $M$ is a point very close to the side $A C$ and the vertex $C$ of this triangle (Fig. 266, b), then

$$
R_{a} \approx c, \quad R_{b} \approx 0, \quad R_{c} \approx 0 ; \quad d_{a}^{\prime} \approx 0, \quad d_{b}^{\prime} \approx 0, \quad d_{c}^{\prime} \approx c
$$

and

$$
R_{a}+R_{b}+R_{c} \approx d_{a}^{\prime}+d_{b}^{\prime}+d_{c}^{\prime}
$$

where the ratio $\frac{R_{a}+R_{b}+R_{c}}{d_{a}^{\prime}+d_{b}^{\prime}+d_{c}^{\prime}}$ can be made arbitrarily close to 1.]

question:
114. a) Prove the following theorem of Pappus ${ }^{1}$: let parallelograms $A B B_{1} A_{1}$ and $A C C_{1} A_{2}$ be constructed on the sides $A B$ and $A C$ of triangle $A B C$, with both these parallelograms lying outside the triangle $A B C$ (Fig. $28, \alpha$) or both lying on the same side of the line $A B$, respectively $A C$, as the triangle itself (Fig. 28, b); $D$ is the point of intersection of the lines $B_{1} A_{1}$ and $C_{1} A_{2}$; $B C C_{2} B_{2}$ is a parallelogram constructed on the side $B C$ such that $B B_{2} \# C C_{2} \# A D$. Prove that the area of the parallelogram $B C C_{2} B_{2}$ is equal to the sum of the areas of the parallelograms $A B B_{1} A_{1}$ and $A C C_{1} A_{2}$. [If angle $A$ of the triangle is a right angle and the parallelograms $A B B_{1} A_{1}$ and $A C C_{1} A_{2}$ are squares, then Pappus' theorem obviously reduces to the Pythagorean theorem; see Fig. 28, c.]

b)* Derive the result of problem 111 b) from Pappus' theorem.

Note. Pappus' theorem is closely related to the distributive (or distributive) property of the so-called skew (or pseudoscalar) product of vectors, for in the notation of Fig. $28, a$

$$

& S_{B A A_{1} B_{1}}=\overline{B A} \times \overline{B B}_{1}=\overline{B A} \times \overline{A A}_{1} \\
& S_{C A A_{2} C_{1}}=\overline{A C} \times \overline{A A_{2}} \text { and } S_{B C C_{2} B_{2}}=\overline{B C} \times B B_{2}=\overline{B C} \times \overline{A D}
\end{aligned}
$$

1) Pappus of Alexandria - an ancient Greek mathematician of the era of the decline of ancient mathematics (late 3rd century AD).
(See, for example, § 4 of the article by V. G. Boltyansky and I. M. Yaglom, Vectors and their applications in geometry, Encyclopedia of Elementary

& =S_{B A A_{1} B_{1}}+S_{C A A_{2} C_{1}} .

reference_solution:
114. a) Let the line $A D$ intersect the sides $B C$ and $B_{2} C_{2}$ of the parallelogram $B C C_{2} B_{2}$ at points $K$ and $L$; furthermore, let $E$ and $F$ be the points of intersection of the lines $B B_{2}$ and $A_{1} B_{1}$, $C C_{2}$ and $A_{2} C_{1}$. On the other hand, $B^{\prime} C^{\prime}=B C=a$ (since the segment $B^{\prime} C^{\prime}$ is symmetric to $B C$

question:
53. a) A circle is divided into $p$ equal sectors, where $p$ is a prime number. In how many different ways can these $p$ sectors be painted using $n$ colors, if it is allowed to paint several (and even all) sectors with the same color, and two colorings are considered different only if they cannot be made to coincide by rotating the circle?

b) Use the result from part a) to prove the following theorem of Fermat: if $p$ is a prime number, then $n^{p}-n$ is divisible by $p$ for any $n$.

For other proofs of Fermat's theorem, see, for example, the books by D. O. Shklyarsky, N. N. Chentsov, I. M. Yaglom, Selected Problems and Theorems of Elementary Mathematics, part 1 (Library of the Mathematical Circle, issue 1) and E. B. Dynkin and V. A. Uspenskii, Mathematical Conversations (Library of the Mathematical Circle, issue 6).
reference_solution:
53. a) Each of the $p$ sectors can be painted with $n$ colors. Therefore, two sectors can be painted in $n^{2}$ different ways (each of the $n$ ways to paint one sector can be combined with each of the $n$ ways to paint the second sector), three sectors can be painted in $n^{3}$ different ways (each of the $n^{2}$ ways to paint two sectors can be combined with each of the ways to paint the third), and so on; $p$ sectors can be painted in $n^{p}$ different ways. Here, however, any two colorings are considered different if at least one sector is painted differently. Some of these "different" colorings can be combined by rotating the circle and, therefore, should be considered as one.

Now let's count how many such "different" colorings result from rotating a specific coloring. First of all, it is clear that if all $p$ sectors are painted with one color (there will be as many such colorings as there are different colors, i.e., $n$), then no new coloring will result from any rotation of the circle. If, however, some sectors are painted differently,
then new colorings can result from rotating the circle by angles

$$
\frac{360^{\circ}}{p}, \frac{360^{\circ}}{p} \cdot 2, \frac{360^{\circ}}{p} \cdot 3, \ldots, \frac{360^{\circ}}{p}(p-1)
$$

(during such rotations, the sectors will transition into each other). We will show that for any coloring where at least two sectors are painted differently, none of the $p$ colorings obtained from the initial one by rotating the circle by $0^{\circ}$ (this

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_68334347b64402497ba5g-201.jpg?height=374&width=372&top_left_y=462&top_left_x=164)

Fig. 66. is the initial coloring), $\frac{360^{\circ}}{p}$, $\frac{360^{\circ}}{p} \cdot 2, \ldots, \frac{360^{\circ}}{p} \cdot(p-1)$, will coincide. (Note that for composite $p$ this is not true: for example, rotating the coloring shown in Fig. 66 by $\frac{360^{\circ}}{6} \cdot 2=\frac{360^{\circ}}{3}$ will result in the same coloring.) Indeed, suppose, for example, that rotating by angles $\frac{360^{\circ}}{p} k$ and $\frac{360^{\circ}}{p} m$, where $0 \leqslant k \leqslant(p-1), \quad 0 \leqslant m \leqslant(p-1)$, $k<m$, we get the same coloring. By rotating the circle by $\frac{360^{\circ}}{p} m$ and then by $\frac{360^{\circ}}{p} k$ in the opposite direction, we can see that the initial coloring transitions into itself upon rotating by $\frac{360^{\circ}}{p}(m-k)$. Therefore, this coloring also transitions into itself upon rotations by

$$
\frac{360^{\circ}}{p} \cdot 2(m-k), \frac{360^{\circ}}{p} \cdot 3(m-k), \ldots, \frac{360^{\circ}}{p} \cdot(p-1)(m-k)
$$

It is easy to see that upon rotations by

$$
0^{\circ}, \frac{360^{\circ}}{p}(m-k), \frac{360^{\circ}}{p} \cdot 2(m-k), \ldots, \frac{360^{\circ}}{p} \cdot(p-1)(m-k)
$$

(a total of $p$ angles!), the first sector will sequentially coincide with all the sectors. Otherwise, for some two rotations, for example, by $\frac{360^{\circ}}{p} \cdot q(m-k)$ and $\frac{360^{\circ}}{p} \cdot l(m-k)$, the first sector would have to occupy the same position (since there are only $p$ different possible positions, i.e., as many as there are rotations), which is impossible, as the difference

$$
\frac{360^{\circ}}{p} l(m-k)-\frac{360^{\circ}}{p} q(m-k)=\frac{360^{\circ}}{p}(l-q)(m-k)
$$

is not a multiple of $360^{\circ}$ (since $p$ is a prime number, and $l-q$ and $m-k$ are less than $p$). Thus, for the colorings obtained from the initial one by rotating by $\frac{360^{\circ}}{p} m$ and $\frac{360^{\circ}}{p} k$ to coincide, all sectors must be painted the same color as the first sector, i.e., all with the same color.

Thus, among the $n^{p}$ colorings, $n$ monochromatic colorings are counted once, and each of the remaining colorings is counted $p$ times. Therefore, the total number of different colorings is

$$
\frac{n^{p}-n}{p}+n
$$

b) Since the number of different colorings is always an integer, it follows that if $p$ is prime, then for any $n$ the number $n^{p}-n$ is divisible by $p$. This is Fermat's theorem.

question:
57. Factorial Binomial Theorem. Let us introduce the notation:

$$
a(a-h)(a-2 h) \ldots[a-(n-1) h]=a^{n \mid h}
$$

so that, in particular, $a^{n 10}=a^{n}, a^{1 / h}=a$. Prove that in these notations the following equality holds:

$$
(a+b)^{n h}=a^{n / h}+C_{n}^{1} a^{n-1 \mid h} b+C_{n}^{2} a^{n-2 / h} b^{\eta / h}+\ldots+b^{n \mid h}
$$

The theorem expressed by the last equality is called the factorial binomial theorem. It is clear that it contains as a special case (for $h=0$) the ordinary binomial theorem of Newton.
reference_solution:
57. The theorem is proved by mathematical induction in a way completely analogous to the usual proof of the binomial formula of Newton. It is easy to verify that for $n$, equal to 1 and 2, the factorial binomial theorem is true ${ }^{1}$ ). Now suppose that this theorem is true for the exponent $n$, i.e., that

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_68334347b64402497ba5g-216.jpg?height=95&width=933&top_left_y=1193&top_left_x=89)

and let us show that in this case the theorem will also hold for the exponent $n+1$. Indeed, multiply both sides of the equality expressing our theorem for the exponent $n$ by $a+b+n h$. In the left part, obviously, we will get $(a+b)^{n+1 \mid h}$. In the right part, we previously had a sum, the $i$-th

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_68334347b64402497ba5g-216.jpg?height=65&width=980&top_left_y=1471&top_left_x=74)

1) Note that we indicate here the exponent $n=2$ only as an illustration of our theorem. For the possibility of applying the method of mathematical induction, it is sufficient to convince ourselves that the theorem is true for $n=1$, and then immediately consider the transition from $n$ to $n+1$.
term multiplied by $a+b-n h$ will give us:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& C_{n}^{i} a^{n-i \mid h} b^{i \mid h}(a+b-n h)= \\
& \quad=C_{n}^{i} a^{n-i \mid h} b^{i \mid h}[(a-(n-i) h)+(b-i h)]= \\
& \quad=C_{n}^{i} a^{n-i \mid h}(a-(n-i) h) b^{i \mid h}+C_{n}^{i} a^{n-i \mid h} b^{i \mid h}(b-i h)= \\
& \quad=C_{n}^{i} a^{n-i+1 \mid h} b^{i \mid h}+C_{n}^{i} a^{n-i \mid h} b^{i+1 \mid h} .
\end{aligned}
$$

By the well-known relation $C_{n}^{i-1}+C_{n}^{i}=C_{n+1}^{l}$, it follows from this, just as in the case of the usual binomial theorem of Newton, that after multiplying the right side by $(a+b-n h)$ we will get a sum of terms of the form $C_{n+1}^{i} a^{n+1-\left.i\right|^{h}} b^{i \mid h}$. Thus, it is proved that if the factorial binomial theorem is true for the exponent $n$, then it is true for the exponent $n+1$. And since it is true for $n=1$, it follows that it is valid for any $n$.
