7.16. Point $O$ lies inside the polyhedron $A_{1} \ldots \ldots A_{n}$. Prove that there exist such positive (and therefore all non-zero) numbers $x_{1} \ldots \ldots x_{n}$ that $x_{1} \overrightarrow{O A}_{1}+\ldots+x_{n} \overrightarrow{O A}_{n}=\overrightarrow{0}$.

## § 4. Various Problems
reference_solution: 7.16. Let the extension of the ray $O A_{i}$ beyond point $O$ intersect the polyhedron at point $M; \boldsymbol{P}$ - one of the vertices of the face containing point $M; QR$ - the edge of this face, intersecting the extension of the ray $M P$ beyond point $M$. Then $\overrightarrow{O M}=p \overrightarrow{O P}+q \overrightarrow{O Q}+ \overrightarrow{O R}$, where $p, q, r \geqslant 0$. Since the vectors $\overrightarrow{O A}_{i}$ and $\overrightarrow{O M}$ are oppositely directed, then $\overrightarrow{O A}_{i}+\alpha \overrightarrow{O P}+\beta \overrightarrow{O Q}+\gamma \overrightarrow{O R}=\overrightarrow{0}$, where $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \geqslant 0, P, Q, R$ - some vertices of the polyhedron. Writing such equalities for all $i$ from 1 to $n$ and adding them, we obtain the required.

question: 7.17. Let a, b, c, and d be unit vectors directed from the center of a regular tetrahedron to its vertices, and u be an arbitrary vector. Prove that $(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{u}) \mathbf{a}+(\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{u}) \mathbf{b}+(\mathbf{c}, \mathbf{u}) \mathbf{c}+(\mathbf{d}, \mathbf{u}) \mathbf{d}=4 \mathbf{u} / 3$.
reference_solution:
7.17. First $p$ solution. Any vector $\mathbf{u}$ can be represented in the form $\mathbf{u}=\alpha \mathbf{a}+\beta \mathbf{b}+\gamma \mathbf{c}$; therefore, the proof is sufficient to conduct only for vectors $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}$, and $\mathbf{c}$. Since the center of a regular tetrahedron divides its median in the ratio $1: 3$, we have $(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})=(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c})=(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{d})=-1 / 3$. Considering that $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{0}$, we get $(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{a}) \mathbf{a}+(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) \mathbf{b}+(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c}) \mathbf{c}+(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{d}) \mathbf{d}=\mathbf{a}-(\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{d}) / 3=\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{a} / 3=4 \mathbf{a} / 3$. The proof for vectors $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ is conducted analogously.

Second solution. Consider the cube $A B C D A_{1} B_{1} C_{1} D_{1}$. It is clear that $A B_{1} C D_{1}$ is a regular tetrahedron. Introduce a rectangular coordinate system with the origin at the center of the cube and axes parallel to the edges of the cube. Then $\sqrt{3} \mathbf{a}=(1,1,1), \sqrt{3} \mathbf{b}=(-1,-1,1), \sqrt{3} \mathbf{c}=(-1,1,-1)$, and $\sqrt{3} \mathbf{d}=(1,-1,-1)$. Let $\mathbf{u}=(x, y, z)$. Simple but somewhat cumbersome calculations now lead to the required result.

question: 7.18. From point $M$, lying inside a regular tetrahedron, perpendiculars $M A_{i} (i=1,2$, $3,4)$ are dropped to its faces. Prove that $\overrightarrow{M A}_{1}+\overrightarrow{M A}_{2}+$ $+\overrightarrow{M A_{3}}+\overrightarrow{M A} A_{4}=4 \overrightarrow{M O} / 3$, where $O$ is the center of the tetrahedron.
reference_solution: 7.18. Drop perpendiculars $O B_{i}$ from point $O$ to the faces of the tetrahedron. Let $a_{i}$ be the unit vector in the direction of $\overrightarrow{O B}_{i}$. Then $\left(\overrightarrow{O M}, a_{i}\right) a_{i}+\overrightarrow{M A}_{i}=\overrightarrow{O B}_{i}$. Since the tetrahedron $B_{1} B_{2} B_{3} B_{i}$ is regular, the sum of the vectors $\overrightarrow{O B}_{i}$ is zero. Therefore, $\sum \overrightarrow{M A} A_{i}=\sum\left(\overrightarrow{M O}, \mathbf{a}_{i}\right) \mathbf{a}_{i}=4 \overrightarrow{M O} / 3$ (see problem 7.17).

question: 7.19. From a point $O$ lying inside a convex polyhedron, rays are drawn intersecting the planes of the faces and perpendicular to them. On these rays, from point $O$, vectors are laid off whose lengths are equal to the areas of the corresponding faces. Prove that the sum of these vectors is equal to zero.
reference_solution:
7.19. First solution. We will prove that the sum of the projections of all given vectors onto any line $l$ is zero. For this, consider the projection of the polyhedron onto a plane not perpendicular to the line $l$. The projection of the polyhedron is covered by the projections of its faces in two layers, as the faces can be divided into two types: "visible from above" and "visible from below" (faces projecting into segments can be ignored). Assigning the areas of the projections of the faces of one type a positive sign and the areas of the faces of the other type a negative sign, we get that the sum of the areas of the projections of the faces, taking into account the sign, is zero. Now, note that the area of the projection of a face is equal to the length of the projection of the corresponding vector onto the line $l$ (see problem 2.13), and for faces of different types, the projections of the vectors are oppositely directed. Therefore, the sum of the projections of the vectors onto the line $l$ is also zero.

Second solution. Let $X$ be a point inside the polyhedron, $h_{i}$ be the distance from it to the plane of the $i$-th face. Divide the polyhedron into pyramids with vertex $X$, the bases of which are its faces. The volume $V$ of the polyhedron is equal to the sum of the volumes of these pyramids, i.e., $3 V=\sum h_{i} S_{i}$, where $S_{i}$ is the area of the $i$-th face.

Furthermore, let $\mathbf{n}_{\mathbf{i}}$ be the unit vector of the inner normal to the $i$-th face, $M_{i}$ be an arbitrary point of this face. Then $h_{i} = \left(\overrightarrow{X M}_{i}, \mathbf{n}_{i}\right)$, so $3 V=\sum h_{i} S_{i}=\sum\left(\overrightarrow{X M}_{i}, S_{i} \mathbf{n}_{i}\right)=\sum(\overrightarrow{X O}, \left.S_{i} \mathbf{n}_{i}\right)+\sum\left(\overrightarrow{O M}_{i}, S_{i} \mathbf{n}_{i}\right)=\left(\overrightarrow{X O}, \sum S_{i} \mathbf{n}_{i}\right)+3 V$ (here $O$ is some fixed point of the polyhedron). Therefore, $\sum S_{i} \mathbf{n}_{i}=0$

question:
7.21. Let a, b, and c be arbitrary vectors. Prove that $|\mathbf{a}|+|\mathbf{b}|+|\mathbf{c}|+|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}| \geqslant$ $\geqslant|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}|+|\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}|+|\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{a}|$.

## § 5. Vector Product

The vector product of two vectors a and b is a vector c, the length of which is equal to the area of the parallelogram spanned by the vectors a and b, and it is directed perpendicular to a and b, such that the vectors a, b, and c form a right-handed triplet, i.e., have the same orientation as the thumb (a), index finger (b), and middle finger (c) of the right hand. Notation: $\mathbf{c}=[\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}]$; another notation: $\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}$.
reference_solution:
7.21. Let $a=|\mathrm{a}|, b=|\mathbf{b}|$ and $c=|\mathbf{c}|$. Let $x, y, z$ be the cosines of the angles between vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{c}$, $\mathbf{c}$ and $\mathbf{a}$. The difference between the left and right parts of the required inequality is $a+b+c+\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+2(a b x+b c y+a c z)}-$ $-\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}+2 a b x}-\sqrt{b^{2}+c^{2}+2 b c y}-\sqrt{c^{2}+a^{2}+2 a c z}=$ $=f(x, y, z)$. The numbers $x, y$ and $z$ are related by some inequalities, but we need to prove that $f(x, y, z) \geqslant 0$ for all $x$, $y, z$, not exceeding 1 in absolute value.

$$
\text { The function } \quad \varphi(t)=\sqrt{p+t}-\sqrt{q+t}=\frac{p-q}{\sqrt{p+t}+\sqrt{q+t}}
$$

is monotonic in $t$. Therefore, for fixed $y$ and $z$, the function $f(x, y, z)$ achieves its minimum value when $x=$ $= \pm 1$. Fixing then $x= \pm 1$ and $z$; in this case, the function $f$ achieves its minimum value when $y= \pm 1$. Finally, fixing $x= \pm 1$ and $y= \pm 1$, we obtain that the function $f$ achieves its minimum value when the numbers $x, y, z$ are $\pm 1$. In this case, the vectors $\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{b}$, and $\mathbf{c}$ are collinear, and the inequality is easily verified.

question:
7.22. Prove that
a) $[\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}]=-[\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{a}]$;

b) $[\lambda \mathbf{a}, \mu \mathbf{b}]=\lambda \mu[\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}]$

c) $[a, b+c]=[a, b]+[a, c]$,
reference_solution:
7.22. Assertions a) and b) easily follow from the definition.

c) First solution. Introduce a coordinate system $O x y z$, directing the axis $O x$ along the vector a. It can be verified that the vector product of vectors $\mathbf{2}=(a, 0,0)$ and $\mathbf{u}=(x, y, z)$ is the vector $(0, -a z, a y)$. Indeed, this vector is perpendicular to both vectors, and its length is equal to the product of the length of vector a by the length of the height dropped from the end of vector a to vector a; the consistency of orientations should be verified for different sign combinations of the numbers $y$ and $z$.

Now, the required equality can be easily verified by expressing the coordinates of the vector products involved through the coordinates of vectors b and c.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_3f2bc5f5a1af26514cfag-147.jpg?height=53&width=894&top_left_y=1364&top_left_x=224)
where $\overrightarrow{A B}=\mathbf{b}, \overrightarrow{B C}=\mathbf{c}$ and $\overrightarrow{A A_{1}}=\mathbf{a}$. Since $\overrightarrow{A C}=\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}$, the specified equality means that the sum of the three vectors of the external (or internal) normals to the lateral faces of the prism, the lengths of which are equal to the areas of the corresponding faces, is zero. Let $A^{\prime} B^{\prime} C^{\prime}$ be the section of the prism by a plane perpendicular to the lateral edge. After rotating the normal vectors by $90^{\circ}$ in the plane $A^{\prime} B^{\prime} C^{\prime}$, they transform into vectors $\overrightarrow{A^{\prime} B^{\prime}}, d \overrightarrow{B^{\prime}} C^{\prime \prime}$, and $d \overrightarrow{C^{\prime} A^{\prime}}$, where $d$ is the length of the lateral edge of the prism. It is clear that the sum of these vectors is zero.

question: 7.23. Vectors a and b have coordinates $\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}\right)$ and ( $b_{1}, b_{2}, b_{3}$ ). Prove that the vector [a, b] has coordinates $\left(a_{2} b_{3}-a_{3} b_{2}, a_{3} b_{1}-a_{1} b_{3}, a_{1} b_{2}-a_{2} b_{1}\right)$.
reference_solution: 7.23. Let $\mathbf{a}=a_{1} \mathbf{e}_{1}+a_{2} \mathbf{e}_{2}+a_{3} \mathbf{e}_{3}$ and $\mathbf{b}=b_{1} \mathbf{e}_{1}+b_{2} \mathbf{e}_{2}+b_{3} \mathbf{e}_{3}$, where $\mathbf{e}_{1}, \mathbf{e}_{2}$ and $\mathbf{e}_{3}$ are unit vectors directed along the coordinate axes. To solve the problem, you can use the results of problems 7.22, a - c, after noting that $\left[\mathbf{e}_{1}, \mathbf{e}_{2}\right]=\mathbf{e}_{3},\left[\mathbf{e}_{2}, \mathbf{e}_{3}\right]=\mathbf{e}_{1}$ and $\left[\mathbf{e}_{3}, \mathbf{e}_{1}\right]=\mathbf{e}_{2}$.

question:
7.25. a) Prove that $[a, [b, c]] + [b, [c, a]] + [c, [a, b]] = 0$ (Jacobi identity).

b) Let point $O$ lie inside triangle $ABC$ and $\mathbf{a} = \overrightarrow{OA}$, $\mathbf{b} = \overrightarrow{OB}$, and $\mathbf{c} = \overrightarrow{OC}$. Prove that the Jacobi identity for vectors $\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{b}$, and $\mathbf{c}$ is equivalent to the equality

$$
\mathbf{a} S_{BOC} + \mathbf{b} S_{COA} + \mathbf{c} S_{OAB} = \mathbf{0}
$$
reference_solution:
7.25. a) According to problem 7.24, \(\mathbf{a} \quad [a,[b, c]]=b(c, a)-c(a, b)\), \([\mathbf{b},[\mathbf{c}, \mathbf{a}]]=\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})-\mathbf{a}(\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c})\) and \([\mathbf{c},[\mathrm{a}, \mathbf{b}]]=\mathrm{a}(\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c})-b(a, c)\). By adding these equalities, we obtain the required result.

b) The vectors \([\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}]\), \([\mathbf{c}, \mathbf{a}]\) and \([\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}]\) are perpendicular to the plane \(ABC\) and are collinear, with their lengths equal to \(2 S_{BOC}\), \(2 S_{COA}\) and \(2 S_{AOB}\). Therefore, the vectors \([a, [b, \mathbf{c}]\), \([\mathbf{b},[\mathbf{c}, \mathbf{a}]\) and \([\mathbf{c},[\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}]\) after a \(90^{\circ}\) rotation in the plane \(ABC\) transform into the vectors \(2 \mathrm{a} S_{\text{BOC}}\), \(2 \mathrm{~b} S_{COA}\) and \(2 \mathrm{c} S_{AOB}\).

question: 7.26. The angles at the vertices of a spatial hexagon are right angles, and it has no parallel sides. Prove that the common perpendiculars to pairs of opposite sides of the hexagon are perpendicular to one line.
reference_solution: 7.26. Let a, b and c be vectors defining three non-adjacent sides of a hexagon; $a_{1}, b_{1}$ and $c_{1}$ - vectors of the opposite sides. Since vector $\mathbf{a}_{1}$ is perpendicular to vectors $\mathbf{b}$ and c, then $\mathbf{a}_{1}=\lambda[\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}]$. Therefore, the common perpendicular to vectors a and $\mathbf{a}_{1}$ is given by the vector $\mathbf{n}_{a}=[\mathrm{a},[\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{c}]]$. From the Jacobi identity, it follows that $\mathbf{n}_{a}+\mathbf{n}_{b}+\mathbf{n}_{c}=\mathbf{0}$, i.e., these vectors are perpendicular to one line.

question:
7.28. a) Prove that the planes passing through the bisectors of the faces of a trihedral angle $SABC$ and perpendicular to the planes of these faces intersect along a single line, and that this line is defined by the vector $[\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}]+[\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}]+[\mathbf{c}, \mathbf{a}]$, where $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}$, and $\mathbf{c}$ are unit vectors directed along the edges $SA, SB$, and $SC$.

b) On the edges of a trihedral angle with vertex $O$, points $A_{1}, A_{2}$, and $A_{3}$ are taken such that $OA_{1}=OA_{2}=OA_{3}$. Prove that the bisector planes of its dihedral angles intersect along a line defined by the vector $\overrightarrow{OA}_{1} \sin \alpha_{1}+\overrightarrow{OA}_{2} \sin \alpha_{2}+\overrightarrow{OA}_{3} \sin \alpha_{3}$, where $\alpha_{i}$ is the measure of the plane angle opposite the edge $OA_{i}$.
reference_solution:
7.28. a) Let's prove, for example, that the vector $[a, b]+[b, c]+[c, a]$ lies in the plane П, passing through the bisector of the edge $SAB$ and perpendicular to this edge. The plane II is perpendicular to the vector $a - b$, so it contains the vector $[c, a - b]$. In addition, the plane П contains the vector $[a, b]$, so it contains the vector $[a, b]+[c, a-b]=[a, b]+[b, c]+[c, a]$.

b) Let $\overrightarrow{OA}=\overrightarrow{OA}_{1} \sin \alpha_{1}+\overrightarrow{OA}_{2} \sin \alpha_{2}+\overrightarrow{OA}_{3} \sin \alpha_{3}$. Let's prove, for example, that the plane $OA_{2}A$ bisects the angle between the faces $OA_{2}A_{1}$ and $OA_{2}A_{3}$. For this, it is sufficient to check that the perpendicular to the plane $OA_{2}A$ is the bisector of the angle between the normals to the planes $OA_{2}A_{1}$ and $OA_{2}A_{3}$. The normals to these three planes are given by the vectors $\overrightarrow{OA}_{2} \times \overrightarrow{OA}=\overrightarrow{OA}_{2} \times \overrightarrow{OA}_{1} \sin \alpha_{1}+\overrightarrow{OA}_{2} \times \overrightarrow{OA}_{3} \sin \alpha_{3}$, $\overrightarrow{OA}_{2} \times \overrightarrow{OA}_{1}$, and $\overrightarrow{OA}_{2} \times \overrightarrow{OA}_{3}$. It is easy to see that if $|\mathrm{a}|=|\mathbf{b}|$, then the vector $a + b$ defines the bisector of the plane between the vectors $a$ and $b$. Therefore, it remains to prove that the lengths of the vectors $\overrightarrow{OA}_{2} \times \overrightarrow{OA}_{1} \sin \alpha_{1}$ and $\overrightarrow{OA}_{2} \times \overrightarrow{OA}_{3} \sin \alpha_{3}$ are equal. But $\left|\overrightarrow{OA}_{2} \times \overrightarrow{OA}_{1}\right|=\sin A_{1}OA_{2}=\sin \alpha_{3}$ and $\left|\overrightarrow{OA}_{2} \times \overrightarrow{OA}_{3}\right|=\sin \alpha_{1}$, which completes the proof. The proof for the planes $OA_{1}A$ and $OA_{3}A$ is analogous.

question:
7.30. Prove that vectors with coordinates $\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}\right),\left(b_{1}, b_{2}, b_{3}\right)$ and $\left(c_{1}, c_{2}, c_{3}\right)$ are parallel to one plane if and only if

$$
a_{1} b_{2} c_{3}+a_{2} b_{3} c_{1}+a_{3} b_{1} c_{2}=a_{1} b_{3} c_{2}+a_{2} b_{1} c_{3}+a_{3} b_{2} c_{1}
$$

For those familiar with the concept of matrix multiplication, let us explain the connection between the vector product and the commutator of two matrices. Each vector $\mathrm{a}=\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}\right)$ in three-dimensional space can be associated with a skew-symmetric matrix

$$
A=\left(\begin{array}{rrr}
0 & -a_{3} & a_{2} \\
a_{3} & 0 & -a_{1} \\
-a_{2} & a_{1} & 0
\end{array}\right)
$$

Let vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ be associated with matrices $A$ and $B$. Consider the matrix $[A, B]=A B-B A$ - the commutator of matrices $A$ and $B$. Simple calculations show that the vector $[\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}]$ is associated with the matrix $[A, B]$.

## § 6. Symmetry

Symmetry with respect to a point $A$ is a transformation of space that maps a point $X$ to a point $X^{\prime}$ such that $A$ is the midpoint of the segment $X X^{\prime}$. Other names for this transformation are central symmetry with center $A$ or simply symmetry with center $A$.
reference_solution:
7.30. Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their scalar triple product is zero. Using the formula from problem 7.23, we get that the scalar triple product of the given vectors is

$$
\left(a_{2} b_{3}-a_{8} b_{2}\right) c_{1}+\left(a_{3} b_{1}-a_{1} b_{3}\right) c_{2}+\left(a_{1} b_{2}-a_{2} b_{1}\right) c_{3}
$$

question: 7.31. Given a tetrahedron and a point $N$. Through each edge of the tetrahedron, a plane is drawn parallel to the segment connecting point $N$ with the midpoint of the opposite edge. Prove that all six of these planes intersect at one point.
reference_solution: 7.31. Let $M$ be the center of mass of the tetrahedron, $A$ be the midpoint of the edge through which the plane П passes, $B$ be the midpoint of the opposite edge, and $N^{\prime}$ be the point symmetric to $N$ with respect to point $M$. Since point $M$ is the midpoint of segment $A B$ (see problem 14.3), then $A N^{\prime} \| B N$, which means that point $N^{\prime}$ belongs to the plane П. Therefore, all five planes pass through point $N_{1}$.

question:
7.32. a) Through the midpoint of each edge of a tetrahedron, a plane perpendicular to the opposite edge is drawn. Prove that all five of these planes intersect at one point (the Monge point).

b) Prove that if the Monge point lies in the plane of any face of the tetrahedron, then the foot of the altitude dropped to this face lies on its circumscribed circle.

Symmetry with respect to a plane \(\Pi\) is a transformation of space that translates a point \(X\) into a point \(X'\) such that the plane \(\Pi\) passes through the midpoint of the segment \(XX'\) and is perpendicular to it.
reference_solution:
7.32. a) Let $A$ be the midpoint of edge $a$, and $B$ be the midpoint of the opposite edge $b$. Further, let $M$ be the center of mass of the tetrahedron, $O$ be the center of its circumscribed sphere, and $O^{\prime}$ be the point symmetric to $O$ with respect to point $M$. Since point $M$ is the midpoint of segment $A B$ (Problem 14.3), it follows that $O^{\prime} A \| O B$. But segment $O B$ is perpendicular to edge $b$, so $O^{\prime} A \perp b$, which means that point $O^{\prime}$ lies in the plane passing through the midpoint of edge $a$ and perpendicular to edge $b$. Therefore, all six planes pass through point $O_{2}$.

b) Suppose the Monge point $O^{\prime}$ lies in the plane of face $A B C$. Draw a plane $\Pi$, parallel to this face, through vertex $D$. Since the center $O$ of the circumscribed sphere of the tetrahedron is symmetric to point $O^{\prime}$ with respect to its center of mass $M$, and point $M$ divides the median of the tetrahedron drawn from vertex $D$ in the ratio $3:1$ (Problem 14.3), it follows that point $O$ is equidistant from planes $\Pi$ and $A B C$. It remains to note that if the center of the sphere is equidistant from two parallel section planes, then the projection of the circle of intersection on the second section plane coincides with the second circle of intersection.

question: 7.36. In a convex 5-sided pyramid $S A B C D E$, the lateral edges are equal and the dihedral angles at the lateral edges are equal. Prove that this pyramid is regular.
reference_solution:
7.36. Let $O$ be the projection of vertex $S$ onto the plane of the base of the pyramid. Since the vertices of the base of the pyramid are equidistant from point $S$, they are also equidistant from point $O$, which means they lie on a circle with center $O$. Now, let us assume that $B C = A E$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of side $A B$. Since $M O \perp A B$ and $S O \perp A B$, segment $A B$ is perpendicular to the plane $S M O$, and thus, by symmetry relative to the plane $S M O$, segment $S A$ is transformed into segment $S B$. The dihedral angles at edges $S A$ and $S B$ are equal, so the plane $S A E$ under this symmetry is transformed into the plane $S B C$. Since the circle on which the vertices of the base of the pyramid lie is transformed into itself under this symmetry, point $E$ is transformed into point $C$.

Similarly, it can be proven that $B C = E D = A B = D C$.

question:
7.38. Prove that under symmetry with respect to a line defined by vector $\mathbf{b}$, vector $\mathbf{a}$ transforms into the vector

$$
2 \mathbf{b} \frac{(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})}{(\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{b})} - \mathbf{a}
$$
reference_solution: 7.38. Let $\mathbf{a}^{\prime}$ be the image of vector $\mathbf{a}$ under the considered symmetry; and $\mathbf{u}$ be the projection of vector $\mathbf{a}$ onto the given line. Then $\mathbf{a}^{\prime}+\mathbf{a}=2 \mathbf{u} \quad$ and $\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{b} \frac{(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b})}{(\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{b})}$.

question:
7.40. Prove that no body in space can have a non-zero even number of axes of symmetry.

## § 7. Homothety

Homothety is a transformation of space that maps a point $X$ to a point $X^{\prime}$, with the property that $\overrightarrow{O X^{\prime}}=k \overrightarrow{O X}$ (the point $O$ and the number $k$ are fixed). The point $O$ is called the center of homothety, and the number $k$ is called the coefficient of homothety.
reference_solution: 7.40. Let's fix some axis of symmetry $l$. We will prove that the other axes of symmetry are divided into pairs. First, note that under reflection in the line $l$, an axis of symmetry is transformed into an axis of symmetry. If an axis of symmetry $l^{\prime}$ does not intersect $l$ or intersects it at an angle other than a right angle, then the pair of $l^{\prime}$ will be the axis symmetric to it with respect to $l$. If the axis $l^{\prime}$ intersects $l$ at a right angle, then the pair of $l^{\prime}$ will be the line perpendicular to both $l$ and $l^{\prime}$ and passing through their point of intersection. Indeed, from problem 7.39 it follows that this line is an axis of symmetry.

question: 7.41. Let $r$ and $R$ be the radii of the inscribed and circumscribed spheres of a tetrahedron. Prove that $R \geqslant 3 r$.
reference_solution: 7.41. Let $M$ be the center of mass of the tetrahedron. Under a homothety with center $M$ and coefficient $-1 / 3$, the vertices of the tetrahedron are transformed into the centers of mass of its faces, and thus, the circumscribed sphere of the tetrahedron is transformed into a sphere of radius $R / 3$, intersecting all the faces of the tetrahedron (or touching them). To prove that the radius of this sphere is not less than $r$, it is sufficient to draw planes parallel to the faces of the tetrahedron and tangent to the parts of this sphere lying outside the tetrahedron. Indeed, in this case, this sphere will be inscribed in a tetrahedron similar to the original one and not smaller than it.

question: 7.42. In the plane of a lateral face of a regular quadrilateral pyramid, an arbitrary figure Ф is taken. Let $\Phi_{1}$ be the projection of $Ф$ onto the base of the pyramid, and $\Phi_{2}$ be the projection of $\Phi_{1}$ onto the adjacent lateral face. Prove that the figures Ф and $\Phi_{2}$ are similar.
reference_solution: 7.42. Let $S A B$ be the original face of the pyramid $S A B C D$, and $S A D$ be the second face. Rotate the planes of these faces around the lines $A B$ and $A D$ so that they coincide with the plane of the base (the rotation is performed towards the smaller angle). Consider a coordinate system with the origin at point $A$ and axes $O x$ and $O y$ directed along the lines $A B$ and $A D$. The first projection defines a transformation where the point $(x, y)$ transitions to $(x, k y)$, where $k=\cos \alpha$ ($\alpha$ is the angle between the base and the lateral face); during the second projection, the point $(x, y)$ transitions to $(k x, y)$. Therefore, the composition of these transformations translates the point $(x, y)$ to $(k x, k y)$.

question: 7.43. Prove that inside any convex polyhedron $M$, two polyhedra similar to it with a coefficient of $1 / 2$ can be placed so that they do not intersect.
reference_solution: 7.43. Let $A$ and $B$ be the points of the polyhedron that are farthest from each other. Then the images of the polyhedron $M$ under homotheties with centers at $A$ and $B$ and coefficient $1 / 2$ define the desired arrangement. Indeed, these polyhedra do not intersect, as they are located on opposite sides of the plane passing through the midpoint of segment $A B$ and perpendicular to it. Moreover, they lie inside $M$, since $M$ is a convex polyhedron.

question:
7.46. Let $A_{i}^{\prime}$ and $A_{i}^{\prime \prime}$ be the projections of the vertices of the tetrahedron $A_{1} A_{2} A_{3} A_{4}$ onto the planes $\Pi^{\prime}$ and $\Pi^{\prime \prime}$. Prove that one of these planes can be moved in space so that the 4 lines $A_{i}^{\prime} A_{i}^{\prime \prime}$ become parallel.

Definition. The composition of transformations $F$ and $G$ is called the transformation $G \circ F$, which maps a point $X$ to the point $G(F(X))$.
reference_solution: 7.46. We can assume that the planes $\Pi^{\prime}$ and $\Pi^{\prime \prime}$ are not parallel, otherwise the statement is obvious. Let $l$ be the line of intersection of these planes, and $A_{i}^{*}$ be the point of intersection of the line $l$ with the plane $A_{i} A_{i}^{\prime} A_{i}^{\prime \prime}$. The plane $A_{i} A_{i}^{\prime} A_{i}^{\prime \prime}$ is perpendicular to the line $l$, so $l \perp A_{i}^{\prime} A_{i}^{*}$ and $l \perp A_{i}^{\prime \prime} A_{i}^{*}$. Therefore, if the plane $\Pi^{\prime}$ is rotated around the line $l$ so that it coincides with the plane $\Pi^{\prime \prime}$, then the lines $A_{i}^{\prime} A_{i}^{\prime \prime}$ will be perpendicular to the line $l$.

question: 7.47. Prove that the composition of reflections with respect to two planes intersecting along a line $l$ is a rotation about the line $l$, and that the angle of this rotation is twice the angle of the rotation about the line $l$ that maps the first plane to the second.
reference_solution: 7.47. Consider a section by a plane perpendicular to the line $l$. The required statement then follows from the corresponding planimetric statement about the composition of two axial symmetries (see Prasolov, 8.14, b).

question:
7.48. Prove that the composition of a symmetry with respect to a point $O$ and a rotation about a line $l$ passing through $O$ is also the composition of some rotation about the line $l$ and a symmetry with respect to a plane $\Pi$ passing through the point $O$ and perpendicular to $l$.

Definition. A movement is a transformation that maps each point in space to a point in space such that if $A^{\prime}$ and $B^{\prime}$ are the images of points $A$ and $B$, then $A B = A^{\prime} B^{\prime}$, i.e., a movement is a transformation of space that preserves distances.

A movement that leaves four points in space, not lying in the same plane, fixed, leaves all other points in space fixed as well. Therefore, any movement is determined by the images of four points not lying in the same plane.
reference_solution: 7.48. Let $A$ be some point, $B$ be its image under reflection about point $O$, $C$ be the image of point $B$ under rotation by angle $\varphi$ about line $l$, and $D$ be the image of point $C$ under reflection about plane $P$. Then point $D$ is the image of point $A$ under rotation by angle $180^{\circ}+\varphi$ about line $l$.

question:
7.49. a) Guess that any motion of space is a composition of no more than four symmetries with respect to planes.

b) Prove that any motion of space having a fixed point \( O \) is a composition of no more than three symmetries with respect to planes.

Definition. A motion that is a composition of an even number of symmetries with respect to planes is called a motion of the first kind or a motion that preserves the orientation of space. A motion that is a composition of an odd number of symmetries with respect to planes is called a motion of the second kind or a motion that changes the orientation of space.

We will not prove that a composition of an even number of symmetries with respect to planes cannot be represented as a composition of an odd number of symmetries with respect to planes.
reference_solution:
7.49. a) Let $T$ be some transformation that maps point $A$ to point $B$, different from $A$; $S$ - the symmetry with respect to the plane $\Pi$ passing through the midpoint of segment $AB$ and perpendicular to it. Then $S \circ T(A) = S(B) = A$, i.e., $A$ is a fixed point of the transformation $S \circ T$. Moreover, if $T(X) = X$ for some point $X$, then $AX = T(A)T(X) = BX$. Therefore, point $X$ belongs to the plane $\Pi$, and thus $S(X) = X$. Hence, point $A$ and all fixed points of the transformation $T$ are fixed points of the transformation $S \circ T$.

Take 4 points in space, not lying in the same plane, and consider their images under a given transformation $P$. It is possible to find $k (k \leqslant 4)$ such transformations $S_{1}, \ldots, S_{k}$, which are symmetries with respect to planes, such that the transformation $S_{1} \circ \ldots \circ S_{k} \circ P$ leaves the chosen 4 points fixed, i.e., this transformation leaves all points in space fixed. Therefore, $P = S_{k} \circ \ldots \circ S_{1}$; to prove this statement, one can use the fact that if $S \circ F = G$, where $S$ is a symmetry with respect to a plane, then $S \circ C = S \circ S \circ F = F$, since $S \circ S$ is the identity transformation.

b) For a transformation that leaves point $O$ fixed, one of the 4 points, the images of which determine this transformation, can be taken as point $O$. In all other respects, the proof is analogous to the solution of part a).

question:
7.50. a) Prove that any motion of the first kind, having a fixed point, is a rotation about some axis.

b) Prove that any motion of the second kind, having a fixed point, is a composition of a rotation about some axis (possibly by a zero angle) and a reflection in a plane perpendicular to this axis.
reference_solution:
7.50. a) According to problem $7.49,5$, any motion of the first kind, having a fixed point, is a composition of two symmetries with respect to planes, i.e., a rotation about the line where these planes intersect (see problem 7.47$)$.

b) Let $T$ be the given motion of the second kind, and $I$ be the symmetry with respect to the fixed point $O$ of this transformation. Since $I$ can be represented as a composition of three symmetries with respect to three mutually perpendicular planes passing through the point $O$, $I$ is a transformation of the second kind. Therefore, $\boldsymbol{P}=T \circ I$ is a transformation of the first kind, and $O$ is a fixed point of this transformation. Consequently, $P$ is a rotation about some axis $l$ passing through the point $O$. Therefore, the transformation $T=T \circ I \circ I=P \circ I$ is a composition of a rotation about some line $l$ and a symmetry with respect to a plane perpendicular to $l$ (see problem 7.48).

question:
7.51. A ball lying in the corner of a rectangular box rolls along the side of the box to another corner, with the same point of the ball always touching the side wall. From the second corner, the ball rolls to the third, then to the fourth, and finally returns to the initial corner. During this process, a point $X$ on the surface of the ball moves to point $X_{1}$. After a similar rolling, point $X_{1}$ moves to $X_{2}$, and $X_{2}$ to $X_{3}$. Prove that the points $X, X_{1}, X_{2}$, and $X_{3}$ lie in the same plane.

## § 9. Reflection of Light Rays
reference_solution: 7.51. After rolling, any point $A$ on the surface of the pair moves to the point $T(A)$, where $T$ is a first-order motion having a fixed point - the center of the sphere. According to problem $7.50, \mathrm{a}$, the transformation $T$ is a rotation about some axis $l$. Consequently, the points $X_{1}, X_{2}$ and $X_{3}$ lie in a plane passing through the point $X$ perpendicular to the line $l$.

question: 7.52. A ray of light enters a trihedral angle and is reflected from all three faces once. Prove that in this case, it simply changes direction.
reference_solution: 7.52. Let us associate a rectangular coordinate system Oxyz with the given trihedral angle. A ray of light moving in the direction of the vector ( $x, y, z$ ) will, after reflection from the plane $Oxy$, be traveling in the direction of the vector ( $x, y, -z$ ). Thus, after reflecting from all three faces, it will be moving in the direction of the vector ( $-x, -y, -z$ ).

question:
8.1. a) The areas of all faces of a convex polyhedron are equal. Prove that the sum of the distances from its internal point to the planes of the faces does not depend on the position of the point.

b) The heights of a tetrahedron are \( h_{1}, h_{2}, h_{3} \) and \( h_{4} \); \( d_{1}, d_{2}, d_{3} \) and \( d_{4} \) are the distances from an arbitrary internal point to the corresponding faces. Prove that

$$
\sum\left(d_{i} / h_{i}\right)=1
$$
reference_solution:
8.1. a) Let \( V \) be the volume of a polyhedron, \( S \) be the area of its face, and \( h_{i} \) be the distance from a point \( X \), located inside the polyhedron, to the \( i \)-th face. By cutting the polyhedron into pyramids with apex \( X \) and bases being its faces, we get \( V = S h_{1} / 3 + \ldots + S h_{n} / 3. \) Therefore, \( h_{1} + \ldots + h_{n} = 3 V / S \).

b) Let \( V \) be the volume of a tetrahedron. Since \( h_{i} = 3 V / S_{i} \), where \( S_{i} \) is the area of the \( i \)-th face, then \( \sum\left(d_{i} / h_{i}\right) = \left(\sum d_{i} S_{i}\right) / 3 V \). It remains to note that \( d_{i} S_{i} / 3 = V_{i} \), where \( V_{i} \) is the volume of the pyramid with apex at the chosen point of the tetrahedron and base being the \( i \)-th face, and \( \sum V_{i} = V \).

question:
8.2. a) Prove that a convex polyhedron cannot have exactly 7 edges.

b) Prove that a convex polyhedron can have any number of edges greater than 5 and different from 7.
reference_solution:
8.2. a) Suppose a polyhedron has only triangular faces, and their number is $\Gamma$. Then the number of edges of the polyhedron is $3 \Gamma / 2$, i.e., it is divisible by 3. If the polyhedron has a face with more than three sides, then the number of its edges is at least 8.

b) Let $n \geqslant 3$. Then $2 n$ edges has an $n$-sided pyramid, and $2 n+3$ edges has the polyhedron that results if a triangular pyramid is cut off from the $n$-sided pyramid by a plane passing near one of the vertices of the base.

question: 8.3. A plane intersecting a circumscribed polyhedron divides it into two parts with volumes $V_{1}$ and $V_{2}$; it divides its surface into two parts with areas $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$. Prove that $V_{1}: S_{1}=V_{2}: S_{2}$ if and only if the plane passes through the center of the inscribed sphere.
reference_solution:
8.3. For definiteness, assume that the center $O$ of the inscribed sphere belongs to the part of the polyhedron with volume $V_{1}$.

Consider a pyramid with vertex $O$, the base of which is the section of the polyhedron by the given plane. Let $V$ be the volume of this pyramid. Then $V_{1}-V=r S_{1} / 3$ and $V_{2}+V=r S_{2} / 3$, where $r$ is the radius of the inscribed sphere (see problem 3,7). Therefore, $S_{i}$ : $: S_{2}=V_{1}: V_{2}$ if and only if ( $\left.V_{1}-V\right):\left(V_{2}+\right.$ $+V)=S_{1}: S_{2}=V_{1}: V_{2}$, which means $V=0$, i.e., the point $O$ belongs to the cutting plane.

question: 8.4. In a convex polyhedron, an even number of edges emanate from each vertex. Prove that any section of it by a plane, not containing vertices, is a polygon with an even number of sides.
reference_solution: 8.4. The number of lines connecting the vertices of a polyhedron is finite, so the given plane can be slightly moved so that during the movement it does not intersect any vertex and in its new position it is not parallel to any line connecting the vertices of the polyhedron. We will shift this plane parallel until it exits the polyhedron. The number of vertices of the section will change only when the plane passes through the vertices of the polyhedron, and each time it will pass through only one vertex. If on one side of this plane there are $m$ edges emanating from the vertex, and on the other side $n$ edges, then the number of sides of the section changes by $n-m=(n+m)-2 m=2 k-2 m$, i.e., by an even number. Since after the plane exits the polyhedron, the number of sides of the section is zero, the number of sides of the initial section is even.

question: 8.5. Prove that if any vertex of a convex polyhedron is connected by edges to all other vertices, then this polyhedron is a tetrahedron.
reference_solution:
8.5. If any vertex of a polyhedron is connected by edges to all other vertices, then all faces are triangular.

Consider two faces $A B C$ and $A B D$ with a common edge $A B$. Suppose the polyhedron is not a tetrahedron. Then it has another vertex $E$, different from the vertices of the considered faces. Since points $C$ and $D$ lie on different sides of the plane $A B E$, the triangle $A B E$ is not a face of the polyhedron. If cuts are made along the edges $A B$, $B E$, and $E A$, the surface of the polyhedron will be split into two parts (this would be incorrect for a non-convex polyhedron), and points $C$ and $D$ will lie in different parts. Therefore, points $C$ and $D$ cannot be connected by an edge, as otherwise the cut would not intersect it, but the edges of a convex polyhedron cannot intersect at internal points.

question:
8.7. Each face of a convex polyhedron has a center of symmetry.

a) Prove that it can be dissected into parallelepipeds.

b) Prove that it has a center of symmetry.
reference_solution:
8.7. a) Let's take an arbitrary face of the given polyhedron and its edge $r_{1}$. Since the face is centrally symmetric, it contains an edge $r_{2}$, equal and parallel to $r_{1}$. The face adjacent to the edge $r_{2}$ also has an edge $r_{3}$, equal and parallel to $r_{1}$, and so on. In the end, we get a "belt" of faces defined by the edge $r_{1}$ (it will necessarily close on the edge $r_{1}$). If we cut this "belt" from the surface of the polyhedron, two "caps" $\Pi_{\mathrm{i}}$ and $\Pi_{2}$ will remain. Move the "cap" $\Pi_{i}$ inside the polyhedron by the vector defined by the edge $r_{1}$, and cut the polyhedron along the surface $\mathrm{T}\left(\Pi_{1}\right)$ formed in this way. The part of the polyhedron enclosed between $\Pi_{\mathrm{i}}$ and $\mathrm{T}\left(\Pi_{1}\right)$ can be cut into prisms, and by cutting their bases into parallelograms (see Prasolov, part II, 24.18), we obtain a partition into parallelepipeds. The faces of the polyhedron enclosed between $\mathrm{T}\left(\Pi_{1}\right)$ and $\Pi_{2}$ are centrally symmetric, and the number of its edges is less than that of the original polyhedron by the number of edges of the "belt" parallel to $r_{i}$. Therefore, in a finite number of such iterations, the polyhedron can be cut into parallelepipeds.

b) As in part a), consider the "belt" and "cap" defined by the edge $r$ of the face $\Gamma$. The projection of the polyhedron onto a plane perpendicular to the edge $r$ is a convex polyhedron, the sides of which are the projections of the faces included in the "belt". The projections of the faces of one "cap" form a partition of this polygon into centrally symmetric polygons. Therefore, this polygon is centrally symmetric (see Prasolov, part II, 24.19), which means that for the face $\Gamma$ there exists a face $\Gamma^{\prime}$, the projection of which is parallel to the projection of $\Gamma$, i.e., these faces are parallel; it is also clear that a convex polyhedron can have only one face parallel to $\Gamma$. The faces $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma^{\prime}$ belong to the same "belt", so $\Gamma^{\prime}$ also has an edge equal and parallel to the edge $\boldsymbol{r}$. By conducting similar reasoning for all "belts" defined by the edges of the face $\Gamma$, we obtain that the faces $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma^{\prime}$ have corresponding equal and parallel edges. Since these faces are convex, they are equal. The midpoint of the segment connecting the centers of their symmetries is their center of symmetry.

Thus, for any face, there exists a centrally symmetric face. It remains to prove that all centers of symmetry of pairs of faces coincide. It is sufficient to prove this for two faces that have a common edge. Considering the "belt" defined by this edge, we obtain that the faces parallel to it also have a common edge, and both centers of symmetry of pairs of faces coincide with the center of symmetry of the pair of common edges of the faces.

Therefore, for any face, there exists a centrally symmetric face, and all centers of symmetry of pairs of faces coincide.

question:
8.8. Prove that if all faces of a convex polyhedron are parallelograms, then their number is the product of two consecutive natural numbers.

## §2. Criteria for Non-inscribability and Non-circumscribability of Polyhedra
reference_solution:
8.8. Let's use the solution from problem 8.7. Each "belt" divides the surface of the polyhedron into two "caps." Since the polyhedron is centrally symmetric, both "caps" contain an equal number of faces. Therefore, another "belt" cannot lie entirely within one "cap," i.e., any two "belts" intersect, and they intersect exactly along two faces (parallel edges defining the "belts").

Let \( k \) be the number of different "belts." Then each "belt" intersects with \( k-1 \) other "belts," i.e., it contains \( 2(k-1) \) faces. Since any face is a parallelogram, it belongs to exactly two "belts." Therefore, the number of faces is \( 2(k-1) k / 2 = (k-1) k \).

question:
8.9. Some faces of a convex polyhedron are painted black, the others are white, and no two black faces share an edge. Prove that if the area of the black faces is greater than the area of the white faces, then a sphere cannot be inscribed in this polyhedron.

Can the area of the black faces equal the area of the white faces for the described polyhedron?
reference_solution:
8.9. We will prove that if no two black faces of a circumscribed polyhedron share a common edge, then the area of the black faces does not exceed the area of the white ones. In the proof, we will use the fact that if two faces of a polyhedron touch a sphere at points $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$, and $AB$ is their common edge, then $\triangle ABO_{1} = \triangle ABO_{2}$. We will divide the faces into triangles by connecting each point of contact between the polyhedron and the sphere with all the vertices of the corresponding face. From the previous remark and the condition, it follows that each black triangle can be paired with a white triangle of equal area. Therefore, the sum of the areas of the black triangles is not greater than the sum of the areas of the white triangles.

A circumscribed polyhedron - a regular octahedron - can be colored such that the area of the black faces equals the area of the white ones, and no two black faces share a common edge.

question: 8.10. Some faces of a convex polyhedron are painted black, and the rest are painted white, with no two black faces sharing an edge. Prove that if there are more black faces than half, then it is impossible to inscribe a sphere in this polyhedron.
reference_solution: 8.10. We will prove that if a sphere is inscribed in a polyhedron and no two black faces share a common edge, then the number of black faces is not greater than the number of white faces. In the proof, we will use the fact that if $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$ are the points of tangency of the sphere with the faces sharing a common edge $A B$, then $\triangle A B O_{1}=\triangle A B O_{2}$, and therefore, $\angle A O_{1} B = \angle A O_{2} B$. Consider all the angles at which edges of the corresponding face are drawn from the points of tangency of the sphere with the faces. From the previous remark and the condition, it follows that each such angle of a black face can be matched with an equal angle of a white face. Therefore, the sum of the black angles is not greater than the sum of the white angles. On the other hand, the sum of such angles for one face is $2 \pi$. Consequently, the sum of the black angles is $2 \pi n$, where $n$ is the number of black faces, and the sum of the white angles is $2 \pi m$, where $m$ is the number of white faces. Thus, $n \leqslant m$.

question: 8.11. Some vertices of a convex polyhedron are painted black, and the rest are white, with at least one end of each edge being white. Prove that if there are more black vertices than half, then this polyhedron cannot be inscribed in a sphere.
reference_solution:
8.11. Suppose a polyhedron is inscribed in a sphere and no two black vertices are connected by an edge, then the number of black vertices is not greater than the number of white vertices.

Let the planes tangent to the sphere with center $O$ at points $\boldsymbol{P}$ and $Q$ intersect along the line $A B$. Then any two planes passing through the segment $P Q$ cut the same angle on the plane $A B P$ as on the plane $A B Q$. Indeed, these angles are symmetric with respect to the plane $A B O$. Now consider for each vertex of your polyhedron the angles that are cut on the tangent plane by the dihedral angles between the faces meeting at that vertex. From the previous statement$11^{*}$

163
it follows from the conditions that each angle at a black vertex can be matched with an equal angle at a white vertex. Therefore, the sum of the black angles is not greater than the sum of the white angles. On the other hand, the sum of such angles for one vertex is $\pi(n-2)$, where $n$ is the number of faces of the polyhedral angle at that vertex (for proving this, it is convenient to consider a section of the polyhedral angle by a plane parallel to the tangent plane). It is clear then that if instead of these angles we consider the angles that complement them to 180$)^{\circ}$ (i.e., the exterior angles of the polygonal section), their sum for any vertex will be equal to $2 \pi$. As before, the sum of the black such angles is not greater than the sum of the white ones. On the other hand, the sum of the black angles is $2 \pi n$, where $n$ is the number of black vertices, and the sum of the white angles is $2 \pi m$, where $m$ is the number of white vertices. Therefore, $2 \pi n \leqslant 2 \pi m$, i.e., $n \leqslant m$.

question:
8.14. Prove that $\mathrm{B}-\mathrm{P}+\Gamma=2$ (Euler's formula).





The translation is provided as requested, maintaining the original text's line breaks and format.
reference_solution:
8.14. First solution. Let $M$ be the projection of a polyhedron onto a plane that is not perpendicular to any of its faces; with such a projection, all faces are projected into polygons. Edges that project into sides of $M$ divide the polyhedron into two parts. Consider the projection of one of these parts (Fig. 58). Let $n_{1}, \ldots, n_{h}$ be the numbers of edges of the faces of this part, $B_{j}$ be the number of internal vertices of this part, and $B^{\prime}$ be the number of boundary vertices of $M$. The sum of the angles of the polygons into which the polygon $M$ is divided is, on one hand, $\sum \pi\left(n_{i}-2\right)$, and on the other hand, $\pi\left(B^{\prime}-2\right)+2 \pi B_{1}$. Therefore, $\sum n_{i}-2 k=B^{\prime}-2+2 B_{1}$, where $k$ is the number of faces of the first part. Writing the same equation for the second part of the polyhedron and adding these two equations, we obtain the required result.

Second solution. Consider a sphere of radius 1 with center $O$ located inside the polyhedron. The angles of the arc $A O B$, where $A B$ is an edge of the polyhedron, divide the surface of the sphere into spherical polygons. Let $n_{i}$ be the number of sides of the $i$-th spherical polygon, $\sigma_{i}$ be the sum of its angles, and $S_{i}$ be its area. According to problem 4.44, $S_{i}=\sigma_{i}-\pi\left(n_{i}-2\right)$. Adding all such equations for $i=1, \ldots, \Gamma$, we get $4 \pi=2 \pi B-2 \pi P+2 \pi \Gamma$

question:
8.15. a) Prove that the sum of the angles of all faces of a convex polyhedron is equal to twice the sum of the angles of a planar polygon with the same number of vertices,
b) Consider for each vertex of a convex polyhedron the difference between \(2 \pi\) and the sum of the planar angles converging at this vertex. Prove that the sum of all these values is \(4 \pi\).
reference_solution:
8.15. Let $\Sigma$ be the sum of all the angles of the faces of a convex polyhedron. In part (a), it is required to prove that $\Sigma=2 (V - 2) \pi$, and in part (b), it is required to prove that $2 B \pi - \Sigma = 4 \pi$. Therefore, both problems are equivalent.

If a face contains $k$ edges, then the sum of its angles is $(k-2) \pi$. When summing over all faces, each edge is counted twice, as it belongs to exactly two faces. Therefore, $\Sigma=(2 P - 2 \Gamma) \pi$. Hence, $2 B \pi - \Sigma = 2 \pi (B - P + \Gamma) = 4 \pi$.

question: 8.16. Let $\Gamma_{k}$ be the number of $k$-sided faces of an arbitrary polyhedron, $\mathrm{B}_{h}$ be the number of its vertices where $k$ edges meet. Prove that $2 \mathrm{P}=3 \mathrm{~B}_{3}+$ $+4 \mathrm{~B}_{4}+5 \mathrm{~B}_{5} \ldots=3 \Gamma_{3}+4 \Gamma_{4}+5 \Gamma_{5}+\ldots$
reference_solution: 8.16. Each edge can be associated with two vertices connected by it. In this case, a vertex where $k$ edges meet appears $k$ times. $\quad$ Therefore, $2 \mathrm{P}=3 \mathrm{~B}_{3}+4 \mathrm{~B}_{4}+5 \mathrm{~B}_{5}+\ldots$ On the other hand, each edge can be associated with two faces adjacent to it. In this case, a $k$-sided face appears $k$ times. Therefore, $2 \mathrm{P}=3 \Gamma_{3}+4 \Gamma_{4}+5 \Gamma_{5}+\ldots$

question:
8.17. a) Prove that in any convex polyhedron, there will be either a triangular face or a trihedral angle.

b) Prove that for any convex polyhedron, the sum of the number of triangular faces and the number of trihedral angles is not less than 8.
reference_solution:
8.17. a) Suppose that a certain market polyhedron has neither triangular faces nor three-edged vertices. Then $B_{3}=\Gamma_{3}=0$, and therefore, $2 \mathrm{P}=4 \Gamma_{4}+5 \Gamma_{5}+\ldots \geqslant 4 \Gamma$ and $2 \mathrm{P}=4 \mathrm{~B}_{4}+5 \mathrm{~B}_{5}+\ldots \geqslant 4 \mathrm{~B}$ (see problem 8.16). Consequently, $4 B-4 P+4 \Gamma \leqslant 0$. On the other hand, $\mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{P}+\Gamma=2$. A contradiction is obtained.

b) According to Euler's formula $4 \mathrm{~B}+4 \Gamma=4 \mathrm{P}+8$. Substitute the following expressions for the quantities involved in this formula: $\quad 4 \mathrm{~B}=4 \mathrm{~B}_{3}+4 \mathrm{~B}_{4}+4 \mathrm{~B}_{5}+\ldots, \quad 4 \Gamma=4 \Gamma_{3}+4 \Gamma_{5}+$ $+4 \mathrm{\Gamma}_{5}+\ldots \quad$ and $\quad 4 \mathrm{P}=2 \mathrm{P}+2 \mathrm{P}=3 \mathrm{~B}_{3}+4 \mathrm{~B}_{\overline{4}}+5 \mathrm{~B}_{5}+\ldots$ $\ldots+3 \Gamma_{3}+4 \Gamma_{4}+5 \Gamma_{5}+\ldots$ After simplification, we obtain $\mathrm{B}_{3}+\Gamma_{3}=8+\mathrm{B}_{5}+2 \mathrm{~B}_{6}+3 \mathrm{~B}_{7}+\ldots+\Gamma_{5}+2 \Gamma_{6}+3 \Gamma_{7} \ldots \geqslant$ $\geqslant 8$.

question: 8.18. Prove that in any convex polyhedron, there is a face with fewer than six sides.
reference_solution:
8.18. Suppose that any face of a certain convex polyhedron has at least six sides. Then $\Gamma_{3}=\Gamma_{\overline{4}}=$ $=\Gamma_{5}=0$, and therefore $2 P=6 \Gamma_{6}+7 \Gamma_{8}+\ldots \geqslant 6 \Gamma$ (see problem 8.16), i.e., $P \geqslant 3$. Moreover, for any polyhedron $2 P=3 B_{3}+4 B_{\mathbf{4}}+\ldots \geqslant 3 B$. Adding the inequalities $P \geqslant 3 \Gamma$ and $2 P \geqslant 3 B$, we get $P \geqslant \Gamma+B$. On the other hand, $P=$ $=\Gamma+B-2$. A contradiction is obtained.

Remark. Similarly, it can be proved that in any convex polyhedron there is a vertex from which fewer than six edges emanate.

question:
8.20. Given a convex polyhedron, all faces of which have 5, 6, or 7 sides, and all polyhedral angles are trihedral. Prove that the number of pentagonal faces is 12 more than the number of heptagonal faces.

## § 4. Traversals of Polyhedra
reference_solution: 8.20. Let $a, b$ and $c$ be the numbers of faces with 5, 6 and 7 sides respectively. Then $\mathrm{P}=(5 a+6 b+7 c) / 2, \Gamma=a+$ $+b+c$ and, since by condition three edges emanate from each vertex, $V=(5 a+6 b+7 c) / 3$. Multiplying all these expressions by 6 and substituting them into the formula $6(\mathrm{~V}+\Gamma-\mathrm{P})=12$, we obtain the required.

question: 8.21. A planet has the shape of a convex polyhedron, and cities are located at its vertices, with each edge being a road. Two roads are closed for repair. Prove that it is possible to travel from any city to any other city via the remaining roads.
reference_solution:
8.21. Let $A$ and $B$ be given cities. First, we will prove that it was possible to travel from $A$ to $B$ before the closure of two roads for repair. Consider the projection of the polyhedron onto some line that is not perpendicular to any of its edges (in such a projection, the vertices of the polyhedron do not merge). Let $A^{\prime}$ and $B^{\prime}$ be the projections of points $A$ and $B$, and $M^{\prime}$ and $N^{\prime}$ be the extreme points of the projection of the polyhedron (points $M^{\prime}$ and $N^{\prime}$ are the projections of vertices $M$ and $N$). If we move from vertex $A$ such that the movement in the projection is in the direction from $M^{\prime}$ to $N^{\prime}$, then eventually we will end up at vertex $N$. Similarly, we can travel from vertex $B$ to $N$. Thus, it is possible to travel from $A$ to $B$ (via $N$).

If the path from $A$ to $B$ passes through a closed road, there are still two detours along the faces for which this edge is common. The second closed road cannot be on both of these detours at the same time.

question: 8.22. A direction is indicated on each edge of a convex polyhedron; at the same time, at least one edge enters and at least one edge exits from each vertex. Prove that there exist two faces that can be traversed, moving in accordance with the introduced orientation of the edges.
reference_solution: 8.22. Let's exit from some vertex of the polyhedron and walk along the edges in the direction indicated on them until we find a vertex that we have already visited before. The path from the first passage through this vertex to the second forms a "loop" that divides the polyhedron into two parts. Consider one of them and find a face with the required property on it. The boundary of each of the two parts can be traced, moving in accordance with the introduced orientation. If the considered figure is itself a face, then everything is already proven. Therefore, we will assume that it is not a face, i.e., on the boundary there is a vertex from which an edge exits (or enters) that does not lie on the boundary of the figure. We will pass along this edge and continue to move along the edges in the indicated direction (or in the opposite direction) until we either exit to the boundary or get a loop. The path divides the figure into two parts; the boundary of one of them can be traced in accordance with the orientation (Fig. 51). We will do the same with this part, and so on. After several such operations, only one face will remain, possessing the required property. For the other part obtained at the very first step, a second required face can be found analogously.

question: 8.24. A plane intersects the sides of a spatial polygon $A_{1} \ldots A_{n}$ (or their extensions) at points $B_{1}, \ldots, B_{n}$; the point $B_{i}$ lies on the line $A_{i} A_{i+1}$. Prove that $\frac{A_{1} B_{1}}{A_{2} B_{1}} \cdot \frac{A_{2} B_{2}}{A_{3} B_{2}} \cdot \ldots \cdot \frac{A_{n} B_{n}}{A_{1} B_{n}}=1$, and that an even number of points $B_{i}$ lie on the sides of the polygon (and not on their extensions).
reference_solution:
8.24. Consider the projection onto a line perpendicular to a given plane. All points $B_{i}$ are projected onto a single point $B$, while points $A_{1}, \ldots, A_{n}$ are projected onto $C_{1}, \ldots, C_{n}$. Since the ratios of segments lying on the same line are preserved under projection, we have

$$
\frac{A_{1} B_{1}}{A_{2} B_{1}} \cdot \frac{A_{2} B_{2}}{A_{3} B_{2}} \cdots \frac{A_{n} B_{n}}{A_{1} B_{n}}=\frac{C_{1} B}{C_{2} B} \cdot \frac{C_{2} B}{C_{3} B} \cdots \frac{C_{n} B}{C_{1} B}=1
$$

The given plane divides space into two parts. Moving from vertex $A_{i}$ to $A_{i+1}$, we transition from one part of space to the other only if the point $B_{i}$ lies on the side $A_{i} A_{i+1}$. Since, after completing the traversal of the polygon, we return to the original part of space, the number of points $B_{i}$ lying on the sides of the polygon is even.

question: 8.25. Given four lines, no three of which are parallel to the same plane. Prove that there exists a spatial quadrilateral, the sides of which are parallel to these lines, and the ratio of the sides parallel to the corresponding lines is the same for all such quadrilaterals.
reference_solution: 8.25. Let a, b, c, and d be vectors parallel to given lines. Since any three vectors in space, not lying in the same plane, form a basis, there exist such non-zero numbers $\alpha, \beta$, and $\gamma$ that $\alpha \mathbf{a}+\beta \mathbf{b}+\gamma \mathbf{c}+\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{0}$. The vectors $\alpha \mathrm{a}, \beta \mathrm{b}, \gamma \mathbf{c}$, and d are the sides of some quadrilateral. Now let $\alpha_{1} a, \beta_{1} \mathbf{b}, \gamma_{1} \mathbf{c}$, and $\boldsymbol{d}$ be the vectors of the sides of another such quadrilateral. Then $\alpha_{1} a+\beta_{1} b+\gamma_{1} c+d=0=\alpha a+$ $+\beta \mathbf{b}+\gamma \mathbf{c}+\mathbf{d}$, i.e., $\left(\alpha_{1}-\alpha\right) \mathbf{a}+\left(\beta_{1}-\beta\right) \mathbf{b}+\left(\gamma_{1}-\gamma\right) \mathbf{c}=\mathbf{0}$. Since the vectors a, b, and c do not lie in the same plane, then $\alpha=\alpha_{1}$, $\beta=\beta_{1}$, and $\gamma=\gamma_{1}$.

question:
8.26. a) How many pairwise non-equal spatial quadrilaterals exist with one and the same set of side vectors?

b) Prove that the volumes of all tetrahedra defined by these spatial quadrilaterals are equal.
reference_solution:
8.26. a) We fix one of the vectors of the sides. It can be followed by any of the three remaining vectors, and then by any of the two remaining ones. Therefore, there are exactly 6 different quadrilaterals.

b) Let $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}$, and $\mathbf{d}$ be the given vectors of the sides. Consider the parallelepiped defined by the vectors $\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{b}$, and $\mathbf{c}$ (Fig. 61); its diagonal is the vector $\mathbf{d}$. A simple enumeration shows that all 6 different quadrilaterals are among the quadrilaterals whose sides are the edges of this parallelepiped and its diagonal $\mathbf{d}$ (it is convenient to fix the vector $\mathbf{d}$ during enumeration). The volume of each corresponding tetrahedron is $1/6$ of the volume of the parallelepiped.

question: 8.32. On the sides $AB, BC, CD$ and $DA$ of a spatial quadrilateral $ABCD$ (or on their extensions), points $K, L, M$ and $N$ are taken such that $AN = AK$, $BK = BL$, $CL = CM$ and $DM = DN$. Prove that there exists a sphere that is tangent to the lines $AB, BC, CD$ and $DA$.
reference_solution:
8.32. Since $A N = A K$, there exists a circle $S_{1}$ in the plane $D A B$ that is tangent to the lines $A D$ and $A B$ at points $N$ and $K$. Similarly, there exists a circle $S_{2}$ in the plane $A B C$ that is tangent to the lines $A B$ and $B C$ at points $K$ and $L$. We will prove that the sphere containing circles $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ is the desired one. This sphere is tangent to the lines $A D, A B$, and $B C$ at points $N, K$, and $L$ (points $B, C$, and $D$ lie outside this sphere). It remains to verify that this sphere is tangent to the line $C D$ at point $M$.

Let $S_{3}$ be the section of the given sphere by the plane $B C D$, and let $D N^{\prime}$ be a tangent to $S_{3}$. Since $D C = \pm D M \pm M C$, and $D M = D N = D N^{\prime}$ and $M C = C L$, the length of the segment $D C$ is equal to the sum or difference of the lengths of the tangents drawn from points $C$ and $D$ to the circle $S_{3}$. This means that the line $C D$ is tangent to the circle $S_{3}$. Indeed, let $a = d^{2} - R^{2}$, where $d$ is the distance from the center of the circle $S_{3}$ to the line $C D$ and $R$ is the radius of $S_{3}$; $P$ is the foot of the perpendicular dropped from the center of the circle $S_{3}$ to the line $C D$; $x = C P$ and $y = D P$. Then the lengths of the tangents $C L$ and $D N^{\prime}$ are $\sqrt{x^{2} + a}$ and $\sqrt{y^{2} + a}$. Suppose

$\left|\sqrt{x^{2} + a} \pm \sqrt{y^{2} + a}\right| = |x \pm y| \neq 0$. We will prove that then $a = 0$. Squaring both sides, we get $\sqrt{\left(x^{2} + a\right)\left(y^{2} + a\right)} = \pm x y \pm a$. Squaring again, we get $a\left(x^{2} + y^{2}\right) = \pm 2 a x y$. If $a \neq 0$, then $(x \pm y)^{2} = 0$, i.e., $x = \pm y$. The equality $2\left|\sqrt{x^{2} + a}\right| = 2|x|$ holds only if $a = 0$.

question:
8.33. Let $a, b, c$ and $d$ be the lengths of the sides $AB, BC$, $CD$ and $DA$ of a spatial quadrilateral $ABCD$.

a) Prove that if none of the three relations $a+b=c+d, a+c=b+d$ and $a+d=b+c$ are satisfied, then there exist exactly 8 distinct spheres that are tangent to the lines $AB, BC, CD$ and $DA$.

b) Prove that if at least one of the specified relations is satisfied, then there exist infinitely many distinct spheres that are tangent to the lines $AB, BC$, $CD$ and $DA$.
reference_solution:
8.33. a) Let's introduce coordinates on the lines $A B, B C, C D$ and $D A$, taking points $A, B, C$ and $D$ as the origins of the coordinates, respectively, and the directions of the rays $A B, B C, C D$ and $D A$ as the positive directions. According to the result of problem 8.32, we will look for points $K$, $L, M$ and $N$ on the lines $A B, B C, C D$ and $D A$ such that $A N = A K, B K = B L, C L = C M$ and $D M = D N$, i.e., $\overrightarrow{A K} = \mathbf{x}, \overrightarrow{A N} = \alpha \mathbf{x}, \overrightarrow{B C} = \mathbf{y}, \overrightarrow{B K} = \beta \mathbf{y}, \overrightarrow{C M} = \mathbf{z}, \overrightarrow{C L} = \gamma \mathbf{z}, \overrightarrow{D N} = \mathbf{u}$ and $\overrightarrow{D M} = \delta \mathbf{u}$, where $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta = \pm 1$. Since $\overrightarrow{A B} = \overrightarrow{A K} + \overrightarrow{K B}$, we have $a = x - \beta y$. Similarly, $b = y - \gamma z, c = z - \delta u$ and $d = u - \alpha x$. Therefore, $u = d + \alpha x, z = c + \delta d + \delta \alpha x, y = b + \gamma c + \gamma \delta d + \gamma \delta \alpha x$ and $x = a + \beta b + \beta \gamma c + \beta \gamma \delta d + \beta \gamma \delta \alpha x$. From the last equation, we get $(1 - \alpha \beta \gamma \delta) x = a + \beta b + \beta \gamma c + \beta \gamma \delta d$. Consequently, if $1 - \alpha \beta \gamma \delta = 0$, then the equation $a \pm b \pm c \pm d = 0$ holds; it is clear that the equation $a - b - c - d = 0$ cannot hold. Therefore, in this case, $\alpha \beta \gamma \delta \neq 1$, which means $\alpha \beta \gamma \delta = -1$. The numbers $\alpha, \beta, \gamma = \pm 1$ can be chosen arbitrarily, and the number $\delta$ is determined by these numbers. There are 8 different sets of numbers $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$, and for each set, there is a unique solution for $x, y, z, u$. Moreover, all numbers $x, y, z, u$ are non-zero, so all 8 solutions are distinct.

b) First solution. Let's consider, for example, the case when $a + c = b + d$, i.e., $a - b + c - d = 0$. In this case, we should set $\beta = -1, \beta \gamma = 1, \beta \gamma \delta = -1$ and $\alpha \beta \gamma \delta = 1$, i.e., $\alpha = \beta = \gamma = \delta = -1$. The system of equations for $x, y, z, u$ considered in part (a) of the problem has infinitely many solutions: $u = d - x, z = c - d + x$ and $y = b - c + d - x = a - x$, where the number $x$ is arbitrary.

The other cases are handled similarly: if $a + b = c + d$, then $\alpha = \gamma = -1$ and $\beta = \delta = 1$, and if $a + d = b + c$, then $\alpha = \gamma = 1$ and $\beta = \delta = -1$.

Second solution. In each of the three cases when the specified conditions are met, a quadrilateral pyramid with vertex $B$ can be constructed, whose lateral edges are equal and parallel to the sides of the given quadrilateral, and the base is a parallelogram, with the sums of the lengths of opposite edges being equal (see Fig. 64). Therefore, there exists a ray with which the edges of the pyramid, and hence the sides of the quadrilateral, form equal angles (problem 6.63). Let the plane $\Pi$, perpendicular to this ray, intersect the lines $A B, B C, C D$ and $D A$ at points $P, Q, R$ and $S$, and the corresponding lateral edges of the pyramid at points $P', Q', R'$ and $S'$. Since the points $P', Q', R'$ and $S'$ lie on the same circle, and the lines $P Q$ and $P' Q', Q R$ and $Q' R'$, etc., are parallel, we have $\angle(P Q, P S) = \angle(P' Q', P' S') = \angle(R' Q', R' S') = \angle(R Q, R S)$, i.e., the points $P, Q, R$ and $S$ lie on the same circle (see Prasolov, 1, p. 36); let $O$ be the center of this circle. Since the lines $A P$ and $A S$ form equal angles with the plane $\Pi$, we have $A P = A S$. Therefore, the corresponding sides of the triangles $A P O$ and $A S O$ are equal, and hence the distances from the point $O$ to the lines $A B$ and $A D$ are equal. Similarly, it can be shown that the point $O$ is equidistant from all the lines $A B, B C, C D$ and $D A$, i.e., the sphere with center $O$ and radius equal to the distance from the point $O$ to these lines exists. By moving the plane $\Pi$ parallel, we obtain an infinite number of spheres.

Remark. For each vertex of the spatial quadrilateral $A B C D$, one can consider two bisector planes passing through the bisectors of its external and internal angles perpendicular to them. It is clear that $O$ is the point of intersection of the bisector planes. The following sets of four bisector planes intersect along one line: in the case $a + c = b + d$, all 4 internal; in the case $a + b = c + d$, internal at vertices $A$ and $C$ and external at vertices $B$ and $D$; in the case $a + d = b + c$ - internal at vertices $B$ and $D$ and external at vertices $A$ and $C$,

9.5. Let us draw perpendiculars to the faces through their centers. question:
9.7. a) Prove that it is possible to choose 4 vertices of a cube such that they will be the vertices of a regular tetrahedron. In how many ways can this be done?

b) Prove that it is possible to choose 4 planes of the faces of an octahedron such that they will be the planes of the faces of a regular tetrahedron. In how many ways can this be done?
reference_solution:
9.7. a) If $A B C D A_{1} B_{1} C_{1} D_{1}$ is a cube, then $A B_{1} C D_{1}$ and $A_{1} B C_{1} D$ are regular tetrahedra.

b) It is easy to verify that the midpoints of the edges of a regular tetrahedron are the vertices of an octahedron. From this, it is clear that one can choose 4 faces of the octahedron such that they are the planes of the faces of the regular tetrahedron, and this can be done in two ways.

question: 9.8. Prove that on the edges of a cube, 6 points can be chosen such that they will be the vertices of an octahedron.
reference_solution: 9.8. Let the edge of the cube $A B C D A_{1} B_{1} C_{1} D_{1}$ be equal to 4a. Take points on the edges emanating from vertex $A$, at a distance of $3 a$ from it. Similarly, take 3 points on the edges emanating from vertex $C_{1}$. Using the equality $3^{2}+3^{2}=1+$ $+4^{2}+1$, it is easy to verify that the lengths of all edges of the polyhedron with vertices at the selected points are $3 \sqrt{2} a$.

question:
9.9. a) Prove that it is possible to choose 8 vertices of a dodecahedron such that they are the vertices of a cube. How many ways can this be done?

b) Prove that it is possible to choose 4 vertices of a dodecahedron such that they are the vertices of a regular tetrahedron.
reference_solution:
9.9. a) From the solution to problem 9.2, it is clear that there exists a cube whose vertices are located at the vertices of the dodecahedron. Moreover, one edge of the cube is located on each face of the dodecahedron. It is also clear that choosing any of the five diagonals of a certain face of the dodecahedron as an edge of the cube uniquely determines the entire cube. Therefore, there are 5 different cubes with vertices at the vertices of the dodecahedron.

b) By placing the cube such that its vertices are located at the vertices of the dodecahedron, it is then possible to place a regular tetrahedron such that its vertices are located at the vertices of that cube.

question:
9.10. a) Prove that it is possible to choose 8 faces of an icosahedron such that they will be the planes of the faces of an octahedron. How many ways can this be done?

b) Prove that it is possible to choose 4 planes of the faces of an icosahedron such that they will be the planes of the faces of a regular tetrahedron.
reference_solution:
9.10. a) From the solution to problem 9.4, it is clear that 8 faces of the icosahedron can be embedded such that they become faces of an octahedron. In this case, from each vertex of the icosahedron, exactly one edge does not lie in the plane of the octahedron's face. Therefore, the choice of any one of the three edges emanating from a certain vertex of the icosahedron as the edge not lying in the plane of the octahedron's face uniquely determines the octahedron. Therefore, there are 5 different octahedra whose faces lie in the planes of the icosahedron's faces.

b) By selecting 8 planes of the icosahedron's faces such that they become the planes of the octahedron's faces, one can choose 4 planes from them such that they are the planes of the faces of a regular tetrahedron.

question: 9.11. Consider a convex polyhedron, the vertices of which are the centers of the faces of some regular polyhedron. Prove that this polyhedron is also regular. (It is called the polyhedron dual to the original.)
reference_solution: 9.11. When rotating about the line connecting the vertex of the original polyhedron with its center, which transforms the polyhedron into itself, the centers of the faces adjacent to this vertex map to themselves, i.e., they become vertices of a regular polyhedron. Similarly, considering a rotation about the line connecting the center of a face of the original polyhedron with its center, we obtain that the polyhedral angles of the dual polyhedron are regular. Since any two polyhedral angles of the original polyhedron can be aligned by rotation, all faces of the dual polyhedron are equal. And since any two faces of the original polyhedron can be aligned, all polyhedral angles of the dual polyhedron are equal.

question:

b) Prove that the cube and octahedron are dual to each other.

c) Prove that the dodecahedron and icosahedron are dual to each other.
reference_solution:
9.12. To prove this, it is sufficient to note that if the original polyhedron has $m$-sided angles at the vertices and $n$-sided faces, then the dual polyhedron will have $n$-sided angles at the vertices and $m$-sided faces.

R e m a r k. The solutions to problems 9.2 and 9.4 are actually two different solutions to the same problem. Indeed, if a dodecahedron exists, then there exists a dual polyhedron - an icosahedron (and vice versa).

question: 9.13. Prove that if the radii of the inscribed spheres of two dual regular polyhedra are equal, then: a) the radii of their circumscribed spheres are equal; b) the radii of the circumscribed circles of their faces are equal.
reference_solution:
9.13. a) Let $O$ be the center of the original polyhedron, $A$ one of its vertices, and $B$ the center of one of the faces with vertex $A$. Consider the face of the dual polyhedron, formed by the centers of the faces of the original polyhedron, adjacent to vertex $A$. Let $C$ be the center of this face, i.e., the point of intersection of this face with the line $O A$. It is clear that $A B \perp O B$ and $B C \perp O A$. Therefore, $O C: O B = O B: O A$, i.e., $r_{2}: R_{2} = r_{1}: R_{1}$, where $r_{1}$ and $R_{1}$ (respectively $r_{2}$ and $R_{2}$) are the radii of the inscribed and circumscribed spheres of the original polyhedron (respectively the dual polyhedron).

b) If a plane is at a distance $r$ from the center of a sphere of radius $R$, then it intersects the sphere in a circle of radius $\sqrt{R^{2}-r^{2}}$. Therefore, the radius of the circumscribed circles of the faces of a polyhedron inscribed in a sphere of radius $R$ and circumscribed about a sphere of radius $r$ is $V \sqrt{R^{2}-r^{2}}$. In particular, if for two polyhedra $R$ and $r$ are equal, then the radii of the circumscribed circles of their faces are also equal.

question:
9.14. A face of a dodecahedron and a face of an icosahedron lie in the same plane, and moreover, their opposite faces also lie in the same plane. Prove that all other vertices of the dodecahedron and icosahedron are located in two planes parallel to these faces.

## § 3. Projections and Sections of Regular Polyhedra
reference_solution:
9.14. If a dodecahedron and an icosahedron are inscribed in the same sphere, then the radii of their inscribed spheres are equal (Problem 9.13, a), i.e., they are equal to the distances between their opposite faces. We will call the "center of a spherical face" of the dodecahedron (or icosahedron) the point of intersection of the circumscribed sphere with the line passing through its center and the center of one of its faces. Fix one of the centers of the spherical faces of the dodecahedron and consider the distances from it to the vertices; among these distances, there are exactly 4 different ones. To solve the problem, it is sufficient to prove that this set of four different distances coincides with the same set for the icosahedron.

It is easy to verify that the centers of the spherical faces of the dodecahedron are the vertices of the icosahedron, and the centers of the spherical faces of the resulting icosahedron are the vertices of the original dodecahedron. Therefore, any distance between the center of a spherical face and a vertex of the dodecahedron is a distance between a vertex and the center of a spherical face of the icosahedron.

question: 9.15. Prove that the projections of a dodecahedron and an icosahedron onto planes parallel to their faces are regular polygons.
reference_solution:
9.15. To prove this, it is sufficient to note that the faces of the polyhedron coincide with themselves upon rotation, aligning the projection of the upper face with the projection of the lower face. Thus, the projection of the dodecahedron is a 10-sided polygon that coincides with itself upon rotation by \(36^{\circ}\) (Fig. 69, a), while the projection of the icosahedron is a hexagon that coincides with itself upon rotation by \(60^{\circ}\) (Fig. 69, b).
