question: 103. Prove that the bases of the perpendiculars dropped from the intersection point of the diagonals of an inscribed quadrilateral to its sides are the vertices of a quadrilateral into which a circle can be inscribed. Find the radius of this circle if the radius of the given circle is $R$, the distance from its center to the intersection point of the diagonals is $d$, and the diagonals of the inscribed quadrilateral are perpendicular.
reference_solution:
103. Let (Fig. 26) $P$ be the point of intersection of the diagonals, and $K$, $L, M, N$ be the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from $P$ to $A B$,

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-091.jpg?height=368&width=359&top_left_y=761&top_left_x=165)

Fig. 26. Since the quadrilateral $P K B L$ is cyclic, $\widehat{P K L}=\widehat{P B C}$, similarly $\widehat{P K N}=\widehat{P A D}$; but $\widehat{P B C}=\widehat{P A D}$, as they subtend the same arc. Therefore, $K P$ is the bisector of angle $N K L$; hence, the bisectors of the angles of quadrilateral $K L M N$ intersect at point $P$, which is the center of the circle inscribed in $K L M N$. Now let the diagonals $A C$ and $B D$ be perpendicular, $R$ be the radius of the given circle, and $d$ be the distance from $P$ to its center. $|A P| \cdot|P C|=R^{2}-d^{2}$. The radius of the desired circle $r$ is equal, in particular, to the distance from $P$ to $K L$. Denoting $\widehat{K L P}=\widehat{A} B P=\alpha, \widehat{P B C}=\beta$, we find

$\left.r=|P L| \sin \alpha=|P B| \sin \beta \sin \alpha=|P B| \frac{|P C|}{|B C|} \right\rvert\, \frac{|A P|}{|A B|}=$

$$
\begin{aligned}
&=\left(R^{2}-d^{2}\right) \frac{|P B| \cdot|A C|}{|B C| \cdot|A B| \sin (\alpha+\beta)} \frac{\sin (\alpha+\beta)}{|A C|}= \\
&=\left(R^{2}-d^{2}\right) \frac{2 S_{A B C}}{2 S_{A B C}} \frac{1}{2 R}=\frac{R^{2}-d^{2}}{2 R}
\end{aligned}
$$

Answer: $\frac{R^{2}-d^{2}}{2 R}$.

question: 104. The diagonals of an inscribed quadrilateral are perpendicular. Prove that the midpoints of its sides and the bases of the perpendiculars dropped from the point of intersection of the diagonals to the sides lie on one circle. Find the radius of this circle if the radius of the given circle is $R$, and the distance from its center to the point of intersection of the diagonals of the quadrilateral is $d$.
reference_solution:
104. Let (Fig. 27) $ABCD$ be the given quadrilateral, $P$ the point of intersection of the diagonals, $K$ the midpoint of $BC$, and $L$ the midpoint of $AD$. We will prove that the line $LP$ is perpendicular to $BC$. Denoting by $M$ the point of intersection of $LP$ with $BC$, we have $\widehat{BPM} = \widehat{LPD} = \widehat{ADP} = \widehat{PCB}$. Therefore, $PM \perp BC$. Hence, $OK \parallel LP$. Analogously, $PKLO$, and $KOLP$ is a parallelogram, $|LK|^2 + |PO|^2 = 2(|LP|^2 + |PK|^2) = 2\left(\frac{|AD|^2}{4} + \frac{|BC|^2}{4}\right) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 4R^2 = 2R^2$.

(If the chords $AD$ and $BC$ are moved so that they have a common endpoint, and the corresponding arcs continue one another, a right triangle is formed with legs $|AD|$ and $|BC|$ and a diameter of $2R$, meaning $|AD|^2 + |BC|^2 = 4R^2$.) Therefore, $|LK|^2 = 2R^2 - d^2$ and points $L$ and $K$ lie on a circle with center $S$ at the midpoint of $PO$ and radius $\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{2R^2 - d^2}$. But $\triangle LMK$ is a right triangle, $MS$ is the median, $|MS| = \frac{1}{2}|LK| = \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{2R^2 - d^2}$, i.e., $M$ lies on the same circle.

$$
\text{Answer: } \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{2R^2 - d^2}.
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-092.jpg?height=338&width=344&top_left_y=382&top_left_x=733)

question:
105. Prove that if a quadrilateral is inscribed in a circle of radius $R$, and is also circumscribed about a circle of radius $r$, and the distance between the centers of these circles is $d$, then the following relation holds:

$$
\frac{1}{(R+d)^{2}}+\frac{1}{(R-d)^{2}}=\frac{1}{r^{2}}
$$

There are infinitely many quadrilaterals that are simultaneously inscribed in the larger circle and circumscribed about the smaller circle. (One of the vertices can be any point on the larger circle.)
reference_solution:
105. From the two previous problems, it follows that if the diagonals of an inscribed quadrilateral are perpendicular, then the projections of the intersection point of the diagonals of this quadrilateral onto its sides serve as the vertices of a quadrilateral that can be inscribed in a circle and circumscribed around a circle, and the radii of the inscribed and circumscribed circles and the distance between their centers are completely determined by the radius of the circle circumscribed around the original quadrilateral and the distance from its center to the intersection point of the diagonals of the inscribed quadrilateral. Consequently, when the diagonals of the original quadrilateral rotate around their intersection point, the quadrilateral formed by the projections of this point will rotate, remaining inscribed in the same circle and circumscribed around the same circle. It is also easy to show, taking into account the expressions for the radii of the inscribed and circumscribed circles obtained in the two previous problems, that the proposed relationship for such quadrilaterals holds.

To complete the proof, we need to prove that any "inscribed-circumscribed" quadrilateral can be obtained from an inscribed quadrilateral with mutually perpendicular diagonals in the above-mentioned way. Indeed, if $K L M N$ is an "inscribed-circumscribed" quadrilateral, $P$ is the center of the inscribed circle, then by drawing lines perpendicular to the bisectors of $\grave{K} P, L P, M P, N P$ and passing through $K, L, M$ and $N$ respectively, we obtain a quadrilateral $A B C D$ (see Fig. 26). In this case, $\widehat{B P K}=\widehat{K L B}=90^{\circ}-\frac{1}{2} M L K \quad$ (we used, in particular, the fact that in the quadrilateral $P K B L$ the opposite angles are right and, therefore, it is inscribed). Similarly, $\widehat{K P A}=\widehat{K N A}=90^{\circ}-\frac{1}{2} \widehat{M N K}$, and, therefore, $\widehat{B P A}=\widehat{B P K}+\widehat{K P A}=$
$=180^{\circ}-\frac{1}{2}(\widehat{M L K}+\widehat{M N K})=90^{\circ}$. Thus, all angles $B P A$, $A P D, D P C$ and $C P B$ are right, i.e., $P$ is the intersection point of the diagonals $A B C D$, and the diagonals themselves are perpendicular. It is not difficult to show that $A B C D$ is an inscribed quadrilateral, since $\widehat{A B C}+\widehat{A D C}=\widehat{P B L}+\widehat{P B K}+\widehat{P D N}+\widehat{P D M}=\widehat{P K L}+\widehat{P L K}+\widehat{P M N}+$ $\left.+\widehat{P N M}=\frac{1}{2} \widehat{(N K L}+\widehat{K L M}+\widehat{L M N}+\widehat{M N K}\right)=180^{\circ}$.

question:
106. a) Two tangents are drawn to a given circle from point $\mathrm{K}$. Let $A$ and $B$ be the points of tangency, and $C$ be the point of intersection of the tangents. Draw an arbitrary line $l$, tangent to the given circle, not passing through $A$ and $B$. Let $u$ and $v$ be the distances from $A$ and $B$ to $l$, and $w$ be the distance from $C$ to $l$. Find $\frac{u^{w}}{w^{2}}$, if $\widehat{A C B}=\alpha$.

b) A polygon is circumscribed around a circle. Let $l$ be an arbitrary line tangent to the circle and not coinciding with any side of the polygon. Prove that the ratio of the product of the distances from the vertices of the polygon to $l$ to the product of the distances from the points of tangency of the sides of the polygon with the circle to $l$ does not depend on the position of the line $l$.

c) Let $A_{1} A_{2} \ldots A_{2 n}$ be a $2 n$-sided polygon circumscribed around a circle, and $l$ be an arbitrary tangent to the circle. Prove that the product of the distances from the vertices with odd indices to $l$ and the product of the distances from the vertices with even indices to $l$ are in a constant ratio, independent of $l$ (assuming that $l$ does not contain any vertices of the polygon).
reference_solution:
106. a) Let $l$ intersect $A C$ and $B C$ at points $K$ and $N$ and touch the circle at point $M$ (Fig. 28). Denote $|A C| = |B C| = a, \quad |A K| = |K M| = x, \quad |B N| = |N M| = y$. Clearly,

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-093.jpg?height=302&width=433&top_left_y=503&top_left_x=166)

Fig. 28. $\frac{w^{2}}{u v} = \frac{(a-x)(a-y)}{x y}$, but by the cosine theorem for $\triangle C K N$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& (x+y)^{2} = (a-x)^{2} + (a-y)^{2} - \\
& - 2(a-x)(a-y) \cos \alpha \Rightarrow x y = \\
& = a^{2} - a x - a y - (a-x)(a-y) \times \\
& \quad \times \cos \alpha \Rightarrow 2 x y = \\
& = (a-x)(a-y)(1 - \cos \alpha) \Rightarrow \\
& \quad \Rightarrow \frac{x y}{(a-x)(a-y)} = \sin ^{2} \frac{\alpha}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\frac{u v}{w^{2}} = \sin ^{2} \frac{\alpha}{2}$. (Similarly, other cases of the position of the line $l$ are considered.)

b) We use the result of problem 106 a). Multiplying the corresponding equalities for all angles of the $n$-gon, we obtain the square of the desired ratio, and the ratio itself will be equal to

$$
\frac{1}{\sin \frac{\alpha_{1}}{2} \sin \frac{\alpha_{2}}{2} \cdots \sin \frac{\alpha_{n}}{2}}
$$

where $\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \ldots, \alpha_{n}$ are the angles of the polygon.

c) We use the result of problem 106 a). If we denote the points of tangency of the sides $A_{1} A_{2}, A_{2} A_{3}, \ldots, A_{2 n-1} A_{2 n}, A_{2 n} A_{1}$ with the circle by $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{2 n-1}, B_{2 n}$, and the distances from $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{2 n}$ to $l$ by $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{2 n-1}, x_{2 n}$, and the distances from $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{2 n}$ to $l$ by $y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{2 n}$, then we get

$$
\frac{x_{1}^{2}}{y_{2 n} y_{1}} = \frac{1}{\sin ^{2} \frac{\alpha_{1}}{2}}, \frac{x_{2}^{2}}{y_{1} y_{2}} = \frac{1}{\sin ^{2} \frac{\alpha_{2}}{2}}, \ldots, \frac{x_{2 n}^{2}}{y_{2 n-1} y_{2 n}} = \frac{1}{\sin ^{2} \frac{\alpha_{2 n}}{2}}
$$

( $\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \ldots, \alpha_{2 n}$ are the angles of the polygon). Multiplying the equalities containing $x_{1}, x_{3}, \ldots, x_{2 n-1}$, and dividing by the product of the remaining equalities, we get

$$
\left(\frac{x_{1} x_{2} \ldots x_{2 n-1}}{x_{2} x_{4} \ldots x_{2 n}}\right)^{2} = \left(\frac{\sin \frac{\alpha_{2}}{2} \sin \frac{\alpha_{4}}{2} \ldots \sin \frac{\alpha_{2 n}}{2}}{\sin \frac{\alpha_{1}}{2} \sin \frac{\alpha_{3}}{2} \ldots \sin \frac{\alpha_{2 n-1}}{2}}\right)^{2}
$$

question: 113. In triangle $ABC$, a line is drawn intersecting sides $AC$ and $BC$ at points $M$ and $N$ such that $|MN| = |AM| + |BM|$. Prove that all such lines are tangent to the same circle.
reference_solution:

Let's construct a circle (Fig. 29) that is tangent to the lines $M N$, $A C$, and $B C$ in such a way that the points of tangency $P$ and $Q$ with the lines $A C$ and $B C$ are outside the segments $C M$ and $C N$ (this will be the circle inscribed in the triangle $M C N$). If $R$ is the point of tangency with $M N$, then $|M P|=|M R|,|N Q|=|N R|$, hence $|M N|=|M P|+|N Q|$, but by the condition $|M N|=|M A|+|N B|$. Therefore, one of the points $P$ or $Q$ (in the figure, $P$) lies inside the corresponding side, while the other lies on its extension. In this case,

\[
\begin{aligned}
|C P|=|C Q|=\frac{1}{2}(|C P| & +|C Q|)= \\

question: 121. The diagonals divide a convex quadrilateral into four triangles. The radii of the circles inscribed in these triangles are equal. Prove that the given quadrilateral is a rhombus.
reference_solution:
121. First, let's prove that the diagonals of the given quadrilateral are bisected at the point of intersection, i.e., that the quadrilateral is a parallelogram. Let \(ABCD\) be the given quadrilateral, and \(O\) the point of intersection of the diagonals. Suppose \(|BO| \leq |OD|, |AO| \leq |OC|\); consider \(\triangle OA_1B_1\), symmetric to \(\triangle OAB\) with respect to point \(O\); obviously, the radius of the circle inscribed in \(\triangle OA_1B_1\) is less than the radius of the circle inscribed in \(\triangle OCD\), but by the condition, they are equal.

Thus, \(O\) is the midpoint of both diagonals. Now, let's prove that all sides of the quadrilateral are equal. We will use the formula \(S = pr\) (where \(S\) is the area, \(p\) is the semiperimeter, and \(r\) is the radius of the inscribed circle of the triangle). Since \(\triangle ABO\) and \(\triangle BOC\) have equal areas and radii of the inscribed circles, their perimeters are also equal, i.e., \(|AB| = |BC|\).

question: 123. For quadrilateral $A B C D$, it is known that the radii of the circles inscribed in triangles $A B C$, $B C D$, $C D A$, $D A B$ are equal to each other. Prove that $A B C D$ is a rectangle.
reference_solution:
123. From the condition of the problem, it follows that $ABCD$ (Fig. 30) is a convex quadrilateral. Consider the parallelogram $AC C_{1} A_{1}$, in which sides $A A_{1}$ and $C C_{1}$ are equal and parallel to the diagonal $BD$. Triangles $A D A_{1}$, $C D C_{1}$, and $C_{1} D A_{1}$ are equal to triangles $A B D$, $B C D$, and $A B C$, respectively. Therefore, the segments connecting $D$ with the vertices $A, C, C_{1}, A_{1}$ divide the parallelogram into 4 triangles, which have equal radii of the inscribed circles.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-096.jpg?height=314&width=350&top_left_y=1255&top_left_x=730)

Fig. 30. If $O$ is the point of intersection of the diagonals of the parallelogram $A C C_{1} A_{1}$, then $D$ must coincide with $O$ (if $D$, for example, is inside $\triangle C O C_{1}$, then the radius of the circle inscribed in $\triangle A D A_{1}$ is greater than the radius of the circle inscribed in $\triangle A O A_{1}$ and even more so in $\triangle C D C_{1}$). Thus, $ABCD$ is a parallelogram, but, moreover, from problem 121 it follows that $A C C_{1} A_{1}$ is a rhombus, i.e., $ABCD$ is a rectangle.

question: 124. Given a right triangle $A B C$, angle $C$ is right, $O$ is the center of the inscribed circle, $M$ is the point of tangency of the inscribed circle with the hypotenuse, the circle with center at $M$, passing through $O$, intersects the angle bisectors of angles $A$ and $B$ at points $K$ and $L$, different from $O$. Prove that $K$ and $L$ are the centers of the circles inscribed in triangles $A C D$ and $B C D$, where $C D$ is the altitude of triangle $A B C$.

125. On the sides $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ of triangle $ABC$, squares $BCDE$, $ACFG$, and $BAHK$ are constructed outwardly. Let $FCDQ$ and $EBKP$ be parallelograms. Prove that triangle $APQ$ is an isosceles right triangle.

126. $A B C D$ is a rectangle, $E$ is a point on $B C$, $F$ is on $D C$, $E_{1}$ is the midpoint of $A E$, $F_{1}$ is the midpoint of $A F$. Prove that if $\triangle A E F$ is equilateral, then triangles $D E_{1} C$ and $B F_{1} C$ are also equilateral.
reference_solution:
126. Since $\widehat{F E_{1} E}=\widehat{F C E}=90^{\circ}$, the quadrilateral $F E_{1} E C$ is cyclic, $\widehat{F C E_{1}}=\widehat{F E E_{1}}=60^{\circ}$. Similarly, the quadrilateral $F E_{1} A D$ is cyclic and $\widehat{E_{1} D F}=\widehat{E_{1} A F}=60^{\circ}$, i.e., $\triangle D E_{1} C$ is equilateral. The same can be proven for $\triangle B F_{1} C$ being equilateral.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-097.jpg?height=349&width=955&top_left_y=1157&top_left_x=150)

question: 127. Quadrilateral $A B C D$ is inscribed in a circle. Let $O_{1}, O_{2}, O_{3}, O_{4}$ be the centers of the circles inscribed in triangles $A B C, B C D, C D A, D A B$, and $H_{1}, H_{2}, H_{3}$, $\mathrm{H}_{4}$ be the points of intersection of the altitudes of the same triangles. Prove that $\mathrm{O}_{1} \mathrm{O}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3} \mathrm{O}_{4}$ is a rectangle, and quadrilateral $H_{1} H_{2} H_{3} H_{4}$ is equal to quadrilateral $A B C D$.
reference_solution: 127. 128. Note that if $O$ is the center of the circle inscribed in triangle $ABC$, then $\widehat{BOC}=90^{\circ}+\frac{1}{2} \hat{A}$. Indeed, $\widehat{BOC}=$ $=180^{\circ}-\frac{1}{2}(\hat{B}+\hat{C})=90^{\circ}+\frac{1}{2} \hat{A}$. Since $\widehat{BO_{1}A}=\widehat{BO_{4}A}$, the quadrilateral $ABO_{1}O_{4}$ is cyclic (Fig. $31, a$), therefore, the external angle to $\widehat{BO_{1}O_{4}}$ is $\widehat{BAO_{4}}=\frac{1}{2} \widehat{BAD}$. Similarly, the angle external to $\widehat{BO_{1}O_{2}}$ is $\frac{1}{2} \widehat{BCD}$. But $\frac{1}{2} \widehat{(BAD}+\overline{BCD}=90^{\circ}$, hence, $\widehat{O}_{4} \widehat{O}_{1} O_{2}=90^{\circ}$.

question: 128. Given a triangle $ABC$, $D$ is an arbitrary point on the plane. Prove that the points of intersection of the altitudes of triangles $ABD$, $BCD$, and $CAD$ are the vertices of a triangle equal in area to the given one.

129. Two circles intersect at points $A$ and $B$. An arbitrary line passes through $B$ and intersects the first circle again at $C$, and the second circle at $D$. The tangents to the first circle at $C$, and to the second circle at $D$ intersect at point $M$. A line through the intersection of $A M$ and $C D$ is parallel to $C M$,
intersecting $A C$ at point $K$. Prove that $K B$ is tangent to the second circle.
reference_solution:
129. Let us denote (Fig. 32) by $O$ the intersection of $A M$ and $D C$. Draw a tangent through $B$ to the second circle and denote the intersection of this tangent with $A C$ by $K$ (as in the problem statement). It is clear that the statement of the problem is equivalent to the statement that $K O \| C M$.

Let the angle subtended by $\overline{A B}$ in the first circle be $\alpha$, and in the second circle be $\beta$; then

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \widehat{B C M}=\widehat{B A C}, \quad \widehat{B D M}=\widehat{B A D}, \\
& \widehat{D M C}=180^{\circ}-\widehat{B D M}-\widehat{B C M}=180^{\circ}-\widehat{B A D} \cdots \widehat{B A C}=180^{\circ}-\widehat{D A C},
\end{aligned}
$$

thus, $A D M C$ is a cyclic quadrilateral, $\overline{A M C}=\beta$.

Furthermore, if the tangent $B K$ intersects $D M$ at point $L$, then $\widehat{K B O}=$ $=\widehat{L B D}=\widehat{B D L}=\widehat{C A M}$; hence, the quadrilateral $K A B O$ is also cyclic and $\widehat{K O A}=\widehat{K B A}=\beta$, i.e., $K O \| C M$ (the same consideration applies to other relative positions of points $D, B$ and $C$).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-099.jpg?height=325&width=558&top_left_y=333&top_left_x=335)

Fig. 32.

question: 130. On the legs $AC$ and $BC$ of a right triangle, squares $ACKL$ and $BCMN$ are constructed outward. Prove that the quadrilateral bounded by the legs and the lines $LB$ and $NA$ is equal in area to the triangle formed by the lines $LB$, $NA$, and the hypotenuse $AB$.

131. The sides of a convex quadrilateral are divided into $(2 n+1)$ equal parts each. The corresponding division points of opposite sides are connected to each other. Prove that the area of the central quadrilateral is $1 /(2 n+1)^{2}$ of the area of the entire quadrilateral.
reference_solution:
131. The statement of our problem follows from the following two facts.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-099.jpg?height=296&width=329&top_left_y=1237&top_left_x=241)
a)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-099.jpg?height=347&width=389&top_left_y=1223&top_left_x=609)

Fig. 33.

1) If points \( K, L, M, \) and \( N \) are taken on the sides of quadrilateral \( ABCD \) (Fig. 33, a) such that the sides \( AB, BC, CD, \) and \( DA \) are divided by these points in the same ratio \(\left(\frac{|BK|}{|KA|} = \frac{|CM|}{|MD|} = \frac{|BL|}{|LC|} = \frac{|AN|}{|ND|}\right)\), then the segments \( KM \) and \( LN \) are also divided by their point of intersection in the same ratio.

Indeed, from the fact that lines \( KL \) and \( NM \) are parallel to diagonal \( AC \), it follows that

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{|KP|}{|PM|} & = \frac{|LP|}{|PN|} = \frac{|KL|}{|NM|} = \frac{|KL|}{|AC|} \cdot \frac{|AC|}{|NM|} = \\
& = \frac{|BK|}{|BA|} \cdot \frac{|AD|}{|ND|} = \frac{|BK|}{|BA|} \cdot \frac{|BA|}{|KA|} = \frac{|BK|}{|KA|}
\end{aligned}
\]

2) If points \( K_1 \) and \( K, M_1 \) and \( M \) are taken on the sides \( AB \) and \( CD \) of the quadrilateral (Fig. 33, b) such that

\[
\frac{|K_1 K|}{|AB|} = \frac{|M_1 M|}{|CD|} = \frac{1}{m}, \quad |AK_1| = |KB|, \quad |DM_1| = |CM|
\]

then the area of quadrilateral \( K_1 K M M_1 \) is \(\frac{1}{m}\) of the area of quadrilateral \( ABCD \). Indeed, \( S_{BKC} = \frac{|BK|}{|BA|} S_{ABC}, S_{AM_1D} = \frac{|M_1D|}{|CD|} S_{ACD} = \frac{|BK|}{|BA|} S_{ACD} \). Therefore, \( S_{AKCM_1} = \left(1 - \frac{|BK|}{|BA|}\right) S_{ABCD} = \frac{|AK|}{|BA|} S_{ABCD} \). Similarly, \( S_{K_1 K M M_1} = \frac{|K_1 K|}{|AK|} S_{AKCM_1} \). Thus, \( S_{K_1 K M M_1} = \frac{|K_1 K|}{|AB|} S_{ABCD} = \frac{1}{m} S \).

question: 132. The line passing through the midpoints of the diagonals $A C$ and $B D$ of quadrilateral $A B C D$ intersects sides $A B$ and $D C$ at points $M$ and $N$. Prove that $S_{D C M}=S_{A N B}$.
reference_solution:
132. Let $K$ be the midpoint of $DB$, and $L$ be the midpoint of $AC$. $S_{ANM}=S_{CNM}$ (since $|AL|=|LC|$), similarly $S_{BNM}=S_{DMN}$, from which the statement of the problem follows.

question: 133. In parallelogram $A B C D$, vertices $A, B, C$ and $D$ are connected to the midpoints of sides $C D, A D, A B$ and $B C$. Prove that the area of the quadrilateral formed by these lines is $1 / 5$ of the area of the parallelogram.
reference_solution:
133. If (Fig. 34) $M$ is the midpoint of $DC$, $N$ is the midpoint of $BC$, $K$ and $L$ are the points of intersection of $DN$ with $AM$ and $AB$ respectively, then $\frac{|KM|}{|AK|} = \frac{|DM|}{|AL|} = \frac{1}{4}$, i.e., $|AK| = \frac{4}{5}|AM|$, therefore,

$$
S_{ADK} = \frac{4}{5} S_{ADM} = \frac{4}{5} \cdot \frac{1}{4} S = \frac{1}{5} S
$$

( $S$ is the area of the parallelogram). Thus, the area of the desired figure will be $S - 4 S_{ADK} = S - \frac{4}{5} S = \frac{1}{5} S$.

question: 134. Prove that the area of the octagon formed by the lines connecting the vertices of a parallelogram to the midpoints of the opposite sides is $1 / 6$ of the area of the parallelogram.
reference_solution:
134. Let (Fig. 35) $Q$ be the midpoint of $A D$, $N$ be the midpoint of $B C$, $M$ be the midpoint of $D C$, and $K, P, R$ be the points of intersection of $D N$ and $A M$, $Q C$ and $D N$, $Q C$ and $A M$. Then $|D K|=\frac{2}{5}|D N|,\left|D P_{\mid}=\right| P N|, \quad Q P|=$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-101.jpg?height=310&width=387&top_left_y=287&top_left_x=166)

Fig. 35.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =|P C|, \left.\quad|Q R|=\frac{1}{3} \right\rvert\, Q C:, \frac{S_{R P K}}{S_{Q P D}}= \\
& =\frac{|R P|}{|Q P|} \cdot \frac{K P \mid}{\mid D P}=\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{1}{5}=\frac{1}{15} \\
& S_{R P K}=\frac{1}{15} \cdot \frac{S}{8}=\frac{S}{120} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, from the quadrilateral considered in the previous problem, four triangles of area $\frac{S}{120}$ are cut off; thus, the area of the desired octagon will be $\frac{S}{5}-\frac{4 S}{120}=\frac{S}{6}$.

question: 135. On the sides $AC$ and $BC$ of triangle $ABC$, two parallelograms $ACDE$ and $BCFG$ are constructed outwardly. The extensions of $DE$ and $FD$ intersect at point $H$. On side $AB$, a parallelogram $ABML$ is constructed, with sides $AL$ and $BM$ equal and parallel to $HC$. Prove that the parallelogram $ABML$ is equal in area to the sum of the parallelograms constructed on $AC$ and $BC$.

136. Through the ends of the smaller base of a trapezoid, two parallel lines are drawn intersecting the larger base. The diagonals of the trapezoid and these lines divide the trapezoid into seven triangles and one pentagon. Prove that the sum of the areas of the three triangles adjacent to the lateral sides and the smaller base of the trapezoid is equal to the area of the pentagon.
reference_solution:
136. Let's denote the areas as shown in Fig. 36. Then \( s_{1} + x + s_{2} = s_{2} + y + s_{3} = \frac{1}{2} \left( x + y + s_{2} + Q \right) \). Thus,

\[
s_{1} + x + s_{2} + s_{2} + y + s_{3} = x + y + s_{2} + Q \Rightarrow s_{1} + s_{2} + s_{3} = Q
\]

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-101.jpg?height=189&width=448&top_left_y=1329&top_left_x=210)

question:
137. Let $A B C D$ be a parallelogram, $E$ lies on line $A B$, $F$ lies on line $A D$ ($B$ is on segment $A E$,
$D$ is on segment $A F$), $K$ is the intersection point of lines $E D$ and $F B$. Prove that quadrilaterals $A B K D$ and $C E K F$ are equal in area.
reference_solution: 137. If $S$ is the area of the parallelogram (Fig. 37), then $S_{A B K} + S_{K C D} = \frac{1}{2} S$. On the other hand, $S_{D E C} = S_{E K C} + S_{K C D} = \frac{1}{2} S$, which means $S_{A B K} + S_{K C D} = S_{E K C} + S_{K C D}$, i.e., $S_{A B K} = S_{E K C}$; analogously, $S_{A K D} = S_{K C F}$; adding the last two equalities, we get $S_{A B K D} = S_{C E K F}$.

question: 138. Given a triangle $A B C$. On the rays $A B$ and $C B$, segments $|A K|=|C M|=|A C|$ are laid off. Prove that the radius of the circumcircle of $\triangle B K M$ is equal to the distance between the centers of the inscribed and circumscribed circles of $\triangle A B C$, and that the line $K M$ is perpendicular to the line connecting the centers of the inscribed and circumscribed circles.
reference_solution:
138. Let (Fig. $38, a$ ) $O$ be the center of the circumscribed circle, and $I$ be the center of the inscribed circle. Drop perpendiculars from $O$ and $I$ to $AB$ and $BC: ON, OP, IL, IQ$. If $a, b, c$ are the lengths of the sides $BC, AC$, and $AB$ of the triangle, it is easy to find $|BK|=|c-b|, |BM|=|a-b|$, $|BN|=\frac{c}{2}, |BP|=\frac{a}{2}, |BL|=|BQ|=\frac{a+c-b}{2}, |NL|=\frac{|a-b|}{2}$, $|PQ|=\frac{c-b}{2}$ (see problem 18, section $\left.\mathrm{I}\right)$.

Therefore, if we draw lines through $O$ parallel to the sides $AB$ and $BC$, intersecting the perpendiculars dropped from $I$, we get $\triangle ORS$, similar to $\triangle BKM$ with a coefficient of $1 / 2$. But the circle constructed on $OI$ as a diameter is circumscribed around $\triangle ORS$. Consequently, the radius of the circle circumscribed around $\triangle BKM$ is $|OI|$. For the proof of the second part of the problem, note that if we lay off $\left|OR_{1}\right|=|OR|$ on the line $OS$, and $\left|OS_{1}\right|=|OS|$ on the line $OR$, then the line $S_{1}R_{1}$ will be parallel to $KM$ (Fig. 38, b), but $\widehat{OR_{1}S_{1}}+\widehat{IOR_{1}}=$ $=\widehat{ORS}+\overline{IOS}=90^{\circ}$, i.e., $S_{1}R_{1} \perp OI$.

question: 140. Let $P, Q$ and $M$ be the points of intersection of the diagonals and the extensions of the opposite sides of a cyclic quadrilateral, respectively. Prove that the orthocenter of triangle $P Q M$ coincides with the center of the circle circumscribed around the given quadrilateral (Brocard).
reference_solution:
140. Let the radius of the circle be denoted by $R$, and the distances from $P, Q$, and $M$ to the center by $a, b$, and $c$. Then (see problem 87) $|Q P|^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}-2 R^{2},|Q M|^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2 R^{2},|P M|^{2}=c^{2}+a^{2}-2 R^{2}$. If $O$ is the center of the circle, then for $Q O$ to be perpendicular to $P M$, it is necessary and sufficient that the condition

$$
\left.\left|Q P^{2}-\right| Q M\right|^{2}=|P O|^{2}-|O M|^{2}
$$

or

$$
\left(a^{2}+b^{2}-2 R^{2}\right)-\left(b^{2}+c^{2}-2 R^{2}\right)=a^{2}-c^{2} .
$$

Similarly, the perpendicularity of other segments can be verified.

question: 141. Prove that if a circle can be inscribed in a quadrilateral, then: a) the circles inscribed in the two triangles into which the given quadrilateral is divided by a diagonal touch each other; b) the points of contact of these circles with the sides of the quadrilateral are the vertices of an inscribed quadrilateral.
reference_solution:
141. a) Consider the quadrilateral $A B C D$; let $K$ and $L$ be the points of tangency of the incircles of $\triangle A B C$ and $\triangle A C D$,

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-103.jpg?height=398&width=388&top_left_y=214&top_left_x=164)

Fig. 39. with the line $A C$. Then (see problem 18, section I)

\[
\begin{aligned}
& |K L|=|| A L|-| A K||= \\
& \left.=\frac{1}{2} \right\rvert\,(|A B|+|A C|-|B C|)- \\
& -(|A D|+|A C|-|C D|)= \\
& \left.=\frac{1}{2}|| A B|+| C D|-| A D \right\rvert\,- \\
& -|B C| \mid .
\end{aligned}
\]

But if $A B C D$ is a circumscribed quadrilateral, then $|A B|+\mid C D_{1}=$ $=|A D|+|B C|$ and $|K L|=0$.

b) If $K, L, M, N$ are the points of tangency of the incircle with the sides of the quadrilateral, and $K_{1}, L_{1}, M_{1}, N_{1}$ are the points of tangency of the incircles of $\triangle A B C$ and $\triangle A C D$ (Fig. 39), then $N_{1} K_{1}\left\|N K, M_{1} L_{1}\right\| M L$.

We will prove that $K_{1} L_{1} \| K L$ and $N_{1} M_{1} \| N M$. Since the incircles of $\triangle A C B$ and $\triangle A C D$ touch each other on the diagonal at point $P$, then $A N_{1}=A P=A M_{1}$, i.e., $N_{1} M_{1} N N M$. Therefore, the quadrilateral $K_{1} L_{1} M_{1} N_{1}$, like the quadrilateral $K L M N$, is inscribed.

question: 142. Prove that if $A B C D$ is a cyclic quadrilateral, then the sum of the radii of the circles inscribed in triangles $A B C$ and $A C D$ is equal to the sum of the radii of the circles inscribed in triangles $B C D$ and $B D A$.
reference_solution:
142. Let (Fig. 40, a, b) $O_{1}, O_{2}, O_{3}, O_{4}$ be the centers of the circles inscribed in $\triangle A B C, \triangle B C D, \triangle C D A$ and $\triangle D A B$. Since $\mathrm{O}_{1} \mathrm{O}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3} \mathrm{O}_{4}$ is a rectangle (see problem 127),
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-103.jpg?height=302&width=784&top_left_y=1033&top_left_x=226)

Fig. 40.

then $\left|O_{1} O_{3}\right|=\left|O_{2} O_{4}\right|$. If $K$ and $L$ are the points of tangency of the circles inscribed in $\triangle A B C$ and $\triangle A C D$ with $A C$, then $\left.|K L|=\frac{1}{2}|| A B \right\rvert\,+$ $+|C D|-|B C|-|A D| \mid$ (see problem 141). Similarly, if $P$ and $Q$ are the points of tangency of the corresponding circles with $B D$, then $|P Q|=$ $=|K L|$. Draw a line through $O_{3}$ parallel to $A C$, intersecting the extension of $O_{1} K$. We obtain $\triangle O_{1} O_{3} M$, similarly construct $\triangle \mathrm{O}_{2} O_{4} R$. These two right triangles are equal, since they have $\left|O_{1} O_{3}\right|=\left|O_{2} O_{4}\right|$, $\left|O_{3} M\right|=|K L|=|P Q|=\left|O_{4} R\right|$. Therefore, $\left|O_{1} M\right|=\left|O_{2} R\right|$, but $\left|O_{1} M\right|$ is equal to the sum of the radii of the circles inscribed in $\triangle A B C$ and $\triangle A C D$, and $\left|O_{2} R\right|$ is equal to the sum of the radii of the circles inscribed in $\triangle A C D$ and $\triangle B D A$.

question: 143. $A B C$ is an isosceles triangle $(|A B| = |B C|)$, and $B D$ is its height. A circle with radius $B D$ rolls along the line $A C$. Prove that while the vertex $B$ is inside the circle, the arc of the circle located inside the triangle has a constant length.
reference_solution: 143. Let $\breve{K L}$ be an arc of a circle located inside triangle $A B C$. By extending sides $A B$ and $B C$ beyond point $B$, we obtain arc $\overline{M N}$, which is symmetric to $\breve{K L}$ with respect to the diameter parallel to $A C$. Since $\widehat{A B C}$ is measured by the arc $\frac{1}{2}$ ( $\breve{K L}+$ $+\widehat{M N})=\breve{K L}$, it follows that the arc $\breve{K L}$ has a constant length, corresponding to a central angle equal to $\widehat{A B C}$.

question: 146. Prove that if perpendiculars are dropped from an arbitrary point on a circle to the sides of an inscribed $2 n$-gon, then the products of the lengths of these perpendiculars taken alternately will be equal.
reference_solution:
146. Let (Fig. 43) $A$ be a given point, $A_{k}$ be some vertex of a $2n$-gon, $B_{k-1}$ and $B_{k}$ be the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from $A$ to the sides enclosing $A_{k}, \alpha_{k}$ and $\beta_{k}$ be the angles formed by the line $A A_{k}$ with these

Fig. 43. sides $\quad\left(\beta_{k}={\widehat{A A_{k} B}}_{k-1}, \quad \alpha_{k}=\right.$ $=\widehat{A A_{k} B_{k}}$ ). Since a circle can be circumscribed around the quadrilateral $A B_{k-1} A_{k} B_{k}$, then $\widehat{A B_{k-1}} B_{k}=$

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{\left|A B_{k-1}\right|}{\left|A B_{k}\right|}=\frac{\sin \beta_{k}}{\sin \alpha_{k}} \\
\frac{\left|A B_{k-1}\right|\left|A B_{k+1}\right|}{\left|A B_{k}\right|^{2}}=\frac{\sin \beta_{k} \sin \alpha_{k+1}}{\sin \alpha_{k} \sin \beta_{k+1}}
\end{gathered}

Multiplying these equalities for $k=2,4, \ldots, 2 n$, replacing the index $2 n+1$ with 1, we obtain the required result ( $\sin \alpha_{k}=\sin \beta_{k+1}$, $\left.\sin \beta_{1}=\sin \alpha_{2 n}\right)$).

148. Let the lengths of the sides of a triangle be \(a, b, c\), and \(b = \frac{a+c}{2}\).

a) From the equality \(p r = \frac{1}{2} b h_{b}\) (where \(p\) is the semiperimeter, \(r\) is the radius of the inscribed circle, and \(h_{b}\) is the height dropped to side \(b\)), we get \(\frac{a+b+c}{2} r = \frac{1}{2} b h_{b}\); but \(a+c = 2b\), so \(h_{b} = 3r\).

b) This statement follows from the fact that \(r = \frac{h_{b}}{3}\), and the point of intersection of the medians divides each in the ratio \(2:1\).
c) Extend the bisector \(BD\) to intersect the circumscribed circle at point \(M\) (see Fig. 44). If we prove that the incenter \(O\) divides \(BM\) in half, then our statement will also be proven. (Draw the diameter \(BN\); then the line connecting the centers of the inscribed and circumscribed circles will be parallel to \(NM\), and \(\widehat{BMN} = 90^\circ\).) But \(\triangle COM\) is isosceles because \(\widehat{COM} = \widehat{OCM} = \frac{\hat{C}}{2} + \frac{\hat{B}}{2}\). Therefore, \(|CM| = |OM|\). From the condition \(b = \frac{a+c}{2}\) and the property of the bisector, we get \(|CD| = \frac{a}{2}\). Let \(K\) be the midpoint of \(CB\); \(\triangle CKO = \triangle CDO \quad (|CK| = |CD|, \widehat{KCO} = \widehat{OCD})\); hence \(\widehat{BKO} = \widehat{CDM}\), and \(\widehat{DCM} = \widehat{OBK} = \frac{\hat{B}}{2}, |CD| = |BK|\), so \(\triangle BKO = \triangle CDM, |CM| = |BO|\), thus \(|BO| = |OM|\), which is what we needed to prove.

d) Take any point on the bisector. Let the distances to sides \(BC\) and \(BA\) be \(x\), and to side \(AC\) be \(y\). We have

\[
\frac{ax + cx + by}{2} = S_{\triangle} \Rightarrow b(2x + y) = 2S_{\triangle} \Rightarrow 2x + y = h_{b}
\]

e) If \(L\) is the midpoint of \(BA\), then the quadrilateral we need is homothetic to the quadrilateral \(BCMA\) with a coefficient of \(1/2\) (see part c).

question:
149. Bretschneider's Theorem (Cosine Rule for Quadrilaterals). Let $a, b, c, d$ be the consecutive side lengths of a quadrilateral, $m$ and $n$ the lengths of its diagonals, $\hat{A}$ and $\hat{C}$ the measures of two opposite angles. Then the following relation holds:

$$
m^{2} n^{2}=a^{2} c^{2}+b^{2} d^{2}-2 a b c d \cos (\hat{A}+\hat{C})
$$
reference_solution:
149. Let in quadrilateral $A B C D$ (Fig. 15)

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
|A B|=a, & B C|=b, \quad| C D \mid=c \\
|D A|=d, & |A C|=m, \quad|B D|=n
\end{array}
$$

Construct triangle $A K B$ on side $A B$ outward, similar to triangle $A C D$, such that $\widehat{B A K}=\widehat{D C A}, \widehat{A B K}=\widehat{C A D}$. On side $A D$, construct $\triangle A M D$, similar to $\triangle A B C$, $\widehat{D A M}=\widehat{B C A}, \widehat{A D M}=\widehat{C A B}$ (Fig. 45). From the corresponding similarity, we get

$$
|A K|=\frac{a c}{m}, \quad|A M|=\frac{d b}{m}, \quad|K B|=\left\lvert\, D M_{i}=\frac{a d}{m}\right.
$$

Moreover, $\widehat{K B D}+\widehat{M D B}=\widehat{K B A}+\widehat{A B D}+\widehat{B D A}+\widehat{A D M}=\widehat{C A D}+$ $+\widehat{A B D}+\widehat{B D A}+\widehat{C A B}=180^{\circ}$, i.e., quadrilateral $K B D M$ is a parallelogram. Therefore, $|K M|=|B D|=n$. But $\widehat{K} A \widehat{M}=\hat{A}+\hat{C}$. By the cosine theorem for $\triangle K A M$, we have

$$
n^{2}=\left(\frac{a c}{m}\right)^{2}+\left(\frac{d b}{m}\right)^{2}-2\left(\frac{a c}{m}\right)\left(\frac{d b}{m}\right) \cos (\hat{A}+\hat{C})
$$

from which $m^{2} n^{2}=a^{2} c^{2}+b^{2} d^{2}-2 a b c d \cos (\hat{A}+\hat{C})$.

question: 151. Prove that if $A B C$ is an equilateral triangle, $M$ is an arbitrary point in the plane, not lying on the circumcircle of $A B C$, then there exists a triangle whose side lengths are $|M A|$, $|M B|$, and $|M C|$ (Pompeiu's theorem). Find the angle of this triangle opposite the side equal to $|M B|$, if $\widehat{A M C}=\alpha$.
reference_solution: 151. If $|M B|$ is the greatest of the segments $|M A|,|M B|, |M C|$, then applying Bretschneider's theorem (problem 149) to the quadrilateral $A B C M$, we get that $|M B|^{2}=|M A|^{2}+|M C|^{2}-$ $-2|M A| \cdot|M C| \cos \left(\widehat{A M C}+60^{\circ}\right), \quad$ i.e. $\quad|M B|<|M A|+|M C|$, since $\cos \left(\widehat{A M C}+60^{\circ}\right) \neq-1$.

question:
152. Consider a circle in which a regular $(2 n+1)$-gon $A_{1} A_{2} \ldots A_{2 n+1}$ is inscribed. Let $A$ be an arbitrary point on the arc $A_{1} A_{2 n+1}$.

a) Prove that the sum of the distances from $A$ to the vertices with even indices is equal to the sum of the distances from $A$ to the vertices with odd indices.

b) Construct equal circles that are tangent to the given circle at points $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{2 n+1}$. Prove that the sum of the lengths of the tangents drawn from $A$ to the circles tangent to the given circle at the vertices with even indices is equal to the sum of the lengths of the tangents drawn to the circles tangent to the given circle at the vertices with odd indices.
reference_solution:
152. a) Let $A$ be an arbitrary point on the circle (on the arc $\widehat{A_{2 n+1} A_{1}}$). Denote the side of the polygon by $a$, and the length of the diagonal connecting vertices separated by one vertex by $b$. By Ptolemy's theorem for the quadrilateral $A A_{k} A_{k+1} A_{k+2}$

$$
\left|A A_{k}\right| a+\left|A A_{k+2}\right| a=\left|A A_{k+1}\right| b, \quad k=1,2, \ldots, 2 n-1
$$

Similar relations can be written for the quadrilaterals $A_{2 n} A_{2 n+1} A A_{1}$ and $A_{2 n+1} A A_{1} A_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left|A A_{1}\right| a+\left|A A_{2 n+1}\right| b=\left|A A_{2 n}\right| a \\
& \left|A A_{2 n+1}\right| a+\left|A A_{1}\right| b=\left|A A_{2}\right| a
\end{aligned}
$$

By adding all these equations, keeping the vertices with even indices on the right and those with odd indices on the left, we obtain the required statement.

b) Our statement follows from part a) and the results of problems 20 and 21.

question:
153. Theorem of Leibniz. Let $M$ be an arbitrary point in the plane, and $G$ the centroid of triangle $ABC$. Then the following equality holds: $3|M G|^{2}=|M A|^{2}+|M B|^{2}+|M C|^{2}-$

$$
-1 / 3\left(|A B|^{2}+|B C|^{2}+|C A|^{2}\right)
$$

154. Let $A B C$ be an equilateral triangle with side $a$, and $M$ be some point on the plane, located at a distance $d$ from the center of the triangle $A B C$. Prove that the area of the triangle with sides equal to the segments $|M A|,|M B|,|M C|$, is expressed by the formula $S=\frac{\sqrt{\overline{3}}}{12}\left|a^{2}-3 d^{2}\right|$.
reference_solution:
154. Consider the case when point $M$ (Fig. 46) lies inside triangle $A B C$. Rotate triangle $A B M$ around $A$ by an angle of $60^{\circ}$ so that $B$ moves to $C$. We obtain triangle $A M_{1} C$, equal to $\triangle A B M$. Triangle $A M M_{1}$ is equilateral, hence the side lengths of $\triangle C M M_{1}$ are equal to the segments $|MA|$, $|MB|$, and $|MC|$. Similarly, we obtain points $M_{2}$ and $M_{3}$. The area of the hexagon $A M_{1} C M_{3} B M_{2}$ (Fig. 46) is twice the area of $\triangle A B C$, i.e., it is equal to $a^{2} \sqrt{3} / 2$. On the other hand, the area of this hexagon is composed of three equilateral triangles: $\triangle A M M_{1}$, $\triangle C M M_{3}$, $\triangle B M M_{2}$, and three triangles equal to the desired one. Therefore,

$$
\begin{array}{r}
3 S+\frac{|M A|^{2}+|M B|^{2}+|M C|^{2}}{4} \sqrt{3}= \\
=\frac{a^{2} \sqrt{3}}{2}
\end{array}
$$

Using the result from problem 153, we get

$$
3 S+\frac{\left(3 d^{2}+a^{2}\right) \sqrt{3}}{4}=\frac{a^{2} \sqrt{\overline{3}}}{2}
$$

from which $S=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{12}\left(a^{2}-3 d^{2}\right)$.

question: 155. The extensions of sides $A B$ and $D C$ of a convex quadrilateral $A B C D$ intersect at point $K$, and the extensions of sides $A D$ and $B C$ intersect at point $L$, such that segments $B L$ and $D K$ intersect. Prove that if one of the three relations $|A B|+|C D|=$ $=|B C|+|A D|,|B K|+|B L|=|D K|+|D L|,|A K|+$ $+|C L|=|A L|+|C K|$ holds, then the other two also hold.
reference_solution: 155. Show that each of these conditions is necessary and sufficient for the existence of a circle inscribed in a quadrilateral $A B C D$ (see also problem 19, section I).

The extensions of sides $A B$ and $D C$ of the convex quadrilateral $A E C D$ intersect at point $K$, and the extensions of sides $A D$ and $B C$ intersect at point $L$, such that segments $B L'$ and $D K$ intersect. reference_solution: 156. Show that each of these conditions is necessary and sufficient for there to exist a circle that is tangent to the lines $A B, B C, C D$ and $D A$, with its center located outside the quadrilateral $A B C D$.

question: 159. On the sides of a quadrilateral, squares are constructed outwardly. Prove that the segments connecting the centers of opposite squares are equal in length and perpendicular to each other.
reference_solution: 159. Let $O_{1}, O_{2}, O_{3}, O_{4}$ be the consecutive centers of squares. We will perform sequential rotations in the same direction around the points $O_{1}, O_{2}, O_{3}, O_{4}$ by $90^{\circ}$. Reasoning as in the previous problem, we will show that the resulting transformation leaves all points of the plane fixed. Therefore (see problem 140, section I), each of the two pairs of rotations: around $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$ and around $O_{3}$ and $O_{4}$ can be replaced by a central symmetry relative to the same point 0. In this case, $\triangle O_{1} O O_{2}$ and $\triangle \mathrm{O}_{3} \mathrm{OO}_{4}$ are isosceles right triangles with right angles at vertex 0. Therefore, triangle $\mathrm{O}_{2} \mathrm{OO}_{4}$ is obtained from triangle $\mathrm{O}_{1} \mathrm{OO}_{3}$ by a rotation around $O$ by $90^{\circ}$, i.e., $\mid O_{1} O_{3}:=O_{2} O_{4}!$, $\mathrm{O}_{1} \mathrm{O}_{3}!\mathrm{O}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}$.

160. Let $ABC$ be a given triangle, $A_1B_1C_1$ be triangle $\Delta$, and $A_2B_2C_2$ be triangle $\delta$ (where $A_1$ and $A_2$ are the centers of triangles constructed on $BC$), the sides of triangle $ABC$ are $a, b, c$ as usual.

a) The fact that triangles $A_1B_1C_1$ and $A_2B_2C_2$ are equilateral follows, for example, from the result of problem 158.

b) Let's find the distance from $A_1$ to $M$ - the point of intersection of the medians of triangle $ABC$. Let $N$ be the point of intersection of the line $A_1M$ and the altitude to side $BC$, and $K$ be the point of intersection of the same altitude with the line passing through $A_1$ parallel to $BC$ (obviously, $N$ lies on the extension of the altitude beyond point $A$, and $K$ lies on the extension beyond line $BC$, see Fig. 48). If $D$ is the midpoint of $BC$, then

\[
\begin{aligned}
& \left|A_1D\right| = \frac{a}{6} \sqrt{3}, \left|AN\right| = 2 \left|A_1D\right| = \frac{a \sqrt{3}}{3} \\
& \left|NK\right| = h_a + \left|A_1D\right| + \left|AN\right| = h_a + \frac{a \sqrt{3}}{2}
\end{aligned}
\]

($h_a$ - the altitude from vertex $A$),

\[
\left|A_1K\right| = \left| \frac{a}{2} - c \cos \hat{B} \right|
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
& \left|A_1M\right|^2 = \frac{1}{9} \left|A_1N\right|^2 = \frac{1}{9} \left( \left|NK\right|^2 + \left|A_1K\right|^2 \right) = \\
& = \frac{1}{9} \left( h_a^2 + a h_a \sqrt{3} + \frac{3}{4} a^2 + \frac{a^2}{4} - a c \cos \hat{B} + c^2 \cos^2 \hat{B} \right) = \\
& = \frac{1}{9} \left( \frac{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}{2} + 2 S \sqrt{3} \right)
\end{aligned}
\]

(We used the equalities $S = \frac{1}{2} a h_a$, $h_a^2 + c^2 \cos^2 \hat{B} = c^2$, and the cosine theorem.) The distances $B_1M$ and $C_1M$ are found similarly, and all of them, as can be easily seen, are equal. In the same way, we find the squares of the distances from $M$ to points $A_2, B_2, C_2$. They are equal to $\frac{1}{9} \left( \frac{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}{2} - 2 S \sqrt{3} \right)$

c) Using the result of the previous part, since $S_{\Delta} = \frac{3}{4} \left|A_1M\right|^2 \sqrt{3}$, $S_{\delta} = \frac{3}{4} \left|A_2M\right|^2 \sqrt{3}$, it is easy to obtain the required statement.

question:
161. Given an arbitrary triangle $A B C$. On the line passing through vertex $A$ and perpendicular to side $B C$, two points $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$ are taken such that $\left|A A_{1}\right|=$ $=\left|A A_{2}\right|=|B C|$ ( $A_{1}$ is closer to line $B C$ than $A_{2}$).

Similarly, on the line perpendicular to $A C$ and passing through $B$, points $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$ are taken such that $\left|B B_{1}\right|=\left|B B_{1}\right|=|A C|$. Prove that segments $A_{1} B_{2}$ and $A_{2} B_{1}$ are equal in length and perpendicular to each other.
reference_solution: 161. We will prove that triangles $C B_{1} A_{2}$ and $C A_{1} B_{2}$ are obtained from each other by a rotation about point $C$ by an angle of $90^{\circ}$. Indeed, $\triangle C A A_{1}=\triangle C B B_{1}\left(B B_{1}{ }^{\prime}=A C, \quad B C==^{\prime} A A_{1}^{\prime}, \widehat{C B B_{1}}=\right.$ $=\widehat{C A A_{1}}$ ), and since $A A_{1} \perp B C$ and $B B_{1} \perp A C$, then $B_{1} C \perp A_{1} C$. Similarly, $A_{2} C$ and $B_{2} C$ are equal and perpendicular.

question: 162. Prove that the midpoints of the sides of a triangle, the feet of the altitudes, and the midpoints of the segments of the altitudes from the vertices to their point of intersection lie on one circle, the "nine-point circle" (Euler).
reference_solution:
162. Let $A B C$ be a given triangle, $H$ the point of intersection of its altitudes, $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ the midpoints of segments $A H, B H, C H$, $A A_{2}$ the altitude, and $A_{3}$ the midpoint of $B C$.

For convenience, let's assume that $\triangle A B C$ is an acute triangle. Since $\widehat{B_{1} A_{1} C_{1}}=\widehat{B A C}$ and $\triangle B_{1} A_{2} C_{1}=\triangle B_{1} H C_{1}$, it follows that $\widehat{B_{1} A_{2} C_{1}}=\widehat{B_{1} H C_{1}}=180^{\circ}-\widehat{B A C}$, i.e., points $A_{1}, B_{1}, A_{2}, C_{1}$ lie on the same circle. It is also easy to see that $\widehat{B_{1} A_{3} C_{1}}=\widehat{B H C_{1}}=180^{\circ}-\widehat{B A C}$, i.e., points $A_{1}, B_{1}, A_{3}, C_{1}$ also lie on the same (and therefore the same) circle. From this, it follows that all 9 points mentioned in the problem lie on the same circle. The case of an obtuse triangle $A B C$ is considered similarly. Note that the nine-point circle is homothetic to the circumcircle with the center at $H$ and a coefficient of $1 / 2$. (This is how triangles $A B C$ and $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ are positioned.) On the other hand, the nine-point circle is homothetic to the circumcircle with the center at the intersection of the medians of triangle $A B C$ and a coefficient of $-1 / 2$. (This is how triangles $A B C$ and the triangle with vertices at the midpoints of its sides are positioned.)

question: 163. Let $H$ be the orthocenter of a triangle, $D$ the midpoint of one of its sides, and $K$ one of the intersection points of the line $H D$ with the circumcircle (with $D$ between $H$ and $K$). Prove that $D$ is the midpoint of the segment $H K$.
reference_solution: 163. Our statement follows from the fact that $D$ lies on the nine-point circle, and the nine-point circle is homothetic to the circumcircle with center $H$ and coefficient $1 / 2$ (see problem 162).

question:
164. Let $M$ be the point of intersection of the medians of a triangle, $E$ be the foot of some altitude, and $F$ be one of the points of intersection of the line $M E$ with the circumscribed circle ($M$ is between $E$ and $F$). Prove that $|F M|=2|E M|$.

In problems 165-168, $a, b$ and $c$ denote the lengths of the sides of the triangle, $p$ is the semiperimeter, $R$ is the radius of the circumscribed circle, and $r$ is the radius of the inscribed circle.
reference_solution: 164. Our statement follows from the fact that $E$ lies on the nine-point circle, and the nine-point circle is homothetic to the circumcircle with center $M$ and coefficient $-1 / 2$ (see problem 162).

question: 166. Prove that the square of the distance between the centroid and the circumcenter of a triangle is equal to $R^{2}-\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}{9}$.
reference_solution: 166. Use Leibniz's formula (problem 153), taking as $M$ the center of the circumscribed circle.

question: 167. Prove that the square of the distance between the centroid of a triangle and the center of the inscribed circle is equal to $\frac{1}{9}\left(p^{2}+5 r^{2}-16 R r\right)$.
reference_solution:
167. Use Leibniz's formula (Problem 153), taking as \( M \) the center of the inscribed circle. To calculate, for example, \( |M A|^{2} \), drop a perpendicular \( M K \) to \( A B \); we have \( |M K|=r \), \( |A K|=p-a \), hence, \( |A M|^{2}=(p-a)^{2}+r^{2} \).

Similarly, \( |M B|^{2} \) and \( |M C|^{2} \) are calculated. When simplifying the right-hand side, use the result of Problem 165.

question:
168. Let $d$ be the distance between the centers of the inscribed and circumscribed circles of a triangle. Prove that

$$
d^{2}=R^{2}-2 R r \quad(\text { Euler }) .
$$
reference_solution:
168. Let $O$ be the center of the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$, and $O_{1}$ be the center of the inscribed circle. $M$ is the intersection point of the angle bisector of $\angle B$ with the circumcircle (Fig. 49). Since the point $O_{1}$ is at a distance $d$ from the center $O$, then $\left|B O_{1}\right| \cdot \left|O_{1} M\right| = R^{2} - d^{2}$. The triangle $O_{1} C M$ is isosceles: $\left|O_{1} M\right| = |C M|$, because $\widehat{C O_{1} M} = \frac{1}{2}(\hat{B} + \hat{C})$ and $\widehat{O_{1} C M} = \frac{1}{2}(\hat{B} + \hat{C})$.

By drawing the diameter $M K$ and dropping a perpendicular $O_{1} D$ to $B C$, we obtain two similar right triangles $M K C$ and $O_{1} B D$, from which $\frac{|M K|}{|M C|} = \frac{\left|B O_{1}\right|}{\left|O_{1} D\right|}$, but $\quad |M K| = 2 R$, $\left|O_{1} D\right| = r, \quad |M C| = \left|M O_{1}\right|, \quad$ hence,

Fig. 49. $2 R r = \left|B O_{1}\right| \cdot \left|O_{1} M\right| = R^{2} - d^{2}$.

question:
169. Prove that the nine-point circle (see problem 162) is tangent to the incircle of the triangle (Feuerbach).

## § 3. Geometric Loci. Belonging of Points to Lines and Circles
reference_solution:
169. Let $G$ be the centroid of triangle $ABC$, $O$ the circumcenter, $I$ the incenter, and $O_{1}$ the center of the nine-point circle. $G$ lies on the segment $OO_{1}$, and $|OG|=2|GO_{1}|$. If $\widehat{OGI}=\varphi$, then

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}
|O I_{1}|^{2} & =|OG|^{2}+|GI|^{2}-2|OG|\cdot|GI|\cos\varphi \\
|O_{1}I|^{2} & =|GI|^{2}+|GO_{1}|^{2}+2|GI|\cdot|GO_{1}|\cos\varphi
\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Multiplying the second equation by 2 and adding it to the first, we get

$$
2|O_{1}I|^{2}+|OI|^{2}=|OG|^{2}+2|GO_{1}|^{2}+3|GI|^{2}
$$

Considering that $|GO_{1}|=\frac{1}{2}|GO|$, we get

$$
|O_{1}I|^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left(3|GI|^{2}+\frac{3}{2}|GO|^{2}-|OI|^{2}\right)
$$

From the results of problems 165-168, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
& |O_{1}|^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{p^{2}}{3}+\frac{5}{3}r^{2}-\frac{16}{3}Rr+\frac{3}{2}R^{2}-\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}{6}-R^{2}+2Rr\right)= \\
& =\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{p^{2}}{3}+\frac{5}{3}r^{2}-\frac{10}{3}Rr+\frac{R^{2}}{2}-\frac{1}{3}p^{2}+\frac{1}{3}r^{2}+\frac{4}{3}Rr\right)= \\
& =\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{R^{2}}{2}-2Rr+2r^{2}\right)=\left(\frac{R}{2}-r\right)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $|O_{1}I|=\left|\frac{R}{2}-r\right|$, which means the incircle and the nine-point circle are internally tangent.

question: 170. Given two points $A$ and $B$. Prove that the set of points $M$ such that $|A M|^{2}-|M B|^{2}=k$ (where $k$ is a given number), is a line perpendicular to $A B$.
reference_solution:
170. Prove that if $D$ is the projection of $M$ onto $A B$, then

$$
|A D|^{2}-|B D|^{2}=|A M|^{2}-|M B|^{2}.
$$

question:
172. Prove that for the perpendiculars dropped from points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ to the sides $B C, C A$, and $A B$ of triangle $A B C$ to intersect at one point, it is necessary and sufficient that

$\left|A_{1} B\right|^{2}-\left|B C_{1}\right|^{2}+\left|C_{1} A\right|^{2}-\left|A B_{1}\right|^{2}+\left|B_{1} C\right|^{2}-\left|C A_{1}\right|^{2}=0$.

173. Prove that if the perpendiculars dropped from points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ to the lines $B C, C A$ and $A B$ respectively intersect at one point, then the perpendiculars dropped from points $A, B$ and $C$ to the lines $B_{1} C_{1}$, $C_{1} A_{1}$ and $A_{1} B_{1}$ also intersect at one point.
reference_solution: 173. From the result of problem 172, it follows that the condition for the perpendiculars dropped from $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ to the sides $B C, C A$ and $A B$ to intersect at one point is the same as the condition for the perpendiculars dropped from $A, B$ and $C$ to $B_{1} C_{1}, C_{1} A_{1}$ and $A_{1} B_{1}$ to intersect at one point.

question: 181. Let a line intersect one circle at points $A$ and $B$, and another circle at points $C$ and $D$. Prove that the points of intersection of the tangents to the first circle drawn at points $A$ and $B$ with the tangents drawn to the second circle at points $C$ and $D$ (considering the points where the tangents to different circles intersect) lie on one circle, the center of which lies on the line passing through the centers of the given circles.
reference_solution:
181. Let (Fig. 50) $K$ and $L$ be the points of intersection of the tangent to the second circle passing through $D$ with the tangents to the first circle passing through $B$ and $A$, and let $M$ and $N$ be the other two points. It is easy to see that $\widehat{D K B}=\widehat{C M A}$ (each of these angles is equal to half the difference of the angles corresponding to the arcs $\breve{A B}$ and $\overline{C D}$). Therefore (in our figure) $\widehat{L} \widehat{M N}+\widehat{L K M}=180^{\circ}$.

Thus, the quadrilateral $K L M N$ is cyclic. Further, we have

$$
\frac{D K}{\mid K B}=\frac{\sin \widehat{D B K}}{\sin B \overline{D K}}=\frac{\sin \frac{1}{2} \widetilde{A B}}{\sin \frac{1}{2} \widetilde{D C}}
$$

Similarly, the ratios of the lengths of the tangents drawn through points $L, M$, and $N$ are found.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-114.jpg?height=413&width=404&top_left_y=503&top_left_x=682)

Fig. 50. All these ratios are equal to each other; hence, the center of the circle circumscribed around $K L M N$ lies on the line passing through the centers of the given circles (see problem 175).

question: 183. Given a triangle $ABC$. Consider all possible pairs of points $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ such that $\left|A M_{1}\right|:\left|B M_{1}\right|:\left|C M_{1}\right|=\left|A M_{2}\right|:\left|B M_{2}\right|:\left|C M_{2}\right|$. Prove that all lines $M_{1} M_{2}$ pass through a fixed point on the plane.
reference_solution:
183. Let $\left|A M_{1 \mid}:\right| B M_{1}\left|: C M_{1}\right|=p: q: r$. Then the set of points $M$ such that

$$
\left(r^{2}-q^{2}\right) A M{ }^{2}+\left(p^{2}-r^{2}\right) ;\left.B M\right|^{2}+\left(q^{2}-p^{2}\right) ; C M ;^{2}=0
$$

is a straight line passing through $M_{1}, M_{2}$ and the center of the circumcircle of $\triangle A B C$ (see problem 176).

question: 185. Let $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ be the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from the vertices $A, B$, and $C$ of triangle $ABC$ to the line $l$. Prove that the perpendiculars dropped from $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ to $BC, CA$, and $AB$, respectively, intersect at one point.
reference_solution: 185. Let $\left|A A_{1}\right|=a,\left|B B_{1}\right|=b, \quad\left|C C_{1}\right|=c,\left|A_{1} B_{1}\right|=x$, $\left|B_{1} C_{1}\right|=y, \quad\left|C_{1} A_{1}\right|=z$. Then $\left|A B_{1}\right|^{2}=a^{2}+x^{2}, \mid B_{1} C^{2}=c^{2}+y^{2}$, $\left|C A_{1}{ }^{2}=c^{2}+z^{2},\right| A_{1} B=b^{2}+x^{2},\left|B C_{1}\right|^{2}=b^{2}+y^{2}, \mid C_{1} A^{2}=a^{2}+z^{2}$. Now it is easy to verify the condition of problem 172.

question: 186. Given an equilateral triangle $A B C$ and an arbitrary point $D$; $A_{1}, B_{1}$, and $C_{1}$ are the centers of the circles inscribed in triangles $B C D, A C D$, and $A B D$. Prove that the perpendiculars dropped from vertices $A, B$, and $C$ to $B_{1} C_{1}, C_{1} A_{1}$, and $A_{1} B_{1}$ respectively, intersect at one point.
reference_solution:
186. Let $|A D|=x,|B D|=y,|C D|=y,|A B|=a$. Denote by $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ the points of tangency of the incircles of triangles $B C D, C A D, A B D$ with sides $B C, C A, A B$. The perpendiculars drawn through points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ to sides $B C, C A$, and $A B$ coincide with the perpendiculars erected to the same sides at points $A_{2} ; B_{2}, C_{2}$.

But $\left|B A_{2}\right|=\frac{a+y-z}{2},\left|A_{2} C\right|=\frac{a+z-y}{2}$; similarly $\left|A C_{2}\right|=$ $=\frac{a+x-y}{2}, \quad\left|C_{2} B\right|=\frac{a+y-x}{2}, \quad\left|A B_{2}\right|=\frac{a+x-z}{2}, \quad\left|B_{2} C\right|=$ $=\frac{a+z-x}{2}$. Now it is easy to verify the condition of problem 172.

question: 187. Given three pairwise intersecting circles. Prove that the three common chords of these circles pass through one point.
reference_solution: 187. Apply the condition proved in problem 173, taking points $A, B$ and $C$ as the centers of the circles, and points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ as one of the intersection points of the circles ( $A_{1}$ - one of the intersection points of the circles with centers $B$ and $C$ and so on.)

question: 188. On the lines $A B$ and $A C$, points $M$ and $N$ are taken respectively. Prove that the common chord of the two circles with diameters $C M$ and $B N$ passes through the orthocenter of $\triangle A B C$.
reference_solution: 188. Let's take the third circle with diameter $B C$. The common chords of the 1st and 3rd, as well as the 2nd and 3rd circles, are the altitudes of the triangle dropped from vertices $B$ and $C$. Therefore (see problem 187), the common chord of these circles also passes through the orthocenter of triangle $A B C$.

191. We have

$$
\frac{\left|A C_{1}\right|}{\left|C_{1} B\right|}=\frac{S_{A C C_{1}}}{S_{C C_{1} B}}=\frac{\frac{1}{2}|A C| \cdot\left|C C_{1}\right| \sin \widehat{A C C_{1}}}{\frac{1}{2}\left|C C_{1}\right| \cdot|C B| \sin \widehat{O_{1} C B}}=\frac{|A C|}{|B C|} \frac{\sin \widehat{A C C_{1}}}{\sin \widehat{C_{1} C B}}
$$

By obtaining similar equalities for the ratios $\frac{\left|B A_{1}\right|}{\left|A_{1} C\right|}$ and $\frac{\left|C B_{1}\right|}{\left|B_{1} A\right|}$, and multiplying them, we obtain the required statement.

question: 192. Ceva's Theorem. For the lines $A A_{1}, B B_{1}, C C_{1}$ to intersect at one point (or all three to be parallel), it is necessary and sufficient that $R=1$ (see problem 191) and at the same time, an odd number (i.e., one or all three) of the points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ lie on the sides of the triangle, and not on the extensions of the sides.
reference_solution:
192. Let's show that if the lines $A A_{1}, B B_{1}$, and $C C_{1}$ intersect at one point (denote it by $M$), then $R^{*}=1$ (and consequently, $R=1$; see problem 191). By the Law of Sines for $\triangle A M C$

$$
\frac{\sin \widehat{A C C_{1}}}{\sin \widehat{A_{1} A C}}=\frac{|A M|}{|M C|}
$$

Writing similar equalities for triangles $A M B$ and $B M C$ and multiplying them, we obtain the required statement. Conversely, if $R=1$ and all points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ lie on the sides of the triangle (or only one of them), then, drawing lines $A A_{1}$ and $B B_{1}$, denote their intersection point by $M_{1}$; let the line $C M_{1}$ intersect $A B$ at point $C_{2}$. Considering the conditions of the problem and the necessity of the condition $R=1$ that has been proven, we will have $\frac{|A C_{1}|}{|C_{1} B|}=\frac{|A C_{2}|}{|C_{2} B|}$, and points $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ lie simultaneously either on the segment $A B$ or outside it. Therefore, $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$ coincide.

question: 193. Theorem of Menelaus. For points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ to lie on the same line, it is necessary and sufficient that $R=1$ (see problem 191) and at the same time, an even number (i.e., zero or two) of the three points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ lie on the sides of the triangle, and not on their extensions.
reference_solution: 193. Let $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ lie on the same line. Draw a line through $C$ parallel to $A B$, and denote by $M$ the point of its intersection with the line $A_{1} B_{1}$. From the similarity of the corresponding triangles, we get $\frac{\left|B A_{1}\right|}{\left|A_{1} C\right|}=\frac{\left|B C_{1}\right|}{\mid C M}, \frac{\left|C B_{1}\right|}{\mid B_{1} A}=\frac{|C M|}{\left|A C_{1}\right|}$. Replacing the corresponding ratios in the expression $R$ (see problem 191), we obtain that $R=1$. The converse statement is proved similarly to how it was done in problem 192 (draw the line $B_{1} A_{1}$, denote by $C_{2}$ the point of its intersection with $A B$, etc.).

question: 194. Prove that if three lines passing through the vertices of a triangle intersect at one point, then the lines symmetric to them with respect to the corresponding angle bisectors of the triangle also intersect at one point or are parallel.
reference_solution: 194. Check that if for the given lines $R^{*}=1$, then it will also be the case for the symmetric ones. At the same time, if a line passing through, for example, vertex $A$ intersects side $B C$, then the line symmetric to it with respect to the bisector of angle $A$ will also intersect side $B C$.

question: 195. Let $O$ be an arbitrary point in the plane, $M$ and $N$ be the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from point $O$ to the internal and external angle bisectors of $\angle A$ of $\triangle ABC$, $P$ and $Q$ are similarly defined for $\angle B$, and $R$ and $T$ are defined for $\angle C$. Prove that the lines $MN$, $PQ$, and $RT$ intersect at one point or are parallel.
reference_solution: 195. If $A_{0}, B_{0}, C_{0}$ are the midpoints of segments $A O, B O, C O$ respectively, then the constructed lines turn out to be symmetric to the lines $A_{0} O, B_{0} O, C_{0} O$ with respect to the angle bisectors of triangle $A_{0} B_{0} C_{0}$ (see problem 194).

question: 196. Given a triangle $A B C$. On the radii of the inscribed circle, drawn to the points of tangency, points are taken that are at equal distances from its center; these points are connected to the opposite vertices. Prove that the three resulting lines intersect at one point.
reference_solution: 196. Let $K$ be a point on the radius perpendicular to side $AC$, and $L$ be on the radius perpendicular to side $AB$. Line $BK$ intersects $AC$ at $B_{1}$, and line $CL$ intersects $AB$ at point $C_{1}$. Draw a line through $K$ parallel to $AC$, and let $M$ and $N$ be its points of intersection with $AB$ and $BC$. Clearly, $\frac{\left|A B_{1}\right|}{\left|B_{1} C\right|}=\frac{|M K|}{|K N|}$. By drawing a line through $L$ parallel to $AB$, intersecting $AC$ and $BC$ at points $P$ and $Q$, we have $\frac{\left|B C_{1}\right|}{\left|C_{1} A\right|}=\frac{|Q L|}{|L P|}$. We will perform a similar construction for the third radius. Replacing the ratios in $R$ (see problem 192), we note that for each segment in the numerator, there is an equal segment in the denominator, for example: $|M K|=|L P|$.

question: 197. For the diagonals $A D, B E$ and $C F$ of a hexagon $A B C D E F$ inscribed in a circle to intersect at one point, it is necessary and sufficient that the equality $|A B| \cdot|C D| \cdot|E F|=$ $=|B C| \cdot|D E| \cdot|F A|$ holds.
reference_solution: 197. Consider the triangle $A C E$, through the vertices of which the lines $A D, C F$ and $E B$ are drawn. The sines of the angles formed by these lines with the sides of the triangle $A C E$ are proportional to the chords on which they stand (for example, $\sin \widehat{C A D}=\frac{C D}{2 R}$, where $R$ is the radius of the circle); therefore, the condition $R^{*}=1$ (see problem 192) is equivalent to the condition given in the problem.

question:
198. Let two tangents $A M$ and $A N$ (where $M$ and $N$ are the points of tangency) and two secants be drawn from a point $A$ outside a circle, and let $P$ and $Q$ be the points of intersection of the circle with the first secant, and $K$ and $L$ be the points of intersection with the second. Prove that the lines $P K, Q L$, and $M N$ either intersect at one point or are parallel.

From this, derive a method for constructing a tangent to a given circle passing through a given point using only a straightedge.
reference_solution:
198. Note (Fig. $51, a$ ), that $\triangle A P M$ is similar to $\triangle A M Q$, $\triangle A P L$ is similar to $\triangle A K Q$, $\triangle A K N$ is similar to $\triangle A L N$; from these similarities we obtain

$$
\frac{P M}{|M Q|}=\frac{A M}{|\overline{A Q}|}, \quad \frac{Q K}{|P L|}=\frac{|A Q|}{|A L|}, \quad \frac{|L N|}{|N K|}=\frac{|A L|}{|A N|}
$$

Multiplying these equalities and considering that $|A M|=|A N|$, we get that $\frac{|P M| \cdot|Q K| \cdot|L N|}{|M Q| \cdot|P L| \cdot |N K|}=1$, and this (see problem 197) is the necessary and sufficient condition for the lines $M N, P K$ and $Q L$ to intersect at one point.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-117.jpg?height=277&width=465&top_left_y=336&top_left_x=154)
a)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-117.jpg?height=273&width=433&top_left_y=334&top_left_x=656)

b)

Fig. 51.

The method of constructing a tangent using a single ruler is clear from Fig. 51, b. The numbers $1,2, \ldots$ indicate the sequence of drawing the lines.

question: 200. A circle intersects side $A B$ of triangle $A B C$ at points $C_{1}$ and $C_{2}$, side $C A$ at points $B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$, and side $B C$ at points $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$. Prove that if the lines $A A_{1}, B B_{1}$, and $C C_{1}$ intersect at one point, then the lines $A A_{2}, B B_{2}$, and $C C_{2}$ also intersect at one point.
reference_solution:
200. By the property of secants drawn from an external point to a circle, or by the property of segments of chords of a circle passing through one point, we have \( \left|B C_{1}\right| \cdot \left|B C_{2}\right| = \left|B A_{1}\right| \cdot \left|B A_{2}\right| \), \( \left|C B_{1}\right| \cdot \left|C B_{2}\right| = \left|C A_{1}\right| \cdot \left|C A_{2}\right| \), \( \left|A B_{1}\right| \cdot \left|A B_{2}\right| = \left|A C_{1}\right| \cdot \left|A C_{2}\right| \).

It is now easy to verify that if the statement of Ceva's theorem (equality \( R=1 \)) holds for points \( A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1} \), then it also holds for points \( A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2} \). From the statement of the problem, it follows that either all three points \( A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2} \) lie on the corresponding sides of the triangle, or only one of them (see problem 192).

question: 201. On the sides $AB, BC$, and $CA$ of triangle $ABC$, points $C_{1}, A_{1}$, and $B_{1}$ are taken. Let $C_{2}$ be the point of intersection of the lines $AB$ and $A_{1} B_{1}, A_{2}$ be the point of intersection of the lines $BC$ and $B_{1} C_{1}, B_{2}$ be the point of intersection of the lines $AC$ and $A_{1} C_{1}$. Prove that if the lines $A A_{1}, B B_{1}$, and $C C_{1}$ intersect at one point, then the points $A_{2}, B_{2}$, and $C_{2}$ lie on one line.
reference_solution: 201. Writing the equality $R=1$ (according to Ceva's and Menelaus' theorems - see problems 192 and 193) for the points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1} ; A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{2}$; $A_{2}, B_{1}, C_{1} ; A_{1}, B_{2}, C_{1}$, we obtain that for the points $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ $R=1$ as well. Now it remains to prove that either all three points $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ lie on the extensions of the sides of the triangle (which will be the case if the points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ lie on the sides of the triangle), or only one is on the extension (if one of the points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$ lies on the sides of the triangle), and then use Menelaus' theorem (see problem 193).

question: 203. Given a triangle $A B C$. Let's define a point $A_{1}$ on the side $B C$ as follows: $A_{1}$ is the midpoint of the side $K L$ of a regular pentagon $M K L N P$, where vertices $K$ and $L$ lie on $B C$, and vertices $M$ and $N$ lie on $A B$ and $A C$. Similarly, points $C_{1}$ and $B_{1}$ are defined on the sides $A B$ and $A C$. Prove that the lines $A A_{1}$, $B B_{1}$, and $C C_{1}$ intersect at one point.
reference_solution:
203. If $a$ is the length of the side of pentagon $M K L N P$, $b$ is the length of the side of the pentagon with one side on $A B$, and $c$ is the length of the side of the pentagon, with one side on $A C$, then

$$
\frac{\left|B A_{1}\right|}{\mid C_{1} B}=\frac{a}{b}, \quad \frac{\left|A C_{1}\right|}{\left|A B_{1}\right|}=\frac{b}{c}, \quad \frac{\left|C B_{1}\right|}{\left|C A_{1}\right|}=\frac{c}{a}
$$

Multiplying these equalities, we find that $R=1$, and we will use Ceva's theorem (problem 192).

question: 215. Given numbers $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ and $k$. Let $x, y, z$ be the distances from a point $M$ inside a triangle to its sides. Prove that the set of points $M$ such that $\alpha x + \beta y + \gamma z = k$, is either empty, or a segment, or coincides with the set of all points of the triangle.
reference_solution:
215. Show that if $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ are two different points belonging to a certain set, then any point $M$ on the line segment $M_{1} M_{2}$ inside the triangle also belongs to this set. For this, denoting by $x_{1}, y_{1}, z_{1}$ the distances from $M_{1}$ to the sides of the triangle, and by $x_{2}, y_{2}, z_{2}$ the distances from $M_{2}$, we can express the distances $x, y, z$ from $M$ to the sides in terms of these quantities and the distances between $M_{1}, M_{2}, M$. For example, if $\left|M_{1} M\right|=$ $=k\left|M_{1} M_{2}\right|$ and the directions $\vec{M}_{1} \vec{M}$ and $\vec{M}_{1} \vec{M}_{2}$ coincide, then $x=$ $=(1-k) x_{1}+k x_{2}, y=(1-k) y_{1}+k y_{2}, z=(1-k) z_{1}+k z_{2}$.

From this it follows that if the equality holds for three points inside the triangle that do not lie on the same line, then it will hold for all points of the triangle.

Remark. The statement of the problem remains true for any convex polygon. Moreover, all points of the plane can be considered, but in this case, the distances from the points to the line, located on different sides of it, should be taken with opposite signs.

question: 217. Prove that if there exists a circle tangent to the lines $A B, B C, C D$ and $D A$, then its center and the midpoints of $A C$ and $B D$ lie on the same line.
reference_solution:
217. Let $A B C D$ be a circumscribed quadrilateral, $O$ - the center of the inscribed circle, $M_{1}$ - the midpoint of $A C$, $M_{2}$ - the midpoint of $B D$, $r$ - the radius of the circle (the distances from $O$ to the sides are equal to $r$), $x_{1}, y_{1}, z_{1}, u_{1}$ - the distances from $M_{1}$ to $A B, B C, C D, D A$, $x_{2}, y_{2}$, $z_{2}, u_{2}$ - the respective distances from $M_{2}$ to the same sides. Since $|A B|+|C D|=|B C|+|D A|$, then

$$
|A B| r-|B C| r+|C D| r-|D A| r=0
$$

Moreover,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& |A B| x_{1}-|B C| y_{1}+|C D| z_{1}-|D A| u_{1}=0 \\
& |A B| x_{2}-|B C| y_{2}+|C D| z_{2}-|D A| u_{2}=0
\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the points $O, M_{1}, M_{2}$ lie on the same line (see the remark to problem 215).

Similarly, other cases of the positions of points $A, B, C$ and $D$ and the center of the circle are considered. In this case, the relationships that arise between the segments $|A B|,|B C|$, $|C D|,|D A|$ (see problems 155,156) need to be used, and according to the remark to problem 215, if any two points turn out to be located on different sides of some line, then the corresponding distances should be assigned different signs.

question: 235. Let $H$ be the orthocenter of a triangle, and $F$ be an arbitrary point on the circumcircle. Prove that the Simson line corresponding to point $F$ passes through one of the points of intersection of the line $F H$ with the nine-point circle (see problems 162, 233).
reference_solution: 235. Since the midpoint of $F H$ lies on the nine-point circle (see problem 162), it is sufficient to show that the Simson line corresponding to point $F$ also bisects $F H$. Let $K$ be the projection of $F$ onto one of the sides of the triangle, $D$ the foot of the altitude to that same side, $H_{1}$ the point where this altitude intersects the circumcircle, ! $H_{1} D_{\mid}=\mid H D$ (see problem 108), $L$ the point where the Simson line intersects the same altitude, and finally, $M$ a point on the line $H H_{1}$ such that $F M \| K D$; then $\triangle F M H_{1}=\triangle K D L(|F M|=\mid K D$; both are right triangles and $\widehat{D L K}=\widehat{M H_{1} F}$, since the altitude of the triangle is the Simson line corresponding to the vertex from which it is drawn, and we can use the statement from problem 234). It is also not difficult to show that the directions of $\overrightarrow{H_{1} M}$ and $\overrightarrow{D L}$ coincide, i.e., $F K H L$ is a parallelogram, from which our statement follows.

question: 236. Prove that on the Euler line of triangle $ABC$ there exists a point $P$ such that the distances from the centroids of triangles $ABP$, $BCP$, $CAP$ to the vertices $C$, $A$, and $B$ respectively are equal to each other (see problem 232).
reference_solution: 236. Show that the required property is possessed by a point $P$ on the Euler line for which $P O_{1}=O H_{1}$ (where $O$ is the center of the circumscribed circle, $H$ is the orthocenter); in this case, for each triangle, the distance from the centroid to the opposite vertex of the original triangle is $-\frac{4}{3} R$, where $R$ is the radius of the circumcircle of $\triangle A B C$.

question: 237. Let $P$ be a point inside triangle $ABC$ such that the angles $APB$, $BPC$, and $CPA$ are $120^{\circ}$ (assuming that the angles of triangle $ABC$ are less than $120^{\circ}$). Prove that the Euler lines of triangles $APB$, $BPC$, and $CPA$ intersect at one point (see problem 232).
reference_solution: 237. Let $C_{1}$ be the center of the circumcircle of $\triangle A P B$, and $C_{2}$ the point symmetric to $C_{1}$ with respect to $A B$. Similarly, for triangles $B P C$ and $C P A$, define points $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}, B_{1}$ and $B_{2}$. Since triangles $A C_{1} B, A C_{2} B, B A_{1} C, B A_{2} C, C B_{1} A, C B_{2} A$ are isosceles with angles of $120^{\circ}$ at the vertices, triangles $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ and $A_{2} B_{2} C_{2}$ are equilateral (see problem 158). By calculating the angles of the quadrilateral with vertices $P, A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$, it can be proven that these points ($P, A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$) lie on the same circle. Furthermore, if $H$ is the orthocenter of triangle $A P B$, then since $|P H|=\left|C_{1} C_{2}\right|$, $P H C_{2} C_{1}$ is a parallelogram, and the line $C_{1} H$ (the Euler line of triangle $A P B$) passes through the midpoint of $P C_{2}$. Since $P C_{2}$ is a chord of the circle with center $C_{1}$, $C_{1} H$ is perpendicular to $P C_{2}$. Thus, the three Euler lines coincide with the perpendicular bisectors of the segments $P C_{2}, P B_{2}$, and $P A_{2}$. Since points $P, A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ lie on the same circle, these lines intersect at its center, which is the center of the equilateral triangle $A_{2} B_{2} C_{2}$. From the result of problem 161, it follows that these three Euler lines intersect at the centroid of triangle $A B C$.

question: 238. A quadrilateral $A B C D$ is inscribed in a circle. Let $M$ be the point of intersection of the tangents to the circle at points $A$ and $C, N$ be the point of intersection of the tangents drawn through $B$ and $D, K$ be the point of intersection of the angle bisectors of angles $A$ and $C$ of the quadrilateral, $L$ be the point of intersection of the angle bisectors of angles $B$ and $D$. Prove that if one of the statements is true: a) $M$ lies on the line $B D$; b) $N$ lies on the line $A C$; c) $K$ lies on $B D$; d) $L$ lies on $A C$, then the other three statements are also true.
reference_solution:
238. A necessary and sufficient condition for the fulfillment of all four points is the equality $|A B| \cdot|C D|=|A D| \cdot|B C|$. For points a) and b), this follows from the theorem about the bisector of the interior angle of a triangle, for points c) and d) - from the result of problem 50.

*) For more detailed information about the family of Simson lines, see the book: Vasilyev N. B., Gutenmakher V. L. Lines and Curves, - Moscow: Nauka, 1978,

question: 239. Prove that 4 lines, each of which passes through the bases of two perpendiculars dropped from the vertex of an inscribed quadrilateral to the sides not containing it, intersect at one point.
reference_solution:
239. Let $ABCD$ be the given quadrilateral. We will assume that angles $A$ and $D$ are obtuse, and $B$ and $C$ are acute. Let the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from vertex $A$ be denoted by $M$ and $N$, and from vertex $C$ by $K$ and $L$ (see Fig. 64a), and let $R$ be the intersection point of $MN$ and $LK$. Note that $A, K, N, C, L, M$ lie on the same circle with diameter $AC$. We will show that $MK \parallel LN$: $\widehat{MKL} = \widehat{MAL} = \hat{D} - 90^\circ = 90^\circ - \hat{B} = \widehat{KCB} = \widehat{KLN}$ (where $\hat{D}$ and $\hat{B}$ are the angles of the quadrilateral). Thus,

\[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{|MR|}{|RN|} = \frac{|MK|}{|LN|} = \frac{\sin \widehat{MCK}}{\sin \widehat{LAN}} = \\
& \quad = \frac{\sin (\hat{C} - 90^\circ + \hat{B})}{\sin (\hat{A} - 90^\circ + \hat{B})} = \frac{\sin (90^\circ - \hat{A} + \hat{B})}{\sin (\hat{A} + \hat{B} - 90^\circ)} = \frac{\cos (\hat{A} - \hat{B})}{\sin (\hat{A} + \hat{B} - 90^\circ)}
\end{aligned}
\]

Now let $P$ and $Q$ be the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from vertex $B$, and let $S$ be the intersection point of $MN$ and $PQ$ (see Fig. 64b). Since $\widehat{PNB} = \widehat{PAB} = \hat{C}$, it follows that $PN \parallel DC$, i.e., $MQNP$ is a trapezoid (since $ANBP$ is a cyclic quadrilateral with diameter $AB$). Thus,

\[
\frac{|MS|}{|SN|} = \frac{|MQ|}{|PN|} = \frac{|AB| \cos (\hat{A} + \hat{D} - 180^\circ)}{|AB| \sin (\hat{B} + \hat{A} - 90^\circ)} = \frac{\cos (\hat{A} - \hat{B})}{\sin (\hat{B} + \hat{A} - 90^\circ)}
\]

(We used the fact that $MQ$ is the projection of $AB$ onto $DC$: the angle between $AB$ and $DC$ is $\hat{A} + \hat{D} - 180^\circ$.) Therefore, points $R$ and $S$ divide $MN$ in the same ratio, i.e., they coincide; hence, the three lines intersect at one point. It is easy to show now that all four lines intersect at this same point.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-129.jpg?height=367&width=429&top_left_y=748&top_left_x=166)
a)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-129.jpg?height=398&width=390&top_left_y=719&top_left_x=683)

b)
