question: 240. $A B$ and $C D$ are two chords of a circle; $M$ is the point of intersection of the perpendiculars erected to $A B$ at point $A$ and to $C D$ at point $C; N$ is the point of intersection of the perpendiculars erected to $A B$ and $C D$ at points $B$ and $D$. Prove that the line $M N$ passes through the point of intersection of $B C$ and $A D$.
reference_solution:
240. Let's find in what ratio $B C$ divides $M N$. This ratio is equal to the ratio

$$
\frac{S_{M C B}}{S_{C B N}}=\frac{|M C| \cdot|C B| \sin \widehat{M C B}}{|B N| \cdot|C B| \sin \widehat{N B C}}=\frac{M C \cdot \cos \widehat{B C D}}{|B N| \cos \widehat{C B A}}
$$

Similarly, the ratio in which $A D$ divides $M N$ is $\frac{|A M| \cos \widehat{B A D}}{|N D| \cos \widehat{A D C}}$. But these ratios are equal, since $\widehat{B C D}=\widehat{B A D}$, $\widehat{C B A}=\widehat{C D A}$, and $\triangle A M C$ is similar to $\triangle B N D$, and therefore $\frac{|M C|}{|B N|}=\frac{|A M|}{|N D|}$.

question: 241. Given a circle $S$ and a tangent to it $l$. Let $N$ be the point of tangency, $NM$ be a diameter. A fixed point $A$ is taken on the line $NM$. Consider an arbitrary circle passing through $A$, with its center on $l$. Let $C$ and $D$ be the points of intersection of this circle with $l$, and $P$ and $Q$ be the points of intersection of the lines $MC$ and $MD$ with $S$. Prove that the chords $PQ$ pass through a fixed point on the plane.
reference_solution:
241. Since the circle with diameter $C D$ passes through a fixed point $A$ on $M N$ ($M N \perp C D$), then

$$
|C N| \cdot|N D|=|N A|^{2}(1)
$$

is a constant value. Let $K$ be the intersection point of $P Q$ with $M N$. We will show that $\frac{|N K|}{|K M|}$ is a constant value. Note that $\widehat{P N Q}=180^{\circ}-\widehat{P M Q} ;$ therefore, $\frac{|M K|}{|K N|}=\frac{S_{\triangle P M Q}}{S_{\triangle P Q N}}=\frac{|P M| \cdot|M Q|}{|P N| \cdot|N Q|}=\frac{|M N|}{|C N|} \cdot \frac{|M N|}{|N D|}=\frac{|M N|^{2}}{|A N|^{2}}$ (we used the equality (1) and the fact that $\triangle M N P$ is similar to $\triangle M N C$, and $\triangle M N Q$ is similar to $\triangle M N D$).

question: 242. Given three pairwise non-intersecting circles. Let $A_{1}, A_{2}, A_{3}$ be the three points of intersection of the common internal tangents to any two of them, and $B_{1}, B_{2}, B_{3}$ be the corresponding points of intersection of the external tangents. Prove that these points lie on four lines, three on each ( $A_{1}, A_{2}, B_{3} ; A_{1}$, $\left.B_{2}, A_{3} ; B_{1}, A_{2}, A_{3} ; B_{1}, B_{2}, B_{3}\right)$ .
reference_solution: 242. Check that points $A_{1}, A_{2}, A_{3}$ and $B_{1}, B_{2}, B_{3}$ lie on the sides of triangle $\mathrm{O}_{1} \mathrm{O}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}$ ( $\mathrm{O}_{1}, \mathrm{O}_{2}, \mathrm{O}_{3}$ - centers of circles) or on the extensions of these sides and the ratio of the distances from each of these points to the corresponding vertices of triangle $\mathrm{O}_{1} \mathrm{O}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}$ is equal to the ratio of the radii of the corresponding circles. Then, one can use Menelaus' theorem (see problem 193) for each of these sets of three points.

question: 243. The diameter of the circle inscribed in triangle $ABC$, passing through the point of tangency with side $BC$, intersects the chord connecting the other two points of tangency at point $N$. Prove that $AN$ bisects $BC$.
reference_solution:
243. Let $O$ be the center of the inscribed circle, $K$ and $L$ be the points of tangency with sides $AC$ and $AB$, and the line passing through $N$ parallel to $BC$ intersects sides $AB$ and $AC$ at points $R$ and $M$. The quadrilateral $OKMN$ is inscribed ( $\widehat{ONM}=\widehat{OKM}=90^{\circ}$ ), therefore, $\widehat{OMN}=\widehat{OKN}$; similarly, $\widehat{ORN}=\widehat{OLN}$, but $\widehat{OLN}=\widehat{OKN}$, hence, $\widehat{ORN}=\widehat{OMN}$ and $\triangle ORM$ is isosceles, $ON$ is the height; thus,

$$
|RN|=|NM|
$$

question: 244. A circle is inscribed in triangle $ABC$. Let $M$ be the point of tangency of the circle with side $AC$, and $MK$ be a diameter. The line $BK$ intersects $AC$ at point $N$. Prove that $|AM|=|NC|$.
reference_solution:
244. If the sides of $\triangle A B C$ are $|B C|=a, \mid C A=b$, $|A B|=c$, then, as we know (see problem 18, section 1), $\mid M C:=$ $=\frac{a+b-c}{2}$. Draw a line through $K$ parallel to $A C$, and denote its points of intersection with $A B$ and $B C$ as $A_{1}$ and $C_{1}$. The incircle of $\triangle A B C$ is an excircle (touching $A_{1} C_{1}$ and the extensions of $B A_{1}$ and $B C_{1}$) for $\triangle A_{1} B C_{1}$. But $\triangle A_{1} B C_{1}$ is similar to $\triangle A B C$. Therefore, the excircle of $A B C$ will touch $A C$ at point $N$; denote the points of tangency with the extensions of $B A$ and $B C$ as $R$ and $L$. We have

$$
|B R|=|B L|=\frac{1}{2}(|B R|+|B L|)=\frac{1}{2}(a+b+c)
$$

thus,

$$
|A N|=|A R|=|R B|-|B A|=\frac{a+b-c}{2}=|M C| .
$$

question: 245. A circle is inscribed in triangle $ABC$, $M-$ is the point of tangency of the circle with side $BC$, $MK$ is a diameter. Line $AK$ intersects the circle at point $P$. Prove that the tangent to the circle at point $P$ bisects side $BC$.
reference_solution: 245. Draw a line through $K$ parallel to $B C$. Let $L$ and $Q$ be the points of intersection of the tangent at point $P$ with the line $B C$ and the constructed parallel line, and let $N$ be the point of intersection of $A K$ with $B C$. Since $|C N| = |B M|$ (see problem 244), it is sufficient to prove that $|N L| = |L M|$, but $|P L| = |L M|$, so we need to prove that $|P L| = |N L|$. Since $\triangle P L N$ is similar to $\triangle P Q K$, in which $|P Q| = |Q K|$, then $|P K| = |N L|$ and $|C L| = |L B|$.

question: 246. The line $l$ is tangent to the circle at point $A$, let $CD$ be a chord of the circle parallel to $l$, and $B$ be any point on the line $l$. The lines $CB$ and $DB$ intersect the circle again at points $L$ and $K$. Prove that the line $LK$ bisects the segment $AB$.
reference_solution:
246. Let $M$ and $N$ be the points of intersection of line $L K$ with lines $l$ and $C D$. Then $|A M|^{2}=|M L| \cdot|M K|$. From the similarity of triangles $K M B$ and $D K N$, it follows that $\frac{|M K|}{|K N|}=\frac{|M B|}{|D N|}, \quad|M K|=$ $=\frac{|K N| \cdot|M B|}{|D N|}$. From the similarity of triangles $C N L$ and $M L B$ it follows that $\frac{|M L|}{|L M|}=\frac{|M B|}{|C N|},|M L|=\frac{|L N| \cdot|M B|}{|C N|}$.

Thus,

$$
|M K| \cdot|M L|=\frac{|K N| \cdot|L N|}{|C N| \cdot|D N|}|M B|^{2}=|M B|^{2}
$$

i.e. $|M A|^{2}=|M B|^{2},|M A|=|M B|$.

question: 247. Given two intersecting circles. Let $A$ be one of their points of intersection. From an arbitrary point lying on the extension of the common chord of the given circles, two tangents are drawn to one of them, touching it at points $M$ and $N$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the points of intersection (different from $A$) of the lines $M A$ and $N A$ with the second circle. Prove that the line $M N$ bisects the segment $P Q$.
reference_solution:
247. Let (Fig. 65) $B$ be the second common point of the circles,

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-131.jpg?height=526&width=410&top_left_y=839&top_left_x=162)

Fig. 65. $C$ is a point on the line $A B$, from which tangents are drawn, and, finally, $K$ is the intersection point of the lines $M N$ and $P Q$. Using the Law of Sines and the result from problem 50, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{|P M|}{|M A|}=\frac{|P M|}{\sin \widehat{P B M}} \cdot \frac{\sin \widehat{P B M}}{|M A|}= \\
& =\frac{|B M|}{\sin \widehat{B P M}} \cdot \frac{\sin \widehat{P B M}}{|M A|}= \\
& =\frac{|B M|}{|M A|} \cdot \frac{\sin \widehat{P B M}}{\sin \widehat{B P M}}= \\
& =\sqrt{\frac{|C B|}{|C A|}} \cdot \frac{\sin \widehat{P B M}}{\sin \widehat{B P M}} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, denoting the angle $\widehat{A M B}$ by $\alpha$ and the angle $\widehat{A P B}$ by $\beta$ (where $c$ and $\rho$ are constants), we get

$$
\frac{|P M|}{|M A|}=\sqrt{\frac{|C B|}{|C A|}} \cdot \frac{\sin (\alpha+\beta)}{\sin \beta}
$$

Similarly, we find

$$
\frac{|A N|}{|N Q|}=\sqrt{\frac{|C A|}{|C B|}} \cdot \frac{\sin \beta}{\sin (\alpha+\beta)}
$$

But by Menelaus' theorem (see problem 193), $\frac{|P M|}{|M A|} \cdot \frac{|A N|}{|N Q|} \cdot \frac{|Q K|}{|K P|}=1$. Therefore, $\frac{|Q K|}{|K P|}=1$.

question: 248. On the height $B D$ of triangle $A B C$ as a diameter, a circle is constructed, intersecting sides $A B$ and $B C$ at points $K$ and $L$. The lines tangent to the circle at points $K$ and $L$ intersect at point $M$. Prove that the line $B M$ bisects side $A C$.
reference_solution: 248. Draw a line through $M$ parallel to $A C$, until it intersects points $A_{1}$ and $C_{1}$ on lines $B A$ and $B C$. We have $\widehat{A_{1} K M}=90^{\circ}-\widehat{D K M}=90^{\circ}-\widehat{K B D}=\widehat{B A D}=\widehat{K A_{1} M}, \quad$ therefore, $\triangle K M A_{1}$ is isosceles and $\left|A_{1} M\right|=|M K|$. Similarly, $\left|M C_{1}\right|=|M L|$, but $|K M|=|M L|$, hence, $\left|A_{1} M\right|=\left|M C_{1}\right|$, i.e., line $B M$ bisects $A C$.

question: 249. The line $l$ is perpendicular to the segment $A B$ and passes through $B$. A circle with its center on $l$ passes through $A$ and intersects $l$ at points $C$ and $D$. The tangents to the circle at points $A$ and $C$ intersect at $N$. Prove that the line $D N$ bisects the segment $A B$.
reference_solution:
249. Let $M$ be the intersection point of $ND$ and $AB$, and $P$ be the intersection point of the tangents to the circle at points $A$ and $D$. Since the lines $NC$, $AB$, and $PD$ are parallel, from the similarity of the corresponding triangles we get

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{|AM|}{|DP|}=\frac{|AN|}{|NP|}, \quad|AM|=|DP| \frac{|AN|}{|NP|}, \\
\frac{|MB|}{|NC|}=\frac{|MD|}{|ND|}=\frac{|AP|}{|NP|}, \quad|MB|=|NC| \frac{|AP|}{|NP|},
\end{gathered}
$$

but $|DP|=|AP|,|NC|=|AN|$, therefore, the right-hand sides of expressions (1) and (2) are equal, i.e., $|AM|=|MB|$.

question: 250. A circle is circumscribed around $\triangle A B C$. Let $N$ be the point of intersection of the tangents to the circle passing through points $B$ and $C ; M$ - a point on the circle such that $A M \| B C, K$ - the point of intersection of $M N$ and the circle. Prove that $K A$ bisects $B C$.
reference_solution:
250. Let's consider that $D$ is the midpoint of $CB$ and $AD$ intersects the circle again at point $K$. We need to prove that the tangents to the circle at points $B$ and $C$ intersect on the line $MK$.

Consider the quadrilateral $CMBK$. For the tangents to the circle at points $C$ and $B$ to intersect on the diagonal $MK$, it is necessary and sufficient (see problem 238) that $\frac{|CM|}{|CK|} = \frac{|MB|}{|BK|}$. However, $\frac{|CM|}{|CK|} = \frac{|AB|}{|CK|} = \frac{|BD|}{|DK|} = \frac{|CD|}{|DK|} = \frac{|AC|}{|BK|} = \frac{|MB|}{|BK|}$. (In the first and last equalities, we used the fact that, due to the parallelism of $AM$ and $CB$, $|CM| = |AB|$, $|AC| = |MB|$; in the second and fourth - the similarity of triangles $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle CDK$, $\triangle ADC$ and $\triangle KDB$; in the third - the fact that $AD$ is a median.)

251. Let $O$ be the center of the circle, $N_1, M_1, P_1, R_1$ be the points symmetric to points $N, M, P, R$ respectively with respect to the line $OA$, and $K$ be the intersection point of the lines $N_1R_1$ and $QS$. We need to prove that the points $R_1, S$, and $K$ coincide. The points $N_1, M_1$, and $B$ lie on the same line, symmetric to the line $NMC$; $N_1, P_1$, and $R_1$ also lie on the same line, symmetric to the line $NPR$ (Fig. 66). The points $B, N_1, Q$, and $K$ lie

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-132.jpg?height=456&width=417&top_left_y=1136&top_left_x=670)

Fig. 66. on the same circle, since $\widehat{BN_1K} = \widehat{M_1N_1P_1} = \widehat{MNP} = \widehat{PQM} = \widehat{BQK}$. The points $B, N_1, Q, R_1$ also lie on the same circle, since $\widehat{N_1R_1B} = \widehat{N_1P_1P} = \widehat{N_1QP} = \widehat{N_1QB}$.

Therefore, the five points $B, N_1, Q, R_1, K$ lie on the same circle, but the points $N_1, R_1$, and $K$ lie on the same line, so $R_1$ and $K$ coincide.

question:
252. Given a semicircle with diameter $A B . C$-point on the semicircle, $D$-the foot of the perpendicular
dropped from $C$ to $A B$. Consider three circles: the first circle, with center $O_{1}$, touches segments $A D, D C$ and arc $\breve{A C}$; the second, with center $O_{2}$, touches segments $D B, D C$ and arc $\widehat{B C}$; the third, with center $O_{3}$, is inscribed in triangle $A B C$. Prove that $O_{3}$ coincides with the midpoint of segment $\mathrm{O}_{1} \mathrm{O}_{2}$.
reference_solution:
252. Let (Fig. 67) $O$ be the midpoint of $AB$, $N_{1}$ and $N_{2}$ be the points of tangency of circles $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$ with $AB$, $O_{3}$ be the midpoint of $O_{1}O_{2}$, $N_{3}$ be the foot of the perpendicular dropped from $O_{3}$ to $AB$, $a$ and $b$ be the legs of the triangle ($|CB|=a, |AC|=b$), $c$ be the hypotenuse, $r_{1}$ and $r_{2}$ be the radii of the circles with centers $O_{1}$ and $O_{2}$. We will prove that $|AN_{2}|=|AC|=b$, $|BN_{1}|=|BC|=a$. Let $|BN_{1}|=x$, $|BD|=\frac{a^{2}}{c}$, $|N_{1}D_{i}|=r_{1}=x-\frac{a^{2}}{c}$, $|OO_{1}|=\frac{c}{2}-r_{1}=\frac{c}{2}-x+\frac{a^{2}}{c}$, $|N_{1}O|=x-\frac{c}{2}$. Applying the Pythagorean theorem to $\triangle OO_{1}N_{1}$:

$$
\left(\frac{c}{2}-x+\frac{a^{2}}{c}\right)^{2}=\left(x-\frac{c}{2}\right)^{2}+\left(x-\frac{a^{2}}{c}\right)^{2}
$$

from which $x^{2}=a^{2}$, $x=a$, i.e., $r_{1}=a-\frac{a^{2}}{c}$. Similarly, $|AN_{2}|=b$, $r_{2}=b-\frac{b^{2}}{c}$. Now it is easy to find

$$
|O_{\overline{3}}N_{3}|=\frac{r_{1}+r_{2}}{2}=\frac{a+b-\frac{a^{2}}{c}-\frac{b^{2}}{c}}{2}=\frac{a+b-c}{2}=r
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the inscribed circle, and

$$
|AN_{3}|=\frac{1}{2}(|AN_{1}|+|AN_{2}|)=\frac{1}{2}[c-|BN_{1}|+b]=\frac{1}{2}[b+c-a]
$$

i.e., $N_{\mathbf{3}}$ coincides with the point of tangency of the inscribed circle.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-133.jpg?height=277&width=451&top_left_y=1132&top_left_x=180)

Fig. 67.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-133.jpg?height=382&width=373&top_left_y=1041&top_left_x=701)

Fig. 68.

question: 253. Let $A B C D E F$ be a cyclic hexagon. Denote by $K$ the intersection point of $A C$ and $B F$, and by $L$ the intersection point of $C E$ and $F D$. Prove that the diagonals $A D, B E$ and the line $K L$ intersect at one point (Pascal).

254. $A B C D$ is a cyclic quadrilateral. The perpendicular to $B A$, erected at point $A$, intersects the line $C D$ at point $M$; the perpendicular to $D A$, erected at point $A$, intersects the line $B C$ at point $N$. Prove that $M N$ passes through the center of the circle.
reference_solution: 254. Let $L$ and $P$ be the points of intersection of the lines $A M$ and $A N$ with the circle. As follows from problem 253, the lines $B L$, $D P$, and $M N$ intersect at one point. But $B L$ and $D P$ are diameters, intersecting at the center of the circle, hence $M N$ passes through the center of the circle.

question: 255. On each side of a triangle, two points are taken such that all six segments connecting each point with the opposite vertex are equal to each other. Prove that the midpoints of these six segments lie on a single circle.
reference_solution:
255. We will prove that the center of the desired circle coincides with the orthocenter (the point of intersection of the altitudes). Let $B D$ be the altitude, $H$ be the point of intersection of the altitudes, and $K$ and $L$ be the midpoints of the constructed segments emanating from vertex $B, |B K|=|B L|=l, M$ be the midpoint of $B D$ (Fig. 69). Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
& |K H|^{2}=|L H|^{2}=|M H|^{2}+|K M|^{2}=l^{2}-|B M|^{2}+|M H|^{2}= \\
& =l^{2}-\frac{|B D|^{2}}{4}+\left(|B H|-\frac{|B D|}{2}\right)^{2}=l^{2}+|B H|^{2}-|B H| \cdot|B D|= \\
& =l^{2}-|B H|(|B D|-|B H|)=l^{2}-|B H| \cdot|H D|
\end{aligned}
$$

It remains to prove that the products of the segments of the altitudes, into which each is divided by their point of intersection, are equal. Draw the altitude $A E$. Due to the similarity of $\triangle B H E$ and $\triangle A H D$, we have $|B H| \times$ $\times|H D|=|A H| \cdot|H E|$, which is what we needed to prove.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-134.jpg?height=363&width=434&top_left_y=1177&top_left_x=196)

Fig. 69.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-134.jpg?height=511&width=362&top_left_y=1034&top_left_x=682)

Fig. 70.

question: 256. In triangle $ABC$, on the rays $AB$ and $CB$, segments $|AM|=|CN|=p$ are laid out, where $p$ is the semiperimeter of the triangle (with $B$ lying between $A$ and $M$ and between $C$ and $N$). Let $K$ be the point on the circumcircle of $\triangle ABC$ that is diametrically opposite to $B$. Prove that the perpendicular dropped from $K$ to $MN$ passes through the incenter of the inscribed circle.
reference_solution:
256. Let (Fig. 70) the lengths of the sides of triangle $ABC$ be: $|BC|=a, |CA|=b, |AB|=c$. Draw lines through the center of the inscribed circle parallel to $AB$ and $BC$, intersecting $AK$ and $KC$ at points $P$ and $Q$; in triangle $OPQ$ we have $\widehat{POQ}=\hat{B}$, $|OQ|=\frac{a+b-c}{2}=p-c$, $|OP|=\frac{b+c-a}{2}=p-a$, but by the condition $\widehat{NBM}=\hat{B}$, $|NB|=p-a$, $|MB|=p-c$. Therefore, $\triangle POQ = \triangle NBM$. If we take $M_1$ on the line $OP$ such that $\left|OM_1\right| = |OQ|$, and on $OQ$ - point $N_1$ such that $\left|ON_1\right| = |OP|$, then $\triangle ON_1M_1 = \triangle NBM$ and the corresponding sides $BM$ and $OM_1$, $BN$ and $ON_1$ will be parallel. Thus, $N_1M_1 \| NM$. We will prove that $OK \perp NM$: since in quadrilateral $OPKQ$ two opposite angles are right, it is cyclic, hence $\widehat{OKP} = \widehat{OQP}$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-135.jpg?height=417&width=323&top_left_y=453&top_left_x=164)

Fig. 71. Further, we have $\widehat{KOP} + \widehat{OM_1N_1} = \widehat{KOP} + \widehat{OQP} = \widehat{KOP} + \widehat{OKP} = 90^\circ$, which means that $OK \perp M_1N_1$.

question: 257. From a certain point on the circumcircle of an equilateral triangle $ABC$, lines parallel to $BC$, $CA$, and $AB$ are drawn and intersect $CA$, $AB$, and $BC$ at points $M$, $N$, and $Q$. Prove that $M$, $N$, and $Q$ lie on the same line.
reference_solution: 257. Let, for definiteness, $P$ lie on the arc $\widehat{A C}$ (Fig. 71). Points $A$, $M, P, N$ lie on the same circle, hence $\widehat{N M P}=\widehat{N A P}$. Similarly, $P, M$, $Q, C$ lie on the same circle, $\widehat{P M Q}=$ $=180^{\circ}-\widehat{P C Q}=180^{\circ}-\widehat{P A N}=180^{\circ}-\widehat{P M N}$.

question: 258. Points $A$ and $A_{1}, B$ and $B_{1}, C$ and $C_{1}$ are symmetric with respect to line $l, N$ is an arbitrary point on $l$. Prove that the lines $A N, B N, C N$ intersect the lines $B_{1} C_{1}, A_{1} C_{1}, A_{1} B_{1}$ respectively at three points lying on one line.
reference_solution:
258. Let's first consider the limiting case when point $N$ is at "infinity"; in this case, lines $A N$, $B N$, and $C N$ are parallel to line $l$. Let the distances from points $A, B$, and $C$ to line $l$ be $a, b$, and $c$ (for convenience, assume that $A, B$, and $C$ are on the same side of $l$). Lines parallel to $l$ and passing through $A, B$, and $C$ intersect lines $B_{1} C_{1}, C_{1} A_{1}$, and $A_{1} B_{1}$ at points $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$. It is easy to see that $\frac{\left|A_{1} C_{2}\right|}{\left|C_{2} B_{1}\right|}=\frac{a+c}{c+b}$, $\frac{\left|B_{1} A_{2}\right|}{\left|A_{2} C_{1}\right|}=\frac{b+a}{a+c}$, $\frac{\left|C_{1} B_{2}\right|}{\left|B_{2} A_{1}\right|}=\frac{c+b}{b+a}$. Multiplying these equalities, we get that the statement of Menelaus' theorem holds (it is also necessary to check that an odd number of points from $A_{2}, B_{2}$, and $C_{2}$ lie on the extensions of the sides of triangle $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$). Therefore, points $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ lie on the same line.

The general case can be reduced to the one considered, for example, by projecting the given arrangement of triangles from some point in space onto another plane. In this way, we can ensure that the symmetry of the triangles is not violated, and point $N$ will move to infinity.

We can avoid spatial considerations. Introduce a coordinate system, choosing the $x$-axis as line $l$ and taking the origin at point $N$. Perform the transformation $x^{\prime}=\frac{1}{x}, y^{\prime}=\frac{y}{x}$. In this transformation, points on the $x$-axis ($y=0$) will move to the line $y^{\prime}=0$; points symmetric with respect to the $x$-axis will move to points symmetric with respect to the line $y^{\prime}=0$; lines will move to lines; lines passing through the origin will move to lines parallel to the line $y^{\prime}=0$ (this transformation is essentially the projection mentioned above). After such a transformation, we obtain the arrangement already considered.

question: 259. Through the intersection point of the altitudes of a triangle, two mutually perpendicular lines are drawn. Prove that the midpoints of the segments cut off by these lines on the sides of the triangle (on the lines forming the triangle) lie on one straight line.
260. Prove that three lines, symmetric to an arbitrary line passing through the orthocenter of a triangle with respect to the sides of the triangle, intersect at one point.
reference_solution:
260. Let (Fig. 72) $ABC$ be a given triangle, and $H$ be the point of intersection of its altitudes. Note that the points symmetric to $H$ with respect to its sides

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-136.jpg?height=354&width=337&top_left_y=1223&top_left_x=748)

Fig. 72. lie on the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ (see problem 108). If $H_{1}$ is the point symmetric to $H$ with respect to side $BC$, then the line $l_{1}$, symmetric to $l$ with respect to the same side, passes through $H_{1}$. When $l$ is rotated around $H$ by an angle $\varphi$, the line $l_{1}$ rotates around $H_{1}$ by the same angle $\varphi$ in the opposite direction. Therefore, if $P$ is the second point of intersection of the line $l_{1}$ with the circumcircle, then the radius $OP$ ($O$ being the center of the circumcircle) rotates around $O$ by an angle $2\varphi$ in the corresponding direction. The same reasoning applies to the other two lines symmetric to $l$. However, if $l$ coincides with one of the altitudes of the triangle, the statement of the problem is obvious (the point $P$ will coincide with the corresponding vertex of the triangle). Therefore, this statement is always true.

question:
261. Two equal non-intersecting circles are given. On two common internal tangents, take two arbitrary points $F$ and $F^{\prime}$. From both points, one more tangent can be drawn to each circle. Let the tangents drawn from points $F$ and $F^{\prime}$ to one circle meet at point $A$, and to the other at point $B$. It is required to prove that:
1) the line $A B$ is parallel to the line connecting the centers of the circles (in the case of unequal circles, it passes through the point of intersection of the external tangents);
2) the line connecting the midpoints of $F F^{\prime}$ and $A B$ passes through the midpoint of the segment connecting the centers of the given circles.

(This problem was proposed to the readers of the journal "Bulletin of Experimental Physics and Elementary Mathematics" by Professor V. Ermakov. This journal was published in Russia in the last century. The problem was published in the 14 (2)-th issue of the journal for 1887. A prize - literature on mathematics - was promised to the readers for solving the problem.)
reference_solution:
261. Consider the general case of arbitrary circles. Let points $F$ and $F^{\prime}$ be located as shown in Fig. 73. The notation is clear from the figure. We will prove that there exists a circle inscribed in the quadrilateral $A K B M$, after which we will use the result of problem 242. For this, it is sufficient to prove that

$$
|B F|+\left|B F^{\prime}\right|=\left|A F^{\prime}\right|+|F A| \text {. }
$$

Considering that $|B L|=|B T|$, and $|F S|=|F T|$, we get $|B F|=$ $=|B L|-|F S|$ and similarly $|F A|=|F Q|-|A E|,\left|B F^{\prime}\right|=$ $=\left|F^{\prime} P\right|-|B L|,\left|F^{\prime} A\right|=|A E|-\left|F^{\prime} R\right|$. Substituting these expressions into (1), we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
&|B L|-|F S|+\left|F^{\prime} P\right|-|B L|= \\
&=|F Q|-|A E|+|A E|-\left|F^{\prime} R\right| \Rightarrow \\
& \Rightarrow\left|F^{\prime} R\right|+\left|F^{\prime} P\right|=|F Q|+|F S| \Rightarrow|P R|=|S Q| .
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, the other cases of the positions of points $F$ and $F^{\prime}$ on the tangents are considered (taking into account the results of problems 155,

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-137.jpg?height=419&width=601&top_left_y=1007&top_left_x=319)

Fig. 73.

question:
262. Given a triangle $A B C$; $A A_{1}, B B_{1}$, and $C C_{1}$ are its altitudes. Prove that the Euler lines of triangles $A B_{1} C_{1}, A_{1} B C_{1}, A_{1} B_{1} C$ intersect at a point $P$ on the nine-point circle, such that one of the segments $P A_{1}, P B_{1}, P C_{1}$ is equal to the sum of the other two segments (Victor Thebault, American Mathematical Monthly; see problems 162,232).

## § 4. Geometric Inequalities and Problems on Maximum-Minimum
reference_solution:
262. Let $H$ be the point of intersection of the altitudes of triangle $ABC$, and let $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ be the midpoints of segments $AH, BH, CH$. Note that triangles $AB_{1}C_{1}, A_{1}BC_{1}, A_{1}B_{1}C$ are similar to each other (corresponding vertices are denoted by the same letters), and $A_{2}, B_{2}$, and $C_{2}$ are the centers of the circumcircles of these triangles. First, let's prove the following statement: three lines passing through points $A_{2}, B_{2}$, and $C_{2}$ and equally positioned relative to triangles $AB_{1}C_{1}, A_{1}BC_{1}, A_{1}B_{1}C$, intersect at one point on the nine-point circle.

Note that the lines $A_{2}B_{1}, B_{2}B$, and $C_{2}B_{1}$ are equally positioned relative to triangles $AB_{1}C_{1}, A_{1}BC_{1}$, and $A_{1}B_{1}C$ and intersect at point $B_{1}$, which lies on the nine-point circle. Since points $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ lie on the nine-point circle, it is obvious that three lines obtained from lines $A_{2}B_{1}, B_{2}B$, and $C_{2}B_{1}$ by rotating them by the same angle around points $A_{2}, B_{2}$, and $C_{2}$ respectively, will also intersect at one point located on the nine-point circle.

Now let $P$ be the point of intersection of the Euler lines of triangles $AB_{1}C_{1}, A_{1}BC_{1}, A_{1}B_{1}C$. Denote $\widehat{PA_{2}A}=\varphi$. For convenience, we will assume that triangle $ABC$ is acute-angled, and point $P$ lies on the arc $B_{1}A_{2}$ of the nine-point circle (Fig. 74).

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \widehat{PA_{2}A_{1}}=180^{\circ}-\varphi, \\
& \widehat{PA_{2}B_{1}}=180^{\circ}-\varphi-\widehat{B_{1}A_{2}A_{1}}=180^{\circ}-\varphi-\widehat{B_{1}C_{1}A_{1}}=2 \hat{C}-\varphi \\
& \widehat{PA_{2}C_{1}}=180^{\circ}-\varphi+180^{\circ}-2 \hat{B}=360^{\circ}-\varphi-2 \hat{B} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the chords $\left|PA_{1}\right|,\left|PB_{1}\right|$, and $\left|PC_{1}\right|$ are proportional to the sines of the angles subtended by them, we need to prove that one of the three quantities $\sin \varphi, \sin (2 \hat{C}-\varphi), -\sin (2 \hat{B}+\varphi)$ (in our case, the first one) is equal to the sum of the other two, i.e.,

$$
\sin \varphi=\sin (2 \hat{C}-\varphi)-\sin (2 \hat{B}+\varphi) .
$$

But in triangle $AA_{2}H_{1}\left|AA_{2}\right|=R,\left|AH_{1}\right|=2R \cos \hat{A}(R$ is the radius of the circumcircle, $R \cos \hat{A}$ is the distance from the center of the circumcircle $A_{2}$ to $\left.B_{1}C_{1}\right), \widehat{H_{1}AA_{2}}=\hat{A} \lessdot 2 \hat{B}-180^{\circ}$. By the sine theorem for $\triangle AA_{2}H_{1}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{2 \cos \hat{A}}{\sin \varphi}= & -\frac{1}{\sin (2 \hat{B}+\hat{A}+\varphi)} \Rightarrow \\
& \Rightarrow-2 \cos \hat{A} \sin (2 \hat{B}+\hat{A}+\varphi)=\sin \varphi \Rightarrow \\
& \Rightarrow-\sin (2 \hat{B}+2 \hat{A}+\varphi)-\sin (2 \hat{B}+\varphi)=\sin \varphi \Rightarrow \\
& \Rightarrow \sin (2 \hat{C}-\varphi)-\sin (2 \hat{B}+\varphi)=\sin \varphi
\end{aligned}
$$

which is what we needed to prove.

Thus, we have proved our statement in the case of an acute-angled triangle.

The case of an obtuse-angled triangle $ABC$ is considered in the same way.

question: 263. Prove that if in triangle $ABC$ angle $B$ is obtuse and $|AB|=\frac{|AC|}{2}$, then $\hat{C}>\frac{1}{2} \hat{A}$.
reference_solution: 263. Let $D$ be the midpoint of $AC$. Construct a perpendicular to $AC$ at $D$ and denote by $M$ the point of intersection of this perpendicular with $BC$. $\triangle AMC$ is isosceles, so $\widehat{MAC} = \widehat{BCA}$. By the given condition, $\triangle ABD$ is also isosceles, $\widehat{ABD} = \widehat{BDA}$, $\widehat{ABM} > 90^{\circ}$ (by the given condition), $\widehat{ADM} = 90^{\circ}$, hence $\widehat{MBD} > \widehat{MDB}$ and $|MD| > |BM|$. Therefore, $\widehat{MAD} > \widehat{MAB}$ (if we reflect $B$ symmetrically with respect to the line $AM$, we get a point $B_1$ inside the angle $MAD$, since $MD \perp AD$ and $|MD| > |MB| = |MB_1|$); thus, $\hat{C} > \hat{A} - \hat{C}$, $\hat{C} > \frac{1}{2} \hat{A}$.

question: 264. Prove that the circumcircle of a triangle cannot pass through the center of an excircle. (An excircle is tangent to one side of the triangle and the extensions of the other two sides. For each triangle, there are three excircles.)
reference_solution: 264. If the circle touches the extensions of sides $A B$ and $A C$ and its center is $O$, it is easy to find that $\widehat{B O C}=180^{\circ}-\left(90^{\circ}-\frac{\hat{B}}{2}\right)-$ $-\left(90^{\circ}-\frac{\hat{C}}{2}\right)=\frac{\hat{B}+\hat{C}}{2}=90^{\circ}-\frac{\hat{A}}{2}$. Therefore, $\widehat{B O C}+\widehat{B A C}=$ $=90^{\circ}+\frac{\hat{A}}{2} \neq 180^{\circ}$.

question: 266. Prove that if the medians drawn from vertices $B$ and $C$ of triangle $ABC$ are perpendicular, then $\operatorname{ctg} \hat{B} + \operatorname{ctg} \hat{C} \geqslant 2 / 3$.
reference_solution:
266. If $A D$ is the altitude, $A N$ is the median, and $M$ is the point of intersection of the medians, then

$\operatorname{ctg} \hat{B}+\operatorname{ctg} \hat{C}=\frac{|D B|}{|A D|}+\frac{|C D|}{|A D|}=\frac{|C B|}{|A D|} \geqslant \frac{|C B|}{|A N|}=\frac{|C B|}{3|M N|}=\frac{2}{3}$.

question: 268. From an external point $A$ to a circle, two tangents $A B$ and $A C$ are drawn, and the midpoints of these tangents $D$ and $E$ are connected by a line $D E$. Prove that this line does not intersect the circle.
reference_solution:
268. If $|O A|=a, R$ is the radius of the circle, and $K$ is the intersection point of $O A$ and $D E$, it is easy to find that

$$
|O K|=a-\frac{a^{2}-R^{2}}{2 a}=\frac{a^{2}+R^{2}}{2 a}>R
$$

question: 270. In triangle $A B C$, the angles are related by $3 \hat{A}-\hat{C}<\pi$. Angle $B$ is divided into four equal parts by lines intersecting side $A C$. Prove that the third segment, counting from vertex $A$, into which side $A C$ is divided, is less than $|A C| / 4$.
reference_solution:
270. Let $K, L$ and $M$ be the points of intersection of the drawn lines with $AC$. Denote $|AC|=b, |BC|=a, |AB|=c, |BL\rangle=l$. By the angle bisector theorem for the internal angle, we find $|LC|=\frac{ba}{a+c}$; applying this theorem again for $\triangle BCL$, we get

$$
|LM|=|LC| \frac{|BL|}{|BL|+|BC|}=\frac{ba}{a+c} \cdot \frac{l}{l+a}=\frac{ba}{a+c}\left(1-\frac{a}{a+l}\right)
$$

but $\widehat{BLA}=\frac{\hat{B}}{2}+\hat{C}=\frac{\pi-A+\hat{C}}{2}>\hat{A}$ (since $\hat{C}>3\hat{A}-\pi$), so $c>l$ and

$$
|LM|=\frac{ba}{a+c}\left(1-\frac{a}{a+l}\right)<\frac{ba}{a+c}\left(1-\frac{a}{a+c}\right)=b \frac{ac}{(a+c^2)} \leqslant \frac{b}{4}
$$

question: 271. Let $a, b, c, d$ be the lengths of the consecutive sides of a quadrilateral. Prove that if $S$ is its area, then $S \leqslant (ac + bd) / 2$, and equality holds only for a cyclic quadrilateral with perpendicular diagonals.
reference_solution: 271. If $A B C D$ is the given quadrilateral, then take the quadrilateral $A B_{1} C D$, where $B_{1}$ is symmetric to $B$ with respect to the perpendicular bisector of the diagonal $A C$. Obviously, the areas of $A B C D$ and $A B_{1} C D$ are equal, and the sides of $A B_{1} C D$ in order are $b$, $a, c, d$. The inequality $S \leqslant \frac{1}{2}(a c+b d)$ for the quadrilateral $A B_{1} C D$ is obvious. Equality will hold if $\widehat{D A B_{1}}=\widehat{B_{1} C D}=90^{\circ}$, i.e., the quadrilateral $A B_{1} C D$ is inscribed, with two opposite angles each $90^{\circ}$; hence, $A B C D$ is also inscribed (in the same circle) and its diagonals are perpendicular.

question: 272. Prove that if the lengths of the bisectors of a triangle are less than 1, then its area is less than $\sqrt{3} / 3$.
reference_solution:
272. Consider two cases:
1) The given triangle $A B C$ is acute-angled. Let $\hat{B}$ be the largest angle: $60^{\circ} \leqslant \hat{B}<90^{\circ}$. Since the angle bisectors of angles $A$ and $C$ are less than 1, the heights of these angles $h_{A}$ and $h_{C}$ are also less than 1. We have

$$
S_{A B C}=\frac{h_{A} h_{C}}{\sin \hat{B}}<\frac{\sqrt{\overline{3}}}{3}
$$

2) If one of the angles of the triangle, for example $B$, is not acute, then the sides enclosing it are less than the corresponding bisectors, i.e., less than 1, and the area does not exceed $\frac{1}{2}|A B| \cdot|A C|$, i.e.,

$$
S_{A B C} \leqslant \frac{1}{2}<\frac{\sqrt{\overline{3}}}{3} .
$$

question: 273. Prove that triangle $ABC$ will be acute, right, or obtuse depending on whether the expression $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}-8 R^{2}$ is positive, zero, or negative ( $a, b, c$ are the sides of the triangle, $R$ - the radius of the circumscribed circle).
reference_solution: 273. Let $c$ be the largest side, opposite vertex $C$. If $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}-8 R^{2}>0$, then $a^{2}+b^{2}>8 R^{2}-c^{2}>c^{2}$ (since $c<2 R$), i.e., the triangle is acute-angled. Conversely, let the triangle be acute-angled; then $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}=2 m_{c}^{2}+\frac{3}{2} c^{2}\left(m_{c}\right.$ - the median to side $c$); therefore, the smaller the median, the smaller $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}$, but the median is maximal when $C$ is the midpoint of the arc, and decreases as $C$ moves along the arc; when the triangle becomes right-angled, $a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}-8 R^{2}=0$.

question: 274. Prove that if the lengths of the sides of a triangle are related by the inequality $a^{2}+b^{2}>5 c^{2}$, then $c$ is the length of the smallest side.
reference_solution: 274. Suppose the opposite, for example, that $c \geqslant a$; then $2 c \geqslant$ $\geqslant c+a>b$; squaring the inequalities and adding them, we get $5 c^{2}>a^{2}+b^{2}-$ a contradiction.

question:
275. In triangle $ABC$, angle $B$ is the middle in size: $\hat{A}<\hat{B}<\hat{C} ; I$ is the incenter,

O is the circumcenter, $H$ is the orthocenter. Prove that $I$ lies inside $\triangle B O H$.
reference_solution:
275. It is not difficult to prove that the bisector of angle $B$ is also the bisector of angle $O B H$ (the same is true for angles $O A H, O C H$). Figure 76, b shows the cases of an acute triangle (a) and an obtuse triangle (b). The solution is the same in both cases.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-141.jpg?height=350&width=442&top_left_y=1252&top_left_x=173)
a)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-141.jpg?height=411&width=429&top_left_y=1191&top_left_x=652)
b)

Fig. 76.

Let, for example, $\hat{C} \geqslant 90^{\circ}$ (Fig. 76, b). The bisector of angle $B$ is the bisector of $O B H$, and the bisector of angle $A$ is the bisector of angle $O A H$. Further, $\widehat{B A H}=90^{\circ}-\hat{B}|B H|$. If $K$ and $M$ are the points of intersection of the bisectors of angles $A$ and $B$

$$
\frac{|H K|}{|K O|}=\frac{|A H|}{|A O|}=\frac{|A H|}{R}>\frac{|B H|}{R}=\frac{|B H|}{|O B|}=\frac{|H M|}{|M O|}
$$

Thus, $|H K|>|H M|$ and the point of intersection of the bisectors of angles $A$ and $B$ lies inside $\triangle B O H$.

question: 277. In triangle $A B C$, point $M$ lies on side $B C$. Prove that $(|A M|-|A C|)|B C| \leqslant(|A B|-$ $-|A C|)|M C|$
reference_solution:
277. Draw a line through $M$ parallel to $A C$, intersecting $A B$ at point $K$. It is easy to find

$$
\left|A K_{i}=C M\right| \frac{|A B|}{|C B|}, \quad|M K|=|M B| \frac{|A C|}{|C B|} .
$$

Since $|A M| \leqslant|A K|+|K M|$, by substituting $|A K|$ and $|K M|$, we get

$$
\begin{gathered}
|A M| \leqslant \frac{|C M| \cdot|A B|}{|B C|}+\frac{|M B| \cdot|A C|}{|C B|} \\
|A M||B C| \leqslant|C M| \cdot|A B|+(|B C|-|M C|)|A C|, \\
\quad(|A M|-|A C|)|B C| \leqslant(|A B|-|A C|)|M C|,
\end{gathered}
$$

which is what we needed to prove.

question: 283. The vertex of an angle of measure $\alpha$ is at point $O$. $A$ is a fixed point inside the angle. Points $M$ and $N$ are taken on the sides of the angle such that $\widehat{M A N}=\beta(\alpha+\beta<$ $<180^{\circ}$ ). Prove that if $|A M|=|A N|$, then the area of quadrilateral OMAN reaches a maximum (among all possible quadrilaterals obtained by varying $M$ and $N$).
reference_solution:
283. Let $M_{1}$ and $N_{1}$ be two other points on the sides of the angle (Fig. 78). Then $\quad{\widehat{M_{1} A N_{1}}}_{1}=\beta, \quad \widehat{A M_{1} M}=360^{\circ}-\alpha-\beta-\widehat{O N_{1} A}>$ $>180^{\circ}-\widehat{N_{1} A}=\widehat{A N_{1} N}$. From this, considering that $\widehat{M_{1}} \widehat{A M}=\widehat{N_{1} A N}$,
we get that $\left|M_{1} A\right|<\left|A N_{1}\right|$ and, therefore, $S_{M_{1} A M}<S_{A N_{1} N}$; thus, $S_{O M_{1} A N_{1}}<S_{O M A N}$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-144.jpg?height=264&width=426&top_left_y=304&top_left_x=208)

Fig. 78.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-144.jpg?height=336&width=356&top_left_y=230&top_left_x=687)

Fig. 79.

question:
286. Let $A B C D$ be a cyclic quadrilateral. The diagonal $A C$ is equal to $a$ and forms angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with the sides $A B$ and $A D$. Prove that the area of the quadrilateral is bounded by the values

$$
\frac{a^{2} \sin (\alpha+\beta) \sin \beta}{2 \sin \alpha} \text { and } \frac{a^{2} \sin (\alpha+\beta) \sin \alpha}{2 \sin \beta}
$$
reference_solution:
286. Let $\sin \alpha \geqslant \sin \beta$ for definiteness; take a point $K$ on the extension of $AB$ such that $\widehat{B K C}=\beta$ (Fig. 81); since $\widehat{C} B K = \widehat{A D C}$ (since $A B C D$ is cyclic), $\triangle K B C$ is similar to $\triangle A C D$,

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6282cf4a54d2a9633c48g-145.jpg?height=419&width=285&top_left_y=273&top_left_x=160)

Fig. 81. but $|B C| \geqslant |C D|$, therefore, $S_{B C K} \geqslant S_{A D C}$ and $S_{A K C} \geqslant S_{A B C D}$, but

$$
S_{A K C}=\frac{a^{2} \sin (\alpha+\beta) \sin \alpha}{2 \sin \beta},
$$

i.e.,

$$
S_{A B C D} \leqslant \frac{a^{2} \sin (\alpha+\beta) \sin \alpha}{2 \sin \beta}
$$

Similarly, it can be shown that $S_{A B C D} \geqslant \frac{a^{2} \sin (\alpha+\beta) \sin \beta}{2 \sin \alpha}$.

question: 287. Given an angle of size $\alpha$ with vertex at point $O$ and a point $A$ inside it. Consider all possible quadrilaterals $O M N N$, where vertices $M$ and $N$ are located on the sides of the angle and such that $\widehat{M A N} = \beta\left(\alpha+\beta>180^{\circ}\right)$. Prove that if among these quadrilaterals there is a convex quadrilateral such that $|M A|=|A N|$, then this quadrilateral has the smallest area among all considered quadrilaterals.
reference_solution: 287. Consider another position of points $M_{1}$ and $N_{1}\left(\widehat{M_{1} A N_{1}}=\beta\right)$ and show, taking into account the condition (that $\alpha+\beta>180^{\circ}$), that the "added" triangle has a greater area than the triangle whose area is reduced (analogous to the solution of problem 283).

question:

293. Let the ratios $\frac{|A M|}{|M C|}, \frac{|C N|}{|N B|}$ and $\frac{|M L|}{|L M|}$ be denoted by $\alpha, \beta$ and $\gamma$. Then we will have (see the solution of problem 35) $\frac{P}{Q}=\alpha \beta \gamma$, $S=Q(\alpha+1)(\beta+1)(\gamma+1)$. Then we will use the inequality

2. In space, two segments $A B$ and $A_{1} B_{1}$ are given. Prove that the distance between their midpoints $M$ and $M_{1}$ does not exceed half the sum of the distances $A A_{1}$ and $B B_{1}$ between the endpoints of the segments and is not less than (the absolute value of) half the difference of the distances $A A_{1}$ and $B B_{1}$.

In which case $M M_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\left(A A_{1}+B B_{1}\right)$? And when $M M_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\left|A A_{1}-B B_{1}\right|$?

2. Draw through the midpoint $M_{1}$ of the segment $A_{1} B_{1}$ the segments $M_{1} A^{\prime} \# A_{1} A$ and $M_{1} B^{\prime} \# B_{1} B$ (Fig. $60, a$). In this case, the quadrilateral $M_{1} A_{1} A A^{\prime}$ will be a parallelogram ${ }^{1}$); therefore, $A A^{\prime} \# A_{1} M_{1}$. Similarly, the quadrilateral $M_{1} B_{1} B B^{\prime}$ is also a parallelogram ${ }^{1}$); therefore, $B B^{\prime} \# B_{1} M_{1}$. It is clear that the parallel segments $A A^{\prime}$ and $B B^{\prime}$, drawn through the endpoints of the segment $A B$, lie in the same plane $\ell$, passing through the line $A B$. Now, connect the point $M$ with the points $A^{\prime}$ and $B^{\prime}$; in this case, in the triangles $M A A^{\prime}$ and $M B B^{\prime}$ (lying in the same plane $\pi$!), we will have: $\angle M A A^{\prime}=\angle M B B^{\prime}$ (since $A A^{\prime} \| B B^{\prime}$), $M A=M B$ (since the point $M$ is the midpoint of the segment $A B$), and $A A^{\prime}=B B^{\prime}$ (since $A A^{\prime}=A_{1} M_{1}, B B^{\prime}=B_{1} M_{1}$, and the segments $A_{1} M_{1}$ and $B_{1} M_{1}$ are equal). Therefore, these triangles are equal, and thus $A^{\prime} M=B^{\prime} M$ and $\angle A^{\prime} M A=\angle B^{\prime} M B$. From the latter equality, it follows that the points $A^{\prime}, M$, and $B^{\prime}$ of the plane $\pi$ lie on the same straight line; thus, the "broken line" $A^{\prime} M B^{\prime}$ forms one segment, and the point $M$ is the midpoint of the side $A^{\prime} B^{\prime}$ of the triangle $A^{\prime} M_{1} B^{\prime}$.

Since $M_{1} A^{\prime}=A_{1} A$ and $M_{1} B^{\prime}=B_{1} B$, it remains for us to prove that the median $M_{1} M$ of the triangle $A^{\prime} M_{1} B^{\prime}$ does not exceed the half-sum of its sides $M_{1} A^{\prime}$ and $M_{1} B^{\prime}$ and is not less than their half-difference. But this is established elementarily: extend the median $M_{1} M$ beyond the point $M$ to a distance $M Q=M_{1} M$ and connect $Q$ with $A^{\prime}$ (Fig. '60, b). From the equality of the triangles $M_{1} B^{\prime} M$ and $Q A^{\prime} M$, we have $M_{1} B^{\prime}=Q A^{\prime}$; therefore,

$$
2 M_{1} M=M_{1} Q

and

$\left|M_{1} A^{\prime}-M_{1} B^{\prime}\right|=\left|M_{1} A^{\prime}-A^{\prime} Q\right| \leqslant M_{1} Q \leqslant M_{1} A^{\prime}+A^{\prime} Q=M_{1} A^{\prime}+M_{1} B^{\prime}$, which is what we needed to prove.

4. Let the convex quadrilateral $A B C D$ be such that $A C+C D \geqslant A B+B D$. Prove that in this case, vertex $A$ of the quadrilateral is closer to vertex $B$ than to vertex $C$.

Does the statement of this problem remain valid if the quadrilateral $A B C D$ is not convex?
reference_solution:
4. We will prove the required statement by contradiction. If the convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ (Fig. 61, $\partial$) is such that $AB \geqslant AC$, then $\angle BCA \geqslant \angle ABC$; but in this case, obviously,

$$
\angle BCD > \angle BCA \geqslant \angle ABC > \angle DBC
$$

and considering $BD > CD$. Adding this last inequality to the initial inequality $AB \geqslant AC$, we get that

$$
AB + BD > AC + CD
$$

But this contradicts the condition of the problem; hence, our assumption that $AB \geqslant AC$ was incorrect.

It is not difficult to see that if the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is non-convex, then the inequalities $AC + CD \geqslant AB + BD$ and $AB \geqslant AC$ are compatible (Fig. $61, e$).

5. a) Let $N$ be the point symmetric to point $M$ with respect to the common midpoint $S$ of segments $AD$ and $BC$ (Fig. 62). In this case, quadrilaterals $AMDN$ and $BMCN$ are parallelograms, with the second one lying inside the first. If one convex quadrilateral lies inside another, then the perimeter of the former is less than the perimeter of the latter; therefore,

$$
MA + MD + ND + NA \geqslant MB + MC + NB + NC
$$

or

$$
2MA + 2MD \geqslant 2MB + 2MC
$$

i.e.,

$$
MA + MD \geqslant MB + MC
$$

which is what we needed to prove.

It is easy to see that the equality $MA + MD = MB + MC$ holds only when point $M$ coincides with $A$ or $D$ (in this case, the degenerate "parallelograms" $AMDN$ and $BMCN$ coincide—they become the segment $AD$ taken twice).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_d4ffc236376258137647g-125.jpg?height=271&width=456&top_left_y=661&top_left_x=177)

Fig. 62. coincide—they become the segment $AD$ taken twice).

b) Let's take point $M$ on the plane to be point $A$ first, and then point $D$; then, by the condition of the problem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
& AD \geqslant AB + AC \\
& AD \geqslant BD + CD
\end{aligned}
$$

from which it follows that

$$
2AD \geqslant AB + AC + BD + CD
$$

On the other hand, by the triangle inequality, we have

$$
AD \leqslant AB + BD \quad \text{and} \quad AD \leqslant AC + CD
$$

which means,

$$
2AD \leqslant AB + BD + AC + CD
$$

From comparing inequalities (I) and (II), it follows that

$$
AD = AB + BD + AC + CD
$$

but this is possible only if both inequalities (*) and both inequalities (**) turn into equalities.

The first of the inequalities (**) turns into an equality only if point $B$ lies on segment $AD$, and the second if point $C$ lies on segment $AD$; thus, both points $B$ and $C$ must lie on segment $AD$. Now, for example, the first of the equalities (*) (since we know that these inequalities turn into equalities!) gives

$$
AC + CD = AB + AC
$$

i.e.,

$$
AB = CD
$$

But the last equality is equivalent to the fact that segments $AD$ and $BC$ have a common midpoint $S!$

8. Let $\Phi_{1}, \Phi_{2}$, and $\Phi_{3}$ be three arbitrary figures.

a) Prove that the sum of the distances from $\Phi_{1}$ to $\Phi_{2}$ and from $\Phi_{2}$ to $\Phi_{3}$ is not less than the distance from $\Phi_{1}$ to $\Phi_{3}$:

$$
\rho\left(\Phi_{1}, \Phi_{2}\right)+\rho\left(\Phi_{2}, \Phi_{3}\right) \geqslant \rho\left(\Phi_{1}, \Phi_{3}\right)
$$

b) Can the inequality

$$
\rho\left(\Phi_{1}, \Phi_{2}\right)+\rho\left(\Phi_{2}, \Phi_{3}\right)<\rho\left(\Phi_{3}, \Phi_{1}\right)
$$

hold?

Sometimes it is convenient to characterize the deviation of figure $\Phi_{1}$ from figure $\Phi_{2}$ by the maximum of the previously defined distances from $\Phi_{1}$ to $\Phi_{2}$ and from $\Phi_{2}$ to $\Phi_{1}$. The resulting quantity is called the distance between figures $\Phi_{1}$ and $\Phi_{2}$ and is denoted by $\mathrm{P}\left(\Phi_{1}, \Phi_{2}\right)$; thus:

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(\Phi_{1}, \Phi_{2}\right)=\max \left[\rho\left(\Phi_{1}, \Phi_{2}\right), \rho\left(\Phi_{2}, \Phi_{1}\right)\right]
$$

It is clear that the distance $\mathrm{P}\left(\Phi_{1}, \Phi_{2}\right)$ is already symmetric: for any two figures $\Phi_{1}$ and $\Phi_{2}$, it is always

$$
\mathrm{P}\left(\Phi_{1}, \Phi_{2}\right)=\mathrm{P}\left(\Phi_{2}, \Phi_{1}\right)
$$

Moreover, $\mathrm{P}\left(\Phi_{1}, \Phi_{2}\right)=0$ in the case when figures $\Phi_{1}$ and $\Phi_{2}$ coincide $\left.{ }^{1}\right)$.

8. Since the greatest of the distances from a point of figure $\Phi_{1}$ to the nearest point of figure $\Phi_{2}$ is $a$, figure $\Phi_{2}$ contains a point $B$ such that the distance from point $A$ of figure $\Phi_{1}$ to point $B$ of figure $\Phi_{2}$ does not exceed $a$. Furthermore, since the greatest of the distances from a point of figure $\Phi_{2}$ to the nearest point of figure $\Phi_{3}$ is $b$, for point $B$

question: 12. Let $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{1000}$ be any 1000 points on the plane. Prove that on any circle of radius 1, there exists a point $M$ such that the sum of the distances from $M$ to the points $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{1000}$ is not less than 1000.

( $M_{1} A_{1}+M_{2} A_{1}=2$, if the point $A_{1}$ lies on the segment $M_{1} M_{2}$, and $M_{1} A_{1}+M_{2} A_{1}>2$ in all other cases). Therefore,

\left(M_{1} A_{1}+M_{2} A_{1}\right)+ & \left(M_{1} A_{2}+M_{2} A_{2}\right)+\ldots+\left(M_{1} A_{1000}+M_{2} A_{1000}\right)= \\
= & \left(M_{1} A_{1}+M_{1} A_{2}+\ldots+M_{1} A_{1000}\right)+ \\
& +\left(M_{2} A_{1}+M_{2} A_{2}+\ldots+M_{2} A_{1000} \geqslant 2000\right.

## 2. ANGLE ESTIMATES

A central place in this cycle of problems is occupied by closely related problems 25-32, which begin with relatively simple questions and quickly lead to very complex problems or to issues that no one can solve today. Some of the unsolved problems related to angle estimates may turn out to be not very difficult, and we recommend that the reader try to answer some of the questions posed below and not yet answered, or to formulate new problems related to those collected here.

When solving problems in this cycle, it is important to keep in mind the certain "treacherousness" of the issues considered here: problems that are quite simple in their conditions often turn out to be quite difficult, and the complexity of two seemingly very similar problems often turns out to be quite different. For example, while problem 25 g) is relatively simple, an exactly analogous problem about estimating the largest of the angles formed by $n$ points has not been solved yet, although many famous mathematicians have tried to solve it. Similarly, while the second of two very close problems 32 and 34 (see the comments on this on p. 33) is solved quite easily, the first turns out to be one of the most difficult in the entire book. It is also instructive to compare problems 31 a) and 32 a) with their stereometric analogs 31 b) and 32 b) (or even to compare the very simple problem 33 a) with problem 33 b)), illustrating the typical sharp increase in difficulties in combinatorial geometry when transitioning from planimetric problems to stereometric or "multidimensional" ones (see the comments on p. 33 in connection with problem 32).

question: 16. A heptagon $A_{1} A_{2} A_{3} A_{4} A_{5} A_{6} A_{7}$ is inscribed in a circle. Prove that if the center of this circle lies inside the heptagon, then the sum of the angles at vertices $A_{1}, A_{3}$ and $A_{5}$ is less than $450^{\circ}$.

17. Let $M$ be an arbitrary point lying inside a regular $n$-gon. Prove that there exist two vertices $A$ and $B$ of the $n$-gon such that

$$
\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right) \cdot 180^{\circ} \leqslant \angle A M B \leqslant 180^{\circ}
$$
reference_solution:
17. Let $AB$ be the closest to the considered point $M$ among all diagonals and sides of our regular $n$-gon. If point $M$ lies on the diagonal $AB$, then $\angle AOB = 180^{\circ}$; if it does not lie on $AB$, then since point $M$ lies inside the polygon, there will be a neighboring vertex $C$ of $B$ such that $C$ and $M$ lie on the same side of the line $AB$ (make a sketch). It is clear that $\angle BAC = \frac{1}{2n} \cdot 360^{\circ} = \frac{180^{\circ}}{n}$. But point $M$ is no farther from the diagonal $AB$ than from $AC$; therefore, it lies between the bisector $AK$ of the angle $\angle BAC$ and the diagonal $AB$ (possibly on $AK$), and thus,

$$
\angle MAB \leqslant \angle KAB = \frac{180^{\circ}}{2n}
$$

analogously,

$$
\angle MBA \leqslant \frac{180^{\circ}}{2n}
$$

Now we have

$$
\angle AMB < 180^{\circ}
$$

and

$$
\angle AMB = 180^{\circ} - \angle MAB - \angle MBA \geqslant 180^{\circ} - \frac{180^{\circ}}{n} = 180^{\circ} \left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)
$$

which is what we needed to prove.

question:
18. In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$, the bisector $AD$, the median $BM$, and the altitude $CH$ intersect at one point.

a) Prove that the angle $A$ of the triangle is greater than $45^{\circ}$.

b) Specify all possible values that $\angle A$ can have under the conditions of the problem.
reference_solution:
18. a) It is not difficult to construct $\triangle ABC$ with a given (acute) angle $\angle A = \alpha$ such that the bisector $AD$, the altitude $CH$, and the median $BM$ intersect at one point $Q$: it is sufficient to lay off on side $AU$ of angle $UAV = \alpha$ an arbitrary segment $AC$, drop a perpendicular $CH$ (the altitude of the future triangle $ABC$) from $C$ to $AV$, and connect the midpoint $M$ of segment $AC$ with the point $Q$ of intersection of $CH$ and the bisector $AW$ of angle $UAV$ (and of triangle $ACB$); the line $MQ$ will be the median of the desired triangle, and the point $B$ of intersection of $MQ$ and $AV$ will be its vertex (Fig. 71). From the construction, in particular, it follows that the given angle $\alpha$ determines the desired triangle "uniquely up to similarity": this means that by replacing segment $AC$ with any other segment $AC'$, we will arrive at

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_d4ffc236376258137647g-137.jpg?height=377&width=404&top_left_y=301&top_left_x=188)

Fig. 71. $\triangle AC'B'$ with $\triangle ACB$, i.e., the angles of $\triangle ABC$ are completely determined by the given angle $\alpha$ (if $\alpha \leqslant 45^{\circ}$), and it follows that $AE > CE$: On the other hand, since $\angle AEC = \alpha$, $\triangle ACE$ is isosceles; line $CH \perp AE$ is its bisector and, therefore, $EQ$ is the third bisector of $\triangle ACE$. But since $AE > CE$, $EQ$ intersects $AM$ at a point $F$ located between $M$ and $C$ (since $\frac{AF}{FC} = \frac{AE}{CE} > 1$, and $\frac{AM}{MC} = 1$), from which it follows that $FQ$ intersects side $AB$ of triangle $AMB$, i.e., $E$ is located between $A$ and $B$. But from this it follows that $\angle ACB > \angle ACE \geqslant 90^{\circ}$, which is what we needed to prove.

b) First of all, note that as the angle $UAV = \alpha$ increases from 0 to $90^{\circ}$, the angle $\angle ACB = \gamma$ corresponding to $\alpha$ monotonically decreases. 26. a) On a plane, four points are given. Prove that from these points, one can choose three that form the vertices of a right or obtuse triangle; however, the arrangement of the points can be such that no three of them form the vertices of an obtuse triangle ${ }^{1}$ ).

b) On a plane, five points are given. Prove that from these points, one can choose three that form the vertices of a triangle with the largest angle $\geqslant 108^{\circ}$; however, the arrangement of the points can be such that no triangle formed by these points has an angle greater than $108^{\circ}$.

c) On a plane, six points are given. Prove that from these points, one can choose three that form the vertices of a triangle with the largest angle $\geqslant 120^{\circ}$; however, the arrangement of the points can be such that no triangle formed by these points has an angle greater than $120^{\circ}$.

For what arrangements of four, respectively five and six, points on a plane can one not choose three that form the vertices of a triangle with an angle greater than $90^{\circ}$, respectively greater than $108^{\circ}$ or greater than $120^{\circ} ?$

In connection with problems 26 a) - c), we can repeat almost everything said about problems 25 a) - d). Let us consider, as before, $n$ points $M_{1}, M_{2}, M_{3}, \ldots, M_{n}$ on the plane; the angles $M_{2} M_{j} M_{k}$ formed by these points are denoted by $\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \alpha_{3}, \ldots, \alpha_{N}$, where $N$ is the total number of all considered angles. The largest of all these angles we denote by $\beta$:

$$
\beta=\max _{J} \alpha_{J} \quad J=1,2,3, \ldots \text { or } N,
$$

and the smallest possible value of the largest angle $\beta$, achievable with a suitable choice of the system $\mathscr{P}_{n}=\left\{M_{1}, M_{2}, \ldots, M_{n}\right\}$ of points on the plane, we denote by $\underline{\beta}$ (or by $\underline{\beta}(n)$, since the considered quantity obviously depends on $n$):

$$
\begin{array}{r}
\beta=\min _{\mathscr{P}_{n}} \beta=\min _{\mathscr{S}_{n}} \max _{J} \alpha_{J} \quad J=1,2, \ldots \text { or } N ; \\
\qquad \mathscr{P}_{n}=\left\{M_{\mathrm{1}}, M_{2}, \ldots, M_{n}\right\}
\end{array}
$$

Then, from the above-discussed problem of estimating the angles of triangles and from the results of problems 26 a) - c), it follows that

$$
\underline{\beta}(3)=60^{\circ}, \quad \underline{\beta}(4)=90^{\circ}, \quad \underline{\beta}(5)=108^{\circ} \quad \text { and } \quad \underline{\beta}(6)=120^{\circ} ;
$$

thus, in the case of all possible systems $\mathscr{P}_{5}=$ $=\left\{M_{1}, M_{2}, M_{3}, M_{4}, M_{5}\right\}$ of five points on the plane, the largest angle $\beta$ among the $N(=30)$ angles determined by these points is always within the limits

$$
108^{\circ} \leqslant \beta \leqslant 180^{\circ}
$$

(it is clear that $\beta=180^{\circ}$ if any three of our five points lie on the same line).

Problems 26 a) - c) are no more difficult than problems 25 a) - c); on this basis, one might assume that the general problem of determining the value of $\beta(n)$ is not difficult and, most likely, has the following answer: $\underline{\beta}(n)=180^{\circ}-\frac{360^{\circ}}{n} \cdot\left(=180^{\circ}-2 \bar{\alpha}(n) ; \quad\right.$ this formula, obviously, is valid for $n=3,4,5$ and 6). A careful analysis of the results of problems 25 a) - c) and 26 a) - c) reveals only one noticeable difference between them, which can be perceived as a signal that the problems of estimating the possible values of the smallest angle $\alpha\left(=\min _{J} \alpha_{j}\right)$ and the largest angle $\beta\left(=\max _{J}\right)$ may differ both in the nature of the answers and in the difficulty of the solution: while in all problems 25 a) - c) (and in the general problem 25 d)) the largest value $\bar{\alpha}$ of the smallest angle is always realized for a unique system $\mathscr{P}_{n}$ of points on the plane, in problems 26 a) - c) the smallest value $90^{\circ}$, respectively $108^{\circ}$ and $120^{\circ}$, of the angle $\beta=\max \alpha$, is achieved for an infinite number of different (i.e., not similar to each other) systems $\mathscr{P}_{n}$ of points on the plane (where $n=4,5,6$). However, this "signal" should not be ignored, - and indeed, the following problems 27 a) - c) are already quite different from problems 26 a) - c): they are noticeably more difficult than these problems and problems 25 a) - c).

Let's start again with constructing a convex polygon $T$ (the convex hull of our points; see the beginning of the solution to problem 25), inside and on the boundary of which all our points are located, and the vertices coincide with some of them. Next, if point $D$ lies inside $\triangle A B C \equiv T$ (Fig. 73, a), then since $\angle A D B + \angle B D C + \angle C D A = 360^{\circ}$, at least one of the angles $A D B, B D C, C D A$ will be $\geqslant \frac{360^{\circ}}{3} = 120^{\circ}$ (i.e., $>90^{\circ}; >108^{\circ}$); if point $E$ lies inside an $m$-sided polygon $T$ with vertices at $m$ of our points, where $m \geqslant 4$, it is sufficient to divide $T$ into triangles using diagonals emanating from one vertex (Fig. 73, b). Thus, it remains to consider the case where the given points are the vertices of a convex polygon.

However, the sum of the angles of a convex $n$-sided polygon, where $n=4,5$ and 6, is respectively $180^{\circ}(4-2)=360^{\circ}, 180^{\circ} \cdot 3$, and $180^{\circ} \cdot 4$; therefore, at least one angle of a convex quadrilateral is $\geqslant \frac{360^{\circ}}{4}=90^{\circ}$, at least one angle of a convex pentagon is $\geqslant \frac{3 \cdot 180^{\circ}}{5}=108^{\circ}$, and at least one angle of a convex hexagon is $\geqslant \frac{4 \cdot 180^{\circ}}{6}=120^{\circ}$, which proves the statement of the problem.

From the solutions to problems a) - c), it follows that no three of our points form a triangle with an angle greater than $90^{\circ}$, respectively greater than $108^{\circ}$ or $120^{\circ}$, only in the case when the points are the vertices of a convex equiangular quadrilateral (rectangle), an equiangular pentagon, or an equiangular hexagon (see also the beginning of the solution to problem 27).

question:
28. Let $A, B, C, D$ be any four points on a plane; $\alpha=\alpha_{1}$ and $\alpha_{2}$ be the two smallest of the 12 angles formed by these points, and $\beta=\beta_{1}$ and $\beta_{2}$ be the two largest angles (so that $\alpha=. \alpha_{1} \leqslant \alpha_{2} \leqslant \ldots \leqslant \leqslant \beta_{2} \leqslant \beta_{1}=\beta$). Prove that

a) $0 \leqslant \alpha_{2} \leqslant 45^{\circ}$

b) $72^{\circ} \leqslant \beta_{2} \leqslant 180^{\circ}$.

For which quadruples of points $A, B, C, D$ are the values $\alpha_{2}=45^{\circ}$ and $\beta_{2}=72^{\circ}$ achieved?
reference_solution:
28. a) If all our points belong to a segment, then the two smallest angles are equal to 0 (i.e., $\alpha_{2} \equiv 0$; compare with problem 29); if point $D$ belongs to $\triangle A B C$, then two angles of the triangle, say, $A$ and $B$, are acute and smaller than the "parts" $B A D$ and $C A D$, respectively $A B D$ and $C B D$, of these angles $<45^{\circ}$; thus, we are left to consider the case of a convex quadrilateral $A B C D$ (see the beginning of the solution to problem 25). Since, for example, $\angle A B D + \angle B D A + \angle D A C + \angle B A C = 180^{\circ}$ and $\angle C B D + \angle B D C + \angle B C A + \angle D C A = 180^{\circ}$, each set of four angles contains an angle that does not exceed $45^{\circ}\left(=\frac{180^{\circ}}{4}\right)$, which proves that $\alpha_{2} \leqslant 45^{\circ}$. If $A B C D$ is a square (and only in this case!), then $\alpha_{2}$ equals $45^{\circ}$.
b) If all our points belong to a segment, then the two largest angles are equal to $180^{\circ}$ (i.e., $\beta_{2}=180^{\circ}$; see problem 29); if $D$ is a point inside triangle $A B C$, then two of the three "internal" angles $A D B$, $B D C$, and $C D A$ will be $\geqslant 90^{\circ}$. Now let $A B C D$ be a convex quadrilateral and $D$ its largest angle. In this case, $\angle D \geqslant 90^{\circ}$; moreover, $\angle D A B + \angle A B C + \angle B C D + \angle C D B + \angle B D A = 360^{\circ}$, and thus, at least one of these five angles $\geqslant 72^{\circ}\left(=\frac{360^{\circ}}{5}\right)$, which establishes that $\beta_{2} \geqslant 72^{\circ}$.

Equality $\beta_{2}=72^{\circ}$ is achieved if each of the five angles in the last sum is equal to $72^{\circ}$.

36. a) From one point in space, three rays emanate. Prove that at least one of the pairwise angles between these rays does not exceed $120^{\circ}$; however, the rays can be drawn such that no pairwise angle between them is less than $120^{\circ}$.

b) From one point in space, four rays emanate. Prove that at least one of the pairwise angles between these rays does not exceed $\alpha$, where $\cos \alpha = -\frac{1}{3}$ (and thus, $\alpha \approx 109^{\circ} 28^{\prime} 16^{\prime \prime}$); however, the rays can be drawn such that no pairwise angle between them is less than $\alpha$.

c) From one point in space, five rays emanate. Prove that at least one of the pairwise angles between these rays does not exceed $90^{\circ}$; however, the rays can be drawn such that no angle between them is acute.

d) Prove that the statement of part c) remains valid for six rays in space.

Let $l_{1}, l_{2}, \ldots, l_{n}$ be $n$ rays in space. The smallest of the pairwise angles between these rays is denoted by $\psi$, and let $\varphi(n)$ be the smallest such angle such that, regardless of the $n$ rays,

$$
\psi \leqslant \varphi(n)
$$

(in other words,

$$
\psi=\min _{i, j} \angle\left(l_{i}, l_{j}\right), \quad \text { where } \quad i, j=1,2, \ldots \text { or } n
$$

and

$\varphi(n)=\sup _{Q_{n}} \psi=\sup _{Q_{n}} \min _{i, j} \angle\left(l_{i}, l_{j}\right), \quad i, j=1,2, \ldots, n ;$

$$
Q_{n}=\left\{l_{1}, l_{2}, \ldots, l_{n}\right\}
$$

or even $\varphi(n)=\max \min \angle\left(l_{i}, l_{j}\right)$, since the maximum of the values $\psi=\min _{i} \angle\left(l_{i}, l_{j}\right), i, j=1,2, \ldots$ or $n$, considered for all possible systems $Q_{n}=\left\{l_{1}, l_{2}, \ldots, l_{n}\right\}$ of $n$ rays in space, is always achieved; clearly, the angle $\varphi(n)$ depends on the number $n$). Obviously,

$$
\varphi(2)=180^{\circ} ;
$$

further, from the result of problem 36, it follows that

$$
\varphi(3)=120^{\circ} . \quad \varphi(4)=\alpha \approx 109^{\circ} 28^{\prime} 16^{\prime \prime} ; \quad \varphi(5)=\varphi(6)=90^{\circ} .
$$

It is also proven that

$$
\begin{gathered}
\varphi(7) \approx 77^{\circ} 51^{\prime} 58^{\prime \prime}, \quad \varphi(8) \approx 74^{\circ} 52^{\prime} 10^{\prime \prime}, \quad \varphi(9) \approx 70^{\circ} 31^{\prime} 44^{\prime \prime}, \\
\varphi(12) \approx 63^{\circ} 26^{\prime} 06^{\prime \prime} \quad \text { and } \quad \varphi(24) \approx 44^{\circ} 42^{\prime} 52^{\prime \prime}
\end{gathered}
$$

(see Chapter VI of the book by L. Fejes Tóth [24] and the article by R. M. Robinson [49]); however, the exact value of $\varphi(n)$ for any $n>9$ and $n \neq 12,24$ is apparently unknown, although fairly plausible hypotheses about the magnitude of the angle $\varphi(n)$ have been proposed for all $n$ in the interval $123$; in particular, a relatively simple $k$-dimensional variant of problem 35.

Fig. 9. statement was formulated quite a long time ago; however, it was not easy to prove. Only in the 1960s, in different countries, several proofs were found that \(\triangle PQR\) cannot have the smallest perimeter among all the triangles depicted in Fig. 9. For proofs using geometric differentiation (see [l], p. 317 and following), see, for example, [7], pp. \(81-83\) or V. A. Zalgaller [52].
reference_solution:
38. a) The areas of triangles having a common angle are in the ratio of the products of the lengths of the sides enclosing this angle (since \( S_{A B C} = \frac{1}{2} a b \sin C \)); therefore, in the notation of Fig. 9 (p. 37)

\[
\frac{S_{A P R}}{S_{A B C}} = \frac{A P \cdot A R}{A B \cdot A C} ; \quad \frac{S_{B P Q}}{S_{B A C}} = \frac{B P \cdot B Q}{B A \cdot B C}, \quad \frac{S_{C Q R}}{S_{C B A}} = \frac{C Q \cdot C R}{C B \cdot C A}
\]

If all these ratios were greater than \(\frac{1}{4}\), then by multiplying their right-hand sides, we would have

\[
\frac{A P \cdot A R \cdot B P \cdot B Q \cdot C Q \cdot C R}{A B^{2} \cdot B C^{2} \cdot C A^{2}} > \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{3} = \frac{1}{64}
\]

or

\[
\frac{A P \cdot B P}{A B^{2}} \cdot \frac{B Q \cdot C Q}{B C^{2}} \cdot \frac{C R \cdot A R}{A C^{2}} > \frac{1}{64}.
\]

But since \(A P + B P = A B\), by the well-known theorem on the arithmetic and geometric means of two quantities \((a b \leqslant \left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)^{2}\) for any \(a, b > 0\), since \(\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)^{2} - a b = \left(\frac{a-b}{2}\right)^{2} \geqslant 0\)), we have \(A P \cdot B P \leqslant \left(\frac{A P + B P}{2}\right)^{2} = \frac{A B^{2}}{4}\), i.e., \(\frac{A P \cdot B P}{A B^{2}} \leqslant \frac{1}{4}\) and similarly

\[
\frac{B Q \cdot C Q}{B C^{2}} \leqslant \frac{1}{4}, \quad \frac{C R \cdot A R}{A C^{2}} \leqslant \frac{1}{4}
\]

Therefore,

\[
\frac{A P \cdot B P}{A B^{2}} \cdot \frac{B Q \cdot C Q}{B C^{2}} \cdot \frac{C R \cdot A R}{A C^{2}} \leqslant \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{3} = \frac{1}{64}
\]

The obtained contradiction proves the required statement.

b) Let \(A_{1} B_{1}, B_{1} C_{1}, C_{1} A_{1}\) be the midlines of \(\triangle A B C\). We will call corresponding those sides of triangles \(A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}\) and \(P Q R\) whose endpoints lie on the sides of the same angle of \(\triangle A B C\). Then two cases may arise: either there is a pair of non-intersecting corresponding sides, for example, \(P Q\) and \(C_{1} A_{1}\), i.e., \(P Q\) lies entirely inside \(\triangle C_{1} B A_{1}\) (Fig. 86, a) or inside trapezoid \(A C A_{1} C_{1}\) (Fig. 86, b), or all corresponding sides intersect pairwise (Fig. 86, c). In this case, if \(P Q\) lies entirely inside trapezoid \(A C A_{1} C_{1}\) and, for example, \(R\) lies on segment \(A B_{1}\), then \(P R\) lies inside \(\triangle A C_{1} B_{1}\) (Fig. 86, b); if \(R\) lies on segment \(B_{1} C\), then \(Q R\) lies inside \(\triangle B_{1} A_{1} C\). Therefore, only two cases remain to be considered: either there is a side of the inscribed triangle, for example, \(P Q\), lying inside the corresponding triangle \(C_{1} B A_{1}\) (possibly on its boundary), or all corresponding pairs of sides of triangles \(P Q R\) and \(A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}\) intersect.

First, consider the first case (Fig. 86, a) and prove that \(S_{B P Q} \leqslant S_{P Q R}\). Obviously,

\[
\frac{S_{B P Q}}{S_{P Q R}} = \frac{\frac{1}{2} P Q \cdot B H}{\frac{1}{2} P Q \cdot R H_{1}} = \frac{B H}{R H_{1}}
\]

where \(B H \perp P Q\) and \(R H_{1} \perp P Q\); this ratio is equal to \(\frac{B N}{N R} \leqslant \frac{B N_{1}}{N_{1} R} = 1\), where \(N\) and \(N_{1}\) are the points of intersection of \(B R\) with \(P Q\) and \(C_{1} A_{1}\) (since \(A_{1} C_{1}\) is the midline of the triangle). Therefore,

\[
\frac{S_{B P Q}}{S_{P Q R}} \leqslant 1,
\]

which is what we needed to prove.

Now consider the second case (Fig. 86, c). Since \(P Q\) intersects \(C_{1} A_{1}\), either

\[
S_{P Q R} > S_{Q P B_{1}}
\]

since with the common base \(P Q\), the height \(R H_{2}\) of \(\triangle P Q R\) is greater than the height \(B_{1} H_{1}\) of \(\triangle B_{1} P Q\) (since point \(R\) is farther from vertex \(K\) of angle \(P K A\) than \(B_{1}\). Similarly, we find that

\[
\begin{aligned}
& S_{Q P B_{1}} > S_{A_{1} P B_{1}} \\
& S_{A_{1} P B_{1}} = S_{A_{1} C_{1} B_{1}} = \frac{1}{4} S_{A B C}
\end{aligned}
\]

From the comparison of the obtained results, it follows that

\[
S_{P Q R} > \frac{1}{4} S_{A B C}
\]

and hence,

\[
S_{A R P} + S_{C Q R} + S_{B P Q} < \frac{3}{4} S_{A B C}
\]

Among the three terms in the left-hand side, at least one is not greater than \(\frac{1}{4} A B C\) (see problem a)) and, therefore, is less than \(S_{P Q R}\), which is what we needed to prove.

question:
39. On the extensions of the sides of angles $A, B, C$ of triangle $A B C$, segments equal to the opposite sides are laid out (Fig. 10). Show that the area of the resulting hexagon $\geqslant 13 S$, where $S$ is the area of triangle $A B C$. Can this estimate be improved?

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_d4ffc236376258137647g-038.jpg?height=445&width=521&top_left_y=1004&top_left_x=137)

Fig. 10.
reference_solution:
39. Since the areas of two triangles having an equal angle are in the ratio of the products of the sides enclosing this angle (see the beginning of the solution to problem 38a)), then (see Fig. 10 on p. 37, where it is assumed that $B C=A U=A V=a, C A=B W=B X=b, A B=C Y=$ $=C Z=\dot{c})$

$$
\frac{S_{A X V}}{S_{A B C}}+\frac{S_{A U V}}{S_{A B C}}=\frac{(b+c)^{2}}{b c}+\frac{a^{2}}{b c}=\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}{b c}+2
$$

and

$$
S_{A X Y}+S_{A U V}=\left(\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}{b c}+2\right) S
$$

It is logical that

$$
S_{B U Z}+S_{B W X}=\left(\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}{a c}+2\right) S
$$

and

$$
S_{C V W}+S_{C Y Z}=\left(\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}{a b}+2\right) S
$$

And since, obviously,

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{A X Y}+S_{B Z U}+S_{C V W}+S_{A U V}+S_{B W X}+S_{C Y Z} & = \\
& =S_{U V W X Y Z}+2 S_{A B C}=S_{U V W X Y Z}+2 S
\end{aligned}
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
& S_{U V W X Y Z}=\left[\left(\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}{b c}+2\right)+\left(\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}{a c}+2\right)+\right. \\
& \left.+\left(\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}}{a b}+2\right)\right] S-2 S= \\
& \quad=\left[\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}\right)\left(\frac{1}{a b}+\frac{1}{a c}+\frac{1}{b c}\right)+4\right] S
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we only need to use the fact that

$$
\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{a b} \geqslant 2, \quad \frac{b^{2}+c^{2}}{b c} \geqslant 2, \quad \frac{a^{2}+c^{2}}{b c} \geqslant 2
$$

(because, for example, $\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{a b}-2=\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}-2 a b}{a b}=\frac{(a-b)^{2}}{a b} \geqslant 0$ ) and) $\frac{c^{2}}{a b}+\frac{b^{2}}{a c}+\frac{a^{2}}{b c}=\frac{a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}}{a b c} \geqslant 3$, since

$$
\frac{a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}}{a b c}-3=\frac{a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}-3 a b c}{a b c}=
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& =\frac{(a+b+c)\left(\alpha^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}-a b-a c-b c\right)}{a b c}= \\
& =\frac{1}{2} \frac{(a+b+c)\left[\left(a^{2}+b^{2}-2 a b\right)+\left(a^{2}+c^{2}-2 a c\right)+\left(b^{2}+c^{2}-2 b c\right)\right]}{a b c}= \\
& \quad=\frac{1}{2} \frac{(a+b+c)\left[(a-b)^{2}+(a-c)^{2}+(b-c)^{2}\right]}{a b c} \geqslant 0 .
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{array}{r}
\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}\right)\left(\frac{1}{a b}+\frac{1}{a c}+\frac{1}{b c}\right)=\left(\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{a b}+\frac{a^{2}+c^{2}}{a c}+\frac{b^{2}+c^{2}}{b c}\right)+ \\
+\left(\frac{c^{2}}{a b}+\frac{b^{2}}{a c}+\frac{a^{2}}{b c}\right) \geqslant 2+2+2+3=9
\end{array}
$$

and thus,

$$
S_{U V W X Y Z}=\left[\left(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}\right)\left(\frac{1}{a b}+\frac{1}{a c}+\frac{1}{b c}\right)+4\right] S \geqslant 13 S
$$

It is obvious that if triangle $A B C$ is equilateral (i.e., $a=b=c$) - and only in this case - $S_{U V W X Y Z}=13 S$.

question:

Can the estimate contained in this problem be improved?

40. Let the points of intersection of the "main" diagonals $A D, B E$ and $C F$ of the hexagon $A B C D E F$ be denoted by $P, Q$ and $R$ (Fig. 87). In this case,

$S_{A Q B}+S_{B Q C}+S_{C R D}+S_{D R E}+S_{E P F}+S_{F P A} \leqslant$

$$
\leqslant S_{A B C D E F}-S_{P Q R} \leqslant S
$$

therefore, the area of at least one of these six triangles $\leqslant \frac{1}{6} S$ (where equality is possible only if $\triangle P Q R$ "collapses" into a point). Suppose, for example, $S_{D R E} \leqslant \frac{1}{6} S$; in this case, if $C F \| D E$, then $S_{D E C}=S_{D E R} \leqslant \frac{1}{6} S$, and if $C F \forall D E$ and, say,
