Fig. 87. point $C$ is closer to the line $D E$ than $F$, then $S_{C D E}<S_{D R E} \leqslant \frac{1}{6} S$.

The inequality in the problem cannot be improved, since the areas of all triangles cut off by the diagonals $A C, \quad B D, \ldots, E A$ from a regular hexagon $A B C D E F$ of area $S$ are equal to $\frac{1}{6} S$.

1) Since $a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3} \geqslant 3 a b c$ for all $a, b, c \geqslant 0$, then

$$
\frac{x+y+z}{3} \geqslant \sqrt[3]{x y z}
$$

for all $x, y, z \geqslant 0$ (to prove this, it is sufficient to set $a^{3}=x, b^{3}=y, c^{3}=z$ in the original inequality) — in this form, the last inequality (relating the arithmetic mean and the geometric mean of three numbers) is used in the solution of one of the following problems.

question:
44*. Let $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ be two triangles with sides $a_{1}, b_{1}, c_{1}$, and $a_{2}, b_{2}, c_{2}$, respectively, and let $a=\sqrt{\frac{a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}}{2}}$, $b=\sqrt{\frac{b_{1}^{2}+b_{2}^{2}}{2}}, \quad c=\sqrt{\frac{c_{1}^{2}+c_{2}^{2}}{2}} . \quad$ Prove that there exists a triangle $T$ with sides $a, b, c$ and that, if $S_{1}, S_{2}$ and $S$ are the areas of triangles $T_{1}, T_{2}$ and $T$, then

a) $S \geqslant \sqrt{S_{1} S_{2}}$

b) $S \geqslant \frac{1}{2}\left(S_{1}+S_{2}\right)$.

In what cases do the inequalities in parts a) and b) become equalities?
reference_solution:
44. In solving this problem, the algebraic inequality (err ${ }^{1}$ )

$$
(A X+B Y)^{2} \leqslant\left(A^{2}+B^{2}\right)\left(X^{2}+Y^{2}\right)
$$

(where $A, B, X, Y$ are positive numbers), the validity of which follows from the fact that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(A^{2}+B^{2}\right)\left(X^{2}+Y^{2}\right)- & (A X+B Y)^{2}= \\
& =A^{2} Y^{2}+B^{2} X^{2}-2 A B X Y=(A Y-B X)^{2} \geqslant 0
\end{aligned}
$$

from this proof of the inequality (*), it follows that equality in it is achieved only when $A Y=B X$, or when $A: B=X: Y$.

Notice now that if, say, $a$ is the largest of the segments $a, b, c$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
& a^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left(a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}\right)<\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(b_{1}+c_{1}\right)^{2}+\left(b_{2}+c_{2}\right)^{2}\right]= \\
& \quad=\frac{1}{2}\left[\left(b_{1}^{2}+b_{2}^{2}\right)+\left(c_{1}^{2}+c_{2}^{2}\right)\right]+\left(b_{1} c_{1}+b_{2} c_{2}\right) \leqslant \\
& \leqslant b^{2}+c^{2}+\sqrt{\left(b_{1}^{2}+b_{2}^{2}\right)\left(c_{1}^{2}+c_{2}^{2}\right)}=b^{2}+c^{2}+(\sqrt{2} b)(\sqrt{2} c)=(b+c)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

(here the inequality (*) is used, where $A=b_{1}$, $B=b_{2}, X=c_{1}, Y=c_{2}$), and thus, $a<b+c$, i.e., the triangle $T$ with sides $a, b$, and $c$ exists.

Further, let $h_{1}, h_{2}$, and $h$ be the heights of the triangles $T_{1}, T_{2}$, and $T$, dropped, say, on the sides of length $a_{1}, a_{2}$, and $a$; in this case, obviously,

$$
S_{1}=\frac{1}{2} a_{1} h_{1}, \quad S_{2}=\frac{1}{2} a_{2} h_{2} \quad \text { and } \quad S=\frac{1}{2} a h
$$

1) Compare problems 289 and following in the book by D. O. Shklyarsky, N. N. Chentsov, and I. M. Yaglom, mentioned in the footnote on page 39.

On the other hand, applying the cosine theorem to the triangles $T \equiv A B C, T_{1} \equiv A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$, and $T_{2} \equiv A_{2} B_{2} C_{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
& a c \cos B=\frac{a^{2}+c^{2}-b^{2}}{2}=\frac{\left(a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}\right)+\left(c_{1}^{2}+c_{2}^{2}\right)-\left(b_{1}^{2}+b_{2}^{2}\right)}{4}= \\
& =\frac{a_{1}^{2}+c_{1}^{2}-b_{1}^{2}}{4}+\frac{a_{2}^{2}+c_{2}^{2}-b_{2}^{2}}{4}=\frac{1}{2}\left(a_{1} c_{1} \cos B_{1}+a_{2} c_{2} \cos B_{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Squaring both sides of the last equality, we get

$$
a^{2} c^{2} \cos ^{2} B=\frac{1}{4}\left(a_{1} c_{1} \cos B_{1}+a_{2} c_{2} \cos B_{2}\right)^{2}
$$

from which, using (*) again (where now we need to put $A=a_{1}$, $B=a_{2}, X=c_{1} \cos B_{1}$ and $\left.Y=c_{2} \cos B_{2}\right)$, we have

$$
a^{2} c^{2} \cos ^{2} B \leqslant \frac{1}{4}\left(a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}\right)\left(c_{1}^{2} \cos ^{2} B_{1}+c_{2}^{2} \cos ^{2} B_{2}\right)
$$

or, since $a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}=2 a^{2}$,

$$
c^{2} \cos ^{2} B \leqslant \frac{1}{2}\left(c_{1}^{2} \cos ^{2} B_{1}+c_{2}^{2} \cos ^{2} B_{2}\right)
$$

where equality holds only in the case when

$$
a_{1}: a_{2}=c_{1} \cos B_{1}: c_{2} \cos B_{2}
$$

On the other hand, $c^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\left(c_{1}^{2}+c_{2}^{2}\right)$; subtracting the last inequality from this equality (and using the fact that $1-\cos ^{2} \alpha=$ $=\sin ^{2} \alpha$ for all $\left.\alpha\right)$, we get

$$
c^{2} \sin ^{2} B \geqslant \frac{1}{2}\left(c_{1}^{2} \sin ^{2} B_{1}+c_{2}^{2} \sin ^{2} B_{2}\right)
$$

But, obviously (make a drawing!), $c \sin B=h, \quad c_{1} \sin B_{1}=h_{1}$ and $c_{2} \sin B_{2}=h_{2} ;$ thus, we have

$$
h^{2} \geqslant \frac{1}{2}\left(h_{1}^{2}+h_{2}^{2}\right)
$$

where the conditions for equality are the same as above.

Now we can proceed to solving problems b) and a) (in this exact order!).

b) Obviously (here we again use the inequality (*), as well as the fact that $\left.a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}=2 a^{2}, h_{1}^{2}+h_{2}^{2} \leqslant 2 h^{2}\right)$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
{\left[\frac{1}{2}\left(S_{1}+S_{2}\right)\right]^{2}=\left[\frac{1}{4}\left(a_{1} h_{1}+a_{2} h_{2}\right)\right]^{2} } & \leqslant\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{2}\left[\left(a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}\right)\left(h_{1}^{2}+h_{2}^{2}\right)\right] \leqslant \\
& \leqslant\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{2} 2 a^{2} \cdot 2 h^{2}=\frac{1}{4}(a h)^{2}=S^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

and thus,

$$
\frac{1}{2}\left(S_{1}+S_{2}\right) \leqslant S
$$

where equality holds only if

$$
a_{1}: a_{2}=c_{1} \cos B_{1}: c_{2} \cos B_{2}
$$

and

$$
a_{1}: \alpha_{2}=h_{1}: h_{2}=c_{1} \sin B_{1}: c_{2} \sin B_{2}
$$

i.e., if $\cos B_{1}: \cos B_{2}=\sin B_{1}: \sin B_{2}, \quad$ i.e., $\operatorname{tg} B_{1}=\operatorname{tg} B_{2}, \quad$ and $B_{1}=B_{2}$, after which our conditions take the form

$$
a_{1}: a_{2}=c_{1}: c_{2}
$$

which (together with the equality $B_{1}=B_{2}$) means the similarity of triangles $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$.
a) Since

$$
\left[\frac{1}{2}\left(S_{1}+S_{2}\right)\right]^{2}=S_{1} S_{2}+\left[\frac{1}{2}\left(S_{1}-S_{2}\right)\right]^{2} \geqslant S_{1} S_{2}
$$

it follows from the result of problem b) that

$$
S \geqslant \frac{1}{2}\left(S_{1}+S_{2}\right) \geqslant \sqrt{S_{1} S_{2}}
$$

in this case, since $S=\frac{1}{2}\left(S_{1}+S_{2}\right)$, only if triangles $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ are similar, and $\frac{1}{2}\left(S_{1}+S_{2}\right)=\sqrt{S_{1} S_{2}}$, only if $S_{1}-S_{2}=0$, i.e., if triangles $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ are equal in area, then equality in problem a) holds only if triangles $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ are similar and equal in area, i.e., if they are congruent.

reference_solution:
48. Let the rectangle $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1} D_{1}$ with sides $A_{1} B_{1}=a$ and $A_{1} D_{1}=b$ and area $S$ cut off triangles $A K L, B M N, C P Q$ and $D R T$ from an equal rectangle $A B C D$ (Fig. 101, a). Extend these four triangles to rectangles $A K L A^{\prime}, B M N B^{\prime}, C P Q C^{\prime}$ and $D R T D$ (this operation can be understood as a peculiar "folding of the corners" of the paper rectangle $A B C D$) and prove that

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_d4ffc236376258137647g-186.jpg?height=348&width=796&top_left_y=272&top_left_x=218)
a)

()

Fig. 101.

the triangles $A^{\prime} K L$, $B^{\prime} M N$, $C^{\prime} P Q$ and $D^{\prime} R T$ depicted with thin lines in Fig. 101, a do not intersect pairwise; from this it will follow that

$$
S_{\triangle A K L}+S_{\triangle B M N}+S_{\triangle C P Q}+S_{\triangle D R T} = \frac{1}{2} S
$$

Indeed, two "adjacent" triangles, say $A^{\prime} K L$ and $B^{\prime} M N$, cannot intersect because any line $l$ parallel to $A D \| B C$ that intersects the segment $L M$ of the side $A B$ of the rectangle $A B C D$ separates them from each other. If "opposite" triangles, for example $A^{\prime} K L$ and $C^{\prime} P Q$ (Fig. 101, b), have a common point $F$, then a line passing through $F$ and parallel to $A D \| B C$ intersects the hypotenuses $K L$ and $P Q$ of these triangles at points $U$ and $V$ such that $U V A_{1} D_{1} = b$.

question:
49. A raft is floating through a straight channel that is 1 unit wide and turns $90^{\circ}$ from its initial direction (see Fig. 12). Prove that if the area of the raft is $2 \sqrt{2}$ (or larger), it will definitely not be able to turn the corner and continue moving through the channel.

The estimate obtained in problem 49 is rather rough; in reality, a raft that can navigate the described channel should have a significantly smaller area than $2 \sqrt{2} (\approx 2.83)$. On the other hand, it is not difficult to provide examples of rafts that can navigate the channel described in the problem; for instance, a square raft with an area of 1 or a semicircular raft with an area of $\frac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.57$ (Fig. 12b); it is also not difficult to construct a raft with a larger area that can
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_d4ffc236376258137647g-042.jpg?height=432&width=770&top_left_y=271&top_left_x=197)

Fig. 12.

turn in our channel. American mathematician J. Hamming [53] suggested that the largest raft satisfying the conditions of the problem has an area of $\left.\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{2}{\pi}(\approx 2.31)\right)$, but this hypothesis has not yet been proven (nor disproven).
reference_solution:
49. Enclose the raft $F$, which we assume has an area $\geqslant 2 \sqrt{2}$ and has not yet reached the bend of the channel, in the smallest possible rectangle $P \equiv \Lambda_{1} B_{1} B_{2} A_{2}$,

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_d4ffc236376258137647g-186.jpg?height=518&width=396&top_left_y=1039&top_left_x=694)

Fig. 102. bounded by the banks of the channel and two segments perpendicular to the banks (Fig. 102). Since the area of the raft is $\geqslant 2 \sqrt{2}$, the area of the rectangle $P$ of width 1 is even more $>2 \sqrt{2}$; therefore, if $A$ and $B$ are the points where the sides $A_{1} A_{2}$ and $B_{1} B_{2}$ of the rectangle, which are perpendicular to the channel, touch $F$, then $A B \geqslant A_{1} B_{1} \geqslant 2 \sqrt{2}$. From this, exactly as in the solution of problem 81 below, it is established that if the raft can pass the bend of the channel, then during its movement, the segment $A B$ (and thus the entire raft) will rotate relative to its initial position by an angle $>45^{\circ}$.

Now consider the position of the raft $F$ when it has rotated exactly $45^{\circ}$; in this case, the rectangle $P$, which we assume is rigidly attached to the raft, will also rotate by $45^{\circ}$ relative to its initial position (the rectangle $P$ may, of course, extend beyond the channel during the raft's movement). At this moment, the sides of the rectangle, which initially coincided with the banks of the channel, will coincide with some lines $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ perpendicular to the bisector of the angle formed by the channel; the distance between $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ is 1.

The lines $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ cannot descend "lower" than the lines $l_{1}^{0}$ and $l_{2}^{0}$ depicted in Fig. 102, as otherwise the intersection of the strips bounded by $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ with the channel would split into two parallelograms of area $\sqrt{2}$ (recall that both the width of the channel and the distance between $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ are 1) and (consisting of one piece!) the raft would be enclosed in one of these parallelograms, i.e., its area would be even $\leqslant \sqrt{2}$. But if $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ are located "higher" than the lines $l_{1}^{0}$ and $l_{2}^{0}$, then the area of the intersection of the strip bounded by $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ with the channel differs from the area of the two parallelograms of area $\sqrt{2}$ bounded by $l_{1}^{0}$ and $l_{2}^{0}$ (they are shaded in Fig. 102) in that from the total area of the parallelograms, two "small" parallelograms $K L M N$ and $P Q R T$ are subtracted, and equal but overlapping parallelograms $K^{\prime} O M^{\prime} N^{\prime}$ and $O Q^{\prime} R^{\prime} T^{\prime}$ are added. This proves that the area of the intersection of the strip bounded by $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ (containing the rectangle $P$, and thus the raft $F$) with the channel is less than the total area of the $2 \sqrt{2}$ shaded parallelograms in Fig. 102, and therefore, even more, the area of the raft $F$ will be $<2 \sqrt{2}$!

question: 50. Prove that any triangular section of a tetrahedron (triangular pyramid) by area is smaller than at least one of its faces.
reference_solution:
50. Let us preliminarily prove that if in space there are two non-parallel lines \(a\) and \(b\), and from three consecutive points \(A_1, A_2, A_3\) on line \(a\) perpendiculars \(A_1B_1, A_2B_2, A_3B_3\) are dropped to line \(b\), then \(A_2B_2\) is less than one of the two segments \(A_1B_1\) and \(A_3B_3\). Indeed, let us draw through line \(b\) a plane \(M\) parallel to line \(a\) (Fig. 103) and let \(A_1', A_2', A_3'\) be the projections of points \(A_1, A_2, A_3\) onto plane \(M\). Based on the theorem of three perpendiculars, we conclude that \(A_1'B_1, A_2'B_2, A_3'B_3 \perp b\). Since the segment \(A_2'B_2\) is obviously less than one of the two segments \(A_1'B_1, A_3'B_3\), then the segment \(A_2B_2\) is less than one of the two segments \(A_1B_1, A_3B_3\), which was to be proved.

Now let us proceed to solving the given problem.

\(1^\circ\). Suppose in a triangular pyramid (tetrahedron) \(ABCD\) the section \(RCD\) passes through the edge \(CD\) (Fig. 104, a). In triangles \(ACD\), \(RCD\), and \(BCD\) with the common base \(CD\), the heights dropped to this side are the perpendiculars considered above. Since \(R\) lies between \(A\) and \(B\), then \(S_{RCD}\) is less than the area of one of the triangles \(ACD\) and \(BCD\).

\(2^\circ\). Suppose the section \(APR\) passes through the vertex \(A\) of the tetrahedron (Fig. 104, b). Connect \(P\) with the opposite vertex \(D\) of triangle \(BCD\). Then in the tetrahedron \(PABD\) the triangular section \(PAR\) passes through the edge \(AP\); therefore, either \(S_{PAR} < S_{PAB}\) or \(S_{PAR} < S_{APD}\). In the first case, we have \(S_{PAR} < S_{ABC}\), since \(\triangle PAB\) is a part of triangle \(ABC\); in the second case, applying to the section \(ADP\) of the tetrahedron \(ABCD\) the result from point \(1^\circ\), we find that \(S_{APD}\) is less than the area of one of the faces \(ACD\) or \(ABD\), and therefore the same holds for \(S_{P \text{d}}\). Thus, our assertion is shown for this type of triangular sections.

\(3^\circ\). Finally, consider the section \(PQR\) of the most general type (Fig. 104, c). Connect an arbitrary vertex \(P\) of triangle \(PQR\), lying on the edge \(AC\) of the tetrahedron, with the ends \(B\) and \(D\) of the opposite edge \(BD\). According to what was proved in point \(2^\circ\), \(S_{PQR}\) is less than the area of at least one face of the tetrahedron \(PABD\). But for any face of the tetrahedron \(PABD\), there is an equal or larger face of the tetrahedron \(CABD\). Indeed, the face \(ABD\) is common to these two tetrahedrons, \(\triangle PAB\) and \(\triangle PAD\) are parts of \(\triangle ABC\) and \(\triangle ADC\), respectively, and \(S_{PBD}\) is less than either \(S_{BAD}\) or \(S_{BCD}\), since \(PBD\) is a section of the tetrahedron \(ABCD\) passing through its edge. From this, the theorem follows.

question:
54. a) In a unit square $K$, there is some figure $\Phi$ (which may consist of several separate pieces). Prove that if $\Phi$ does not contain a pair of points whose distance is 0.001, then the area of $\Phi$ does not exceed 0.34.

b) Can you improve the estimate of the area of $\Phi$ given in the condition of part a)?
reference_solution:
54. a) Let's consider the sides of the square $K$ to be horizontal and vertical, and parallel shift the figure $\Phi$ by a distance of 0.001 in the direction of one of the sides of the square, say, from left to right. Since $\Phi$ does not contain points that are 0.001 units apart, the figure $\Phi'$ obtained by this shift does not intersect with $\Phi$; furthermore, both are located within a rectangle, three sides of which coincide with the sides of $K$, and the fourth is obtained by shifting the right side of $K$ by 0.001 to the right. Now, shift $\Phi$ by the same distance 0.001 in the direction forming a $60^{\circ}$ angle with the initial shift direction, say, to the right and up (Fig. 111, a, where $\boldsymbol{a}^{\prime}$ and $\boldsymbol{a}^{\prime \prime}$ are the vectors of the considered shifts). The resulting figure $\Phi^{\prime \prime}$ is contained within the square $K_{1}$ with side 1.001, obtained by shifting the right and top sides of $K$ by 0.001 outward (and even in a slightly smaller rectangle, which is not important to us); moreover, it, like $\Phi^{\prime}$, does not intersect with $\Phi$. Furthermore, $\Phi^{\prime \prime}$ does not intersect with $\Phi^{\prime}$ either. Indeed, if a point $A$ of the plane simultaneously belongs to both $\Phi^{\prime}$ and $\Phi^{\prime \prime}$, and $A^{\prime}$ and $A^{\prime \prime}$ are the points of the figure $\Phi$ that are translated to point $A$ by the first and second of the considered shifts, respectively, then $\overline{A^{\prime} A} = \boldsymbol{a}^{\prime}$ and $\overline{A^{\prime \prime} A} = \boldsymbol{a}^{\prime \prime}$; therefore, in the triangle $A A^{\prime} A^{\prime \prime}$, we have $A A^{\prime} = A A^{\prime \prime} = 0.001$ and $\angle A^{\prime} A A^{\prime \prime} = 60^{\circ}$, and thus $A^{\prime} A^{\prime \prime} = 0.001$, while the figure $\Phi$ does not contain such two points $A^{\prime}$ and $A^{\prime \prime}$ by the given condition.

Thus, the three non-overlapping figures $\Phi$, $\Phi^{\prime}$, and $\Phi^{\prime \prime}$ of the same area $s$ (since these figures are congruent) are located in the square $K_{1}$ of area $(1.001)^2$, from which it follows that

$$
s \leqslant \frac{(1.001)^2}{3} < 0.34
$$

b) Of course, the estimate of 0.34 for the area of the figure $\Phi$ obtained in part (a) is not the best possible; for example, we noted above that the figure $\Phi$ (as well as $\Phi'$ and $\Phi''$) is contained not only in the square $K_{1}$ but also in a smaller rectangle, the area of which is easy to estimate. However, such a refinement of the solution in part (a) leads only to a very minor improvement in the obtained result; therefore, we will now somewhat supplement the corresponding reasoning.

Note that our conclusion that the figures $\Phi^{\prime}$ and $\Phi^{\prime \prime}$ do not have common points remains valid for any two figures $\Phi_{1}$ and $\Phi_{2}$ obtained from $\Phi$ by parallel shifts (translations) by vectors $a_{1} = \widehat{O M}_{1}$ and $a_{2} = \widehat{O M}_{2}$, such that the vector $\bar{M}_{1} M_{2}$ (which corresponds to the shift translating $\Phi_{1}$ to $\Phi_{2}$) has a length of 0.001. However, if the lengths of the vectors $a_{1}$ and $a_{2}$ differ from 0.001, we cannot be sure that the figures $\Phi_{1}$ and $\Phi_{2}$ do not intersect with $\Phi$. Therefore, we will replace the last conclusion with a much weaker statement that at least one of these two figures has a "not too large" intersection with $\Phi$: indeed, if the area of the figure $\Phi$ is $s$, then at least one of the two (non-intersecting!) figures $\Phi_{1}$ and $\Phi_{2}$, for example, the figure $\Phi_{1}$, intersects $\Phi$ by a part with an area $\leqslant \frac{1}{2} s$. From this, it follows that the area of the union of the figures $\Phi$ and $\Phi_{1}$ does not exceed $\frac{3}{2} s$.

Now, let's return to the figures $\Phi^{\prime}$ and $\Phi^{\prime \prime}$ defined in the solution of part (a) and assume that the vectors $a^{\prime} = \overline{O M^{\prime}}$ and $a^{\prime \prime} = \widetilde{\sigma^{\prime \prime}}$ corresponding to their shifts in length and position on the plane coincide with the sides of the rhombus $O M^{\prime} M_{1} M^{\prime \prime}$ with diagonal $O M_{1}$, where $\overline{O M}_{1} = a_{1}^{\prime}$ (Fig. 111, b). Since in this case $\Phi_{1}$ is obtained from $\Phi'$ by a shift of 0.001, $\Phi^{\prime}$ does not intersect $\Phi_{1}$. Similarly, it can be shown that $\Phi^{\prime \prime}$ does not intersect $\Phi_{1}$, i.e., that $\Phi^{\prime}$ and $\Phi^{\prime \prime}$ do not intersect with the union $\Phi \cup \Phi_{1}$ of the figures $\Phi$ and $\Phi_{1}$. Thus, the total area covered by the figures $\Phi, \Phi_{1}, \Phi^{\prime}$, and $\Phi^{\prime \prime}$ is at least

$$
\frac{3}{2} s + s + s = \frac{7}{2} s
$$

However, all these figures are clearly contained within the square $\bar{K}$ with side $1 + 0.001 \sqrt{3} < 1.0018$ (and even in a slightly smaller $\bar{K}$, which, however, only slightly changes the estimate obtained below). Therefore, it follows that

$$
\frac{7}{2} s < (1.0018)^2 \quad \text{and, hence,} \quad s < \frac{2}{7} (1.0018)^2 < 0.287
$$

Note. The estimate $s < 0.287$ obtained in the solution of part (b) is also, of course, not exact; it would be desirable to improve it (or even find the exact value of inf $s$, achievable under the conditions given in the problem), which, however, seems to be quite difficult.

The formulations of problems 56 a) and b) are quite close to each other; however, the gap between the numbers $\frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{1}{9}$ mentioned in these problems is very significant. One can, however, assume that such a large gap is not due to the essence of the matter but rather to our inability to fill this gap. The fact is that the result of problem a) is clearly precise, i.e., it cannot be improved (why?). However, the result of problem b) is not definitively precise. Concrete examples of systems of squares covering a given unit square while satisfying the conditions of the problem, as well as some general considerations, suggest that from each such system of squares, one can select non-overlapping squares whose total area is not less than $\frac{1}{4}$

(while this latter estimate cannot be improved!); however, no one has been able to prove this conjecture. It has only been proven (by several different methods, see A. S. Sokolov [57], R. Rado [58], V. A. Zalgaller [59]), that Rado's conjecture is true for systems of equal squares with mutually parallel sides, but it has not been possible to determine how significant the assumption of the equality of the covering squares is. (in other words, we first select from the system $\mathscr{K}$ a subsystem $\mathscr{L}$ with the largest possible area $s(\mathscr{L})$, and then we find the system $\mathscr{K}$ for which the value $\max s(\mathscr{L})$ is the smallest $\left.{ }^{3}\right)$):

reference_solution:
56. a) First, we will exclude from consideration all those segments of the covering that are entirely covered by one or several of these segments. After this, we will enumerate all the remaining segments in a certain order as follows. We will assume that our original segment \( O \) of length 1 is positioned horizontally. We will call the first one of the remaining covering segments the one that covers the left end of segment \( O \) (note that such a segment can only be one, since if there were two, the one with the left end further to the left could be discarded). Next, we will call the second one the segment of the covering that contains the right end of the first segment. We claim that such a segment can also be only one. Indeed, let there be two such segments: \( O_{1} \) and \( O_{2} \), and let the left end of \( O_{1} \) be to the left of the left end of \( O_{2} \). In this case, if the right end of \( O_{1} \) is to the right of the right end of \( O_{2} \), then segment \( O_{2} \) is entirely contained within \( O_{1} \) (and therefore was previously excluded from consideration); if the right end of \( O_{1} \) is to the left of the right end of \( O_{2} \), then segment \( O_{1} \) is entirely covered by segment \( O_{2} \) and the first segment (make the corresponding drawings!).

Similarly, there is a unique segment that covers the right end of the second segment; we will call this segment the third, and so on. Note that no two segments, both with even or both with odd numbers, intersect: indeed, if, for example, the first and third segments intersected, they would cover the entire second segment, which, by assumption, cannot be. Further, the total length of all the remaining covering segments is certainly not less than 1 (the length of segment \( O \)). From this it follows that either the total length of all the "odd" segments is not less than \( \frac{1}{2} \), or the total length of all the "even" segments is not less than \( \frac{1}{2} \). And this shows that there exist non-intersecting covering segments whose total length is not less than \( \frac{1}{2} \).

An example of a segment \( O \), covered in a "checkerboard pattern" by an even number of "white" and "black" (or "even" and "odd") segments of equal length, only touching at their ends (or overlapping by arbitrarily small parts), shows that the estimate obtained in this problem cannot be improved.

b) We will choose the largest of the covering squares (denote it \( K_{1} \)) and discard all squares intersecting with it (not exceeding its size); it is clear that if the area of square \( K_{1} \) was \( k_{1}^{2} \), then the area not covered by \( K_{1} \) and covered by the discarded squares will be \( \leqslant 8 k_{1}^{2} \) (since it represents a "strip" surrounding the contour of \( K_{1} \) with a width \( \leqslant k_{1} \)). Then we will choose the largest of the remaining squares and again discard all squares intersecting with the considered square \( K_{2} \). Continuing in this manner, we will select a system of non-overlapping squares, the total area of which is not less than eight times the area of the discarded squares - from which the statement of the problem follows.

Remark. The method proposed in the solution to part b) of the problem can also be used in the ("one-dimensional") problem a), where it is also possible to start with the largest of the covering segments \( O_{i} \) of the considered segment \( O \); then, discarding all segments intersecting the selected segment \( O_{1} \), take the largest of the remaining ones, and so on. In this way, we will obtain systems of non-overlapping segments with a total length \( \geqslant \frac{1}{3} \). However, while in problem a) the estimate obtained in this way can easily be strengthened and brought to the best possible result, in the case of problem b) the situation turns out to be quite different (see p. \( 45-47 \)).

question: 58. In a rectangle of area 5 sq. units, nine polygons of area 1 are placed; prove that among them there are two polygons, the area of the common part of which is not less than $\frac{1}{9}$.
reference_solution:
58. Let the areas of all pairwise intersections of the considered polygons $M_{1}, M_{2}, \ldots, M_{9}$ be less than $\frac{1}{9}$; then the area of the part of polygon $M_{2}$ not covered by polygon $M_{1}$ is greater than $1-\frac{1}{9}=\frac{8}{9}$; the area of the part of polygon $M_{3}$ not covered by either polygon $M_{1}$ or polygon $M_{2}$ is greater than $1-\frac{1}{9}-\frac{1}{9}=\frac{7}{9}$; the area of the part of polygon $M_{3}$ not covered by either polygon $M_{1}$, polygon $M_{2}$, or polygon $M_{3}$ is greater than $1-\frac{1}{9}-\frac{1}{9}-\frac{1}{9}=\frac{6}{9}$; ...; the area of the part of polygon $M_{9}$ not covered by any of the polygons $M_{1}, M_{2}, \ldots, M_{8}$ is greater than $1-\underbrace{\frac{1}{9}-\frac{1}{9}-\ldots-\frac{1}{9}}_{8 \text { times }}=\frac{1}{9}$

1) If the number of points were 101, they could coincide with the endpoints $A B$ and with (99) division points of $A B$; however, for $n>101$, the stated assertion is undoubtedly true (why?).

Therefore, the area of the union of polygons $M_{1}, M_{2}, \ldots, M_{9}$ in this case should be greater than

$$
1+\frac{8}{9}+\frac{7}{9}+\frac{6}{9}+\ldots+\frac{1}{9}=5
$$

which, however, contradicts the assumption that all polygons are located within a rectangle of area 5.

The obtained contradiction proves the assertion of the problem.

question:
61. Prove that

a) every convex polygon of area 1 can be enclosed in a parallelogram of area 2;

b) a triangle of area 1 cannot be enclosed in a parallelogram of area $<2$.

$62^{*}$. Prove that

a) every convex polygon of area 1 can be enclosed in a triangle of area 2;

b) a parallelogram of area 1 cannot be enclosed in a triangle of area $<2$.

It is noteworthy that there is a peculiar "parallelism" between problems 61 and 62, which can be formulated as follows:

Prove that every convex polygon M of area 1 can be enclosed in

\begin{gathered}
\text { parallelogram } \\
\text { triangle }
\end{gathered}

of area 2; however, if M is a

## triangle

parallelogram

ecto

of area 1, then it cannot be enclosed in

parallelogram of area $<2$.

triangle
reference_solution:
61. a) Let $AB$ be a side of a convex polygon $M$ of area $1$, and $C$ be the point of the polygon $M$ farthest from $AB$ (or one of such points if $M$ has a side parallel to $AB$). The line $AC$ divides the polygon $M$ into two parts $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ (Fig. 119; one of these parts may not exist). If $D_{1}$ and $D_{2}$ are the points of the polygons $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$, respectively, farthest from the line $AC$ (or some of such points), $l \parallel AB$ passes through the point $C$, and $l_{1} \parallel AC$ and $l_{2} \parallel AC$ pass through the points $D_{1}$ and $D_{2}$, then the lines $AB, l, l_{1}$, and $l_{2}$ form a certain parallelogram $\Pi$ enclosing $M$ inside.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_d4ffc236376258137647g-228.jpg?height=287&width=471&top_left_y=855&top_left_x=699)

Fig. 119.

Since the polygons $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ are convex, $M_{1}$ contains $\triangle AD_{1}C$, and $M_{2}$ contains $\triangle AD_{2}C$. The line $AC$ divides the parallelogram $\Pi$ into two parallelograms $\Pi_{1}$ and $\Pi_{2}$, such that

$$
S_{AD_{1}C} = \frac{1}{2} S_{\Pi_{1}} \quad \text{and} \quad S_{AD_{2}C} = \frac{1}{2} S_{\Pi_{2}}
$$

From this, it follows that

$$
S_{\Pi} = S_{\Pi_{1}} + S_{\Pi_{2}} = 2 S_{AD_{1}C} + 2 S_{AD_{2}C} \leq 2 S_{M_{1}} + 2 S_{M_{2}} = 2 S_{M} = 2
$$

which is what we needed to prove (if $S_{\Pi} < 2$, we can increase this parallelogram so that it continues to enclose $M$ inside itself).

b) Let $\Pi$ be a parallelogram containing the triangle $ABC$ of area 1. Reduce $\Pi$ by sliding its sides parallel to themselves until they "touch" the vertices of the triangle; let $A$ be the vertex through which two sides of the resulting parallelogram $\Pi \equiv APQR$ (Fig. 120) pass. Draw a line $l \parallel PQ \parallel AR$ through $C$; denote the points of intersection of $l$ with $AB$ and $AP$ by $D$ and $E$. Then, obviously,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& S_{CBD} \leq S_{CBE} = \frac{1}{2} S_{CQPE} \\
& S_{CAD} \leq S_{CAE} = \frac{1}{2} S_{CRAE}
\end{aligned}
$$

from which the desired result follows:

$$
S_{ABC} = S_{CBD} + S_{CAD} \leq \frac{1}{2} S_{CQPE} + \frac{1}{2} S_{CRAE} = \frac{1}{2} S_{APQR}
$$

i.e.,

$$
S_{APQR} \geq 2 S_{ABC} = 2
$$

(if $C$ is an interior point of the side $QR$, then $S_{APQR} = 2$ only if $B$ coincides with $P$).

63. Let $M$ be a convex polygon of area $S$ and $l$ be an arbitrary line. Prove that

a) in $M$ one can inscribe a triangle, one side of which is parallel to $l$ and the area of which is $\geqslant \frac{3}{8} S$;

b) the polygon $M$ and the line $l$ can be chosen such that in $M$ one cannot inscribe a triangle, one side of which is parallel to $l$ and the area of which is $>\frac{3}{8} S$.

Let the distance between $l_{1}$ and $l_{2}$ be denoted by $d$, and draw three more lines parallel to $l$: $l_{1}^{\prime}, l_{0}$, and $l_{2}^{\prime}$, dividing our "strip" into four narrower "strips" of width $\frac{d}{4}$. Let $p$ be the side of $M$ passing through $P$ (it could be one of two such sides); similarly, $q, r$, and $s$ are the sides of the polygon passing through $Q, R$, and $S$, respectively. The area of the trapezoid $T_{1}$,

Ashkinuze, Ideas and Methods of Affine and Projective Geometry, Part 1, Affine Geometry, Moscow, Uchpedgiz, 1962).
bounded by the lines $l_{0}, l_{1}, p$, and $q$, is obviously $P Q \cdot \frac{d}{2}$; similarly, the area of the trapezoid $T_{2}$, bounded by $l_{0}, l_{2}, r$, and $s$, is $R S \cdot \frac{d}{2}$. Since the union of trapezoids $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ contains $M$ (possibly coinciding with $M$), we have

$$
S_{M} \leqslant S_{T_{1}} + S_{T_{2}} = P Q \cdot \frac{d}{2} + R S \cdot \frac{d}{2} = (P Q + R S) \cdot \frac{d}{2}
$$

Now consider $\triangle A R S$ and $\triangle B P Q$, inscribed in the polygon $M$. Clearly, $S_{A R S} = \frac{1}{2} R S \cdot \frac{3}{4} d ; S_{B P Q} = \frac{1}{2} P Q \cdot \frac{3}{4} d$, therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
& S_{A R S} + S_{B P Q} = (R S + P Q) \cdot \frac{3}{8} d = \\
& = \frac{3}{4}(P Q + R S) \cdot \frac{d}{2} \geqslant \frac{3}{4} S_{M}
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus,

or $S_{A R S} \geqslant \frac{3}{8} S_{M} \quad$ or $\quad S_{B P Q} \geqslant \frac{3}{8} S_{M}$,

which proves the statement of the problem.

b) Let $M$ be a regular hexagon $A B C D E F$, and $l$ be parallel to the side $A B$ of the hexagon (Fig. 124). Further, let $P Q R$ be the inscribed triangle of the largest possible area in $M$, one side of which, $P Q$, is parallel to $A B$. If $P$ and $Q$ lie on the sides $A F$ and $B C$ of the hexagon, respectively, then, obviously, the vertex $R$ must belong to $D E$. Let the length of the side of the hexagon be 1 and the distance $A P = B Q$ be denoted by $a$. In this case, it is easy to calculate that

$$
\hat{P} Q = A B + P G + Q H = 1 + \frac{a}{2} + \frac{a}{2} = 1 + a
$$

and

$$
h_{P Q} = R S - A G = \sqrt{3} - \frac{a \sqrt{3}}{2} = (2 - a) \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}
$$

thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{P Q R} = \frac{1}{2}(1 + a)(2 - a) \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(2 + a - a^2) = \\
= \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\left[2 \frac{1}{4} - \left(a - \frac{1}{2}\right)^2\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, for $S_{P Q R}$ to be the largest possible, it is necessary that $a - \frac{1}{2} = 0, a = \frac{1}{2}$; then

$$
S_{P Q R} = \frac{9}{4} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} = \frac{9 \sqrt{3}}{16}
$$

The area of the entire hexagon $M$ is

$$
6 S_{O A B} = 6 \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} = \frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{2}
$$

($O$ is the center of the hexagon); hence, the largest inscribed triangle in $A B C D E F$, one side of which is parallel to $A B$, has an area equal to $\frac{3}{8} S_{A B C D E F}$, which is what we needed to prove.

question:
65. In the same circle $K$, a convex polygon $M=A_{1} A_{2} \ldots A_{n}$ and a convex polygon $M^{\prime}=A_{1}^{\prime} A_{2}^{\prime} \ldots A_{n}^{\prime}$ are inscribed, the vertices of which are the midpoints of the arcs subtended by the sides of the $n$-gon $M$ (Fig. 23, b). Prove that if $P$ and $S$, respectively $P^{\prime}$ and $S^{\prime}$, are the perimeter and area of the polygons $M$ and $M^{\prime}$, then:
a) $P^{\prime} \geqslant P$

b) $S^{\prime} \geqslant S$

with equality in both cases holding only for a regular $n$-gon $M$.

The theorem of problem 65 suggests an important result concerning convex $n$-gons. It is clear that if the polygon $M$ of this problem is irregular, then the polygon $M^{\prime}$ is "more regular" than the polygon $M$. The latter statement means the following: if $M$ has one largest side of length $a$ and one smallest side of length $b<a$ (note that these sides correspond to the largest and smallest arcs subtended by the sides of $M$!), then the largest side $a^{\prime}$ of the polygon $M^{\prime}$ will be less than $a$, and its smallest side $b^{\prime}$ will be greater than $b$, so that

$$
a^{\prime}-b^{\prime}<a-b
$$

i.e., the "spread" between the side lengths will decrease. If, for example, $M$ has several sides of the same maximum length $a$, then, of course, it may happen that the largest side of $M^{\prime}$ will have the same length $a$ (this will be the case if $M$ has two adjacent sides of length $a$); however, in this case, the number of sides of length $a$ will be less in the polygon $M^{\prime}$ than in $M$ (and also the number of sides having the smallest length $b$, if $M$ had several such sides, will be less in $M^{\prime}$ than in $M$). Therefore, if we repeatedly apply the construction used in problem 65, i.e., from the polygon $M^{\prime}$ we move to the polygon $M^{\prime \prime}$, the vertices of which are the midpoints of the arcs of the circle subtended by the sides of $M^{\prime}$; then from $M^{\prime \prime}$ using the same method we move to a new polygon $M^{\prime \prime \prime}$, and so on, we will obtain a sequence

$$
M \rightarrow M^{\prime} \rightarrow M^{\prime \prime} \rightarrow M^{\prime \prime \prime} \rightarrow \ldots
$$

of "more regular" polygons inscribed in our circle (in the sense that the difference between the lengths of the largest and smallest side of the polygon will continuously decrease $\left.{ }^{1}\right)$ ), and the perimeters and areas of these polygons will monotonically increase. These considerations suggest (but do not prove!) the conclusion that among all $n$-gons inscribed in a given circle, the regular $n$-gon has the largest perimeter and area (see problem 71 below).
reference_solution:
65. Since $\triangle O A_{1} A_{2}$, formed by the center $O$ of the circle $K$ with radius 1 and two points $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$ on it, such that $\angle A_{1} O A_{2}=2 \alpha$ (see Fig. 23,6 on p. 58), obviously has the base $A_{1} A_{2}=$ $=2 \sin \alpha_{1}$ and area $S_{O A_{1} A_{2}}=\frac{1}{2} \sin 2 \alpha_{1}$, the perimeter $P$ and area $S$ of the convex $n$-gon $M$ inscribed in the unit circle $K$, whose sides correspond to the central angles $2 \alpha_{1}, 2 \alpha_{2}, \ldots$ $\ldots, 2 \alpha_{n}$, are (we assume here that the center of the circle is inside $M$)

$$
P=-2\left(\sin \alpha_{1}+\sin \alpha_{2}+\ldots+\sin \alpha_{n}\right)
$$

and

$$
S=\frac{1}{2}\left(\sin 2 \alpha_{1}+\sin 2 \alpha_{2}+\ldots+\sin 2 \alpha_{n}\right)
$$

Thus, problems a) and b) reduce to proving the inequalities

a) $\sin \alpha_{1}+\sin \alpha_{2}+\ldots+\sin \alpha_{n} \leqslant$

$$
\leqslant \sin \frac{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}{2}+\sin \frac{\alpha_{2}+\alpha_{3}}{2}+\ldots+\sin \frac{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{n}}{2}
$$

respectively

b) $\sin 2 \alpha_{1}+\sin 2 \alpha_{2}+\ldots+\sin 2 \alpha_{n} \leqslant \sin \left(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}\right)+$

$$
+\sin \left(\alpha_{2}+\alpha_{3}\right)+\ldots+\sin \left(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{n}\right)
$$

where $0<\alpha_{i}<90^{\circ}, i=1,2, \ldots, n$ and $\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+\ldots+\alpha_{n}=180^{\circ}$.

But, for example.

$$
\begin{gathered}
2\left[\sin \left(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}\right)+\sin \left(\alpha_{2}+\alpha_{3}\right)+\ldots+\sin \left(\alpha_{n}+\alpha_{1}\right)\right]- \\
-2\left(\sin 2 \alpha_{1}+\sin 2 \alpha_{2}+\ldots+\sin 2 \alpha_{n}\right)= \\
=\left[2 \sin \left(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}\right)-\left(\sin 2 \alpha_{1}+\sin 2 \alpha_{2}\right)\right]+ \\
+\left[2 \sin \left(\alpha_{2}+\alpha_{3}\right)-\left(\sin 2 \alpha_{2}+\sin 2 \alpha_{3}\right)\right]+\ldots \\
\ldots+\left[2 \sin \left(\alpha_{n}+\alpha_{1}\right)-\left(\sin 2 \alpha_{n}+\sin 2 \alpha_{1}\right)\right]= \\
=\left[2 \sin \left(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}\right)-2 \sin \left(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}\right) \cos \left(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}\right)\right]+ \\
+\left[2 \sin \left(\alpha_{2}+\alpha_{3}\right)-2\left(\sin \left(\alpha_{2}+\alpha_{3}\right) \cos \left(\alpha_{2}-\alpha_{3}\right)\right]+\ldots\right. \\
\ldots+\left[2 \sin \left(\alpha_{n}+\alpha_{1}\right)-2 \sin \left(\alpha_{n}+\alpha_{1}\right) \cos \left(\alpha_{n}-\alpha_{1}\right)\right]= \\
=2 \sin \left(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}\right)\left[1-\cos \left(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}\right)\right]+2 \sin \left(\alpha_{2}+\alpha_{3}\right)\left[1-\cos \left(\alpha_{2}-\alpha_{3}\right)\right]+\ldots \\
\ldots+2 \sin \left(\alpha_{n}+\alpha_{1}\right)\left[1-\cos \left(\alpha_{n}-\alpha_{1}\right)\right] \geqslant 0
\end{gathered}
$$

where equality holds if and only if $\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}, \alpha_{2}=\alpha_{3}, \ldots, \alpha_{n}=\alpha_{1}$, i.e., if $\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{2}=\ldots=\alpha_{n}$, and the $n$-gon $M$ is regular.

The inequality a) is proved in the same way.

question:
67. a) Two points $A$ and $B$ in a plane, the distance between which is 1, are connected by a convex broken line $A P_{1} \ldots P_{n} B$ (i.e., such a broken line that the polygon $A P_{1} P_{2} \ldots P_{n} B$ is convex). Prove that if the sum of the exterior angles of the broken line at points $P_{1}, P_{2}, \ldots, P_{n}$ is $\alpha < 180^{\circ}$, then the length of the broken line does not exceed $1: \cos \frac{\alpha}{2}$.

b) Find the convex polygon with a side of length $a$ and the sum of the exterior angles at the vertices not adjacent to this side equal to $120^{\circ}$, which has the largest area.
reference_solution:
67. a) First of all, note that if the considered broken line consists of only two segments \( A P \) and \( P B \) (Fig. 129, a), then the theorem is valid. Indeed, extend the line \( A P \) beyond point \( P \) and on the extension, lay off the segment \( P Q = P B \). Since \(\triangle B P Q\) is isosceles, \(\angle B Q A = \frac{180^{\circ} - \angle B P Q}{2} = \frac{180^{\circ} - \alpha}{2}\); therefore, point \( Q \) lies on the arc of the circle constructed on segment \( A B \) that subtends the angle \(\frac{180^{\circ} - \alpha}{2}\). The central angle corresponding to arc \( A B \) of this circle is \(180^{\circ} - \alpha\); since the chord \( A B = 1 \), it follows that the radius of the circle is \(\frac{1}{2 \cos \frac{\alpha}{2}}\). But \( A Q = A P + P B \) does not exceed the diameter of this circle; therefore,

\[
A P + P B \leqslant \frac{1}{\cos \frac{\alpha}{2}}
\]

which is what we needed to prove. In this case, \( A P + P B = \frac{1}{\cos \frac{\alpha}{2}} \) only if triangle \( A P B \) is isosceles.

Now let's prove the theorem by mathematical induction. Assume that our statement is true for all \( n \)-segment broken lines, and we will prove that in this case it will also be true for an \((n+1)\)-segment broken line \( A P_{1} P_{2} \ldots P_{n} B \). Extend the sides \( A P_{1} \) and \( P_{3} P_{2} \) of the convex polygon \( A P_{1} P_{2} \ldots P_{n} B \) until they intersect at point \( P \) (Fig. 128, ). Since the sum of the exterior angles of the broken line at \( P_{1} \) and at \( P_{2} \) is less than \( 180^{\circ} \), point \( P \) will lie on the extension of \( A P_{1} \) beyond point \( P_{1} \). Further, the exterior angle \( Q P P_{2} \) of triangle \( P_{1} P P_{2} \) is equal to the sum of the exterior angles \( P P_{1} P_{2} \) and \( P P_{2} P_{1} \) of the polygon \( A P_{1} P_{2} \ldots P_{n} B \); from this it follows that the sum of the exterior angles of the \( n \)-segment broken line \( A P P_{3} P_{4} \ldots P_{n} B \) at \( P, P_{3}, P_{4}, \ldots, P_{n} \) will be equal to the sum \(\alpha\) of the exterior angles of the \((n+1)\)-segment broken line \( A P_{1} P_{2} \ldots P_{n} B \). Since we assume that the theorem has already been proven for all \( n \)-segment broken lines, the length of the broken line \( A P P_{3} P_{4} \ldots P_{n} B \) does not exceed \(\frac{1}{\cos \frac{\alpha}{2}}\). But the length of the broken line \( A P_{1} P_{2} \ldots P_{n} B \) is obviously less than the length of the broken line \( A P P_{3} \ldots P_{n} B \) (since \( P_{1} P_{2} \) is a side of the polygon).

The area of a convex polygon with side \( A B = a \) and a given sum of exterior angles at vertices other than \( A \) and \( B \) equal to \( 120^{\circ} \), is greater than \(\frac{a^{2} \operatorname{tg} \frac{120^{\circ}}{2}}{4} = \frac{a^{2} \sqrt{3}}{4}\), is proven similarly to the solution of part a).

question:
70**. a) Prove that among all convex quadrilaterals with given angles and a given perimeter, the one with the largest area is the quadrilateral in which a circle can be inscribed.

b) Prove that among all convex $n$-gons with given angles and a given perimeter, the one with the largest area is the $n$-gon in which a circle can be inscribed.

The formulations of problems 69 and 70 a) are very similar to each other. This similarity becomes even more noticeable if we recall that all quadrilaterals have the same sum of angles, which is $360^{\circ}$, so that problems 69 and 70 a) can be stated as follows:

a) Among all quadrilaterals with given sides (and a given sum of angles, equal to $360^{\circ}$), the one with the largest area is the quadrilateral that can be inscribed in a circle.

b) Among all quadrilaterals with given angles and a given sum of sides, the one with the largest area is the quadrilateral in which a circle can be inscribed.

The analogy between problems 69 and 70 a) is not accidental and has deep foundations, the explanation of which, however, would take us too far.

The generalization of the result of problem 69, analogous to the statement of problem 70 b) and arising when the quadrilateral is replaced by an arbitrary $n$-gon, also holds; however, the simplest proof of this proposition relies on the (general) isoperimetric theorem (see problems 76 and 77 and the related text; see, for example, the book [27] or $\$ 5$ of the book [29]).

reference_solution:
71. a) If an n-sided polygon \( M \) inscribed in a circle \( S \) is not regular, then it must have a side that is smaller than the side \( a \) of the regular n-sided polygon \( M_{0} \) inscribed in \( S \). Furthermore, we can also assume that \( M \) has a side larger than \( a \): indeed, this is not the case only if \( M \) is entirely inscribed in an arc of \( S \) that is less than \(\frac{1}{n}\) of \( S \); but then \( M \) is contained within the segment cut off from the circle bounded by \( S \) by a side of \( M_{0} \), and in this case, it is sufficient to reflect this segment symmetrically about the corresponding side of \( M_{0} \) to verify the inequality \( S_{M} < S_{A B C} \); indeed, from Fig. 136, it is immediately clear that point \( B_{1} \) is closer to the midpoint of the arc \( A B C \) of \( S_{0} \) than point \( B \), and thus, \(\triangle A B_{1} C\) has a greater height than \(\triangle A B C\). Therefore, from the polygon \( M \), we transition to a polygon \( M_{1} \), one of whose sides will already be equal to \( a \); in this case, \( S_{M_{1}} > S_{M} \).

Furthermore, if \( M_{1} \) differs from \( M_{0} \), then we transform it in the described manner into a new polygon \( M_{2} \), which has more sides equal to \( a \) than \( M_{1} \) and such that \( S_{M_{2}} > S_{M_{1}} \). By performing these transformations several times, we will arrive at the polygon \( M_{0} \), and in the process of transforming the polygons, their areas will only increase; therefore, \( S_{M_{0}} > S_{M} \).

b) The solution to the problem is almost identical to the solution of part a); the only difference lies in proving that the perimeter of the polygon increases when \(\triangle A B C\) is replaced by \(\triangle A B_{1} C\) (see Fig. 136). On the extensions of \( A B \) and \( A B_{1} \), we lay off segments \( R D = B C \) and \( B_{1} D_{1} = B_{1} C \) (the corresponding constructions are reproduced on Fig. 136 with dashed lines). Since \(\angle A B C\) and \(\angle A B_{1} C\) are external angles of the isosceles triangles \( D B C \) and \( D_{1} B_{1} C \), we have

\[
\angle A D C = \angle A D_{1} C = \frac{1}{2} \angle A B C \left( = \frac{1}{2} \angle A B_{1} C \right)
\]

therefore, points \( D \) and \( D_{1} \) belong to the arc of the circle constructed on the segment \( A C \) as a chord, which contains \(\frac{1}{2} \angle A B C\), and with the arrangement of the sides of \(\triangle A B C\) and \(\triangle A B_{1} C\) as shown in Fig. 136, the chord \( A D_{1} \) will be closer to the center \( S_{0} \) of this arc than the chord \( A D \), from which it follows that

\[
A B_{1} + B_{1} C = A D_{1} > A D = A B + B C
\]

question:
73. Let $R$ and $r$ be the radii of the circumscribed and inscribed circles of a convex $n$-gon (see Fig. 24, a and b). Prove that

$$
\frac{R}{r} \geqslant \sec \frac{180^{\circ}}{n}
$$

In which case is the ratio $\frac{R}{r}$ exactly equal to $\sec \frac{180^{\circ}}{n}$?

In the case $n=3$, from the theorem of problem 73, it follows that the radii $R$ and $r$ of the circumscribed and inscribed circles of an arbitrary triangle

$$
\frac{R}{r} \geqslant \sec \frac{180^{\circ}}{3}=\sec 60^{\circ}=2, \quad \text { i.e. } \quad R \geqslant 2 r
$$

thus, in this case, it reduces to the well-known relationship between the radii of the two main circles associated with a triangle (see, for example, problem 94 a) from the book [4] and many other problems in the last section of this book).
reference_solution:
73. From the formulas (see p. 65)

$$
2 n R \sin \frac{180^{\circ}}{n} \geqslant P \quad \text { and } \quad P \geqslant 2 n r \operatorname{tg} \frac{180^{\circ}}{n}
$$

where $P$ is the perimeter of the $n$-sided polygon $M$, it directly follows that

$$
2 n R \sin \frac{180^{\circ}}{n} \geqslant 2 n r \operatorname{tg} \frac{180^{\circ}}{n}
$$

i.e.

$$
\frac{R}{r} \geqslant \left(\operatorname{tg} \frac{180^{\circ}}{n}\right):\left(\sin \frac{180^{\circ}}{n}\right)=\sec \frac{180^{\circ}}{n}
$$

(where, obviously, equality holds only in the case of a regular $n$-sided polygon $M$).

question:
76. Prove that a circle has a greater area than any convex polygon with the same perimeter.

The result of problem 76 makes the following (famous!) "isoperimetric theorem for convex figures" highly plausible: among all plane convex figures of a given perimeter ${}^{1}$), the circle has the largest area—indeed, by the theorem of problem 76, the area of the circle is greater than the area of any convex polygon with the same perimeter, and any convex figure $F$ can be replaced by a convex polygon close to it (for example, inscribed in $F$). However, the reasoning provided cannot serve as a proof of the "isoperimetric theorem for convex figures" (at least because in this reasoning we do not specify the meaning of the phrase "replace a figure with another, close to it," which deprives us of any possibility to discuss how close the areas and perimeters of "close" figures are); therefore, readers interested in this general theorem will have to refer to other literature (see, for example, books [27], [29], [30] or the article [1]).
reference_solution:
76. We have already noted several times that for a regular

$$
\frac{P}{S^{2}}=4 n \operatorname{tg} \frac{180^{\circ}}{n}
$$

(see p. 67), and for an $n$-sided polygon that is not regular,

$$
\frac{P^{2}}{S}>4 n \operatorname{tg} \frac{180^{\circ}}{n}
$$

On the other hand, for a circle with area $S=\pi r^{2}$ and perimeter (circumference) $P=2 \pi r$, it is clear that

$$
\frac{P^{2}}{S}=\frac{4 \pi^{2} r^{2}}{\pi r^{2}}=4 \pi
$$

However, since (see, for example, pp. 64-65) the number $n \operatorname{tg} \frac{180^{\circ}}{n}$ is equal to the area $S$ of a regular $n$-sided polygon $m$ circumscribed around a circle of unit radius, and this is equal to the area of the circle itself, then $4 n \operatorname{tg} \frac{180^{\circ}}{n}>4 \pi$, from which it follows that for a circle the ratio $\frac{P^{2}}{S}$ is less than for a polygon.

question: 80. Let $P$ be the perimeter of a convex polyhedron $M$, i.e., the sum of the lengths of all its edges, and $D$ be the diameter of $M$. Prove that $P > 3D$.
reference_solution: 80. Let $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$ be two farthest vertices of $M$; $A_{1} A_{2}=D$ is the diameter of $M$ (see problem 78). Draw planes perpendicular to $A_{1} A_{2}$ through all the vertices of the polyhedron; it is clear that the "outermost" of these will be the planes $\pi_{1}$ and $\pi_{2}$, passing through $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$ (if $M$ contained a point $B$ located, say, on the other side of $\pi_{2}$ from $A_{1}$, then $A_{1} B > A_{1} A_{2} = D$). The planes drawn will divide the surface of $M$ into a series of layers. Each of these layers consists of at least three pieces of faces (some of which may be entire faces), separated from each other by segments of the edges of $M$ (which may be entire edges); it is clear that in each layer there will be no more than three such edge segments leading from one of our planes to the next plane. Since the length of such an edge segment is not less than the distance between the planes, the sum of the lengths of all "transverse" (i.e., not parallel to the drawn planes) edges of $M$ is not less than three times the distance between the outermost planes, i.e., $\geqslant 3 D$; equality here is impossible (why?).

question:
103. Let $K_p$, $K_{v}$, and $T p$ be a circle, a square, and an equilateral triangle of diameter 1. Prove that:

a) $\delta(1, K_p)=\delta(2, K_p)=1 ; \delta(3, K_p)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(\approx 0.86) ;$ $\delta(4, K_p)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\approx 0.71) ; \delta(5, K_p)=\frac{1}{4} \sqrt{10-2 \sqrt{5}}(\approx 0.59) ;$ $\delta(6, K_p)=\delta(7, K_p)=\frac{1}{2}(=0.5)$ (in other words, in this problem it is required to prove that a circle of diameter 1 cannot be divided into two parts, the diameter of each of which is $\delta(3, K_p)\left(=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$. However, as for the estimates (!!), they turn out to be exact, as shown by the following problem.
reference_solution:
103. a) This problem is about dividing a circle $Kp$ of unit diameter into $n$ "possibly smaller" parts $F_{1}, \ldots, F_{n}$, where the phrase "possibly smaller" has the following precise meaning: it is required that the diameter of the largest (by diameter) of the parts be as small as possible (i.e., we are looking for the value of $\min \max F_{i}$). We will consider different values of $n$.

$1^{\circ} . n=1$. The equality $\delta(1, Kp)=1$ is obvious: since $\delta(1, F)=1$ for all $F$.

$2^{\circ} . n=2$. It is clear that if the circle $Kp$ is divided into two parts $F_{1}$ and $F_{2}$, then the boundary circle $Okr$ is also divided into two parts $f_{1}$ and $f_{2}$. (If the entire circle $Okr$ belongs to one of the parts $F_{1}$ or $F_{2}$ of the circle $Kp$, then the diameter of the corresponding part of $Kp$ will be 1.) Let $A$ be one of the points of contact of the segments $f_{1}$ and $f_{2}$ of the circle $Okr$ (each of which can consist of many parts), and $B$ be the point diametrically opposite to $A$. Clearly, the part of the circle $Okr$ that contains point $B$ has a diameter of 1; therefore,

$$
\delta(2, Kp)=1 \quad(=\delta(1, Kp))
$$

$3^{\circ} . n=3$. If the circle $Kp$ is divided into three parts $F_{1}, F_{2}$, and $F_{3}$, then the boundary circle $Okr$ is also divided into three parts $f_{1}, f_{2}$, and $f_{3}$. (Here, too, we can ignore the possibility that one of the parts $F_{1}, F_{2}$, and $F_{3}$ of the circle $Kp$ does not contain any points of $Okr$.) In this case, the (arc) length of at least one of the parts $f_{1}, f_{2}$, and $f_{3}$ of the circle $Okr$ (each of which can consist of many arcs) will be $\geqslant 120^{\circ}$; but in such a case, this part of $Okr$ will necessarily contain points that are at an arc distance $\geqslant 120^{\circ}$ from each other, i.e., such points that the chord connecting them spans an arc $\geqslant 120^{\circ}$, and thus the chord itself is $\geqslant \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ (since $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \sin 60^{\circ}$ is the length of the chord of the circle $Kp$ that spans an arc of $120^{\circ}$). It is clear that the circle $Kp$ can be divided into three parts with a diameter of $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ (Fig. $183, a$); therefore,

$$
\delta(3, Kp)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}
$$

$4^{\circ} . n=4, 5$ or 6. Just as above, we conclude that if the circle $Kp$ is divided into four, five, or six parts, then at least one of the corresponding parts $f_{1}, f_{2}, \ldots$ of the circle $Okr$ will have an (arc) length $\geqslant 90^{\circ}\left(=\frac{360^{\circ}}{4}\right)$, respectively $\geqslant 72^{\circ}\left(=\frac{360^{\circ}}{5}\right)$, and $\geqslant 60^{\circ}\left(=\frac{360^{\circ}}{6}\right)$. But in such a case, this part of the circle $Okr$ will contain points that are at an angular distance $\geqslant 90^{\circ}$, respectively $\geqslant 72^{\circ}$, and $\geqslant 60^{\circ}$ from each other, i.e., points that are at a distance $\geqslant \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$, respectively $\geqslant \frac{1}{4} \sqrt{10-2 \sqrt{5}}$, and $\geqslant \frac{1}{2}$ (the values $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}=\sin 45^{\circ}, \frac{1}{4} \sqrt{10-2 \sqrt{5}}=\sin 36^{\circ}$, and $\frac{1}{2}=\sin 30^{\circ}$ are the lengths of the chords of the circle $Okr$ that span arcs of $90^{\circ}$, $72^{\circ}$, and $60^{\circ}$). It is clear that the circle $Kp$ can be divided into four parts with a diameter of $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$, into five parts with a diameter of $\frac{1}{4} \sqrt{10-2 \sqrt{5}}$, and into six parts with a diameter of $\frac{1}{2}$ (Fig. $183, \sigma-$); therefore, $\delta(4, Kp)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} ; \quad \delta(5, Kp)=\frac{1}{4} \sqrt{10-2 \sqrt{5}}, \quad \delta(6, Kp)=\frac{1}{2}$.

104*. Prove that any plane figure of diameter 1 can be divided

a) into 3 parts of diameter $\leqslant \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(\approx 0.86)$;

b) into 4 parts of diameter $\leqslant \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\approx 0.71)$;

c) into 7 parts of diameter $\leqslant \frac{1}{2}(=0.5)$.

Thus, we have

$$
\delta_{2}(2)=1, \quad \delta_{2}(3)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \quad \delta_{2}(4)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \quad \text { and } \quad \delta_{2}(7)=\frac{1}{2}
$$

However, in addition to these results, the trivial equality

$$
\delta_{1}(n)=\frac{1}{n}, \quad n=1,2,3, \ldots
$$

where the index 1 below indicates that this concerns the partitioning of one-dimensional figures, i.e., segments, and the almost equally obvious relation ${ }^{1}$

$$
\delta_{k}(n)=1 \quad \text { for } \quad n \leqslant k,
$$

no exact values of the quantities $\delta(n)$ are known.

The value of $\delta_{2}(3)$ was essentially found by K. Borsuk [91] in 1932-1933 (see also D. Gale [86]); the values of $\delta_{2}(4)$ and $\delta_{2}(7)$ were calculated in 1956 by the German geometer H. Lenz [96], who thoroughly studied the possible values of $\delta_{2}(n)$ for small $n$. The fact that in all equalities (!!!) we have $\delta_{2}(n)=\delta_{2}(n, K p)^{2}$ does not provide us with any significant information: it was previously conjectured that $\delta_{2}(n)=\delta(n, K p)$ for all $n$ (and even that $\delta_{3}(n)=\delta_{3}(n, B)$, where $B$ is a ball, and that this pattern extends to multidimensional spaces), but these hypotheses were not confirmed. We do not even know whether there is any value of $n$ different from $1,2,3,4$, and 7 such that $\delta_{2}(n)=\delta(n, K p)$; in any case, this equality does not hold for $n=5$ and $n=6$ (try to prove this yourself!).

From the solutions to the stereometric variant of Borsuk's problem by H. Hadwiger [94] and B. Grünbaum [87], the estimates follow: $\delta_{3}(4) \leqslant \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\delta_{3}(5) \leqslant \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$. It is also known that for $n \geqslant k+1$ the equality $\delta_{k}(k+1)=\delta\left(k+1, B^{(k)}\right)$ holds, where $B^{(k)}$ is a $k$-dimensional ball, however, apart from the fact that we do not yet have sufficient arguments to justify this hypothesis, this conjecture itself does not provide much information, as the values of $\delta\left(k+1, B^{(k)}\right)$ are unknown for any $k>3^{1}$.

1) This follows, for example, from the existence in $k$-dimensional Euclidean space of a so-called regular simplex (analogous to a regular triangle in the plane or a regular tetrahedron in space), having $k+1$ vertices, each pair of which is at a distance of 1 from each other (see the footnote on p. 32).

) Note also that the equalities $\delta_{2}(1)=\delta(1, K p), \quad \delta_{2}(2)=\delta(2, K p), \quad \delta_{2}(3)=\delta(3, K p), \delta_{2}(4)=\delta(4, K p)$, and $\delta_{2}(7)=\delta(7, K p)$ have a completely different nature: indeed, $\delta_{2}(1)=\delta(1, F)$ for any (planar) figure $F$ (and therefore, of course, for a circle!); $\delta_{2}(2)=\delta(2, F)$ for a series of planar figures $F$, including the circle $K p$ (and the regular triangle $T p$); at the same time, the equalities $\delta_{2}(3)=\delta(3, F), \quad \delta_{2}(4)=\delta(4, F)$, and $\delta_{2}(7)=\delta(7, F)$ hold only for $F \equiv K p$ (prove this!).

For other unsolved problems related to Borsuk's problem, see V. G. Boltyansky and I. Ts. Gohberg [17] and B. Grünbaum [19].

In conclusion, let us note that the main problems of this series, 103 and 104 (and many of the preceding ones), also have the familiar "minimax" form. Indeed, the number $\delta(n, F)$, for example, can be described as follows. For each fixed partition $\mathscr{R}_{n}$ of the figure $F$ into $n$ parts $f_{1}, f_{2}, \ldots, f_{n}$, we define the number

$$
\delta\left(\mathscr{R}_{n}\right)=\max _{i} d\left(f_{i}\right) ; \quad i=1,2,3, \ldots \text { or } n
$$

where $d(f)$ is the diameter of the figure $f$; further, considering all possible partitions of $F$ into $n$ parts, we seek the quantity

$$
\delta(n, F)=\min _{\mathscr{R}_{n}} d\left(\mathscr{R}_{n}\right)=\min _{\mathscr{R}_{n}} \max _{i} d\left(f_{i}\right)
$$

Finally, the characteristic $\delta_{2}(n)$ of the set $\mathfrak{M}_{2}(1)=\mathfrak{M}_{2}$ of all planar (two-dimensional) figures $F$ of diameter 1 is defined as follows:

$$
\delta(n)=\max _{F \in \mathbb{M}_{2}} \delta(n, F)=\max _{F} \min _{\mathscr{R}_{n}} \max _{i} d\left(f_{i}\right)
$$

Similarly, the problems related to Lebesgue's problem (see problems 93-100) also have a minimax form. For example, the radius of the circumscribed circle $K$ of a figure $F$ can be defined as the radius $R$ of the smallest circle $K=K(0, \rho)$ (where $O$ is the center of $K$, and $\rho$ is its radius) containing $F$ inside itself:

$$
R=\min \rho, \text { where } K(O, \rho) \supset F
$$

(here $\supset$ is the set-theoretic inclusion sign of one set in another; the notation $K \supset F$ reads: "the figure $F$, understood as a set of points, is entirely contained within the circle $K$"). After this, the radius $R_{0}\left(=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\right)$ of the Jung circle is defined as

$$
R_{0}=\max _{F \in M_{2}(1)} R=\max _{F} \min _{K} \rho ; \quad K(O, \rho) \supset F, \quad F \in \mathfrak{M}_{2}(1),
$$

where $\mathfrak{M}_{2}(1)$ is the set of all possible planar "two-dimensional" figures of diameter $1^{2}$).

question:
108. Let a circle $K$ of radius 1 and smaller circles $K_{1}, K_{2}$, $K_{3}, \ldots$ be given. Prove that

a) the smallest number of circles $K_{1}, K_{2}, \ldots$, needed to cover circle $K$, is always $\geqslant 3$;

b) if the radii of circles $K_{1}, K_{2}, \ldots$ are less than $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, then this number will be $\geqslant 4$

c) if the radii of circles $K_{1}, K_{2}, \ldots$ are less than $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$, then this number is $\geqslant 5$.

Can the estimates in parts a) - c) be improved?
reference_solution:
108. a) Since the circle $K$ cannot be divided into two parts with a diameter less than 1 (see problem 103 a) above), it cannot be covered by two circles $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ with diameters $<1$, otherwise the diameter of the part of $K$ covered by $K_{1}$ and the diameter of the "remainder" (entirely covered by the circle $K_{2}$) would both be less than 1.

b) - c) The results of these problems follow from the fact that $\delta(3, K p)=$ $=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, respectively $\delta(4, K p)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$ (see the same problem 103 a)).

The fact that the estimates of problems b), c) cannot be improved is shown by Fig. 51, a, b (p. 111); for problem a) this is obvious (since $K$ can even be covered by a single circle of diameter 1).

question:
116. Let $m$ be a convex polygon, and $M$ (the larger) a convex polygon obtained from $m$ by shifting all sides of $m$ outward by a distance of 1 (Fig. 56). Prove that

$$
n(1, M) \geqslant v(2, m)
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_d4ffc236376258137647g-117.jpg?height=334&width=396&top_left_y=286&top_left_x=193)

Fig. 56.
reference_solution:
116. Consider $n=n(1 ; N)$ non-intersecting circles $k_{1}$, $k_{2}, \ldots, k_{n}$ of radius 1, located inside the polygon $M$; it is not difficult to see that the centers of all these circles will belong to the polygon $m$ (why?). Now replace these $n$ circles with concentric circles $K_{1}, K_{2}, \ldots, K_{n}$ of radius 2. We claim that the new $n$ circles will completely cover $m$. Indeed, if there were a point $A \in m$ not covered by any of the $n$ "large" circles $K_{1}, K_{2}, \ldots, K_{n}$, then the centers of all these circles would be at a distance $\geqslant 2$ from $A$ and the number of circles filling $M$, $k_{1}, k_{2}, \ldots, k_{n}$, could be increased by adding a circle $k_{n+1}$ of radius 1 with center $A$, obviously not extending beyond the boundaries of $M$ and not intersecting any of the preceding $n$ circles, which, however, contradicts the definition of the number $n(1, M)$. Thus, the polygon $m$ can be covered by $n$ circles of radius 2, from which, by the definition of the number $v(2, n)$, it follows that

$$
n \geqslant v(2, m)
$$

question:
5. a) Given a quadruple of positive numbers ( $a, b$, $c, d$ ). From it, a new quadruple ( $a b, b c, c d, d a$ ) is obtained according to the following rule: each number is multiplied by the next one, the fourth by the first. From the new quadruple, a third one is obtained by the same rule, and so on. Prove that in the sequence of quadruples obtained, ( $a, b, c, d$ ) will never appear again, except in the case when $a=b=c=d=1$.

b) Given an arbitrary set of 1s and -1s of length $2^{k}$. From it, a new set is obtained according to the following rule: each number is multiplied by the next one; the last $2^{k}$-th number is multiplied by the first. The same operation is performed on the new set of 1s and -1s, and so on. Prove that eventually a set consisting entirely of ones will be obtained.
reference_solution:
5. a) Suppose the quadruple ( $a, b, c, d$ ) has reappeared.

First, let's prove that in this case $a b c d=1$.

Let $a b c d=p$. Then the product of the numbers in the second quadruple is $p^{2}$, in the third $-p^{4}$, in the fourth $p^{8}, \ldots$ Clearly, if $p \neq 1$, the sequence of products will not have two identical numbers, and consequently, all resulting quadruples will be different. Therefore, $p=1$.

Now consider the second quadruple: $a b, b c, c d, d a$; since $a b c d=1$, it is easy to verify that the fourth quadruple will be $b^{2} c^{2}, c^{2} d^{2}, d^{2} a^{2}, a^{2} b^{2}$. Thus, the fourth quadruple is obtained from the second by squaring and rearranging. Similarly, the sixth quadruple is obtained from the fourth, the eighth from the sixth, and so on.

If not all numbers in the second quadruple are equal to one, then the largest of them is greater than one. Then the largest number in the $2n$-th quadruple will increase without bound as $n$ grows, which contradicts the fact that they periodically repeat.

Thus, $a b=b c=c d=d a=1$, and from this it is easy to conclude that $a=b=c=d=1$.

b) For $n=1$, the statement of the problem is clearly true.

Assume that it is true for $n=k$, and we will prove its validity for $n=k+1$.

Write the first three lines:

$$
\begin{gathered}
x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, x_{1}, \ldots, x_{2 k+1} \\
x_{1} x_{2}, x_{2} x_{3}, x_{3} x_{1}, \ldots, x_{2 k+1} x_{1}, \\
x_{1} x_{3}, x_{2} x_{4}, x_{3} x_{5}, \ldots, x_{2 k+1} x_{2}
\end{gathered}
$$

It is easy to see that the numbers in the odd positions and the numbers in the even positions form the lines $x_{1}, x_{3}, \ldots, x_{2 k+1-1}$ and $x_{2}, x_{4}, \ldots, x_{2 k+1}$, which transform "every other step" as required by the condition. Since by the induction hypothesis a line of length $2^{k}$ eventually transforms into a line of all ones, the original line of length $2^{k+1}$ will also transform into a line of all ones.
$\nabla$ It can be proven that from a string $x$ of length $m=2^{\circ} r$, where $r$ is odd, a string of all ones will be obtained if and only if $x$ consists of $r$ identical blocks of length $2^{\text {k }}$, i.e., has a period of $2^{k}$ (see [5], problem 134).

question: 7. In the cells of an $m \times n$ table, some numbers are written. It is allowed to simultaneously change the sign of all numbers in a certain column or a certain row. Prove that by repeatedly performing this operation, the given table can be transformed into one where the sums of the numbers in any column and any row are non-negative.
reference_solution: 7. Among all the tables that can be obtained from the given variables by changing signs in rows and columns, we take the one for which the sum $\Sigma$ is maximal. Such a table T exists, since the number of ways to place signs before the numbers in the $m \times n$ table is finite - $2^{m n}$ (the number of ways to change signs in rows and columns is even smaller: $2^{m+n-1}$ ). In table $\mathrm{T}$, the sum of the numbers in each row and each column is non-negative. Indeed, if the sum of the numbers in some row (or column) of table T were negative, then by changing the sign in this row (column), we would obtain a table with a greater sum $\sum$ of all numbers, which contradicts the choice of table T.

question:
11. Prove that for any three infinite sequences of natural numbers

$$
\begin{aligned}
& a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, \ldots \\
& b_{1}, \quad b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}, \ldots \\
& c_{1}, \quad c_{2}, \ldots, c_{n}, \ldots
\end{aligned}
$$

there exist indices $p$ and $q$ such that $a_{p} \geqslant a_{q}, b_{p} \geqslant b_{q}$, $c_{p} \geqslant c_{q}$.
reference_solution:
11. Since the numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, \ldots$ are natural, there exists a sequence of indices $i_{1}, i_{2}, \ldots, i_{n}, \ldots$, such that $a_{i_{1}} \leqslant a_{i_{2}} \leqslant \ldots \leqslant a_{i_{n}} \leqslant \cdots \quad\left(a_{l_{1}}\right.$ is the smallest number in the sequence $a_{n}, a_{l_{2}}$ is the smallest of the following, and so on). Similarly, from the sequence of indices $i_{1}, i_{2}, \ldots, i_{n}, \ldots$, we can select a sequence $j_{1}, j_{2}, \ldots, j_{n}, \ldots$, for which

$$
b_{l_{1}} \leqslant b_{l_{2}} \leqslant \ldots \leqslant b_{l_{n}} \leqslant \ldots
$$

It is clear that the sequence $a_{f_{1}}, a_{f_{2}}, \ldots, a_{I_{n}}, \ldots$ remains non-decreasing. Now it remains to select a non-decreasing sequence $c_{k_{1}}, c_{k_{2}}, \ldots, c_{k_{n}}, \ldots$ from the sequence $c_{f_{1}}, c_{l_{2}}, \ldots, c_{l_{n}}, \ldots$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
& a_{k_{1}} \leqslant a_{k_{2}} \leqslant \ldots \leqslant a_{k_{n}} \leqslant \ldots \\
& b_{k_{1}} \leqslant b_{k_{2}} \leqslant \ldots \leqslant b_{k_{n}} \leqslant \ldots \\
& c_{k_{1}} \leqslant c_{k_{2}} \leqslant \ldots \leqslant c_{k_{n}} \leqslant \ldots
\end{aligned}
$$

from which the statement of the problem follows.

$\nabla$ In the solution, we used the fact that in any (even infinite) set of natural numbers, there is a smallest number. This fact seems obvious; it is equivalent to the principle of mathematical induction (PI).

Thus, these figures cannot cover the rectangle with an area of 456, and therefore, there exists a circle with a diameter of 1 that does not intersect any of the squares.

question: 13. On the extensions of sides $A B, B C, C D$ and $D A$ of a convex quadrilateral $A B C D$, points $A^{\prime}$, $B^{\prime}, C^{\prime}, D^{\prime}$ are taken such that $\overrightarrow{B B^{\prime}}=\overrightarrow{A B}, \overrightarrow{C C^{\prime}}=\overrightarrow{B C}, \overrightarrow{D D^{\prime}}=\overrightarrow{C D}$ and $\overrightarrow{A A^{\prime}}=\overrightarrow{D A}$. Prove that the area of quadrilateral $A^{\prime} B^{\prime} C^{\prime} D^{\prime}$ is 5 times the area of quadrilateral $A B C D$.
reference_solution:
13. The median divides the area of the triangle in half. Therefore (Fig. 27) $S_{A B C}=S_{C B B^{\prime}}=S_{C B^{\prime} C^{\prime}}$. From this it follows that $S_{B B^{\prime} C^{\prime}}=2 S_{A B C}$.

Similarly, the equalities $S_{C C^{\prime} D^{\prime}}=2 S_{B C D^{\prime}}$; $S_{D D^{\prime} A}=2 S_{C D A^{\prime}}$; $S_{A A^{\prime} B^{\prime}}=2 S_{D A B^{\prime}}$ are proved.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-111.jpg?height=578&width=463&top_left_y=565&top_left_x=104)

Fig. 27

Fig. 28

Adding these 4 equalities, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& S_{B B^{\prime} C^{\prime}}+S_{C C^{\prime} D^{\prime}}+S_{D D^{\prime} A^{\prime}}+S_{A A^{\prime} B^{\prime}}= \\
&=2\left(S_{A B C}+S_{B C D}+S_{C D A}+S_{D A B}\right)=4 S
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $S_{A^{\prime} B^{\prime} C^{\prime} D^{\prime}}=4 S+S=5 S$.

question: 15. Given positive integers $a_{0}, a_{1}$, $a_{2}, \ldots, a_{99}, a_{100}$. It is known that $a_{1}>a_{0}, a_{2}=3 a_{1}-$ $-2 a_{0}, \quad a_{3}=3 a_{2}-2 a_{1}, \ldots, a_{100}=3 a_{99}-2 a_{98}$. Prove that $a_{100}>2^{99}$.
reference_solution:
15. By the condition $a_{1}-a_{0} \geqslant 1$. Further, $a_{2}-a_{1}=2\left(a_{1}-a_{0}\right)$, $a_{3}-a_{2}=2\left(a_{2}-a_{1}\right), \ldots, a_{100}-a_{99}=2\left(a_{99}-a_{98}\right) . \quad$ Multiplying these 99 equalities, both sides of which are positive, and canceling the common factors $a_{2}-a_{1}, a_{3}-a_{2}, \ldots, a_{99}-a_{98}$ on both sides, we get

$$
a_{100}=a_{99}+2^{99}\left(a_{1}-a_{0}\right) \geqslant 2^{99}
$$

$\nabla$ A more precise estimate by induction $a_{k} \geqslant 2^{k}, a_{k+1}-a_{k} \geqslant$ $\geqslant 2^{k}(k=1,2, \ldots)$ shows that $a_{100} \geqslant 2^{100}$.

question: 16. Prove that there do not exist integers $a$, $b, c, d$ such that the expression $a x^{3}+b x^{2}+c x+d$ equals 1 when $x=19$ and equals 2 when $x=62$.
reference_solution:
16. Let $P(x)=a x^{3}+b x^{2}+c x+d$. The difference

$$
P(62)-P(19)=a\left(62^{3}-19^{3}\right)+b\left(62^{2}-19^{2}\right)+c(62-19)
$$

is divisible by 43 and cannot equal 1.

$\nabla$ In general, for any polynomial $P(x)$ with integer coefficients, the difference $P\left(x_{1}\right)-P\left(x_{2}\right)$, where $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ are different integers, is divisible by $x_{1}-x_{2}$ (P6).

question:
19. $a, b, c, d$ - positive numbers, the product of which is equal to 1. Prove that

$$
a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2}+a b+a c+a d+b c+b d+c d \geqslant 10
$$
reference_solution:
19. From the inequality $x^{2}+y^{2} \geqslant 2 x y$ it follows that

$$
\begin{gathered}
\left(a^{2}+b^{2}\right)+\left(c^{2}+d^{2}\right) \geqslant 2(a b+c d) \geqslant 4 \sqrt{a b c d} \geqslant 4 \\
a b+c d \geqslant 2, \quad b c+a d \geqslant 2, \quad a c+b d \geqslant 2
\end{gathered}
$$

$\nabla$ Using the general theorem on the arithmetic and geometric means, the problem can be solved in another way, and it can also be proven that for any $n$ positive numbers with a product of 1, the sum of their squares is not less than $n$, and the sum of $n(n-1) / 2$ of their pairwise
