Fig. 29 products is not less than $n(\boldsymbol{n}-$ $-1) / 2$.

question: 22. From the midpoint $M$ of the base $AC$ of an isosceles triangle $ABC$, a perpendicular $MH$ is dropped to the side $BC$. Point $P$ is the midpoint of the segment $MH$. Prove that $AH \perp BP$.
reference_solution: 22. Drop the altitude $A D$ in $\triangle A B C$ (Fig. 30). Then in $\triangle A D C$, the segment $M H$ will be the midline, i.e., $D H=C H$. The right triangles $B H M$ and $A D C$ are similar, since $\angle D A C=$ $=90^{\circ}-\angle C=\angle H B M$, and after rotating one of them by $90^{\circ}$, the corresponding sides will become parallel; at this point, the corresponding medians $B P$ and $A H$ will also become parallel, which means that before the rotation, $A H \perp B P$.

question: 24. $x, y, z$ - arbitrary pairwise distinct integers. Prove that $(x-y)^{5}+(y-z)^{5}+$ $+(z-x)^{5}$ is divisible by $5(y-z)(z-x)(x-y)$.
reference_solution:
24. The quotient is equal to $x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}-2 x y-2 y z-2 x z$. To verify the required identity, it is convenient to set $x-y=u_{0}$, $y-z=v$, then $z-x=-(u+v)$, and prove the identity

$$
(u+v)^{5}=u^{5}+v^{5}+5 u v(u+v)\left(u^{2}+u v+v^{2}\right)
$$

using the binomial formula (P6):

$$
(u+v)^{5}=u^{5}+5 u^{4} v+10 u^{3} v^{2}+10 u^{2} v^{3}+5 u v^{4}+v^{5}
$$

question: 25. For the numbers $a_{0}, a_{1}, \ldots, a_{n}$, it is known that $a_{0}=$ $=a_{n}=0$ and that $a_{k-1}-2 a_{k}+a_{k+1} \geqslant 0$ for all $k$ $(k=1,2, \ldots, n-1)$. Prove that all $a_{k}$ are non-positive.
reference_solution:
25. Solving this problem is aided by Fig. 31: the broken line with vertices at points ( $k, a_{k}$ ) is "convex" because $a_{k+1}-a_{k} \geqslant a_{k}-a_{k-1}$ (i.e., the slope of each subsequent segment is greater than the previous one), so the entire line, except for the ends, lies below the base $0 k$

Suppose that for some $m \geqslant 1$ it will be $a_{m-1} \leqslant 0$, $a_{m}>0$. Then $a_{n}-a_{n-1} \geqslant a_{n-1}-$ $-a_{n-2} \geqslant \ldots \geqslant a_{m+1}-a_{m} \geqslant a_{m}-$ $-a_{m-1}>0$ and therefore $a_{n}>a_{n-1}>$ $>\ldots>a_{m}>0$, which contradicts the condition $a_{n}=0$.

question:
26. Given positive numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{m}$, $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$, such that $a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{m}=b_{1}+$ $+b_{2}+\ldots+b_{n}$. Prove that in an empty table with $m$ rows and $n$ columns, no more than $m+n-1$ positive numbers can be placed so that the sum of the numbers in the $i$-th row equals $a_{i}$, and the sum of the numbers in the $k$-th column equals $b_{k}$.

Third All-Russian Olympiad, 1963 (Moscow)

| Class |  |  |  |  |  |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 8 | 27 | 28 | $29 a$ | 30 | $31 a$ |
| 9 | 32 | 33 | 34 | 316 | 28 |
| 10 | 35 | 36 | 37 | 296 | 28 |
| 11 | 38 | 28 | 39 | 40 | 296 |
reference_solution:
26. Consider the table $m \times n$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-114.jpg?height=306&width=419&top_left_y=772&top_left_x=635)

Fig. 31

and let's reason by induction, assuming that the statement is already proven for tables with a smaller sum $m+n$. For a $1 \times 1$ table, the statement is obvious. Choose the smallest of the $m+n$ given numbers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{m}, b_{1}$, $b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$ - let it be $a_{1}$. Place $a_{1}$ in the top-left corner, then cut off the first row; it remains to solve the problem for the $(m-1) \times n$ table and the set of numbers $a_{2}, \ldots, a_{m}, b_{1}-a_{1}$, $b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$, which we can do by the induction hypothesis.

Another, typically "olympiad" solution. Draw a segment of length $d=a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{m}=b_{1}+b_{2}+\ldots+b_{n}$ and divide it in two ways: into $m$ "red" segments of lengths $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{m}$ and $n$ "blue" segments of lengths $b_{1}, b_{2}, \ldots, b_{n}$. There will be $(n-1)+(m-1)$ division points and thus $m+n-1$ small segments. It remains to write the length of each of these segments (the intersection of some red $a_{i}$ and some blue $b_{j}$) in the corresponding cell of the table (located at the intersection of the $i$-th row and the $j$-th column),

question: 27. Out of five given circles, any four pass through one point. Prove that there exists a point through which all five circles pass.
reference_solution:
27. Let the 1st, 2nd, 4th, and 5th circles pass through point $A$; the 1st, 3rd, 4th, and 5th circles through point $B$; and the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 5th circles through point $C$.

We see that all three points $A, B$, and $C$ cannot be distinct, as they lie on the 4th and 5th circles, and two circles have no more than two points of intersection. Therefore, some two of the points $A, B$, and $C$ must coincide (P9).

Suppose, for example, that $A=B$. Then all the circles pass through point $A$.

question:
29. a) Each diagonal of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ divides its area in half. Prove that $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.
b) Given a convex hexagon $ABCDEF$. It is known that each of the diagonals $AD, BE$, and $CF$ divides its area in half. Prove that these diagonals intersect at one point.
reference_solution:
29. a) Let $O$ be the point of intersection of the diagonals of quadrilateral $ABCD$. Since triangles $ABD$ and $BCD$ have equal areas and a common base $BD$, their heights dropped from vertices $A$ and $C$ are equal, i.e., points $A$ and $C$ are equidistant from $BD$, hence

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-115.jpg?height=306&width=418&top_left_y=1143&top_left_x=139)

Fig. 32 $AO = OC$. The same can be proven for $BO = OD$.

Thus, the diagonals of quadrilateral $ABCD$ are bisected by their point of intersection, which means that $ABCD$ is a parallelogram.

b) First solution. Suppose that in some convex hexagon $ABCDEF$, the diagonals connecting opposite vertices divide the area in half and at the same time do not intersect at a single point. Then their points of intersection $P, Q$, and $R$ are the vertices of a triangle lying inside the hexagon (Fig. 32).

The areas of quadrilaterals $ABCD$ and $BCDE$ are equal, so the areas of triangles $ABP$ and $EPD$ are also equal, since

$$
S_{ABP} = S_{ABCD} - S_{BCDP} = S_{BCDE} - S_{BCDP} = S_{EPD}
$$

Similarly, we obtain that

$$
S_{BCR} = S_{EFR} \text{ and } S_{AQF} = S_{CQD^{*}}
$$

From the equality of the areas of the triangles, the following proportions are derived:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& AP \cdot BP = EP \cdot DP \\
& CQ \cdot DQ = AQ \cdot FQ \\
& ER \cdot FR = BR \cdot CR
\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying these equalities, we get

$$
AP \cdot BP \cdot CQ \cdot DQ \cdot ER \cdot FR = AQ \cdot BR \cdot CR \cdot DP \cdot EP \cdot FQ
$$

But this is impossible because $AP > AQ, \quad BP > BR, \quad CQ > CR, \quad DQ > DP, \quad ER > EP, \quad FR > FQ$, so the product on the right is less than the product on the left. The contradiction obtained shows that the diagonals $AD, BE$, and $CF$ intersect at a single point (i.e., that $FQ = QR = RP = 0$).

Second solution. This solution is based on the use of a geometric transformation - homothety. Since the areas of quadrilaterals $ABCD$ and $BCDE$ are equal, the areas of triangles $ABD$ and $BDE$ are also equal (they are smaller than the areas of the corresponding quadrilaterals by $S_{BCD}$). These triangles have a common base $BD$. From the equality of the areas, it follows that the heights dropped from vertices $A$ and $E$ to $BD$ are equal, i.e., points $A$ and $E$ are equidistant from $BD$. Therefore, $AE \parallel BD$. Similarly, it is established that $CE \parallel BF$ and $DF \parallel AC$. Thus, triangles $BDF$ and $ACE$ are similar.

Let $P$ be the point of intersection of the diagonals $AD$ and $BE$. Consider a homothety with center at point $P$ and coefficient $PE : PB$. Under this homothety, point $B$ will map to point $E$, and point $D$ will map to point $A$, the line $DF$ will map to the line $AC$, and $BF$ will map to $EC$.

Since $F$ is the point of intersection of lines $DF$ and $BF$, it will map to the point of intersection of lines $AC$ and $EC$, i.e., point $C$. Therefore, points $F, P$, and $C$ lie on the same line, which means that the diagonals $AD, BE$, and $CF$ intersect at point $P$.

question: 30. Natural numbers $a$ and $b$ are coprime. Prove that the greatest common divisor of the numbers $a+b$ and $a^{2}+b^{2}$ is 1 or 2.
reference_solution:
30. If $a^{2}+b^{2}$ and $a+b$ are divisible by $d$, then $(a+b)^{2}-$ $-\left(a^{2}+b^{2}\right)=2 a b$ is also divisible by $d$. Therefore, $2 a^{2}=2 a(a+b)$ $-2 a b$ and $2 b^{2}=2 b(a+b)-2 a b$ are divisible by $d$.

But if $a$ and $b$ are coprime, then $a^{2}$ and $b^{2}$ are also coprime, so $2 a^{2}$ and $2 b^{2}$ cannot both be divisible by any $d>2$. (Here the fundamental theorem of arithmetic is used, see P2.)

question:
31. Two points $A$ and $B$ are fixed on a circle, while point $M$ runs through the entire circle. From the midpoint $K$ of segment $M B$, a perpendicular $K P$ is dropped onto the line $M A$.

a) Prove that all lines $K P$ pass through one point,

b) Find the set of points $P$.
reference_solution:
31. a) Let $C$ be the point diametrically opposite to point $A$. The angle $A M C=$ is right. Since $M K=K B$ and $P K$ is a median, the line $P K$ intersects the segment $B C$ at its midpoint: $B H=H C$. Therefore, all lines $P K$ pass through the point $H$, the midpoint of segment $B C$.

b) From a) it follows that the set of points $P$ lies on a circle constructed with $A H$ as its diameter. Since $\angle H B A$ is right, this circle passes through the point $B$.

question: 33. A chessboard of size $6 \times 6$ is covered with 18 dominoes of size $2 \times 1$ (each domino covers two cells). Prove that for any such covering, the board can be cut into two parts along a horizontal or vertical line without cutting any domino.
reference_solution:
33. Suppose that a set of dominoes can be laid on a board in such a way that each of the horizontal and vertical lines dividing the board into cells intersects at least one domino.

There are 10 such lines in total. Each of these lines divides the board into 2 parts, each consisting of an even number of cells. In any of these parts, there is some number of uncut dominoes. These dominoes occupy an even number of cells. The remaining cells are occupied by halves of cut dominoes, and since their number is even, the number of cut dominoes is also even.

Thus, each of the 10 lines cuts no fewer than two dominoes, and since each domino is intersected by only one line, the number of cut dominoes is no less than 20.

However, the total number of dominoes covering the board is 18.

$\nabla$ It is interesting to determine for which rectangles $m \times n$ (with even $m$) the analogous statement holds. This question is addressed in the solution to problem M63 from the "Quantum Problems" (see "Quantum," 1971, No. 10).

question: 34. Given $n$ distinct positive numbers $a_{1}$, $a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$. From them, all possible sums with any number of addends (from 1 to $n$) are formed. Prove that among these sums, there will be at least $n(n+1) / 2$ pairwise distinct sums.
reference_solution:
34. We can assume that the numbers are arranged in ascending order: $a_{1}<a_{2}<\ldots<a_{n}$. Consider the numbers:

$$
\begin{array}{llll}
a_{1}, & a_{2}, & \ldots, a_{n-2}, & a_{n-1}, \\
a_{1}+a_{n}, & a_{2}+a_{n}, \ldots, a_{n-2}+a_{n}, \\
a_{1}+a_{n-1}+a_{n}, & \ldots, & \ldots, a_{n-2}+a_{n-1}+a_{n}, \\
\ldots & \ldots, & a_{n-1}+a_{n}, \\
a_{1}+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{n} & &
\end{array}
$$

Obviously, each number is greater than the previous one; thus, all the listed numbers are distinct. Their quantity is $n+(n-1)+\ldots+1=n(n+1) / 2$, which meets the requirements of the problem.

Note also that the first $n$ natural numbers provide an example of $n$ distinct numbers from which no more than $n(n+1) / 2$ distinct sums can be formed (these sums are all natural numbers from 1 to $1+2+\ldots+n=n(n+1) / 2$).

question: 35. In triangle $ABC$, the angle bisectors from vertices $A$ and $B$ are drawn. Then, from vertex $C$, lines parallel to these bisectors are drawn. Points $D$ and $E$ are the intersections of these lines with the bisectors, and these points are connected. It turns out that lines $DE$ and $AB$ are parallel. Prove that triangle $ABC$ is isosceles.
reference_solution:
35. From the equality of angles (Fig. 34), it follows that point $A$ lies on the circle passing through points $C, D$, and $E$, and also that point $B$ lies on this circle, with $D E \| A B$.

question: 36. Given an infinite arithmetic progression, the terms of which are positive integers. One of them is a perfect square. Prove that the progression contains infinitely many squares.
reference_solution: 36. Let the difference of the progression be $d$ and one of its terms $a=m^{2}$, where $m$ is a natural number. Then the number $(m+1 / d)^{2}=$ $=m^{2}+2 m k d+k^{2} d^{2}=a+d\left(2 k m+k^{2}\right)$ is also a term of the progression for any natural $k$. We have thus indicated an infinite number of terms of the progression that are squares of natural numbers.

question: 42. Prove that $m(m+1)$ is not a power of an integer for any natural $m$.
reference_solution: 42. Suppose that the number $m(m+1)$ is the $k$-th power of some natural number. Since the numbers $m$ and $m+1$ are coprime, each of them must be the $k$-th power of a natural number. But this is impossible: if $\boldsymbol{m}=\boldsymbol{a}^{\text {k }}$, then already $(a+1)^{k}>(a+1) a^{k-1}=a^{k}+a^{k-1}>m+1(k>1)$.

question: 44. Given an arbitrary set of $n$ integers $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{2 k+1}$. From it, a new set is obtained: $\frac{a_{1}+a_{2}}{2}, \quad \frac{a_{2}+a_{3}}{2}, \ldots, \frac{a_{n-1}+a_{n}}{2}, \quad \frac{a_{n}+a_{1}}{2} ;$ from this set - the next one by the same rule and so on. Prove that if all the resulting numbers are integers, then all the original numbers are equal.
reference_solution:
44. No matter what set of $n$ numbers $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ (not all equal to each other) we take, after a certain number of steps, the maximum number in the set will decrease, and the minimum number will increase.

From this, it is clear that the maximum number cannot remain an integer all the time, unless we end up with a set of equal numbers $(a, a, a, \ldots a)$.

Suppose from the set $z_{1}, z_{2}, \ldots, z_{n}$, a set of equal numbers is obtained for the first time:

$$
\frac{z_{1}+z_{2}}{2}=\frac{z_{2}+z_{3}}{2}=\ldots=\frac{z_{n-1}+z_{n}}{2}=\frac{z_{1}+z_{n}}{2}
$$

Then the numbers $z_{i}$ are equal every other one. For odd $n$, this is impossible.

Suppose $n$ is even. Let's see from what set the set $(a, b, a, b, a, b, \ldots, a, b)$ can be obtained. Let

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{y_{1}+y_{2}}{2}=\frac{y_{3}+y_{4}}{2}=\frac{y_{n}+y_{n-1}}{2}=a ; \\
& \frac{y_{2}+y_{3}}{2}=\frac{y_{4}+y_{5}}{2}=\frac{y_{n}+y_{1}}{2}=b
\end{aligned}
$$

Then

$$
y_{1}+y_{2}+\ldots+y_{n}=2 a n, \quad y_{2}+y_{3}+\ldots+y_{n}+y_{1}=2 n b_{1}
$$

i.e., $2 a n=2 n b$ and $a=b$.

Thus, a set of pairwise equal numbers cannot be obtained, which proves the statement of the problem.

question:
45. a) In a convex hexagon $A B C D E F$ all angles are equal. Prove that

$$
A B-D E=E F-B C=C D-F A
$$

b) Conversely, prove that from six segments, the lengths of which are $a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, a_{4}, a_{5}, a_{6}$ and satisfy the relations $a_{1}-a_{4}=a_{5}-a_{2}=a_{3}-a_{6}, \quad$ a convex hexagon with equal angles can be constructed.
reference_solution:
45. a) The measure of each angle of the hexagon is $120^{\circ}$, and therefore, its opposite sides are parallel. We can assume that $A B \geqslant D E$ (Fig. 36).

Now, let's construct parallelograms $A B C K, C D E L, A F E M$. If points $K, L, M$ do not coincide, then all angles of triangle $K L M$ are $60^{\circ}$, from which

Fig. 36 $K L=L M=K M$ and, therefore,

$$
A B-D E=C D-F A=F E-B C
$$

b) We can assume that $a_{1}>a_{4}$. Construct an equilateral triangle $K L M$ with sides

$$
\begin{aligned}
K L=L M=M K & =a_{1}-a_{4}= \\
& =a_{3}-a_{6}=a_{5}-a_{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

On the extension of $K L$, mark the segment $L C=a_{4}$, on the extension of $L M$, mark the segment $M E=a_{6}$, and on the extension of $M K$, mark the segment $K A=a_{2}$, and construct parallelograms $A K C B, C L E D, A F E M$. The resulting hexagon $A B C D E F$ is the desired one.

question: 47. Perpendiculars are dropped from the vertices of a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ to its diagonals. Prove that the quadrilateral formed by their feet is similar to the original one.
reference_solution:
47. Let $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}, D_{1}$ be the bases of the perpendiculars dropped from the vertices $A, B, C$, and $D$ to the diagonals $B D$ and $A C$, $O$ be the point of intersection of the diagonals, and $\alpha$ be the measure of the acute angle between them (Fig. 37). Then $O A_{1} = O A \cdot \cos \alpha ; O B_{1} = O B \cdot \cos \alpha ;$ $O C_{2} = O C \cdot \cos \alpha_{1} O D_{1} = O D \cdot \cos \alpha$. Therefore, triangles $A_{1} O B_{1}, B_{1} O C_{2}, C_{1} O D_{1} \equiv D_{1} O A_{1}$ are similar to triangles $A O B$, BOC, COD, and DOA with a similarity coefficient of $\cos \alpha$.

From this, it follows that quadrilaterals $A B C D$ and $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1} D_{1}$ are similar.

$\nabla$ Note that the second of the quadrilaterals is obtained from the first by the composition of the following transformations: symmetry relative to the bisector of the acute angle between the diagonals and homothety with center $O$ and coefficient $\cos \alpha$.

question:
51. $a, b$ and $n$ are fixed natural numbers. It is known that for any natural $k (k \neq b)$,
the number $a-k^{n}$ is divisible without remainder by $b-k$. Prove that $a=b^{n}$.
reference_solution:
51. Since $k^{n}-b^{n}=(k-b)\left(k^{n-1}+k^{n-2}b+\ldots+b^{n-1}\right)$, then $k^{n} - b^{2}$ is divisible by $k-b$.

Thus, $\left(k^{2}-b^{n}\right)-\left(k^{n}-a\right)=a-b^{n}$ is divisible by $\boldsymbol{k}-\boldsymbol{b}$ for any $k \neq b$, but this can only be true when $a=b^{n}$.

question:
55. $ABCD$ is a circumscribed trapezoid; $E$ is the point of intersection of the diagonals $AC$ and $BD$; $r_{1}, r_{2}, r_{3}, r_{4}$ are the radii of the circles inscribed in triangles $ABE, BCE$, $CDE, DAE$ respectively. Prove that

$$
\frac{1}{r_{1}}+\frac{1}{r_{3}}=\frac{1}{r_{2}}+\frac{1}{r_{4}}

question: 58. A circle is circumscribed around triangle $A B C$. Chords connecting the midpoint of arc $A C$ with the midpoints of arcs $A B$ and $B C$ intersect sides $A B$ and $B C$ at points $D$ and $E$. Prove that segment $D E$ is parallel to side $A C$ and passes through the center of the inscribed circle of triangle $A B C$.
reference_solution:
58. Let $L, M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of the arcs $AB, BC$ and $CA$, $O$ be the center of the inscribed circle of triangle $ABC$, and $D$ and $K$ be the points of intersection of the segment $LN$ with the sides $AB$ and $AC$ (Fig. 42).

We will prove that the quadrilateral $ADOK$ is a rhombus (at the same time, we will solve problem 237). For this, it is sufficient to verify that the diagonals $AO$ and $DK$ serve as axes of symmetry for this quadrilateral.

Indeed, $AM \perp LN$, since $\overline{LB}+\widetilde{BM}+\widetilde{AN}=180^{\circ}$; therefore, points $D$ and $K$ are symmetric with respect to the line $AM$ (the bisector of angle $BAC$), and points $A$ and $O$ are symmetric with respect to the line $LN$ (the bisector of angle $ANB$).

From this, it follows that $DO \parallel AC$; similarly, we can prove that $EO \parallel AC$, where $E$ is the point of intersection of the segment $MN$ with the side $BC$. Thus, points $D, O$ and $E$ lie on the same line, parallel to $AC$.

question: 61. In the people's militia, there are 100 people, and every evening three people go on duty. Prove that it is impossible to organize the duty schedule so that any two people are on duty together exactly once.
reference_solution:
61. Let's take one of the militiamen. If the required distribution of duties were possible, the remaining 99 militiamen would have to break into pairs, each of which would stand duty with the chosen militiaman, but this is impossible since 99 is an odd number.

$\nabla$ The problem of for which $n$ it is possible to select a system of triples from the elements $\{1,2, \ldots, n\}$ such that each pair appears in exactly one triple (a Steiner triple system), is discussed in detail in the books [58], [64].

question:
65*. Rounding a number means replacing it with one of the two nearest integers.

Given $n$ numbers. Prove that they can be rounded in such a way that the sum of any $m$ rounded numbers ( $1 \leqslant m \leqslant n$ ) differs from the sum of these same unrounded numbers by no more than $(n+1) / 4$.
reference_solution:
65. Let $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots x_{n}$ be given numbers, numbered in the order of increasing their fractional parts $\alpha_{1}=x_{1}-\left[x_{i}\right]$.

We will round the first $k$ of these numbers down, and the rest up; $k$ will be chosen below. It is easy to see that the largest error in rounding will accumulate in the calculation of one of the sums

$$
x_{1}+x_{2}+\ldots+x_{k} \text { or } x_{k+1}+x_{k+2}+\ldots+x_{n \cdot l}
$$

The absolute value of the first error is

$$
\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+\ldots+\alpha_{k} \leqslant k \alpha_{k v}
$$

And the second

$$
\left(1-a_{k+1}\right)+\ldots+\left(1-\alpha_{n}\right) \leqslant(n-k)\left(1-a_{k+1}\right)
$$

Now let's choose $k$ so that the inequalities

$$
k a_{k} \leqslant(n+1) / 4 \text { and }(n-k)\left(1-\alpha_{k+1}\right) \leqslant(n+1) / 4 .
$$

are satisfied. For this, it is sufficient to take the largest $k$ for which the first inequality holds; then $\alpha_{k+1}>\frac{n+1}{(k+1)}$, so the second inequality is also satisfied $1-\alpha_{k+1}<1-\frac{n+1}{4(k+1)} \leqslant \frac{n+1}{4(n-k)}$ (since $\frac{n+1}{4(k+1)}+\frac{n+1}{4(n-k)}=\frac{(n+1)^{2}}{4(k+1)(n-k)} \geqslant 1$ for $0<k<n)$.

$\nabla$ For odd $n$, the error estimate given in the condition is exact (example: $x_{1}=x_{2}=\ldots=x_{n}=1 / 2$). For even $n$, it can be slightly improved by replacing $\frac{n+1}{4}$ with $\frac{n+1}{4}-\frac{1}{n+1}$ (example: $x_{1}=x_{2}=\ldots=x_{n}=\frac{n}{2(n+1)}$).

question: 66. A tourist who arrived in Moscow by train wandered around the city all day. After having dinner at a cafe on one of the squares, he decided to return to the station and do so only by streets he had walked an odd number of times before. Prove that he can always do this.
reference_solution: 66. A tourist can walk from the cafe along any route with one condition: upon reaching a square, they choose the next street from those they have walked an odd number of times before. It is not hard to see that such a street exists for any intersection, except for the station (indeed, the tourist approached the intersection one more time than they left it), and also that the resulting route cannot pass along the same street twice. Since the number of streets is finite, the tourist will eventually arrive at the station.

question:
67. a) A certain commission met 40 times. Each time, 10 people were present at the meetings, and no two members of the commission were together at more than one meeting.

Prove that the number of commission members is greater than 60.

b) Prove that from 25 people, it is impossible to form more than 30 commissions of 5 people each, such that no two commissions have more than one member in common.
reference_solution:
67. a) First solution. Each pair of commission members could meet at no more than one meeting. At each meeting, there were $C_{10}^{2}=45$ pairs. Since there were 40 meetings, at least $1800=45 \cdot 40$ pairs could be formed from the commission members. However, from 60 (no less) people, no more than $C_{60}^{2}=60 \cdot 59 / 2 = 1770$ pairs can be formed. Therefore, there must be a person who attended at least 7 meetings. All the people he met are different, and their total number is $7 \cdot 9 > 59$. Contradiction.

b) This problem is solved in exactly the same way as a) (any solution is valid).
$\nabla$ It is interesting that the estimate given here is exact: 30 commissions of 5 people each, satisfying the problem's conditions, can be formed.

question: 68*. Given two coprime numbers \( p > 0 \) and \( q > 0 \). An integer \( n \) is called good if it can be represented as \( n = px + qy \), where \( x \) and \( y \) are non-negative integers, and bad otherwise. a) Prove that there exists an integer \( c \) such that out of two integers \( n \) and \( c - n \), one is always good, and the other is bad. b) How many bad non-negative numbers are there?
reference_solution:
68. Answer: b) $(p-1)(q-1) / 2$. If $p$ and $q$ are coprime natural numbers, then every integer $z$ can be represented as $z=p x+q y$ (P2). Every such representation is derived from some fixed $z p a+q b$ by the general formula $z=p(a-q t)+q(b+p t)$, where $t$ is an integer, and there exists a unique representation for which $0 \leqslant x \leqslant q-1$.

Each integer $z$ is associated with a pair $(x, y)$ of integers such that $0 \leqslant x \leqslant q-1, z=p x+q y$. Different numbers correspond to different pairs, and $z$ will be good only if $y \geqslant 0$. (If $z=p x+q y$ is a good number, then for $x=q t+r \geqslant 0, \quad 0 \leqslant r \leqslant q-1, \quad$ there is a representation $z=$ $=p r+q(y+t)$.

Now notice that if the number $z=p x+q y, 0 \leqslant x \leqslant q-1$ is good, then the number $z^{\prime}=(q-1-x) p+(-1-y) q$ is bad, and vice versa, if $z$ is bad, then $z^{\prime}$ is good. The points $(x, y)$ and $(q-1-x,-1-y)$ are symmetric with respect to the point $\left(x_{0}, y_{0}\right)=\left(\frac{q-1}{2},-\frac{1}{2}\right)$, and the numbers $z$ and $z^{\prime}$ are symmetric with respect to the point $z_{0}=p x_{0}+q y_{0}=(p q-p-q) / 2$, since $z+z^{\prime}=p q-p-q=2 z_{0}=c$.

Thus, part a) is proven: a good number $z$ corresponds to a bad (symmetric to it) $c-z=z^{\prime}$ and vice versa.

Since the smallest good number is 0, the largest bad number will be $c$, and the total number of bad numbers will be $(c+1) / 2=$, $=(p-1)(q-1) / 2$.

$\nabla$ It is very useful, when analyzing the solution to this problem, to refer to a geometric illustration: pairs $(x, y)$ are points on a lattice, $p x+q y=z-$ are lines passing through them, etc. (see "Kvant", 1973, No. 11, solution to problem M194).

question: 70. Prove that the sum of the lengths of the edges of a polyhedron is greater than $3 d$, where $d$ is the distance between the most distant vertices of the polyhedron.
reference_solution:
70. Let $A$ and $B$ be two vertices of a polyhedron, separated by a distance $d$. Through points $A$ and $B$, we draw planes perpendicular to the line $A B$.

It is clear that the entire polyhedron is contained between these two planes. Through each vertex of the polyhedron, we draw a plane perpendicular to $A B$. Consider two adjacent planes among those drawn. Between them, there are, obviously, at least three edge segments. The projection of each segment onto the line $A B$ is not less than the length of this segment, and among

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-131.jpg?height=367&width=445&top_left_y=924&top_left_x=149)

Fig. 47 them, there are certainly segments that are not parallel to $A B$. Therefore, the total length of all such segments, i.e., the sum of the lengths of the edges, is greater than $3 \cdot A B = 3d$.

In simpler terms, this solution can be explained as follows: the projection of the polyhedron's skeleton onto the segment covers it at least three times.

question: 72. On each of the planets in a certain system, there is an astronomer observing the nearest planet. The distances between the planets are all different. Prove that if the number of planets is odd, then some planet is not observed by anyone.
reference_solution:
72. Let's take the two closest planets to each other. Clearly, the astronomers on these planets are looking at each other.

There are still $n-2$ planets and $n-2$ astronomers left. If at least one of them is looking at one of the already chosen planets, then there won't be enough astronomers for one of the $n-2$ planets. If no one else is looking at these two planets, then the same reasoning can be applied again: we choose two of the closest planets from the remaining $n-2$ planets, and so on. Since $n$ is odd, in the end, there will be one planet that no one is observing.

question:
73. a) Points $B$ and $C$ lie inside the segment $A D$. Prove that if $A B$ equals $C D$, then for any point $P$ on the plane, the inequality $P A + P D \geqslant P B + P C$ holds.

b) Points $A, B, C$, and $D$ are marked on the plane. It is known that for any point $P$, the inequality $P A + P D \geqslant P B + P C$ holds. Prove that points $B$ and $C$ lie on the segment $A D$ and $A B = C D$.
reference_solution:
73. a) If point $P$ lies on line $A D$, the statement is obvious.

Let $P$ not lie on $A D$ and $O$ be the midpoint of segment $A D$. Let $P^{\prime}$ be the point symmetric to point $P$ with respect to $O$. Quadrilaterals $B P C P^{\prime}$ and $P^{\prime} A P D$ are parallelograms and $A P + P D = A P^{\prime} + A P > P^{\prime} B + P B = B P + P C$.

b) In the condition, $P$ is an arbitrary point. Choosing $P = A$, we get $A D \geqslant A B + A C$. Now let $P = D$; then $A D \geqslant B D + D C$. Adding these inequalities, we obtain $2 A D \geqslant A B + A C + B D + C D$.

On the other hand, it is always true that $A D \leqslant A C + C D$ and $A D \leqslant A B + B D$. Moreover, equality in each of these inequalities is possible only when the three points lie on the same line. Adding them, we get $2 A D \leqslant B D + A B + A C + C D$. Comparing this with the previously obtained result, we get $2 A D = B D + A B + A C + C D$. From this, it immediately follows that points $A, B, C$, and $D$ lie on the same line and all the previously listed inequalities are equalities; from them, it follows that points $B$ and $C$ lie on segment $A D$ and $A B = C D$.

question:
75. a) Eighth-graders are lined up in a row. In front of each of them stands a seventh-grader who is shorter than them. Prove that if the row of eighth-graders is arranged by height and the row of seventh-graders is also arranged by height, then each eighth-grader will still be taller than the seventh-grader standing in front of them.

b) A regiment of soldiers is arranged in a rectangle such that in each row, the soldiers are standing by height. Prove that if in each column the soldiers are also arranged by height, then in each row they will still be standing by height.
reference_solution:
75. a) It is sufficient to prove that the $k$-th tallest eighth-grader is taller than the $k$-th tallest seventh-grader. Let $A$ be the $k$-th tallest seventh-grader. Then there are at least $k$ seventh-graders (including $A$) who are not shorter than $A$. All $k$ eighth-graders standing behind them are taller than $A$. Therefore, the $k$-th tallest eighth-grader is taller than $A$.

b) This reduces to problem a): the same reasoning can be applied to any two columns.

question: 76. On a grid paper, a rectangle $A B C D$ is drawn, with its sides lying on the grid lines, and $A D$ is $k$ times greater than $A B$ ($k$ is an integer). Consider all possible paths that follow the grid lines and lead from $A$ to $C$ in the shortest way. Prove that among these paths, those in which the first segment lies on $A D$ are $k$ times more numerous than those in which the first segment lies on $A B$.
reference_solution:
76. Let there be a rectangle $ABCD$ on a grid paper of size $m \times n$ cells (Fig. 48). Denote the number of paths leading from vertices $B_{1}, D_{1}, B_{2}, D_{2}$, and $A_{2}$ to $C$ along the grid lines by $b_{1}, d_{1}, b_{2}, d_{2}$, and $a_{2}$ respectively. The statement of the problem is that $d_{1} / b_{1} = n / m$. We will prove this by induction on $m+n$ (P1), and for any, not necessarily integer, ratio $n / m = k$. The base case of the induction ($m=1$ or $n=1$) is obvious. We will assume that $m>1, n>1$. By the induction hypothesis applied to smaller rectangles of sizes $(m-1) \times n$ and $m \times (n-1)$,

$$
\frac{a_{2}}{b_{2}} = \frac{n}{m-1} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{d_{2}}{a_{2}} = \frac{n-1}{m}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{d_{1}}{b_{1}} = \frac{d_{2} + a_{2}}{b_{2} + a_{2}} = \frac{d_{2} / a_{2} + 1}{b_{2} / a_{2} + 1} = \frac{(n-1) / m + 1}{(m-1) / n + 1} = \frac{n}{m}
$$

$\nabla$ Essentially, in solving this problem, the following equalities have been proven:

$$
C_{m+n-1}^{m-1} = n C_{m+n-1}^{m} = (m+n-1) C_{m+n-2}^{m-1}
$$

(in our problem $n = k m$). Knowing the formula for the numbers $C_{n}^{m}$ (P10), these equalities are not hard to verify; but one can, conversely, use these equalities to derive the general formula for the "combination numbers" $C_{n}^{m}$.

question: 79. In a certain city, for any three intersections $A, B$, and $C$, there is a path leading from $A$ to $B$ that does not pass through $C$. Prove that from any intersection to any other, there are at least two non-intersecting paths (an intersection is a place where at least two streets meet; the city has at least two intersections).
reference_solution:
79. Let's call the length of a path the number of segments it consists of. Let $n-$ be the length of the shortest path from $A$ to $B$. We will prove the statement of the problem by induction on $n$.

For $n=1$, besides the shortest path $AB$, there exists a path that goes from $A$ to a crossroad $C \neq A$, which is 1 unit away from $B$, and does not pass through $B$.

Suppose $n>1$, and let $D$ be the closest crossroad to $A$ on the shortest path from $A$ to $B$. By the induction hypothesis, there exist two non-intersecting paths $p$ and $q$ from $D$ to $B$. We will go from $A$ along a path $l$ that does not pass through $D$. If this path does not intersect with paths $p$ and $q$, then the proof is complete. If, however, it intersects, say, path $p$ for the first time, then we should continue along $p$ directly to $B$. The resulting path does not intersect with $q$.

b) In an acute-angled triangle \(ABC\), the height \(AH\) is equal to the median \(BM\) and is also equal to the angle bisector \(CD\). Prove that triangle \(ABC\) is equilateral.

85. a) In a certain natural number, the digits were arbitrarily rearranged. Prove that the sum of the obtained number and the original number is not equal to $\underbrace{999 \ldots 9}_{1967 \text { digits }}$.

b) The digits of a certain number were rearranged and the obtained number was added to the original number. Prove that if the sum is $10^{10}$, then the original number was divisible by 10.
reference_solution:
85. a) If the sum of two numbers $a$ and $b$ consists of only nines, then there cannot be any carry-over of units to the next place when adding these numbers. Therefore, $S(a+b)=S(a)+S(b)$, where $S(x)$ is the sum of the digits of the number $x$. If $S(a)=S(b)$, then $S(a+b)$ is even and cannot equal $9 \cdot 1967$.

b) If the last digit of the number $a$ is not zero, then the sum of its last digit and the last digit of the number $b$ equals 10, and the sums of the digits in each of the other nine places equal 9. From this, it follows that $2 S(a)=9 \cdot 9+10=91$, which is impossible. 86. a) Draw a line $l$ such that in each of the half-planes into which the plane is divided by this line, there are two of the given points. It is clear (Fig. 51) that two projectors placed at points in one of these half-planes can illuminate the other half-plane.

b) Draw a plane such that four of the given points lie on one side of it, and the other four on the other side. Using the problem a), it is not difficult to prove that projectors placed at four points in one of the half-spaces can illuminate the other half-space.

A far-reaching generalization of this problem was found ten years later by two namesakes - "olympiad participants" of different generations [70]. It turns out that any $n$ given angles $\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}, \ldots, \alpha_{n}, \alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+\ldots+\alpha_{n}=360^{\circ}$, can be placed at the given $n$ vertices such that they cover the entire plane.

question: 88. Prove that there exists a number divisible by $5^{1000}$ and not containing any zeros in its decimal representation.
reference_solution:
88. The number $5^{1000}$ ends with 5. Let the $k$-th digit from the end in the decimal representation of this number be 0, and all subsequent digits be different from 0. Add $5^{1000} \cdot 10^{k-1}$ to this number. As a result, we get a number divisible by $5^{1000}$, in which the last $k$ digits are different from 0. Continuing this procedure, we can obtain a number in which the last 1000 digits are different from 0. Now, discard all digits except the last 1000. The resulting number, obviously, is also divisible by
$5^{1000}$. $(-6 ; 2)$.

question: 91. "THE SUICIDAL KING". On a chessboard of size $1000 \times 1000$, there is a black king and 499 white rooks. Prove that, regardless of the initial arrangement of the pieces, the king can place himself under attack by a white rook, no matter how the whites play. (Moves are made in the same way as in regular chess.)
reference_solution:
91. If the king moves from the bottom left corner of the board to the top right corner along the diagonal, at some point he will inevitably be under attack by a white rook.

To prove this, it is sufficient to note that after the king's first move, all white rooks must be above the third rank and to the right of the third file (after which the king will be under attack on the next move).

Similarly, before the king's move to the top right corner, all rooks must be below the 998th rank and to the left of the 998th file.

In total, before his last move along the diagonal, the king will make 997 moves. During this time, each rook must make 2 moves (change the rank and file it was initially on), but there are 499 rooks, and this would require $2 \cdot 499=998>997$ moves.

93. First, note that the number $k$ is coprime with 10. Indeed, there exists a number divisible by $k$ and starting with 1. The reversed number is also divisible by $k$ and ends with 1.

Now, let's take a number starting with the digits 500 and divisible by $k: 500 a b c \ldots z$ (where $a, b, c, \ldots z$ are the digits of this number). Then the following numbers are divisible by $k$:

1) $z \ldots c b a 005$.
2) The sum $z \ldots c b a 00500 \ldots 0$

$500 a b c \ldots z$

$z \ldots c b a 01000 a b \ldots z$.

3) The reversed last number $z \ldots b a 00010 a b \ldots z$.
4) The difference $z \ldots b a 0100 a b \ldots z$

$\frac{z \ldots b a 0001 a b \ldots z}{9900 \ldots 0}$

From this, it is clear that 99 is divisible by $k$.

question: 94. In an octagon, all angles are equal, and the side lengths are integers. Prove that the opposite sides of the octagon are equal to each other.
reference_solution:
94. Let $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{8}$ be the lengths of the sides of the octagon (Fig. 53). From the equality of all its angles, it immediately follows that its opposite sides are parallel. By extending two pairs of opposite sides $a_{1}$ and $a_{5}, a_{3}$ and $a_{7}$, we obtain a rectangle from which our octagon can be made by cutting off the corners.

From the equality of the opposite sides of this rectangle, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{a_{8}}{\sqrt{2}}+a_{1}+\frac{a_{2}}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{a_{6}}{\sqrt{2}}+a_{5}+\frac{a_{4}}{\sqrt{2}} & , \text { or } a_{5}-a_{1} \Rightarrow \\
& =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\left(a_{8}+a_{2}-a_{6}-a_{4}\right) .
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $a_{t}$ are integers, and $\sqrt{2} / 2$ is irrational, then $a_{5}=a_{1}$. Similarly, the equality of the lengths of the other pairs of opposite sides can be proven.

question: 97. Among the students admitted to the University of Peoples' Friendship, exactly 50 people know English, exactly 50 people know French, and exactly 50 people know Spanish. Prove that the students can be divided into 5 (not necessarily equal) groups such that in each group there are exactly 10 people who know English, exactly 10 people who know French, and exactly 10 people who know Spanish. (It is assumed that some students may either not know any of these languages or know any number of them.)
reference_solution:
97. First, we will prove that it is possible to choose a group of students in which each language is known by exactly two people.

We will denote each student by a set of the initial letters of the names of the languages they know. Thus, student a knows English but not the others, student if knows Spanish and French but not English; student aif knows all three languages.

If $N_{au} \neq 0, N_{a\phi} \neq 0$ and $N_{u\phi} \leqslant 0$, then we choose the group $(au, a\phi, u\phi)$.

100. The sequence $a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots$ is formed according to the following rule:

$$
a_{1}=1, a_{2}=a_{1}+\frac{1}{a_{1}}, \ldots, a_{n}=a_{n-1}+\frac{1}{a_{n-1}}
$$

Prove that $a_{100}>14$.
reference_solution:
100. We will immediately prove the two-sided estimate $141$ we have $a_{k}^{2}=a_{k-1}^{2}+2+\frac{1}{a_{k-1}^{2}}$, and $a_{k}>1$. Therefore, $a_{k-1}^{2}+2<a_{k}^{2}<a_{k-1}^{2}+3$.

By summing these inequalities for all $1 \leqslant k \leqslant n$, we get (taking into account that $a_{1}=1$)

$$
2 n-1<a_{n}^{2}<3 n-2
$$

from which $\sqrt{2 n-1}<a_{n}<\sqrt{3 n-2}$. For $n=100$ we get the required inequalities $14<a_{100}<18$.

Perpendiculars are dropped from point $O$: $OA_1$ to side $BC$, $OB_1$ to side $CA$, and $OC_1$ to side $AB$. Similarly, perpendiculars are dropped from point $O'$: $O'A_1'$ to $B'C'$, $O'B_1'$ to $C'A'$, and $O'C_1'$ to $A'B'$. 101. Let's translate $\Delta A^{\prime} B^{\prime} C^{\prime}$ parallel so that point $O^{\prime}$ moves to point $O$. The vertices of the resulting triangle will be denoted, as before, by $A^{\prime}, B^{\prime}$, and $C^{\prime}$.

Since $\angle A^{\prime} O B = \angle A_{1} O B_{1}$ and by the condition $O A^{\prime} : O B^{\prime} = O B_{1} : O A_{1}$, then

Therefore, $\triangle A_{1} O C \sim \triangle C_{1}^{\prime} O A^{\prime}$ and $\triangle B O C \sim \triangle C_{1}^{\prime} O B_{1}$, from which it follows that the segment $O C^{\prime}$ lies on the line $O C$ and $O C \cdot O^{\prime} C_{1}^{\prime} = O A \cdot O^{\prime} A_{1}^{\prime} = O B_{1} \cdot O^{\prime} B_{1}^{\prime}$.

question: 106. The medians of triangle $ABC$ divide it into six triangles. It turns out that four of the circles inscribed in these triangles are equal. Prove that triangle $ABC$ is equilateral.
reference_solution:
106. The areas of all six triangles into which a given triangle is divided by its medians are equal.

Due to the equality of the radii of the inscribed circles and the formula $S=p r$, it follows that the perimeters of four of such triangles are equal.

Since two of them adjoin one side, say $AB$ (Fig. 58), then $AM=MB$, therefore $MK$ is the median and height of $\triangle AMB$ and $AC=BC$.

If the radii of the circles inscribed in triangles $ALM$ and $AKM$ are equal, then these triangles are equal (as triangles with equal areas, bases, and perimeters), and $AL=AK$, i.e., $AC=AB$ and triangle $ABC$ is equilateral.

If the perimeters of triangles $CLM$ and $KMB$ are equal, then using the equality of the lengths of the tangents drawn from one point, we get: $CL+LM+CM=2 \cdot CL+2x=$ $=2 \cdot BK+2x$ (where $x$ is the distance from point $M$ to the point of tangency with the corresponding circle). From this, it follows that $AC=$ $=AB$.

question:
107. Prove that the equation

$$
x^{2}+x+1=p y
$$

has solutions in integers $(x, y)$ for infinitely many primes $p$.
reference_solution:
107. The proof of this statement resembles Euclid's proof of the infinitude of the set of prime numbers (P2).

Suppose that the equation $x^{2}+x+1=p y$ has integer solutions $(x, y)$ only for a finite number of prime numbers $p_{1}, p_{2}, \ldots, p_{m}$.

Let $P=p_{1} p_{2} \ldots p_{m}$. Then the number $P^{2}+P+1$ is not divisible by any of the numbers $p_{1}, p_{2}, \ldots, p_{m}$ and, consequently, has a prime divisor $q$ that does not coincide with any of these numbers. Thus, the equation $x^{2}+x+1=q y$ has an integer solution $\left(P,\left(P^{2}+P+1\right) / q\right)$. This leads to a contradiction.

$\nabla$ A more general problem is discussed in the book [60] (VIII, problem 108). 108. Answer: The maximum possible value of $c_{1}$ is 24.

If the first place is awarded to one skater by all judges, then $c_{1}=9$. If the first places are awarded to two skaters, then one of them received at least 5 first places, and the other four places he received are no higher than fourth, so $c_{1} \leqslant 5 \cdot 1+4 \cdot 4=21$.

If the first places are awarded to three skaters, then, since the other places they received are no higher than fourth, the total number of places for all these skaters is no more than $1 \cdot 9 + 3 \cdot 9 + 4 \cdot 9 = 72$. Therefore, $c_{1} \leqslant 24$. If the first place is awarded to four skaters, then their total number of places is no more than 90, so the sum of points for one of them is no more than 22. The case where 5 or more skaters receive the first place is impossible (there are not enough points from 1 to 4 for them).

Thus, $c_{1} \leqslant 24$. We will show how to construct an example with $c_{1}=24$.

If the judges distributed the points as follows: each of the three best skaters received places $1,1,1,3,3,3,4,4,4$, each of the next three received places $2,2,2,5,5,5,6,6,6$, and the rest received points arbitrarily, then the resulting distribution will have $c_{1}=24$.

question: 116. In the center of a field shaped as a square, there is a wolf, and at the vertices of the square, there are four dogs. The maximum speed of each dog is 1.5 times the maximum speed of the wolf. Prove that the dogs have the ability to keep the wolf within the square.
reference_solution:
116. Let v be the maximum speed of the wolf. Draw two lines through the point where the wolf is located, parallel to the diagonals of the square. These lines intersect the contour of the square at points $C_{1}, C_{2}, C_{3}, C_{4}$.

Since the speed of movement of each of the points $C_{1}, C_{2}, C_{3}$, and $C_{4}$ is no more than $v \sqrt{2}<\frac{3}{2} v$, the dogs will be able to be in these four points at any moment and, consequently, will not let the wolf escape.

question: 120. Given a natural number $n$. Let us write down all fractions of the form $\frac{1}{p q}$, where $p$ and $q$ are coprime, $0 < p < q \leq n$. Prove that the sum of all such fractions is $1 / 2$.
reference_solution:
120. The approved task can be proven by induction.

For $n=1$ it is valid: $\frac{1}{1 \cdot 1}=1$. When transitioning from $n-1$ to $n$, we need to discard all fractions $\frac{1}{p q}$ with coprime $p$ and $q$, for which $p<q, p+q=n, p$ and $q$ are coprime, and add all fractions of the form $\frac{1}{p n}$, where $p<n, p$ and $n$ are coprime.

Let $\frac{1}{p q}$ be one of the discarded fractions.

Since

$$
\frac{1}{p q}=\frac{1}{p(n-p)}=\frac{1}{p n}+\frac{1}{(n-p) n}
$$

the removal of this fraction from the sum is compensated by the appearance of two new fractions $\frac{1}{p n}$ and $\frac{1}{(n-p) n}$, which satisfy the conditions of the problem.

Thus, when transitioning from $n-1$ to $n$, the sum does not change.

question: 121*. In space, $n$ points are arranged such that any three of them form a triangle, one of whose angles is greater than $120^{\circ}$. Prove that these points can be labeled as $A_{1}$, $A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}$ in such a way that each of the angles $A_{i} A_{j} A_{k}$, where $1 \leqslant i<j<k \leqslant n$, will be greater than $120^{\circ}$.
reference_solution:
121. Let's choose from our system of points two, the distance between which is the greatest: let, for example, these be points $A$ and $B$.

We will prove that each of the angles $X A Y$ (and $X B Y$), where $X$ and $Y$ are some of the given points, is less than $120^{\circ}$. Indeed, since in triangles $A X B$ and $A Y B$ the side $A B$ is the largest, then $\angle A X B > 120^{\circ}$ and $\angle A Y B > 120^{\circ}$. Therefore, $\angle X A B > 120^{\circ}$, which, as we have seen, is impossible. We will number the given points, setting $A_{1} = A, A_{2}$ - the closest point to $A$ in the system, $A_{3}$ the closest to $A$ from the remaining points, $\ldots, A_{k}$ - the closest from the points that have not yet received a number, $\ldots, A_{n} = B$. We will prove that such numbering satisfies the condition of the problem.

Since $\angle A_{1} A_{i} A_{k} > 120^{\circ}$ for $1 < i < k \leq n$, and $\angle A_{1} A_{i} A_{k} > 120^{\circ}$ for $1 < i < k \leq n$, it follows from the inequality $\angle A_{k} A_{t} A_{l} \leq 120^{\circ}$ that the sum of the planar angles of the trihedral angle with vertex $A_{i}$ would be greater than $360^{\circ}$.

Thus, $\angle A_{i} A_{i} A_{k} > 120^{\circ}$ for any $1 \leq i < k \leq n$. The value $120^{\circ}$ here cannot be replaced by a smaller one.

The relation «$\angle A_{i} A_{i} A_{k} > 120^{\circ}$» has the same properties as the relation $\kappa A_{1}$ lies between $A_{l}$ and $A_{k}$ for points on a line, i.e., that this relation allows us to establish an "order" in the given set. The value $120^{\circ}$ here cannot be replaced by a smaller one.

question:
124. Consider a convex pentagon with all sides of equal length.

a) Prove that there exists a point inside it, lying on the longest diagonal, from which all sides are visible at angles not exceeding a right angle.

b) Prove that the circles constructed on its sides as diameters do not cover the entire pentagon.
reference_solution:
124. a) If $K$ is the midpoint of the largest diagonal $AD$ of a convex pentagon $ABCDE$, all sides of which are equal to $a$, then $\angle AKE = \angle EKD = 90^{\circ}$. Since $AC \leq AD$, it follows that $\angle BAC > \angle DAE$; therefore, $\angle BAK > \angle KAE$. From this, it follows that points $A$ and $B$ lie on the same side of the line $EK$. Similarly, it is proved that points $C$ and $D$ also lie on the same side of the line $EK$. From this, it immediately follows that $\angle BKA > 60^{\circ}$ and $\angle CKD > 60^{\circ}$ (the angle opposite the larger side of a triangle is larger); but this is impossible, since $\angle AKB + \angle BKC + \angle CKD = 180^{\circ}$. Therefore, $\angle BKC < 90^{\circ}$.

We have proved that point $K$ satisfies the condition of the problem.

b) If a point $M$ is taken on the extension of the segment $EK$, very close to point $K$, then all angles $AMB, BMC, CMD, DME$, and $EMA$ will be acute. Therefore, point $M$ cannot belong to any of the semicircles constructed on the sides of the pentagon as diameters.

question:
125. On the board, the equation is written

$$
x^{3}+\ldots+x^{2}+\ldots+x+\ldots=0
$$

Two players play a game. The first player places an integer, different from zero (positive or negative), in any of the empty spaces. Then the second player places an integer in one of the remaining spaces. Finally, the first player places an integer in the last free space. Prove that the first player can play in such a way that regardless of the second player's move, all three roots of the resulting equation will be integers.
reference_solution: 125. If the first player puts -1 before $x$ in the first degree, and on his second move he places the opposite number of what the second player placed on the last remaining spot, then the polynomial will be of the form $x^{3}-a x^{2}-x+a=$ $=\left(x^{2}-1\right)(x-a)$. The roots of this polynomial are $-1,1, a$-integers.

question:
127. $h_{k}$ - apothem of a regular $k$-gon inscribed in a circle of radius $R$. Prove that

$$
(n+1) h_{n+1}-n h_{n}>R
$$
reference_solution:
127. The inequality of the problem is equivalent to the relations

$$
(n+1) \cos \frac{\pi}{n+1}-n \cos \frac{\pi}{n}>1
$$

or

$$
n\left(\cos \frac{\pi}{n+1}-\cos \frac{\pi}{n}\right)>1-\cos \frac{\pi}{n+1}
$$

i.e.,

$$
n \sin \frac{\pi}{2 n(n+1)} \cdot \sin \frac{\pi(2 n+1)}{2 n(n+1)}>\sin ^{2} \frac{\pi}{2(n+1)}
$$

The last inequality is valid because

$$
\sin \frac{\pi(2 n+1)}{2 n(n+1)}>\sin \frac{2 \pi n}{2 n(n+1)}=\sin \frac{\pi}{n+1}>\sin \frac{\pi}{2(n+1)}
$$

and

$$
n \sin \frac{\pi}{2 n(n+1)} \geqslant \sin \frac{n \pi}{2 n(n+1)}=\sin \frac{\pi}{2(n+1)}
$$

(here we used the inequality \( n|\sin \alpha| \geqslant|\sin n \alpha| \), which is easily proved by induction).

128. Let $a_{i_{1}}=\max _{1 \leqslant i \leqslant n} a_{i}$. Choose $a_{i_{2}}$ - the largest of the numbers in the denominator of the fraction with numerator $a_{i_{1}}, a_{i_{3}}$ - the largest of the numbers in the denominator of the fraction with numerator $a_{i_{2}}$, and generally $a_{i_{k}}$ the largest of the numbers in the denominator of the fraction with numerator $a_{i_{k-1}}$.

Clearly, we will eventually arrive at $a_{i_{1}}: a_{i_{r+1}}=a_{i_{1}}$.

If the numbers 1, 2, ..., $n$ are arranged in a circle, then $i_{k+1}$ and $i_{k}$ (as well as $i_{r}$ and $i_{1}$) will be adjacent or one apart; hence, $r \geqslant n / 2$.

The given sum is greater than

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{a_{i_{1}}}{2 a_{l_{2}}}+\frac{a_{l_{2}}}{2 a_{i_{3}}}+\ldots+\frac{a_{i_{r}}}{2 a_{i_{1}}} & \\
& =\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{a_{l_{1}}}{a_{i_{2}}}+\frac{a_{l_{2}}}{a_{i_{3}}}+\ldots+\frac{a_{i_{r}}}{a_{i_{1}}}\right)=\frac{1}{2} S_{0}
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the arithmetic mean is not less than the geometric mean (P8), then

$$
\frac{s}{r} \geqslant \sqrt[r]{\frac{a_{l_{1}}}{a_{i_{2}}} \cdot \frac{a_{l_{2}}}{a_{l_{3}}} \cdots \frac{c_{i_{r}}}{a_{i_{1}}}}=1
$$

i.e., $S$ is not less than $r$. Therefore, the given sum is greater than $n / 4$.
$\nabla$ It might seem that a stronger inequality is always true:

$$
\frac{a_{1}}{a_{2}+a_{3}}+\frac{a_{2}}{a_{3}+a_{4}}+\ldots+\frac{a_{n}}{a_{1}+a_{2}} \geqslant \frac{n}{2}
$$

(such a hypothesis was proposed in 1954 by American mathematician Shapiro). Indeed, this has been gradually proven for odd $n \leqslant 11$ and even $n \leqslant 12$, but it is false for even $n \geqslant 14$ and odd $n \geqslant 27$ (counterexamples were initially devised for larger $n$). The exact estimate $\gamma_{n} \cdot \frac{n}{2}$, which should replace $\frac{n}{2}$ in (*), is unknown for each $n$, but V. G. Drinfeld - one of the winners of the olympiad, who continued working on this problem - managed to achieve a remarkable result in the same year 1969: he found the best estimate $\gamma \cdot \frac{n}{2}$, suitable for all $n$. This number $\gamma=\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \gamma_{n}$ is the ordinate of the point where the common tangent to the graphs of the functions $y=e^{-x}$ and $y=\frac{2}{e^{x / 2}+e^{x}}$ intersects the Oy axis; $\gamma \approx 0.989$.

question: 130. Prove that if the product of three positive numbers is 1, and the sum of these numbers is strictly greater than the sum of their reciprocals, then exactly one of these numbers is greater than 1.
reference_solution: 130. Let $x, y, \frac{1}{x y}$ be these numbers. If $x+y+\frac{1}{x y}>\frac{1}{x}+$ $+\frac{1}{y}+x y$, then after transformations we get $(x-1)(y-1) \times$ $\times\left(\frac{1}{x y}-1\right)>0$, from which it is clear that exactly one of the factors must be positive.

question: 132. The digits of a certain seventeen-digit number are written in reverse order. The resulting number is added to the original. Prove that at least one of the digits of their sum will be even.
reference_solution:
132. Assume the opposite. Write down two numbers one under the other and add them column by column. Since the last digit of the sum is odd, the sum of the first digits must also be odd. Therefore, a one does not carry over from the previous column. This means that the sum of the digits in the second column, and consequently in the second-to-last column, is less than 10. Note that a one does not carry over from the second column to the third, which could only happen if the sum of the digits in the second column were 9, and the sum of the digits in the first column were greater than 10, but then a 0 would stand in the second column of the sum.

By now, if we discard the last two and the first two digits of the given number and apply the same reasoning to the resulting 13-digit, then 9-digit, and finally 5-digit numbers, we will find that a one cannot carry over to the middle column from the previous column. Since the digits in the middle columns are the same, the middle digit of the sum will be even.

As can be seen from the solution, the statement of the problem is true for $(4k+1)$-digit numbers. Simple examples ($12+21, 506+605, \ldots$) show that for numbers with a different number of digits, it is not true.

question: 134. Five segments are such that any three of them can form a triangle. Prove that at least one of these triangles is acute.
reference_solution:
134. Let $a \leqslant b \leqslant c \leqslant d \leqslant e-$ be the lengths of given segments. Suppose that no three of these segments can form an acute triangle. Then, since in a non-acute triangle the square of the length of the largest side is greater than or equal to the sum of the squares of the lengths of the other sides, the following inequalities hold: $c^{2} \geqslant a^{2}+b^{2}, d^{2} \geqslant c^{2}+b^{2}, \quad e^{2} \geqslant d^{2}+c^{2}$

Adding them, we get $e^{2} \geqslant a^{2}+2 b^{2}+c^{2} \geqslant a^{2}+2 a b+b^{2}$, from which $e \geqslant a+b$, i.e., a triangle cannot be formed from segments of lengths $e, a$ and $b$.

question: 138. In triangle $ABC$, a line $MO$ is drawn through the midpoint $M$ of side $BC$ and the center $O$ of the inscribed circle of the triangle. This line intersects the altitude $AH$ at point $E$. Prove that the segment $AE$ is equal to the radius of the inscribed circle.
reference_solution:
138. First solution. Let $P$ be the point of tangency of the inscribed circle with side $BC$, and $PQ$ the diameter of the inscribed circle. In the solution to problem 112, it was proven that $AQ \parallel MO$, so $AEOQ$ is a parallelogram, hence $OQ = AE = r$.

Second solution. Let $a, b, c$ be the lengths of the sides of the triangle opposite vertices $A, B, C$ respectively. We can assume that $b > c$. Drop a perpendicular $OP$ from point $O$ to $BC$. Then

\[
\begin{gathered}
MC = \frac{a}{2} ; \quad PC = \frac{a + b - c}{2} ; \quad HC = \frac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2}{2a} ; \\
\frac{EH}{OP} = \frac{HM}{PM} = \frac{HC - MC}{PC - MC} = \frac{2HC - a}{b - c} = \\
= \frac{a^2 + b^2 - c^2 - a^2}{a(b - c)} = \frac{b + c}{a} ; \\
\frac{AE}{r} = \frac{AH}{r} - \frac{EH}{r} = \frac{a + b + c}{a} - \frac{b + c}{a} = 1
\end{gathered}
\]

from which $AE = r$.

question: 139. Prove that for each natural number $k$ there are infinitely many natural numbers $t$, not containing zeros in their decimal representation, such that $t$ and $k t$ have the same sum of digits.
reference_solution:
139. If the number $k$ is written as $k=\overline{a_{n} a_{n-1} \ldots a_{0}}$ and $t$ is a number consisting of $m>n$ nines: $t=\underbrace{99 \ldots 9}_{m}=10^{m}-1$, then

$$
k t=a_{n} a_{n-1} \ldots\left(a_{0}-1\right) \underbrace{99 \ldots 9\left(9-a_{n}\right)\left(9-a_{n-1}\right) \ldots\left(9-a_{1}\right)\left(10-a_{0}\right)}_{m \text { L上丨 }} .
$$

The sum of the digits of $k t$ is the same as that of $t$: it is equal to $9 m$.

question: 140. Two equal rectangles are positioned such that their contours intersect at eight points. Prove that the area of the common part of these rectangles is greater than half the area of each of them.
reference_solution:
140. Let $a$ and $b$ be the lengths of the sides of each rectangle. If the contours of the rectangles intersect at eight points, then on each side of any of them, there are exactly two points of intersection with the adjacent sides of the other. If there are fewer than two points of intersection on any side, then there will be fewer than eight such points in total. Therefore, no side of one rectangle can intersect two parallel sides of the other.

Now let $A$ and $C$ be the points where the sides of length $a$ intersect; $B$ and $D$ be the points where the sides of length $b$ intersect (Fig. 63). The segments $A C$ and $B D$, as can be easily seen, serve as the angle bisectors of the angles formed by the sides passing through points $A, C$ and $B, D$ respectively; therefore, $A C \perp B D$. The area $S$ of the quadrilateral $A B C D$ is equal to $A C \cdot B D$, and since $A C \geqslant b, B D \geqslant a$, then $S \geqslant a b / 2$.
