question: 141. Cards have all five-digit numbers from 11111 to 99999 written on them. Then these cards are placed in one chain in a random order. Prove that the resulting 444,445-digit number cannot be a power of two.
reference_solution:
141. We will prove that any such number is divisible by $11111 \mathrm{n}$, and therefore is not a power of two. To do this, note that $10^{5}$ when divided by 11111 leaves a remainder of $1: 10^{5}=9 \cdot 1111+1$. Therefore, any of the obtained numbers gives the same remainder when divided by 11111 as the sum of all the numbers on the cards.

It is also not difficult to show that any such number is divisible by 9. But this sum, as can be easily seen, is equal to $\frac{11111+99799}{2} \times$ $\times\left(10^{5}-1\right)$, i.e., it is divisible by 11111.

question: 142*. All natural numbers, in decimal notation of which there are no more than $n$ digits, are divided into two groups. The first group includes all numbers with an odd sum of digits, and the second group includes all numbers with an even sum of digits. Prove that if $1 \leqslant k<n$, then the sum of the $k$-th powers of all numbers in the first group is equal to the sum of the $k$-th powers of all numbers in the second group.
reference_solution:
142. Let $D_{1}$ be the set of 10 digits $\{0,1,2, \ldots, 9\}$; $A_{1}=\{0,2, \ldots, 8\}$ - the set of even digits, $B_{1}=\{1,3, \ldots, 9\}$ - the set of odd digits. In general, for any $n$, denote by $D_{n}$ the set of all numbers with no more than $n$ digits, $A_{n}$ and $B_{n}$ - its subsets of numbers with even and odd sums of digits ( $D_{n}=A_{n} \cup B_{n}$ ). Note that $B_{n}$ and $A_{n}$ each contain, counting the number consisting of all zeros, $5 \cdot 10^{n-1}$ elements. The sum of all elements $x$ of a set $X$ will be briefly written as: $\sum x$ over $x \in X$. We need to prove that $\sum a^{k}$ over $a \in A_{n}$ is equal to $\sum b^{k}$ over $b \in B_{n} ;$ this sum we will denote $S_{n}^{(k)}$.

For $n=2, k=1$, the statement of the problem reduces to the obvious equality (where $a \in A_{1}, p \in A_{1}, b \in B_{1}, q \in B_{1}$ ):

$$
\sum(10 a+p)+\sum(10 b+q)=\sum(10 a+q)+\sum(10 b+p)
$$

both sides are equal to $5\left(\sum 10 d+\sum r\right)$ over all $d_{1}: \in D_{1}, r \in D_{1}, S_{2}^{(l)} \Rightarrow$  $b, q$ enter each sum 5 times ( $a$ on the left - paired with five $p$ and vice versa).

We will illustrate further calculations with the example of $n=3$. We will find the sum over all $a \in A_{1}, p \in A_{2}, b \in B_{1}, q \in$ $\in B_{2}$ (below $d \in D_{1}, r \in D_{2}$ ):

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sum(10 a+p)^{2}+\sum(10 b+q)^{2}=50 \cdot 10^{2}\left(\sum a^{2}+\sum b^{2}\right)+ \\
& \quad+2 \cdot 10\left(\sum a \cdot p+\sum b \cdot q\right)+5 \sum p^{2}+5 \sum q^{2}= \\
& =10^{2} \sum d^{2}+2 \cdot 10\left(\sum a \cdot \sum p+\sum b \cdot \sum q\right)+5 \sum r^{2}= \\
& =5 \cdot 10^{3} \sum d^{2}+20 \sum d S_{2}^{(1)}+5 \sum r^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

It is clear that the sum $\sum(10 a+q)^{2}+\sum(10 b+p)^{2}$ is transformed in the same way. Here we used the identities $\left((x+y)^{2}=x^{2}+2 x y+y^{2}\right.$ and $\sum u v=\sum u \cdot \sum v$ (sum over all $u \in U, v \in V)$.

Now we will prove the general statement by induction on $n$. For this, we will use the formulas

$$
\begin{array}{r}
(x+y)^{k}=x^{k}+C_{k}^{1} x^{k-1} y+C_{k}^{2} x^{k-2} y+\ldots+C_{k}^{k-1} x y^{a-1}+y^{k}= \\
=x^{k}+\sum C_{k}^{l} x^{k-1} y^{l}+y^{k}
\end{array}
$$

/(the values of the "binomial coefficients" $C_{k}^{l}, 1 \leqslant j \leqslant k-1$, do not play a role in our reasoning) and $\sum u v=\sum u \sum v_{\text {。 }}$ Suppose that for $n$-digit numbers and any $1 \leqslant k<n$ the required equality is proved: $\sum p^{f}=\sum q^{f}=S_{n}^{(j)}$ (where $p \in A_{n}, q \in$ $\in B_{n}$ ). We will transform the sum of the $k$-th powers of numbers from $A_{n+1}, k<n+$ +1 (below we sum over $a \in A_{1}, p \in A_{n}, b \in B_{1}, q \in B_{n_{9}}$ $\left.d \in D_{1}, r \in D_{n}, 1 \leqslant j \leqslant k-1\right):$

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \sum(10 a+p)^{k}+\sum(10 b+q)^{k}=5 \cdot 10^{n-1} \cdot 10^{k}\left(\sum a^{k}+\sum b^{k}\right)+ \\
& +\sum C_{k}^{l} \cdot 10^{k-1}\left(\sum a^{k-1} p^{f}+\sum b^{k-1} q^{f}\right)+5\left(\sum p^{k}+\sum q^{k}\right)= \\
& \quad=5 \cdot 10^{n+k-1} \sum d^{k}+\sum_{i} C_{k}^{l} \cdot 10^{k-j} S_{k}^{(j)} \sum d^{k-1}+5 \sum r^{k}
\end{aligned}
$$

It is clear that the sum of the $k$-th powers of numbers from $B_{n+1}$ is equal to the same expression (it is only necessary to swap the letters $p$ and q).

$\nabla$ Similar identities hold in any $d$-ary number system for even $d$, for example, in binary, where - for small $n$ it can be easily verified directly.

question:
143*. The vertices of a regular $n$-gon are colored with several colors (each with one color) such that points of the same color are vertices of a regular polygon. Prove that among these polygons, there will be two equal ones.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-044.jpg?height=239&width=750&top_left_y=723&top_left_x=239)
reference_solution:
143. We will call a system of unit vectors $e_{1}, e_{2}, \ldots, e_{m}$ (with a common origin $O$) symmetric if, upon rotation by an angle $2 \pi k / m$ (for some $k < m$), it transforms into itself. The sum of the vectors in such a system is clearly zero, as it does not change upon rotation by an angle $2 \pi / m \leq 2 \pi_{\text{s}}$.

In particular, a symmetric system is formed by vectors pointing to the consecutive vertices of a regular $m$-gon: for them, $k=1$.

Let us subject all unit vectors with origin $O$ to the transformation $e \rightarrow D^{\prime} e$ ($l$-fold twisting): increase the angle from the initial direction $O x$ to $e$ by $l$ times; the resulting vector will be taken as $D^{\prime} e$. Under such a transformation $D^{t}$, a symmetric system of vectors will transform into a symmetric one if and only if $k l$ is not divisible by $m$ (the angle $2 \pi k / m$ between adjacent vectors $\boldsymbol{e}_{i}, \boldsymbol{e}_{i+1}$ will increase by $l$ times; subtracting from $2 \pi k l / m$ a multiple of $2 \pi$, we obtain that the angle between $D^{\prime} e_{i}$ and $D^{\prime} e_{i+1}$ is equal to $2 \pi r / m$, where $r$ is the remainder of the division of $k l$ by $m$). If, however, $k l$ is divisible by $m$ (in particular, when $k=m$), then all vectors $D^{\prime} e_{i}$ will merge into one.

After these remarks, let us proceed to solving the problem. Suppose that the vertices of an $n$-gon can be colored with several colors such that the vertices of the same color form regular polygons: an $l$-gon, a $q_{1}$-gon, a $q_{2}$-gon, ..., ..., a $q_{s}$-gon, where $l < q_{1} < q_{2} < \ldots < q_{s}$. We can thus divide the symmetric system of vectors drawn to the vertices of the $n$-gon into $s+1$ symmetric systems of $l_{1}$, $q_{1}, q_{2}, \ldots, q_{s}$ vectors. So far, there is no contradiction: the sum of each of them is zero, and the total sum is also zero. But if we subject all our vectors to an $l$-fold twisting, a contradiction will arise: all $l$ vectors of the first system will merge into one, so their sum will become non-zero, while the other systems - of $q_{i} (i=1,2, \ldots, s)$ vectors and of all $n$ vectors - will remain regular, since the angles between adjacent vectors in them are $2 \pi l / q_{1} < 2 \pi, 2 \pi l / q_{2} < 2 \pi, \ldots, 2 \pi l / n < 2 \pi$, so the sum in them remains equal to $\mathbf{0}$.

$\nabla$ This remarkable solution was devised by A. Lifshitz; at this Olympiad, he was already a member of the jury, and no one among the schoolchildren managed to solve the problem.

The idea of "l-fold twisting" of vectors becomes more transparent if we consider vectors as complex numbers; the transformation $D^{t}$ is simply raising to the power $z \rightarrow z^{b}$ of complex numbers $z$ with $|z|=1$; a symmetric system of vectors is a geometric progression $u, и \varepsilon, и \varepsilon^{2}, \ldots, и \varepsilon^{m}$, where $|u|=1$ and $\varepsilon$ is some $m$-th root of $1, \varepsilon \neq 1$; if the argument of the number $\varepsilon$ - the angle between adjacent vectors in the system is equal to $2 \pi k / m$, then such a system, as can be shown, consists of vectors pointing to the vertices of a regular $\mathrm{m} / \mathrm{d}$-gon, where $d$ is some divisor of $m, d<m$, and in each vertex there are $d$ vectors.

The solution to this problem shows that any partition of the set of integers $\boldsymbol{Z}$ into several non-intersecting (infinite in both directions) arithmetic progressions is obtained only in this way: $\boldsymbol{Z}$ is divided into $d$ progressions with the same difference $d$, then, perhaps, one (or several) of them is divided into progressions with the same difference, and so on. The application of complex numbers in number-theoretic problems, similar to the one described in our solution, is called the "method of trigonometric sums."

question: 144. Prove that for any natural $n$ there exists a number composed of the digits 1 and 2, divisible by $2^{n}$.
reference_solution:
144. This can be proven by induction. For $n=1$, the number 2 should be taken. If $A=2^{n} \cdot B-n$ is an $n$-digit number divisible by $2^{n}$, then one of the numbers $2 \cdot 10^{n}+A$ or $1 \cdot 10^{n}+A$ is divisible by $2^{n+1}$, because one of the numbers $5^{n}+B$ or $2 \cdot 5^{n}+B$ is even.

$\nabla$ The desired number for each $n$ is exactly one; moreover, all $n$-digit numbers composed of the digits 1 and 2 give different remainders when divided by $2^n$. Using this, another solution to the problem can be obtained.

question: 147*. In a square with a side of 1, several circles are placed, the diameter of each of which is less than 0.001. The distance between any two points of any two circles is not equal to 0.001. Prove that the total area covered by the circles does not exceed 0.34.
reference_solution:
147. Consider the figures $F_{1}$ and $F_{2}$, obtained from the given figure $F$ (a union of circles) by translations along vectors of length 0.001, forming an angle of $60^{\circ}$ with each other.

The three figures $F, F_{1}, F_{2}$ do not overlap and lie within a square with side length 1.001. Therefore, the area $S$ of each of them is less than

$$
(1.001)^{2} / 3 < 0.34
$$

$\nabla$ Similarly, for the spatial analog of this problem, we can obtain the estimate (1.001$)^{2} / 4 < 0.26$.

On the plane, the estimate can be significantly refined: for example, it can be proven that $S < 0.287$ ("Kvant", 1972, No. 8, p. 58).

question:
148*. Three vessels contain a whole number of liters of water each. It is allowed to pour from any vessel into any other as much water as the latter already contains. Prove that by several such pourings one can empty one of the vessels. (The vessels are large enough: each can hold all the available water.)

翻译结果如下：

148*. Three vessels contain a whole number of liters of water each. It is allowed to pour from any vessel into any other as much water as the latter already contains. Prove that by several such pourings one can empty one of the vessels. (The vessels are large enough: each can hold all the available water.)
reference_solution:
148. Let the vessels $A, B$, and $C$ contain $a, b$, and $c$ liters of water, respectively, with $0<a \leqslant b \leqslant c$. It is sufficient to achieve, through several pourings, that one of the vessels will contain less than $a$ liters of water (by repeating this procedure, we can reduce the amount of water in one vessel to 0). We divide $b$ by $a$ with a remainder: $b=a d+r, 0 \leqslant r<a$. We will pour water from $B$ and $C$ into $A$, (in $A$ there will be $2 a, 2^{2} a, 2^{3} a, \ldots, 2^{k} a$ liters of water) in such a way that exactly $d a$ liters are poured from $B$; then $B$ will have $r<a$ liters left. We can act this way since $d$, like any natural number, can be and uniquely represented as the sum of some of the numbers $1,2,2^{2}, \ldots, 2^{k}, \ldots$ The corresponding portions of water $2^{k} a$ should be taken from $B$, the rest - from $C$.

In this process, no more water will be poured from $C$ than from $B$, from which the last portion is taken, so there will be enough water in $C$.

question: 149. Prove that if for numbers $p_{1}, p_{2}, q_{1}, q_{2}$ the inequality $\left(q_{1}-q_{2}\right)^{2}+\left(p_{1}-p_{2}\right)\left(p_{1} q_{2}-\right.$ - $\left.p_{2} q_{1}\right)<0$ holds, then the quadratic trinomials $x^{2}+p_{1} x+q_{1}$ and $x^{2}+p_{2} x+q_{2}$ have real roots and between the two roots of each of them lies a root of the other,
reference_solution:
149. The condition that the roots of the quadratic polynomials $f_{1}(x)=x^{2}+p_{1} x+q_{1}$ and $\mathrm{f}_{2}(x)=x^{2}+p_{2} x+q_{2}$ are real and interlaced is equivalent to the graphs $y=f_{1}(x)$ and $y=f_{2}(x)$ intersecting at a point $(x_{0}, y_{0})$ lying below the x-axis: $y_{0}<0$. Solving the equation $f_{1}(x)=f_{2}(x)$, we find $x_{0}=\left(q_{2}-q_{1}\right) /\left(p_{2}-p_{1}\right)$ and $y_{0}=$ $=R\left(p_{1}-p_{2}\right)^{2}$, where

$$
R=\left(q_{1}-q_{2}\right)^{2}+\left(p_{1}-p_{2}\right)\left(p_{1} q_{2}-p_{2} q_{1}\right) .
$$

$\nabla$ The expression $R$ equals zero if and only if $f_{1}$ and $f_{2}$ have a common (possibly complex) root. Such a polynomial in the coefficients of two given polynomials $f_{1}$ and $f_{2}$ of any degrees is called their "resultant".

question: 150. Projections of a body onto two planes - circles. Prove that these circles have equal radii.
reference_solution: 150. If the planes are parallel, this is obvious. Let them not be parallel. Then the projection of the body onto the line $l$ of intersection of the planes can be obtained as the projection onto $l$ of each of the projections of this body onto one and the other plane. (Everywhere we are talking about orthogonal projections: the set of bases of perpendiculars.) But the projection of a circle onto a line in its plane is a segment of length equal to the diameter of the circle.

question: 151. Several numbers are written in a circle. If for some four consecutive numbers $a, b, c, d$ it turns out that $(a-d)(b-c)<0$, then the numbers $b$ and $c$ can be swapped. Prove that such an operation can be performed only a finite number of times.
reference_solution: 151. As a result of the sorting operation, the sum $S$ of the pairwise products of adjacent numbers increases (in this sum $a b+$ $+b c+c d$ is replaced by $a c+c b+b d$, and $a b+c d<a c+b d_{\text {n }}$ if $(a-d)(b-c)<0$.) However, the sum $S$ can take only a finite number of different values (P13).

question:
152. a) Prove that a line dividing a given triangle into two polygons of equal area and equal perimeter passes through the center of the circle inscribed in the triangle.

b) Prove an analogous statement for an arbitrary polygon in which a circle can be inscribed.

c) Prove that all lines dividing both the area and the perimeter of a triangle in half intersect at one point.
reference_solution:
152. Let's immediately solve the general problem b). Suppose a line $l$ intersects the contour of a circumscribed polygon at points $R$ and $Q$ and divides its perimeter in half. Then the broken line consisting of two segments $O R$ and $O Q$, where $O$ is the center of the circle, divides its area in half; this is proven in the same way as the formula $S=\operatorname{Pr} / 2$ for the area of a circumscribed polygon with perimeter $P$: one needs to draw segments from the center $O$ to all vertices of the polygon and write the area of each triangle as half the product of the length of the base and the height, which is equal to the radius of the circle. Therefore, if the line $R Q$ also divides the area in half, the point $O$ must lie on this line.

$\nabla$ An interesting question is how many such lines (for a triangle and for an $n$-sided polygon) can exist that divide both the area and the perimeter in half («Kvant», 1972, № 7, p. 35).

question:
154. a) At vertex $A_{1}$ of a regular 12-sided polygon $A_{1} A_{2} \ldots A_{12}$, there is a minus sign, while the others have plus signs. It is allowed to simultaneously change the sign to the opposite in any six consecutive vertices of the polygon. Prove that it is impossible to achieve, after several such operations, that vertex $A_{2}$ has a minus sign, and the other vertices have plus signs.

b) Prove the same statement if it is allowed to change the signs in any four consecutive vertices of the polygon.

c) Prove the same statement if it is allowed to simultaneously change the sign in any three consecutive vertices of the polygon.
reference_solution:
154. a) Let's divide all 12 vertices into 6 pairs of opposite vertices: $A_{1} A_{7}, A_{2} A_{8}, A_{3} A_{9}, \ldots, A_{6} A_{12}$. With each operation, only one vertex in each pair changes its sign. Therefore, in pairs $A_{2} A_{8}, \ldots, A_{6} A_{12}$, after the $(2 k-1)$-th operation, the signs will be different, and after the $2 k$-th operation, they will be the same (in the pair $A_{1} A_{7}$, it will be the opposite). Therefore, it cannot happen that in the pair $A_{2} A_{8}$ the signs are different, while in the pair $A_{3} A_{9}$ they are the same.

b) Consider the partition into 4 groups of three vertices: $A_{1} A_{5} A_{9}, A_{2} A_{6} A_{10}, A_{3} A_{7} A_{11}, A_{4} A_{8} A_{12}$ and reason similarly as above. The parity of the number of minuses in each group changes with each operation, and the parity in groups $A_{2} A_{6} A_{10}$ and $A_{3} A_{7} A_{11}$ is the same.

c) Similar reasoning for the partition into 3 groups $A_{1} A_{1} A_{7} A_{10}, A_{2} A_{5} A_{6} A_{11}, A_{3} A_{8} A_{9} A_{12}$.

$\nabla$ Generally, it can be determined which sets can be transformed into each other by changing the signs of $k$ consecutive vertices of an $n$-gon. The answer is as follows: associate each set $\varepsilon_{1}, \varepsilon_{2}, \ldots, \varepsilon_{n}$ of numbers $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{k}= \pm 1$ at the vertices of the $n$-gon with a set of $d$ numbers $\left(x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{d}\right)$, where $d=$ GCD $(n, k)$, as follows

$$
x_{i}=\varepsilon_{i} e_{i+d} \cdots \varepsilon_{i+n-d^{*}}
$$

Then two sets $\left(\varepsilon_{i}\right),\left(\varepsilon_{i}^{\prime}\right)$ can be transformed into each other if and only if either the corresponding sets $\left(x_{i}\right),\left(x_{i}^{\prime}\right)$ are the same, or $k / d$ is even and the sets $\left(x_{i}\right),\left(x_{i}^{\prime}\right)$ are opposite: $x_{i}=-x_{i}^{\prime}$ for all $t$.

question:
155*. On an infinite sheet of graph paper, $N$ cells are painted black. Prove that it is possible to cut out a finite number of squares from the sheet such that the following two conditions are met:

1) all black cells will lie within the cut-out squares
2) in any cut-out square, the area of black cells will constitute no less than $1 / 5$ and no more than $4 / 5$ of the area of this square.

The problems 156-158, proposed to 10th-grade students on the second day of the olympiad, were preceded by the following text:

«You are offered three problems. A correct solution to any of them presents serious challenges and requires a lot of time. Choose one of these problems and try to make as much progress as possible.

Before the end of the session, prepare a "summary of results" for the problem you worked on: list the facts you have proven, indicate examples in which you were able to figure out, formulate hypotheses that seem correct to you.»
reference_solution:
155. We can act by the "binary search" method. Cut out a large square $K_{0}$ of $2^{n} \times 2^{n}$ cells from the plane, containing all the black cells and at least four times as many white cells; then the area of the black cells is less than $1 / 5$ of the area of the square $K_{0}$. Cut $K_{0}$ into four squares $K_{1}$ of $2^{n-1} \times 2^{n-1}$ cells. In each of $K_{1}$, the black cells occupy no more than $4 / 5$ of its area, so either it satisfies both conditions 1) and 2), or it can be cut again into four squares $K_{2}$, and so on, down to $2 \times 2$ squares, from which all empty ones should be discarded, and all with one, two, and three shaded cells should be kept.

$\nabla$ Similar problems can be formulated for a line divided into unit segments (with constants $1 / 3$ and $2 / 3$), for space divided into cubes (with constants $1 / 9$ and $8 / 9$).

question:
157. a) Consider the function $f(x, y)=x^{2}+x y+$ $+y^{2}$. Prove that for any point $(x, y)$ there exist integers $(m, n)$ such that $f(x-m, y-n)=$ $=(x-m)^{2}+(x-m)(y-n)+(y-n)^{2} \leqslant 1 / 2$.

b) * Denote by $\bar{f}(x, y)$ the minimum of the numbers $f(x-m, y-n)$ for all integers $m$ and $n$. The statement of part a) was that for all $x, y$ the inequality $f(x, y) \leqslant 1 / 2$ holds.

Prove that in fact the stronger inequality $f(x, y) \leqslant 1 / 3$ holds. Find all points for which the equality $\bar{f}(x, y)=1 / 3$ is achieved.
c) * Consider the function $\left.f_{a}(x, y)=x^{2}+a x y^{\prime}+\right]$ $+y^{2}(0 \leqslant a \leqslant 2)$. Find some number $c$ depending on $a$ such that for all $(x, y)$ the inequality $\left|f_{a}(x, y)\right| \leqslant c$ holds. Try to find the best possible estimate.
reference_solution:
157. For each point $(x, y)$ on the plane, we need to find a point $(m, n)$ on the integer lattice for which the value $f_{a}(x-m, y-n)$ is as small as possible, and to find an upper estimate of this minimum $\vec{f}_{a}(x, y)=\min _{m, n} f_{a}(x-m, y-n)$. It is convenient to call the quantity $\left.\sqrt{f_{a}\left(x_{1}-x_{2}, y_{1}-y_{2}\right.}\right)$ the "distance" between points $\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right)$ and $\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right)$, by analogy with the usual distance $\sqrt{f_{0}\left(x_{1}-x_{2}, y_{1}-y_{2}\right)}=\sqrt{\left(x_{1}-x_{2}\right)^{2}+\left(y_{1}-y_{2}\right)^{2}}$. Note that for this distance, the exact estimate is: $\ldots_{0}(x, y) \leqslant 1 / 2$. Indeed, for each square $m-\frac{1}{2} \leqslant x \leqslant m+\frac{1}{2}$, $n-\frac{1}{2} \leqslant y \leqslant n+\frac{1}{2}$, the distance from any of its points $(x, y)$ to the center $(m, n)$ is no more than $\sqrt{2} / 2$, and for any vertex of such a square, it is equal to $\sqrt{2} / 2$, i.e., $f_{0}\left(x_{0}, y_{0}\right)=1 / 2$.

Let's try to construct a partition of the plane into figures $\Phi_{m, n}$ for other "distances" $\sqrt{\vec{f}_{a}}, 0<a<2$, based on the following criterion: a point $(x, y)$ belongs to $\Phi_{m, n}$ if the "distance" from it to $(m, n)$ is less than (or not greater than) the distance to any other lattice point. It is sufficient to find the figure $\Phi_{00}$ with the center at $(0 ; 0)$; the others will be obtained from it by translations of the centers by vectors with coordinates $(m ; n)$; since such translations preserve the distance $\sqrt{\widetilde{f}_{a}}$, they also preserve the principle by which points of the region with a given center are selected. Now we use the fact that the square of the distance $f_{a}$ is a quadratic function of the coordinates. The set of points closer to $(0 ; 0)$ than to $(m ; n)$ is simply a half-plane: the inequality

$$
x^{2}+a x y+y^{2} \leqslant(x-m)^{2}+a(x-m)(y-n)+(y-n)^{2}
$$

is equivalent to the linear inequality

$$
(2 m+a n) x+(2 n+a m) y \leqslant m^{2}+a m n+n^{2}
$$

To find the figure $\Phi_{00}$, we would need to take the intersection of all such half-planes (for all $(m ; n)$, different from $(0 ; 0)$). It turns out that it is sufficient to take only six of them, corresponding to the six pairs $(0 ; \pm 1),( \pm 1 ; 0),(1 ;-1),(-1 ; 1)$. This will become clear when we verify that the intersection of these six half-planes (this is a convex hexagon $(-1 \leqslant 2 x+a y \leqslant 1, -1 \leqslant a x+2 y \leqslant 1, -1 \leqslant x-y \leqslant 1$) does not intersect with its images under parallel translations by vectors $(m ; n)$ (more precisely, it has only common boundary segments with them, see Fig. 65); thus, $\Phi_{00}$ cannot be smaller than this

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-168.jpg?height=594&width=641&top_left_y=711&top_left_x=288)

Fig. 65

hexagon, and therefore coincides with it. The maximum of $f_{a}(x, y)$ for $(x, y) \in \Phi_{\text {оо }}$ is achieved at the vertices of this hexagon, since when moving along any segment of a straight line $x=b+u t, y=1$ $=c+v t$, the square of the distance $f_{a}(b+u t, c+v t)$ depends on $t$ as a quadratic trinomial with a positive coefficient $u^{2}+a u v+v^{2}$ at $t^{2}$, so $f_{a}$ takes its maximum value at the endpoints of the segment. By finding the coordinates of the vertices (see Fig. 65) and substituting them into the expression for $f_{a}$, we obtain the exact estimate for $f_{a} ; f_{a} \leqslant 1 /(a+2)$. The same estimate is valid for $a=2$, when $f_{2}(x, y)$ is simply the square of the difference between $x+y$ and the nearest integer: the exact estimate $\bar{f}_{2}(x, y) \leqslant 1 / 4$.
$\nabla$ The main idea of solving this problem - partitioning the plane into regions containing given centers, where each point belongs to the nearest center - is used in various problems of analysis, geometry, and number theory (see [71]).

question: 159. In rectangle $A B C D$, point $M$ is the midpoint of side $A D$, and point $N$ is the midpoint of side $B C$. On the extension of segment $D C$ beyond point $D$, point $P$ is taken. Denote the intersection point of lines $P M$ and $A C$ as $Q$. Prove that $\angle Q N M = \angle M N P$.
reference_solution:
159. Let $R$ be the point of intersection of the lines $Q N$ and $C D$, and $O$ the center of the rectangle $A B C D$. From $O M=O N$ it follows that $P C = C R$, and therefore triangle $P N R$ is isosceles (with $N C$ being both the median and the altitude of this triangle).

The statement of the problem follows from the equality of angles $\angle M N P = \angle N P R$ and $\angle Q N M = \angle Q R P$.

question:
162. a) Let $a, m, n$ be natural numbers, $a>1$. Prove that if $a^{m}+1$ is divisible by $a^{n}+1$, then $m$ is divisible by $n$.

b) Let $a, b, m, n$ be natural numbers, where $a$ is coprime with $b$ and $a>1$. Prove that if $a^{m}+b^{m}$ is divisible by $a^{n}+b^{n}$, then $m$ is divisible by $n$.
reference_solution:
162. First, let's prove the following two statements.

a) if \(a^{k}+b^{k}\) is divisible by \(a^{n}+b^{n}\), then \(a^{k-n}-b^{k-n}\) is also divisible by \(a^{n}+b^{n}\);

b) if \(a^{t}-b^{t}\) is divisible by \(a^{n}+b^{n}\), then \(a^{l-n}+b^{t-n}\) is also divisible by \(a^{n}+b^{n}\).

These statements easily follow from the mutual simplicity of \(\boldsymbol{a}\) and \(b\) and the identities

\[
\begin{gathered}
a^{k}+b^{k}=a^{k-n}\left(a^{n}+b^{n}\right)-b^{n}\left(a^{k-n}-b^{k-n}\right) \\
a^{l}-b^{l}=a^{l-n}\left(a^{n}+b^{n}\right)-b^{n}\left(a^{l-n}+b^{l-n}\right)
\end{gathered}
\]

Divide \(m\) by \(n\) with a remainder: \(m=q n+r\), where \(0 \leqslant r<n\); subtracting \(q\) times \(n\) from \(m\), we get \(r\).

From the problem statement and statements a) and b), it follows that \(a^{r}+(-1)^{a} b^{r}\) is divisible by \(a^{n}+b^{n}\); but \(0 \leqslant\left|a^{r}+(-1)^{a} b^{r}\right|<a^{n}+b^{n}\). Therefore, it follows that \(r=0\) (and in this case \(q\) is odd!).

question: 163. A triangular table is constructed according to the following rule: the top row contains a natural number $a$, and below each number $k$ on the left, $k^{2}$ is written, and on the right, the number $k+1$ is written. For example, when $\boldsymbol{a}=2$, the table shown in Fig. 9 is obtained. Prove that in each row of such a table, all numbers are distinct.
reference_solution:
163. Suppose that in some rows of the table, the same numbers appear. Let $n$ be the number of the highest such row, and $p$ and $q$ be the equal numbers in this row.

Since there are no equal numbers in the $(n-1)$-th row, $p$ and $q$ are obtained from numbers $r$ and $s$ in this row through different operations: let $p=r^2, q=s+1$, then $s=r^2-1$.

On the path leading from the top number $a$ to the number $s$, there could have been squaring and adding of ones. The largest number that could have been squared was $r-1$ (since $s=r^2-1$). This means that the number $s$ could have been obtained from the last square encountered on the path in no fewer than $r^2-1-(r-1)^2=2r-2$ steps, with one being added at each step. Thus, the number $s$ was obtained from $a$ in no fewer than $2r-1$ steps (i.e., $n-2 \geq 2r-1$). But in the same row as $s$ stands $r$, and any number obtained from $a$ in such a number of steps is no less than $a+2r-1 > r$. Therefore, there were no squaring operations in obtaining $s$, so $q$ is the rightmost, smallest number in the $n$-th row, which contradicts the equality $p=q$.

$\nabla$ The analysis of the solution shows that the squaring operation can be replaced by any function $f$ that takes natural values and such that $f(n+1) - f(n) > n+1$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-172.jpg?height=415&width=473&top_left_y=1091&top_left_x=576)

Fig. 67

question: 164*. Given several squares, the sum of whose areas is 1. Prove that they can be placed without overlapping in a square of area 2.
reference_solution:
164. Arrange the squares in descending order of their sides and start placing them from the largest $x \times x$, from left to right along the bottom side of the square area $\sqrt{2} \times \sqrt{2}$ (Fig. 67); as soon as the next square does not fit - it protrudes beyond the right side of the area, - we draw a horizontal line along the top side of the left square and start a new row. Let $x=h_{1}, h_{2}, h_{3} \ldots$ be the sides of the squares adjacent to the left side of the area. We need to prove that the height $h=h_{1}+h_{2}+h_{3}+\ldots$ is less than $\sqrt{2}$, i.e., that the squares will run out before they protrude beyond the top side of the area.

Estimate their total area. Mentally move each of the left squares with sides $h_{k}(k=2,3, \ldots)$ to the end of the previous $(k-1)$-th row. It will protrude beyond the right side, so after such a procedure, the area of the squares in the $(k-1)$-th row will be at least $(\sqrt{2}-x) h_{k}$; in the 1-st row, we do not count the large left square. Thus, the total area of all the squares, which is 1 by condition, is not less than

$$
x^{2}+(\sqrt{2}-x)\left(h_{2}+h_{3}+\ldots\right)=x^{2}+(\sqrt{2}-x)(h-x)
$$

From this, we can obtain an estimate for $h$. Since $\sqrt{2}-x>0$, from the inequality $x^{2}+(\sqrt{2}-x)(h-x) \leqslant 1$ it follows that

$$
h \leqslant \frac{1-x^{2}}{\sqrt{2}-x}+x=3 \sqrt{2}-\sqrt{2}\left(2-x \sqrt{2}+\frac{1}{2-x \sqrt{2}}\right) \leqslant \sqrt{2}
$$

since the number in the parentheses of the form $t+\frac{1}{t}$ is not less than 2. (equality is possible only when $x=\sqrt{2} / 2$). This problem and its variants are discussed in the note [67].

question: 165. $O$ is the intersection point of the diagonals of a convex quadrilateral $A B C D$. Prove that the line passing through the points of intersection of the medians of triangles $A O B$ and $C O D$ is perpendicular to the line passing through the points of intersection of the altitudes of triangles $B O C$ and $A O D$.
reference_solution:
165. Points $K, L, M, N$ - the intersections of the altitudes of triangles $A O B, B O C, C O D$ and $D O A$ - are the vertices of a parallelogram, two sides of which lie on lines passing through points $A$ and $C$ perpendicular to $B D$, and the other two - on lines passing through points $B$ and $D$ perpendicular to $A C$ (Fig. $68, a$).

Points $K^{\prime}, L^{\prime}, M^{\prime}$ and $N^{\prime}$ - the intersections of the medians of triangles $A O B, B O C, C O D$ and $D O A$ - are the vertices of a parallelogram, two sides of which are parallel to $B D$ and divide the segment $A C$ into three equal parts, and the other two are parallel to $A C$ and divide the segment $B D$ into three equal parts (Fig. 68,6).

It is clear that the sides of these parallelograms are respectively perpendicular. We will prove that the parallelograms are similar; from this it will follow that if one of them is rotated by $90^{\circ}$, not only its sides but also its diagonals will become parallel to the diagonals of the other, i.e., $K^{\prime} M^{\prime} \perp K M$ (and $L^{\prime} N^{\prime} \perp L N$), which is required. For the similarity of the parallelograms, the sides need to be proportional. The lengths of sides $K^{\prime} L^{\prime}$ and $K N$ are $A C / 3$ and $B D / 3$. The projection of side $K L$ onto the line $B D$ coincides with the projection of segment $A C$ onto this line, so $K L = A C \cdot \operatorname{ctg} \varphi$, where $\varphi$ is the acute angle between the lines $A C$ and $B D$; similarly, $K N = B D \cdot \operatorname{ctg} \varphi$. Thus, the sides of both parallelograms are in the ratio $A C: B D$, from which the similarity follows.

If the angle $\varphi$ is a right angle, then all points $K, L, M, N$ coincide, and the problem loses its meaning.

question: 166. Each of the nine lines divides the square into two quadrilaterals, the areas of which are in the ratio $2: 3$. Prove that at least three of these nine lines pass through one point.
reference_solution:
166. Each line dividing a square into two trapezoids (or rectangles) with an area ratio of $2: 3$, divides the median line of the square, running along the midlines of these trapezoids, in the same ratio; this follows from the formula: the area of a trapezoid is equal to the product of the height and the length of the median line.

There are four points that divide one of the median lines in the ratio $2: 3$ (Fig. 69), and nine lines, so in one of these points, three lines must intersect (P9).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-174.jpg?height=247&width=260&top_left_y=801&top_left_x=789)

Fig. 69

question: 170. A point $O$ inside a convex polygon forms an isosceles triangle with every pair of its vertices. Prove that this point is equidistant from the vertices of the polygon.
reference_solution:
170. For triangle $ABC$, it is easy to prove: if a point lies inside this triangle and triangles $AOB_1$, $BOC$, $COA$ are isosceles, then at least two of the angles $\angle AOB$, $\angle BOC$, $\angle COA$ are greater than $120^{\circ}$. Let these angles be $\angle AOB$ and $\angle BOC$. Then $AO = BO = OC$. Using this special case as
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-176.jpg?height=326&width=712&top_left_y=221&top_left_x=238)

Fig. 70

a lemma, let's now prove the statement of the problem for a polygon. If $A$ and $B$ are any two of its vertices, then either the angle formed by the extensions of $AO$ and $BO$ beyond point $O$ contains a vertex $C$ of the polygon, or this angle intersects a side $DE$ of the polygon (Fig. 70). In the first case, the point lies inside $\triangle ABC$ and, as proved above, $AO = BO = CO$. In the second case, $O$ lies inside $\triangle BDE$ and $\triangle ADE$, so $AO = DO = EO = BO$.

question:
174. At the trial, 14 coins were presented as physical evidence. The expert found that coins from 1st to 7th are counterfeit, and from 8th to 14th are genuine. The court, however, only knows that counterfeit coins weigh the same, genuine coins weigh the same, and that counterfeit coins are lighter than genuine ones. The expert has at his disposal a balance scale without weights.

a) The expert wants to prove to the court that the coins from 1st to 7th are counterfeit. How can he do this using only three weighings?

b) Show that with three weighings, he can prove even more: that the coins from 1st to 7th are counterfeit, and from 8th to 14th are genuine.
reference_solution:
174. Let's present the solution to part b). The expert should conduct the following three weighings.

$1^{\circ}$. The expert places the 1st coin on the left pan and the 8th coin on the right pan. Since the right pan outweighs, the court sees that the 1st coin is counterfeit and the 8th coin is genuine.

$2^{\circ}$. The 2nd, 3rd, and 8th coins are placed on the right pan, and the 9th, 10th, and 1st coins are placed on the left pan. The left pan outweighs, and the court

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-179.jpg?height=182&width=300&top_left_y=441&top_left_x=237)

$a$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-179.jpg?height=301&width=278&top_left_y=723&top_left_x=244)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-179.jpg?height=234&width=241&top_left_y=396&top_left_x=653)

$\delta$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-179.jpg?height=330&width=361&top_left_y=701&top_left_x=578)

Fig. 73

is convinced that the 2nd and 3rd coins are counterfeit, and the 9th and 10th coins are genuine.

$3^{\circ}$. The expert places the 4th, 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th, 9th, and 10th coins on the left pan, and the rest on the right pan. The right pan outweighs, and the court sees that there are more genuine coins on the right pan than on the left, and more counterfeit coins on the left pan than on the right. This convinces the court that the 4th, 5th, 6th, and 7th coins are counterfeit, and the 11th, 12th, 13th, and 14th coins are genuine.

$\nabla$ Similarly, the verification of $2^{k}-1$ counterfeit and $2^{k}-1$ genuine coins can be carried out in $k$ weighings for any $k \geqslant 1$.

question: 175. Prove that a nine-digit number, in the notation of which all digits except zero are used, and which ends with the digit 5, cannot be a perfect square of an integer.
reference_solution: 175. Suppose there exists a perfect square $D=A^{2}$ satisfying the conditions of the problem. The number $A$, obviously, ends in the digit 5, i.e., $A=10 a+5$. Therefore, $D=100 a(a+1)+25$ ends in 25. The number $a(a+1)$ ends in either 2, 6, or 0. Therefore, the third digit from the right of the number $D$ is 6. Thus, $D=1000 k+625$. We see that $D$ is divisible by $5^{3}=125$, and therefore also by $5^{4}$. Therefore, $k$ is divisible by 5, and thus the fourth digit from the right of the number $D$ is either 0 or 5, which is impossible.

question: 176. Given $n$ points, $n>4$. Prove that it is possible to connect them with arrows so that from any point to any other point it is possible to get by following either one arrow or two (any two points can be connected by an arrow in only one direction; it is possible to follow an arrow only in the direction indicated on it).
reference_solution:
176. The problem is solved by induction. For $n=3, n=5$ and $n=6$ the required systems of points are shown in Fig. $73, a-c$, while Fig. 73,2 shows one way to transform a system of $n$ points $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}$, connected by arrows as needed, into the required system with $n+2$ points $A_{1}$, $A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}, A_{n+1}, A_{n+2}$. For this, we add arrows from $A_{n+1}$ to all points $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}$; from each point $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}$, we draw an arrow to $A_{n+2}$; finally, from $A_{n+2}$, we draw an arrow to point $A_{n+1}$.

By the principle of complete induction, the statement of the problem is true for all odd $n \geqslant 3$ and all even $n \geqslant 6$.

For $n=4$, the required system of points does not exist.

question: 177. Given an angle with vertex $O$ and a circle tangent to its sides at points $A$ and $B$. From point $A$, a ray is drawn parallel to $OB$, intersecting the circle at point $C$. Segment $OC$ intersects the circle at point $E$, and lines $AE$ and $OB$ intersect at point $K$. Prove that $OK=KB$.
reference_solution:
177. Let $P$ and $Q$ be points

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-180.jpg?height=277&width=396&top_left_y=513&top_left_x=664)

Fig. 74 shows the points of intersection of the tangent to the given circle at point $C$ with the sides of the angle. Since $A P = P C$, $\triangle A P C$ and consequently $\triangle O P Q$ are isosceles. Therefore, $A O = C Q = O B = B Q$ (Fig. 74).

Note that $\angle O A E = \angle O C A = \angle C O Q$, and $\angle A O B = \angle C Q B$. From the similarity of $\triangle O A K \sim \triangle Q O C$, it follows that:

$$
\frac{O K}{O A} = \frac{C Q}{O Q} = \frac{1}{2}
$$

Thus, $O K = O A / 2 = O B / 2$. The equality of angles $\angle O A E = \angle A C O$ follows from the theorem about the angle between a tangent and a chord.

question:
178. Real numbers \(a, b, c\) are such that for all numbers \(x\) satisfying the condition \(-1 \leqslant x \leqslant 1\), the inequality

\[
\left|a x^{2}+b x+c\right| \leqslant 1
\]

is satisfied. Prove that for these values of \(x\), the inequality

\[
\left|c x^{2}+b x+a\right| \leqslant 2
\]

is also satisfied.
reference_solution:
178. Let $f(x)=a x^{2}+b x+c, g(x)=c x^{2}+b x+a$. Since $f(1)=g(1)$ and $f(-1)=g(-1)$, then $|g(1)| \leqslant 1$ and $|g(-1)| \leqslant 1$, in addition, $|c|=|f(0)| \leqslant 1$.

Suppose there exists a point $x$ for which $|g(x)|>2$. Then the vertex of the parabola $y=g(x)$ is the point with coordinates ( $x_{0}, g\left(x_{0}\right)$ ), and $\left|x_{0}\right| \leqslant 1$ and $\left|g\left(x_{0}\right)\right|>2$. Completing the square, we get $g(x)=c\left(x-x_{0}\right)^{2}+g\left(x_{0}\right)$. Substitute into this equation the closest to $x_{0}$ of the numbers -1 and 1 (for definiteness, let's assume it is 1). Then $\left|1-x_{0}\right| \leqslant 1$ and therefore $\left|g\left(x_{0}\right)\right|=\left|g(1)-c\left(1-x_{0}\right)^{2}\right| \leqslant \mid g(1)+$. $|+| c|\leqslant 1+| c \mid \leqslant 2$, which contradicts the inequality $g\left(x_{0}\right)>2$.

The example of the polynomial $f(x)=2 x^{2}-1$ shows that the estimate $|g(x)| \leqslant 2$ cannot be improved. (In this case $g(x)=-x^{2}+2$.)

question: 180. The quadratic trinomial \( f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c \) is such that the equation \( f(x) = x \) has no real roots. Prove that the equation \( f(f(x)) = x \) also has no real roots.
reference_solution:
180. If the equation $f(x)=x$ has no roots, then either $f(x)>x$ for all $x$ (if $a>0$), or $f(x)<x$, or $f(f(x))<f(x)<x$, which means that the equation $f(f(x))=x$ has no roots.

$\nabla$ The statement of the problem is true not only for a quadratic trinomial, but also for any continuous function.

question: 181. On an infinite grid of white paper, $n$ cells are painted black. At moments $t=1,2, \ldots$ all cells on the sheet are simultaneously repainted according to the following rule: each cell $K$ acquires the color that the majority of three cells had in the previous moment: the cell $K$ itself and its neighbors to the right and above (if two or three of these cells were white, then $K$ becomes white; if two or three of them were black, then $K$ becomes black). a) Prove that after a finite time, there will be no black cells left on the sheet; b) Prove that the black cells will disappear no later than at moment $t=n$.
reference_solution:
181. a) Note that if we add several more black cells to the given set of black cells, then after recoloring, only additional black cells may appear. Add cells to the initial set $M$ so that a black square of $m \times m$ cells is formed.

After $2 m-1$ steps, nothing will remain of the square (and thus of $M$).

b) Let the set of black cells that results from $M$ after $t$ steps be denoted by $M_{t}$. We will prove by induction on $n$ that for any set $M$ of $n$ cells, $M_{n}$ is empty. (For $n=1$ this is clear.) Suppose this is proven for sets of fewer than $n$ cells, and consider an arbitrary set $M$ of $n$ cells. We can assume that $M$ lies on the coordinate plane $Oxy$ in the quadrant $x \geqslant 0, y \geqslant 0$, with at least one cell from $M$ in the strips $0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1$ and $0 \leqslant y \leqslant 1$ (Fig. 75). Then, by the induction hypothesis, $M_{n-1}$ does not intersect the quadrant $x \geqslant 0, y \geqslant 1$ (cells in the strip $0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1$ do not affect what happens for $x \geqslant 1$), so $M_{n-1}$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-182.jpg?height=403&width=397&top_left_y=471&top_left_x=164)

Fig. 75

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-182.jpg?height=516&width=406&top_left_y=373&top_left_x=657)

Fig. 76

lies in the strip $0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1$. Similarly, it can be shown that $M_{n-1}$ lies in the strip $0 \leqslant y \leqslant 1$. Therefore, $M_{n-1}$ can contain only one cell, and $M_{n}$ is empty.

$\nabla$ More complex problems of this type are discussed in the article [74].

question:
182. On the sides of an acute-angled triangle $A B C$, three similar acute-angled triangles $A C_{1} B$, $B A_{1} C$, and $C B_{1} A$ are constructed outwardly (such that $\angle A B_{1} C=\angle A B C_{1}=\angle A_{1} B C$; $\left.\angle B A_{1} C=\angle B A C_{1}=\angle B_{1} A C\right)$.

a) Prove that the circumcircles of triangles $A C_{1} B$, $B A_{1} C$, and $C B_{1} A$ intersect at one point.

b) Prove that the lines $A A_{1}$, $B B_{1}$, and $C C_{1}$ also intersect at the same point.
reference_solution:
182. Let $D$ be the point of intersection of $A A_{1}$ and $B B_{1}$. Since $\angle A_{1} C A = \angle B_{1} C B$ (Fig. 76) and $A_{1} C : B C = A C : B_{1} C$, triangles $A_{1} C A$ and $B_{1} C B$ are similar, therefore, $\angle D B C = \angle D A_{1} C$. Hence, points $B, D, C, A_{1}$ lie on the same circle. It is also proven that points $A, D, C, B_{1}$ lie on the same circle, i.e., point $D$ is the point of intersection of the circumcircles of triangles $A_{1} B C$ and $A B_{1} C$.

Now, note that $\angle A D B = 180^{\circ} - \angle A D B_{1} = 180^{\circ} - \angle A C_{1} B$, so points $A, D, B$ and $C_{1}$ lie on the same circle. Thus, $D$ is the point of intersection of all three circumcircles, and as proven earlier - line $C C_{1}$ passes through point $D$.

question: 183. $N$ people are not acquainted with each other. Some of them need to be introduced to each other so that no three people have the same number of acquaintances. Prove that this can be done for any $N$.
reference_solution:
183. This problem can be solved by the method of mathematical induction. Such a solution is also possible.

Let us number $N$ people with numbers from 1 to $N$ and introduce person with number $i$ to person with number $j$ if $|i-j| \leqslant$
$\leqslant N / 2$. It is easy to see that with this method of introduction, only people with numbers $k$ and $N-k$ will have the same number of acquaintances. Therefore, no three people will have the same number of acquaintances.

question: 185. Given a triangle with area 1 and sides $a, b, c$. It is known that $a \geqslant b \geqslant c$. Prove that $b \geqslant \sqrt{2}$.
reference_solution: 185. Since $1 \leqslant bc / 2 \leqslant b^{2} / 2, b \geqslant \sqrt{2}$.

question: 186. Given a convex $n$-gon with pairwise non-parallel sides and a point inside it. Prove that through this point, no more than $n$ lines can be drawn, each of which divides the area of the $n$-gon in half.
reference_solution:
186. Let each of the two lines bisect the area of polygon $M$. Then in each of the two vertical angles formed by these lines, there lie parts of the polygon of equal area (in Fig. 78, these are $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$).

Consider together with the given polygon $M$ its symmetric counterpart $M^{\prime}$ relative to point $O$. If $k$ lines pass through point $O$, each of which bisects the area, then in each of the $2 k$ angles into which the $k$ lines divide the plane, there should lie a point of intersection of the contours of $M$ and $M^{\prime}$. But on each side of polygon $M$ there are no more than two such intersection points. Therefore, if $M$ has $n$ sides, the number of intersection points is no less than $2 k$ and no more than $2 n$, from which it follows that $k \leqslant n$.

question:
187. Prove that if \(x_{1}, x_{2}, x_{3}, x_{4}, x_{5}\) are positive numbers, then

\[
\begin{aligned}
\left(x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}+x_{4}+x_{5}\right)^{2} & \geqslant \\
& \geqslant 4\left(x_{1} x_{2}+x_{2} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{4}+x_{4} x_{5}+x_{5} x_{1}\right)
\end{aligned}
\]
reference_solution:
187. If $x_{2} \geqslant x_{1}$, then the inequality follows from the identity

$$
\begin{gathered}
\left(x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}+x_{4}+x_{5}\right)^{2}- \\
-\left(x_{1}-x_{2}+x_{3}-x_{4}+x_{5}\right)^{2}= \\
=4\left(x_{1}+x_{3}+x_{5}\right)\left(x_{2}+x_{4}\right)= \\
=4\left(x_{1} x_{2}+x_{2} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{4}+x_{4} x_{5}+x_{5} x_{1}\right)+ \\
\quad+4 x_{5}\left(x_{2}-x_{1}\right)+4 x_{1} x_{4}
\end{gathered}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-184.jpg?height=304&width=330&top_left_y=302&top_left_x=735)

Fig. 78

If $x_{1}>x_{2}$, then from the similarly provable identity

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \left(x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}+x_{4}+x_{5}\right)^{2}-\left(x_{1}-x_{2}-x_{3}+x_{4}-x_{5}\right)^{2}= \\
& \quad=4\left(x_{1} x_{2}+x_{2} x_{3}+x_{3} x_{4}+x_{4} x_{5}\right)+4 x_{3}\left(x_{1}-x_{2}\right)+4 x_{2} x_{4}
\end{aligned}
$$

$\nabla$ In general, the inequality

$$
\left(x_{1}+x_{2}+\ldots+x_{n}\right)^{2} \geqslant c_{n}\left(x_{1} x_{2}+x_{2} x_{3}+\ldots+x_{n} x_{1}\right)
$$

is satisfied for the following (largest) $c_{n}: c_{2}=2, c_{3}=3, c_{4} \Rightarrow$ $=4$ (and for these $n$ the inequality is valid for all $x_{i}$, not necessarily positive), and also for $c_{n}=4$ for all $n \geqslant 5$ (for $x_{i}>0$). The last statement is obtained from the proven case for $n=5$ by induction: if the indices are cyclically shifted so that $x_{n+1}$ is the smallest, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left(x_{1}+x_{2}+\ldots+x_{n+1}\right)^{2}-\left(x_{1}+x_{2}+\ldots+x_{n}\right)^{2} & \\
& \geqslant-4 x_{1} x_{n}+4 x_{1} x_{n+1}+4 x_{n} x_{n+1}
\end{aligned}
$$

since

$$
2 x_{n+1}\left(x_{2}+\ldots+x_{n-1}\right)+\left(x_{n+1}-2 x_{1}\right)\left(x_{n+1}-2 x_{n}\right) \geqslant 0
$$

question:
191. a) Each side of a convex hexagon is greater than 1. Will there always be a diagonal longer than 2?

b) In a convex hexagon $A B C D E F$, the lengths of the diagonals $A D, B E$, and $C F$ are greater than 2. Will there always be a side longer than 1?
reference_solution:
191. a) Answer: not always. Example: if on each side of an equilateral triangle with side 2 isosceles triangles with height $1 / 10$ are constructed, then all sides of the resulting hexagon will be greater than 1, while all diagonals will not exceed 2.

b) Answer: always: Among the three diagonals $A D, B E$, and $F C$, there will be two for which the angle $\alpha$ between them is not less than $60^{\circ}$. Let these be, for example, $A D$ and $B E$. Construct the parallelogram $B E D K$. Since $B E=D K>2, A D>2$ and $\angle A D K=\alpha \geqslant 60^{\circ}$, then $A K \gtrdot 2$, but $A B+B K \geqslant A K$. Therefore, either $A B>1$, or $E D=B K>1$.

question: 193*. On the plane, there are $n$ vectors, each of length 1. The sum of all $n$ vectors is the zero vector. Prove that the vectors can be numbered in such a way that for all $k=1,2, \ldots$ ..., n the following condition is satisfied: the sum of the first $k$ vectors has a length of no more than 2.
reference_solution:
193. Let's lay out all vectors from some point $O$.

We will prove that if $k$ vectors have already been chosen with a sum of $s=\overrightarrow{O S}$ (Fig. 80) $|s| \leqslant 1$, then from the remaining vectors, one can either choose a single vector $a$ such that $|s+a| \leqslant 1$, or

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-187.jpg?height=349&width=251&top_left_y=441&top_left_x=165)

Fig. 80 two vectors $b$ and $c$, for which $|s + b + c| \leqslant 1$. Indeed, if among the remaining vectors there is a vector $a$ for which $\angle(a, s) \geqslant 120^{\circ}$, then $|s+a| \leqslant 1$. If such a vector does not exist, then since there are vectors of the system on both sides of the line $O S$, one can choose as $b$ a vector from one of the two half-planes that forms the largest angle with the vector $s$. Similarly, in the other half-plane, the vector $c$ is chosen. Clearly, one of the angles $-\angle(c, s)$ or $\angle(b, s)$ is obtuse, and $\angle(b, c) > 120^{\circ}$. Suppose, for example, that $\angle(b, s) > 90^{\circ}$. Then $|s+b| < 1$ and therefore $|s+b+c| \leqslant 1$. Thus, if we add to the system with sum $s$ first the vector $b$ and then $c$, the sum after each step will be less than $\sqrt{2}$.

$\nabla$ We have proved that in condition 2, $\sqrt{2}$ can be replaced. More subtle arguments show that the vectors can always be numbered such that the sum of the first $n$ of them is no more than $\sqrt{5} / 2$, and this estimate is already precise: the example of $2n+1$ vectors - one $(-1,0)$, $n$ of $\left(1 / n, \sqrt{1-1 / n^{2}}\right)$, and $n$ of $\left(1 / n, -\sqrt{1-1 / n^{2}}\right)$ shows that the constant $\sqrt{5} / 2$ cannot be replaced by a smaller one.

$\nabla$ A similar theorem (it is called the Steinitz lemma) can be proved for $m$-dimensional space, and (for any "norm" of vectors) the corresponding Steinitz constant does not exceed $m$. . $^{*}$ )

question: 195. Given a square $A B C D$. Points $P$ and $Q$ lie on sides $A B$ and $B C$ respectively, such that $B P = B Q$. Let $H$ be the foot of the perpendicular dropped from point $B$ to segment $P C$. Prove that angle $D H Q$ is a right angle.
reference_solution:
195. Let $F$ be the point of intersection of the lines $B H$ and $A D$ (Fig. 81). From the equality of triangles $A B F$ and $B P C$ (by the leg and acute angle), it follows that $A F = B P = B Q$ and $F D = C Q$; therefore, $Q C D F$ is a rectangle.

The circle circumscribed around it passes through the point $H$ ($F C$ is the diameter of this circle, and $\angle F H C = 90^{\circ}$). Since $D Q$ is also a diameter, then $\angle D H Q = 90^{\circ}$.

question: 198. On the legs $CA$ and $CB$ of an isosceles right triangle $ABC$, points $D$ and $E$ are chosen respectively such that $CD = CE$. The extensions of the perpendiculars dropped from points $D$ and $C$ to the line $AE$ intersect the hypotenuse $AB$ at points $K$ and $L$ respectively. Prove that $KL = LB$.
reference_solution: 198. Rotate triangle $A B C$ around vertex $C$ by $90^{\circ}$ so that point $A$ moves to $B$. Then $E$ will move to point $F$ on line $A C$, for which $F B\|C L\| D K$ and $F C=C D$, therefore $B L=$ $=L K$.

question:
199. On an $8 \times 8$ chessboard, two players are playing a game of "cat and mouse." The first player has one token - the mouse, and the second player has several tokens - the cats. All tokens move the same way: one cell to the right, left, up, or down. If the mouse reaches the edge of the board, it can jump off the board on its next move. If a cat and the mouse land on the same cell, the cat eats the mouse.

The players take turns, and the second player moves all of their cats in one turn (different cats can move in different directions). The mouse starts. It tries to jump off the board, while the cats try to eat it before it does.

a) Suppose there are only two cats. The mouse is already placed on some cell not on the edge. Can the cats be placed on the edge of the board in such a way that they can catch the mouse?

b) Suppose there are three cats, but the mouse gets an extra move: it makes two moves in a row on its first turn. Prove that the mouse can escape from the cats, regardless of the initial positions of the tokens.
reference_solution:
199. a) Answer: it is possible. Regardless of the mouse's position, the cats should be placed so that the mouse is on a segment between them, parallel to one of the diagonals of the board, and in response to any move of the mouse, the cats should be moved so that the mouse remains between them on a line parallel to the diagonal.
b) Draw two segments through the mouse, parallel to the diagonals, and exclude the cells of these segments. In one of the four remaining parts of the board, there are no cats, and the mouse must go to this part in the direction towards the edge. It is clear that the cats will not be able to catch it, since after any move of the cats, there will be a part of the board free of cats in front of the mouse in the direction of its movement.

question:
200. a) Prove that the numbers $1,2,3, \ldots, 32$ can be arranged in such an order that for no two numbers their half-sum equals any of the numbers placed between them.

b) Can the numbers $1,2,3, \ldots, 100$ be arranged in such an order that for no two numbers their half-sum equals any of the numbers placed between them?
reference_solution:
200. a) To achieve the required arrangement, in one half of the line, we will write even numbers, and in the other half - odd numbers. In this case, the half-sum of any two numbers from different halves will not be an integer and therefore will not be contained between them. Then, we will perform a similar procedure with the first and second halves: we will divide each of them into two quarters and place numbers of the form $4k, 4k+2, 4k+1$, and $4k+3$ respectively: in this case, the half-sum of numbers from different quarters in the left half will be odd, and in the right half - even, and therefore will not be contained between them. Next, we will divide each quarter in half, where the role of "even" and "odd" numbers will now be played by numbers with different remainders when divided by 8, and so on. In the end, we will get such an arrangement:

$$
8,24,16,32,4,20,12,26,6,22,14,30,2,18,10,26 \text{, }
$$

$$
7,23,15,31,3,19,11,27,5,21,13,29,1,17,9,25 \text{. }
$$

b) To prove this statement for any number $N$ of numbers, it is sufficient to prove it for $N=2^n$ (extra numbers can be discarded; for example, from the arrangement of $128=2^n$ numbers, we can discard numbers greater than 100 and get the required arrangement for $N=100$ numbers). The main idea has already been shown in the solution to part a); more formally and concisely, the proof can be presented as induction on $n$.

For $n=1$ and $n=2$, the statement is obvious: the arrangements $(1,2)$ and $(2,4,1,3)$ work. If $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_N$ is an arrangement of $N=2^n$ numbers $1,2, \ldots, N$ that satisfies the condition, then

$$
2a_1, 2a_2, \ldots, 2a_N, 2a_1-1, 2a_2-1, \ldots, 2a_N-1
$$

will be an arrangement of $2N=2^{n+1}$ numbers $1,2, \ldots, 2N$, which, as it is not difficult to verify, also satisfies the condition: for numbers from different halves - by parity considerations, for numbers from the same half - by the induction hypothesis.

question: 202. Given a convex polygon into which no triangle of area 1 can be placed. Prove that this polygon can be placed in a triangle of area 4.
reference_solution:
202. Consider the set of vertices of a given polygon $P$ and choose three of them $-A, B, C$- such that the area of triangle $A B C$ is the largest. (It is clear that the area of triangle $A B C$ is not less than the area of any triangle that can be placed inside polygon $P$. We will use further specific cases of this fact.)

Let $M$ be an arbitrary point of polygon $P$. Since the area of triangle $M B C$ is not greater than $S_{A B C}$, $M$ lies in a strip whose axis of symmetry is the line $B C$, and whose width is twice the height of $\triangle A B C$ dropped from vertex $A$. By conducting the same reasoning for $\triangle M A B$ and $\triangle M C A$, we obtain that all points of the poly-

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-190.jpg?height=514&width=477&top_left_y=487&top_left_x=555)

Fig. 82 gon belong to the intersection of the three constructed strips - triangle $A^{\prime} B^{\prime} C^{\prime}$ (Fig. 82), the area of which is equal to $4 S_{A B C}=4$.

$\nabla$ A similar argument was already encountered in problem 80, where we essentially established that $\triangle A^{\prime} B^{\prime} C^{\prime}$ is the set of points $M$ for which all three areas $S_{\text {mAB, }} S_{\text {mBC }}, S_{\text {mCA }}$ do not exceed $S_{A B C}$.

question:
203. On the segment $0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1$, a function $f$ is given. It is known that this function is non-negative and $f(1)=1$. Moreover, for any two numbers $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ such that $x_{1} \geqslant 0, x_{2} \geqslant 0$ and $x_{1}+x_{2} \leqslant 1$, the inequality

$$
f\left(x_{1}+x_{2}\right) \geqslant f\left(x_{1}\right)+f\left(x_{2}\right)
$$

a) Prove that for any function $\mathfrak{f}$ satisfying the listed conditions, for all $x$ the inequality $f(x) \leqslant 2 x$ holds.

b) Is it true that for all $x$

$$
f(x) \leqslant 1.9 x ?
$$
reference_solution:
203. a) The function $f$ is monotonically non-decreasing on the interval $[0,1]$, since from $1 \geqslant x \geqslant y \geqslant 0$ it follows that $f(x)=f((x-y)+y) \geqslant$ $\geqslant f(x-y)+f(y) \geqslant f(y)$. In addition, $f(2 x) \geqslant 2 f(x)$ for all $x_{1}$. Using this, we obtain:

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\text { for } \frac{1}{2}1,9 \cdot 0,51=0,969
$$

question:
205. a) From triangle $A B C$, by rotating around the center of the circumscribed circle by some angle less than $180^{\circ}$, we obtained triangle $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$. Corresponding segments $A B$ and $A_{1} B_{1}$ intersect at point $C_{2}$, $B C$ and $B_{1} C_{1}$ at point $A_{2}$, and $C A$ and $C_{1} A_{1}$ at point $B_{2}$. Prove that triangles $A_{2} B_{2} C_{2}$ and $A B C$ are similar.

b) From quadrilateral $A B C D$, inscribed in a circle, by rotating around the center by some angle less than $180^{\circ}$, we obtained quadrilateral $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1} D_{1}$. Prove that the points of intersection of the corresponding lines at the rotation: $A B$ and $A_{1} B_{1}$, $B C$ and $B_{1} C_{1}$, $C D$ and $C_{1} D_{1}$, $D A$ and $D_{1} A_{1}$, serve as the vertices of a parallelogram.
reference_solution:
205. If the chord $Q_{1} Q_{2}$ of a circle with center $O$ is obtained by rotating the chord $P_{1} P_{2}$ by an angle $\alpha$ around the point $O$, then the intersection point $R$ of the lines $P_{1} P_{2}$ and $Q_{1} Q_{2}$ can be obtained by rotating the midpoint $M$ of the chord $P_{1} P_{2}$ around the center $O$ by an angle $\alpha / 2$ (in this case, the point $M$ will transition to some point $M^{\prime}$ on the segment $O R$) and then applying a homothety with center $O$ and coefficient $k = 1 / \cos (\alpha / 2) = O R : O M = O R : O M^{\prime}$. Apply these considerations to solve the problem.

a) The triangle $A_{2} B_{2} C_{2}$ is obtained by the described transformations from the triangle $K L M$, formed by the midpoints of the sides of triangle $A B C$. Since $\triangle K L M \sim \triangle A_{2} B_{2} C_{2}$ and $\triangle K L M \propto \triangle A B C$, we get $\triangle A B C \propto \triangle A_{2} B_{2} C_{2}$.

b) The quadrilateral from the problem condition is obtained by a similarity transformation from the quadrilateral formed by the midpoints of the sides of quadrilateral $A B C D$. But the midpoints of any sides of any quadrilateral are the vertices of a parallelogram.

question: 210. Prove that from the digits 1 and 2, one can form $2^{n+1}$ numbers, each of which is $2^{n}$-digit long, and any two of which differ in at least $2^{n-1}$ digits.
reference_solution:
210. For $n=1$, the four numbers $11,21,12,22$ satisfy the condition. We will prove the statement of the problem by induction.

Let $a^{\prime}$ denote the number obtained from $a$ by replacing the digit 1 with 2 and 2 with 1, and let $ab$ denote the number obtained by appending the number $b$ to $a$. Suppose we have constructed the set $A_{n}$ consisting of $2^{n+1}$ numbers, each of which is $2^{n}$-digit, and any two of which differ in at least $2^{n-1}$ digits. Consider the set $A_{n+1}$, consisting of numbers $aa$ and $aa^{\prime}$, where $a \in A_{n}$. All such numbers are $2^{n+1}$-digit, and there are a total of $2^{n+2}$ of them. Moreover, any two of them differ in at least $2^{n}$ digits. Indeed, the numbers $aa$ and $aa^{\prime}$, as well as the numbers $aa$ and $bb^{\prime}$ for any $a$ and $b$, differ exactly in $2^{n}$ digits (in the digits where $a$ and $b$ differ, $a^{\prime}$ and $b$ coincide, and vice versa); the numbers $aa$ and $bb$ differ in at least $2^{n}$ digits by the induction hypothesis. The statement is proved.

question: 211. In the plane, there is a finite set of polygons, each two of which have a common point. Prove that some line intersects all these polygons.
reference_solution: 211. Let's project all polygons onto some straight line. The projection of each polygon is a segment, and by the condition, any two segments have a common point. From this, it follows that all segments have a common point (to convince yourself of this, it is enough to consider the given line as a number line and take the smallest of the right ends of these segments). The line perpendicular to the given one and passing through the marked point intersects all polygons.

question: 212. Prove that for positive $a, b, c$ the inequality $a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}+3 a b c>$ $>a b(a+b)+b c(b+c)+a c(a+c)$ holds.
reference_solution:
212. Without loss of generality, we can assume that $a \geqslant b \geqslant c$. Then $c(a-c)(b-c) \geqslant 0$, from which $c^{3} + abc \geqslant ac^{2} + bc^{2}$. It is sufficient to prove that $a^{3} + b^{3} + 2abc \geqslant ab(a+b) + a^{2}c +$

question: 213. Three flies are crawling along the sides of triangle $ABC$ in such a way that the centroid of the triangle they form remains in the same place. Prove that it coincides with the centroid of triangle $ABC$, given that one of the flies has crawled along the entire perimeter of the triangle. (The centroid of a triangle is the point of intersection of its medians.)
reference_solution: 213. If one of the flies is at vertex $A$, then the center of gravity of the triangle formed by the flies is located in triangle $A D E$ (Fig. 88), where $D E: B C=1$ $\vDash 2: 3$. Since one of the flies has been to all vertices, the center of gravity of the "triangle of flies" should belong to the three shaded triangles in the figure. The only common point of these triangles is the center of gravity of the given one.

215. Let $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}$ be the points of intersection of the lines with the lower edge of the strip, numbered in order (from left to right), and $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{n}$ be the points of intersection with the upper edge (also from left to right). We will number the paths starting from points $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}$ in order with the numbers $1, 2, \ldots, n$. From the rules of constructing the paths, the following properties follow.

$1^{\circ}$ Each segment of each line is traversed by exactly one path.

$2^{\circ}$ Adjacent paths, the $k$-th and $(k+1)$-th, touch at vertices, and the $k$-th path always lies to the left of the $(k+1)$-th path (for each $k=1, 2, \ldots, n-1$). Non-adjacent paths do not have any common points.

$3^{\circ}$ The $k$-th path ends at point $B_{k}$.

Now let's prove all the statements of the problem.

a) Consider all paths with odd numbers. According to property $1^{\circ}$, they cannot have common points, and their number is at least $n / 2$.

b) Let's count the total number of segments on all paths in two ways. Each segment $A_{i} B_{n+1-t}$ of one of the lines is divided by points of intersection with the other lines into $n$ segments. Therefore, the total number of segments is $n^{2}$. According to $1^{\circ}$, we should get the same sum $n^{2}$ by summing the number of segments in all $n$ paths. Therefore, at least one of the summands will be no less than $n$.

Of course, statement b) also follows from g).

c) Let's estimate the number of segments in the two extreme paths, the 1st and the $n$-th.

These paths bound convex sets lying to the left of the 1st path and to the right of the $n$-th path; the first path lies within the angle $A_{1} P B_{1}$, and the second within the angle $A_{n} P B_{n}$, where $P$ is the point of intersection of the lines $A_{1} B_{n}$ and $A_{n} B_{1}$. The other lines $A_{2} B_{n-1}, A_{3} B_{n-2}, \ldots, A_{n-1} B_{2}$ can have a common segment only with one of the two extreme paths (specifically, with the one that lies on the other side of this line from the point $P$). Therefore, the total number of segments in the two extreme paths is no more than $4 + (n-2)$ segments. Therefore, in one of them, there are no more than $\frac{n}{2} + 1$ segments.

d) Consider the middle path, i.e., the path with number $m = (n+1) / 2$ if $n$ is odd and $m = n / 2$ if $n$ is even, and prove that it passes through all the lines (Fig. 89). Indeed, it divides the strip into two regions: each of the segments $A_{1} B_{n}$ and $A_{2} B_{n-1}, \ldots, A_{n} B_{1}$ starts in one of the regions (possibly on the boundary) and ends in the other and, therefore, has a common point with the middle path, and hence (by the rule of constructing paths) - a common segment.

$\nabla$ It would be interesting to obtain good lower and upper bounds for the number of segments in the maximum (by the number of segments) path.

question:
217. Given a polynomial $P(x)$ with

a) natural coefficients;

b) integer coefficients.

Denote by $a_{n}$ the sum of the digits in the decimal representation of the number $P(n)$. Prove that there is a number that occurs in the sequence $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}, \ldots$ infinitely many times.
reference_solution:
217. a) As such a number $S$, one can take the sum of all the digits in the representation of all the coefficients of the polynomial $P(x)$: then for any $n \geqslant n_{0}$, where $n_{0}$ is chosen so that $10^{n_{0}}$ is greater than all the coefficients, $a_{10}{ }^{n}=S$.

b) The result of a) can be applied to the polynomial $Q(x)=$ $=P(x+d)$, where $d$ is a large natural number; in this case, it turns out that for a sufficiently large $n_{0}=n_{0}(d)$, for any $n \geqslant n_{0}$, the sum of all the digits of the number $Q\left(10^{n}\right)=a_{10^{n}+d}$ is the same. Of course, it is necessary to check the condition that all $10^{n}+d$ coefficients of $Q(x)$ are of the same sign.

For a sufficiently large $d>0$, the coefficients of the polynomial $Q(x)=P(x+d)$ have the same sign as the leading coefficient of the polynomial $P(x)=p_{0} x^{n}+p_{1} x^{n-1}+\ldots+p_{n}$. We outline two ways of proving this.

$1^{\circ}$ The coefficients of the polynomial

$$
\begin{aligned}
& Q(x)=p_{0}(x+d)^{n}+p_{1}(x+d)^{n-1}+\ldots+p_{n}= \\
& \quad=p_{0}\left(x^{n}+C_{n}^{1} x^{n-1} d+\ldots+C_{n}^{n-1} x d^{n-1}+d^{n}\right)+ \\
& +p_{1}\left(x^{n-1}+C_{n-1}^{1} x^{n-2} d+\ldots+d^{n-1}\right)+\ldots+p_{n}= \\
& \quad=q_{0} x^{n}+q_{1}(d) x^{n-1}+\ldots+q_{n}(d)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $q_{k}(d), k=0,1, \ldots, n$, are polynomials in $d$, and $q_{k}(d)$ has degree $k$ with the leading term $p_{0} C_{n}^{k} d^{k}$ (while $q_{0}$ simply equals $p_{0}$). Then for a sufficiently large $d>d_{0}$, each $q_{k}(d)$ will have the same sign as $p_{0}$.

$2^{\circ}$. If the first few coefficients $p_{0}, p_{1}, \ldots, p_{n-k}$ of the polynomial $P(x)$ have the same sign, then upon shifting $P(x) \rightarrow(x+d)=Q(x)$ by $d$, a polynomial is obtained in which the coefficients $q_{0}, q_{1}, \ldots q_{n-\text { n }}$ have the same sign, and the next coefficient $q_{n-k+1}=p_{0} C_{n}^{n-k+1} d^{n-k+1}+$ $+p_{1} C_{n-1}^{n-k} d^{n-k}+\ldots+p_{n-k} d+p_{n-k+1}$ will have the same sign for a sufficiently large $d$. Thus, in $n-1$ shifts, we can transform any polynomial $P(x)$ into one in which all coefficients have the same sign as $p_{0}$.

$\nabla$ Here, only the fact was used that the numbers $C_{n}^{k}$—the coefficients of the binomial $(a+b)^{n}=\sum_{k=1}^{n} C_{n}^{k} a^{k} b^{n-k} \quad$ (see P6) —are positive integers.

question: 220. On the table, there are 50 correctly running clocks. Prove that at some moment, the sum of the distances from the center of the table to the ends of the minute hands will be greater than the sum of the distances from the center of the table to the centers of the clocks.
reference_solution:
220. The idea of the solution can be expressed in one phrase: the sum of the distances to the ends of the minute hands on average (over time) is greater than the sum of the distances to the centers of the clocks. The proof can be conducted as follows.

Consider the sums $s_{1}$ and $s_{2}$ of the distances from the center of the table $O$ to the ends of the minute hands at two moments in time, 30 minutes apart. The quantity $s_{1}+s_{2}$ is greater than $2 s_{0}$, where $s_{0}$ is the sum of the distances from $O$ to the centers of the clocks, because in each triangle

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-203.jpg?height=402&width=533&top_left_y=718&top_left_x=149)

Fig. 93

Fig. 94

in the triangle $O M_{1} M_{2}$, the sum of the lengths of the two sides $O M_{1}$ and $O M_{2}$ is greater than twice the length of the median located between them (Fig. 94). Therefore, at least one of the numbers $s_{1}$ or $s_{2}$ is greater than $s_{0}$.

question:
221. A row of 1000 numbers is written in a row. Below it, a second row of numbers is written according to the following rule: under each number $a$ in the first row, a natural number is written indicating how many times $a$ appears in the first row. From the second row, a third row is similarly constructed: under each number $b$ in the second row, a natural number is written indicating how many times $b$ appears in the second row. Then, from the third row, a fourth row is constructed in the same way, from the fourth row - a fifth row, and so on.

a) Prove that some row coincides with the next one.

b) Moreover, prove that the 11th row coincides with the 12th.

c) Provide an example of such an initial row for which the 10th row does not coincide with the 11th.
reference_solution:
221. The solution to part a) follows from these two considerations: (1) under each number $a$ in the $m$-th row ($m \geqslant 2$), there is a number not less than $a$; (2) each of these numbers does not exceed 1000. To solve part b), we also need to consider that if a number $a$ in the $m$-th row ($m \geqslant 2$) is strictly less than the number $b$ below it, then $b \geqslant 2a$: several groups of $a$ numbers (each group stands under equal numbers) merge into one group of $b$ numbers; from this, by induction, it follows that in such a situation $b \geqslant 2^{m-1}$. But $2^{m-1} \leqslant 1000$ only for $m \leqslant 10$. An example of a sequence for which the 10th row does not match the 11th row is:

$$
0,1,2,2,4,4,4,4,8,8, \ldots, 8, \ldots, \underbrace{256, \ldots, 256}_{8}, \underbrace{488, \ldots, 488}_{258}
$$

Here are the successive transformations:
№ $21,1,2,2,4, \ldots, 4,8, \ldots, 8, \ldots, 256, \ldots, 256,488, \ldots, 488$
№ $32,2,2,2,4, \ldots, 4,8, \ldots, 8, \ldots, 256, \ldots, 256,488, \ldots, 488$
№ $10256,256, \ldots$
..., $256,488, \ldots, 488$
№ $11512,512, \ldots$
..., 512, $488, \ldots, 488$.

$\nabla$ Similarly, for a sequence of $n$ numbers, where $2^{k-1} \leqslant n < 2^{k}$, it can be proven that the $(k+2)$-th row will coincide with the $(k+1)$-th, but the $(k+1)$-th may still not coincide with the $k$-th.
