question: 223. Natural numbers $x_{1}, x_{2}$ are less than 10000. From them, a sequence $x_{1}, x_{2}$, $x_{3}, \ldots, x_{n}$ is constructed, where the number $x_{3}$ is equal to $\left|x_{1}-x_{2}\right|$, the number $x_{4}$ is the smallest of the numbers $\left|x_{1}-x_{2}\right|,\left|x_{2}-x_{3}\right|$, $\left|x_{1}-x_{3}\right|$, the number $x_{5}$ is the smallest of the numbers $\left|x_{1}-x_{2}\right|,\left|x_{1}-x_{3}\right|,\left|x_{1}-x_{4}\right|,\left|x_{2}-x_{3}\right|,\left|x_{2}-x_{4}\right|$, $\left|x_{3}-x_{4}\right|$ and so on (each subsequent number is the smallest of the absolute differences between the previous numbers). Prove that $x_{21}=0$ must be true.
reference_solution:
223. If the first three numbers are rearranged in descending order, then for all members of the sequence, the condition $x_{k} \leqslant x_{k-r}-x_{k-1}$ will be satisfied, and the sequence will become decreasing: $x_{1} \geqslant x_{2} \geqslant x_{3} \geqslant \ldots \geqslant x_{21}$. If we assume that $x_{21} \geqslant$ $\geqslant 1$, then from $x_{k-2} \geqslant x_{k}+x_{k-1}$ it would follow that $x_{20} \geqslant 1, x_{19} \geqslant 2$, $\alpha_{18} \geqslant 3, x_{17} \geqslant 5, \ldots$ The only thing left is to write down 21 members of the "Fibonacci sequence" (P21)

$$
1,1,2,3,5,8,13, \ldots, 6745,10916
$$

to obtain the contradiction $x_{1} \geq 10$ 000.

question:
225*. On the plane, vectors $\boldsymbol{a}, \boldsymbol{b}, \boldsymbol{c}, \boldsymbol{d}$ are given, the sum of which is 0. Prove the inequality

$$
|a|+|b|+|c|+|d| \geqslant|a+d|+|b+d|+|c+d|
$$
reference_solution:
225. The right side of the inequality, like the left, is symmetric with respect to \(a, b, c\) and \(d\) (provided their sum is 0); since \(b+c=-(a+d)\) and so on, it is equal to half the sum of the lengths of all pairwise sums of the given vectors. Considering this, for a given quadruple of vectors with a sum of 0, we can choose the notation such that the broken line composed of vectors \(\overrightarrow{A B}=\boldsymbol{a}, \overrightarrow{B C}=\boldsymbol{b}, \overrightarrow{C D}=\boldsymbol{c}, \overrightarrow{D A}=\boldsymbol{d}\) is self-intersecting. For this, it is sufficient that the vectors \(a, b, c\), laid off from one point \(O\), lie in the same half-plane, and \(\boldsymbol{a}\) and \(\boldsymbol{c}\) lie on the same side of the line passing through \(O\) and parallel to \(b\). Then

\[
|a+d|+|c+d|=B D+A C \leqslant|b|+|d|
\]

It remains to add to this

\[
|b+d|=|a+c| \leqslant|a|+|c|
\]

Another solution, based on the idea of averaging the projections of vectors in all possible directions, allows reducing the two-dimensional and even three-dimensional versions of this problem to proving an analogous inequality for numbers, i.e., to the one-dimensional version \([73]\).

question: 227. On a square sheet of paper, $n$ rectangles with sides parallel to the sides of the sheet are drawn. No two of these rectangles have any common interior points. Prove that if all the rectangles are cut out, the number of pieces into which the remaining part of the sheet will split is no more than $n+1$.
reference_solution: 227. Let's mark 4 vertices (angles at these vertices are $90^{\circ}$ or $270^{\circ}$) on each of the $k$ pieces into which the remaining part of the sheet has split. Each of the $4 k$ marked points is a vertex of one of the $n$ cut-out rectangles or the original one, and if any point is marked twice, then two rectangles are adjacent to it. Therefore, $4 k \leq 4 n+4$, from which $k \leq$ $\leqslant n+1$.

question: 228. Three pedestrians are walking along three straight roads at constant speeds. At the initial moment, they were not on the same straight line. Prove that they can be on the same straight line no more than twice.
reference_solution:
228. Three points $\left(x_{0}, y_{0}\right),\left(x_{1}, y_{1}\right),\left(x_{2}, y_{2}\right)$ lie on the same straight line if and only if

$$
\left(x_{1}-x_{0}\right)\left(y_{2}-y_{0}\right)-\left(x_{2}-x_{0}\right)\left(y_{1}-y_{0}\right)=0 .
$$

If $x_{i}$ and $y_{i}(i=0,1,2)$ are linear functions of time $t_{\text {, }}$, then (*) becomes a quadratic equation in terms of $l$; it has no more than two roots.

question:
229. On a $99 \times 99$ chessboard, a figure (this figure will be different in parts a), b), and c)) is marked. In each cell of the figure $F$, there is a beetle. At some point, the beetles fly up and land again in the cells of the same figure $F$; in this process, several beetles could land in the same cell. After the flight, any two beetles that were in adjacent cells ended up in adjacent cells again or in the same cell. (Cells are considered adjacent if they share a side or a vertex.)

a) Let the figure $F$ be the "central cross," i.e., the union of the middle vertical and middle horizontal lines (Fig. 12,a). Prove that in this case, some beetle either returned to its original place or moved to an adjacent cell.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-062.jpg?height=433&width=796&top_left_y=1022&top_left_x=183)

a

6

Fig. 12

b) Is the statement true if the figure is a "window frame," i.e., the union of the central cross and all the boundary cells of the board (Fig. 12, b)?

c)* Is the statement true if the figure is the entire board?
reference_solution:
229. a) We can assume that the beetle from the central cell has moved to the right by $k \geqslant 2$ cells. Let's write in each of the 49 cells of the rightmost column how many cells the beetle has moved horizontally from the corresponding cell; a move to the right is considered positive, and a move to the left is negative. Clearly, for the rightmost beetle, the displacement is negative, and the numbers we write in adjacent cells differ by no more than 2. Moving along the row from the central cell to the right, we must somewhere *cross 0*, so one of the written numbers is 1, 0, or -1, i.e., one of the beetles must move no more than one cell.

b) Answer: the statement is false. In Fig. 97, an example is given where all beetles end up far from their initial cells (on the left, the numbers we assign to each beetle are shown, and on the right, where the beetles with the corresponding numbers should fly).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-206.jpg?height=378&width=822&top_left_y=866&top_left_x=180)

Fig. 97

cells (on the left, the numbers we assign to each beetle are shown, and on the right, where the beetles with the corresponding numbers should fly).

c) Answer: true. We will prove this statement immediately for a rectangle of $m \times n$ cells. For squares $1 \times 1$, $2 \times 2$, and the rectangle $1 \times 2$, it is obvious. (In general, for rectangles $1 \times n$ and $2 \times n$, it can be easily proven in the same way as part a).) Let the dimensions of the rectangle be $m \times n$ greater than $2: 2 < m \leqslant n$. We will prove that from it (by cutting off the outermost rows), we can obtain a smaller rectangle $\Pi$, all beetles from which again land in $\Pi$, so it will be sufficient to show that in $\Pi$ there is a "nearly stationary" beetle.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-207.jpg?height=51&width=894&top_left_y=123&top_left_x=144)
the number of moves it takes for a chess king to move from $A$ to $B$: the set of cells $M$ (on a grid) that are at a distance no greater than $r$ from a given cell $C$, for any $r=1,2, \ldots$, fills a square $(2 r+1) \times(2 r+1)$ with the central cell $C$. By the condition, the beetle from cell $K$ lands in such a cell $f(K)$ that for cells $A, B$ at a distance of 1, $\rho(f(A), f(B)) \leqslant 1$. Then for any two cells $A$ and $B$,

$$
\rho(f(A), f(B)) \leqslant \rho(A, B).
$$

In the rectangle $m \times n$ ($m \leqslant n$), we will call "outermost" cells those whose distance from some cells of the rectangle is $n-1$. If $m < n$, such cells occupy two outermost rows (the shorter sides of the rectangle) and in the square $n \times n$, they occupy four outermost rows (the border). Note that the distance $\rho$ between two cells of opposite outermost rows is $n-1$, and for any other two cells, it is less.

If no beetle lands in any of the outermost rows, then by removing this row, we obtain the required rectangle $\Pi$ with dimensions $m \times (n-1)$; from any cell $K$, the beetle flies to a cell $f(K)$ in $\Pi$.

Otherwise, we can take $\Pi$ as the rectangle obtained from the given one by cutting off all the outermost rows. Indeed, we can mark several (two, three, or four) cells $K_{l}$ such that in each outermost row, one of the cells $f(K_{l})$ is contained. Since $\rho(M, K_{l}) \leqslant n-2$ for any cell $M$ in $\Pi$ and each cell $K_{l}$, then according to (*), $\rho(f(M), f(K_{l})) \leqslant n-2$, and from the remark about opposite rows, it follows that $f(M)$ is contained in $\Pi$.

Now the proof is clearly carried out by induction (by $n=\max \{m, n\}$ or by $m+n$). Moreover, it follows from it that there will always be a $2 \times 2$ square that maps to itself.

$\nabla$ This problem is one of the discrete variants of the famous Brouwer's fixed-point theorem, which states that a continuous mapping of a convex set into itself has a fixed point.

question:
231. Given a natural number \( n \). A sequence of natural numbers \( a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{k} (k \geqslant n) \) is called universal for the given \( n \) if any permutation of the numbers \( 1, 2, \ldots, n \) (i.e., any sequence of \( n \) numbers in which each of the numbers \( 1, 2, \ldots, n \) appears exactly once) can be obtained by removing some elements from it. For example, the sequence \( (1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 1, 3) \) is universal for \( n=3 \), while the sequence \( (1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 3, 1) \) is not universal, as it is impossible to obtain the permutation \( (3, 1, 2) \) by removing any elements from it. The goal of this problem is to estimate the number of elements in the shortest universal sequence (for a given \( n \)).

a) Provide an example of a universal sequence with \( n^{2} \) elements.

b) Provide an example of a universal sequence with \( n^{2}-n+1 \) elements.

c)* Prove that any universal sequence consists of at least \( n(n+1) / 2 \) elements.

question:
233. At the vertices of a regular $n$-gon with center at point $O$, numbers $(+1)$ and $(-1)$ are placed. In one step, it is allowed to change the sign of all numbers located at the vertices of any regular $k$-gon with center $O$ (we also allow 2-gons, understanding a 2-gon as a segment with midpoint at point $O$). Prove that in cases a), b), c) there exists an initial arrangement of $(+1)$ and $(-1)$ such that it is impossible to obtain a set of all $(+1)$ in any number of steps:

a) $n=15$

b) $n=30$

c) $n$ is any number greater than 2;

d)* Try to explain for an arbitrary $n$, what is the largest number $K(n)$ of different arrangements of $(+1)$ and $(-1)$, among which none can be obtained from another in several steps. Prove, for example, that $K(200)=2^{80}$.
reference_solution:
233. Let's first note several facts relevant to the case of any natural $n$. There are a total of $2^n$ arrangements of the numbers +1 and -1 at the vertices of a regular $n$-gon. We will call two arrangements equivalent if one can be transformed into the other (and vice versa) using the operations specified in the problem statement - changing the signs at the vertices of regular $n$-gons. Any two such operations "commute" - the result does not depend on the order in which they are performed; repeating any operation twice can also be excluded - it is equivalent to the identity operation, which does not change the arrangement. At the same time, we can limit ourselves to operations of changing signs at the vertices of regular $p$-gons with a prime number of vertices $p$ (we will call them "generators"); the set of vertices of a regular $n$-gon for any $n$ divisible by $p$ can be divided into $n / p$ generating $p$-gons.

Before moving on, let's consider specific problems.

a) For $n=15$, there are a total of 8 generating $p$-gons: 5 triangles and 3 pentagons. We will denote the unit (consisting of all +1) arrangement by $E$. Any arrangement equivalent to $E$ is determined by specifying some subset of these 8 $p$-gons; there are $2^8$ different subsets (including the empty one) - this is less than the total number of $2^{15}$ arrangements. Therefore, there are arrangements that are not equivalent to $E$.

b) For $n=30$, the total number of generating $p$-gons is $15+10+6=31$, so additional considerations are needed to solve the problem. Note that we can limit ourselves to a smaller number of generators: for example, from each pair of symmetric polygons (triangles and pentagons) relative to the center, we can leave only one - changing the signs in it, as well as in three (five) "digons" containing its vertices, is equivalent to changing the signs in the other, symmetric to it. There remain $15+5+3=23$ generators, thus, there are no more than $2^{23}<2^{30}$ arrangements equivalent to $E$.

c) Let's show how to find the exact number $T(n)$ of arrangements equivalent to $\boldsymbol{E}$ for any $n$. Note that the number of arrangements equivalent to some other arrangement $A$ of +1 and -1 is also $T(n)$: all of them are obtained by element-wise multiplication of the signs of the arrangement $A$ by any arrangement from the class equivalent to $E$. Let $K(n)$ be the number of "equivalence classes" - the maximum number of pairwise non-equivalent arrangements; then

$$
K(n)=2^n / T(n).
$$

Let $n$ contain $s$ different prime factors:

$$
n=p_{1}^{\alpha_{1}} p_{2}^{\alpha_{2}} \ldots p_{s}^{\alpha_{s}}
$$

Let $p_{1} p_{2} \ldots p_{s}=q ; \quad n / q=m$. Divide the regular $n$-gon into $m$ regular $q$-gons. The problem of calculating $T(n)$ reduces to the simpler problem of calculating $T(q)=T\left(p_{1} \ldots p_{s}\right)$; after all, each of the generating $p_{i}$-gons is contained in only one of the $q$-gons, - in other words, changes of signs occurring in different $q$-gons are independent, therefore

$$
T(n)=(T(q))^{m}, \quad K(n)=(K(q))^{m}.
$$

Start with the case $s=2$: let $n=p_{1} p_{2}$. Number the vertices of the $n$-gon by the numbers $0,1, \ldots, n-1$. Write these numbers

|  | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 0 | 0 | 6 | 12 | 3 | 9 |
| 1 | 10 | 1 | 7 | 13 | 4 |
| 2 | 5 | 11 | 2 | 8 | 14 |

Fig. 100. Each number from 0 to 14 is uniquely determined by its remainders when divided by 5 and by 3 in the $p_{1} \times p_{2}$ table so that the numbers in one column give the same remainder when divided by $p_{1}$, in one row - when divided by $p_{2}$. This can be done because the pair of remainders ( $r_{1}, r_{2}$ ) from division by $p_{1}$ and $p_{2}$ uniquely determines the number from 0 to $n$ (Fig. 100). Arrangements of numbers +1 and -1 at points on the circle correspond to arrangements of numbers $\sigma\left(r_{1}, r_{2}\right)=+1$ and -1 in the cells of the table ( $r_{1}$ - row number, $r_{2}$ - column number), changing signs in $p_{1}$ and $p_{2}$-gons - changing signs $\sigma$ in rows and columns. Any arrangement can be reduced to one where there are only +1 in the first row and the first column by these operations. Such "reduced" arrangements will be pairwise non-equivalent; indeed, when the signs of $q$ in rows and columns are changed, the value of the product

$$
\sigma\left(r_{1}, r_{2}\right) \sigma\left(0, r_{2}\right) \sigma\left(r_{1}, 0\right) \sigma(0,0)
$$

is preserved (the set of such values for all $\left(r_{1}, r_{2}\right), 1 \leqslant r_{1} \leqslant p_{1}-1,1 \leqslant r_{2} \leqslant p_{2}-1$ determines the equivalence class), Therefore

$$
K\left(p_{1} p_{2}\right)=2^{\left(p_{1}-1\right)\left(p_{2}-1\right)}, \quad T\left(p_{1} p_{2}\right)=2^{p_{1}+p_{2}-1}.
$$

In particular, $K(15)=2^{8}, T(15)=2^{7} ; K(10)=2^{4}$. The last equality allows us to find $K(200) ; n=200=2^{3} \cdot 5^{2}, q=10$, $m=20, K(200)=(K(10))^{20}=2^{4 \cdot 20}=2^{80}$.

Similar considerations allow us to find $K(n)$ for any $s$. Let $q=p_{1} p_{2} \ldots p_{s}$; the number $k$ from 0 to $q-1$ is uniquely determined by the remainders $r_{1}, r_{2}, \ldots, r_{s}$ from division by $p_{1}, p_{2}, \ldots, p_{s}$ (the "Chinese Remainder Theorem", P2); with arrangements $\sigma\left(r_{1}, r_{2}, \ldots, r_{s}\right)$ - functions on the set of tuples $r_{i}, 0 \leqslant r_{t} \leqslant p_{1}-1(1 \leqslant i \leqslant s)$, taking values +1 and -1, - it is allowed to perform operations of simultaneous replacement of signs in one "row", consisting of $p_{l}$ tuples, where the $i$-th coordinate $r_{i}$ is arbitrary - changes from 0 to $p_{l}-1$, and the other $s-1$ numbers $r_{i}$ are fixed (for each $i=1,2, \ldots, s)$; by these operations, any arrangement can be reduced to one where $\sigma\left(r_{1}, r_{2}, \ldots, r_{s}\right)=+1$, if at least one $r_{1}$ is equal to 0; the resulting reduced arrangements are non-equivalent (the product $2^{5}$ of the values of $\sigma$ for tuples obtained from a given one by replacing some coordinates with zeros is preserved). Write the answer for $q=p_{1} p_{2} \ldots p_{s}$ and for any $n=q m$ of the form ( $\mathbf{2}$ ):

$$
\begin{aligned}
& K(q)=2^{\left(p_{1}-1\right) \cdots\left(p_{s}-1\right)} ; \quad K(n)=2^{\varphi(n)}, \\
& \quad \text { where } \varphi(n)=n\left(1-\frac{1}{p_{1}}\right) \cdots\left(1-\frac{1}{p_{s}}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

In particular, $K(30)=2^{8}, T(30)=2^{22}$.

$\nabla$ The function $\varphi(n)$ that arose here somewhat unexpectedly is well known in number theory: it is the Euler's function, expressing the number of natural numbers less than $n$ and coprime with it [ 23$]$.

question: 235. On a plane, there is a non-self-intersecting closed broken line, no three vertices of which lie on the same straight line. We will call a pair of non-adjacent segments special if the extension of one of them intersects the other. Prove that the number of special pairs is even.
reference_solution:
235. A line passing through some segment $B C$ of a broken line intersects an even or odd number of other segments depending on whether the adjacent segments $A B$ and $C D$ lie on the same or different sides of the line $B C$ (in the latter case, we will call $B C$ a "zigzag"); indeed, the parity of the number of intersections of the broken line with the line $B C$ is determined by whether points $A$ and $D$ are in the same or different half-planes relative to it (Fig. 101, a). However, on any closed broken line, the number of "zigzags" is even: traveling along this broken line and noting whether we turn left or right at each vertex, we change the direction of the turn from left to right and from right to left an equal number of times. From these two facts, the statement of the problem follows.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-216.jpg?height=346&width=939&top_left_y=918&top_left_x=104)

Fig. 101

An even shorter proof is obtained if we use the fact that the sides of the angle formed by extending any two adjacent segments $A B$ and $B C$ beyond point $B_{\text {s }}$ are intersected an even number of times by the broken line (Fig. 101, b).

question: 236. On a plane, several points not lying on the same line are marked, and a number is written near each. It is known that if a line passes through two or more of the marked points, then the sum of all the numbers written near these points is zero. Prove that all the numbers are zero.
reference_solution: 236. Let the number $a_{x}$ be written at the marked point $X$, and let $n_{x}>1$ lines pass through it, containing other marked points. The sum of the numbers on each of them is 0 by condition. The total sum of the numbers on all $n_{x}$ lines (in which $a_{x}$ participates $n_{x}$ times) is $s+(n_{x}-1)a_{x}=0$, where $s$ is the sum of all numbers written next to the marked points. The assumption $s \neq 0$ leads to an obvious contradiction: for each point $X$, the sign of the number $a_{x}$ is opposite to the sign of the sum $s$ of these numbers; therefore, $s=0$ and $a_{x}=0$ for all $X$.

240*. In a certain country, it is possible to travel from any city to any other city without passing through other cities. The cost of each such trip is known. Two travel routes have been compiled through the cities of the country. Each city appears exactly once in each of these routes. The routes were compiled according to the following principle: the starting point of the route is chosen arbitrarily, and at each subsequent step, among the cities that the route has not yet passed through, the one with the lowest cost of travel from the previous city is chosen (if there are several such cities, any one of them is chosen); and so on until all cities have been passed through. When compiling the second route, the starting city is also chosen arbitrarily, and at each subsequent step, among the cities that the route has not yet passed through, the one with the highest cost of travel from the previous city is chosen. Prove that the total cost of travel along the first route is not greater than the total cost of travel along the second route.
reference_solution:
239. Let's use the definition of the limit of a sequence (P21). If for all $n \geqslant N$ and some $k$ the inequalities

$$
\left|a_{n}-a_{n+1} / 2\right|<\varepsilon \text { and }\left|a_{N}\right| / 2^{k}<\varepsilon,
$$

hold, then for $m \geqslant N+k$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left|a_{m}\right|<\frac{1}{2}\left|a_{m-1}\right|+\varepsilon<\frac{1}{2^{2}}\left|a_{m-2}\right|+\frac{\varepsilon}{2} & +\varepsilon<\ldots \\
\ldots<\frac{1}{2^{m-N}}\left|a_{N}\right|+\frac{\varepsilon}{2^{m-N+1}}+\ldots & +\frac{\varepsilon}{2^{2}}+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}+\varepsilon< \\
& <\frac{1}{2^{k}}\left|a_{N}\right|+2 \varepsilon<3 \varepsilon
\end{aligned}
$$

241. At each vertex of a convex polyhedron $M$, three edges meet. It is known that each of its faces is a polygon around which a circle can be circumscribed. Prove that a sphere can be circumscribed around this polyhedron.

$242^{*}$. The polynomial $x^{10}+* x^{9}+* x^{8}+\ldots$ $\ldots+* x^{2}+* x+1$ is written. Two players play a game. First, the first player replaces any of the asterisks with some number, then the second player replaces any of the remaining asterisks with a number, then the first player again replaces one of the asterisks with a number, and so on (a total of 9 moves). If the resulting polynomial has no real roots, the first player wins; if it has at least one root, the second player wins. Can the second player win regardless of the first player's moves?
reference_solution: 241. Two circles, in which the faces adjacent to the edge $A B$ of the polyhedron are inscribed, uniquely determine a sphere on which these circles lie, and thus all the vertices of these two faces. If $B C$ and $B D$ are two other edges emanating from $B$, then the circle containing points $B, C, D$ (circumscribed around the face containing them) also belongs to the sphere, so the vertices of the faces adjacent to the edge $B C$ all lie on the same sphere. Now we can similarly consider the faces adjacent to the edge emanating from $C$, and thus reach any vertex of the polyhedron - all of them lie on the same sphere: for any of them, a chain of edges can be constructed, ending at this vertex and starting from the edge $A B$.

246. a) Let's divide ten digits $0,1,2, \ldots, 9$ into two groups of 5 digits each (for example, from 0 to 4 - one group, from 5 to 9 - the other). It is sufficient to use boxes where both digits are taken from the same group, since such two digits are present in any three-digit number.

b) In addition to the 10 boxes $00,11, \ldots, 99$, which will inevitably be occupied, at least 30 more boxes are required to accommodate tickets with three different digits: there are a total of $10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8=720$ such tickets, and in each box with the number $\overrightarrow{pq}(p \neq q)$, no more than $3 \cdot 8=24$ of them can be placed ( $\overline{zpq}, \overline{pzq}$, and $\overline{pqz}$, where $z=$ any digit different from $p$ and $q$).

c) Let $x$ be the smallest number of boxes occupied by numbers starting with a certain digit ( $x \geqslant 1$ ); since all digits are equal, we can assume that the fewest numbers start with 9 and these numbers are $-\overline{99}, \overline{98}, \ldots, \overline{9y}$. where $y=10-x$. Then any ticket $\overline{9pq}$, where $p<y, q<y$, cannot be placed in boxes $\overline{9p}$ and $\overline{9q}$, i.e., the box $\overline{pq}$ must be occupied. Thus, at least all $y^{2}$ boxes with numbers where both digits are from 0 to $y-1$ are occupied, and at least $x^{2}$ boxes starting with one of the digits from $y$ to 9 (at least $x$ for each of these $x$ digits), i.e., in total, at least

$$
y^{2}+x^{2}=(10-x)^{2}+x^{2} \geqslant 50 \text { boxes. }
$$

d), e) For given natural numbers $k$ and $s, k<s$, denote by $F(k, s)$ the smallest of the numbers $x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+\ldots+x_{k}^{2}$ where $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{k}$ are natural numbers that sum to $s$; the value of $F(k, s)$ can be expressed in terms of $k$ and $s$ - the smallest value of the sum of squares is achieved when the numbers $x_{1}$ are "almost equal"; more precisely, if $s=k q+r, 0 \leqslant r<k$, then $k-r$ of them are equal to $q$ and $r$ of the remaining are $q+1$, so that

$$
F(k, s)=(k-r) q^{2}+r(q+1)^{2}=k q^{2}+r(2 q+1)
$$

It is convenient to consider a more general problem - for $k$-digit "tickets" with $s$ "digits" from 0 to $s-1$ (in our problem $s=10$). We will prove that the smallest number $M(k, s)$ of boxes with numbers $\overline{pq}$ ( $0 \leqslant p<s, 0 \leqslant q<s$ ), in which tickets can be placed by erasing $k-2$ digits, is equal to $F(k-1, s)$.

In particular, in problem d)

$$

and the answer to problem e) is given by the table

The inequality $M(k, s) \geqslant F(k-1, s)$ can be proven by induction on $k+s$, reasoning as in part c):

$$

To place tickets in $F(k-1, s)=x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+\ldots+x_{k-1}^{2}$ boxes, it is sufficient, as in part a), to divide $s$ digits into $k-1$ groups (of $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{k-1}$ digits) and leave boxes where both digits are from the same group (see [77]).

question:
247. Given a square sheet of grid paper $100 \times 100$ cells. Several non-intersecting broken lines are drawn along the sides of the cells and have no common points. These broken lines strictly lie inside the square, and their ends exit onto its boundary. Prove that, besides the vertices of the square, there is a node (inside or on the boundary) that does not belong to any broken line.

$248^{*}$. Given natural numbers $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ and $y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{m}$. The sums $x_{1}+x_{2}+\ldots+x_{n}$ and $y_{1}+y_{2}+\ldots+y_{m}$ are equal to each other and less than $m n$. Prove that in the equality $x_{1}+x_{2}+\ldots+x_{n}=$ $=y_{1}+y_{2}+\ldots+y_{m}$, some terms can be erased so that the equality remains true.
reference_solution: 247. Let's color all nodes in a checkerboard pattern in black and white. On the boundary, there are 4.99 nodes (excluding the vertices) - an equal number of black and white nodes. Let all of them serve as endpoints of broken lines. Then there is an equal number of broken lines with two white and two black ends. Therefore, the total number of white and black nodes lying on the broken lines inside the board is also the same. (On broken lines with white ends, there is one more black node, and on broken lines with black ends, there is one more white node.) But in total, inside the board, there are $99^{2}$ - an odd number - of nodes, so at least one of them does not lie on a broken line.

The one of the squares $K_{l}$ and $K_{l}$, whose center is farther from these axes (by the sum of distances, or by the largest of them), contains the center of the other. But this contradicts the rule of choosing squares.

a) Prove that the weights can be placed in such an order that the left pan is heavier first, then the right pan, then the left pan again, then the right pan again, and so on.

question: 253. Inside the quadrilateral $A B C D$, a point $M$ is marked such that $A B M D$ is a parallelogram. Prove that if $\angle C B M=\angle C D M$, then $\angle A C D=$ $=\angle B C M$.
reference_solution: 253. Let $E$ be the vertex of triangle $A D E$, obtained by translating triangle $B M C$ (by vector $B A$, Fig. 103). Then $M D E C$ is a parallelogram, the angles $E A D$, $C B M$, $C D M$, and $E C D$ are equal, and the points $A$, $C$, $E$, and $D$ lie on the same circle. Therefore, the angles $A C D$, $A E D$, and $B C M$ are also equal.

question: 254. Prove that for no natural $m$ the number $1978^{m}-1$ is divisible by $1000^{m}-1$.
reference_solution:
254. If $1978^{m}-1$ were divisible by $1000^{m}-1=d$, then the number $1978^{m}-1000^{m}=2^{m} \quad(989^{m} - 500^{m})$ would also be divisible by $d$. But this is impossible, since $989^{m} - 500^{m} < d$ and $d$ is odd.

$$
\left|x_{m}-x_{k}\right| \geqslant \frac{1}{|m-k|}
$$

holds.
reference_solution:
257. The sequence $4\{n \sqrt{2}\}$, where $\{x\}=x-[x]$ is the fractional part of the number $x$ ($n=1,2,3, \ldots$), satisfies the condition of the problem. Indeed, if $p$ and $q$ are natural numbers, $p\frac{1}{4 q^{2}}
$$

here $l=[m \sqrt{2}]-[k \sqrt{2}]<m \sqrt{2}-k \sqrt{2}+1 \leqslant(m-k)(\sqrt{2}+1)<$ $<(4-\sqrt{2})(m-k)$.

question: 258. Let $f(x)=x^{2}-x+1$. Prove that for any natural number $m>1$ the numbers $m, f(m)$, $f(f(m)), \ldots$ are pairwise coprime.
reference_solution:
258. Since $f(1)=f(0)=1$, the constant term $P_{n}(0)$ of the polynomial $P_{n}(x)=\underbrace{f(\ldots(f(x)) \ldots))}_{n}$ is equal to 1. Therefore, for any integer $m$, the remainder of the division of $P_{n}(m)$ by $m$ is 1.

Replacing $m$ with $m^{\prime}=P_{k}(m)$, we get that $P_{n+k}(m)$ and $m^{\prime}=P_{k}(m)$ are coprime.

$\nabla$ From the fact that there exists a sequence ( $\left.P_{\mathrm{n}}(2)\right)$, all terms of which are pairwise coprime, it immediately follows that the set of prime numbers is infinite.

question: 259. Prove that there exists a number $A$ such that in the graph of the function $y=A \sin x$, one can inscribe no fewer than 1978 pairwise distinct squares. (A square is called inscribed if all its vertices belong to the graph.)
reference_solution:
259. Let $M$ be any point of intersection of the graph $y = A \sin x$ with its image $x = -A \sin y$ after a $90^{\circ}$ rotation around the origin (Fig. 105). Then the point $M$ and its images

$K, L$, and $N$ after a $90^{\circ}$, $180^{\circ}$, and $270^{\circ}$ rotation around $C$ belong to the graph $y = A \sin x$, so the square $M K L N$ is inscribed in this graph. For sufficiently large $A$, the point $M$ of intersection of the graphs can be chosen in more than 1978 ways, at different distances from the point $O$; for example, for $A > 1978.2 \pi$, one point of intersection can be taken from the $k$-th wave of the original and the $k$-th wave of the rotated trajectory (waves are counted from $O$). Here, the theorem on the existence of a root of a continuous function that changes sign (see P5) is used: it is not difficult to derive the visually obvious fact that the graphs intersect on the specified segments.

question: 261. A regular $n$-sided polygon of area $S$ is inscribed in a circle of radius $R$. A point is marked on each side of the $n$-sided polygon. Prove that the perimeter of the $n$-sided polygon with vertices at the marked points is not less than $2 S / R$.
reference_solution:
261. Let $A_{i}$ be the vertices of an inscribed $n$-gon ( $i=1$, 2. $\ldots, n, n$); $b_{l}$ - a segment connecting two marked points on its sides emanating from $A_{i}$; $O$ - the center of the circle (Fig. 106):
$s_{i}$ and $s_{i}^{\prime}$ - the areas of triangles with base $b_{l}$, the vertices of which are $A_{l}$ and $O$, respectively, and $s_{i}^{\prime}$ is taken with a negative sign if $A_{i}$ and $O$ lie on the same side of the line containing $b_{i}$. Then $s_{i}+s_{i}^{\prime} \leqslant b_{i} R / 2$ for each $i$ and the sum $s_{1}^{\prime}+s_{2}^{\prime}+\ldots$ $\ldots+s_{n}^{\prime}$ is equal to the area of the polygon with vertices at the marked points (the sign + or - of the number $s_{i}^{\prime}$ indicates whether the side $b_{i}$ is visible from point $O$ inside or outside). Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
s=s_{1}+s_{2}+\ldots+s_{n}+s_{1}^{\prime}+s_{2}^{\prime}+\ldots+ & +s_{n}^{\prime} \leqslant \\
& \leqslant\left(b_{1}+b_{2}+\ldots+b_{n}\right) R / 2
\end{aligned}
$$

question:
262. A chip is placed in the corner of an $n \times n$ chessboard. Each of the two players, in turn, moves it to an adjacent square (one that shares a side with the current square). It is not allowed to move to a square that the chip has already visited. The player who cannot make a move loses.

a) Prove that if $n$ is even, the player who starts the game can ensure a win, and if $n$ is odd, the second player wins.

b) Who wins if the chip is initially placed not on a corner square, but on an adjacent one?
reference_solution:
262. a) If $n$ is even, the entire board can be divided into rectangles of size $1 \times 2$ cells («dominoes»). The first player will always have the opportunity to make a move (and thus win) if they follow this strategy: if the chip is on one of the cells of a certain domino, then they place it on the second cell of the same domino («cover» the domino).

If $n$ is odd, then all cells of the board, except the starting one - the corner, can be divided into dominoes. Now a similar strategy will be winning for the second player.

b) Answer: the first player always wins. For even $n$, the strategy is the same as in a). For odd $n$, the board should again be divided into dominoes, except for the corner cell; by coloring the board in a checkerboard pattern, it is easy to see that the second player will never be able to move to the corner cell, therefore

Fig. 107 the first player wins by following the same «covering» domino strategy.

question:
264. The numbers $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$ belong to the interval $[a ; b]$, where $0<a<b$. Prove the inequality

$\left(x_{1}+x_{2}+\ldots+x_{n}\right)\left(\frac{1}{x_{1}}+\frac{1}{x_{2}}+\ldots+\frac{1}{x_{n}}\right) \leqslant \frac{(a+b)^{2}}{4 a b} n^{2}$.
reference_solution:
264. First solution. Using the inequality $a b \leqslant \leqslant(a+b)^{2} / 4$, for any number $c>0$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P=\left(x_{1}+x_{2}+\ldots+x_{n}\right)\left(\frac{1}{x_{1}}+\frac{1}{x_{2}}+\ldots+\frac{1}{x_{n}}\right)= \\
= & \left(\frac{x_{1}}{c}+\ldots+\frac{x_{n}}{c}\right)\left(\frac{c}{x_{1}}+\ldots+\frac{c}{x_{n}}\right) \leqslant \\
& \leqslant \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{x_{1}}{c}+\frac{c}{x_{1}}+\frac{x_{2}}{c}+\frac{c}{x_{2}}+\ldots+\frac{x_{n}}{c}+\frac{c}{x_{n}}\right)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the function $f(t)=\frac{c}{t}+\frac{t}{c}$ attains its maximum value on $[a ; b]$ at one of the endpoints; choose $c$ such that these values coincide: $f(a)=f(b)$, i.e., take $c=\sqrt{a b}$. Then for $a \leqslant t \leqslant b$, we have $f(t) \leqslant \sqrt{a / b} + \sqrt{b / a}$. Therefore,

$$
P \leqslant n^{2}(\sqrt{a / b}+\sqrt{b / a})^{2} / 4 = n^{2}(a+b)^{2} / 4 a b
$$

Second solution. Place equal weights at points on the arc of the hyperbola $y=\Rightarrow =1 / x, a \leqslant x \leqslant b$, with abscissas $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}$. The center of mass of these weights is a point with abscissa $p=\left(x_{1}+x_{2}+\ldots+x_{n}\right) / n$ and ordinate $q=\left(\frac{1}{x_{1}}+\frac{1}{x_{2}}+\ldots+\frac{1}{x_{n}}\right) / n$ - this point will lie within the segment bounded by the arc of the hyperbola and the segment connecting its ends. Clearly, the point $(p ; q)$ in this segment for which the value $p q$ is the largest should be sought on the segment - the upper boundary of the segment (see Fig. 108). For points $(p ; q)$ on the line containing this segment, $q$ can be written as a linear function of $p$, then $p q$ will be a quadratic trinomial in $p$ (vanishing at $p=0$). To avoid writing it out explicitly - though this is not difficult - notice that at $p=a$ and $p=b$ it takes equal values $a \cdot \frac{1}{a}=b \cdot \frac{1}{b}=1$; therefore, its maximum value is attained halfway between these points and is equal to $(a+b)\left(\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}\right) / 4$. From this follows the required inequality.

$\nabla$ From the second solution, it is easy to derive a corollary: segments of any line between the points of intersection with the hyperbola $y=1 / x$ and its "asymptotes" - the coordinate axes (shown by dashed lines in the figure) are equal.

Returning to the original problem, note that for even $n$ the inequality gives an exact estimate of the left-hand side, and for odd $n$ it can be slightly refined. (For $n=5$, this problem was recently proposed in the USA Olympiad, see problem 7.22 in the book [41].)

question: 266*. Prove that for any tetrahedron, there exist two planes such that the ratio of the areas of the projections of the tetrahedron onto these planes is not less than $\sqrt{2}$
reference_solution:
266. Let's draw planes \( p \) and \( p' \) through two opposite edges \( a \) and \( b \) of a tetrahedron. Let \( h \) be the distance between them. We will only consider projections of the tetrahedron onto planes \( q \) perpendicular to \( p \), and among these, we will find those for which the ratio of the areas is not less than \( \sqrt{2} \). The projection of the tetrahedron onto the plane \( q \) is a trapezoid with bases \( a_q' \) and \( b_q' \) - the projections of \( a \) and \( b \) onto \( q \), and height \( h \) (in a special case, if the projection of one of the edges \( a \) or \( b \) consists of a single point, the trapezoid degenerates into a triangle); the area of the projection is \( \left(a_q' + b_q'\right) h / 2 \). To trace how this quantity depends on the inclination of the edges \( a \) and \( b \) to the plane \( q \), consider the vectors \( \boldsymbol{a} \) and \( \boldsymbol{b} \) represented by the edges of the tetrahedron (Fig. 110). Clearly, we can assume that \( a \geqslant b \) and the angle \( \gamma \) between the vectors \( \boldsymbol{a} \) and \( \boldsymbol{b} \) does not exceed \( 90^\circ \). If we draw them from the same point \( O \) - then instead of the lengths of the projections of the tetrahedron's edges onto the plane \( q \), we can talk about the lengths of the projections of the vectors \( \boldsymbol{a} \) and \( \boldsymbol{b} \) onto a line (in a plane parallel to \( p \) and \( p' \)). The sum of the projections onto the line \( l_1 \), parallel to the vector \( \boldsymbol{a} + \boldsymbol{b} \), is \( |\boldsymbol{a} + \boldsymbol{b}| \), and onto the line \( \boldsymbol{l}_2 \) perpendicular to \( a, b \sin \gamma \); the ratio of these two quantities is not less than \( \sqrt{2} \):

\[
|a+b|^2 = a^2 + b^2 + 2ab \geqslant a^2 + b^2 \geqslant 2b^2 \geqslant 2b^2 \sin^2 \psi
\]

\(\nabla\) Note that for a regular tetrahedron, the estimate \( \sqrt{2} \) is the best: the area of any of its projections is between \( a^2 / 3 \) and \( a^2 / (2 \sqrt{2}) \), where \( a \) is the length of the edge.
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-234.jpg?height=548&width=728&top_left_y=410&top_left_x=223)

Fig. 110

267. Let

$$
f(x)=\left(x-a_{1}\right)^{2}+\ldots+\left(x-a_{n}\right)^{2}
$$

By completing the square in this quadratic trinomial, we get

$$
f(x)=n\left(x-b_{n}\right)^{2}+f\left(b_{n}\right)
$$

when verifying this equality, it is necessary to take into account that $n b_{n}=a_{1}+$ $+a_{2}+\ldots+a_{n}$.

For $n=1$, the required inequalities are obvious ( $C=D$ ). To prove them using mathematical induction, it is sufficient to prove the inequalities

$$
0 \leqslant f\left(b_{n+1}\right)-f\left(b_{n}\right) \leqslant\left(a_{n+1}-b_{n+1}\right)^{2}
$$

since when adding one more number $a_{n+1}$ to $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$, the value of $C$ increases by $\left(a_{n+1}-b_{n+1}\right)^{2}$, and $D$ by $\left(a_{n+1}-b_{n+1}\right)^{2}+f\left(b_{n+1}\right)-f\left(b_{n}\right)$. The left inequality immediately follows from equality (*) when $x=b_{n+1}$; the right one follows from the equalities

$$
\begin{gathered}
(n+1) b_{n+1}=n b_{n}+a_{n+1}, \quad n\left(b_{n+1}-b_{n}\right)=a_{n+1}-b_{n+1} \\
f\left(b_{n+1}\right)-f\left(b_{n}\right)=n\left(b_{n+1}-b_{n}\right)^{2}=\left(a_{n+1}-b_{n+1}\right)^{2} / n .
\end{gathered}
$$

$\nabla$ The identity (*), expressing the sum of the squares of the distances to $n$ points through the square of the distance to their "center of mass" (or "mean value"), is constantly used in probability theory, statistics, and its analogs on the plane and in space - in geometry.

question: 271. In the parliament, each of its members has no more than three enemies. Prove that the parliament can be divided into two chambers so that each parliamentarian will have no more than one enemy in the same chamber. (It is assumed that if $B$ is an enemy of $A$, then $A$ is an enemy of $B$.)
reference_solution: 271. First, let's arbitrarily distribute the parliamentarians into two chambers. If in one of the chambers a member $A$ has at least two enemies, then in the other chamber $A$ has no more than one enemy. We will move $A$ to the other chamber; as a result, the total number $s$ of enemy pairs in both chambers decreases. Since $s$ is a non-negative integer, such a decrease can only be performed a finite number of times, and in the end, we will obtain the required partition into chambers.

272. All binary-rational fractions with denominators $2, 4, 8, 16$, etc., are easily obtained.

To obtain the fraction $1 / n$ from the pair $(0 ; 1)$, it is sufficient to choose $n$ different binary-rational numbers with a sum of 1 and take their arithmetic mean; for example, for $n=5:$

$$
\frac{1}{5}=\frac{\frac{3}{4}+\frac{3}{4^{2}}+\frac{3}{4^{3}}+\frac{3}{4^{4}}+\frac{1}{4^{4}}}{5}
$$

(a similar set can be constructed for any $n$).

Now, notice that if we can obtain $t$ from the pair of numbers $(0 ; 1)$ according to some plan, then by the same plan from the pair of numbers $(1,0)$ we will obtain $1-t$ (everywhere the numbers $x$ will be replaced by $1-x$ - the operation "arithmetic mean" preserves this replacement), and from the pair $(0 ; r)$ by the same plan we will obtain $(0 ; r t)$ (everywhere $x$ will be replaced by $r x$). Thus, if we have already obtained $1 / n$ and all numbers $k /(n-1), k=1,2, \ldots, n-1$, then we can obtain $1-\frac{1}{n}=\frac{n-1}{n}$ and all $\frac{k}{n}=\frac{n-1}{n} \cdot \frac{k}{n-1}$.

question:
273. A decreasing sequence $x_{n}$ of positive numbers is such that for any natural $n$

$$
x_{1}+\frac{x_{4}}{2}+\frac{x_{9}}{3}+\ldots+\frac{x_{n^{2}}}{n} \leqslant 1
$$

Prove that for any natural $n$

$$
x_{1}+\frac{x_{2}}{2}+\frac{x_{3}}{3}+\ldots+\frac{x_{n}}{n} \leqslant 3
$$
reference_solution:
273. Consider segments of the number series $x_{m} / m, k^{2} \leqslant m \leqslant$ $\leqslant(k+1)^{2}-1 \quad(k=1,2,3, \ldots), \quad k$-th segment consists of $(k+1)^{2}-k^{2}=2 k+1$ numbers from $x_{k^{2}} / k^{2}$ to $x_{(k+1)^{2}-1} /\left((k+1)^{2}-1\right)$.

By replacing each term $x_{m} / m$ in the $k$-th segment with the largest term in the segment $x_{k^{2}} / k^{2}$, we obtain that the sum of the numbers in this segment is no greater than

$$
\frac{(2 k+1) x_{k^{2}}}{k^{2}} \leqslant \frac{3 k x_{k^{2}}}{k^{2}}=\frac{3 x_{k^{2}}}{k}
$$

Now for any natural number $n$ we get

$$
\frac{x_{1}}{1}+\frac{x_{2}}{2}+\ldots+\frac{x_{n}}{n} \leqslant 3\left(\frac{x_{1}}{1}+\frac{x_{4}}{2}+\frac{x_{9}}{3}+\ldots+\frac{x_{q^{2}}}{q}\right)
$$

where $q$ is the smallest number for which $q^{2}>n$.

question: 274. On a plane, there are several points. For some pairs $A, B$ of these points, vectors $\overrightarrow{A B}$ are taken, such that in each point, the number of vectors starting from it is equal to the number of vectors ending at it. Prove that the sum of all selected vectors is 0.
reference_solution: 274. Let's choose any point $O$ and represent each of the vectors $\overrightarrow{A B}$ as $\overrightarrow{O B}-\overrightarrow{O A}$. In the sum of all vectors, each vector $\overrightarrow{O M}$, where $M$ is one of the given points, will appear as many times with a minus sign as with a plus sign, so the entire sum is 0.

question:
279. Natural numbers $p$ and $q$ are coprime. The segment $[0 ; 1]$ is divided into $p+q$ equal segments. Prove that in each of these segments, except for the two extreme ones, there lies exactly one of the $p+q-2$ numbers

$$
\frac{1}{p}, \frac{2}{p}, \ldots, \frac{p-1}{p}, \frac{1}{q}, \frac{2}{q}, \ldots, \frac{q-1}{q}
$$
reference_solution:
279. Since $p$ and $q$ are coprime, each of them is coprime with $n=p+q$. Therefore, all numbers

$$
\frac{l}{p}, \frac{l}{q}, \frac{i+j}{n} \quad(i=1,2, \ldots, p-1 ; j=1,2, \ldots, q-1)
$$

are distinct. Note that $\frac{l+1}{p+q}$ always lies between $\frac{l}{p}$ and $\frac{l}{q}$; therefore, it is clear that all fractions $\frac{l}{p}, \frac{l}{q}$ lie in different segments $\left[\frac{k}{n}, \frac{k+1}{n}\right], k=1,2, \ldots, n-2$.

280. Let $e_{l}$ be a unit vector directed along the line $l_{l}$. Put $e_{i} e_{l+1}=c_{l} (i=1,2, \ldots, 1978), e_{1979} e_{1}=c_{1979}$ ( $c_{l}$ - the cosine of the angle between $e_{l}$ and the next vector $\left.\boldsymbol{e}_{l+1}\right) ;$ let $\overrightarrow{O A}_{l}=a_{i} e_{l}$. The condition of perpendicularity of the lines $A_{i-1} A_{i+1}$ and $l_{i}$ is equivalent to:

$$
\left(a_{t-1} e_{i-1}-a_{i+1} e_{i+1}\right) e_{l}=0, \quad a_{i-1} c_{i-1}=a_{i+1} c_{l} .
$$

We can, by taking $a_{1}$ arbitrarily, choose $a_{3,} a_{6}, \ldots, a_{197}, a_{2}$, $a_{4}, \ldots, a_{1978}$ so that all 1979 conditions (*) are satisfied, except perhaps one: $a_{1978} c_{1978}=a_{1} c_{1979}$. But, multiplying all 1978 equalities

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{a_{3}}{a_{1}}=\frac{c_{1}}{c_{2}}, \frac{a_{5}}{a_{3}}=\frac{c_{3}}{c_{4}}, \ldots, \frac{a_{1979}}{a_{1977}}=\frac{c_{1977}}{c_{1978}}, \\
\frac{a_{2}}{a_{1979}}=\frac{c_{1979}}{a_{1}}, \frac{a_{4}}{a_{2}}=\frac{c_{2}}{c_{3}}, \ldots, \frac{a_{1978}}{a_{1976}}=\frac{c_{1976}}{c_{1977}},
\end{gathered}
$$

we will precisely obtain the missing 1979th equality after simplifications.

question:
281*. The final sequence $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ of numbers 0 and 1 must satisfy the following condition: for any integer $k$ from 0 to $n-1$, the sum

$$
a_{1} a_{k+1}+a_{2} a_{k+2}+\ldots+a_{n-k} a_{n}
$$

is an odd number.

a) Come up with such a sequence for $n=25$.

b) Prove that such a sequence exists for some $n>1000$.
reference_solution:
281. The value specified in the problem condition

$$
p_{k}=a_{1} a_{k+1}+a_{2} a_{k+2}+\ldots+a_{n-k} a_{n}
$$

is conveniently calculated as follows: the sequence $A_{n}=\left(a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}\right)$ is signed under itself with a shift of $k$ digits; in this case, $p_{k}=p_{k}\left(A_{n}\right)$ is the number of digits where ones are present in both rows.

A sequence $A_{n}$ of length $n$ satisfies the problem condition if all $p_{k}\left(A_{n}\right)$ for $0 \leqslant k \leqslant n-1$ are odd.

The following construction allows constructing $A_{l}=A_{n} \sqcup A_{m}$ of length $l=1$ 238
$=(2 m-1) n-(m-1)=2 m n-m-n+1$. Replace each 1 in $A_{n}$ with the block $A_{m} \underbrace{0 \ldots 0}_{m-1}$ of $2 m-1$ digits, each 0 in $A_{n}$ with a block of $2 m-1$ zeros, and discard the last $m-1$ zeros. When calculating $p_{k}$ for $A_{l}$ using the method described above for any shift $k$, each block $A_{m}$ in the upper row touches only one block $A_{m}$ in the lower row; if $k=(2 m-1) q+r$ or $k=(2 m-1) q-r$, where $0 \leqslant r \leqslant m-1$, $0 \leqslant q \leqslant n-1$, then $p_{k}\left(A_{l}\right)=p_{q}\left(A_{n}\right) \cdot p_{r}\left(A_{m}\right)$, since exactly $p_{q}\left(A_{n}\right)$ pairs of blocks $A_{m}$ touch each other and they are shifted by $r$ digits. From this, it is clear that the constructed sequence $A_{l}=A_{n} \sqcup A_{m}$ satisfies the problem condition along with $A_{n}$ and $A_{m}$.

This construction allows creating the answer $A_{25}=A_{4} \sqcup A_{4}$ for part (a) from $A_{4}=1101$:

$$
A_{25}=110100011010000000000 \text{. } 1101 .
$$

Further, $A_{25} \sqcup A_{25}$ already has $2 \cdot 25^{2}-50+1=1201-$ more than 1000 digits, as required in part (b),

$\nabla$ There are other series of sequences that satisfy the problem condition. One of them was devised by the olympiad participant A. A. Razborov. It is interesting to obtain their complete description. A similar problem can be considered on a circle.

question: 282. A convex quadrilateral $A B C D$ is divided by its diagonals into four triangles. Prove that if the radii of all four inscribed circles in these triangles are equal to each other, then the quadrilateral $A B C D$ is a rhombus.
reference_solution:
282. Suppose the diagonals of the quadrilateral $ABCD_{\text{s}}$ intersect at point $O$, and are not perpendicular to each other, for example, that angle $AOB$ is acute. Construct points $A'$ and $B'$, symmetric to $A$ and $B$ with respect to point $O$. The radii of the circles inscribed in triangles $A'OB$ and $B'OC$ are less than the radius $n$ of the circle inscribed in $\triangle AOB$ (the areas of all these triangles are equal, and the perimeter of $\triangle AOB$ is smaller), so the tangents drawn from points $A$ and $B$ to the circles of radius $r$ inscribed in angles $BOC$ and $AOD$ intersect the rays $OA'$ and $OB'$ at points $C$ and $D$, which are farther from $O$ than $A'$ and $B'$ respectively, so that the segment $CD$ cannot touch the circle of radius $r_2$ inscribed in $\triangle OA'B'$.

Thus, under the conditions of the problem, the lines $AC$ and $BD$ are perpendicular to each other and, considering the equality of the radii of the inscribed circles, serve as the axes of symmetry of the quadrilateral $ABCD$. Therefore, this quadrilateral is a rhombus.

question:
283*. On a line, points $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n}$ are arranged in order such that the lengths of the segments $A_{1} A_{2}, A_{2} A_{3}, \ldots, A_{n-1} A_{n}$ do not exceed 1. It is required to mark $k-1$ of the points $A_{2}, \ldots, A_{n-1}$ in red so that the lengths of any two of the $k$ parts into which the segment $A_{1} A_{n}$ is divided by the red points differ by no more than 1. Prove that this can always be done:

a) for $k=3$

b) for each natural number $k<n-1$.

14th All-Union Olympiad, 1980 (Saratov)

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_7b8a6b2625543c3dae75g-075.jpg?height=146&width=662&top_left_y=1477&top_left_x=273)
reference_solution:
283. a) Let's consider possible arrangements $T$ of a pair of red points ($A_{l}, A_{r}$) that divide the segment $A_{0} A_{n}$ into three parts: $A_{0} A_{l}, A_{l} A_{r}, A_{r} A_{n}$. Let the largest of these parts be denoted by $M$, and the smallest by $m$. From all the arrangements $T$, we select those for which $M$ is minimal, and from these, we select the one (or one of those) for which $m$ is maximal. We will prove that for such an arrangement $T = (A_{l}, A_{r})$, the condition $M - m \leq 1$ will be satisfied.

Suppose for this arrangement $M - m > 1$. If the parts $M$ and $m$ are adjacent, then by moving the red boundary between them by one segment, we obtain an arrangement $T'$ where the smallest part is greater than $m$ and (possibly or) the largest part is less than $M$, which contradicts the choice of $T$. If $m = A_{0} A_{1}$ and $M = A_{r} A_{n}$, then either the arrangement $(A_{l+1}, A_{r})$ has a smallest part greater than $m$, or $A_{l+1} A_{r} \leq m$. In the latter case, we can repeat the same procedure several more times. During this process, we cannot repeat ourselves because the newly obtained arrangement is "better" in the sense that it either has a strictly smaller length of the largest part $M$, or the $M$ are the same but there are fewer parts equal to $M$, or both these numbers are the same but $m$ is larger, or (with equal $m$) there are fewer parts equal to $m$. Since the total number of arrangements is finite, after several repetitions of the procedure, we will arrive at an arrangement that cannot be "improved," i.e., $M - m \leq 1$.

question:
285. The vertical side $AB$ of the square $ABCD$ is divided into $n$ segments such that the sum of the lengths of the segments with even numbers is equal to the sum of the lengths of the segments with odd numbers. Through the points of division, segments parallel to the side $AD$ are drawn, and then each of the resulting $n$ strips is divided into two parts - left and right - by the diagonal $BD$.

Prove that the sum of the areas of the left parts with odd numbers is equal to the sum of the areas of the right parts with even numbers (in Fig. 13, these parts are shaded).
reference_solution:
285. If $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ are the sums of the areas of the left parts with even and odd numbers, and $S_{3}$ and $S_{4}$ are the analogous sums for the right parts, then

$$
S_{2}+S_{4}=S_{3}+S_{1}=S_{3}+S_{4}=S_{1}+S_{2}
$$

question: 287. Points $M$ and $P$ are the midpoints of sides $B C$ and $C D$ of the convex quadrilateral $A B C D$. It is known that $A M + A P = a$. Prove that the area of quadrilateral $A B C D$ is less than $a^{2} / 2$.
reference_solution:
287. $S_{A B C D}=2 S_{A M P C}$. Let $A M=x$, then

$$
S_{A M C D}<2 S_{A M P} \leqslant x(a-x) \leqslant \frac{a^{2}}{4}
$$

question: 290. On the shore of a large round lake, there are several settlements. Some of them are connected by ferry routes. It is known that two settlements are connected by a route if and only if the two next settlements in the counterclockwise direction are not connected by a route. Prove that from any settlement to any other settlement, one can travel by ferry, and with no more than two transfers.
reference_solution: 290. Let $A, B$ and $C$ be three consecutive points on the shore of a lake. From the condition, it follows that $A$ and $B$ are connected if and only if $B$ and $C$ are not connected. Thus, all points are divided into pairs of adjacent points connected by a steamboat route. Moreover, any two such pairs are connected, i.e., one of the points of the first pair is connected to some point of the second pair.

question: 291. A six-digit number, written with six different non-zero digits, is divisible by 37. Prove that by rearranging the digits of this number, you can obtain at least 23 other different six-digit numbers that are divisible by 37.
reference_solution: 291. Along with the number $N=\overline{a b c d e f}$, the numbers $\overline{a b c}+\overline{d e f}$, $\overline{b c a f d e}$, and $\overline{c a b d e f}$ are also divisible by 37.

question: 305. On a circle, points $A, B, M$ and $N$ are given. From point $M$, chords $M A_{1}$ and $M B_{1}$ are drawn, perpendicular to the lines $N B$ and $N A$ respectively. Prove that the lines $A A_{1}$ and $B B_{1}$ are parallel.
reference_solution: 305. It is sufficient to prove that $\angle B_{1} M A=\angle A A_{1} B_{1}=$ $=\angle A_{1} B_{1} B$.

question:
307. The table has 4 rows. In the first row, arbitrary natural numbers are written, which may include identical ones. The second row is filled as follows: from left to right, the numbers in the first row are examined, and under the number $a$, the number $k$ is written if $a$ appears for the $k$-th time in the first row. Similarly, the third row is written based on the second row, and the fourth row is written based on the third row.

Prove that the second and fourth rows are always the same.
reference_solution: 307. If in some column of the table the first three numbers, counting from the top, are $a, m$ and $n$, then each of the numbers $1,2, \ldots, m-1, m$ will appear in the second row to the left of the number $m$ at least $n$ times, and any number greater than $m$ will appear fewer than $n$ times.

question: 309. Equilateral triangles $A B C, C D E$ and $E H K$ (vertices are listed counterclockwise) are placed on a plane such that $\overrightarrow{A D}=\overrightarrow{D K}$. Prove that triangle $B H D$ is also equilateral.
reference_solution: 309. When rotated by $60^{\circ}$ around vertex $C$, triangle $C A D$ will transform into triangle $C B E$, and when rotated by $60^{\circ}$ around point $H$, triangle $H B E$ will transform into triangle $H D K$.

question:
310. In a certain village, there are 1000 residents. Every day, each of them shares the news they learned yesterday with all their acquaintances. It is known that any news eventually becomes known to all residents of the village.

Prove that it is possible to choose 90 residents such that if they are all simultaneously informed of some news, it will become known to all residents of the village within 10 days.
reference_solution: 310. We will say that residents $X, A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{k}, Y$ form a chain if $X$ is acquainted with $A_{1}, A_{2}$ is acquainted with $A_{3}, \ldots, A_{k}$ is acquainted with Y. From the condition, it follows that any two residents are connected by some chain. We will consider that there are no closed chains (i.e., chains where $X$ is acquainted with $Y$). Let's take the longest chain $X-A_{1}-A_{2}-\ldots-A_{10}-\ldots-A_{k}-Y$. If $k \leqslant 19$, then the news told by $A_{10}$ will be known to all residents of the village in 10 days. If $k \geqslant 20$, we will separate residents $X, A_{1}, \ldots, A_{10}$ and all those who are connected to them not through $A_{11}$ (there are at least 11 of them). The remaining group of residents still satisfies the condition of the problem. Repeating the already described procedure 89 times (and selecting their own $A_{10}$ at each step), we will either exhaust all residents at some step or leave no more than $1000-89 \cdot 11=21$, from which we will select one more as described above. If there are closed chains in the village, they can be broken while preserving the conditions of the problem.

question:
311. For numbers $a$ and $b$, it is known that the inequality

$$
a \cos x + b \cos 3x > 1
$$

has no solutions. Prove that $|b| \leqslant 1$.
reference_solution: 311. We have $f(\pi n)=(-1)^{n} a+(-1)^{n} b ; \quad f(\pi / 3)=a / 2-b$; $(2 \pi / 3)=-a / 2+b$. Therefore $|a+b| \leqslant 1,|a-2 b| \leqslant 2$.

question: 314*. Is it possible to color all cells of some rectangular table in white and black so that there are an equal number of white and black cells, and in each row and each column, more than $3 / 4$ of the cells are of one color?

315. Prove that if the quadrilaterals $A C P H$, $A M B E$, $A H B T$, $B K X M$, $C K X P$ are parallelograms, then the quadrilateral $A B T E$ is also a parallelogram (the vertices of all quadrilaterals are listed counterclockwise).
reference_solution: 315. It follows from the condition that $\overrightarrow{A E}=\overrightarrow{M B}=X \vec{K}=P \vec{C}=H \vec{A}=\overrightarrow{B T}$.

question: 317. In a football tournament, 18 teams played 8 rounds - each team played against eight different teams. Prove that there will be three teams that have not played against each other yet.
reference_solution: 317. For any team, there will be 9 teams that it has not yet played against, and among these nine, there will be two that have not played against each other.

question:
318. Points $C_{1}, A_{1}, B_{1}$ are taken on the sides $A B, B C$, and $C A$ of triangle $A B C$ respectively, such that

$$
A C_{1}: C_{1} B=B A_{1}: A_{1} C=C B_{1}: B_{1} A=1 / 3
$$

Prove that the perimeter $P$ of triangle $A B C$ and the perimeter $p$ of triangle $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$ are related by the inequalities

$$
\frac{1}{2} P<p<\frac{3}{4} P
$$
reference_solution: 318. Let $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}$ be points on the sides $B C, C A$, and $A B$ such that $A C_{2} / C_{2} B = B A_{1} / A_{1} C = C B_{2} / B_{2} A = 3$. The perimeter of the hexagon $A_{1} A_{2} B_{1} B_{2} C_{1} C_{2}$ is $3 / 4 P$ and is greater than the perimeter of the triangle $A_{1} B_{1} C_{1}$. Next, write the triangle inequality for the triangles $A_{2} C_{1} B_{1}, C_{1} B_{2} A_{1}, A_{1} B_{1} C_{2}$.

question: 320. A student needs to copy a convex polygon that fits inside a circle of radius 1. First, the student laid out the first side, then drew the second from its end, the third from the end of the second, and so on. Upon completing the construction, the student found that the polygon did not close, and the first and last vertices drawn were separated by a distance $d$. It is known that the angles were laid out accurately, and the relative error in laying out the length of each side did not exceed the number $p$. Prove that $d \leqslant 4 p$.
reference_solution: 320. Let $A$ and $B$ be the endpoints of the constructed broken line. Project the broken line onto the line $AB$. The relative error of each segment is $p$, so the sum of the absolute errors of all segments does not exceed $4 p$, hence $d \leqslant 4 p$.

question:
329. a) Let $m$ and $n$ be natural numbers. Prove that if for some non-negative integers $k_{1}, k_{2}, \ldots, k_{n}$ the number $2^{k_{1}}+2^{k_{2}}+\ldots+2^{k_{n}}$ is divisible by $2^{m}-1$, then $n \geqslant m$.

b) Does there exist a natural number that is divisible by $\underbrace{111 \ldots 1}$ and has a sum of digits less than $m$?
reference_solution:
329. a) From all numbers of the form $2^{k_{1}}+2^{k_{2}}+\ldots+2^{k_{n}}$ that are divisible by $2^{m}-1$, we select the numbers with the smallest $n$, and from the obtained numbers, we select the number with the smallest $k_{1}+k_{2}+\ldots+k_{n}$. All numbers in the set $(k_{1}, k_{2}, \ldots, k_{n})$ are distinct. If $n<m$, then $k_{i} \leqslant m-1$ and $2^{k_{1}}+2^{k_{2}}+\ldots+2^{k_{n}}<2^{m}-1$. Contradiction.

b) It does not exist. Let $P=a_{1} 1^{2}+\ldots+a_{r}$ be the smallest number divisible by $M=\underbrace{11 \ldots 1}_{m}$ and having a sum of digits less than $m$. Then $r \geqslant m$ and the number $P_{1}=P-\left(10^{r}-10^{r-m}\right)$, which is divisible by $M$, is smaller than $P$ and has a sum of digits not exceeding the sum of the digits of $P$.

question: 330. A non-negative real number is assigned to each vertex of a cube, with the sum of all these numbers being 1. Two players play the following game: the first player chooses any face of the cube, the second player chooses another face, and finally, the first player chooses a third face. It is not allowed to choose faces parallel to the already chosen ones. Prove that the first player can play in such a way that the number corresponding to the common vertex of the three chosen faces does not exceed $1 / 6$.
reference_solution: 330. Among eight numbers, there are three that do not exceed y/6, and two of them will be at the ends of the diagonal of one of the faces. The player should choose this face first.

question: 334. Inside a tetrahedron, a point $M$ is chosen. Prove that at least one edge of the tetrahedron is seen from point $M$ at an angle whose cosine is no greater than $-1 / 3$.
reference_solution: 334. Let $A M, B M, C M$ and $D M$ be segments of length 1, laid out on the rays connecting point $M$ with the vertices of the tetrahedron. The line $D M$ intersects the triangle $A B C$ at some point $P$. If the cosines of the angles $A M D, B M D$ and $C M D$ are greater than $-1 / 3$, then these angles are less than $\varphi=\arccos (-1 / 3)$, and the angles $A M B, B M P$ and $C M P$ are greater than $\pi-\varphi$. We can assume that $\angle A P B \geqslant 120^{\circ}$. Then, writing the cosine theorem for triangles $A P B$ and $A M B$, we get that $\cos \angle A M B < -1 / 3$.

question:
336. A closed broken line $M$ has an odd number of vertices - sequentially $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{2 n+1}$. Denote by $S(M)$ a new closed broken line, the successive vertices $B_{1}, B_{2}, \ldots, B_{2 n+1}$ of which are the midpoints of the segments of the broken line $M: B_{1}$ - the midpoint of segment $A_{1} A_{2}, B_{2}$ - the midpoint of $A_{3} A_{4}, \ldots, B_{n+1}$ - the midpoint of $A_{2 n+1} A_{1}, B_{n+2}$ - the midpoint of $A_{2} A_{3}, \ldots, B_{2 n+1}$ - the midpoint of $A_{2 n} A_{2 n+1}$. Prove that in the sequence of broken lines constructed in this way

$$
M_{1}=S(M), M_{2}=S\left(M_{1}\right), M_{3}=S\left(M_{2}\right), \ldots, M_{k}=S\left(M_{k-1}\right)
$$

there will be a closed broken line homothetic to the original broken line $M$.
reference_solution:
336. Let $\quad 0$-point, for which $\overrightarrow{O_{1}}+\overrightarrow{O A_{2}}+\ldots$ ... $+\overrightarrow{O A}_{2^{n+1}}=0$. Choose $k$ such that $2^{k}-1$ is divisible by
$2 n+1$. Then the broken line $M_{k}$ will be homothetic to $M$ with respect to $O$ with a coefficient of $2^{-k}$.

question:
341. Prove that for all positive values of $x$ the inequality

$$
2^{12} \sqrt{x}+2^{\sqrt[4]{x}} \geqslant 2 \cdot 2^{\sqrt[6]{x}}
$$

holds.
reference_solution: 341. $2^{\sqrt[12]{\sqrt{x}}}+2^{\sqrt[4]{x}} \geqslant 2 \cdot 2^{\frac{\sqrt[4]{x}+\sqrt{x}}{2}} \geqslant 2 \cdot 2^{\sqrt[6]{x}}$.

question: 345. In a square table of $n \times n$ cells, $n-1$ cells are marked. Prove that by permuting the rows among themselves and the columns among themselves, it is possible to achieve that all the marked cells lie below the diagonal of the table.
reference_solution: 345. A column without marked cells is swapped with the rightmost column, and the last row of the resulting table is swapped with some row containing marked cells. The problem is reduced to a $(n-1) \times(n-1)$ table.

question:
346. Prove that for any natural number $n$ and any real number $a$, the inequality

$$
|a||a-1||a-2| \ldots|a-n| \geqslant\langle a\rangle \frac{n!}{2^{n}}
$$

holds, where $\langle a\rangle$... is the distance from the number $a$ to the nearest integer to it, $n!=1,2, \ldots, n$.

348*. The vertices of the tetrahedron KLMN lie inside, on the faces, or on the edges of another tetrahedron $A B C D$. Prove that the sum of the lengths of all the edges of the tetrahedron $K I M N$ is less than $4 / 3$ of the sum of the lengths of all the edges of the tetrahedron $A B C D$.

17th All-Union Olympiad, 1983 (Kishinev)

| Class | 1st day |  |  |  | 2nd day |  |  |  |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| 8 | 349 | 350 | 351 | 352 | 360 | 361 | 362 | 363 |
| 9 | 353 | 354 | 355 | 356 | 364 | 365 | 366 | 367 |
| 10 | 357 | 354 | 358 | 359 | 360 | 368 | 369 | 370 |
reference_solution: 348. Let the face $K L M$ of the tetrahedron $K L M N$ have the largest perimeter. Let $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}, D_{1}$ be the projections of points $A, B, C, D$ onto the plane $K L M$ and let $\Gamma$ be the broken line bounding the projection of the tetrahedron $K L M N$ onto this plane. Let $P_{R S T Q}$ be the sum of the lengths of all six segments connecting the points $R, S, T$ and $Q$. Then 1) $P_{K L M N} \leqslant 2 P_{K L M} ; \quad$ 2) $\quad P_{K L M} \leqslant P_{\Gamma} ;$ 3) $\quad P_{\Gamma} \leqslant$ $\left.\leqslant \frac{2}{3} P_{A_{1} B_{1} C_{1} D_{1}} ; 4\right) P_{A_{1} B_{1} C_{1} D_{1}} \leqslant P_{A B C D}$.

question: 351. Three circles touched each other externally at points $X, Y, Z$. Then the radii of these circles were increased by more than $2 / \sqrt{3}$ times, keeping the centers. Prove that every point of triangle $X Y Z$ is covered by at least one of the enlarged circles.
reference_solution: 351. Let $O$ be a point inside triangle XYZ. Connect it with the centers $O_{1}, O_{2}, O_{3}$ of the given circles and the points $X, Y, Z$. One of the six resulting angles (acute!) is not less than $60^{\circ}$ (for example, angle $O_{1} X A$). Then $A O < O X / \sin 60^{\circ} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} O X$.

question: 357. The magnitudes $\alpha$ and $\beta$ of two acute angles satisfy the equation $\sin ^{2} \alpha+\sin ^{2} \beta=\sin (\alpha+\beta)$. Prove that $\alpha+\beta=\pi / 2$.
reference_solution: 357. From the condition, it follows that $\sin \alpha(\sin \alpha-\cos \beta)=$ $=\sin \beta(\cos \alpha-\sin \beta)$. If $\sin \alpha>\cos \beta$ and $\cos \alpha>\sin \beta$, then $\sin ^{2} \beta+\cos ^{2} \beta<1$. The inequalities $\sin \alpha<\cos \beta, \cos \alpha<\sin \beta$ are also impossible. Therefore, $\sin \alpha=\cos \beta, \cos \alpha=\sin \beta$.

question:
358. The vertices of the tetrahedron $ABCD$ are orthogonally projected onto two planes. Points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}$, $D_{1}$ and $A_{2}, B_{2}, C_{2}, D_{2}$ are the projections of the corresponding vertices. Prove that one of the planes can be moved in space so that the lines $A_{1} A_{2}$, $B_{1} B_{2}, C_{1} C_{2}, D_{1} D_{2}$ become parallel.

359 *. A schoolboy is practicing solving quadratic equations. After solving another quadratic equation and verifying that it has two roots, he forms the following equation according to the rule: the constant term is equal to the larger root, the coefficient of the variable $x$ is equal to the smaller root, and the coefficient of $x^{2}$ is equal to one. Prove that this exercise cannot continue indefinitely. What is the maximum number of equations he might have to solve?
reference_solution: 358. Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ be given planes and $l$ be their line of intersection. It is sufficient to rotate the plane $\alpha$ around the line $l$ until it coincides with the plane $\beta$ (points $A_{1}, B_{1}, C_{1}, D_{1}$ rotate together with the plane $\alpha$).

question:
366. Inside triangle $ABC$, an arbitrary point $O$ is chosen. Prove that the following equality holds:

$$
S_{A} \cdot \overrightarrow{O A} + S_{B} \cdot \overrightarrow{O B} + S_{C} \cdot \overrightarrow{O C} = 0
$$

where $S_{A}, S_{B}, S_{C}$ are the areas of triangles $BCO$, $CAO$, and $ABO$ respectively.
reference_solution: 366. Let $\boldsymbol{e}_{1}, \boldsymbol{e}_{2}, \boldsymbol{e}_{3}$ be unit vectors in the same direction as vectors $\overrightarrow{O A}, \overrightarrow{O B}, \overrightarrow{O C} ; \angle B O C=\alpha, \angle C O A=\beta, \angle A O B=\gamma$. It is sufficient to prove that $e_{1} \sin \alpha+e_{2} \sin \beta+e_{3} \sin \gamma=0$. For this, we should consider the triangle $P Q R$, the sides of which are respectively parallel to $O A, O B$ and $O C$, and use the equality $\quad \overrightarrow{P Q}+\overrightarrow{P R}+\overrightarrow{Q P}=0$.

question: 367. Prove that among any $2 m+1$ different integers, not exceeding $2 m-1$ in absolute value, one can find three numbers whose sum is 0.
reference_solution: 367. Induction on $m$: for $m=1$ the statement is true. Let it be true for $m=k-1$ ($k \geqslant 2$). Consider any set $A$ consisting of $2 k+1$ numbers, not exceeding $2 k-1$ in absolute value. If among them there are $2 k-1$ numbers not exceeding $2 k-3$ in absolute value, then everything is clear. Otherwise, we can assume that in $A$ there are either the numbers $2 k-1, 2 k-2$ and $-2 k+1$, or $2 k-1, 2 k-2$ and $-2 k-2$. In the first case, consider the pairs $(1 ; 2 k-2), \quad(2 ; 2 k-3), \ldots$ $\ldots,(k-1, \quad k) \quad$ and $\quad(0, \quad-2 k+1), \quad(-1, \quad-2 k+2), \ldots$ ..., $(-k+1,-k)$. At least one pair consists of numbers belonging to $A$. In the second case, similarly, the pairs $(1,2 k-3), \ldots,(k-2, k)$ and $(0,-2 k+1),(-1,-2 k), \ldots$ $\ldots,(-k+1,-k)$ are considered.

question: 369. The set $M$ consists of $k$ pairwise non-intersecting segments lying on the same line. It is known that any segment of length not greater than 1 can be placed on the line so that its ends belong to the set $M$. Prove that the sum of the lengths of the segments that make up $M$ is not less than $1 / k$.
reference_solution: 369. If on a line there are non-intersecting segments $\Delta_{1}$ and $\Delta_{2}$ with lengths $\alpha$ and $\beta$, then the set of lengths of segments with endpoints belonging to $\Delta_{1}$ and $\Delta_{2}$ fills some segment of length $\alpha+\beta$. Therefore, if $\delta_{1}, \delta_{2}, \ldots, \delta_{k}$ are the lengths of the given segments, then $\delta_{1}+\left(\delta_{1}+\delta_{2}\right)+\left(\delta_{1}+\delta_{3}\right)+\ldots+\left(\delta_{1}+\delta_{k}\right)+\ldots+\left(\delta_{k-1}+\right.$ $\left.+\delta_{k}\right)+\delta_{k}=k\left(\delta_{1}+\delta_{2}+\ldots+\delta_{k}\right) \geqslant 1$.

question:
371. a) The product of some $n$ integers is equal to $n$, and their sum is zero. Prove that the number $n$ is divisible by 4.

b) Let $n$ be a natural number divisible by 4. Prove that there exist $n$ integers whose product is equal to $n$, and their sum is zero.
reference_solution:
371. a) If $n$ is not divisible by 4, then among the factors there is only one even number, and therefore their sum is not equal to 0.

b) Answer: for $n=4k$, $n=2 \cdot(-2k) \cdot 1^{3k-2} \cdot(-1)^{k}$, if $k$ is even, and $n=(-2)(-2k) \cdot 1^{3k} \cdot(-1)^{k-2}$, if $k$ is odd.

question:
375. Prove that for all real $x>0, y>0$ and for all real $\alpha$ the inequality

$$
x^{\sin ^{2} \alpha} \cdot y^{\cos ^{2} \alpha}<x+y
$$

holds.
reference_solution: 375. $x^{\sin ^{2} \alpha} \cdot y^{\cos ^{2} \alpha} \leqslant \max (x, y)<x+y$.

question: 380. In a row, n different real numbers were written in increasing order. Under them, in the second row, the same numbers were written, but perhaps in a different order. For each pair of numbers written one under the other, their sum was calculated. These sums formed the third row. It turned out that the numbers in the third row are also arranged in increasing order. Prove that the first row coincides with the second.
reference_solution: 380. If the first row contains numbers $a_{1}<a_{2}<\ldots$ $\ldots<a_{m}<a_{m+1}<\ldots<a_{n}$, and the second row consists of numbers $a_{k_{1}}, a_{k_{2}}, \ldots, a_{k_{m}}, a_{k_{m+1}}, \ldots, a_{k_{n}}$, then the third row contains numbers $a_{1}+a_{k_{1}}, a_{2}+a_{k_{2}}, \ldots, a_{m}+a_{k_{m}}$. Let $a_{1} \neq a_{k_{1}}$. Then $a_{1}=a_{k_{m}}$ for some $\dot{m} \geqslant 2$. By the condition $a_{1}+a_{k_{1}}<a_{m}+a_{k_{m}}$, $a_{2}+a_{k_{2}}<a_{m}+a_{2}, \ldots, a_{m-1}+a_{k_{m-1}}<a_{m}+a_{k_{m}}$, from which $a_{k_{2}}<a_{m}, a_{k_{3}}<a_{m}, \ldots, a_{k_{m-1}}<a_{m}$. question: 406*. On a plane, $n$ lines ($n>2$) are drawn, dividing the plane into several regions. Some of these regions are colored, with the condition that no two colored regions can touch along a boundary. Prove that the number of colored regions does not exceed $\frac{1}{3}\left(n^{2}+n\right)$.
reference_solution: 406. If all the lines are pairwise parallel, the statement is obvious. Let $m_{2}, m_{\mathrm{s}}, \ldots, m_{k}$ be the numbers of colored regions having $k$ sides. Then $m_{2} \leqslant n$. Moreover, each line is divided by the others into no more than $n$ parts, so the total number of parts of the lines is no more than $n^{2}$. Therefore, $2 m_{2}+3 m_{3}+\ldots \leqslant n^{2}$. Finally, $m_{2}+m_{3}+\ldots+m_{k}+\ldots \leqslant$ $\leqslant \frac{m_{2}}{3}+\frac{2 m_{2}+\ldots+k_{m_{k}}}{3} \leqslant \frac{n(n+1)}{3}$.

question: 437. Prove that the sum of all numbers of the form $\frac{1}{m^{n}}$, where $m, n$ are natural numbers and $1 \leqslant m<n \leqslant 1986$, is not an integer.

## QUADRILATERAL IN A PARALLELOGRAM
reference_solution:

Then $2 a^{2}+2 b^{2}=c^{2}+4 m^{2}$. Let $P$ be the point of intersection of line $C N$ with the circumcircle. Considering the chords $P C$ and $A B$ intersecting at point $N$, we get $P N \cdot m=c^{2} / 4$.

If it is given that $O M \perp C N$, then $M$ is the midpoint of chord $F C$, $P N=2 C M-C N=m / 3$, $P N \cdot m=m^{2} / 3=c^{2} / 4$, and $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2} / 2+2 m^{2}=2 c^{2}$.

Conversely, if it is given that $a^{2}+b^{2}=2 c^{2}$, then $m^{2}=\frac{a^{2}+b^{2}}{2}-\frac{c^{2}}{4}=\frac{3}{4} c^{2}$, $P N \cdot m=c^{2} / 4=m^{2} / 3$, from which $P N=m / 3$. Since $M N=m / 3$ and $C M=2 m / 3$, $M$ is the midpoint of chord $P C$ and, therefore, $O M \perp C N$.

reference_solution:

## CHAIN OF PIGLETS
reference_solution:
6.2. a) Let $M$ lie on the arc $A_{1} A_{2}$ of the circle $O$ (figure a). Rotate the triangle $A_{1} M A_{2}$ around the vertex $A_{2}$ by $60^{\circ}$ so that the segment $A_{2} A_{2}$ lies on the segment $A_{0} A_{2}$. Prove that then the vertex $M$ will fall on the point $K$ lying on the segment $A_{0} M$. The triangle $K M A_{2}$ will be equilateral. From this, it will follow that $A_{1} M + A_{2} M = A_{0} K + K M = A_{0} M$.

Another solution to the same problem can be easily obtained using Ptolemy's theorem: for any inscribed (convex) quadrilateral $A B C D$

$$
A C \cdot B D = A B \cdot C D + B C \cdot A D
$$

It is sufficient to apply this theorem to the quadrilateral $A_{0} A_{1} M A_{2}$; since $A_{0} A_{1} = A_{1} A_{2} = A_{0} A_{2}$, it follows from the equality

$$
A_{1} A_{2} \cdot A_{0} M = A_{0} A_{1} \cdot A_{2} M + A_{0} A_{2} \cdot A_{1} M
$$

that $A_{0} M = A_{2} M + A_{1} M$.

Note that Ptolemy's theorem can be proven using a diagram very similar to our figure a (but using not just a simple rotation, but a similarity transformation). The plan of the proof is as follows: find a point $K$ on the diagonal $A C$ such that the triangles $A K D$ and $B C D$ are similar $(\angle A K D = \angle B C D)$, then $A K \cdot B D = B C \cdot A D$; prove that in this case the triangles $K C D$ and $A B D$ are similar $(\angle K D C = \angle A D B)$, then $K C \cdot B D = A B \cdot C D$ and as a result $(A K + K C) B D = A C \cdot B D = B C \cdot A D + A B \cdot C D$.

b) Let a new circle touch the circle $O$ externally at the point $M$, lying on the arc $A_{1} A_{2}$. Recall that the square of the tangent is equal to the product of the segments of any secant (from a given point to the points of intersection with the circle). Draw a secant through the points $A_{0}, A_{1}, A_{2}$ and the point $M$ and denote by $P_{0}, P_{1}, P_{2}$ their second points of intersection with the new circle (figure b). We need to prove that

$$
\sqrt{A_{0} M \cdot A_{0} P_{0}} = \sqrt{A_{1} M \cdot A_{1} P_{1}} + \sqrt{A_{2} M \cdot A_{2} P_{2}}
$$

In part a) we proved that

$$
A_{0} M = A_{1} M + A_{2} M
$$

It remains to note that the new circle is obtained from the old one by a homothety (similar transformation) with the center at the point $M$, therefore

$$
\frac{M P_{0}}{A_{0} M} = \frac{M P_{1}}{A_{1} M} = \frac{M P_{2}}{A_{2} M} = k
$$

where $k$ is the ratio of the radii of the circles, from which

$$
\frac{A_{0} P_{0}}{A_{0} M} = \frac{A_{1} P_{1}}{A_{1} M} = \frac{A_{2} P_{2}}{A_{2} M} = 1 + k
$$

i.e., each term in (1) differs from the corresponding term in (2) only by the factor $\sqrt{1 + k}$. Therefore, (2) implies (1).

Consider the case when the new circle touches the circle $O$ internally on your own.

c) This problem reduces to the previous one using the following beautiful technique (discussed in detail in the second volume of I. M. Yaglom's "Geometric Transformations").

Let $r$ be the radius of the equal circles. Draw new circles (shown dashed in the figure): one through the points $A_{0}, A_{1}$, and $A_{2}$ with center $O$ and another with center $N$ and radius $r$. Then (and this is the main property of our transformation) the tangent drawn from the point $N$ to the circle of radius $r$ with center $A_{i}$ ($i=0,1,2$) will be equal to the tangent drawn from the point $A_{i}$ to the circle of radius $r$ with center $N$. This, of course, is obvious - these two tangents are opposite sides of a rectangle. But this reduces the problem in c) to the problem in b).
