question: 7.4. Prove that the plane cannot be covered with equal convex heptagons.
reference_solution:
7.4. This task is much more complicated than the previous ones. The idea of the solution is as follows. Suppose that such a covering is possible. We will calculate the average angle of a heptagon in two ways. On the one hand, the average angle in a heptagon is $\frac{5 \cdot 180^{\circ}}{7}$. On the other hand, at each node of the covering, at least three angles meet, so the average angle of the heptagon is no more than $\frac{360^{\circ}}{3}=120^{\circ}$. But $120^{\circ}<\frac{900^{\circ}}{7}$. This is a contradiction.

Let's implement this idea rigorously. Suppose it is possible to cover the plane with equal heptagons. Let $s$ be the area of the heptagon, and $d$ be the diameter of the smallest circle containing the heptagon. Consider a circle of large radius $R$ and concentric circles of radii $R-d$ and $R+d$ (see figure).

The number of heptagons that are completely inside the circle of radius $R$ is certainly greater than $N_{1}=\pi(R-d)^{2} / s$.

The total sum of the angles of these heptagons is not less than

$$
\Sigma_{1}=5 \pi N_{1}=5 \pi^{2}(R-d)^{2} / s
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_20eb9f6ef2c568605a63g-56.jpg?height=362&width=373&top_left_y=882&top_left_x=720)

Fig. 7.4.

On the other hand, the number of heptagons intersecting the circle of radius $R$ is less than $N_{2}=$ $=\pi(R+d)^{2} / s$. Therefore, the number of nodes of the covering located within the circle of radius $R$ is less than $7 N_{2} / 3$ (each heptagon has 7 vertices, but each of them is counted at least 3 times). The total sum of the angles at each node is $2\pi$, and for all nodes, it is no more than

$$
\Sigma_{2}=2 \pi \cdot 7 N_{2} / 3=14 \pi^{2}(R+d)^{2} /(3 s)
$$

Obviously, it must be $\Sigma_{2} \geqslant \Sigma_{1}$, from which we get

$$
14(R+d)^{2} \geqslant 15(R-d)^{2}
$$

But for sufficiently large $R$ (with a fixed $d$), the last inequality is impossible. (Check this!) We have reached a contradiction.

Remark. In our reasoning, we did not use the equality of the polygons, but only the equality of their areas $-s$, the boundedness of their sizes (constant $d$), and convexity (at each node, at least three vertices meet).

question: 7.6. A circle is covered by several arcs. These arcs may overlap each other, but none of them covers the entire circle. Prove that it is possible to select several of these arcs such that they also cover the entire circle and their total length does not exceed $720^{\circ}$.
reference_solution: 7.6. The ends of all arcs divide the circle into several parts (we take the "smallest" parts, so that none of them contain the ends of the arcs inside and, by condition, are covered by one or several arcs). If any of these parts is covered by three or more arcs, then we select from these arcs two that extend the farthest clockwise and counterclockwise (however, this may turn out to be the same arc - in which case we select just that one), and discard the other arcs. After several such operations, we will achieve that all parts of the circle are covered by no more than two arcs.

question: 7.7. The corridor is completely covered by several carpet runners, the width of which is equal to the width of the corridor. Prove that some of the runners can be removed so that the remaining ones do not overlap and cover at least half of the corridor. (It is assumed that any runner can be removed without changing the position of the others.)
reference_solution:
7.7. Reasoning as in the previous problem, first prove that some of the paths can be removed so that the remaining ones cover the corridor, and no more than two layers.

Now, let's number the paths from left to right in the order of their left ends. All the odd-numbered paths do not intersect with each other, and the same is true for the even-numbered ones. Either the sum of the lengths of all even-numbered paths or all odd-numbered paths is not less than half the length of the corridor. (This problem, as well as the next one, is a rephrasing of the well-known Rado's problem.)

## SNAIL AND OBSERVERS
reference_solution:
7.8. This problem resembles the previous one, but the previous reasoning does not apply. Specifically, if several carpets cover one area, it is generally not possible to select a smaller number of carpets that cover all the others (figure $a$;
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_20eb9f6ef2c568605a63g-58.jpg?height=288&width=540&top_left_y=853&top_left_x=344)

the area covered by all four carpets is shaded). Therefore, we will proceed differently. We will select the largest carpet $K_{1}$. Let its area be $s_{1}$. Remove all carpets that overlap with $K_{1}$. In this process, the area of the floor that becomes free of carpets does not exceed $8 s_{1}$ (figure b). Among all the remaining carpets, except $K_{1}$, we again select the carpet $K_{2}$ of maximum area $s_{2}$ and remove the carpets that intersect with it, freeing an area of the floor that does not exceed $8 s_{2}$. Continuing this process, we will obtain a set of pairwise non-overlapping carpets $K_{1}, K_{2}, \ldots$, which cover more than $1 / 9$ of the floor area (prove this).

7.9. We will represent time on the OT axis (see figure). The observation time will be represented by a segment \(AB\) of length 6. We will also mark segments of length 1 on the OT axis, representing the observation intervals of each observer.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_20eb9f6ef2c568605a63g-59.jpg?height=120&width=691&top_left_y=285&top_left_x=263)

The segment \(AB\) will be covered by segments of length 1. question: 8.6. On a grid paper with a cell side of 1, a circle of radius 10 is drawn. Prove that inside this circle there are at least 250 grid nodes. (Nodes are called points where the grid lines intersect.)
reference_solution: 8.6. Construct a circle of radius 9, concentric with the given circle. Consider all the $1 \times 1$ squares, the sides of which are parallel to the grid lines, and the centers of which lie at the grid nodes and inside the circle of radius 10. Prove that these squares completely cover the constructed circle of radius 9; compare the sum of the areas of these squares with the area of the circle.

question:
8.8. On graph paper, a closed broken line is drawn, all segments of which have the same length, and all vertices lie at the grid nodes. Prove that the number of segments of such a broken line is necessarily even.

BEE AND HONEYCOMBS
reference_solution: 8.8. Introduce a coordinate system, taking any two mutually perpendicular lines on the grid paper as coordinate axes, and the width of a cell as 1. Let $x_{i}$ and $y_{i}$ be the projections of the segments of the broken line onto the coordinate axes (taking into account the sign). Then $x_{1}+x_{2}+\ldots$ $\ldots+x_{n}=0 ; y_{1}+y_{2}+\ldots+y_{n}=0 ; x_{i}^{2}+y_{i}^{2}=\boldsymbol{c}$. (Try to answer this question: what remainders when divided by 4 can $c$ - the sum of two squares of integers - give?) Clearly, we can assume that at least one of the $2 n$ numbers $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots, x_{n}, y_{1}, y_{2}, \ldots, y_{n}$ is odd - otherwise, all of them can be divided by a suitable power of 2 and the problem can be reduced to this case. After that, only two possibilities need to be considered: (1) all numbers $x_{i}, y_{i}$ are odd, (2) for each $i$, one of the numbers $x_{i}, y_{i}$ is odd, the other is even, and show that in both cases $n$ must be even.

question: 9.2. On a plane, there are $n$ points such that any triangle with vertices at these points has an area no greater than 1. Prove that all these points can be placed in a triangle of area 4.
reference_solution:
9.2. Among all triangles with vertices at the given points, we select the triangle of the largest area $s \leqslant 1$. Through each of its vertices, we draw a line parallel to the opposite side. The area of the triangle formed by these lines, as it is easy to see, is $4 s \leqslant 4$.

Prove that this triangle covers all $n$ points. In the proof, you can use the fact that all triangles with a given base $a$ on the plane, having an area $s$ (or a smaller area), are contained within a strip between two lines parallel to the base $\alpha$ and at a distance $h=2 s / a$ from it.

question:
9.3. a) Prove that in a circle of radius 1, it is impossible to select more than five points such that all pairwise distances between them are greater than 1.
b) Prove that in a circle of radius 10, it is impossible to place 450 points such that the distance between any two points is greater than 1.

c) Prove that it is possible to place 400 points in this circle.

NEIGHBORHOOD OF A POLYGON
reference_solution:
9.3. a) Suppose this is possible, and let $A_{1}, A_{2}, \ldots, A_{6}$ be six such points inside a circle of radius 1, the pairwise distances between which are greater than 1. Draw radii from the center of the circle through each of these points. (Clearly, no two points lie on the same radius.) At least 2 of these 6 radii form an angle not exceeding $60^{\circ}$, and the distance between any two points on these radii is not more than 1. Contradiction.

b) Suppose this is possible. Describe a circle of radius $r=0.5$ around each point. By the condition, these circles do not have common points and are located within a circle of radius $R=10.5$, concentric with the original circle of radius 10. Therefore, the sum of their areas $450 \pi r^{2}=450 \pi / 4$ does not exceed the area of this circle $\pi R^{2}=(21 / 2)^{2} \pi=441 \pi / 4$, from which $450 \leqslant 441$. Contradiction.

c) Check that for a sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ (for example, $\varepsilon=0.02$), more than 400 centers of a grid of regular hexagons with side $\frac{1+\varepsilon}{2}$, covering the plane, can fit inside a circle of radius 10. The distance between the centers of adjacent hexagons is $1+\varepsilon$, i.e., greater than 1. The number of centers inside the circle can be estimated using the same method used in problems 7.4 and 8.6: hexagons whose centers lie within a circle of radius 10 definitely cover a concentric circle of radius $10-\frac{1+\varepsilon}{2}$, and the problem reduces to verifying the inequality

$$
400 \cdot \frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{8} \cdot(1.02)^{2}<\pi(9.49)^{2}
$$

question: 9.6. A paratrooper is somewhere in a forest of area $S$. The shape of the forest is unknown to him, but he knows that there are no clearings in the forest. Prove that he can get out of the forest by traveling a distance of no more than $2 \sqrt{\pi S}$ (it is assumed that the paratrooper can move along a path of a pre-determined shape).
reference_solution:
9.6. The paratrooper will certainly exit the forest if he walks along a circle of radius \( r = \sqrt{S / \pi} \). Indeed, if the entire circumference of this circle were inside the forest, the area of the forest would be greater than \( \pi r^2 = S \).

Formally, the problem is solved, but we will show how one could naturally arrive at such a solution and verify that the estimate \( 2 \sqrt{\pi S} \) is, in some sense, the best possible.

Notice that the path must be either closed or at least contain points of self-intersection. Indeed, otherwise, no matter how long the path \( L \) is, there exists a forest in the form of a very narrow strip along the path \( L \) such that its area does not exceed \( S \) (see the figure). By refining these arguments, one can show that the paratrooper must follow some closed route \( L \). To ensure that the paratrooper can exit the forest regardless of its shape, it is necessary and sufficient that the area enclosed by the line \( L \) is not less than \( S \). Moreover, if the route \( L \) is chosen to be the shortest possible, in the worst-case scenarios, the paratrooper will have to walk the entire (or almost the entire) route \( L \) to exit the forest. Thus, the problem of choosing a "good strategy" reduces to the following question: among all closed curves enclosing an area \( s \), find the curve of the smallest length. The answer, as is known, is given by a circle. (For more details, see, for example, the book by G. Rademacher and O. Toeplitz "Numbers and Figures," Fizmatgiz, 1962, pp. 169-174).

question: 9.7. Prove that if in the conditions of the previous problem the forest is convex, then there exists a path guaranteeing an exit from the forest with a length of no more than $\sqrt{2 \pi S}$.
reference_solution:
9.7. The paratrooper must move along a semicircle of radius $\sqrt{2 s / \pi}$. The length of this semicircle, 
guaranteeing an exit, is exactly $\sqrt{2 \pi S}$. The proof that this path works is obvious (cf. problem 9.6).

question:
10.5. Prove that in any convex 11-gon, there exist two diagonals such that the smaller angle between the lines on which they lie does not exceed $5^{\circ}$ (the angle between parallel lines is considered to be $0^{\circ}$).

## PERIMETER ESTIMATION
reference_solution:
10.5. First, let's calculate the number of diagonals in a convex $n$-gon. In each of the $n$ vertices, $(n-3)$ diagonals converge, but in the product $n(n-3)$, each diagonal is counted twice, as it connects 2 vertices. Therefore, a convex $n$-gon has $n(n-3) / 2$ diagonals. In particular, an 11-gon has $\frac{11 \cdot 8}{2}=44$ diagonals.

Draw 44 lines through a fixed point $P$ on the plane, parallel to the diagonals of the given 11-gon. These lines will divide the full angle of $360^{\circ}$ around point $P$ into 88 parts, and the smallest of these parts will not exceed $\frac{360^{\circ}}{88}$, which is less than $5^{\circ}$.

question:
10.6. The midpoints of adjacent sides of a convex polygon are connected by segments. Prove that the perimeter of the polygon formed by these segments is not less than half the perimeter of the original polygon.

## SQUARE IN A TRIANGLE
reference_solution:
10.6. For a triangle, the statement of the problem is obvious (the inequality turns into an equality), so we will assume that the number \( n \) of the polygon's sides is at least four.

Draw all \( n \) diagonals in this \( n \)-sided polygon, connecting its vertices every other one. Each of these diagonals is twice as long as the parallel segment connecting the midpoints of the sides of the given \( n \)-sided polygon (figure a). Therefore, the statement of the problem is equivalent to the fact that the sum of these \( n \) diagonals is greater than the perimeter of the \( n \)-sided polygon. To prove the latter statement, note that even the sum of
the pieces of these diagonals adjacent to the vertices of the polygon (in figure b they are outlined with thick lines) is greater than the perimeter of the \( n \)-sided polygon.

question:
4. For each pair of real numbers $a$ and $b$, consider the sequence of numbers $p_{n}=[2\{a n+b\}]$. Any $k$ consecutive terms of this sequence will be called a word. Is it true that any ordered set of zeros and ones of length $k$ will be a word of the sequence defined by some $a$ and $b$ for $k=4$; for $k=5$?

Note: $[c]$ - integer part, $\{c\}$ - fractional part of the number $c$.
reference_solution:
4. We will represent numbers as points on a unit circle (numbers with the same fractional part correspond to the same point on the circle, see the comment to the solution of problem 6 for 10th grade of the 1997 competition). Then the sequence $x_{n}=\{a n+b\}$ corresponds to a sequence of points on the circle obtained from $\{b\}$ by $n$-fold rotation by the arc $\{a\}$. In this case, $p_{n}=\left[2 x_{n}\right]$.

It is easy to see that if $x_{n} \in[0 ; 1 / 2)$, i.e., the point $x_{n}$ lies on the upper semicircle, then $p_{n}=0$; if $x_{n}$ lies on the lower semicircle, then $p_{n}=1$.

a) Let's construct sequences $p_{n}$ in which all words of length 4 starting with zero appear. There are eight such words. The other eight words can be obtained by replacing $(a, b)$ with $(a, b+1 / 2)$. Indeed, under such a replacement, the points $x_{n}$ are replaced by diametrically opposite points, so $p_{n}$ is replaced by $1-p_{n}$.

Examples: Consider $a$ and $b$ such that the sequence $x_{n}$ forms regular figures (see table).

| Regular Figures | $a$ | $b$ | Required words from $p_{n}=\left[2 x_{n}\right]$ |
| :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Octagon | $1 / 8$ | 0 | $0000,0001,0011,0111$ |
| Square | $1 / 4$ | 0 | 0110 |
| "Biangle" | $1 / 2$ | 0 | 0101 |
| Triangle | $1 / 3$ | 0 | 0010 |

b) Let's prove that the word 00010 cannot be realized for any $a$ and $b$. Suppose this word is realized. Consider three consecutive members of the sequence $x_{n}, x_{n+1}$, and $x_{n+2}$.

If the points $x_{n}$ and $x_{n+2}$ are diametrically opposite, then the next point is obtained from the previous one by a $90^{\circ}$ rotation, and it is clear that the word 000 cannot appear in the sequence $p_{n}$.

If the points $x_{n}$ and $x_{n+2}$ are not diametrically opposite, then they divide the circle into two different arcs. There are two possible situations: $x_{n+1}$ lies on the larger arc (as in Fig. 31a), and $x_{n+1}$ lies on the smaller arc (as in Fig. 31b).

Suppose $x_{n+1}$ lies on the larger arc, then any other points $x_{m}, x_{m+1}$, and $x_{m+2}$ are arranged in the same way, as they are obtained from the points $x_{n}, x_{n+1}$, and $x_{n+2}$ by the same angle rotation. But then three such points cannot be on the upper semicircle, which means the word 000 will not appear in the sequence $p_{n}$ - a contradiction.

Suppose $x_{n+1}$ lies on the smaller arc $x_{n} x_{n+2}$. Then any points $x_{m}, x_{m+1}$, and $x_{m+2}$ are arranged in the same way, so if $x_{m}$ and $x_{m+2}$ lie on the upper semicircle, then the point $x_{m+1}$ also lies there, which means the word 010 will not appear in the sequence $p_{n}$.

Thus, we have considered all cases and proved that the word 00010 cannot appear.

Comment. If we split $p_{n}$ into segments consisting only of zeros or only of ones (with a segment of zeros followed by a segment of ones, and a segment of ones followed by a segment of zeros), then the lengths of any two such segments will differ by no more than 1. This problem relates to symbolic dynamics, as discussed in article [82].

question: 5. In a botanical key, plants are described by one hundred characteristics. Each characteristic can either be present or absent. A key is considered good if any two plants differ in more than half of the characteristics. Prove that in a good key, no more than 50 plants can be described.
reference_solution:
5. Let $m$ be the number of plants in a good determinant. We estimate the total number of differences between all pairs of plants across all characteristics. The number of pairs of plants is $\frac{m(m-1)}{2}$, and each pair differs in at least 51 characteristics, so the total number of differences $S \geqslant 51 \frac{m(m-1)}{2}$.

We estimate $S$ in another way. Let $m_{i}$ be the number of plants possessing characteristic $i$, then the number of pairs of plants that characteristic $i$ distinguishes is $m_{i}\left(m-m_{i}\right)$, and the total number of differences between plants is:

$$
S=m_{1}\left(m-m_{1}\right)+m_{2}\left(m-m_{2}\right)+\ldots+m_{100}\left(m-m_{100}\right)
$$

By a known inequality (see fact 26$), m_{i}\left(m-m_{i}\right) \leqslant \leqslant \frac{m^{2}}{4}$. Therefore,

$$
S \leqslant 100 \frac{m^{2}}{4}=25 m^{2}
$$

Thus, $51 \frac{m(m-1)}{2} \leqslant S \leqslant 25 m^{2}$, from which $m \leqslant 51$.

It remains to prove that $m \neq 51$. Suppose $m=51$, then we get the strict inequality $m_{i}\left(m-m_{i}\right)n)$ and asserts that under some natural assumption, there are codes of the corresponding size. In the condition of our problem $n=100, d=51$, and the solution demonstrates the Plotkin bound for these parameters: the size of the code does not exceed 34. It turns out that this bound is achievable: one can devise a code with 34 messages.

question: 2. An infinite sequence of numbers $x_{n}$ is defined by the conditions: $x_{n+1}=1-\left|1-2 x_{n}\right|$, and $0 \leqslant x_{1} \leqslant 1$. Prove that the sequence, starting from some point, is periodic a) in the case b) and only in the case, if $x_{1}$ is rational.
reference_solution:
2. a) If $0 \leqslant x_{n} \leqslant 1$, then $0 \leqslant x_{n+1} \leqslant 1$. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}
0 \leqslant x_{n} \leqslant 1 \Rightarrow -1 \leqslant 1-2 x_{n} & \leqslant 1 \Rightarrow \\
& \Rightarrow 0 \leqslant\left|1-2 x_{n}\right| \leqslant 1 \Rightarrow 0 \leqslant x_{n+1} \leqslant 1
\end{aligned}
$$

If $x_{n}$ is rational, then $x_{n+1}$ is rational, and its denominator is no greater than that of $x_{n}$. Indeed, let $x_{n}=\frac{p_{n}}{q_{n}}$ be an irreducible fraction. Then

$$
x_{n+1}=1-\left|\frac{q_{n}-2 p_{n}}{q_{n}}\right|=\frac{q_{n}-\left|q_{n}-2 p_{n}\right|}{q_{n}}.
$$

If this fraction is irreducible, its denominator is the same as that of $x_{n}$; if it is reducible, the denominator will decrease after reduction.

Thus, all terms of the sequence are rational numbers between 0 and 1, i.e., proper fractions. But there are only a finite number of proper fractions with denominators no greater than a given value $q$. Therefore, some terms of the sequence will repeat, and from that point on, the sequence will be periodic.

b) First method. By expanding the absolute value in $x_{n+1}=1-|1-2 x_{n}|$, we get either $x_{n+1}=2 x_{n}$ or $x_{n+1}=2-2 x_{n}$. Therefore, $x_{n+1}=a_{1}+2 b_{1} x_{n}$, where $a_{1}$ is an integer, and $b_{1} = \pm 1$. Similarly, $x_{n+2}=a_{2}+4 b_{2} x_{n}$. Continuing this process, we get

$$
x_{n+k}=a_{k}+2^{k} b_{k} x_{n}
$$

where $a_{k}$ is an integer, and $b_{k} = \pm 1$.

Suppose $x_{n+k}=x_{n}$. Then $x_{n}$ is a solution to the linear equation with integer coefficients $a_{k}+2^{k} b_{k} x_{n}=x_{n}$. This equation has a unique solution because $2^{k} b_{k} = \pm 2^{k} \neq 1$. This solution is rational, so $x_{n}$ is rational. But then $x_{n-1}$ is rational, $x_{n-2}$ is rational, and so on. Therefore, $x_{1}$ is also rational.

Second method. Write the number $x_{1}$ in binary notation (see fact 12):

$$
x_{n}=0, a_{1} a_{2} a_{3} \ldots
$$

If $a_{1}=0$, then the binary representation of the number $x_{n+1}$ is obtained from the binary representation of the number $x_{n}$ by a shift (verify this):

$$
x_{n+1}=0, a_{2} a_{3} a_{4} \ldots
$$

If $a_{1}=1$, then the binary representation of the number $x_{n+1}$ is obtained from the binary representation of the number $x_{n}$ by a shift with the replacement of all ones with zeros and all zeros with ones (we will call this inversion). We will prove that if $x_{n}$ is periodic, then $a_{n}$ is also periodic. If $x_{n+k}=x_{n}$ and an even number of inversions occurred between them, then $a_{n+k}=a_{n}$. If an odd number of inversions occurred between $x_{n}$ and $x_{n+k}$, then $a_{n+2 k}=1-a_{n+k}=a_{n}$. In both cases, $a_{n}$ is periodic. But a number whose binary representation is periodic is rational (see fact 13).

Comments. $1^{\circ}$. Note that the function $y=f(x)=1-|1-2 x|$ is linear on each of the intervals $[0 ; 1 / 2]$ and $[1 / 2 ; 1]$:

$$
y= \begin{cases}2 x & \text { for } 0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1 / 2 \\ 2-2 x & \text { for } 1 / 2 \leqslant x \leqslant 1\end{cases}
$$

Similarly, the function

$$
y=f_{n}(x)=\underbrace{f(f \ldots f(x) \ldots)}_{n \text { times }},
$$

which maps $x_{1}$ to $x_{n}$, is linear on each of the intervals $\left[\frac{k}{2^{n}} ; \frac{k+1}{2^{n}}\right]$. The graphs of the functions $y=f(x), y=f_{2}(x), y=f_{3}(x)$ are shown in (Fig. 51).
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6455f48598646f41a890g-136.jpg?height=294&width=1020&top_left_y=447&top_left_x=178)

Fig. 51

$2^{\circ}$. For each $T=2,3, \ldots$, there is at least one point with period $T$ - for example, the abscissa of the last point of intersection of the segment $y=x, 0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1$, with the graph of the function $y=f_{T}(x)$, $x_{1}=2^{T} /\left(2^{T}+1\right)$.

Think about the question: how many periodic trajectories exist for each period $T$ (or, almost the same thing, - points $x$ for which $x=f_{T}(x)$, but $x \neq f_{k}(x)$ if $\left.k<T\right)$?

$3^{\circ}$. The problem arose from symbolic dynamics. The function $f(x)=1-|1-2 x|$ is called a "tent map".

question: 3. In triangle $ABC$, the angle bisectors of angles $A$ and $C$ are drawn. Points $P$ and $Q$ are the feet of the perpendiculars dropped from vertex $B$ to these bisectors. Prove that segment $PQ$ is parallel to side $AC$.
reference_solution: 3. Extend segments $B Q$ and $B P$ until they intersect line $A C$ at points $A_{1}$ and $C_{1}$, respectively. In triangle $A B C_{1}$, segment $A P$ is both a bisector and an altitude (Fig. 41). Therefore, this triangle is isosceles $\left(A B=A C_{1}\right)$. Then segment $A P$ is also a median: $B P=C_{1} P$. Similarly, segment $C Q$ is a median of triangle $C B A_{1}$, i.e., $B Q=Q A_{1}$. Therefore, $P Q$ is the midline of triangle $A_{1} B C_{1}$, meaning segment $P Q$ is parallel to $A_{1} C_{1}$, and thus it is also parallel to $A C$.

question: 3. Prove that the equation $x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=x^{3}+y^{3}+z^{3}$ has an infinite number of solutions in integers $x, y, z$.
reference_solution:
3. For example: $x=k\left(2 k^{2}+1\right), y=2 k^{2}+1, z=-k\left(2 k^{2}+1\right)$.

How to come up with these formulas? By eliminating two cubes using the substitution $z=-x$, we obtain the equation $2 x^{2}+y^{2}=y^{3}, 2 x^{2}=(y-1) y^{2}$. If $\frac{y-1}{2}=k^{2}$ is a perfect square, then the solution can be found:

$$
y=2 k^{2}+1, \quad x=k\left(2 k^{2}+1\right)
$$

question: 4. Four grasshoppers sit at the vertices of a square. Every minute, one of them jumps to a point symmetric to it relative to another grasshopper. Prove that the grasshoppers cannot end up at the vertices of a larger square at some point.
reference_solution:
4. $1^{\circ}$. Let's imagine that the square, with grasshoppers sitting at its vertices, is a square on a grid paper (the size of the square is $1 \times 1$). Notice that the grasshoppers always jump to the vertices of the cells: if grasshoppers are placed at the vertices of the cells on the grid paper (these vertices are called nodes of the square grid), then after each jump, each grasshopper will again land on some node of the square grid (Fig. 42). The reason is that a jump is equivalent to a central symmetry of one grasshopper relative to another, and the square grid is centrally symmetric relative to any of its nodes.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6455f48598646f41a890g-126.jpg?height=206&width=246&top_left_y=975&top_left_x=127)

Fig. 42

$2^{\circ}$. Suppose the grasshoppers managed to reach the vertices of a larger square, then, jumping in the reverse order, they should be able to reach the vertices of a smaller square. However, starting from the vertices of the larger square, they will always land on the nodes of a grid consisting of larger squares. In other words, the distance between them cannot be less than the side of the larger square. This is a contradiction.

Comment. If the grasshoppers initially were at the vertices of an arbitrary parallelogram, then they will always jump along a grid of such parallelograms.

question: 4. Two circles intersect at points $A$ and $B$. Tangents are drawn to both circles at point $A$, intersecting the circles at points $M$ and $N$. Lines $B M$ and $B N$ intersect the circles again at points $P$ and $Q$ ( $P$ - on line $B M$, $Q$ - on line $B N$ ). Prove that segments $M P$ and $N Q$ are equal.
reference_solution:
4. The first method. Let the circles be arranged as in Fig. 48. The case of a different arrangement of the circles is considered similarly (see comment).

It is sufficient to prove that

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6455f48598646f41a890g-130.jpg?height=475&width=489&top_left_y=673&top_left_x=129)

Fig. 48 triangles $A Q N$ and $A M P$ are equal. To do this, we will prove that they are similar and that their corresponding sides $A Q$ and $A M$ are equal.

By the inscribed angle theorem, $\angle P = \angle N$ and $\angle Q = \angle M$, hence triangles $A Q N$ and $A M P$ are similar.

To prove the equality of segments $A Q$ and $A M$, we will prove the equality of arcs $A Q$ and $M A$ (arcs are measured counterclockwise). Note that angle $A B Q$ is half of arc $A Q$, and angle $M A N$ is half of arc $A M$ (see fact 15). Therefore, it is sufficient to prove the equality of angles $A B Q$ and $M A N$.

Angle $A B Q$ is an exterior angle of triangle $A B N$, so $\angle A B Q = \angle A N B + \angle B A N$. Angle $M A N$ consists of two angles $B A M$ and $B A N$, but $\angle A N B = \angle B A M$ (each of them is half of arc $A B$ of the circle passing through points $A, B$, and $N$), therefore

$$
\angle M A N = \angle A N B + \angle B A N = \angle A B Q.
$$

The problem is solved.

The second method. By the theorem on a tangent and a secant drawn from the same point, we get:

$$
M P = \frac{A M^2}{M B}, \quad N Q = \frac{A N^2}{N B}
$$

That is, it is sufficient to prove that

$$
\frac{A M^2}{A N^2} = \frac{M B}{N B}
$$

Applying the theorem on the angle between a tangent and a chord, we see that triangles $A M B$ and $N A B$ are similar (Fig. 49). Hence,

$$
\frac{A M}{A N} = \frac{A B}{N B}, \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{A M}{A N} = \frac{M B}{A B}
$$

Multiplying these equalities, we obtain equality (1).

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6455f48598646f41a890g-131.jpg?height=478&width=490&top_left_y=185&top_left_x=756)

Fig. 49

Comment. If the center of one of the circles is inside the other circle, then the picture is different. If the center of each circle is inside the other circle, then a third picture is obtained. In these cases, in the first proof, instead of the equality of angles $A B Q$ and $M A N$, it is necessary to prove that these angles sum up to $180^{\circ}$. The second method of solution remains unchanged. The reader can independently conduct these considerations.

question: 4. $D$ is a point on side $B C$ of triangle $A B C$. Incircles are inscribed in triangles $A B D, A C D$, and a common external tangent (different from $B C$) is drawn to them, intersecting $A D$ at point $K$. Prove that the length of segment $A K$ does not depend on the position of point $D$ on $B C$.
reference_solution:
4. Let's try to guess what the length of segment $A K$ is. Consider the limiting case when point $D$ approaches $C$, then the second circle shrinks to a point, and segment $A K$ turns into a tangent segment to the first circle. It is easy to see that in this case $A K = \frac{A B + A C - B C}{2}$. We will prove that this formula is always true (not just in the limiting case). Let's denote the points of tangency as shown in Fig. 53.

Notice that $A B_{1} = A P, A C_{1} = A Q, K M = K P, K N = K Q$ (these are segments of tangents drawn from the same point).

Moreover, $M N = E F$ - segments of the common tangents to the circles (see fact 17). Let's transform our hypothetical answer (doubled), taking into account these equalities:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& A B + A C - B C = A B_{1} + A C_{1} - E F = A B_{1} + A C_{1} - M N = \\
&= A P + A Q - M N = A P + A Q - (M K + K N) = \\
& \quad (A P - K P) + (A Q - K Q) = 2 A K
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus,

$$
A K = \frac{A B + A C - B C}{2}
$$

The problem is solved.

question: 4. From a convex polyhedron with 9 vertices, one of which is $A$, by parallel translations that map $A$ to each of the other vertices, 8 equal polyhedra are formed. Prove that at least two of these 8 polyhedra intersect (at interior points).
reference_solution:
4. Let's perform a homothety of the original polyhedron $M$ with the center at point $A$ and a coefficient of 2. The volume of the stretched polyhedron $M^{\prime}$ will be 8 times the volume of the polyhedron $M$. We will prove that all 8 "transferred" polyhedra are contained in $M^{\prime}$.

Let vertex $A$ be transferred to vertex $B$, $X$ be an arbitrary point of the polyhedron $M$, and $Y$ be the image of point $X$ under the corresponding parallel translation (Fig. 58). We will prove that point $Y$ belongs to $M^{\prime}$.

The segment $BX$ is entirely contained in the polyhedron $M$, since the polyhedron is convex. Therefore, its midpoint $K$ belongs to the polyhedron. The quadrilateral $ABYX$ is a parallelogram, so $Y$ is obtained from $K$ by a homothety with the center at point $A$ and a coefficient of 2,

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6455f48598646f41a890g-145.jpg?height=231&width=290&top_left_y=268&top_left_x=953)

Fig. 58 therefore, point $Y$ belongs to $M^{\prime}$.

Note that points near vertex $A$ do not belong to any of the "transferred" polyhedra. Indeed, place the polyhedron so that vertex $A$ is higher than all other vertices, then there exists a plane that passes below vertex $A$ but above all other vertices. This plane cuts off a small polyhedron $N$ from the polyhedron $M$, containing point $A$. Clearly, it does not intersect with any of the transferred polyhedra.

Now suppose that the transferred polyhedra do not intersect at interior points, then the volume of the polyhedron $M^{\prime}$ is not less than the sum of the volume of the polyhedron $N$ and the volumes of the transferred polyhedra. But the total volume of the transferred polyhedra is exactly equal to the volume of the polyhedron $M^{\prime}$. Contradiction.

Comments. $1^{\circ}$. The problem easily generalizes to $n$-dimensional space.

$2^{\circ}$. A weaker formulation of the problem was at the XIII International Mathematical Olympiad. It was required to prove that at least two of the nine (not eight) polyhedra intersect.

question: 5*. The extensions of sides $A B$ and $C D$ of a convex quadrilateral $A B C D$ intersect at point $P$, and the extensions of sides $B C$ and $A D$ intersect at point $Q$. Prove that if each of the three pairs of angle bisectors: of the external angles of the quadrilateral at vertices $A$ and $C$, of the external angles at vertices $B$ and $D$, and of the external angles at vertices $Q$ and $P$ (of triangles $Q A B$ and $P B C$ respectively) have a point of intersection, then these three points lie on the same line.
reference_solution:
5*. Drawing a diagram for the problem is very difficult (the points of intersection are far from each other), so we will look for a solution from general considerations. Let's recall that points on the bisector of an angle are equidistant from the sides of this angle.

For each line containing a side of the quadrilateral $ABCD$, let's define a function $f_{i}$ - the oriented distance to this line: if the point lies on the same side of the line as the quadrilateral, we take the usual distance, and if it lies on the opposite side, we take the distance with a negative sign. These four functions $f_{1}$, $f_{2}$, $f_{3}$, $f_{4}$ of the coordinates of the points are linear (see fact 25), i.e., they are written in the form $f_{i}(x, y)=a_{i} x+b_{i} y+c_{i}$.

Note that a point lies on the bisector of an external angle of the quadrilateral if and only if the sum of the values of two functions for the sides of the angle is zero.

For each of the points of intersection of the bisectors mentioned in the condition, we get that the sum of all four functions is zero.

But the sum of linear functions is a linear function, and the set of points where a linear function, different from a constant, takes a constant value, is a line.

The sum of our four functions is not identically zero, since it is positive inside the quadrilateral. Therefore, the points of intersection of the bisectors lie on one line.

Comments. $1^{\circ}$. Knowing the idea of the solution with linear functions, one can make a spatial generalization of the problem.

$2^{\circ}$. There is a simpler problem on the same idea: to find the geometric locus of points in a triangle for which the sum of the distances to two sides is equal to the distance to the third. (The points of intersection of the bisectors with the sides of the triangle satisfy the condition. Therefore, the segments between them also satisfy it.)

$3^{\circ}$. In school mathematics, linear functions are polynomials of degree not higher than the first. In linear algebra, a linear function is a polynomial of degree not higher than the first and without a constant term. In this sense, a linear function of two variables has the form: $f(x, y)=a x+b y$. Functions of the form $a x+b y+c$ are called $a f f i n e$.

question:
6. In a square of grid paper $10 \times 10$, one ship $1 \times 4$, two $1 \times 3$, three $1 \times 2$, and four $1 \times 1$ need to be placed. Ships should not share any points (even vertices) with each other, but they can touch the borders of the square. Prove that

a) if they are placed in the order specified above (starting with the larger ones), the process can always be completed, even if at each step only the current ship is considered, without thinking about the future;

b)* if they are placed in the reverse order (starting with the smaller ones), a situation may arise where the next ship cannot be placed (provide an example).

10 k l a s s
reference_solution:
6. In task "b", it is easy to provide an example of an "unextendable" arrangement of nine ships (Fig. $50, a$).

In task "a", there is a "hidden rock": it seems sufficient to prove that there will be a place for the last single-cell ship. However, in reality, it is necessary to prove that in the process of placement, there will be a place for each subsequent ship.

A ship $1 \times 4$ can be placed. We will prove that the next ship $1 \times 3$ will fit. For this, we mark 8 auxiliary ships $1 \times 3$, parallel to each other, with an interval of two cells (Fig. 50, b). Each placed ship can touch (intersect or touch) no more than two marked ships, so there will be an undisturbed marked ship, where the next ship $1 \times 3$ can be placed.

Suppose the following ships have already been placed: $1 \times 4$, two $1 \times 3$, and fewer than three $1 \times 2$. We will prove that another ship $1 \times 2$ will fit. For this, we mark 12 auxiliary ships $1 \times 2$, parallel to each other, with an interval of two cells (Fig. 50, c). Each placed ship can touch no more than two marked ships, so there will be an undisturbed marked ship.

Similarly, the next single-cell ship will fit. We mark 16 auxiliary ships $1 \times 1$ with an interval of two cells (Fig. 50, d). The placed ships touch no more than 15 marked ships.

question:
6*. Does there exist a polynomial $P(x)$ that has a negative coefficient, while all coefficients of any of its powers $(P(x))^{n}, n>1,$ are positive?

## 11th grade
reference_solution:
6. An important observation is that it is sufficient to find a polynomial such that the coefficients of its square and cube are positive. Any other power can be represented as a product of squares and cubes.

We will call a polynomial

$$
a_{n} x^{n}+a_{n-1} x^{n-1}+\ldots+a_{1} x+a_{0}
$$

positive if all its coefficients are positive: $a_{i}>0$ for $i=0, \ldots, n$.

Consider the polynomial $f(x)=x^{4}+x^{3}+x+1$. It is easy to see that $(f(x))^{2}$ and $(f(x))^{3}$ are positive polynomials, but the polynomial $f(x)$ itself is not positive: the coefficient of $x^{2}$ is zero. However, we need a polynomial with a negative coefficient. The idea is to slightly "perturb" the polynomial $f(x)$.

Consider the polynomial $g(x)=f(x)-\varepsilon x^{2}$ for a sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$. The coefficients of the polynomials $(g(x))^{2}$ and $(g(x))^{3}$ are close to the coefficients of the polynomials $(f(x))^{2}$ and $(f(x))^{3}$ and, therefore, are positive. This statement might seem informal to someone not familiar with mathematical analysis. In this case, it is suggested to take, for example, $\varepsilon=\frac{1}{125}$ and check "by hand" that the corresponding polynomials are positive.

Thus, the answer is given by the polynomial

$$
g(x)=f(x)-\varepsilon x^{2}=x^{4}+x^{3}-\varepsilon x^{2}+x+1
$$

for a sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$.

Comment. For $\varepsilon=0$, the coefficients of the polynomial $f(x)=x^{4}+x^{3}-\varepsilon x^{2}+x+1$ can be written as the number: 11011, then the coefficients of $(f(x))^{2}$ and $(f(x))^{3}$ can be written as the sequences of digits $11011^{2}=121242121$ and $11011^{3}=1334996994331$ (polynomials are multiplied "vertically" in the same way as multi-digit numbers).

## 11th class

question: 6. Prove that for any $k>1$ there exists a power of 2 such that among the $k$ last digits of this power, at least half are nines. (For example, $2^{12}=\ldots 96, 2^{53}=\ldots 992$.)
reference_solution:
6. What can cause a lot of nines in a row in powers of two? - If a power of two is "slightly" less than a number divisible by a high power of ten. For example, $2^{12}+4$ is divisible by $100$, and $2^{53}+8$ is divisible by $1000$.

Let's first try to find numbers of the form $2^{n}+1$ that are divisible by a high power of five. Then we will multiply these numbers by the corresponding power of two and get numbers of the form $2^{k}\left(2^{n}+1\right)$, which are divisible by a high power of ten. Expanding the brackets and discarding the smaller term, we will get the required power of two.

Lemma. For all $k \geqslant 1$, the number $2^{2 \cdot 5^{k-1}}+1$ is divisible by $5^{k}$. We will prove this by induction (see fact 24). The base case ($k=1$) is obvious. Let's prove the induction step: we have

$$
2^{2 \cdot 5^{k-1}}+1=4^{5^{k-1}}+1
$$

Let $a=4^{5^{k-1}}$. By the induction hypothesis, $a+1$ is divisible by $5^{k}$. Then $4^{5^{k}}+1=a^{5}+1=(a+1)\left(a^{4}-a^{3}+a^{2}-a+1\right)$. Since $a+1$ is divisible by $5^{k}$, it is enough to prove that the second factor is divisible by 5. Indeed, $a$ has the form $5m-1$, so all terms in the second factor give a remainder of 1 when divided by 5 (see fact 7), and their sum gives a remainder of zero. The lemma is proved.

Thus, the number $2^{k}\left(2^{2 \cdot 5^{k-1}}+1\right)$ ends with at least $k$ zeros. It is not difficult to verify that for $k>1$, the number of digits in $2^{k}$ does not exceed $k / 2$. Therefore, among the last $k$ digits of the number $2^{2 \cdot 5^{k-1}+k}$, no more than $k / 2$ digits can differ from 9.

Comments. $1^{\circ}$. Similar reasoning can be used to prove that the numbers $4^{0}, 4^{1}, 4^{2}, \ldots, 4^{5^{k}-1}$ give different remainders when divided by $5^{k}$. Try to prove a more general fact: if $x-1$ is divisible by $p^{k}$ ($p>2$ is a prime, $k>0$), but not by $p^{k+1}$, then $x^{n}-1$ is divisible by $p^{k+r}$ if and only if $n$ is divisible by $p^{r}$. This important statement (Hensel's lemma) is often used in number theory.

$2^{\circ}$. At the Leningrad City Olympiad in 1981, there was a similar problem: does there exist a natural power of the number 5, in the hundred least significant digits of which there are at least 30 zeros in a row?

question: 1. Prove that if any number of threes are inserted between the zeros in the number 12008, the resulting number is divisible by 19.
reference_solution:
1. We will prove the statement by induction (see fact 24). Base of induction: 12008 is divisible by 19, indeed, $12008=19 \cdot 632$.

Induction step. We will show that if a number of the given form is divisible by 19, then the next one is also divisible by 19. For this, it is sufficient to prove that the difference of two consecutive numbers is divisible by 19 (see fact 5):

$$
120 \underbrace{3 \ldots 308}_{k \text { threes }}-1203 \ldots 308=1083 \cdot 10^{k} .
$$

This difference is divisible by 19, since $1083=19 \cdot 57$. Our statement is proved by induction.

Comments. $1^{\circ}$. Compare with problem 2 for 8th grade.

$2^{\circ}$. It can be shown that the quotient will have the form $63 \ldots 32$.

question:
1. Prove that

$$
|x|+|y|+|z| \leqslant|x+y-z|+|x-y+z|+|-x+y+z|
$$

where $x, y, z$ are real numbers.
reference_solution:
1. Since the modulus of the sum does not exceed the sum of the moduli (see comment), we have:

$$
|x+y-z|+|x-y+z| \geqslant|(x+y-z)+(x-y+z)|=2|x| \text {. }
$$

Similarly, we obtain the inequalities

$$
\begin{aligned}
& |x-y+z|+|-x+y+z| \geqslant 2|z| \\
& |-x+y+z|+|x+y-z| \geqslant 2|y|
\end{aligned}
$$

Adding all three inequalities and dividing the resulting inequality by 2, we get the required inequality.

Comment. The inequality $|x+y| \leqslant|x|+|y|$ can be proven by case analysis. We provide an elegant proof. Since both sides of the inequality are non-negative, they can be squared, and the inequality will be replaced by an equivalent one. That is, it is sufficient to prove that

$$
|x+y|^{2} \leqslant(|x|+|y|)^{2}
$$

Using the fact that for any $a$ the equality $|a|^{2}=a^{2}$ holds and expanding the brackets, we arrive at the inequality:

$$
x^{2}+2 x y+y^{2} \leqslant x^{2}+2|x||y|+y^{2} .
$$

But this is obvious.

Note also that the inequality holds for vectors as well. The proof remains the same with minor modifications. On the plane, this inequality is equivalent to the triangle inequality.

question: 2. Prove that all numbers 10017, 100117, 1001117, ... are divisible by 53.
reference_solution:
2. We will prove the statement by induction (see fact 24).

Base of induction: 10017 is divisible by 53. Indeed, $10017=53 \cdot 189$.

Step of induction. We will show that if a number of the given form is divisible by 53, then the next one is also divisible by 53. For this, we will compute the difference between two consecutive numbers:

$$
100 \underbrace{1 \ldots 1}_{k \text { ones }} 7-100 \underbrace{1 \ldots 1}_{k-1 \text { one }} 7=(1001-100) \cdot 10^{k}=901 \cdot 10^{k}
$$

(the last $k$ digits cancel out). This difference is always divisible by 53, since $901=53 \cdot 17$.

If the subtrahend is divisible by 53 and the difference is divisible by 53, then the minuend is also divisible by 53 (see fact 5). Our statement is proved by induction.

Comments. $1^{\circ}$. Compare with problem 1 for 9th grade.

$2^{\circ}$. It can be shown that the quotient from dividing the given number by 53 has the form $18 \ldots 89$.

question: 3. Given a convex quadrilateral $A B C D$ and a point $O$ inside it. It is known that $\angle A O B=\angle C O D=120^{\circ}, A O=O B$ and $C O=O D$. Let $K, L$ and $M$ be the midpoints of segments $A B, B C$ and $C D$ respectively. Prove that a) $K L=L M$; b) triangle $K L M$ is equilateral.
reference_solution:
3. а) When rotated $120^{\circ}$ clockwise around point $O$, segment $A C$ transitions to $B D$, which means their lengths are equal (Fig. 59). Segment $K L$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6455f48598646f41a890g-148.jpg?height=367&width=475&top_left_y=1308&top_left_x=126)

Fig. 59 is the midline of triangle $A B C$, so it is parallel to segment $A C$, and its length is half the length of segment $A C$.

Similarly, segment $L M$ is parallel to segment $B D$, and its length is half the length of this segment. Therefore,

$$
K L=\frac{1}{2} A C=\frac{1}{2} B D=L M
$$

б) Since segment $A C$ transitions to $B D$ when rotated $120^{\circ}$, the angle between these segments is $60^{\circ}$. Since segments $K L$ and $L M$ are parallel to segments $A C$ and $B D$, the angle between them is also $60^{\circ}$. Using the statement from part «а», we see that triangle $K L M$ is equilateral.

question: 3. The diagonals of trapezoid $ABCD$ intersect at point $K$. Circles are constructed on the lateral sides of the trapezoid as diameters. Point $K$ lies outside these circles. Prove that the lengths of the tangents drawn from point $K$ to these circles are equal.
reference_solution:
3. Let the lateral sides of the trapezoid be sides $AB$ and $CD$. Denote by $M$ and $N$ the second points of intersection of the lines $AC$ and $BD$ with the circles having diameters $AB$ and $CD$, respectively (Fig. 64). If the line $AC$ is tangent to the circle with diameter $AB$, we set $M=A$; similarly, if the line $BD$ is tangent to the corresponding circle, we set $N=D$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6455f48598646f41a890g-159.jpg?height=263&width=599&top_left_y=565&top_left_x=403)

Fig. 64

By the tangent-secant theorem, the squares of the tangents drawn from point $K$ to the circles are equal to $KM \cdot KA$ and $KN \cdot KD$. This is true even in the cases $M=A$ or $N=D$. Therefore, we need to prove that

$$
KM \cdot KA = KN \cdot KD
$$

Since $\angle AMB$ subtends the diameter, $\angle KMB = 90^\circ$ (see fact 14). This is also true in the case $M=A$, as the tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency. Let the angle $\angle AKB$ be denoted by $\varphi$. From the right triangle $KMB$, we find $KM = KB \cos \varphi$. Similarly, $KN = KC \cos \varphi$. Substituting these formulas into (1), we need to prove that $KB \cdot KA = KC \cdot KD$. This is a known property of a trapezoid, which follows from the similarity of triangles $AKD$ and $CKB$.

Alternative solution. Equation (1) can also be proven more geometrically. For this, we need to prove that points $A$, $M$, $N$, and $D$ lie on the same circle.

Since $\angle BMC = 90^\circ$ and $\angle BNC = 90^\circ$, points $B$, $M$, $N$, and $C$ lie on a circle with diameter $BC$, from which

$$
\angle CMN = \angle CBN = \angle BDA
$$

(since $BC \parallel AD$).

Then $\angle AMN + \angle NDA = 180^\circ$, so points $A$, $M$, $N$, and $D$ lie on the same circle. By the theorem on the product of the segments of a secant and its external part, $KM \cdot KA = KN \cdot KD$.

However, this solution relies heavily on the diagram: it does not work, for example, if at least one of the points $M$ and $N$ lies on the extension of the diagonal. These cases can be analyzed separately (one can also use directed angles). It is more difficult to deal with the cases $M=A$ and $N=D$.

The case $M=A$ can be handled in two ways. The first way is to correctly interpret all statements in the case of coincident points. For example, the condition "points $A$, $M$, $N$, and $D$ lie on the same circle" should be understood as: the line $AK$ is tangent to the circle passing through points $A$, $N$, and $D$.

The second way is as follows: since $M=A$, the lines $AC$ and $AB$ are perpendicular. The lines $AC$ and $CD$ cannot be perpendicular, as then the quadrilateral $ABCD$ would be a parallelogram, not a trapezoid (although for a parallelogram, our statement is obvious). Clearly, the lines $AB$ and $BD$ cannot be perpendicular. Therefore, it is sufficient to swap points $A$ and $B$ and points $C$ and $D$.

question:
3. In triangle $ABC$, $AA_{1}$ is a median, $AA_{2}$ is a bisector, $K$ is a point on $AA_{1}$ such that $KA_{2} \| AC$. Prove that $AA_{2} \perp KC$.

In triangle $ABC$, $AA_{1}$ is a median, $AA_{2}$ is a bisector, $K$ is a point on $AA_{1}$ such that $KA_{2} \| AC$. Prove that $AA_{2} \perp KC$.
reference_solution:
3. First with the allowance. Extend the median $A A_{1}$ by its length and complete the triangle to a parallelogram $A B D C$ (Fig. 66). Let's recall that the bisector divides the base of the triangle into segments proportional to the sides:

$$
\frac{A_{2} B}{A_{2} C}=\frac{A B}{A C}
$$

From the generalized Thales' theorem it follows (see comment) that $K$ divides $A D$ in the same proportion:

$$
\frac{K D}{K A}=\frac{A_{2} B}{A_{2} C}=\frac{A B}{A C}=\frac{C D}{A C}
$$

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6455f48598646f41a890g-165.jpg?height=313&width=429&top_left_y=479&top_left_x=817)

Fig. 66

(Note that we are using Thales' theorem in a somewhat unconventional configuration). This means that point $K$ divides $A D$ in the same ratio as the bisector of angle $A C D$ (by the property of the bisector of a triangle). From this it follows that $C K$ is the bisector! Thus, $A A_{2}$ and $C K$ are perpendicular as the bisectors of the internal alternate angles of parallel lines.

The last property is proved as follows. Let $R$ be the point of intersection of these bisectors. Then

$$
\angle R A C+\angle R C A=\frac{1}{2}(\angle B A C+\angle D C A)=\frac{1}{2} \cdot 180^{\circ}=90^{\circ}
$$

Second method. We use a remarkable property of a trapezoid (see comment): the midpoints of the bases, the point of intersection of the diagonals, and the point of intersection of the lines containing the non-parallel sides lie on the same line.

Extend the segment $C K$ to intersect the line $A B$ at point $C_{1}$ (Fig. 67). From the fact that in trapezoid $A K A_{2} C$ the midpoint $B_{1}$ of the base $A C$, the point of intersection of the diagonals $R$, and the point of intersection of the extensions of the non-parallel sides $A_{1}$ lie on the same line, it follows that $R$ lies on the midline $A_{1} B_{1}$ of triangle $A B C$. Therefore, $C R=R C_{1}$. Thus, in triangle $C A C_{1}$, segment $A R$ is both a median and a bisector, and hence a height.

Comments. $1^{\circ}$. Generalized Thales' theorem.

Let points $A_{1}, A_{2}$, and $A_{3}$ be chosen on line $k$, and points $B_{1}, B_{2}$, and $B_{3}$ on line $l$, such that $A_{1} B_{1}\left\|A_{2} B_{2}\right\| A_{3} B_{3}$. Then

$$
\frac{A_{1} A_{2}}{A_{2} A_{3}}=\frac{B_{1} B_{2}}{B_{2} B_{3}}
$$

To prove this, draw a line parallel to line $l$ through point $A_{2}$. Let it intersect lines $A_{1} B_{1}$ and $A_{3} B_{3}$ at points $C_{1}$ and $C_{3}$, respectively. Then $A_{2} C_{1} B_{1} B_{2}$ is a parallelogram, so $A_{2} C_{1}=B_{2} B_{1}$. Similarly, $A_{2} C_{3}=B_{2} B_{3}$. It remains to use the similarity of triangles $A_{1} A_{2} C_{1}$ and $A_{3} A_{2} C_{3}$.

$2^{\circ}$. Remarkable property of a trapezoid. Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of the bases of the trapezoid, $P$ the point of intersection of the diagonals, and $Q$ the point of intersection of the extensions of the non-parallel sides. The remarkable property of the trapezoid is that these four points lie on the same line. This property is easiest to prove using homothety. There exists a homothety with center $P$ that maps one base of the trapezoid to the other. Therefore, point $P$ lies on line $M N$. Moreover, there exists a homothety with center $Q$ that maps one base of the trapezoid to the other. Therefore, point $Q$ also lies on line $M N$.

![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/2024_05_21_6455f48598646f41a890g-165.jpg?height=322&width=425&top_left_y=1470&top_left_x=821)

Fig. 67

question: 5. Several settlements are connected to the city by roads, but there are no roads between them. A car departs from the city with cargos for all the settlements at once. The cost of each trip is equal to the product of the weight of all cargos in the truck and the distance. Prove that if the weight of each cargo is numerically equal to the distance from the city to the destination, then the total cost of transportation does not depend on the order in which the settlements are visited.
reference_solution:
5. First with the allowance. First, let's prove that the cost of transportation does not change from the permutation of the order of two consecutive trips. In other words, let the car visit some populated point $M$, and then the populated point $N$. We will show that if it had first gone to $N$, and then to $M$, the cost would have been the same.

Let the distances to $M$ and $N$ be $m$ and $n$ respectively. Then the weights of the corresponding cargos are also $m$ and $n$. The cost of transporting the remaining cargos does not change from the permutation of trips to $M$ and $N$. The cost of transporting cargos $m$ and $n$ to cities other than $M$ and $N$ also does not change. Let's calculate the cost of transporting cargos $m$ and $n$ to cities $M$ and $N$. In the first case, this cost is equal to $(m+n) m + n m + n^{2}$: the first term corresponds to the trip to point $M$, the second to the return trip to the city, and the third to the trip to $N$.

Similarly, the cost of transporting cargos $m$ and $n$ in the second case is equal to $(m+n) n + m n + m^{2}$. It is easy to see that these costs are equal. The statement is proved.

Let there be two different orders of visiting populated points. The first order can be transformed into the second by permuting consecutive trips. This statement is not difficult to prove by induction on the number of cities. Note that it is very important in the theory of permutations, see [23], chapter 2. By the proved statement, the total cost of transportation does not change with each such permutation, meaning it does not depend on the order of visiting populated points.

Another way. Let's number the cargos $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n}$ in the order in which they are delivered, then the cost of transportation is

$$
\begin{array}{r}
a_{1}\left(a_{1}+2 a_{2}+2 a_{3}+\ldots+2 a_{n}\right)+a_{2}\left(a_{2}+2 a_{3}+\ldots+2 a_{n}\right)+\ldots \\
\ldots+a_{n-1}\left(a_{n-1}+2 a_{n}\right)+a_{n}^{2}= \\
=a_{1}^{2}+a_{2}^{2}+\ldots+a_{n}^{2}+2 a_{1} a_{2}+2 a_{1} a_{3}+\ldots+2 a_{1} a_{n}+2 a_{2} a_{3}+\ldots \\
\ldots+2 a_{n-1} a_{n}=\left(a_{1}+a_{2}+a_{3}+\ldots+a_{n}\right)^{2}
\end{array}
$$

We obtained an expression that does not depend on the order of numbering the cargos.

question: 5. Initially, four identical right-angled triangles are given. With each move, one of the existing triangles is cut along the altitude (drawn from the right angle) into two other triangles. Prove that after any number of moves, there will be two identical triangles among the triangles.
reference_solution:
5. The first method. First, let's outline the idea of the solution. Note that the order in which the triangles are cut does not matter (in the sense that the final result does not depend on it).

Since we initially have four identical triangles, three of them will have to be cut (Fig. 63). Let's make these three cuts first. As a result, two sets of three identical triangles will form. In each of these sets, we will have to cut two triangles. Let's make these cuts. After this, we will again have four identical triangles!

Now let's present this idea more rigorously. Suppose that after a certain number of cuts, from four identical triangles, we get pairwise different triangles, and let $n$ be the smallest such number. Since the order of the cuts does not matter, let's first make the 7 cuts described above. We will again get 4 identical triangles, for which $n-7$ cuts will be required. But this contradicts the assumption that $n$ is the minimum number of cuts needed to get different triangles.

The second method (going beyond the 9th-grade curriculum). Let the hypotenuses of the original triangles be 1, and their legs be $p$ and $q$. Then all triangles obtained by cutting are similar to the original with a coefficient of the form $p^{m} q^{n}$ (where $m$ and $n$ are non-negative integers). When cutting such a triangle, two similar triangles to the original are obtained with coefficients $p^{m+1} q^{n}$ and $p^{m} q^{n+1}$. Now the problem can be reformulated as follows: in the positive quadrant of the coordinate plane, there are 4 chips at the vertex. Any chip can be replaced by two adjacent ones (above and to the right). Prove that it is impossible to achieve that all chips are in different cells.

Let's use the idea of an invariant (see fact 2). Write the number $2^{-(m+n)}$ in the cell with coordinates $(m, n)$ and call the weight of the chip the number on which it stands. It is not difficult to verify that the sum of the weights of the chips will not change during the process of dividing the chips.

At the initial moment, the sum of the weights of the chips is 4. The sum of the numbers written in all cells is also 4. Indeed,

$$
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} 2^{-(n+m)}=\left(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} 2^{-n}\right) \cdot\left(\sum_{m=0}^{\infty} 2^{-m}\right)=2 \cdot 2=4
$$

The penultimate equality follows from the formula for the sum of an infinite geometric progression.

Therefore, if the chips are in different cells, the sum of their weights is less than 4. Consequently, the transition is impossible.

Comment. A similar method solves the problem of M. Kontsevich's bacterial colonization:

At the vertex of the positive quadrant, there is a bacterium. Every second, one of the bacteria divides into two bacteria, which move to two adjacent cells (above and to the right). Only one bacterium can be in one cell. Prove that in the region $x+y \leqslant 5$, there will always be at least one bacterium.

question:
6. Geologists took 80 cans of preserves on an expedition, the weights of which are all known and different (there is a list). After some time, the labels on the cans became unreadable, and only the custodian knows what is where. He can prove this to everyone (i.e., justify which can contains what),
without opening the cans and using only the preserved list and a two-pan balance with a needle indicating the difference in weight on the pans. Prove that for this purpose

a) four weighings are sufficient;

b) three weighings are insufficient.

Comment. Let's note again that the custodian must justify which can contains what for all 80 cans.

10 t h  g r a d e
reference_solution:
6. a) It will be more convenient for us to work with a number of cans divisible by 3. Therefore, we will introduce one more "fictitious" can with zero weight.

Let's assume that the caretaker first puts the 27 lightest cans on the left pan and the 27 heaviest on the right. This will convince all the geologists that the 27 lightest cans are indeed on the left pan, and the 27 heaviest are on the right. All the cans will be divided into 3 piles of 27 cans each, and the geologists will believe that each of these piles indeed contains cans from that pile.

Now the caretaker will put 9 of the lightest cans from each of the three piles on the left pan, and 9 of the heaviest on the right. In doing so, the geologists will see the actions of the caretaker, and he will not mix cans from different piles.

Now all the cans will be divided into 9 piles of 9 cans each, and the geologists will know which cans are in which pile. The caretaker will put 3 of the lightest cans from each pile on the left pan and 3 of the heaviest on the right. The cans will be divided into 27 piles, and the geologists will believe in the distribution of the cans into piles. It remains to take the lightest can from each pile and put it on the left pan, and the heaviest cans from the piles on the right.

b) With each weighing, the cans are divided into three groups - cans on the left pan, cans on the right pan, and cans not participating in the weighing. The most that the geologists can learn from one weighing is to determine which set of cans lies in each group.

After the first weighing, one of the groups will contain no less than a third of all the cans, i.e., no less than 27 (by the pigeonhole principle, see fact 1); at this point, they will be indistinguishable to the geologists (except for the caretaker). During the second weighing, this group will also be divided into 3 groups, one of which will contain no less than 9 indistinguishable cans for the geologists. During the third weighing, out of these 9 cans, no less than 3 will end up in one of the new groups. Therefore, three weighings are insufficient.
